review:
This is a 2005 game and you can feel it in every tiny bit 20 years later. First thing first, worth playing? Yes, once and for discounted price, few bucks.

Pros:
Nice environments and immersive design
Allies add some variety (though flawed)
Clear progression, easy navigation
Short?

Cons:
Predictable, flat story with wasted potential
Stroggification has zero gameplay impact
Gunplay a bit weaker than Quake 2, 
Annoying AI companions with bad pathing

Rating: Better than six, but not a seven => 6,5/10.

Feels more like Doom than classic Quake
Story: No major spoilers, but cmon, it's been a while and obviously, you're going to kick Strogg ass. You are a one man army. Where whole battalions fail (while yelling in pain during the last moments of their digital lives), YOU WILL save the day (sometimes even without a drip of sweat). It's okay, but it's predictable and flat. 
What I dislike the most is, that there is so much potential killed with lazy writing and I don't know if it was the budget or the timing or what... First half of the game is tedious run and gun business... Then you get stroggified and storywise everyone just goes with it. No security concern, something to prove, just "Medics checked him, he should be good..." cmon, I don't expect realism but at least make it a thrill. Also, Stroggs replace half of your body and how does it affect gameplay? NOTHING changes. You are not faster, you don't jump higher, you don't see with thermal vision, NOTHING. Why did they even bother to make you a cyborg?
Another thrilling moment was Waste disposal level, where there were "zombies" but they were relevant for about 20 minutes and then you just return to the typical gun & run.

Allies: Unlike Quake 2 where you were always alone, here you very often get a friend or two. If they are story important, they can't die and are OP AF. If not, well, they are paper. Another problem is pathing, they will into your way or body block you in fights. I'd rather be without them.

Enemies: There is some variety, on par with Quake 2. Bosses are not very hard, early ones you don't fight directly, the later ones the opposite, nuke them with all you got.

Environment: This is where credit has to be given, environments are very well prepared. Levels have a rather strong tunnel design, but that's good, pathfinding was easy most of the time and parts of human bodies being embedded into machines around you really enriched the immersion. This is where I would love to have a HD pack. 

Gunplay: Sadly, gunplay was better in Quake 2. Here the balance of guns is lacking a bit. Your first assault rifle is one of the strongest weapons as headshots are very much rewarded. Also, it's the only gun with Flashlight. In a game that is DARK! So you are also kinda "forced" to use that one. Other guns are okay, but some are worthless, ie Shotgun or Grenade Launcher.

Finished in about 7 hours, medium difficulty as I went for the story. No Achievements. Overall feel, as I said, ok but not a miracle, Quake 2 was much better experience and had much more personality to it. This felt much more like a Doom game than Quake. Ending suggested continuation to the story but for 20 years nothing, I'd totally love to see a new Quake, but I highly doubt we will be getting anything with Strogg anytime soon :/

review:
This game is deceptive. Looks good, seems to have some fair depth, but the reality is that it's straight-up awful. 

Starting off, following the usual (cheesy) story introduction, you're dumped in the middle of a fight, with only the basic nav controls explained. No interactive tutorial, no chance to get used to the controls and UI. Just dumped in a fight and left to figure out every single relevant interaction in 5 seconds flat. Then, if you survive that ("if")... well, don't expect much else. There's a marker to pick up a mission, but that's it. You're on your own! I'm not one to advocate for games holding your hand every step of the way, but this is just masking poor design under the guise of "freedom". Honestly though, I couldn't stomach getting any further anyway, because...

...the UI is pretty much unforgivable. The basic information displays are largely ignored - absolute velocity for starters. When in space, with little visual reference, this is pretty much mandatory. I also noticed that the primary-fire lasers are limited by some kind of refilling capacitor (standard in games like these), but there is no indication of that on-screen; you're again left guessing. The few details that are visible are done so in a poor slap-dash manner, with irrelevant items instead given more prominent placement. For example, the comms screen, which shows static 98% of the time (and pre-animated heads on occasion), is given marked priority over more vital engine read-outs (the few that exist anyway)

It's not just visual interaction that suffers, but controls too. By default, primary-fire actually launches your secondary missiles as well, despite there being a separate missile-fire key. So, if you don't want every shot of your lasers to near-instantly waste your missile stocks, you have to... completely unmount your current missiles. Hope you don't want them in a hurry during a fight!

This game could have more depth than X3 and it wouldn't matter. The interaction is so poor that it doesn't take long before you're left mashing Alt-F4 in frustration.

review:
This game may have potential, but is ruined by the poor design of the maker.

First off, this game is designed with a complex control system, yet the "tutorial" fails to explain the controls properly, i.e. it mentioned "Dock", "Scan", "Next Target", etc., but never mentioned what keys is linked to these commands. Players have to either RTFM or open the Options menu to find out what are the keys binding.

This has the most noctorious (if the game does have such level of amount of players, that is...) problem of this aspect is the FIRST MISSION -- the player is asked to "Activate the Setellites", and nowhere in the mission briefing nor the game manual explains that, in order to "ACTIVATE" the setellites, you have to "DOCK" with it!! I'll spell it clearly: They assume players will automatically know that ACTIVATE == DOCK == PRESS THE EFFING ENTER KEY WHEN YOU ARE WITHIN 100 UNITS FROM THE SETALLITE.

Then the mission journal is simply useless, it just give you a simple (and most time meaningless) description of WHY YOU GOT THIS MISSION, while never mentioned WHAT you should do and WHERE you mut go, or WHO you should meet. Bravo! Spaceforce team, you surpassed Microsoft Office team in the competition of The Most Useless Documentation.

Economy is a total mess. There is no listings of merchendise price of each star system, no indication of realtime price changes. The G News is supposed to do that, but so far, all I see in there is just 2 items listed, one with peice up, another with price donw, so you are only being informed of prices od 2 items in any time. Item selling price is usually low, in the range of 2~3 digits, even if the item could be the "hot selling items of the day". Ship upgrades are usually in the term of 4~6 digits per pop. Go figure, how many Ores or pirate ships you need to shoot, to fully upgrade even the light fighter you get from the beginning of the game.

Loots, or merchendise are poorly designed, there are items that looks like weapons, but is not equipable, and is only meant for trading, and all this are mixed togather with equipable items. There is no fitering system or tabbing system to seperate all the different items to ease the management of goods. It took me some time to even realized that items with white wording are junks to sell, pink words are equipable tools and purple wording items are equipable weapons. This is never mentioned in the manual.

There are 10 professions, woohoo! Nice! But wait, how do I decide what my profession is? I can't even find any description of what make me a Scientist or an Engineer. Okay, another decoration, I guess.

Voice is totally awesomely stupendously awful. Period. Everyone (includeing the protagonist and main characters) sound like an idiotically idiotic idiot with plain flat tone of a first grader reading from a textbook. Even when I destroyed a pirate ship, the poor sot is blown into thousands of smoldering pieces, he still sound like he is reading a newspaper aloud in bordom at the roadside cafe.

The game is monotonous - chasing behind Jax butt, shoot pirates/aliens, buy new ship, continuew chasing Jax.

Star Map doesn't provide enough information, i.e. if the map contains a dockable Station or not. Many times, when I'm trying to search for better weaponary and stronger ships, I found myself jumping into a void and empty system, then have to travel 70k++ space units (not sure if that's counted in kilometers) to get back to the jump gate. That kind of journey, even with a fully upgraded heavy fighter, at speed level 10, is still a long and boring experience.

EFF-uck! This game doesn't support joystick! My Logitech Extreme 3D filght stick is not recognised, in a SPACE FLIGHT game!! EFF-uck!

There are many many more flaws, I can't be bother to continue any more. 

Conclusion: This game is designed and made by a single basement-dwelling cave man whose cave is under a huge rock. He need to come out and see how others are making games.

review:
Rage is a solid post-apocalyptic FPS that is similar to games like Mad Max and Borderlands. 
Before finding it in the steam store I never heard about it so I was pleasantly surprised. 
I found it very entertaining from start to finish. 
The most important strengths are the very good graphics ( excellent for a game made in 2010 ) and the combat gameplay, which is smooth and fun. 

Mind you, it's very linear. The game's world is somewhat large, but this is not an open world game like Mad Max. Nor is this a complex survival game. The various locations unlock only for quests, and the space between is only for traveling between point A and point B. 
It's just a shooter placed in a post-apocaliptic world with a decent story, with interesting communities of survivors that give you main and side quests, a nice variation of enemy factions and a good selection of weapons. You can upgrade your gear and your vehicles. 
There is no mini-map, so it's difficult finding specific locations when you don't have quests for them any more. 
So don't except a lot of depth in this game, but I didn't mind it being linear, it is nonetheless fun because all aspects are done nicely (combat, graphics, sound). The ending is not good however, the game ends abruptly when things were about to heat up. 
There are a lot of minigames to play in order to earn some extra cash - racing being among them. 
Nice FPS that got under the radar for some reason and never got very popular.

review:
RAGE is a pseudo looter-shooter that tries to do many things, but unfortunately falls short on most fronts. It's also weighed down by half-baked mechanics, repetitive gameplay, and mediocre writing. However, underneath its numerous flaws, and identity crisis lies a very solid FPS well worth a playthrough. Moreover, the thing about this game is that many of its issues work in its favor, such as its dull aesthetics, which serve to reinforce the gritty and post-apocalyptic feel of the world, the claustrophobic dungeons, which work in pairs with the machete-wielding maniacs constantly charging at you, and the short and concise writing, which doesn't get in the way of the gameplay. Ok, the last one is pushing it, but I'm a bit biased, as I'd rather kill people, than to romance them.

Jokes aside, the game has quite a few positives, and not just incidental ones. The gunplay is by far its best feature, being fast-paced and engaging, and featuring few but satisfying weapons, with different ammo types for each situation (although admittedly some of them are gimmicky). Enemies are reactive, and are actually quite competent, as some of the humanoid NPCs use cover strategically and then bumrush you, only to run back to their friends as they take damage; likewise, some of the more 'feral' ones use the environment by climbing the walls and ceiling in order to overwhelm you. The game also features a basic gore system, and they also react in various ways after being shot at by, for instance, kneeling if they've taken enough damage, or limping instead of running if their legs are hurt, and so on.
On top of that, there are numerous constructs and tools you can craft to aid you in combat, such as EMP grenades, turrets, mechanical spiders armed with machine guns, and so on.

Even outside of shooting and looting, the game offers other activities, some basic like dice, others more intricate like a card game that lets you look for/buy cards and then use them to battle NPCs. Although, the one you'll definitely want to play is racing, which is the main way to gain the special currency required to upgrade your vehicle. Or, you can explore the town hubs, and talk to the people, who are surprisingly charismatic, and sometimes offer you quests.

Now, to elaborate on some of the aforementioned issues: For starters, most of the things not immediately related to shooting enemies are quite barebones, like the crafting system. Actually, the game in general is very basic at its core and, as a result, can become quite repetitive, especially considering it peaks relatively early and the gameplay loop barely evolves past the first hour or so, and the writing is barely an incentive to keep going (and if it is for you, prepare to be disappointed).
There is also very little actual playable space in this game. The "open-world" really only serves to connect the towns and dungeons, and there is almost nothing to do when driving from point A to B. Interior cells aren't better off, either - the vast majority of doors are inaccessible, and while some of the dungeons are seemingly huge, they're extremely linear, and most of the time you might as well be walking in a straight line. Invisible walls are a staple in most videogames, but in this case, it's literally all around you, everywhere, all the time, to the point where it hurts the gameplay. The game encourages you to explore in order to find loot, but only when it lets you.

Anyway, some other issues I can think of are: spongey enemies, clunky inventory, no map (!!!), fixed camera while driving, muddy textures/somewhat constant pop-ins, and weird soundtrack choices (as in, the melodies are okay, just not how they're used). None of these really spoiled the experience to me, and I actually quite enjoyed it. Buy it on sale.

review:
Batman Arkham Asylum is my first Arkham game.

Yes, it’s 2025, and I have not played any other than this.

Being released in 2009, this game exceeded my expectations.

And I would say it was way ahead of its time.

The Asylum environment in this game is what captivated me the most. 

Bone-chilling sound effects and minor jump scares are not what I expected from a Batman game.

Well, the boss fights in this game are easy and predictable, though I completed it on HARD difficulty; I still struggle to defeat 10 henchmen at a time.

In some cutscenes, I noticed the background music is completely shut down and only dialogues are there, which makes some intense scenes feel a bit off, but it didn’t bother me much.

Talking about combat, this is some very amazing shit I have experienced.

I just loved how Batman kicks and punches his enemies and breaks bones.

The sound effect realism for every hit is pleasing to the ears.

Well, this game lacked skins; it did offer one skin in a challenge mode, but I know the other 3 games do offer multiple skins to play.

The main quest and missions were simple. The game offers a true detective feeling as we go around following fingerprints, analyzing blood particles, alcohol elements in the atmosphere. The Riddler’s trophies and environment scanning challenges are simple too. Though I haven’t completed all of them, it isn’t much difficult to figure them out.

One thing I experienced: if you’re playing on HARD difficulty, there is literally no chance you’re going to survive a sniper in this game. I don’t know about other difficulties, but there is no way you are going to live if a sniper spots you. They can literally shoot you even if you are gliding.

Talking about gliding, I think the developers haven’t focused on that much. Also, I understand the scale of the Asylum is not huge, so one shouldn’t expect to travel around the Asylum through gliding only.

For me, the story of Arkham Asylum comes into the OKAY category.

It’s a 1-night story, so the broadline plot consists of: 
(SPOILERS START)

Batman catches Joker → Puts him in the Asylum → Joker frees himself → murders numerous people → creates a number of maniacs → plans to spoil the Arkham City water with the TITAN virus or something → injects himself with TITAN in the climax → gets defeated and captured again.

(SPOLIERS END)

Also, I don’t know why the character of Ivy sounds so flirty and lusty. Maybe the original character was written that way; I have no idea.

At last, I must say, it’s an extremely well-made Batman game, and I don’t know what I am going to expect in the next Arkham games.

If you’re new to this Arkham Series, you must start with Asylum.

It’s a 10 for me,

out of 10 :)

review:
Batman: Arkham Asylum – A Breakup Survival Simulator (In Disguise)

Let’s be honest: if you're playing Batman: Arkham Asylum because your girlfriend left you, congratulations, Forget emotional damage, you’re living rent-free in the psychological ruins of Gotham City now. This game forces you to confront your demons.

You boot up the game a wreck, emotionally bankrupt, dignity in foreclosure. But by the time the gates of Arkham clang shut, you’re not crying... you’re calculating. You’re skulking through vents, stalking maniacs, and serving justice like it’s your post-breakup meal prep. The Joker’s unleashing chaos, and suddenly your ex’s “we grew apart” text reads like a lullaby compared to Scarecrow’s psychological warfare. Emotions? Batman locked those away years ago, and so will you by the end of this game.

Batman doesn’t text his ex. Batman doesn’t stalk her Instagram. Batman throws thugs through glass windows and solves cryptic puzzles in the dark, all while nursing trauma so deep it makes your situation look pathetic.

And that’s the beauty of this game, it gets you. It holds your hand and whispers, “Hey, I know life feels like it’s falling apart, but would you like to punch a clown in the face?” Yes. Yes, I would.

The combat? Brutal, like your last conversation. The atmosphere? Darker than your recent search history. The plot? Twisted enough to make you forget her name for at least a few blessed hours. And every time Batman resists the temptations of madness, you too resist texting back, “I miss us.”

In the end, you may be lost in the shadows, but in Arkham, you choose the dark. And somewhere between the gadgets, grit, and gliding through your pain, you’ll find a little piece of yourself again… probably crouched on a gargoyle.

Highly recommend for anyone going through something. A reminder that even when life’s a full-blown circus, you can still throw the last punch.

review:
A legendary game. While "City" refined it a bit, there's a lot of charm and interesting choices in the first game which make it just a fantastic bit of fun.

The biggest downside with this game (all the Arkham games and their derivatives really, but some are better and some are worse) is what I call "derp mode" where you go from being given the controls of a legendary fighter to having a button labeled "get punched in the face". [b]Note:[/b] This is a direct sequel to the [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/17470/Dead_Space_2008/]first game[/url]. It's highly recommended you play that one first (or [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1693980/Dead_Space/]the remake[/url]) before playing this game.

[b]Recommended for:[/b] If you liked the original Dead Space there is a good chance you will like this sequel, but maybe not for all people. Although it definitely feels similar to the original, the action and pacing are much faster. In the original the gameplay was more about walking slowly, getting immersed in the gore and having short bursts of action. In Dead Space 2 it's just running from action scene to action scene.

I saw several people compare it with the movies Alien & Aliens and I absolutely agree with this. You have the slow horror of Alien/Dead Space vs the action horror of Aliens/Dead Space 2. Like I said, the game still feels like a Dead Space game, but the fast gameplay also makes it feel different than the first game. It's up to you whether you like this or not.

Also a warning for new players of Dead Space 2. Currently the game contains a DLC that automatically unlocks all weapons and armor which you can get from the first shop you encounter in the game. I strongly suggest you skip this as it will completely wreck any feeling of progression in the game and also makes the game way too easy. You can also completely remove this if you check [url=https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Dead_Space_2#Weapons_and_suits_unlocked_at_start]this page[/url] on PCGamingWiki.

[b]My experience:[/b] I had an overall nice time playing Dead Space 2, but also some mixed feelings. I personally prefer the slower-paced combat in the original so you can get fully immersed in the gore and such. Also it felt for me it was much shorter then the original, maybe also because of the faster gameplay.

One major point I disliked was the story and the characters. In the first game the story was somewhat generic but still interesting and suited the gameplay. In Dead Space 2 the story is continued, but they really went off the rails here with plot holes so big you could park the Ishimura in them. Maybe that's why the combat is so fast-paced so you don't have time to think about some of the bonkers dialogue and decisions the totally uninteresting characters make.

There is one thing I really liked about Dead Space 2 and that is the Stalker enemies. The way they peek at you from the corners always makes me laugh. It's like playing a game of peekaboo with an oversized introvert mutant chicken. One of the funniest enemies I’ve encountered in a game.

[b]Technical:[/b] I had no technical issues playing the game. [i](Win10, 7800X3D, RX7800XT)[/i]

[b]Personal Rating:[/b] 3/5

[h1]🎮 Dead Space 2 🎮  – Scary, Brutal, and Completely Addicting[/h1]

Dead Space 2 honestly blew me away. I liked the first game a lot, but this one hooked me even harder from the very beginning. The opening scene—where you’re strapped down and forced to run while everything goes to hell—set the tone perfectly. It was one of the few times in a game where I actually felt panicked, like I had zero control, and that feeling stuck with me throughout the whole playthrough.

I really liked Isaac more this time around. Giving him a voice and personality made me care about him instead of just seeing him as a blank character. His struggle with the Marker visions felt heavy, and it gave the horror a psychological edge that made the story a lot more personal.

The combat is still awesome. Dismembering Necromorphs never got old, and the game kept me on my toes with new enemy types that forced me to rethink how I fought. I tried out all the weapons, but honestly, I couldn’t stop using the plasma cutter—it’s simple, brutal, and so satisfying. And the zero-gravity sections? Way better than the first game. Floating around while monsters come at you from every angle was terrifying in the best way.

What really stuck with me, though, was the atmosphere. The Sprawl is such a creepy place, and the sound design messed with me constantly. Half the time I’d hear something skittering in the vents and just freeze, waiting for it to pop out. There were moments where I actually paused the game just to breathe because it got too intense—but that’s exactly why I loved it.

If I’m being honest, it leans a bit more toward action than the first game, which makes it feel a little less “survival horror.” But for me, that mix of bigger action set pieces and terrifying horror moments was perfect.

[h1]Final Score: 9/10[/h1]

review:
This Junta DLC is the first in the line of Tropico 4 DLCs, which have been reduced in price to a more reasonable $2.99 since the game is over a decade old. Beforehand, they sold for about 5 bucks each. You'll still want to buy the Collector's Bundle on sale if you're interested in this game, though.

Anyway, Junta sets the pattern that was to follow, with one new building, trait, outfit, mission, and some decorative items. The mission is pretty good, and surprisingly challenging - it definitely demonstrates the overpoweredness of the new building by putting you in a situation where you actually [i]need[/i] that OPness. The Veteran trait for your Presidente isn't bad, making the Militarists like you more and giving El Presidente a boost in combat for an extra edge against rebel attacks. review:
To preface: I am one of the biggest Civ 5 fans out there, and I think that Civilization V: Brave New World is the pinnacle of the series. That being said, when Beyond Earth was released, every one bashed it for being a broken mess. Some people where bashing it for being too similar to Civ 5, others were bashing it for being too different. Most people however where hoping for an alpha centauri remake, and that is why they were disappointed. I never got to try it.

After all these years, I found Beyond Earth with all the expansions at $11.99 on steam (offer going until Aug 18), so I thought to myself, why the hell not? I downloaded it, and suddenly I am playing it for 23 hours in just 3 days! This is the best Civ experience I had in years! The game is very familiar because it is built on Civ 5 rig, but yet very very fresh.

The Good:

1- The theme and atmosphere is brilliant, especially if you like sci-fi.

2- The technology web is very refreshing, it allows different factions to have widely different units at any point of the game, you can have a tier 3 melee unit and a tier 1 ship, while your opponent has a tier 3 ship and a tier 1 melee unit. This creates very dynamic scenarios, especially in wars.

3- The quest system is incredible and adds a lot of narrative to the game.

4- The affinity system is so good. Affinities are philosophies that your civilization follows to guide your society. The more you invest in one philosophy, the more unique units, buildings and wonders you get. I played the first game focusing on Harmony, which is the philosophy based on integrating with alien biology, via genetic engineering and transgenics. All different affinities can be played aggressively or defensively and achieve victory in different ways.

5- Aliens are a very unique and refreshing take on barbarians.

The Bad:

1- Similar to Civ 5, if you know what you are doing you can beat the AI easily in any war.

2- The alliance system is not implemented well, if your ally goes to war against someone else you are forced to go to war with them, whether its offensive or defensive. In Civ 5, you join your allies only in defensive wars, which makes more sense.

3- Similar to Civ 5 and 6 (and all Civ games to be honest), once you pull ahead far enough, there is no way the AI can catch up with you. Late game is the most boring phase.

The Ugly:

1- The terrain is very ugly, it is difficult to discern what each terrain type is, without hovering over it.

2- The technology web, while nice functionally, is very confusing to look at, you need to use the filters provided if you want to make any sense of anything.

3- Leader portraits are very ugly compared to Civ 5.

4- Some annoying bugs.

In conclusion, I think any fan of the Civ series will have a blast with Beyond Earth, and at the current price for the complete edition, I suggest you do yourself a favor and give it a try.

review:
Darkest Hour: A Hearts of Iron Game is a deeply intricate and compelling grand strategy title that appeals to both history enthusiasts and avid strategy gamers. Building upon the foundations laid by the Hearts of Iron series, Darkest Hour delivers an expansive and detailed simulation of the tumultuous years surrounding World War II, offering players a chance to rewrite history or faithfully recreate it. The game’s scope is monumental, encompassing a broad range of nations, military units, political systems, and diplomatic intricacies, all woven into a complex web of interconnected mechanics that demand careful planning and strategic foresight.

One of the most remarkable aspects of Darkest Hour is its depth of historical detail. The game meticulously models various aspects of the era, from military logistics and industrial capacity to diplomatic negotiations and internal political upheavals. This attention to detail allows players to immerse themselves fully in the geopolitical landscape of the 1930s and 1940s, making each decision feel weighty and consequential. The game also introduces a variety of scenarios, alternate history options, and mod support, which significantly extend its replayability. Whether aiming for a historically accurate campaign or experimenting with unlikely alliances and conflicts, players will find ample opportunities to craft their own version of history.

Gameplay mechanics in Darkest Hour are highly sophisticated, combining real-time strategy elements with turn-based management of resources, technology, and diplomacy. Military management is particularly detailed, with a wide array of unit types, doctrines, and supply systems that require strategic coordination across fronts. The AI, while occasionally challenging, generally provides a formidable opponent, pushing players to adapt and refine their tactics continually. The political system adds another layer of complexity, as players must balance national morale, political stability, and leadership decisions to maintain their power base while pursuing military objectives. The game’s interface, although dense and initially intimidating, becomes more navigable with experience, offering comprehensive tools to manage the chaos of global warfare.

Multiplayer capabilities further enhance the appeal of Darkest Hour, allowing players to engage in large-scale conflicts against friends or other online opponents. The multiplayer mode supports various scenarios and game modes, fostering a competitive environment that tests players’ strategic acumen and adaptability. The community around Darkest Hour is active and passionate, often producing custom mods and scenarios that add new dimensions to gameplay. Such community-driven content enriches the experience, ensuring that the game remains lively and evolving long after its initial release. The multiplayer experience, while demanding in terms of coordination and planning, is highly rewarding for those who enjoy testing their skills against human opponents.

Visually, Darkest Hour’s interface is utilitarian but functional, prioritizing clarity and access to complex information over aesthetic flourish. This design choice makes sense given the game’s depth, as players need to access a vast array of data swiftly during play. The graphics are utilitarian but effective, with detailed maps and unit representations that serve their purpose well. Sound design complements the gameplay, with period-appropriate music and sound effects that evoke the tense atmosphere of wartime. Technical stability is generally good, though some players may encounter occasional bugs or performance hiccups, especially when using extensive mods or custom scenarios. Overall, the presentation is serviceable, prioritizing function over form but never detracting from the immersive experience.

In conclusion, Darkest Hour: A Hearts of Iron Game is a masterful and comprehensive grand strategy title that offers a deep, challenging, and richly detailed simulation of World War II. Its complexity may be daunting for newcomers, but for those willing to invest the time, it provides a rewarding experience that captures the chaos, strategy, and nuance of a pivotal period in history. The game’s extensive depth, mod support, and active community make it a lasting staple for serious strategy enthusiasts. While it may not have the visual polish of more modern titles, its gameplay mechanics and historical fidelity more than compensate, making Darkest Hour a standout in the grand strategy genre and a must-play for fans of historical military simulation.

review:
Dinner Date is a very short indie title about a man waiting for his date to arrive and I fucking hated it.

The main reason I hated this game was mainly due to the usual false expectations scenario. Rather than just completely rip this game apart let me explain what I thought the game was going to be, and then what the game actually is.

What I thought Dinner Date was going to be:

Everything I thought this game was going to be came from what people posted about on the internet. Nothing I am writing in this section is what I hoped the game would be, this is what I expected based on others experiences with it. Like I mentioned above, this is a game about a man waiting for his date to arrive at his house. However, I was under the assumption that this would be 1st person, without any narration, and you are completely free to do whatever you want while you wait for the date. You do not know who the date is, or why this man is possibly being stood up. Maybe this is him being dumped, maybe he murdered her, maybe he doesn’t have a date and he’s lonely, we just don’t know. While waiting for your possible date to arrive, you are free to do whatever you want in your apartment. Doing actions will affect the outcome of “The Date”. Maybe you could eat your entire meal before he/she shows up, would that have an effect? Maybe if you drink the whole bottle of wine you will pass out and miss the date entirely, never knowing if the person came by or not. Maybe you could just sit there and wait the entire time, twiddling your thumbs, eagerly watching the clock. Maybe you could just fucking kill yourself, the point is what sold me on this game was mystery. Every time I looked into this game online, for whatever reason, the game was completely shrouded in mystery, and this made me want to play the game so badly. I was honestly expecting to play this game multiple times just to see what else I could make happen. There could’ve been so many possibilities, so many outcomes, but as you can guess I ended up being tremendously disappointed.

What Dinner Date actually is:

A monologue. The game is literally just a monologue disguised as a video game. If there are any David Cage fanboys reading this, buy this game right now. NOTHING you do while you “wait” for you date matters. I only played this game once and I went in with the intention of killing my character through alcohol abuse, but even though I am drinking down a glass of wine every 5 seconds, the character doesn’t shut up…even while he is drinking. You are forced to listen to this guy whine and complain and there’s nothing you can do about it. Yeah, there are actions, but they are fucking meaningless. I’m pretty sure if someone smoked 47 cigarettes in a row he would maybe cough a few times in the middle of his bitching. The game kept giving me hope that something good would happen. Oh look! He’s getting up! Can I jump out the window? Nope. Can I open my fridge? Nope. Well, can I grab that endless bottle of wine again? Not right now, nope. When I realized that I could just sit back and the game would play itself I decided to stick through to the end, with the hope that maybe something interesting would happen, but of course not. You listen to this guy whine and complain about life for awhile and then that’s it, it just ends. He doesn’t kill himself (sadly), the date never shows up, nothing fucking happens. The best part about the uh experience is the torture is short. My game time for this is 23 minutes and I waiting till the credits ended.

So that’s it, I can’t even recommend this game to people who enjoy monologues, or hearing sad..ish life stories. Rather that waste your time listening to this guys issue’s you could go hang out with your friends, and maybe help them with their problems. I can promise in that situation different outcomes and functionality that makes an impact, I dare you to try and drink as much wine as I did in this game while hearing your friend talk. In other words, real life is more of a video game than Dinner Date.

review:
This game is the biggest pile of pretentious tripe I've ever played, this is coming from someone who's favourite experience from a video game was Dear Esther.

Say what you like about Dear Esther but the point of it was that it was following the inner thoughts of a suicidally depressed man as we got some insight on loss, pain, depression and regret and what does Dinner Date offer us? The Inner thoughts of a boring, pretentious pillock, who's whining because nobody wants to bugger him.

I'm serious, this whole game is just a man, sat at a table, whining because he can't get laid and the worst part is that he has no redeeming qualities. He's racist, narcissistic, boring and full of crap. There is NOTHING worth investing yourself in, it's not even funny boring, it's just boring.

You could honestly get the same experience by going to your kitchen table and sitting there for twenty or so minutes, like you're waiting for a date, listening to a pod cast on the colour baige the entire time. There, you've played Dinner Date, except you can actually eat the food and turn off the podcast.

So, why haven't I spoken about the gameplay? Because there is none! Again, Dear Esther, you can walk around and look at stuff, listen to the monologue or enjoy the scenery. Here, there's NOTHING! You can interact with things, sure but only when the game tells you that it's okay to, otherwise you just hover your hand over it, like you're thinking about doing it. The game even tells you that you aren't in control and you're the character's subconscious, making this no more of a game than one of those College Humour POV videos, except those are funny and often relatable, whereas this is just garbage.

You have dozens of options presented to you, whilst you listen to the insightful inner thoughts of the loathesome protagonist and all that I was able to do was dip bread into a sauce and eat it. Although, I will say that I did find one thing in common with this guy, we were both incredibly bored and clock watching, throughout the experience.

The visuals look like shit, I'm by no means a graphics snob but if you're going to force us to look at something for half an hour at least make it look realistic/nice or at least give it its own style like Facade. But no, this looks like a PS2 game that has gone through a dishwasher, it looks really shoddy.

The final thing I have to say is that everything about this game is still pretentious, despite the fact that it offers NOTHING, it acts like it's high art. It constantly has the div recite poetry with classical music playing in the background, whilst he goes on about how Japanese girls can't hold their liquor and how he can't wait for his date to show up so he can shag her. Bugger off Dinner Date, just bugger off.

During the hit list- I mean... credits, my eyes were drawn to the list of the cast and crew and bugger me backwards... 
Try thinking up the most pretentious pseudonym you can, make it sound french and artsy like: Don Panthane Do Blur or some shit like that. Because the credits is full of those names, it's so full of it.

Don't buy this. If I had a physical copy of this game, I would've taken it out back and pissed on it. Screw this game!

review:
Dinner Date is an experimental game, pushing at the edges of what a game can be. You play as Julian Luxemburg, a 27 year old British man who has been set up on a date with a 20 year old Japanese woman named Meiko. As the evening wears on, it becomes clear that Meiko will not be arriving for that date, leaving Julian alone with his thoughts. 

This is not a game with gameplay in the traditional sense. While the player can move Julian’s arms through a series of keyboard inputs and decide how much bread Julian eats or how much wine he drinks, none of these progress the gameplay in any way. The only progression through the game is the slow tick of the clock above the table and the meandering of Julian’s thoughts through possibilities, fears, and sorrow. 

It’s not a happy game in any way. It’s an experiential game, meant to convey a specific narrative and sensation of being engrossed in that narrative, and a way to experience an event in a safe and empathetic way. 

It’s in the assumptions this game makes about the universality of the experiences it depicts that I really struggled and why, perhaps, the game fell flat for me. Rather than empathising with Julian, I felt a softer version of what I felt when I played [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198031223198/recommended/520720/] Dear Esther. [/url] I felt unsafe, unclean, and grateful that Meiko never turned up to this unsettling evening.

In [url=https://www.npr.org/sections/alltechconsidered/2010/10/18/130646920/dinner-date] interviews [/url] he’s given about the game, Dinner Date’s creator, Jeroen Stout, described the game as an opportunity “to sympathize with someone who is slowly consumed by a sense of inadequacy” and a space to explore “things you can’t tell your friends.” This is fundamentally a game built around empathy and around having an unsafe experience in a safe space, and thus gaining a bit of empathy and a taste of the experience for oneself. Whether the game succeeds or fails at its goal is entirely contingent on well it builds the reality of the story and allows the player to inhabit this fundamentally unpleasant place. To be clear, with what little gameplay, graphics, and general interactivity Dinner Date has, it does a good job of drawing the player into the narrative. Throughout the game’s brief runtime, there is a decided sense of claustrophobia and anxiety as it becomes clear how much the player is trapped in this evening gone wrong. The glasses of wine and cigarettes only highlight the cycle of bad decisions that led to this point, and which will probably lead to more like it. 

As well as the game does with crafting a setting, though, what it didn’t succeed in doing was making me feel sympathy for Julian. Julian’s monologue about his life has the dual function of both creating a sense of anxiety and self-loathing, and telling a story - however brief - of who he is and how he got here. He talks about how he got to this point, his fears and doubts, and what he wanted with the evening. 

In doing so, this stopped being a game I could see myself in. Instead, I saw the mind of every man who has harassed me in the street, the ones who would not stop pestering me for my number, the ones who followed me home and made me feel unsafe. In listening to Julian’s monologue, I saw a bit more of the truths of the men who believed themselves to be entitled to  my company, and I did not sympathise with them. 

That Stout hopes Dinner Date captures some degree of universality and expects empathy worries me. 

It’s hard to put my finger on what exactly makes me uncomfortable about Julian Luxembourg. It may be that he is 27, waiting for a 20 year old woman to come into his apartment so he can have sex with her. It may be how he softly rages when she doesn’t appear, mentally accusing her of sleeping around. It may be the way he repeats that he “deserves” this over the course of the evening, though whether that “this” is the date or the sex is unclear. It may be the way he continues to sit at the table for hours, staring at the door after it’s long become apparent she’s not coming. It may be that he doesn’t call her and instead prefers to linger in the fantasies of what-ifs rather than engaging with her as a person. It’s this long medley of thoughts and actions that sent my hackles up and made me feel uncomfortable to be in this man’s skin. If there is a universality to his thoughts about being stood up, it’s not one I identify with. It’s entirely possible that universality is a male one, but even then, I would hate to believe that the universal male experience is to mentally slut shame a significantly younger woman for not coming to a late evening at an older man’s apartment. 

If the idea of the game is to make me feel empathy as a man spirals into self-loathing, it fails. I see the self-loathing, but the way it manifests is toxic. Self-loathing has a tendency towards toxicity, sure, but that toxicity isn’t inherently misogynistic. There are ways to tell this story that make it actually universal and actually generate some degree of empathy. The story told here is an explanation rather than an event. 

I think, too, this game hits a bit differently, given that I played it the day before getting stood up on a date of my own. It’s in the comparison of my experience and thoughts and Julian’s that the ideas and goals of this game ring truly hollow.

My potential date was meant to meet me for coffee. It was supposed to be the first date I’d been on in years. I went across the city to meet her, fiddling with my nails, my hair, my clothes, my phone on the metro the whole way. She e-mailed me as I was arriving at the coffee shop, telling me she wasn’t going to be able to make it, and I was left there, standing outside the coffee shop, unsure of what to do with my now empty afternoon. 

I got a cup of tea, sat down, and finished the book I’d been trying and failing to read on the metro. 

As I sat and read and drank my tea, I thought through the things that had brought me to that point. I thought about my nervousness about the date, and about the woman I was planning to meet. My mind ran back through all the things I’d planned to talk about, all the jokes I’d tell, and all the things I’d imagined she’d say that I would laugh at and sympathise with in turn. I played through the scenarios I’d imagined, then set them all aside. I did not know why she’d cancelled on me. I wasn’t going to ask because her business was her own. All that mattered was that there was no date, and it was up to me to decide how to move on from that. I could linger, and in so doing, accomplish nothing but misery for everyone, or I could go on with my life, and she hers.

I drank my tea. I went home. I moved on.

This story of my own date is not necessarily a better version of the story Stout chose to tell. However, that it’s a different story speaks volumes about the story he is telling, and about the ideas he believes are inherent. I recognise that my experience as a woman may colour my views on dating and male toxicity. That this is a game meant for men and the male dating experience, and I will therefore never actually be able to find myself in it is an entirely valid possibility. If that is the case, it works, and I humbly accept that, as a non-male, I do not have a clear window on the male experience.

However, if this is a game offering universality and a generally understandable portrait of empathy, it’s worth considering why it doesn’t work from my female perspective. In being locked in Julian’s narrative, I think of my own narrative and though processes. I compare our paths, and to compensate for my own failings, I critique his. review:
Lately, I've been making a habit of trying out games with "Mixed" reviews--often, I find them to be the most interesting. Dinner Date is a game that isn't for everyone; some might not enjoy the concept, others might find it boring. This isn't a game in which the goal is clear,  and the end result isn't necessarily what you would call gratifying.  There are no bosses to defeat or world to save. To me, this game embodies "virtual reality" in a much more emotional sense. 

You are the subconscious of the protagonist, Julian, as he experiences the agony of waiting on his "dinner date" to arrive. This means, you really have no control over what is happening. You can merely observe and react in the most subtle of ways. As the story unfolds before you, you are given a set of choices. Will Julian glance nervously at the clock, have a cigarette to calm his nerves or have another glass of wine as he bemoans his situation? The voiceover acting is very well done, and adds to realism of the game. If you've ever experienced the anxiety of anticipation. and the agony of disappointment, the game expresses both  perfectly.

In order to truly enjoy this game, you have to accept the fact that nothing you do will change its outcome. You are merely along for the ride, guiding Julian's thoughts and actions along the way via a growing number of options by pressing specific buttons on your keyboard, which lead to certain interactions. But it's not as if you're sitting there idle while a long cinematic cutscene plays either; it's an experience you can be a part of from start to finish. As Julian's subconscious, you are like the director with Julian as the actor. Considering the options are numerous, and you can choose them in any order you wish, everybody's experience in the game will be slightly different and unique to them, even if the ending is the same. It gives it a very personal feel which I enjoyed. Overall, this is an overlooked and misunderstood little gem of a game.

review:
DINNER DATE.
Stout Games, 2011

Genres: Casual, Indie, Sad Ass Simulator

Plot: The player assumes the role of Julian Luxemburg, a vaguely British man on a DINNER DATE with a beautiful Japanese woman.

Actually, that was a lie. You don’t assume the role of Julian Luxemburg, a vaguely British man on a date with a beautiful Japanese woman. You actually assume the role of Julian Luxemburg’s subconscious. And you’re actually being stood up by a beautiful Japanese woman. And you actually never see her, so she’s probably not that beautiful. Whether or not she’s even Japanese, I have my doubts.

Anyway, you “play” the game as Julian’s subconscious. What does that mean exactly? It means you don’t actually get full control of your character. Instead, you’re in charge of “the small unconscious actions we all do”--things like making Julian look at his hand, or look at his other hand, or touch his face. You do not, by the way, get to do any of the cool things a subconscious can do, like give Julian the sudden urge to kill or make him have a nightmare about his naked father. No, but you can make him mindlessly snack on a shitload of bread. And before you start to think that your actions can affect the outcome in the game whatsoever, you’re wrong. Nothing you do matters at all. You could do nothing or everything and nothing would change. To be fair, the game tells you this pretty much right away, so good on them.

So, you sit there for awhile doing random meaningless shit and Julian gets progressively drunker and more depressed as he rambles and whines on and on about his life as a total fucking loser and then, after 20 minutes of bullshit, he decides to leave his apartment and the game ends and you feel angry but also a little relieved that it’s over. The end.

Gameplay: What the game lacks in fun stuff, it makes up for in not fun stuff, such as stirring soup, looking at a clock, quoting Lord Byron, and constant whining.

Realism: As I said, you get stood up by your date and spend the evening getting drunk alone while succumbing to crippling doubt and insecurity. I don’t know what that’s like because I’m handsome. 0/10.

Graphics: I had the game set on “exorbitant graphical quality” but my character's fingers looked like mangled dongs.

Overall score: 3 out of 10 stars, which makes sense considering I paid 3 out of 10 dollars for the game.

The following paragraph is my recommendation for Painkiller: Black Edition, because, for some reason, Steam thinks I don't own that game, even though I fucking do. Like, I'm on the store page, and it doesn't even have that green section with the "play now" button. What the fuck. It's in my library. I bought the thing with money. Seriously, what the fuck.

If it becomes too hard for you, you can just use cheats anyway. Sometimes it's funner that way too, just going kill crazy and blasting away like there's no tomorrow. The game also has some sort of... Out of all the Painkillers to get into, the original right here should probably be your first choice.



The following paragraph is an anti-recommendation of Dinner Date, a shitty game that I CAN write a recommendation for, but is not the slightest bit recommendable.

Dinner Date is a boring piece of shit. It is hardly interactive at all, and what little possibility for player input there is is fucking lame and inconsequential; all you can do is look in specific directions and make your ugly seemingly-autistic hands touch things a little bit. Then there's a part where your character actually gets off the damn seat, but then it is still boring and there is still nothing to do but listen to this guy be a negative nansy about stupid shit you don't care about. You can't really do anything as the player because you play as the character's subconscious. Oooooooh... Interesting concept, but it turns out it is not fun at all. Your character got stood up for a date, and he is alone at a dinner table at his house, and all there is to do is listen to this guy whine and wallow in his patheticness. Interesting idea, bad game. And if you want to call it "interactive art" instead of a proper "video game", it fails in that department too. And the graphics suck too. I honestly was looking forward to this game, cause it was a fascinating idea, but the game just sucks. It honestly just sucks. This is a sucky game, and it's not worth any amount of time or money, except for maybe as an example of how NOT to make a game.

Dinner Date's top key feature on its store page reads as follows: "Julian’s story lasts a fully voiced 25 minutes and is told through various unique animations, set in a real-time 3d environment with the unique interface of playing as a subconsciousness, the first of its kind."

25 whole minutes? 25 whole minutes?! 25 WHOLE MINUTES?! 25 WHOLE MINUTES, MAN! 25 whole minutes of SHEEYIT. And then you'll flush that shit down the toilet and forget about it. Or at least try to, because that was pretty traumatizingly nasty and painful shit to take.

The icon for this recommendation shows that of Dinner Date, but this is really a recommendation for Painkiller, and a word of warning for whoever might actually consider buying Dinner Date. Don't do it; Dinner Date is not fun at all. It's just trying to be artsy and intellectual and experimental, but it really just fails as a means of entertainment. This game was honestly just a disappointing waste of time, and I see nothing of value in this experience. Dinner Date can suck a dick. Painkiller, however, is pretty damn enjoyable. Fun! Thrilling! Like any video game (or "interactive art") should be.


If you ever find yourself stuck in the perplexing dilemma of deciding whether to get Painkiller or Dinner Date, this is me telling you to get Painkiller.

The game starts you off by telling you you're not playing the character, which is sort of true. You don't control the character in the traditional sense, instead you play a part of his subconcious, you direct where he looks and what draws his attention. You have some minor impulse control in your repetoir as well, but in the end the guy basically just does what he wants anyway... or at least the game forces you to give him what he wants. 

You play a 27 year old guy who has just been stood up by the 20 year old japanese girl that one of his mates has set him up with. She's pretty, and flirty, and from what I understood of the games dialogue she's something of a party girl. As the story progresses you learn a great deal about the young man you're almost controlling, but on the whole thats about all you do. 

There are few choices offered to you by the game. You get to control where the young man looks, which things draw his attention, and which inconsequential actions he peforms; from staring at the clock to eating a piece of bread or smoking. The game progresses down the same path every time. I'm guessing that eventually, if you try to refrain from eating bread or soup, the game will force you to do so as some of the dialogue comments on the things you're eating. I plan to explore this game further.

On the whole this game really isn't worth it. It's an interesting concept, and the voice acting is interesting... but if you have to miss an out there indie game this year, this is the one to miss.

I won't get in too much on the story, since it's quite short but complex, but it's basically about the experience of being stood up on a dinner date and the effect is has on a persons train of thoughts. The characters reactions are very relatable and it feels very natural and never forced.

review:
A game of intrinsically rewarding actions that is only as interesting as you allow it to be. I say intrinisically rewarding, because there is no extrinsic reason to interact with this game whatsoever. No real goals, no punishments, no achievements. Only the simple tale of a man waiting for his date to arrive. In some ways it's a lot like stage acting. You are cast as a character who has to say the same lines and go through the same set of re-occuring events every time, but unlike stage acting, there is no audience to cheer you on. 

But like acting, the subtleties of your performance are both what make the game interesting and rewarding. Is the character a chronic eater? Is he a tapper, a thinker, a pacer? What sort of subtleties can you add to the performance of the story? If any of this sounds interesting or enticing, then this game is for you. Otherwise, it probably isn't. Whether you like or dislike this game need not necessarily make you a better or worse person for it. But as someone who likes to find a reason to enjoy most things, this is certainly an interesting experiment, and at the lowly price of 3 dollars and no more than 40 minutes of your time, is certainly worth a try in my opinion.

review:
Do not reccommend. 

I'm all for artistic games. I think this medium is a beautiful resource for social commentary, satire, artistic statements, etc. 

BUT. This is none of those things. This is pretentious. I'm honestly not sure if the dev/devs think that this is what art is, or if they just didn't realize how lacking this "game" truly is. I hope it's the latter, because I'd love to see them put out something really good.

But it's just not good. Nothing you do has any impact on anything. Any button press you make simply occupies the visual space while a whiney main character complains about life, makes several references to classic poetry, and vascilates wildly from hating himself, his date, and the world at large. Now, this could have been an interesting set up if anything you did had any relevance. But it doesn't. It's simply a visual toy to occupy you while he bangs on for a half hour. the only real interactivity is the wine swigs, which only serve as a "turn the page" movement every few minutes. Not saying all games need to be combat-heavy, or highly interactive, or have multiple endings. But if you are going to make a game, you need more than a "continue" button. Visual novels do that, and they tend to last 2+ hours. this is 20-30 minutes.

Now, as for the story itself. It could have been intriguing to see. Getting to watch, in real time, a man go through the mental gymnastics associated with being stood up. But 2 things happen. 1. The dialogue is WAY too flowery. The poetry and, what I can only call pretense, in his voice seems forced. As if someone thought "this is how artistic dialogue should be." It doesn't sound natural. If I'm meant to empathize with him, He should sound like a normal person. Not a pretentious cretin. And if he was meant to be unlikable, that didn't come across. I don't care for him. I've met people like him, and I don't care for them either. 2. I could handle the content (with more natural dialogue) if i had a little more control. Not saying we need multiple endings or choice. Just let me control more of him. Let my actions guide his thoughts a little bit. Perhaps I have him walk to the fridge, in which case, he speaks for half a minute on whether he should just trash the idea, save the food, and go do something. Or, perhaps I have him go to the sink, where he gets frustrated seeing all the dishware he dealt with for this failed dinner. Little things like that would make it feel like a game, while keeping the artistry. As it stands, it feels like a Humungous Entertainment game where I'm just clicking on stuff to make pretty things happen.

All in all, there was promise in this, but it was horribly executed. If i could reccommend a better way, I'd say do one of 2 things.
1. De flower the dialogue. Make it more natural. Give us more control of the protagonist, and let our actions (where we go in the room and what we do) guide his musings, in addition to the normal bits of rumination. It'd make a powerful statement on rejection.
2. again, Deflower. But, instead of more control, do about the same thing, but as a short film. This didn't seem to utilize the interactivity of the medium in any more than a token way. So work with that. Make it a non-interactive experience. This could have been cool as a first person film. half an hour, same premise, same set up. but more natural dialogue. I'd watch it, and be willing to reccommend it then.

As it stands, I can't bring myself to reccommend. But I hope to see some more things from this dev/devs.

review:
Usually I really love artistic games and I really like the idea for this game. I also rarely wish I could refund a game I've bought from Steam, even if I dislike it. This is not one of those times. 2.99 is actually way too much for such a lack of game.

Positive things first:
 - I actually did like the monologue and felt badly for the character, pathetic as he was. However, my dislike for the character rose as I realized that my actions did not have any effect on him.
 - ...it's cheap?

Negative things:

 - I don't know about anyone else, but my subconcious desires and fears do have some effect on my life, besides where I look. In fact, that is an incredibly random thing for a "sub-concious" to control. Looking back at the description of the game, I think it should be more evident that the point of the game is not to "play" but to listen. I wouldn't be interested in such a game, but I think they could have avoided a lot of alienation but spelling it out that this was a game like Dear Esther. There is obviously an aundience for this type of game, this really should be described better for this crowd.

 - Again, looking back at the description, I see a lot of "unanswered question" type wonderings, but the game is rather straightforword. Julian does not like his coworkers. He does like Byron. There is no real reason to play after the first "act", because it is all spelled out there. I criticized its lousy gameplay strategy before but now I'm criticizing its storytelling.
   
   Why should I care about Julian? Yes, it sucks that he got stood up, but so what? There is no mystery to him, which is fine in real life, but characters who spend 20 minutes or so talking about themselves should really have something interesting to say. Sure, he likes poetry, but so do a lot of people. And they are probably less insufferable and boring than Julian is. No new information is gathered in each subsequent act and there is no real reason to have the game continue with no new information or insight.

   The game's story got ever-so-slightly more interesting near the end, when someone knocks at the door, and I did feel something at his emotions afterward, but that really doesn't excuse the 20 minutes of boredom proceeding that. Boredom can be used in video games and stories, but it should be rewarded or serve a point.

So, no, I would not recommend this game to anyone. It is not a game, it is not a compelling story, and it isn't even a good sleep aid, since no one could sleep over Julian's whining.

review:
[h1]Victor, is that you?[/h1]
[i]The Dream Machine[/i] Chapter 3 finds you, Victor Neff, inside another person's dream. 

This is probably the chapter that will decide whether you dislike or like (or hate or love) the game going forwards, as it has probably the most esoteric and "video-gamey" puzzles of the entire game. The setting of the chapter (a boat that seems to be stranded in the middle of a large city) is a marvelous idea, and the hierarchical system aboard the ship is a great source of conflict for the characters present in the chapter. Determining whether or not the puzzles are any good is up for debate. Personally I found the puzzles here to be of mixed quality. The puzzles I did enjoy were fantastic, but there were a few puzzles that required some serious trial and error. Perhaps that was just my futile attempts at bashing my head against a brick wall when there was a perfectly obvious door just to the side of me. 

This chapter contains elements of genuine horror and morbidity. My first playthrough was traumatic to some degree. The turn the game takes is fantastically horrifying, and yet done with a certain amount of tact. It's not cheap horror that [i]The Dream Machine[/i] dwells in, that's for sure. It's haunting in a way that you wouldn't expect from a point and click adventure game. 

What [i]The Dream Machine[/i] does well is make lucid a certain feeling regarding dreams. It carries dream logic in a fairly seamless and interesting way, and it is in this chapter that Cockroach Inc. begin to explore the idea of a mind beneath the mind; the concept of the subconscious becomes more and more powerful as the game progresses. 

Were I to score this out of ten, I would bestow upon this chapter an eight. Were you to allow me the specificity of a decimal system, an 8.5. A slight dip in puzzle quality is mostly offset by some fantastic writing and the horror on display. This is, speaking from a puzzle design perspective, the weakest chapter in the game, but is fantastic across the board in other areas. Well worth pushing through to see the rest of the game; it is the hurdle one must pass to reach the gold medal.

review:
The Tiny Bang Story is a hidden object game with minigames and a handful of puzzles, nothing you haven't seen before. It's handdrawn scenery is lovely, and the objects are not too hard to find. If you have trouble finding one, chances are that you are just missing an object that you can open, or you need to solve a minigame first that will give you access to your final missing piece. There is an in-game help that shows you a puzzle piece you might have missed, and you have to "charge" it by catching little flies that are buzzing around. 

I bought TTBS as part of a bundle, and I'm not usually a fan of hidden object games, but they put some effort into keeping it interesting and mostly fun. 

There were a couple of minigames that I found plainly annoying, and my greatest criticism is that you can't skip any of the minigames. They were not difficult, but slow and tedious. Fortunately, that was the exception. 
My only other criticim is that when you have collected all the necesssary pieces, you can leave the level by accident. All scenes or levels have a set of puzzle pieces that you can collect as a bonus, they are not used for any puzzles, it is more an extra achievement. But it happened to me a couple of times that I clicked on the exit without intending to, and that immediately ends the level. A confirmation button would have helped there. 

After finishing all levels you can replay each level individually, though, so if you are a completionist, you can return to a specific level if you want to.

I recommend this game for casual HOG fans. For puzzle fans, though, there isn't enough here to sink your teeth in.

Break your legs jumping 2 feet.

Accidentally call in an airstrike on your own squad and still get thanked for "keeping it immersive."

Final Verdict: 11/10. Not a game. A military-grade friendship simulator with occasional war crimes.

Whether you’re running small co-op missions with friends or diving into huge multiplayer battles, the game always feels unique because no two scenarios play out the same.

The learning curve is steep, but once it clicks, it’s incredibly rewarding. Combined Arms, tactical teamwork, and the sheer freedom to approach missions however you want make this game special. The modding scene is also phenomenal—you can find everything from realistic gear packs to entire new campaigns and total conversions.

Pros:

Huge open-world maps with incredible detail

Realistic ballistics, vehicles, and tactics

Insane amount of mods and community content

Co-op and multiplayer experiences that never get old

Sandbox freedom to create your own scenarios

Cons:

Steep learning curve

Performance can vary on large missions

Verdict:
If you want an authentic and endlessly customizable military simulator, this is the game. After hundreds of hours, I’m still discovering new things to do.

review:
A total disaster.

After staying up all night troubleshooting, I can roughly confirm this: with ARMA 3’s latest update, stability in high-stress scenarios—where dozens of units and objects coexist—has been sacrificed to gain smoother performance in some low-to-moderate stress scenarios.
 
But the reason I fell in love with this game in the first place is exactly its ability to support an overwhelming number of units and objects on screen at once, all running in full real-time simulation. Now? As soon as there are too many elements in a scenario, the game crashes for no obvious reason. I can’t even tell if the issue lies with the units, the objects, or the waypoints—I have no clue what’s actually causing the error. Some scenarios crash the second they finish loading.
 
Before, even if high-stress scenarios turned into a slideshow, I could at least sit back: no need to control units, just wait for the result from the camera view. Now even that bare minimum stability is gone? This experience is so frustrating, and so disappointing. What I want is a highly complex battlefield with diverse, mixed loadouts—a full-on, unfiltered chaos. I don’t even want to control any units; I just want to wait and watch the outcome of a thousand AI bots fighting it out along the waypoints I set. That’s the ARMA 3 I love.
 
I hate protagonist-centric design. I hate these compromises made for the sake of optimization. And I especially hate the game logic where “events only happen when the player is nearby”—I want everything to keep running normally, even in parts of the map I can’t see on screen.
 
Right now, there’s no way to figure out if the problem is with a mod or a map. For now, I can only chalk it up to excessive computational load.

I hope my take is wrong—maybe it’s just that my testing method isn’t rigorous, or that my hardware specs aren’t up to par (something like the VRAM bandwidth of an RTX 4060, for example).

Just my personal opinion.

review:
A disclaimer - it's a game set in Forgotten Realms universe, but don't expect DnD-like gameplay. 

Now what should I say about this game...
Neverwinter is a MMORPG, and a really good one. I was somewhat off for the first few hours, but the game gets better and better with every hour you spend in it. 

A disclaimer #2 - if you don't like timegate mechanic and grinding dailies don't read further.

Let's start with some pros:
+ Setting - I'm definitely a FR lover. You should know that Salvatore helped with writing some of the quests in the game. You will also meet some amazing characters like Bruenor Battlehamer, Drizzt Do'Urden or Minsc&Boo. 
+ Music - wether you're in the heart of Neverwinter, traverse the Underdark or purge the Dread Ring of the undead you'll always be accompanied by really nice tunes. It's an MMO so obviously music does not play THAT BIG of a role, but the tracks playing at the background do not disturb you.
+ Character development(bright part) - it's really well made. While power upgrading does not matter much, traits and boons can passively make your character stronger in different ways(for example make your trap also deal damage over time, and even stronger against immune targets)
+ Combat - you're basically on the move all the time, combat is dynamic, there is a lot of dodging, blocking and watching out for enemy attacks
+ Endgame - that is just my opinion but endgame is great. Dungeons are challenging(unless you get boosted by that 3k+ player), long, bossfights are fun. There is always something to do due to campaigns which not only give great rewards but boost your character stats via boons. Also progress is slow paced but significant enough to see the difference between those two items, 30-40 item levels or that one tier of your artifact. 

Cons
- Hard to earn currency - getting AD as a fresh player is a pain in the arse. Enough said. 
- AD to Zen converting ratio - Zen is that "real money" currency of NW. And while gathering AD to exchange for Vip(1k Zen - 500k AD) is not that big of an issue, trying to get AD to buy Zen while also managing your characters equipment is. Artifact here, refinement stones there, goodbye 120k AD here. 
- Outdated graphics - we're in 2017, yet graphics sometimes feel like a 2012 game. It doesn't look bad, it had actually aged quite well, but I think devs should consider making some upgrades here and there. 
- Character development (sad part) - boons from campaigns are a double edged sword. They greatly increase character capabilities, but good luck getting most of them. Some of them are after huge timegates(ToD, Dread Ring, Underdark) and others are just annoying to start with(Icewind Dale, fuck you).

My final mark would be somewhere around 7 or 8 out of 10. It's definitely a game worth at least trying out.

You can put "perks" for your character and your gun which will give you some bonuses-maluses depending on what you prefer. 

Now that this has been said...

GamersFirst is a really shit company that doesn't care about either its playerbase neither their game in general. Their goal is to make as much money as possible while you're still playing their fucking game until you're out of it.

Each and every time they release a new weapon it will most certainly be incredibly unbalanced for at least 4-5 months, so that the players will be so tempted to buy the damn gun. Buying guns permanently in this game costs A LOT of money, and it's even more retardedly expensive if you want it on more than one character. Oh, and since it's a new gun you'll have to pay some more.

The matchmaking system is retarded. If you're gold, most of the time the servers will force you to go in a gold server but nobody plays in those, so they either go in silver servers and ruin silver's days OR they derank on purpose so they don't have to deal with that. Oh and the anti-cheat system. It can take a while before it does something and sometimes it can ban people that weren't cheating. Meanwhile there's a retard teleporting everywhere and plowing everyone in the server.

Honestly, I think the concept is so beautiful and could be so much better. I'm waiting for another company or group of people to steal APB's main concept and actually put their love and soul into a new game that will be better than this one.

GamersFirst. Such a shitty, shitty company.

review:
Sadly there is nothing between "Thumbs up" and "Thumbs down".
Here's a short list of pros and cons about the game:

Pro:
- Really good character costumization
- Different guns with different playstyles with each gun (and not the same assault rifle 10 times)
- Very teamplay based
- Fun competitive aspect
- Not Pay2Win!!!!!111!1!11!!!eleven!11 (I'll come to that later)

Con:
- One of the toxiest community you will probably ever see
- Not beginner friendly at all
- New players have to progress in the game and expand their arsenal to actually have a chance against experienced players
- Anti-Cheat Engine is a joke
- Matchmaking is broken
-  "Threat" (basically elo or "skill level") system doesn't work at all (there are tons of people who lose on purpose to play with lower ranked people)
- Regular server lags (seriously?)
- Cash Shop is way too expensive (at least not pay2win)
- Since it's not Pay2Win, you have to grind all the good shit

One of the biggest misconception about the game is that people say this game is very "Pay2Win".
This isn't actually true, since about 70% of the guns are actually reskins of guns you can actually buy with ingame currency. The other 30% are guns, you can also buy with "Joker-Tickets" (which is just a pure daily mission grindfest).
Other things you can buy with money in this game, are just pure cosmetics, better cars, more customization options and stuff like that. Nothing that would actually boost your combat effectiveness.
So it's actually "Pay2GrindLess" or even "Pay2Enjoy" since buying a premium subscription gives you an additional 125% boost (wtf) to the money you gain after each match.
The only reason I can think of why people say it's pay2win is because they suffer from shit matchmaking and get thrown to way more experienced players who are willing to spend 35 bucks for those awesome weapon reskins.

The idea and the concept are really good and this game WOULD be fun if there wasn't all the issues I listed above.

review:
This game has a great concept, customisation system, and variety, however, unfortunatly, very poorly executed, in a nutshell, it's a Pay 2 Win GTA-Style MMO that had great potential, but it went down the drain, it's a very fun game for the first few hours you play it, but as the missions spiral on, you start to see the problems seep in through the cracks...
1. As a free player myself, i've noticed it's extremely hard to get anything you want that is upper-class without upgrading to a premium account or using real money.

2. The whole "Cops vs Criminals" thing is broken, the Enforcers cannot make any worthwhile cash if the Criminals don't ready up for a mission, and because of this, there are some desperate Enforcers i've encountered that have begged the Criminals to ready up on low-pop areas, and most of the time nothing will happen, and they get to the point where they actively try to instigate a mission by following you and waiting for you to do something they can use as a means to dispatch against you, and the Criminals are usually grinding for something expensive, as to why they aren't wanting to go on a mission, so if you don't notice one, you'll lose all your money and progress from that 40 minutes of grinding if they kill you. And the Criminals can't do anything about it

3. Another point on Paragragh one, the P2W aspect is a catastrophic problem in matchmaking, even on high-pop areas, the game doesen't effectively balance matches even in mission areas, where it's sorted via skill compatability, not availability, and yet my friends and I (Bronze to Silver threat levels) get frequently put up against Gold-Tier Enforcers, who are either Wallet Warriors, or people who sweat so hard over the game it's not fun.
Also it's kind of ironic seeing that the company who made a Pay-2-Win game is called "GamersFirst".
More Like MoneyFirst.

4.5/10.

Give it a try—who knows, it might just become your turning point.
