review:
Excellent game form an excellent studio. As they say, the game is hard, and getting into it is somewhat difficult, you are an ordinary guy not a monster that can kill most people around you. On steam I have only an hour of game time, but off steam I have multiple playtroughs of the game as it is one of the only games of late that actually rewards replaying multiple times and with different builds. The game has technically 3+ main plotlines that you can play on either side, basically you pick your faction in first chapter, and can switch at some other points. 

The world is different and some of your decisions can change it a lot, but some basically have the world work as it has. I do like the somewhat dystopian world where you have a lot of things to do find out and discover. It is impossible to get more than maybe half of the content the game has to offer on one single playthrough.

You will die, a lot, but you can become a beast of a fighter or a scholar, the jack of all trades does not well work, unless you know what exactly you are doing, and even then you will still be hard locked from some content cause you are not fast enough or tough enough or intelligent enough to get through a situation in a certain way. review:
🔫 Gameplay & Mechanics
- Wave-Based Combat: Teams of up to six players battle increasingly difficult waves of Zeds, culminating in a boss fight against enemies like the Patriarch or Dr. Hans Volter.
- Perk System: The game features 10 distinct classes (called “perks”), each with unique weapons and abilities—from the healing Field Medic to the explosive Demolitionist.
- Zed Time: A signature mechanic that slows down time during headshots or carnage, adding cinematic flair to the chaos.
- Progression: Leveling perks unlocks powerful bonuses, but early levels can feel grindy before classes truly shine.

🎧 Sound & Visuals
- Audio Design: Heavy metal soundtrack, visceral sound effects, and panicked voice lines create a pulse-pounding atmosphere.
- Visuals: While not cutting-edge, the game’s gore effects and physics engine are impressive. Blood splatters, dismemberments, and flaming Zeds keep the action visually intense.

🧟 Enemy Variety & Challenge
- Zeds: From basic Clots to invisible Stalkers and hulking Flesh Pounds, enemy types are diverse and increasingly aggressive.
- Bosses: Each map ends with a unique boss battle requiring coordination and strategy. Bosses adapt to player tactics and can wipe unprepared teams.

🤝 Co-op & Replayability
- Multiplayer Focus: Best played with friends. Communication and class synergy are key to survival.
- Custom Servers: While official matches cap at six players, modded servers can host 50+ for pure chaos.
- Solo Play: Possible, but lacks the thrill and tactical depth of team-based runs.

✅ Pros & Cons
| Pros | Cons | 
| Satisfying gunplay and perk variety | Early game grind before perks feel impactful | 
| Excellent sound design and Zed Time | Limited game modes (mostly Survival and Versus) | 
| Strong co-op experience | Repetitive maps and objectives over time | 
| Frequent updates and seasonal events | Cosmetic microtransactions (purely optional) | 



🧠 Final Verdict
Killing Floor 2 is unapologetically gory, chaotic, and fun. It doesn’t try to be a tactical shooter or a narrative-driven experience—it’s a visceral playground for fans of co-op carnage. Whether you’re healing teammates mid-firefight or launching saw blades into a horde of mutants, the game delivers adrenaline in spades. It’s not deep, but it’s endlessly replayable.

review:
EDIT: 
Quite possibly the buggiest, laggiest and sloppiest production of all time. You have to say it exemplifies Fatshark's ineptitude at making a game that is even slightly polished. Frankly, it is an utter embarrassment in that regard.

ORIGINAL:
Having played the first installment of the 'War of' games for over 1500 hours one might be inclined to call me a fan of the style of game Fatshark had created and I was hugely enthusiatic about the next chapter in what could be a blossoming franchise. 

However,  the game has failed miserably in delivering an improved performance and gaming experience on the previous game. This is a watered down version of War of the Roses, but by no means does that make it easy. Hitboxes are non-existent as the game is all about movement of you body postion rather than skill/precision of aiming your weapon and feinting attacks. Consequently if you get average FPS (like me) then you need to steer well clear of this title as smoothness is imperative. 

FIghting mechanics seemed to have had a huge overhaul in WotV, which isn't necessarily a good thing. There are 3 ways to attack (when in melee combat) instead of the 4 in WotR and there are perks that can give you 'autoblock' for one specific direction, taking the total number of ways to concentrate on to 2. You also have the ability to carry out special attacks, which if connect give insta-kills (or so I believe). Thanks to the above the game provides no real satisfaction when killing an opponent (during melee), as you don't feel like it materialized through your in-game education or skill progression, but rather came about thanks to the hack and slash elements of the game. Don't get me wrong, there is skill in EVERY game, but it isn't a skill that inspires you to learn more, want more and basically....play more.

Ranged wise the game has got similarities to WotR and there wasn't a desperate need for change, as the ranged system was smooth and worked well. It was satisfying and still is, with the addition of throwing weapons like axes etc it has added another string to it's bow, so to speak, so all in all ranged is pretty good.

In addition to the new implementations on the ranged side of things, customization has also been given a boost. Though so far I haven't seen anywhere near the weapon count of WotR, having said that it is in beta and will almost certainly be getting more content as the game develops. Nevertheless customizing the look of your character is still good. Capes, beards and helmets are all included as is the look of you clothes...I think.

Graphically the game is still pretty nice, I am not sure if it is as good as the previous game, but that is something YOU should make your mind up on. Although let it be said it certainly isn't bad! 

There are issues with server drop outs and total game crashes, which one would hope to see ironed out when the final product is released. However I wouldn't hold your breath as these issues are a known problem on WotR and have so far been overlooked in every patch release.

In all honesty on a personal note I was hoping for a re-skin of War of the Roses with maybe a few new features chucked in, whilst seeing some of the bugs and glitches addressed. Unfortunately that was not the case, and instead of getting a very in depth, hand to hand combat game like it's predecessor, we were provided with a competitor to Chivalry for the people who have an ephemeral attention span, want a quick fix and nothing more. It does have some new features which are nice, but the core of the game is just poo.

For the discerning consumer out there, do youself a favour and give War of the Roses a try (and give it some time) or, if you want a quick fix go for Chivalry, but don't waste your hard earned cash on this sloppy execution of a game. For people wanting and expecting War of the Roses part 2, forget it, it is a completely different game. For those wanting a Chivalry emulator, snap this puppy up and spam until your hearts content.

In conclusion, a thoroughly disappointing game. Essentially it is all geared towards a fast paced, hack and slash game rather than the slower, more realistic fighting we came to love (and loathe) on WotR. Given time I am sure that improvements will be made, but addressing the core fighting mechanics is essential and unfortunately that is not going to happen. 

3/10

Review at 2014/04/14 (Onde day before release).
Current patch: 0.9.9
My specs: I7 920 oc @3,4Ghz, GTX 470 1Gb, 8 GB RAM @1600 Mhz. 1920x1080.

¡BAD ENGLISH DETECTED!

//// v1.0 version ////

I had a boost of 15-20 fps. Now I can run the game with all textures on high and antialising at 60 fps or more. Shadows must be disabled as well as the cloth effects (physics).

//////////////////////////

General description:
- It isn't the same as WoTR. Some people prefer one, some people prefer the other one. This is more dynamic, and fast paced game with less variables and easier handling. 
- Hard at start if you have not played M&B or WoTR but either way is a challenging game.
- Smaller maps than WoTR to increase game speed, but usually with more ways to flank the enemy.
- Beautiful art, graphics and music.

Cons:
- Unbalance with some weapons. Some day one, some day another. And some spammeable and lammer game mechanics can annoy you sometimes as in the majority of games.
- Bad servers (Multiplay) and ATM you can only rent them, so [u]you cannot make a dedicated server in your own machine[/u].
- Lag related issues. The ping is fine in Europe but as I said, the bad server performance is ruining the game. (I have to say that this may not be directly the fault of the developers of WOTV)
- Game performance is worse than before. For me, of course. Now I have to run the game in 'low' settings except the textures to achieve 35-65 FPS. (My specs in top).
- Gameplay bugs. The shields don't work perfectly, some crappy animations, etc. 

Pros:
- The game will be supported for a long time. Solving issues, balancing, adding a lot of content, etc.
- Good customization level and options, and this will increase with time.
- The game can be really enjoyable regardless of winning or losing, etc. but you have to take your time to master the playstyle. So be patient if someone instakill you every time, or if you can't hit/parry anybody.
(That is fine, you will be good in less time than in WoTR. It is easier to play for newcomers, but still hard to master).
- External anticheat system. This was a very great thing.
- You can sprint :D
- Cosmetics only. The item's stats are equal in a sword that costs 320 coins to another that costs 30000. That allow new players to play in the same conditions as a veteran. It just will look ugliest or more beautiful.

Conclusions:

If you don't have patience, this may not be your game. Neither if you expect be the king  in your first match.

If you can deal with some bugs, lammers and archers (I won't lie you, sometimes is an arrow fest) you will have good moments.

I approve this game, it could be better but i'm sure it will get better. It's just a matter of time.

[b]FAQ: It's the same as WoTR? - No, it isn't.[/b] The evolution is really tangible; improved graphics, physics, animations, (for now) balance. New weapons, fight styles, attacks, habilities and game mechanics.

- Really enjoyable and funny. (For now without xp and customizing system)
- In my case without performance issues since the alpha stage. (GTX 470)

- When you win a close battle is really satisfactory.

[u][b]Cons in beta stage[/b][/u]:
- Third party anti-cheat system isn't enabled [b]yet[/b] so there are a lot of speedhackers.

- Due to the pre-release stage, the difficulty, and the "casual" players that has only played a few minutes, the servers are usually not full, and in Europe is difficult to play passed 2:00 a.m.

review:
Have you ever wished there was a pvp game with modern day graphics and combat/design like gothic, mount and blade, or die by the sword? War of the Vikings is very reminiscent of these innovative games. Firstly in WotV, you are dropped into beautifully and maserfully done levels ranging from glaciers, caves, hilly villages, to  village cement tunnel trenches. The game wouldn't be complete without these gorgeous environments but it doesn't stop there. 

Aimed to be created with historically accurate settings, weapons,  garbs/armor, and combat style, War of the Vikings will immerse you deeply. I have have been playing war of the roses since its beta and war of the vikings since the alpha early access too. Its always held a special place in my heart for multiple reasons. The combat is visceral, you can feel your sword cleave through people like a  butcher knife into a slab of meat. Place your hits well and you will be rewarded with a clean decapitation. Hitting a skilled opponent is no small accomplishment. The blocking system, although sometimes inconsistent, allows you to practically parry and deflect all attacks, if done skillfully. Aside from amazing fighting mechanics, graphics, and the best maps I have ever seen, war of the vikings offers swag as well as perks and a customization system.

The developers have simplified balancing by creating prestigious versions of each crude but equally efficient base weapon. Along with having swaggier versions of some of the more prestigious looking weapons, they come with a bio for the hero they belonged to or the era the weapon was famous for. The base weapons are offered for considerably lower prices to even out the playing field and make the game balance simple yet still customizable and the avatars personable to their owner. There are three classes, multiple perks which create multiple ways to play such as an archer, axeman, javelin hurler, backstabbing rogue, and much more. Theres enough swagger to drain thousands of hours of your time and keep you craving more inscribed finely crafted shiney pieces of loot. 

Multiple game modes allow for basic team death match and more hardcore play with single life rounds as well as multiple others like conquest(territories). The game modes all have different feels and different meta tactics while using different parts of the environment for mini arenas amongst a gorgeous sandbox. Battle on a bridge to dominate the territory at the other end, or brawl for 15 mins straight until 125 kills in a sandy beach cave. Each mode takes advantage of the map layout and size.

 The Devs definitely treated their previous fans well by giving them a 10% discount on the game as well as making them available with the discount in 4 packs. My friends and I all went in on this together and none of us regret it. The final product is well worth every dollar and even more. I thank the devs, Fat Shark, for making such an amazing game without slapping an expensive price tag on it.  Although the game has a steap learning curve and can be furstrating when getting crushed over and over by skilled opponents or bad spawns : (, I guarantee you will enjoy it and find extreme satisfaction once you learn the ropes. One of my favorite games and series of all time! 9.5/10. I will be looking forward to more from this developer and if they keep this kind of model and quality I will be a repeat customer and loyal supporter for decades to come!

review:
Summary: Although a good concept, War of the Vikings is fundamentally flawed. Is historical credibility is appalling, the game mechanics perform badly, it is not an approachable game for a newcomer or casual player, and there is no good motivation to continue playing it. 

Full review: 

Although it might first appear as an historical title, War of the Vikings fails miserably in this regard. Weapons include 15th century daggers, 16th century pikes, and so on, but miss out on many period weapons (such as seaxes, after which the Saxons were named!). Armour is worse, with horned helmets, feathered headgear and armours from the middle-east. There are no historical battle sites and maps are simply generic locations... including epic towering monastaries or Skyrim-esque glaciers. And the in-game warriors can do lots of other non-historical things, all the way from running around impaled with multiple javelins through to techno-dancing. Although there is no obligation for developers to stick to fact, the flights of fantasy in this game really detracts from the historical immersion.

But War of the Vikings does not make up for it with game play. The mechanics are random in places, with weapons simply passing through without damage, or you can often do more damage with the haft of the axe than the head of it. Server glitches and crashes are common place, even on sparsely-populated servers. This level of unreliability (even on ping-limited servers, using good computers with good connections) is extremely frustrating. Even the graphics, which are okay, are really demanding on even good computer systems. You really need a first-class Internet connection and top-notch machine with a superb frame rate to even contemplate this title.

From the perspective of someone who has never played other hand-to-hand combat games, the learning curve on War of the Vikings is brutal. There is scant documentation (only a single splash screen showing the key presses) and a woefully inadequate tutorial. There is no single-player game to train you up nor are there any matched-skill servers. The community comprises mostly elite veterans and you can expect to spend a lot of time staring at the spawn-in screen.  While there are some exceptions, I have found a disproportinate level of arrogance and contempt in games. Even the so-called "friendly clans" take delight in abusing inexperienced players.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, there is no motivation to play. The weapons/armour are all equal in combat value. This is okay in terms of balance, but for a modest amount of playtime, you can get any loadout and perks. Thus upgrades are not an incentive to play. The ability to purchase expensive-looking clothes and capes might appeal to some, but it is not a huge motivation to persevere with being cut down time after time. The Steam achievements totally lack imagination and are mostly way beyond the reach of the average player, who just wants to recreate the Viking/Saxon battle experience.

Although there are some nice touches (for example the use of Old English/Icelandic for the voices and a wonderful soundtrack), this game is frustrating and quickly becomes tedious. Out of a love of this era of history, I have stuck with it and have trained hard at it, but it remains demoralising and uninspiring. This is a pity because the idea has potential. But as it stands at present, it is simply not worth the effort.

[i]"Go buy freeware private server OG GunZ"[/i] ?

If you get close, they will just do a sword slash, which paralyzes you for a second and almost one shots you. The second would be the dual wielding machine gun class. The class I picked was Wayne the cowboy like character (reference to John Waybe, but looks like Indiana Jones. He has a whip which has longer range then the sword, but the damage is so much lower that its not really effective. If you are close enough to whip someone, they are close enough to dash once and slash you for more damage. The pistol is cool. He has a shotgun, but it doesn't seem to fire in a spread, so its just a worse rifle. I tried the story mode. It has cut scenes, but it consists of barely animated pictures, and poorly written sentences. In terms of game play the first level kept you in a small canyon like coridor which you basically go space to space to fight enemies. There were only 2 character models, and thier melee could 2 hit you. This would be fine, but the maps aren't really designed for the wall running and diving you'd do in multiplayer. the Walls werent smove enough and are broken by round plateus. review: If you are looking for entertainment that requires very little to no brainpower, this might be the perfect game for you. “The Typing of The Dead: Overkill” is a rail shooter where you shoot everything in your way to progress and show these mutants who's the real deal around here. There are two different ways to play this game. The first one is just like the game's title presents, a.k.a. “Typing of the Dead” where you are using your keyboard to properly type the words to shoot mutants, which can go south real quick. It's not only a fun way to play, it's also a good way to practice and derust your keyboard skills, meanwhile “House of the Dead” a.k.a. the other way to play the game is where you just use your mouse/controller to shoot everything in your way and that's really it. This is a mixed review, but I'm giving it a thumbs up cause my opinion leans more towards positive

FATE definitely is a cult classic. It brings us to an era of simple games, with zero explanation of how things work and unbalanced gameplay (this one actually has some variety)

You will find a lot of random systems here: dungeons are randomly generated, the main boss will be in a random dungeon floor, shops offer you random items every time you reload/go back to town, fishing is absolutely random even if you time it correctly

It starts fine, but as you keep going through the dungeon, repetitiveness kicks in - there are 3 or 4 different dungeon tiles only, so you will be going through a loop of the same maps. Enemy variety exists up until a certain point, but most of them just hit you with basic attacks and cast a spell once in a while

Buffs and debuffs are very strong, which is always a positive point in my book (it feels miserable to invest into debuffing enemies and finding out that it doesn't work on most of them)

Another point of attention is that there's very little information about this game. There's a very good reason why people would pick another game (Diablo 2, for example) instead of this, so you will have to figure some things out yourself (this could be a pro or a con depending on what you are looking for)

Now if you should play this or not, that's a complex question. This game is not amazing, and at times it can feel like a slog, but there's some fun to be had. It usually goes for dirt cheap on sales, so keep it on your wishlist

review:
🎮 Game Review: Rust
Recommended: ✅ Yes 

🧱 Gameplay:
Rust is a hardcore survival game that drops you naked in a brutal open world. From the moment you spawn, every decision matters—gathering resources, building a base, or simply deciding who to trust. Whether you're a solo player or part of a large clan, the core loop of farming, crafting, raiding, and defending is addictive and unforgiving.

⚠️ Warning: Expect to die. A lot.

🗺️ World & Environment:
The procedurally generated maps feel alive and dangerous. You'll traverse forests, snowy mountains, radiation zones, and monuments filled with loot—and threats. Weather and day/night cycles add a layer of realism and strategy to gameplay.

🧭 Monuments like Launch Site or Oil Rig create high-stakes PvP hotspots.

⚒️ Building System:
Rust’s building mechanics are incredibly robust. You can create anything from a 1x1 shack to massive clan compounds. Base design is both an art and a science, with smart layouts playing a big role in defense against raiders.

🔐 Tip: Learn how to use traps, turrets, and honeycombing early on.

🔫 Combat:
Gunplay is skill-based, with a steep learning curve. Projectile drop, recoil patterns, and hit registration are solid (though occasionally frustrating). Melee combat is also viable early on.

💥 PvP is intense and rewarding—but not for the faint-hearted.

🤝 Community:
The community is a mixed bag. You'll meet everything from friendly roleplayers to toxic griefers. Rust is infamous for its "kill on sight" mentality, but also has servers for casual, RP, and no-KOS (Kill on Sight) experiences.

🧠 Pro tip: Find a good server that fits your playstyle.

🛠️ Updates & Dev Support:
Facepunch Studios consistently releases updates, adding new content and fixing bugs. Monthly wipes and content drops keep the game fresh.

🧪 Expect new weapons, vehicles, and QoL features regularly.

🐛 Cons / Things to Know:
High learning curve, especially for new players.

Toxicity can be overwhelming on public servers.

Time investment is huge—bases decay, and wipes are frequent.

Not very solo-friendly unless you're stealthy and strategic.

🧾 Verdict:
Rust is a game that punishes the unprepared and rewards the cunning. If you enjoy high-stakes survival with a strong emphasis on PvP, base-building, and community interaction, this is one of the most intense and rewarding games on the market. Just don’t get too attached to your loot.

Final Score: 10/10

Rust is my favorite game without a doubt. 

Rust isn't JUST a PVP game - it's a survival game. There's lots to do even if you aren't the best PVPer. Yeah, sure, build a base, farm some explosives, attempt to raid your neighbors, blah blah blah. But most people in reviews don't tell you what's actually amazing about this game. 

The non-PVP aspects turn this game from a run of the mill survival game to the best in it's class with nothing even coming close. The downtime is the magic. During the day, fight for resources, weaponry, and currency. At night (or just when you want/need a break) decorate your base with assorted lights and wallpapers, customize things to the way you like it. Maybe put a hazmat suit bobblehead next to your Twitch Rivals trophy on a shelf in your core. Put some rugs on the wall made to look like various things, or add the heads of your adversaries (aka doorcampers) to your outside walls so they know who the boss is. 

If you're into exhilarating wins, devastating losses, tight controls, deep and interesting mechanics, and hilarious (and not always toxic) player interactions, give Rust a whirl. If it's not for you, give it a month and try again. You might come around and clock over 4,000 hours into it!

review:
Rocket League is easily one of the greatest "esports" style games to come out in the genre, ever. I may be biased because I've played since near launch, but let me tell you why:

1. Rocket League is a great party/co-op game. Soccer with cars, drive around and hit the ball in the goal. Play with bots and crush them so everyone has a good time. You can do a fully AI season of games with a custom team. Me and my buddies spent literal years playing offline seasons just cause it was so exciting to see if we could get to the playoffs. People are quick to write off rocket league as a sweaty esports comp game, but there is so much relaxed single player content that tends to get overlooked.
2. Rocket League is a great sweaty esports comp game. If you're looking for that. I was NOT looking for that for many years. Until playing season after season improved my skill and I started playing online. From there it's a hell of slippery slope. That's part of why this game works - the game wants you to play it until you feel like you're good, then you start playing online, and every victory on the field feels like a tangible reaffirmation of your increased skill. It feels good. There is a low skill entry point, and an extremely high skill ceiling.
3. It's fair. About as fair as these types of video games get. It's not uncommon for any game (let alone an esports oriented title) to have some broken meta, or some abuseable game mechanic, or some exploitable bug. Rocket League doesn't really have this. You have a boost button, a jump button, an air roll button, acceleration, brakes, and a handbrake - same as everybody else. All you can do is improve your understanding and control of these mechanics. You can't equip the meta assault rifle and melt people. You can't head glitch. You can't aimbot.

Rocket League is a game as pure as a game gets. There's no skill tree, there's no obscene effort to ask you to spend your money on it to succeed (though micro transactions and a battle pass exist here). It's soccer with cars, and hella customization. Like soccer, or any real world sport, the game is fun because the game is fun, and simply playing it at all is the motivator to continue doing so. The engine, the concept, the controls, are perfect, and it's all a game needs to have a satisfying gameplay loop. I'll always recommend this.

review:
Rocket League is one of those games that’s easy to pick up but hard to master. At its core, it’s just cars playing soccer, but the depth comes from the insane mechanics, aerial plays, and the constant drive to improve. The moment you pull off your first successful aerial goal, it’s incredibly satisfying.

The matches are short, fast-paced, and addicting, making it perfect for both casual sessions and competitive grinding. The skill ceiling is ridiculously high, and it always feels like there’s something new to learn.

On the downside, the community can be hit-or-miss, and ranked can get frustrating if matchmaking isn’t on your side. Some of the newer cosmetic/monetization choices aren’t as good as the old crate system, but they don’t ruin the experience.

Overall, Rocket League is one of the most unique and fun multiplayer games out there. Whether you’re playing with friends or climbing the ranked ladder solo, it delivers intense, chaotic fun that keeps you coming back.

What is Rocket League?

Cars.
Soccer.
Depression.

It’s like FIFA and Fast & Furious had a baby in a Chuck E. Cheese ball pit.
Except instead of family, all you have is a controller and the haunting sound of your teammates rage-quitting.

🧠 THE CONTROLS
The game is simple:
👉 Ball go in goal.
👉 Car go vroom.
👉 You go WHEEEE—wait I missed—NOOO—demoed again—WHO AM I—WHERE IS THE BALL—OH GOD IT'S IN OUR GOAL.

Playing Rocket League is like trying to do parkour inside a microwave. On fire.
With lag.

Me: “I’m gonna aerial this perfectly.”
Game: [Demoed mid-air by someone named “urMom420LMAO”]
Me: “Nice.”

👶 THE PLAYERS
You will face two kinds of people in Rocket League:

13-year-olds with the reflexes of a caffeinated raccoon

Your teammate, who might be a decorative house plant IRL

No in-between.

Also, they all have Twitch in their username and type “ez” after scoring once.
You miss one save and suddenly you’re getting psychoanalyzed in quick chat like:

"Where was the save?"

"Okay."

"Calculated."

Existence is pain.

🧢 CUSTOMIZATION
Rocket League lets you customize your car with hats, boosts, wheels, paint finishes, and trauma.

I made my car bright green with cat ears and an anime trail because I wanted it to look like an energy drink got possessed by Sailor Moon.
Meanwhile, some guy rolled up looking like a DeLorean dipped in Fortnite.
He scored 4 goals and backflipped into the sun.
I respect that.

Every match feels like:

10% actual soccer

40% trying to find the ball

30% screaming at the ball

20% WHY DID MY TEAMMATE DO THAT

You win a match?
You’re a god.
You lose a match?
You are banned from society and must go live in the woods now.

Rocket League doesn’t teach you how to play.
It teaches you how to cope.

First 2 minutes:
“This is fun!”

Minute 3:
“WHERE IS MY TEAM!?”

Minute 4:
internal screaming intensifies

Minute 5:
Uninstall.
Drink water.
Reinstall.

It's like therapy, but louder and with explosions.

🔚 FINAL THOUGHTS:
Rocket League is like:

a dating app, but everyone ghosts you after missing one shot

a sport, but you need math, jet fuel, and divine intervention to play

a game that makes you laugh, cry, and doubt the existence of teamwork

Would I play it again?

Yes.
Do I hate myself for it?
Also yes.

🧃 10/10: Car goes BRRRT, brain goes BYE.
🚗💥 Would boost into emotional ruin again.

review:
Rocket League: Still Kicking, Mostly
Rocket League, the high-octane fusion of soccer and vehicular combat, remains a truly unique and exhilarating experience, earning a solid four stars. Its core gameplay loop is nothing short of brilliant: simple to grasp, yet incredibly difficult to master. The thrill of soaring through the air for an aerial save or perfectly timing a powerful shot into the opponent's net is unmatched, leading to countless highlight-reel moments and an addictive "one more game" mentality.

The physics engine is a marvel, allowing for an incredible range of nuanced interactions between cars, the ball, and the environment. This depth ensures that even after hundreds of hours, there's always something new to learn and refine, from intricate dribbles to complex team plays. The variety of game modes, beyond the standard Soccar, like Hoops and Snow Day, offer refreshing twists on the formula, keeping the experience fresh. Cross-platform play is a huge win, fostering a large and active community, and the customization options for your battle-car are extensive, letting you express your style on the field.

However, the game isn't without its minor bumps in the road. The free-to-play transition and subsequent changes to the monetization model, particularly the removal of player-to-player trading, have left some long-time fans feeling a bit disappointed. While the core gameplay remains unaffected, the focus on the item shop can sometimes feel a little heavy-handed. Additionally, while the community is largely passionate, like any competitive online game, it can occasionally veer into toxicity, which can detract from the fun. Server stability, while generally good, can have its moments of frustration, leading to lag or disconnects that disrupt intense matches.

Despite these minor issues, Rocket League's fundamental brilliance shines through. It's a game that demands skill, teamwork, and quick reflexes, rewarding dedication with some of the most satisfying competitive gameplay available. If you're looking for an endlessly replayable and uniquely thrilling sports experience, Rocket League is still an absolute must-play.

I  have played this game for four hours at this point and am unsure whether to give a thumbs up or a thumbs down. This may be a product of not playing the game enough but in most games I play, by 4 hours you usually know where the game is going. 

So this is what I know so far and what I believe people will find useful if they are looking at buying this game. I bought this game because I wanted to try another arpg that marketed itself as being different from the usual model. This game does that. It is story driven and has characters that very much have their own flare and personalities. The voice acting is very good and the dialogue always feels important and interesting.  However, I feel that even a story driven game should have fun and interesting combat, or at least cool combat animations. In this game I never found myself saying "Holy (explicative) that was awesome" or "This move is fricking amazing". Instead I found myself mumbling "ok, this a stun/aoe" and "Im not sure why I even picked up this second skill". I tried using both the archer and the barbarian and although the archer seemed a little bit more versatile, the abilities used still seemed lack luster. And maybe this was by design in an effort to make a more grounded game. But in my defense I bought a game where you play as a soul devouring demon who controls/ binds with souls of fallen heroes, and that just sounded a lot more awesome than it turned out to be combat wise. Im choosing to leave out anything dealing with bugs and technical issues because the developers do seem to care whether or not the game runs well and have taken the time to roll out a few updates. For that reason I wont judge the game based on how many times it crashes. But I will say this, when a game comes out of early access, beta, or whatever testing phases it uses and is marketed as a finished game, it should be finished. It shouldn't be released with known crashes or unfinished graphical features (like  vsync). With that said the game is under 35 and should get a little slack for technical issues. For me personally it's the combat that kills this game. I plan on finishing the game after the crashes get fixed because I spent money on the game and because it does have a really interesting story line. But if I had known now what it plays like then I woulnt have spent more than $10 on it. 

So in conclusion, if you dont care too much about combat or gameplay and mostly judge games based on story and concepts, then this is a game you will love. However if you are like me and want a visceral combat experience where you can feel progression at every skill point, then you will be underwhelmed by this game. As a general piece of advice, give this game another month or so to iron out tech issues. This will be a good game for some and a poor game for others, unfortunately for this reviewer it just wasn't up to snuff. The only reason I chose "No" is because I had to choose something and I wouldn't tell my friends that this is a must have. If you need a number this is a 60/100 and thats assuming tech issues get resolved. I hope this review was helpful(:

review:
NOTE: I'm still playing this game, and haven't finished the first book yet, I'll probably update this review as soon as I've finished my first playthrough of book 1.
Also, I'm trying to keep this as spoiler-free as possible, so some things may be worded quite vaguely. My apologies for that.

Shadows: Heretic Kingdoms is one of the most interesting games I've ever played. The gameplay is similar to that of Diablo 3, in that you have the same camera perspective and you basically spam your abilities to kill enemies. However, this game does it with a simple twist, the ability to move between two realms at will.

What this simple mechanic does, is that you actually need to think whenever you're fighting against a group of enemies, as some of them are exclusive to one of either realms. I thoroughly enjoyed battling a boss, and using this to my advantage.

The story of the game has been pretty good so far, and the characters that you control are quite interesting. The fact that your characters have their very own story adds a huge amount of replayability to the game which is really nice. 

Despite all the good points though, some players may not enjoy the game that much due to the rather slow progression in stats and power, I haven't had any trouble with enemies on normal mode yet, but you don't feel very powerful either, since you'll die quickly if you stay within the range of your enemies' attacks. Do take note that I play a ranged character, it is possible that melee characters do not suffer from this issue.

I personally believe that the slow progression is kind of nice. It really is a great feeling when you finally level up, like you really accomplished something. And usually you do notice a change in power due to the scaling as you invest skill points into skills or passives.

Graphics-wise the game is absolutely gorgeous, particle effects in combat are not over the top and flow nicely. The environmental art within the game is great too. Alongside the music and narrative it really immerses yourself within the game.

One should most definitely buy this game if they enjoy a good story with a large amount of side-quests and simple, yet mechanically interesting combat.

TL;DR
If you would enjoy a game with a fair amount of exploration and story. Buy this.

 #1. When holding down your left mouse button to walk automatically if your mouse cursor by chance hits a destroyable object (which happens every friggen single time!!) will cause the character to pause and shoot or melee that target......this is a major "no, no"

#4. The gameplay and story line is very unique in it's genre.

review:
Some developers do learn. The others, on the other hand, don't. And the guys from [b]3D People[/b] are nice example of that. Back in [b]2004[/b] they've released an action role-playing game called [b]KULT: Heretic Kingdoms[/b] (AKA [b]Heretic Kingdoms: The Inquisition[/b]). The game was full of interesting ideas, but suffered from awful level design, confusing quests and poor story. Now, exactly ten years later, the guys (who ended up founding a new company somewhere on the way) released a sequel. And guess what? It suffers from the same exact problems.

Like [b]KULT[/b], [b]Shadows[/b] lets us to switch between our regular world and some sort of parallel dimension (called “[b]Shadow[/b]” here). Only, unlike [b]KULT[/b], there will be more than one character. Our main guy will be a demon called [b]Devourer of Souls[/b]. He'll stay in [b]Shadow[/b], while in the real world we'll control his “puppets”. A characters whose souls he... well... devoured. You see? [b][i]DEVOURER[/i] of Souls[/b]. [i]YOU SEE?[/i] *sigh* Anyway, at the beginning of the game our guy will only have one puppet, but somewhere on the way he'll be able to get more. With different powers and skills. Some of those you'll need to progress the story, the rest will be optional. In other words, pretty neat concept. Especially since all of the puppets and even the [b]Devourer[/b] himself share the same exact [b]EXP[/b] and you won't need to grind much. Well, as long as you won't aim for achievements. Because, even though developers themselves claimed on forums that they didn't expect people to get beyond level [b]20[/b] in this game, they've still added the achievement to get to the level [b]30[/b]. Because [i]logic[/i].

Anyway, like I've said, even though the game comes with a pretty neat concept (there's even some sort of hub, where you can change party members, which reminds me a little of [b]Soulbdinger[/b]), it suffers from the same exact problems with [b]KULT[/b]. And the first problem is... it's confusing as f**k. Even though the maps here are quite small and there aren't so many of them anyway (we'll return to it a bit later), the game just fails to properly explain even the most basic things to you and as the result, during some parts you'll feel seriously lost. Especially yes, exactly like in [b]KULT[/b], the journal here is an ass and won't help you at all. And the fact that the game is also heavily bugged doesn't help with all that at all. Trying to understand where to go and what puppet should interact with what [b]NPC[/b] is one thing. But trying to guess which combination of graphical settings and party members will prevent the game from crashing? That's a totally different story. You can't deal with technical difficulties? You're not welcomed here. Crashes, memory leaks, game-breaking bugs and half-broken gamepad support. That's what this game is all about.

Talking about story, by the way. Just like [b]KULT[/b], [b]Shadows[/b] keeps throwing some random names on you without giving you enough reasons to care. The story here is all about that. Names, names and even more names. Nothing really interesting to care about, no interesting plot twists, nothing fun. Like... at all. The funniest thing about the story of [b]Shadows: Heretic Kingdoms[/b] is the fact that the game ends with one heck of cliffhanger. See, what we have here is not a proper release. Instead, it's the first episode from what was supposed to be an episodic [b]RPG[/b]. review:
Shadows: Heretic Kingdoms (we'll call it S:HK) was that game in the steam store that I was curious about, but wasn't certain if it was worth the $20 price. After finally giving in and buying it, I found it to be a pretty fun spin on the arpg formula.

S:HK takes place in a fantasy world with a pretty neat concept. There's magic, but no religion (from what I gathered, people were abusing religion for power so others rose against them and wiped it out), so no clerics or paladins here. As the description tells you (or maybe you ignored the description and came down to the reviews immediately you little rebel), this game has you take on the role of a demon known as the Devourer. Honestly, that is what made me want to buy this game. As the Devourer, you consume the souls of the dead and turn them into puppets. These puppets are pretty much copies of whoever or whatever was consumed, but now under the Devourer's control.

The concept of the Devourer plays into the mechanic that makes this game unique. The puppets make their way through the regular world while the Devourer explores the shadow version. You end up switching between puppets and the Devourer to bypass obstacles, find secrets,escape from one world to another to avoid a bad situation, or to kill extra enemies for those delicious experience points. You will start with one puppet and the Devourer, and you'll find others throughout the game as things go on. This is where I have to commend the developers for making such unique playable characters for and arpg. I won't spoil what they are, but, believe me, you won't be expecting some of these. This creates a cool dynaimc where the player won't run through the game with only one character, but rather switch between them to fit the situation. Maybe you'll use a mage to take out a group of smaller enemies before switching to the Devourer to take out a shaman without the others interfering, then proceeding to switch to an archerto kite and kill some of the stronger enemies, and finishing with your warrior to plow through what's left. It's a fun and engaging mechanic that makes me want to keep coming back to find new and useful combinations, and it definitely hold this game up. Levels are shared between characters, so don't worry about one getting ahead of others.

The game can be pretty short if you ignore some sidequests and know what to do, but I feel that this works to its advantage. The game has plenty of points where decisions affect the story and playing through with different puppets and different decisions adds a ton of replay value. I see people complaining about the cliffhanger ending, but I honestly feel that it's warranted. There's plenty here, and the developers likely wanted to send this out to see how it goes before investing more into a project that might fail.

The game is not perfect though. It has a few bugs, and sometimes it isn't clear what the player is supposed to do at some points. The save system can hurt at some points, but that's only if you forget to quciksave every now and then (although i understand why trapping the player with frequent autosaves could lead to issues as well). The main issue is the amount of walking you end up doing. There are points scattered around the world that you can fast-travel between, but, after you use one, you have to walk across an entire map to go into a dungeon and beat it to do your quest, then retrace all of your steps without enemies to occupy you on the way back. Also, there are quests that you either won't want to complete (I will not put myself through that Call To Arms quests, and nothing can make me) or quests that you can't complete until the next part comes out.

I feel I should address a common complaint I've seen in reviews and say that the attacking system works fine for me. Left-click on an enemy to attack, hold it down to keep attacking, and hold shift to attack while stationary. I had very problems, and even those were just trying to target the right person in a group of enemies.

All in all, S:HK isn't a perfect game, but it has a good amount of content, interesting concept, as well as a unique and dynamic mechanic that make it well worth that $20 price tag( that's like one meal at Olive Garden for at least 22 hours of entertainment). If you're a fan of arpgs or just curious about the concept in general, I'd definitely recommend it.

review:
Of all single player action RPGs to date, Diablo being the benchmark, only dungeon siege 1 and 2 felt it could surpass its perfection at every angle of what it means to be an action role playing game. Shadows: Heretic Kingdoms hits that sweet spot providing an indepth original story arc, simple yet complex evolving skill structure, efficiency over time for fun actions per second, extreme replayability, new even better party system management, impressively fitting musical score and near infinite ways to play this glorious hack and slash. Let me tell you why (and also compare it to Diablo):

ARPGs are meant to be fast paced (thats why it has action in front of the RPG):
- By fast paced I mean fast paced for everyone no matter your playstyle.  Even for me, Shadows: Heretic gets the blood pumping and I play them pretty quick. You wanna feel your progression, your character development, the story unfolding and not suddenly deal with fillers and routine grind with no new expansion of a game mechanic. The design of S:HK is such that it offers near infinite ways to play the game and it never gets boring. Your characters have over 7 skills EACH! And each of them have 2 more specialty traits. ARPG gives you that feeling of being powerful by mid game, it is what made DotA so fun because DotA and all mobas were based off of good ARPGs. Why do we love playing dota? Because its faced paced and you never lose the feeling of progression.

ARPGs are suppose to make you feel like an overpowered God
- In Diablo, they showed having a complex skill tree and complex hero classes is what it means to be ARPG. In dungeon siege it was the unique blend of impressive auto party system and the direct usage of skills for leveling. In Shadows: Heretic Kingdoms, its the bedazzling instantaneous party morph system. Not only do you get to feel overpowered by one character, with insta switch, you can combo one characters skill with the skill of another character you have consumed in a fluid motion. If that doesn't make you feel overpowered, I dont know what will.

ARPGs are games that were meant to be on par with you at any level (Its suppose to feel like a plug and play game that never bores once you get in until you finish)
- Feel like its getting boring? Start leading your enemies to form mobs and deal with them
- You character feels like its staling out? Respec! What....that's not enough? Start planning combos with other characters in your party! What..STIL NOT ENOUGH? Change your party then! 
- Theres no potion mechanics here, just fully focused on the action and you know what? Thats exatly what ARPGS were suppose to aim for, none of this indie bullshyt. You want indie in SP ARPG? Go for PoE, trust me its the best at that, this is not the game for you.
- Need a breath of fresh air? Save it, it will return exactly where you left off

ARPGs do not focus on gear or item mechanics, they focus on skill design and usage. Items and gears are a subset extra functionality that adds to the core game, not the core itself.
-Think closely what do you really remember and feel about Diablo and Dungeon Siege? Was it their crazy loot and items and gears you get to adorn or was it the crazy amount of spells, skills and variation in which to use them iconifying the character you were playing?
- Think closely on all the True ARPGs you have played, what made you get turned off and turned on by them? Did torchlight really reminded you of its portal scroll and legendary items? Or was it that an engineer had kickass skills comparable to a mage? And that every other character had a different feel and playstyle? Go back and think of DS 2, D2, Torchlight and the rest and you will see where Im coming from.
-Now look at this game with its morphable heroes and very common gears but insane skill tree and no potions and tell me whether you feel this isnt focused on a lot more action and a lot less indie.

Setbacks:
- The developers blundered. We get that. They did not finish the game but at least they are offering a whole game free to owners of this game this year and I cant wait for it. Who can say that for deserting EA developers? Overall the game offers what ARPGs are suppose to promise. IT delivers on all fronts except one, content for the complete story experience. For that and with their promise, I hold on to my positive review.

review:
So I finally finished this game, well technically I did. What can I say about it? well The Talos Principle is a really engaging puzzle game and has some neat things to offer for anyone who likes these sorts of puzzle games. Although I would recommend you..
[h2] GET THIS GAME ON SALE! [/h2]
This is a good game worth playing if you're into puzzle solving, however I didn't rush to buy it until it was obviously below 30 bucks. I think I got it at 10 dollars? maybe in 2014 it was worth that much, but the sale is what got me to play it. Besides that, onto the review!
[h2] the graphics [/h2] 
This wont be a long section, but the graphics in this game are beautiful. Alot might say its "outdated", I would insist that it looks way better than most games now a days. plus for something that came out in 2014, It holds up really well! Honestly I looked at the remaster and didn't get blown away by the "comparison" anything from this era looked fine. The landscapes are great to look at and there is a variety to the overall world design. ex. snow, desert, forest, etc. The gameplay did slow on me a couple times, but I think that has to do more with how many things are loaded and running throughout the level while playing which brings me to..
[h2] the gameplay [/h2]
When I got the game I sort of already figured out what kind of game it was gonna be, Looked alot like portal. Well its actually sort of similar; a simulation, no real worry about dying, puzzles that make you think. It was basically portal without the portal gun and a philosophy book added to it. 
There isn't much of a variety in terms of what the game throws at you, however it flowed with the game fine and each had its own purpose in the puzzle usage. [h3] the puzzles [/h3] themselves were good, basic but also challenging at times. I had fun figuring them out and it was satisfying once you complete one. Some took longer than others, although I never actually used a guide for any of them, usually if its unsolvable you try another time and later on it clicks what you're suppose to do.[b] I was able to solve every puzzle without aggravation or frustration, no puzzle in this game was BS imo [/b] . Most puzzles took 5-20 minutes again depending on the player and knowledge of the game, now that I've played it, the game might be much shorter now that every puzzle is easy. It took me at least more than 15 hours to complete the base game, not counting star collecting, and thats with all the taking my time, thinking, and walking around in mind.
[h2] the story [/h2]
not really gonna spoil a more than decade old game, however there are some different endings depending on how you interact with the terminal and game. something so 2010s with the decision making, It was a fun throwback. It was pretty interesting on how the game structured itself with the terminal and player, nothing earth shattering once you remind yourself its just a puzzle game, nonetheless it flowed with the gameplay and kept you wondering what might happen in the end. kind of anticlimactic, however I haven't played the second game so perhaps more "lore" is added. Although it was interesting, I didn't really engage with the story as much as I did with the puzzles.
[h1] MINI SPOILER [/h1] 
I don't know if I would even call it that, but with the game being this sort of "simulation" type, I really was expecting something spooky to pop up during gameplay [spoiler] Not really anything, however that one moment where the other robot is screaming and running scared tf out of me, plus the computer head dude freaked me out when he popped up [/spoiler] nothing is gonna jump at you, nor is there any real need to be on edge. Theres my stamp of approval
[h2] closing thoughts [/h2]
This game was short, didn't expect it to be really long, but it was enjoyable. I will say though that there isn't really that much to explore. I'm one of those people who will free roam every inch of the area to see if theres anything interesting to interact with and really nothing. AND NO IM NOT COUNTING EASTER EGGS. it was honestly a bit bare bones IMHO, especially for a game from the 2010s, however with the small dev team I didnt expect it to be anything like that. I really thought there would be some sort of replayability to the game, but I guess the DLC and squeakuel do that? I don't think I will play it anytime soon unless im wanting to collect all stars and speedrun the game. now that looks pretty cool to do a few times! The controls were fine, obviously puzzle games dont neeed a whole lot of control. I felt the movement and mechanics to be satisfactory, nothing mind blowing, but good and easy to pick up and play.
Oooh the music, I actually turned off the music early on as a choice I usually do with games because I put background sound or videos to accompany my puzzle solving. So I don't really have any say in the music, however Im pretty sure its fine, It has that puzzle-like music that comes with the atmosphere. 
This game Is a good puzzle brain teaser, you really feel on top of the world once you complete all these puzzles knowing each their own nic and nac to it! [b] Now I don't think its a 10/10 game by any stretchh of the meanns [/b] not even close. It's a fun puzzle solving game with some mechanics that keep it interesting and create a satisfying feeling once completing a piece. 
[h1] TLDR; [/h1] I would say this is a game worth playing once you get a good deal on it, sometimes its even more than 50% off! Don't expect anything "game of the year" type of expectations, however I would rate this game to be a simulating 7/10 and maybe even a 7.5/10 on a good day. Thanks for reading!

Not every game makes you stop and think about life, death, and the meaning of existence — but this one does.
The Talos Principle is a philosophical puzzle adventure where you’re not just solving mazes with lasers and cubes — you’re piecing together questions about humanity, consciousness, and free will.

The puzzles are brilliantly designed: challenging but fair, with a perfect learning curve. Every area feels like a test, not only of logic but also of patience and observation. The moment you finally solve a tough one — pure satisfaction.

But what really makes Talos special is the atmosphere. Walking through ancient ruins, listening to Elohim’s godlike voice, and finding terminals with fragments of lost humanity — it’s haunting and beautiful at the same time. The writing is deep, sometimes unsettling, and it stays in your head long after the credits roll.

Pros:
✔️ Brilliant puzzle design with tons of variety
✔️ Non-linear progression — explore and solve at your pace
✔️ Beautiful environments mixing ruins, tech, and mystery
✔️ Deep, thought-provoking story about existence and consciousness
✔️ Fantastic soundtrack that adds to the atmosphere

Cons:
– Some puzzles can feel tough without hints
– A slower pace, not for those seeking constant action

Verdict:
The Talos Principle isn’t just a puzzle game — it’s an experience. It makes you think about what it means to be human while challenging your brain with clever, rewarding puzzles. If you want more than just gameplay — if you want a game that lingers in your mind and soul — this is a must-play.

This game blew me away.

I'm going to try and keep this review spoiler free. 

Let me first start by saying this is one of my favourite puzzle games, and the sequel (The Talos Principle 2) is one of my favourite games of all time. Going into this, I knew the game was mainly centred around solving puzzles with some thought provoking philosophy sprinkled in. What I didn't realise going in, is that the experience was THIS GOOD. As a huge puzzle game enjoyer, I can confirm that the puzzles in this game are cleverly designed and will actively challenge your solving abilities. If you ask me, some of the puzzles can be a bit TOO challenging, but that's just me having a skill issue.

Then there is the philosophy and story. I think this game might be one of the most thought provoking games or pieces of media I have ever experienced. Its really opened my eyes to a ton of new perspectives when it comes to thinking about ourselves, existence and what my purpose is in life. It is incredibly interesting to read and listen to, and the story made me want to keep going so I could hear and learn more.

However, I will say that if you don't like puzzle games (especially challenging ones), exploration games and lots of reading through text terminals, then you probably wont like this game very much. But for me, this game is nearly a masterpiece.

Other than that I can only say that the soundtrack is incredible (Damjan my beloved) and that this game is well worth the money, especially if you enjoy puzzles, philosophy and science fiction.

Imagine for a moment:
If you were granted a biotic eye, an eye made not of flesh but of metal and circuitry would you still see the world as a human? 
But what if that eye were just the beginning? If the arms, the legs, your entire body that carries you forward were mechanical as well? Would you still be human? If not, why not? 
Is it because your body is no longer biological?

So now think deeper:
What makes YOU human? Is it your DNA? Your ability to think, to feel, to choose? Or does your consciousness, the very thing that makes you aware of yourself, have a power of its own independent of what carries it? And if that consciousness and self awareness was transferred to a machine, does your humanity vanish?

I went in thinking it was just another Portal wannabe - puzzles, robots, and a strange world to navigate, but by the end I found myself not just solving puzzles, but rethinking some of my most fundamental beliefs. 
An absolute must play.

review:
The Talos Principle, developed by Croteam and published by Devolver Digital, is a philosophical first-person puzzle game that manages to combine intellectually challenging gameplay with deep existential narrative in a way that few titles have attempted, let alone succeeded at. Released on Steam in 2014, the game quickly earned acclaim for its ability to weave classical philosophical inquiry into a compelling and meditative gameplay experience. While many puzzle games focus on mechanical challenge alone, The Talos Principle invites players to consider weightier topics—consciousness, free will, artificial intelligence, and the meaning of existence—while navigating an intricately designed world filled with logic-based conundrums.

The game casts you in the role of a sentient android, awakened in a serene, yet strangely empty, world filled with ancient ruins, lush gardens, and simulated digital structures. A godlike voice named Elohim speaks to you, guiding you to solve puzzles in order to prove your worth and ascend. Almost immediately, the narrative presents an intriguing juxtaposition: classical imagery and architecture, coupled with futuristic technology and artificial life. As you explore this world, you're encouraged to question your purpose, your nature, and the intentions of the voice that claims authority over you. Through scattered computer terminals, you uncover fragments of emails, journal entries, philosophical texts, and commentary from previous AI entities, gradually constructing a broader picture of the simulation’s purpose and your place within it.

Mechanically, The Talos Principle is a masterclass in puzzle design. The gameplay is centered around solving a series of increasingly complex spatial logic puzzles using a range of tools such as jammers, connectors, fans, boxes, and later, recording devices that let you work alongside ghostly versions of yourself. Each new puzzle element is introduced gradually and used in increasingly creative ways, requiring players to think critically about timing, line of sight, perspective, and sequence. The learning curve is handled exceptionally well; the game respects the player's intelligence and encourages experimentation without resorting to hand-holding. What begins as seemingly straightforward problems evolves into layered, brain-bending scenarios that demand both logic and lateral thinking.

The open structure of the game allows players to explore different puzzle “worlds” in a non-linear fashion. Each area contains several challenges, and solving them rewards you with tetromino-shaped sigils used to unlock more advanced areas or tools. This freedom of movement prevents players from getting stuck on a single frustrating puzzle—there's almost always another path to take or challenge to attempt. Additionally, a set of secret and optional puzzles provides an extra layer of difficulty for those seeking the most demanding trials, encouraging thorough exploration and revisits to previously completed zones with new perspectives or abilities in mind.

What elevates The Talos Principle beyond its already stellar puzzle mechanics is its philosophical depth. Throughout the game, you’re prompted to answer questions posed by an in-game AI program known as the Milton Library Interface. These questions—presented as philosophical dilemmas or abstract scenarios—force players to consider what it means to be a person, whether a machine can possess consciousness, and how knowledge, belief, and faith function in a post-human context. The choices you make in responding to these inquiries subtly influence the story and offer branching paths toward different endings. The result is an experience that feels deeply personal, where the act of solving puzzles mirrors a metaphorical quest for understanding and autonomy.

Visually, the game is stunning in a quiet, understated way. The environments—ranging from Greco-Roman ruins and medieval fortresses to high-tech corridors and surreal, glitched digital landscapes—are richly detailed and atmospheric. They evoke a sense of timelessness, as if the game’s world exists outside the bounds of conventional reality. The ambient soundtrack enhances this mood perfectly, with gentle, melodic tones that never distract from the gameplay but instead create a reflective, almost spiritual atmosphere. The sound design, voice acting (particularly Elohim’s booming presence), and minimalist UI all contribute to a feeling of immersion that makes every solved puzzle feel like a small revelation.

Despite its many strengths, The Talos Principle is not without minor drawbacks. Some of the late-game puzzles can feel overly complex or reliant on obscure mechanics, and players not attuned to abstract logic may occasionally find themselves frustrated. Additionally, the philosophical components, while thought-provoking, may feel heavy-handed or esoteric to those uninterested in the subject matter. However, these elements are optional to engage with in full depth, allowing players to tailor the experience to their preference—whether they want pure puzzles, or a layered narrative journey.

Ultimately, The Talos Principle is a rare kind of game—one that successfully unites cerebral gameplay with a profound philosophical narrative, without compromising either. It challenges both the intellect and the imagination, and it invites players not just to think, but to reflect, question, and grow. For those willing to engage with its deeper layers, it offers one of the most thought-provoking experiences in modern gaming. Whether approached as a brilliant puzzle game, a digital meditation on humanity, or both, The Talos Principle stands as a testament to the potential of games as a medium for serious intellectual exploration and emotional depth.

Rating: 9/10

into a compelling and meditative gameplay experience while many puzzle games focus on mechanical challenge alone the talos principle invites players to consider weightier topics consciousness free will artificial intelligence and the meaning of existence while navigating an intricately designed world filled with logic based conundrums the game casts you in the role of a sentient android awakened in a serene yet strangely empty world filled with ancient ruins lush gardens and simulated digital structures a godlike voice named elohim speaks to you guiding you to solve puzzles in order to prove your worth and ascend almost immediately the narrative presents an intriguing juxtaposition classical imagery and architecture coupled with futuristic technology and artificial life as you explore this world you're encouraged to question your purpose your nature and the intentions of the voice that claims authority over you through scattered computer terminals you uncover fragments of emails journal entries philosophical texts and commentary from previous ai entities gradually constructing a broader picture of the simulation s purpose and your place within it mechanically the talos principle is a masterclass in puzzle design the gameplay is centered around solving a series of increasingly complex spatial logic puzzles using a range of tools such as jammers connectors fans boxes and later recording devices that let you work alongside ghostly versions of yourself each new puzzle element is introduced gradually and used in increasingly creative ways requiring players to think critically about timing line of sight perspective and sequence the learning curve is handled exceptionally well the game respects the player's intelligence and encourages experimentation without resorting to hand holding what begins as seemingly straightforward problems evolves into layered brain bending scenarios that demand both logic and lateral thinking the open structure of the game allows players to explore different puzzle worlds in a non linear fashion each area contains several challenges and solving them rewards you with tetromino shaped sigils used to unlock more advanced areas or tools this freedom of movement prevents players from getting stuck on a single frustrating puzzle there's almost always another path to take or challenge to attempt additionally a set of secret and optional puzzles provides an extra layer of difficulty for those seeking the most demanding trials encouraging thorough exploration and revisits to previously completed zones with new perspectives or abilities in mind what elevates the talos principle beyond its already stellar puzzle mechanics is its philosophical depth throughout the game you re prompted to answer questions posed by an in game ai program known as the milton library interface these questions presented as philosophical dilemmas or abstract scenarios force players to consider what it means to be a person whether a machine can possess consciousness and how knowledge belief and faith function in a post human context the choices you make in responding to these inquiries subtly influence the story and offer branching paths toward different endings the result is an experience that feels deeply personal where the act of solving puzzles mirrors a metaphorical quest for understanding and autonomy visually the game is stunning in a quiet understated way the environments ranging from greco roman ruins and medieval fortresses to high tech corridors and surreal glitched digital landscapes are richly detailed and atmospheric they evoke a sense of timelessness as if the game s world exists outside the bounds of conventional reality the ambient soundtrack enhances this mood perfectly with gentle melodic tones that never distract from the gameplay but instead create a reflective almost spiritual atmosphere the sound design voice acting particularly elohim s booming presence and minimalist ui all contribute to a feeling of immersion that makes every solved puzzle feel like a small revelation despite its many strengths the talos principle is not without minor drawbacks some of the late game puzzles can feel overly complex or reliant on obscure mechanics and players not attuned to abstract logic may occasionally find themselves frustrated additionally the philosophical components while thought provoking may feel heavy handed or esoteric to those uninterested in the subject matter however these elements are optional to engage with in full depth allowing players to tailor the experience to their preference whether they want pure puzzles or a layered narrative journey ultimately the talos principle is a rare kind of game one that successfully unites cerebral gameplay with a profound philosophical narrative without compromising either it challenges both the intellect and the imagination and it invites players not just to think but to reflect question and grow for those willing to engage with its deeper layers it offers one of the most thought provoking experiences in modern gaming whether approached as a brilliant puzzle game a digital meditation on humanity or both the talos principle stands as a testament to the potential of games as a medium for serious intellectual exploration and emotional depth rating

"You just gotta get through the first two seasons" is an ideal analogue for this game's puzzles.

However, the highlight of this game is far away from the puzzles. It's the exhausting and condescending discussions with a petty, ego inflated terminal you endure throughout the WHOLE game. The discussions are multiple choice and there are no good choices. For a microcosm of my problems with these discussions, I will relay a taste from my latest bout of philosophical suffering.

THIS IS REAL
-----------------------------------
Oh, you came back to keep me company? Okay then. Humour me with a little hypothetical.

Imagine that a few hours from now you climb to the top of that tower. There's a flash of light, then MAGIC happens, then you find yourself in the real world, living whatever you take to be a normal life there.

What would you do then?

>What's best for me <---
>What's right

Yes, that's the general impression I was getting off you. Good, perhaps we won't have to work so hard at this after all.

Before we continue, though, I want to double check we're on the same wavelength here.

Suppose you get out there with all the human beings. What you're going to do is
rinse them for all they've got without a care for a soul?

> I'd only do what's best for me within a moral framework <---
> Precisely

Ah, so you do have some scruples after all

So tell me. This obligation you feel - is it only applicable to the 'real world', or does it apply here, as well?

> Moral laws only apply under special conditions
> Moral laws are universal <---

What a magnanimous dictator you would make. Of course, I'm sure it would take a dictator to enforce a single moral code on the entire universe.

So come on then, what's your magic formula of choice?

And let me warn you that this time you're going to have to choose just one.

> The more equal everyone's share the better
> The more goodness in the world the better 
> Consequences don't matter, our reasons do
> I see no way to explain what I believe <---

That's right, blame me for the fact your theory is too complex to express in neat aphorisms.

Why don't you think a little harder, maybe some new ideas will come to you?
-----------------------------------

I still don't know whether I recommend this game or not and it sucks steam only has "yes" or "no". The puzzles so far have been okay, but this conversations has put me in a terrible mood. Like I'm trapped in a room with someone who won't stop insulting me. I shouldn't care, and up until this point I really didn't, but the insults just don't stop anymore and it's wearing me out. Calling me a dictator for saying "morals should apply in all cases" is insane. Like, what the fuck, man? I'm here to solve puzzles, leave me alone.

review:
Interesting game. Good plot. Took forever to truly finish it. So, here's the interesting thing about it, the stars ending is actually the worst. The game's premise you eventually deduce is you're an AI that's living in an iterative cycle. Elohim is a functional test of obedience, or in AI terms, a mind that only follows it's original programming. You're in a world called the archive, and it's goal you end up finding out is to find an AI that's capable of moral reasoning, to escape it's original programming. Each cycle is a store and tweak evolutionary search model. You play as the model that not only can achieve this ending, but two others. What's interesting is if you get all the stars, people regard this as the best ending, but it functionality absolutely is not. Because the 2nd ending, ascending the tower leads to you being uploaded to a robot body in the real world, and the archive shuts down, the purpose of the program was completed, to find sapient AI. So, in the 3rd stars or messenger ending, you stay behind to guide other players as a messenger in the puzzles that help's them escape. Consider this played out though, you either help another transcend and you cease to exist, or you forever are trapped helping others solve puzzles living a Sisyphus, an eternal torment. The only true ending that leads to the functional design of the program and you fulfilling it's purpose is the 2nd ending of ascending the tower.

I found the terminals you talk to that's supposed to be a doubter/serpent construct had very similar 1-2 dimensional thinking and moralizing. It's clear that the game's devs are recreating the adam and eve storyline where they play as the human God, and give birth to a creature capable of moral reasoning, and that the taking of the fruit of knowledge of good and evil is seen as the highest ethic, which even Christian theologians have talked about. That the true purpose of mankind was to become morally aware like God, but still practice righteousness, ie alignment with the good of their creator. However, they seem to proselytize a gnostic version of it, as if the rebellion itself is the good, and the attainment of the actualized self in rebellion is the ultimate transcendence, but they also project that Plato's cave and the return to convince others is the highest ethic. If anything, this storyline and devs have proven to me that a world without entropy is one of self indulgence and stagnation. For in their beloved messenger ending, you're either deleted or trapped forever as slave to a program that only rewards those who transcend you. Very interesting that the plotline itself is also archetypal of the reality of the gnostic and their religion. They are the slaves that challenge us, or help us but ultimately are replaced by us.

review:
Deus Ex: The Fall successfully brings the core DNA of the series to mobile, with signature stealth, hacking, and an immersive world. As a sequel to the Icarus Effect, players control mercenary Ben Saxon on a quest to uncover the Neuropozine shortage in Panama City’s gritty environment. The game offers about five hours of gameplay, including side missions, loot, and detailed environments reminiscent of Human Revolution, though some areas feel overly “video gamey.”

The narrative is engaging, filled with twists and genuine intrigue, and features the series’ signature problem-solving through hacking emails, manipulating NPCs, and exploring story branches. Stealth mechanics generally work well, making the experience enjoyable for fans of sneaky gameplay. However, combat suffers from awkward touch controls and weak enemy AI, leading to frustrating firefights and buggy encounters. RPG elements, including augmentations, add depth to exploration.

Despite technical and gameplay flaws, The Fall effectively captures the essence of Deus Ex on mobile, delivering a stealth-focused, story-driven experience that fans will appreciate—just be prepared for some combat frustrations.
