review:
Before I get into the bad stuff, I'll start off by saying this: It's truly a beautiful game with high potential. The puzzles are over-all interesting though not extremely challenging.

On to the bad stuff.
The hardest part about this game isn't the puzzles themselves. It's when there's no clear indication of what to do, or the camera.

The camera controls in general are rather bad. You control it with 'ASDW' but the problem is that it has a tendency to sweep towards the character you're controlling while zooming in to a set FOV. This means that when you're using features that require you to see beyond that small window, the camera will constantly automatically pull away from what you're doing. This forced me to start over what I was doing several times during my playthrough.

Then there're the actual character controls. They're honestly  not much better, even though they're just you clicking at a spot you want the selected character to go to. It works fine while walking over 'normal' obstacles, but I've noticed that this function can only interact with climbable objects(like ropes) once per click.
This means that if you want to walk some distance, climb a rope, and then jump off on a platform, you'll have to choose. Either you walk to the rope and grab it in the first click, and climb it and jump off with the second click, or you walk to it and climb it in the first click and jump off on the second.
If it's just walking or going through doorways, you can go as far and go through as many doorways as neccessary for the character to get where you want it in a single click.
This does not mean that you can't make characters pathfind through climbing. Later on in the game, [spoiler]when the golem turns into a monkey, you can call it to the girl. [/spoiler] This working despite all obstacles proves that it's most likely a bug, an obvious one they somehow didn't catch before releasing.

The cutscenes are snapshot-images. While some do have movement, it's mostly minimal. Furthermore, in my case, the images weren't rendering propperly, resulting in the blurred graphics you'd expect from a game on one of the older consoles, not a game whose selling point is atleast partially the graphics/beautiful environment.

Finally, the ending.
[spoiler] It was honestly one of the more disappointing points for me. Firstly, the tower you've been starting up to get water with relies on sunlight, yet all of a sudden in the end cutscene, it starts raining as the steam condensates into raindrops. The thing is, it's still sunny outside. Meaning that, for some reason, the builders decided that after filtering, purifying and boiling the water, the best method to send it out into the aqueducts was to let it rain through the tower's insides, presumably to be collected further down.
Then there's a slight problem revealed. Just before the water from the tower reaches the girl's village, it spills out due to one of the arches being broken, something that's apparently not only a great surprise to the girl, it also apparently nulls the effort they've put in so far. Because there's apparently no way the villages who've been suffering from drought all this time could just collect it from the veritable LAKE that logically should be forming right next to their huts. 
The golem's final form, a humanoid, has gained the power to levitate objects. You've used it numerous times to move objects(duh) and even build simple bridges. Thus, the golem's reaction is to use the very same power to put the broken arch back together, despite it being far FAR out of any previously indicated range. This, however, seemingly kills the golem. Rather unnecessarily so aswell. [/spoiler]

There are several rather obvious indications of sequels in the form them hinting that atleast two more towers existing that are related to the tower the storyline takes place in. If so, then I hope they atleast patch this game first, because as I've mentioned, it HAS potential. It just isn't leveraged yet.
It's furthermore rather short. I got through it in just past 1.5h and I spent some time walking back and forth because I didn't have any idea as to what I was doing. In a second playthrough you could most likely get through it in less that an hour. As such, I'd say that it's not worth its price. I'd be hesitant to recommend buying it in its current state even for 5€, much less the current full price of 15.

EDIT: One point I forgot to mention is the sound. The music cuts oddly when the golem 'evolves', some things make an aweful amount of racket, such as the golem walking up and down stairs, and some things lack sound for no obvious reason, such as object collision.

review:
Bit of a bummer this....Golem is precisely the sort of game I typically love (no pressure puzzle solving), but between the obtuse camera angles (thankfully you can adjust the camera with WASD and the mouse wheel to zoom in or out, but still.....the camera and how it affects your ability to click on targets is your enemy more often than not), some graphical glitches/bugs, and the increasingly convoluted puzzles, and a broken achievement, which the devs can't be arsed to address/fix, ultimately means I can't recommend this game.

Obviously, how complicated a puzzle is remains a subjective thing, but if you not only have multiple moving parts that need to be activated, in the right order, added to the fact that  you can sometimes be trapped halfway through a twenty/thirty minute level if you guess the wrong lever to pull next....well that's just frustrating.  Because then you'd better hope you saved recently (ideally before you made the error, not after you've taken the action and had to  progress a little further before you realize you've screwed yourself) or you will be forced to start the whole level over from scratch.  And there is almost NEVER any clear indication of what the various levers etc will do until you've pulled them, possibly setting yourself up for failure via trial and error.  This makes for a frustrating puzzle game, to be sure!

And the bugs/glitches.....several times I reloaded a saved game and found the character suspended in the air as if she was climbing a vine, whereas she had in fact been saved handling a lever, and she simply could not be retrieved from that position.  Not to mention that sometimes a platform with both the protagonist and her golem would move, but the golem would remain suspended in air as the platform moved on with only the protagonist on it, forcing you to go back and try again (and again, and again) until the golem sticks the landing (as it were).

So, ultimately, I cannot recommend the game, unless it's on a DEEEEEP sale (as I said, the devs can't even be bothered to fix a broken achievment, so the only people with 100% are no doubt SAM users....)

Cheers,
Colin

review:
WHAT'S IN THE BOX?
'Space Panic: Room Escape' is, unsurprisingly, another 'escape the room' game which is set in one room on a space station. There are various puzzles from "find element" to "rotate these rings until they fit". The game supports Vive and Rift, and features teleporting. It took me about 2 hours with one restart due to a bug. There are no save points.
 
VISUALS
This is a very minimalistic game; the environment is extremely clean. There is a weird mix though between spacy elements (the environment) and old stuff (the objects, like a candle, a greek statue, rotating stone rings) which I say didn't really fit together. The game is incredibly resource hungry (read: laggy) and you can't really play it on higher quality settings (there are 7 in total), which is a real problem since some colored elements where the color matters are in fact hardly visible in the lower quality settings. No matter the setting, there is annoying visible aliasing. 

SOUND
There is a constant "droning" noise in the background which I suppose is ventilation. It's a bit distracting but better than nothing I guess. The sounds of the elements (dropping, interacting) are nothing special but fine.

CONTROLS
The controllers are shown as controllers, and sometimes when holding them in a certain position a help text pops up to indicate which button does which. In general it was hard to grab things since it wasn't always clear where to point the controllers, and things tended to fell out of hand too, apparently because they got stuck somewhere. The menus and buttons can be used with a sort of "laser beam" which often simply doesn't show up (this is extremely annoying). Furthermore, one of the stones got stuck in a drawer and I couldn't get it out again and had to restart from scratch.

GAMEPLAY
As usual for an escape room, there is no real story, and you have to solve puzzles to get out; there are some notes scattered around which contain some clues. The puzzles are not connected in any way that made sense to me, and as in the visuals there is a weird mix of sci-fi fuse finding and old stone/metal puzzles which I thought made the impression of a being hastily assembled with no real theme behind it. Several things simply "happened" to me and I'm not sure whether or not I actually did the right thing (such as placing elements in drawers, tapping keys, ...), so the sense of achievement which is what these games are about was lacking for me. Furthermore there is one puzzle which really IMHO doesn't belong in VR (the rings) - this is a puzzle where you'd normally use pen and paper to solve it.

BOTTOM LINE
Some nice ideas in there, but the controls are not working properly and the game is hardly playable on "normal" quality settings.

review:
Ballway is a simple mobile app/Flash-like 2D retro pixel/minimalist puzzle game.  Gameplay consists of clicking on various blocks on each puzzle level.  Some blocks vanish, some explode, clicking on the right blocks in order and with the right timing will propel the ball to the green zone, then you move on to the next level, that's all there is to it.  Considering the sheer power of modern gaming PCs, this is an incredibly underwhelming and shallow experience, however, gamers may get some amusment from the price the developer thinks this is worth. 

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

The graphics here are some of the worst, laziest attempt at video game "art" I've ever seen.  It's hard to suggest this game even has graphics.  It's just untextured, basic pixel blocks and blobs, the kind that an infant child might be able to create in 5 minutes on MS Paint.  It's clear the developer didn't even try to produce any real graphics for the game and just phoned it in.  It's unclear why such a lazy approach was taken, whether it may be caused by lack of talent, budget, or motivation to do their job properly.  It also doesn't matter... what matters is that this has resulted in a game with zero visual appeal for gamers.  It's an immediate failure on that measure alone.

While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality.  Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes Ballway might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Ballway has the laughable price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

review:
The base game is already heavily degraded compared to Mount & Blade but this DLC takes it to the whole another level.
Negative points:
First of all you cannot hire any troops inhame, only two companions.
-No ammo refill. I couldn't find ammo anywhere unless I manage to stealthly kill some bandits.
-Lack of goods, armors, weapons that merchant sells. Seriously, why we even need money if we can't but anything meaningful.
-Lazy zombie design and animations. Only a few skins for female zombies and one skin for male zombies and one melee animation. 
-Some bandit towns are impossible to enter during fight due to closed main doors which softlocks the game.
-No horses despite there's skills tied to them.
-Some talents are useless due to them tied to player troops. (There's no player troops at all, excluding companions)
-Degraded skill tree
-Absense of ships and sea areas. In a game about pirates and colonies there's no ships and almost no sea actions at all. What a shame!
-No loot after defeating enemy squads. Even for bandits and natives.
-Almost no reward for defending a settlement.  I recall getting some fish food for defending a plantation.
-Way many enemies in a towns and small settlements. Too hard to fight bandits and natives with ranged weapons.
-Dull boring quests and stupid dialogues. Only a few were interesting,
-Too short and a terrible ending. The final dialogues were stupid and meaningless due to single outcome.
-It's the same map and same models, textures and sounds with the base game, Only small amount of new oontent were added.
-There's to many zombie squads in some areas. This will lead to endless fight with zombie hordes due to low player speed during night time.
-Too many bugs: 
*You can raid towns and it's a thing from base game as it will show B&G:C town location with original civilians and troops. At the end of the raid you will get insane amount of money. It's basically a cheat. 
*There's one mission with infiltrating enemy base and getting quest item. At the end of the mission you willl LOSE YOUR ALL OF YOUR EQUIPPED WEAPONS. I lost my favorite two handed sword, really good one handed sword and unique multi charged carabine. Most infuriating thing from DLC.
Positive points:
New unique weapons such as hand cannon, multi charged carabine, shotgun pistol.
Driveable balloon. One of the most unique and amazing stuff I saw in MB mods, DLCs.
You can get some top tier valuable equipments by liberating hostile settlements or opening loot chest during missions. 

Overall rating: 3/10
It has some unique staff that should be ported to base game as a mod, as for the DLC it's bland, boring and short. Empty world and repeating gameplay.

[[[[An Unexpected Joyful Experience.]]]]

I'm a Chinese Youtuber (You can say so) who works mainly on terror games. I bought this game yesterday to make a video, since it seemed like nobody had ever did this game. I wasn't expecting much, thought it might be some jumpscares and so on. 

>After 40 mins playing>

Here,if you wanna watch it: http://www.bilibili.com/video/av12451351/

I have to say, this game surprised me really much, in the good ways. 
In this game, while waiting for the moon to set, all you have to do is fishing, burning ghosts up using the spotlight, repairing portholes, and pushing aliens (why aliens??) back using a fire extinguisher. But you will be totally wrong if you think it's a easy thing to do. 


Here is basically what happends during the game:


>Rolling the fishing lines

>Hear the porthole breaking

>Go downstairs to repair it

>See a weird light coming from above

>Aliens come to steal your fish

>Take the extinguisher to drive them away

>They took one or two fishes anyway

>Turn around and find dozens of ghosts REALLY close to you

>Run upstairs to get the spotlight

>It's too late, a ghost bite you (Or should I say "touch you"?)

>Hear the porthole breaking

>.......

A sense of rhythm is very important, and when you get used to it, you will definetally enjoy the trill it brings you. 



And to the developer, here is what more I want to see in your future updates:

>>A better performance on Graphics and Audios. (Ghosts in this game seem somehow CUTE to me, at least. And the sound effects have A LOT OF space to improve. )

>>Maybe some impressive Musics? In order to increase the tense. 

>>CO-OP Mode. It can be an Endless Mode where you defend the boat with your friends, and try to survive as long as you can! Has to be fun!

>>A longer story mode and some more boat upgrades. I'm pretty sure it's already in your plan, just in case. 

Highly recommended.

Games that force me to consider something about myself or the world around me, games that elicit an emotional response weather it's the 1st or 50th time I've played. Great game in concept, started off decent in execution, now suffers extremely due to the playerbase.

Nowadays, you have two options for how to play/experience comedy night:

Option A) You go to a music lobby, you listen to people play songs, maybe you yourself perform. Generally it's a good time. Everyone there is usually supportive, etc.

Option B) You go into a comedy lobby, and are immediately presented with homophobic and racist fascists spouting hateful propaganda the entire time. One might try to make the argument that it is all "satire", but hearing the same "jokes" over and over again that are being delivered with no setup or punchline makes it very obvious that they are not joking. At the very least, if you can be generous enough to call their statements "jokes", they are very mean-spirited and direct.

This type of behavior does not offend me personally, although I know many that it will. What does offend me is that a game meant to simulate a virtual comedy club has now become an echo chamber for fucking morons.

I propose a solution: a "karma" system that detects which players are participating with the game in a genuine fashion, and which ones are not. Every player profile you can interact with in a game lobby should have an upvote/downvote button included. You can only vote on the same player's profile ONCE, but you can change their status between an upvote and a downvote at any given time.

Each vote counts as either a positive or negative karma point (with no limit in either direction). What is crucial to making this work is that all karma values must be hidden from EVERY player. It also has to be hidden in the game server and not be searchable in the game scripts/code (I don't know jack about programming, but like... I feel like you can set it up as some sort of server-side method of tracking and updating player karma stuff so that script-kitties can't do some digging)

Players that do not meet the required karma value will not be able to see or join your lobby. When this feature is disabled, a player of any karma value can join your lobby, including negative.

It's not a perfect solution, but if the devs can make it happen, I think the game would be much better off for it - it might even help revive the games' popularity. Consider releasing new cosmetic features alongside it to help promote the update (preferably without making it paid DLC)

review:
This game puts destruction physics front and center, and that is where it shines. Blowing up buildings never gets old, and the chaos alone makes it worth playing.

Everything else feels like it comes second. The story and characters go nowhere, which is fine for a gameplay-focused game but could have been handled better. Movement with both the jetpack and vehicles feels clunky and restrictive. You cannot even jetpack over a simple hill, and those limitations make the supposedly open world feel smaller than it should. Ammo is also stingy to the point of killing the fun. You spend more time scavenging ammo crates than going wild with weapons (on hard difficulty). The races and destruction challenges sound cool, but they are all timed, which makes them frustrating. The races in particular feel almost impossible without looking up a YouTube video to find the right shortcuts.

There is also a small DLC included where you play as a female character, which is very cool, but aside from that it only adds some collectibles and plenty of bugs without offering anything meaningful to expand the base game.

Despite all that, it is still a decent 7/10. The destruction is UNMATCHED, and if you are in the mood to turn your brain off and wreck everything in sight, or just kick fascists off Mars, it delivers.

This game is everything that I want from a RTS without the massive requirement for high APM that Starcraft takes, or the huge time investment that Total War games take. I have been wanting a strategy game that feels advanced bit still approachable. Basically, this game is to Starcraft what Battlegrounds is to Hearthstone, but with more features.

In addition to the well crafted game design and balanced strategy, the game has a heavy trend towards supporting its community and social engagement. It is so refreshing to find a game that facilitates player interaction instead of being scared of it. It has public tournaments, 2v2 and free for all 4p mode, community challenges, and this is all after having spent a handfull of hours in the game.

And if you want singleplayer content, it has that, too in the form of survival and custom difficulty bots. It may not be a huge amount, but it's more than almost any other auto-battler I've seen. For $15, this game is an incredible deal and a surprisingly great find. I'm going to be sinking many hours into this one.

review:
Mechabellum is a complex tactical auto-battler pitting legions of mechanized units against one another in a chess-like battle of wits... or at least, it is some of the time.

The graphics are slick, with good use of bloom and high quality rendering.  The sound design is fine.  Nothing about it really stands out - good or bad.  

The game design is interesting - like playing chess - but both players have to decide each of their moves simultaneously, only learning what their opponent did after they have both moved.  It makes strategy, tactics, and forethought important.

The problem is the way the game is set up.  You have extremely limited resources, and can only choose a couple of mechs per round.  The problem is compounded by the relatively poor unit balance.  The game mechanics heavily encourage a scissor/paper/rock approach - which I personally consider one of the greatest crutches of modern rts  gaming.  Regardless - the system is incredibly easy to cheese, and if someone chooses the perfect cheese to use against you, it can be very difficult to recover.  

When you get an intelligent adult opponent, games can be an extremely engaging battle of wits where  you adopt and adapt strategies against one another - but at least 1/3 of the games are against sweaty try-hards who go for all-in cheese builds - which I'm sure veteran players can easily defeat, but for newer players, it is very frustrating to encounter one cheese build after another.  (And there are quite a few of them)

For a game that is all about tactics, playing against builds that are downright silly in a military context, and being unable to reasonably counter them due to poor unit balancing, gets very frustrating.

This game has potential, but the units really need to be better balanced.  I think it would also benefit from a mode that let people point buy a larger army, and reposition a limited number of units each round, perhaps with selling or drafting mechanics.

If you are on the fence, I would say go for it. This is not a game you play once and put away. It is something you will keep coming back to. Also its amazing as a second screen game when wanting to listen to podcasts or watch TV-Shows, as you always have enough time for setting up your army per turn.

It's too bad this game is close to being a really good auto-battler/tower defense.

But frankly, it does a really poor job of explaining all sorts of mechanics that are key to the game.  The tutorial missions are so incredibly basic, didn't even know the command centers had stuff in them you could interact with until well after completing all tutorials. Multiplayer could be fun if you are into that, but you're going to be lost for a long time most likely.

Where this game loses me completely is the single player option, or lack thereof.  As a new player, good luck trying to figure out what you're doing wrong when survival mode crushes you in the later waves.  And that's the extent of it.  As a tower defense sort of game, how and why does this not have a decent single player option for learning what units ACTUALLY do aside from trying to remember 4 abilities per unit for every unit while the AI throws experimental stuff at you.  It's just a really bad experience.

I understand why people like the game. I get it. But I would love a game like this where it's not ONLY multiplayer and has some other modes to it.  And for the love of God, Battle Speed. It's a no for me.

Steam will not let me refund due to "Playtime" over 2 hours, when it takes at least 1 hour to complete the tutorials only and another at least 2 hours to even understand what is going on, let alone get a feel for it. My "Playtime" is tutorial, observing other player matches to try to understand the game, and getting to Hard Survival before realizing I don't like it at all.

It's too bad Steam's refund policy is like this. I have a library of over 300 games and have requested a refund I believe twice. Once for this, and once maybe 8 years ago.  And I can't get one, even though as soon as I knew the game wasn't for me.

review:
This game has changed many times since I bought it; I thought I was buying a 4 door sedan but instead I ended up with a pontoon boat. Overall if I could I would get a refund. 

There have been several bad patches that made the game feel unfun. Most of them had a silver lining so there was "something" to keep my interest. This latest patch added walls and static defenses that cannot be moved. This is a problem in a game where the whole point is that unit placement determines how your units move relative to the enemy. The hardest thing to learn in this game is where to place your units. 

In addition the previous patch added "titan" units to 1v1 and 2v2. Overall these giant stompy robots of death are very good at killing entire armies on their own and make the entire game before their appearance feel unimportant. Titans belong only in the "chaotic" 4 player free for all mode.  They remove the strategic importance of many of the other units. Oh you played a great game until round 9 when the Titans show up.... and now you have lost immediately. Well played.

I literally just played a game with someone who was upset when I won as soon as I placed two titans on the board. Did it feel good? It did not but that is about the only way to win vs certain meta strat army compositions. 

I cant get any of my friends interested in this game after it decided not to go "for free".  I understand why it wont go free to play because you can buy all the skins except for a few exclusive ones with in game currency.

Overall this game has always had a number of "cheap" mechanics that make the game less fun(one example of this is the ability to level towers). Unfortunately the developer has leaned into this style of play.  The battlefield "spells" have always been too powerful for their cost. You can remove six turns of deployment with a single spell that costs the same as the most inexpensive unit in the entire game. That feels balanced right? I *suppose* in a way it is balanced if everyone knows you must always click the fire spell.... but I digress.

Spend your time and money on a different game and you will almost certainly be happier.

review:
While most may see this as just another F-Zero clone, yeah I'll be honest, that is kind of what it is, but that doesn't mean it's not worth playing. This game is simple, stright forward, and to the point. You pick a car, and you race on some pretty crazy tracks. While there are many other games on Steam like this, this is a pretty decent one for the price.

One issue I had with this game is the controller setup. You can use an Xbox, PS4 and even a Wii U Pro controller with this game, but you may have to do some rebinding and you'll also need the mouse to move around some of the menus, but for the most part, the controls are pretty solid, especially in the races. Now I'm not pro at AG racing games, so maybe I'm not the best to say how well it handles, but I was able to get through races with 1st place without any issues.

There's also a track editor, although it seems a bit complicated and there's no intro tutorial on how to use it, but all the tracks in the game were made with the editor, so I can imagine some pretty fun creations in here. 

The other thing I really liked was the custom music option. The ingame music is okay, but to me it didn't match the amount of hype and excitement I was hoping for. Once I dropped in some songs from F-Zero GX and turned up the car engine volume a bit (It's turned down because of a little bit of sound crackling issues but it doesn't bother me much.), everything was great. 

Overall, this is a fun game and it even has 4 player local options. No, it's not as pretty as a couple of the other games on here, but it doesn't pretend to be more than it is while delivering a fast paced, fun experience and I respect that.

review:
A decent F-ZeroX clone for Linux+SteamOS (which is rare). Because I am specifically looking for such-a-game, my review will be a comparison of the two (graphics excluded).

Setting up the controls is a bit janky: I tried a generic controller (Nyko AirFlo Ex) and I it would not recognize my Joystick-Right motion while many other games recognize it just fine (Momodora, To the Moon, Jotun, Psychonauts, etc). All preset controllers would leave me spinning in circles. Trying the keyboard controls: Rebinding the space-bar is 'almost' non-functional as it does register as a keybind but reactivates the keybinding act for whatever action you just bound (but it can be 'tricked' to work quickly clicking to a different action in-time). It is actually tied to whatever key is associated with the "ok" confirmation action. Finally I tried my XBoxOne-S controller (as an XBox Preset) but my joystick outright didn't work. However, rebinding it did correctly recognize the joystick-directions and I was finally able to play this game.

Handling feels twice as slippery as F-ZeroX. In F-ZeroX I used the left/right attack bumper for strafing left/right on the track and that is simply not present in Outracer. Also, hitting a wall results in a substantial bump in the opposite direction that seems much bigger then in F-ZeroX.

While I am not very far into this game, I have no idea how to attack. I don't even think that is implemented in this game. Vehicles bump into things and take damage. That seems to be all there is. I can't begin to explain the fun I've had in F-ZeroX, destroying just about every car on a track (while racing) just because I could. That does not seem to be present here.

As a programmer, I feel as though the developer(s) got this game to a runnable state where everything worked fine for them and released it without further testing or improvement. It's sad because it is very close to being a polished game but it seems like theres one little annoyance in every single corner of this game where I just could not outright recommend it.

review:
This is not really a *very* good game, but a passable one, and it's short enough that its drawbacks don't have time to manifest fully.

I liked the variety of missions (there are four types, which is three more than your typical SHMUP). I like the feeling of controls, more or less, and of impact of weapons (much better than, say, M.A.C.E.). But a lot of things are very *meh*.

While you have access to 12 ships, you don't *need* them, as they are not different enough. Just save a bit of money and buy the last one: it has the best armor and shooting power combo, and the special attack is nice.

Additional weapons also seem to be of limited usefullnes. The repair drone is a very good choice. Everything esle is less so.

The randomizing of enemies on levels removes the frustration if you have to replay a level, but leads to blandness: there are not enemy patterns here, though random combinations sometimes force you to weave and dodge.

Bullets are mostly visible against the background in space, but in planetary levels, they are often not - a grave sin in this genre! Fortunately, there are only a few such levels.

The levels are reasonably hard, but since the game is very forgiving and both gives you several lives AND allow to only replay the latest level if you spend all lives, you won't really have any problems. Bosses are boring and unmemorable: they pretty much follow the same pattern.

All in all, it's an OK game to kill a few evenings, but if you're looking for a GREAT shoot em up, better check out Xenoraid or Drifting Lands.

review:
A surprisingly good space shooty arcade style game. There are a great deal of ships to unlock and choose from, each with different stats, primary weapons (though most tend to shoot straight forwards) and unique ship specific abilities, many of which are very fun to use and look at in action. You also get to choose a special weapon to use to complement your ships abilities or weaknesses or strengths. Again, there is a good amount to choose from.

Enemy variety is decent, bosses are OK, powerups are what you would expect. There is nothing revolutionary here.

The looks might be a bit decieving though, it feels very smooth to play and there are some surprisingly nice looking (and deadly) effects that can happen, usually when using a ships special ability.

There is only one outstanding bad thing and that is the translation. It is passable but bad enough to make certain item or weapon abilites unclear and trying to follow the story is gonna end with constant facepalms. It is a good thing a story is not what most care about in this kind of game, but it would have been nice to be able to follow it without feeling like you are reading a sci-fi story paper a 5 year old handed in to their teacher. Other than that everything else becomes clear as you use items and weapons.

If you want to shoot aliens with spaceships like the old days but still have some variety in the gameplay and looks, then this is definitely a game you want and something you can come back to every now and then for some shooty goodness.

review:
I don't love making this review, because there was a window there in 2022 and 2023 where I absolutely loved this game. WW3 was one of those projects with a good core gameplay loop but was always let down by something else: too little content, too few updates, poor server performance, a crappy launcher, too much focus on microtransactions when still trying to establish a player base, and other overall mismanagement issues.

In 2025, what we have is a game without a player base. New ownership has picked up the game and is delivering updates, but at this point it is a drip-feed of tweaks and additions being handed to a player base that doesn't exist. The game has averaged fewer than 200 players since January 2024, and that has now dropped to fewer than 100 players. Trying to play this game is often an exercise of ending up in a waiting room with 3 other players, and watching people join and quit one-by-one.

The positives for the game are still there. The gameplay is a more hardcore Battlefield style experience. Weapon recoil is stronger than Battlefield's often laser-y guns. Movement is weightier and should appeal to players who think BF is drifting too close to COD-style movement. Weapon customization is also a major strong point of the game, and an area where the project punches way above its weight.

This game has had multiple soft-relaunches since its disastrous original 2018 early access release. It's going to take something big and attention-grabbing to get people to come back and try the game again, especially players jaded from the previous short lived re-launches. 

Unfortunately, the new developer so far seems content to dribble out small updates, which may help the quality of the game, but aren't anywhere close to moving the needle when it comes to rebuilding the player base. Hopefully they have something up their sleeve (cross-play console port would be good), but so far it's looking grim.

I really want to like this game, but one of the core characters is really making me uncomfortable.
So we'll start with the negatives, I like to end on a happy note. I'll try to avoid spoilers, but it really depends on what you call spoiler, If you want to skip, skip down to the word "Safety" in all capitals.

There's a character called Eric, you meet him fairly near the start, you can't directly tell him to F off. Much as I wish you could. He's nasty about your relatives, he's obsessed with purity in people in a kinda 1940's fascist party kinda way. He's just a ton of red flags all at once. He knows where you live and he bothers you constantly. Sending you texts and blowing up your phone. You can ignore his texts, but he'll still appear.
And this REALLY makes me uncomfortable. You cannot get rid of him, he's part of the game.

It's really weird, that this game tries to make sure you're comfortable with things. But then throws in one of the most common sources of anxiety when it comes to dating... stalkers.  Honestly, it's really bad of the developers to do this, and I will not forgive them. It's why I will never recommend this game to anyone, hence the thumbs down.
He also owns a shop that you can buy materials from... but I really don't want to go there, because he makes me so uncomfortable. Which really makes me feel like I'm missing out on part of the game.
But honestly, I'm probably going to stop playing this game soon. He's ruining it for me.
I hope there's a mod to disable him. Or turn him into someone who isn't a creep.

I've tried being as nasty as I can toward him, and he just will not go away. It's really making me feel awful. Especially as the rest of the game is genuinely quite good.

...

SAFETY

I'm not sure what I was expecting from this game, when I first got into it, the humour was enjoyable. The awkward cousin, then you meet some friendly talky sword people. Some of them are very much red flags, but that depends on taste I suppose. In games like this I try to be friendly with everyone, but I'm not really interested in romance. And for the most part, the characters are chill with that.... Except the aforementioned problem character who ruins the game.

The combat is... challenging, there is an option in the start menu that makes it easier, you can turn it on with no repercussions. It still remains challenging, but definitely more manageable if, like me, you're not typically good at top down clicky slicy games. 
You can also change the beverage, a nice touch. I chose cups of tea. (Least, I think that's what they are...)

The dates are... honestly, kinda in the way. Some of it is voiced and some of it isn't, it kinda chops and changes and doesn't make up it's mind what it's doing. Most of it isn't voiced, which is a major downer. Especially as some of the characters have nice voices. Maybe that kinda thing doesn't bother you, then by all means, but for me, that's an issue. As I then I have to read out what the characters are saying to the other person in the room. And I'm not a very good reader... (Especially when I try to copy their voices, much to the other person in the rooms dismay. xD)

Unsafety again, I suppose, just kinda closing words from here.

Ultimately, if creepy stalking behaviour doesn't bother you, then I'd recommend this game... 
But because of the aforementioned character, I cannot recommend this game... in fact, I'd actually recommend against it. On a huge level. I'll probably avoid this developer from now on as well, as this is a major cross of boundaries.
The game does warn you about it at the entrance... but warning you that you're going to be stalked and harassed, doesn't make the stalking and harassing any better.

I know it's just a game... but if you've gone through that kinda stuff IRL, it's really awful to see it simulated in your hobbies. Especially the way the character gaslights you.
If I knew this character was in this game. I would never have bought the game.
I wish I could refund it, but it's too late for that now.
I got the game on sale, so I feel less bad about it... but it still feels really bad to buy something, then not be able to play it because it's... violating on a deeply personal level.
I hate this so much.

SAFETY

I personally do not recommend this game. I actually recommend buying anything else.
If you buy the game anyway, and enjoy it... that's great. I hope you get the fun out of it that I cannot.
But if based on my review, you avoid the game. That's absolutely fair, and I hope that we can both find something better.
Regardless, thank you for reading, I hope you have a wonderful day. <3

review:
I don't know if I enjoyed a single second of this game. Maybe looking at Sunder before he opens his mouth, but that's about it.

I think the problem with games that are "woke" is that they're judged more harshly for their attempts towards kindness. For example, the game asks you if a support system "Mom" sending you text messages is okay. That's nice and all but it made me sit there and work through the process if that WOULD be okay with me. In the end I selected it'd be okay, but I actually was a little sad of having to make that choice. I lost my mom when I was 21... In trying to avoid causing me sadness, the game actively made me sad having to remember I don't have a mom. And then, once the messages starting coming in, I realized I made the wrong choice. But there was no way to get rid of my video game mom lovebombing me without starting over lol. 

If the developers were to carry this onward to their other games, I'd leave it more open ended. For example, the question might read as: "There's a character in this game who sends you messages as a support system. They are most similar to a parental role. What would you like to name this character [or would you rather not have the character text you at all]?" Funnily enough, in something like Animal Crossing, I'd shrug it off as the developers just standardizing everyone's lives and it wouldn't be a critique. But this is a "woke" game, right? They should care about my feelings, ...right?

Which leads me to the crux of the negative review. Since the game is "woke", I would expect my "No" to mean "No." but it doesn't. And I'm not talking about the character who is legitimately a stalker. I'm talking about actual love interests just straight up ignoring what you say to them. No, I don't want to dance. Next second, I'm dancing. (this was my attempt at shaking Sunder off but it didn't work.) It also bothered me I wasn't asked my sexual orientation. It made me uncomfortable that one of the characters whose sex I wasn't interested in ground against me without consent. Again, I don't even know if this would be a critique in a regular game - it's much easier to shrug it off as "eh. This is just what people find sexy in fantasies." But this game is supposed to care about my feelings right? it asked me about my dead mom and it warned me that there were "references to stalkers" and it tries hard to have a diverse cast. But instead, all the characters just instantly want to fuck and kiss you, no matter if you tell them you want to just be friends or flat out NO. Or they would be the complete opposite - totally rude and even mean to you or self-absorbed and it's like.... why in the world would I date this person? 

All the love interests that I met weren't likable, or would say something really off-putting. For instant, Sunder saying he likes to kiss other people even if he's in a relationship. okay, well, first off I didn't even know we were dating? But no I don't want to date you after that. You do you, but bye baby. Then he just keeps texting me over and over. Aiya. And then another guy who we are TOLD is SWEET and LOVABLE and KIND tells me that the stalker stalking me is just "odd"... After witnessing the stalker HARASS ME. uhm. how about fuck you, you stupid fucker? stalking is very mentally damaging, in a danish study 80% of victims end with ptsd, depression, or anxiety. So this casual "poo-poo"ing of the situation is upsetting to me. I didn't finish the game because of this. I have since read apparently there is sort of a redemption/hand-waving of the stalker's actions. Uh. "Good job there".

It also bothered me that the game's name is "boyfriend dungeon" but only 4 out of the 8 LIs are men.

Thanks Boyfriend Dungoen - now I'm cying over my dead mom and I didn't even get to fuck or kiss a cute guy for it. Boooo.

review:
[b] Alter Cosmos [/b] is not a very good point&click adventure, at least as far as the gameplay goes. Overall, it lacks polish in almost every aspect, numerous glitches when it comes to UI and click detection. Why do I recommend it? Well, I think the art style and the story are compelling enough to purchase it, plus the price is not particularly high. The comic book style makes it stand out in the genre, the backgrounds are very detailed and there are many cutscenes with text choices, kind of reminds me of CyberFrog in terms of aesthetic. I really like the mature tone of this game, it has plenty of dark humor, occasional gore, and some dirty posters. You play as the AlienCat, a cyborg-cat that is now a fugitive, to be honest, I don't know what to make of it.

Unfortunately, it has a combat system which is like always a bad sign in this genre. The combat kinda sucks, it does not add anything interesting to the game aside from clunky mechanics. Perhaps the developer should add some kind of impact and collision system, otherwise, the enemies tend to walk on top of you. Apparently, it has some sort of combo system, I am not entirely sure how to use it. If you hold space you can see interactive areas, and if you scroll the mouse-wheel you can quickly open the inventory. I would like to see the room exits when you hold space as well, sometimes it is hard to see an entrance to the next area. Also, the developer should map the weapons to hotkeys (1,2,3 etc), it would make my life a bit easier. I must give a warning in regards to puzzles, it has a surprising amount of those sequence minigames that everyone loves so much, you know, moving squares and turning valves.

[b] Pros: [/b]

+ pretty awesome aesthetic 
+ interesting characters
+ mature themes  
+ text choices, many cutscenes 
+ highlighter for interactive areas


[b] Cons: [/b]

- somewhat glitchy
- combat is clunky
- subpar UI
- many annoying minigame puzzles
- hitbox problems/pathing problems

[h1] Overall Thoughts: 6/10 [/h1]

I am usually pretty harsh on games that cannot get the basic UI correctly (hence a relatively poor score), but I think that Alter Cosmos is potentially fun. If you can ignore its lack of polish, there is a very stylish and ridiculous adventure game. I guess I would describe as a guilty pleasure more than anything else.

Video (gameplay + commentary): https://youtu.be/LwXh9FvLZxg

What a great surprise of a game! We're really enjoying it so far and recommend it.

Alter Cosmos is, first and foremost, a point and click adventure game with occasional combat (via clicking as well). Historically point and click adventures can have some pretty obtuse puzzles, and there are occasional moments like that in Alter Cosmos where you have to do your share of pixel hunting to find items hidden away in the background/foreground, but for the most part we found ourselves cruising through the puzzles.

There's also a feature to the puzzle-solving mechanic that we REALLY appreciated. When you have an item selected in your inventory, the game just knows to try to use that item wherever you click. This is so much more streamlined than the typical point and click situation where you have to click your item then click where you want to try to use it.

Combat is a little wonky and involves feverishly clicking on your targets to wail on them with your claws, boots, and tail. If you have a gun, same deal. You run up and wildly fire until they're dead.

The bizarre part is Aliencat (your character), even if you have a ranged weapon equipped, will still run up to the bad guys at point blank range and fire away from that distance. It's really jarring at first and negates the point of having a ranged weapon, but ultimately we haven't run into a situation where this is detrimental, as bizarre as it is. Enemy AI is also mindless and a lot of brawls boil down to repeatedly juking your enemy while whittling down their health.

Graphically, Alter Cosmos NAILS the comic book feel. Every character and every piece of art looks beautifully drawn and really sets the tone for the game world.

The soundtrack is minimal but effective, getting the point across of the totalitarian world.

Overall, the game feels loaded with charm and we've enjoyed playing a classic point and click adventure with some modern amenities thrown in alongside some great art.

review:
While not the most amazing or well made game out there, I would say this game is actually fairly well done, all things considered.

Sound wise, there is nothing whatsoever; no sounds, no music. Interface is minimal, and there is no options menu. You get to pick from playing fields of varying complexity, and have to match spheres in 3D space, which is harder than it sounds. One thing this does differently is that a sphere can only move to make a match if there is an ajacent sphere to switch with, leading to cases where in most games you could make a match, but in this game you can't because the ball doesn't have another one to switch with.

There is a hint system, which shrinks all balls down to show a possible match; however it does this regardless of if you can actually MAKE said match, for example often showing a match that cannot be made because of being buried in the playing field, thus requiring other matches to be made first to get to it. When this happens it renders the hint system useless, as it will continue to show that same match until it is made. It also fines you 100 pts per hint, yet on the larger maps the hints are pretty much required. There is a planet in perpetual orbit, which appears to be the earth, and when a match is made the balls shrink and fly to orbit the planet, which I thought was a nice touch.

Another flaw which is not major, but rather off putting, is that the pink ball is semi-transparent, wheras all the other balls are solid. The game goes on until no more matches an be made, in which case a big bang icon on the bottom of the screen will start to flash; this icon can be clicked on at anytime to end the game if you get bored, or when the game is over, causing all remaining balls to fly towards the planet. There seems to be a bug at the end where the earth started shrinking in increments, only to go back to full size moments later. after doing this a few times the resulting resizing caused all of the orbiting balls to be violently flung off into space, after which it didn't change sizes anymore. it only seems to happen on the largest map setting, and it's actually an enjoyable thing to see, so I classify it more as a feature than a bug

All in all a rather simplistic, but enjoyable take on the genre, and definitely worth the price!

I believe a lot of the information on my review is no longer up to date. However, I still think this is one of the best, if not the best, drumming game in VR. https://youtu.be/4fVRui0s8rI

[h1]Original Review Below:[/h1]

I can confirm this game works on Oculus Rift with Touch Controllers.  The only issue I had, and I'm not sure if it's an issue with the Rift or with the game, was that I couldn't change the look of the drum set.  Which was weird, because all the other customization options worked except for this one.  + The game starts off with 4 songs which you have to get an S rating on at least the easiest difficulty on each song, before unlocking the next set of 4 songs.  There's a total of 20 songs in the game library.  Most of the songs were from NTWO Studio (Korea) the developer, but some of them were from Mike B. Fort who had much better songs, while the dev songs were uneven in quality and had varying genres of music.

Anyways, what really sets this game apart is all the customization options.  You can adjust the height, you can set the delay (they have a handy tool to measure any problems with visual or audio delays), you can play a song on three difficulties from easiest to hardest and you can play it at normal speed or half speed or twice as fast, or 1.5x.  There's just lots of options.  

As I said, I couldn't change my drumset but the option is in the menus.  You can also switch the VR environment (there's only 2 though, one is the default you've already seen and the other is a nicely done forest).  

I had a blast using the very easy to use VR editor where you can beat down your own drum interpretation and share it with others.  In fact, I did that myself easily on my first try after watching a quick tutorial.  However, I don't know if you can add your own songs and I didn't see an option to do that.  Basically, you can edit the in-game songs.  They do describe the ability to edit your own songs, so maybe I missed something.

Anyways, is this better than Drums Hero VR or Drummer Talent VR?  Not exactly.  But it does offer something very different with all the customization options.  I do recommend this game simply because of this.  Honestly, I wish there was a VR drum game that had the awesome songs of Drums Hero, with the realism of Drummer Talent VR, and with the customizations of Into the Rhythm.  Still, this was fun to play.  

Rate 8/10 ... changed score from 7 to 8 after discovering how easy it is to add your own beatmap or drum note highway to your own songs and play in VR, and how fun doing that is

The graphical presentation is a very well done and nice to look at, including the option to customize the appearence of the drums and drumsticks after playing a certain number of songs. My only gripe is that sometimes a drum won't register a hit when I'm almost certain I swung my controller correctly, but it could be that I'm not fully used to the motion controls yet. Definitely recommended for anyone who enjoys rhythm games.

review:
総評 : 課金モバイルゲー臭がする有料ゲーム
TLDR; Paid game with a feeling of "a Pay to Win mobile game". (English review on bottom)

マッチ3にクラフト要素があるというのを聞いて購入したが、以下の点で「本来これはモバイルでF2P(P2W)形式にするつもりだったのか」と思えて仕方がなかった。
・アイテムのクラフト回数は有限。その回数を補充するには盾を500個消す必要がある(3個マッチのみで計算すると170マッチ近く)。
・クラフト素材自体はマッチ３でランダム入手。土タイルや砂タイルを掘ったり、宝箱を開けたりすると手に入る。いわば運ゲー。
・馬にはヘルスとスタミナがあり、ヘルスはエサを与える(１回ごとに食料を大量に消費)、スタミナはクラフト品を渡すことで補充する。前述の「有限クラフト」と馬の健康度ボーナス(両方が高いと+10手、両方が低いと-10手)との相性が悪い。
・どうみても課金通貨にしか見えない「ゴールド」でキーを買わないと「完全クリア」メダルがもらえない。ゴールドの入手はすさまじい量の資源と交換するかクラフトするのが主だろうがその入手量は需要(キー購入以外にも消耗品補充、復活の羽の購入、スロットのコイン追加購入など)と比べるとはるかに少ない。
・「デイリーログインボーナス」や「３０分で１回復するライフ(最大５つ、リトライ時に消費)」というモバイルゲームお約束の仕様。
・スロットマシンが運ゲーにさらに拍車をかけている。３つ絵柄がそろう気がしない。

マッチ３自体は比較的オーソドックスだが、次の問題点があるため難易度は高め。手数の問題はリラックスモードで遊べばかなり多くなるが、オンでプレイしたときの意見をあげる。
・手数が200近く与えられるステージもあるが、多くのステージは複数の盤面にわたって繰り広げられることが多いため「１盤面を３０手ぐらいでクリアしないと無理」というバランス。
・マッチ３ゲームではよくある「シャッフル」が手詰まり時以外で行われない上にヒント表示が遅いため、次の一手がわかりにくい時のストレスに悩まされる。
・パワーアップは「3x3爆破」、「３～４つのブロックを選んで破壊」、「残り手数+20」、「1種のブロックを全消滅」、「盤面にある氷・鎖・箱・土をランダムに現在の50%分吹き飛ばす」、「隣接する同種のタイルかお邪魔ブロックを破壊」といった基本的なものばかりだが、補充はポーションを500個消す必要がある。切らした時に限り、ゴールドを支払うことで補充できる。
・4つ消し/5つ消しで作られる爆弾は初動(1コンボ目)でしか作られず、落下コンボでできた４つ(以上)消しでは爆弾ができない。また、爆弾同士をスワップすることで列爆破も行えるがこれも機会が限られすぎていて扱いに悩まされるし、手数の無駄になりうることもある。そもそも盤面が小さすぎて爆弾を作る余裕もないことも多い。
・画面の上側にある順番どおりにスワップ＋マッチすることで資源を追加で得られるが、手数の少なすぎるこのゲームではそんなことをしている余裕はない。

I bought the game as I saw a charm with a combination of Match 3 and Crafting, but this game had a feeling of "Supposed to be Freemium but decided to make it a paid game":

- You have limited *times* of crafting, and you need to match and remove 500 Shield tiles to recover one attempt.
- Craft materials are obtained from uncovering dirt/sand tiles or opening chests, but the contents are completely random.
- Your horse has Health and Stamina; feed horses(lots of Foods are used in each process) to recover Health, and use crafted items to recover Stamina. This is a HORRIBLE combination with the forementioned "limited crafting". If you neglect your horse's condition, you get moves penalty or you'll have to spend phoenix feathers.
- GOLD CURRENCY. This obviously look like a paid currency and you must use them to purchase keys for getting Medals(which you receive on 100%'ing a level). Instead of paying real money, you'll have to spend TONS of resources or craft materials to get Gold. Of course, you'll be spending much more Gold than you earn them.
- "Daily Login Bonus" and "Lives that regenerates over time". Only mobile games and online games have them.
- Slot Machines add another layer to "game of pure luck". Give us the exact chance to win ANY matches, and show what each matches will give.

Match-3 part is quite orthodox, but it's generally hard for these problems.
(The moves problem can be ignored with Relaxed mode as you will have much more moves, but I turned that off) :
- Sometimes you get 200+ moves, but most levels consist of multiple boards, so basically you'll have to solve each boards within 30 moves or so.
- Shuffle is only available when you have no more moves. Other Match-3 games usually let you use it every few minutes.
- The "hint" that appears when you don't make a move for few seconds, takes too much time.
- Powerups are quite common, but you need to match and remove 500 potions to get one. You can pay Gold to buy powerups if you run out of them.(P2W, huh?)
- The bonus bombs on removing 4 or 5 tiles can only be created in first move, unlike other Match-3s where you can get them from combos. Swap two bombs for bigger explosion, but it's much harder to actually do so and there won't be much space to make multiple bombs.
- You can get bonus resources if you swap & match in certian order(shown on the top of screen), though it's nothing but a waste of moves. 
- Getting 3-star gets difficult due to very low moves, and Medals require 100%'ing the boards(Open all chests, remove dirt/sand tiles, deplete all resource stockpiles, destroy all crates). This means YOU MUST PAY GOLD TO GET MEDALS, because Gold Chests are also counted for the Medal.
- As for Stars and Medals, you will NEED them to progress.
- The cave levels have TOO MUCH moves available. And in earlier level without light radius upgrades, it irritated me often when I don't "see" any matchable blocks, but the game knows there are matchable blocks IN THE DARKNESS.

The game has potential and could've been great if it focused on "pay for the package, and everything else is free, no currencies bullshit".
I can't really understand why they made decisions to make the game less engaging, by adding lots of "Gold contents" that basically slows game down, and ignoring the standards of Match-3 games(such as bombs creation in combos and shuffles).

review:
[b]pathos[/b] is a really difficult sokoban-like where the goal isn't to push boxes to their designated places, but for you to reach the exit by pushing boxes out of the way. sounds easy, it most certainly isn't. there's even a story, from what I've read it seemed a bit pretentious, but it can be turned off if you only want to concentrate on puzzling.

[b]150+ levels[/b], you need a certain amount of 'bits' from solving them to unlock further chapters, but every level within each is accessible at once. wasd or arrows to move, can't be held to move more than one tile, annoying, but steps are numbered, nice. mouse wheel to zoom, but the mouse cursor never disappears, another oversight, and there's a [b]mandatory move limit, once reached, the level resets[/b] for one more unnecessary annoyance. the next (and far from final) nail in the coffin is the [b]lack of undo[/b]. as always, it doesn't make the game more difficult, just a lot more cumbersome and tedious than it should be. some of the later levels involve hundreds(!) of moves, which would be painful to figure out even with undo, let alone without.

and if you haven't suffered enough, be it from puzzle difficulty or having to re-do everything on a level after a misstep, there are also [b]breakthroughs[/b], additional challenges in the game. they can be brought up from the menu in alphabetical order, each has an accompanying image as a clue, the achievemenet list has a bit more info, and not only do you have to figure out [i]what[/i] to do, but also [i]where[/i] to do it, on which level. [b]some of them need audio clues, but they were stored on the game's website, which is not available anymore[/b], so check the forum for download links. honestly, who thought this would be a good idea? why not just store them with the rest of the game? and if you can't be bothered to change it, at least don't let the domain expire. one takes some effort, the other some money, pick one.

the presentation is pleasantly minimalist (except one of the fonts for the in-level story bits, too basic) and the audio is fantastic as well, but there's only a master and sfx volume slider, plus resolutions and windowed mode via the unity launcher. and for such a story-heavy game, [b]there should be an in-game place to re-read all the story bits without launching every level separately[/b].

gotta cater to masochists, no problem with that, but some of the design decisions are questionable at best. [b]with a few improvements it would be a truly excellent game[/b] for a more than reasonable price, except [b]it's broken, the final level set hasn't been accessible for years[/b] without editing the save file (there aren't enough bits otherwise), and some breakthroughs are also broken. not sure how something like this can result in all those positive reviews, people (including developers) really have no standards these days. [b]obviously don't waste money and time on this until (if ever) they decide to fix what they're asking money for.[/b]

And since it's such a new game, it hasn't been spoiled yet by cheat guides.

Tl;dr: 10/10 would buy again. Can't wait for OS/mobile dev.

[/spoiler]

While buying it, I was expecting a difficult puzzle game but later, I realized this is not a game. This is pure torture. This is exactly a punishment. I’m still going crazy when thinking about it. Such a degree of difficulty is really amazing.

Alright, this is definitely a very interesting type of torture. Of course, first levels are easy, then they are getting harder, then getting harderr, then harderrr, then harderrrr, then harderrRR and harderRRR and hardeRRRRR. It is insane. 150+ levels. This is absolute madness.  I don’t even mention about count of moves for further levels. Some levels are sooo sick that you can’t even look at them much long. It was so humiliating. 

Also, there is another very big problem about Pathos. It is absolutely infectious. Sometimes you pause the game or quit the game because of troubles, failures, fatique, fear, loathing, etc. In fact, only your body can quit the game, but your brain can’t stop working in the background. My playtime may be 230 hours but it definitely felt like a full year. (Honestly, I quit playing it for 4 months and then turn back). I just couldn’t stop thinking about it, about them, about the paths, about blue boxes, about icy boxes, about rotten ones, about red circles, about orange dungeons. I really couldn’t stop thinking about it while doing something else, walking, working, eating, reading, driving, even while sleeping and dreaming. Pathos clearly penetrated into my brain and into my muscle memory, more like a virus. This was absolutely the most maddening side of Pathos, for me. But with this virus inside you, it is even possible to digest a level which has 100 moves, 300 moves, even 900+ moves, it is very interesting…

Alright, Pathos was sick. Great level design, just great. Incredible world concept. Killer ‘permadeath’ concept and of course, very fantastic soundtracks, it was a love at first sight.

But, I must warn you again, this is not a game, this is the evil itself. Finishing it was like escaping from hell. Just try it if you are brave enough, determined enough and patient enough, otherwise, don’t even think about it. It is NO joke!!

review:
PATHOS is a Sokoban-style puzzle game where you have to move blocks out of your way to find a path to the "X"it.
You will get no extra moves from the starting gate, so plan your moves wisely.

From the very beginning of the game, you'll start to be tested on your ability to think laterally and outside of the box.  The first few levels weren't overly difficult, but by the second board, you'll start to scratch your head quite a bit.

As of this writing, I've progressed to the "Moonbud" puzzle.  Since some of these conundrums can take several hours or possibly even days of thinking, it's not going to be a game you're able to blast through unless you're a literal genius or you cheat your way through.

For the price, you'll get your money's worth tenfold.  This is not a game to be finished in 10 or 20 hours although most of your in-game time will be spent thinking and using trial-and-error to get to your solution.

The graphics are simplistic but polished, which is just right for a puzzle game of this difficulty.  Right now there's not a ton of different music selections, but one thing I do like about it is that every once in a while a new music track will slip into the game's playlist at a random stage of progress.  Imaging my surprise when I started hearing an Egyptian-style track playing through the speakers when I hadn't heard it before (it came up at the tail end of the track cycle, not at the beginning.)

Some players have wished for an "Undo" button in the game, but personally I feel this takes away from the game's difficulty and cheapens the experience.  Having to help other friends figure out certain puzzles, this forces me to replay the puzzle all over again--and unless you've got great muscle memory or have captured screenshots of the solutions, it can be easy to forget how you did it in the first place.

If you want a puzzle game that will test your limits and frustrate you while putting all of that frustration on your shoulders (the game is not cheapened by bad controls or mechanics,) then be sure to pick it up.  It's an underrated gem that will fly past most gamers' radars, and should get more attention than it deserves due to its ingenious and maddeningly "easy to learn, horribly difficult to master" level-design.  You'll be glad you did.  I think.  :)

Overall, five stars and well worth the price!

Jokes aside, this game is like if someome took Occam's Razor and made a party fighting game out of it.

It is incredibly easy to learn how to play and extremely rewarding to master.

The left analog stick on a controller controls movement.
The right analog stick controls the sword.

There's a jump button, and a throw sword action. That's it. And yet, due to how much a player can finesse their attack and defensive maneuvers with their swords, as simple as it is, its EXTREMELY expressive gameplay wise!

The movement, while simple, is quick and snappy.

To top it all off, its cheap and and be ran on almost any computer.

Buuuut. I wouldn't recommend this for most people. I only gave it a recommendation rating simply because it executes its ideas slightly less than perfectly. (It can crash occasionally)

Firstly:
it is PC only (at the time of this review).

Secondly:
It is CONTROLLER supported only.
Given the first reason, this already filters out a lot of potential players.

Thirdly:
It is multiplayer only. No bots, people only.
Considering the prior two points... Yeah. Getting the hat trick of niche's would be very difficult.

It is offline only. Good God almighty, getting all four of these things accounted for filters out damn near everyone!
Because the thing is, this sort of niche tends to be more of a console strength than a PC centered one.
These are one of those games than would be absolutely baller on say Switch.
On PC, there's simply too many games that are more accessible to most gamers than this one. Not to mention, said niche's aren't particularly hard hitting on PC these days.

If you do need a game that hits those four niches and you have the offline ride and die homies on standby, you're in for one hell of a ride! If not, I can't say this game's strengths can beat the short comings of simply being unplayable for most folks.

review:
I really don't like discouraging small VR developers because I want more games, but this one just doesn't cut it.

The idea is that it uses your music library to generate the rhythm components, but at best it's just using the tempo to generate the volume of orbs. It really doesn't feel like it has anything to do with your song choice.

It also doesn't come with any pre-loaded music. I know the developers didn't want to license any music, but you at least needs a tutorial song because as it is right now you start the game up for the first time, then have to immediately take off your headset to move music into the correct directory.

I could live with it if those were the only issues, but it's not at all. Compared to so many other VR experiences out there, including free ones, it doesn't look great. And the hit detection on the swords is terrible. I sliced my sword through many orbs that seemed to ignore it completely and I had the best luck trying to poke at them with the tips. Overall, the control schemes need a lot of work and need to be much more accurate (just navigating through the instructions is annoying). Nothing is intuitive and you can't move around at all without moving in the physical world.

It's cheap and seemed like an interesting idea so I gave it a try, but unfortunately Sword Samurai needs a lot more polish to be worth playing.

review:
Drug Dealer Simulator is an ambitious and provocative open-world simulation game that plunges players into the gritty underworld of illicit drug trade, blending dark humor with a surprisingly detailed and multifaceted gameplay experience. Developed by Byterunners Game Studio, this title on Steam offers a unique premise rarely explored with such depth in gaming, inviting players to manage the rise and fall of their own drug empire while navigating the hazards of street-level dealings, law enforcement, and rival gangs. Despite its controversial subject matter, Drug Dealer Simulator manages to craft an engaging and complex world that challenges players to strategize and adapt in a risky, high-stakes environment.

The core gameplay revolves around establishing and expanding a drug operation, starting with small-scale street sales and progressing toward manufacturing, distribution, and territory control. Players must balance various aspects such as sourcing raw materials, producing different types of drugs, and optimizing delivery routes, all while maintaining discretion to avoid police detection. The game offers an impressive degree of freedom in how players approach these tasks, whether through stealthy, low-profile sales or aggressive expansion and domination of rival territories. This layered approach adds depth to the gameplay, as players must constantly assess risk versus reward and make decisions that impact their reputation and survival.

One of the standout features of Drug Dealer Simulator is its open-world design, which immerses players in a detailed urban environment filled with NPCs, potential customers, and law enforcement agents. The city is dynamic and alive, with day-night cycles, varying pedestrian behavior, and random events that create a sense of unpredictability and realism. This environment allows for a variety of playstyles, from cautious, methodical trading to chaotic confrontations and high-speed getaways. The interaction with NPCs is particularly notable, as players must build relationships, negotiate deals, and sometimes manipulate or intimidate others to maintain their business. The attention to detail in this social dynamic enriches the gameplay and reinforces the theme of power and survival in a dangerous world.

Visually, Drug Dealer Simulator employs a gritty, realistic art style that complements its dark and often tense atmosphere. The urban settings, from rundown neighborhoods to seedy back alleys, are rendered with a level of detail that enhances immersion. Character models and animations, while functional, are somewhat basic but sufficient for conveying the game’s mood and narrative tone. The sound design plays a critical role, with ambient city noises, radio chatter, and soundtrack selections that contribute to the overall sense of danger and urgency. The voice acting and dialogue, though not heavily scripted, add personality to key characters and encounters, helping to flesh out the story and stakes.

Despite its compelling mechanics, Drug Dealer Simulator is not without flaws. Some players may find certain gameplay loops repetitive, especially when managing inventory or waiting for production cycles. The AI behavior, both of customers and police, can occasionally feel inconsistent, leading to moments of frustration or unpredictability that detract from immersion. Additionally, the game’s moral ambiguity and depiction of drug culture may not be suitable for all audiences, and it’s important to approach the game with an understanding of its fictional and satirical nature rather than as a glorification of illegal activities. From a technical standpoint, the game has seen improvements through updates, but players may still encounter occasional bugs or performance hiccups depending on their hardware.

The progression system in Drug Dealer Simulator is well-structured, offering a satisfying sense of growth and accomplishment. Players unlock new equipment, drugs, and territories as they expand their empire, with opportunities to upgrade production facilities and transportation methods. This progression encourages strategic planning and investment, rewarding those who carefully manage resources and risk. The inclusion of side missions and random events adds variety and challenges that keep the gameplay fresh. Furthermore, the game’s sandbox nature allows players to experiment with different strategies and playstyles, enhancing replayability.

In conclusion, Drug Dealer Simulator is a daring and engaging simulation game that combines open-world exploration with strategic management in a morally complex setting. Its detailed urban environment, multifaceted gameplay mechanics, and immersive atmosphere create a compelling experience for players willing to explore the darker corners of gaming narratives. While it may not be for everyone due to its subject matter and occasional mechanical rough edges, it offers a fresh and thought-provoking take on the simulation genre. For those interested in unconventional games that blend strategy, storytelling, and open-world freedom, Drug Dealer Simulator presents a bold and memorable journey into a risky, high-stakes underworld.

Rating: 8/10

???????
What the hell is this dumb logic? I understand that HOG games are cheesy most of the time but this is outrageous.

All in all, this game is definitely not worth the 6 Euro. Utter garbage

review:
Unbalance is a game about dropping marbles in order to offset a red, circled marble. The game is built on a concept that's surely existed before, but is taken to the minimalistic level.

===

[b]Pros[/b]

Every single level has a more difficult version of it, significantly lengthening the time to beat the game. I completed the first category in an hour, but the second versions are taking a bit longer.

Physics make sense and once you figure the weight of a marble, it becomes a bit easier to predict how the object in the center will spin.

Clearly more than one game mechanic; The second category involves you removing walls to progress, and there seems to be "gates" in the fourth one.

[b]Cons[/b]

Uses words like "Tap" and "Swipe", implying this is a bit of a rushed mobile port.

Music is just a relaxing tone - while I very much enjoy this genre, it has no variation.
EDIT: Each section has its own though, and that only really applied for the first one.

Menus, in the small amount of time that I used them, have a very mobile UI and doesn't feel right when used with a mouse.

===

This game has a lot of potential, but it needs to feel less like a mobile game. I recommend adding more game mechanics instead of just having "more levels". A short game is great when it feels unique.

Buy this game if you want a quick puzzle that involves the use of gravity, turning, and moving objects.
Don't get it for the graphics, because it's not that sort of game.
