review:
SHORT REVIEW
Wonderful and regularly updated indie game that mixes proper flight simulation with some more adventure/career elements, that satisfy the desire for escape and the great outdoors, allowing you to live them at our own space, whether that's daredevil flying or a more relaxing slow experience. You are a bush pilot in Alaska and have to complete various jobs (delivery etc) or simply fly around for fun. The simulation is focused on STOL (short take-off and landing) with small planes, as the territory you're flying over is w,ild and you would mostly land on improvised airfields. The simulation is rather precise (you can hit rocks and wildlife if you're not careful), graphics are immersive, and control compatibility could be improved. 

LONG REVIEW
This is the kind of game I've been waiting for. I love flight simulation, but I am mostly focused on bush flying on small propeller planes in wild locations, rather than big commercial flights and airports. This title is exactly about this. You are a bush pilot in Alaska (but there are many various maps, including islands and deserts) and have to complete various jobs, or simply enjoy flying about for leisure.

The gameplay is intuitive and rich. You can both use your plane and walk. The flight simulation is accurate: there's a fuel system, the flying and cargo physics are accurate. The game simulates different flying conditions and terrains and you can really interact exhaustively with your plane, including pushing it manually when on the ground. The flying mostly focuses on short trips and short takeoffs and landings on small strips. If you don't enjoy the career mode, you can simply enjoy flying through the maps - however if you are ONLY looking for that, you could just do with Microsoft Flight Simulator or X-Plane. What this game adds to those titles is the proper bush pilot adventure experience: the ability to have jobs to complete, the need to look after yourself and your plane in the wilderness. The fact that you can control a character on foot (in first person) other than the plane, allows for a number of activities that are relevant to flying but cannot be experienced in a traditional simulator. You can physically load cargo on your plane, repair it, upgrade it and refuel it manually (no sliders, you will have to pick up the cargo/tools and walk to the plane to do the job). The availability of a character also enables other dynamics: for instance, there is an (optional) survival mode, with a system of hunger, sleep and stamina, and you can camp and use a variety of tools, which makes the game unique and much more interesting and complete than just a flight simulator. 

The maps are beautifully designed and immersive enough, although I don't believe they represent actual territories and, therefore, they don't rely on photogrammetry. The graphics settings can be really pushed to stellar levels, but my computer doesn't support those. Even with medium resolutions, however, the game is very enjoyable. The day/night cycle is well done, and I like that we can stumble across accurate wildlife.

I haven't yet played any missions, and I'm focusing on exploring the vast territories before I take on any missions. These are optional and can be undertaken at any time. There are three categories of objectives: Exploring, Runways, and Missions.  There are multiple objectives for each category, and the goal of each map is to achieve all of them. I might update the review as soon as I start (or complete!) the missions.

As of today, the game has been constantly updated and considerably expanded with new maps, missions and game dynamics. So the game is very much alive, and it has a community on Discord.

So this is the perfect game for someone who wants to add to the technicality of flight simulation, the thrill and excitement of outdoor adventuring. Whether you like to enjoy the career elements, fly dangerous routes at high speeds with your little bush plane (e.g. flying under bridges or in narrow creeks) or whether you want a more relaxing experience and fly at a leasurly pace to admire the landscape and pick a spot to camp for the night, this is the game for you.

A title like this was long needed. Highly recommended to all lovers of bush flying, but also outdoors and adventure.

review:
This game is a trash fire, but I enjoyed my time with it (at least the first 75%).

I can honestly only recommend this if you like those kind of games like me, or if you like the 3D models enough to push through. Join not-Cloud and not-Zack as you team up with a bunch of girls to reseal an ancient god the evil empire wants to use for evil! Also you meet not-Game of Thrones man. All the guys are much worse than the girls, to not much surprise.

Also if you can't read Japanese, you will get very lost as there's lots of talking, so I wouldn't recommend it in that case.

Bad:
- The game lags if you look at too many halberds. I'm on a high-end computer that can run VR and this game lags badly when looking at certain things. Menu's get really unresponsive too (to counter this, stare at the ground or avoid looking at the halberds!)
- The encounter rate is *way* too high. I got lost in the 封印の地 at the end and gained so many levels before I realized running away was a 100% success rate. (btw the solution is Green -> Red -> Yellow -> Blue, first time the gate didn't activate for me so I wrote it off, then had to dig for what little info there was online). It's really a drag trying to explore a dungeon or heading for a chest when you get into 3 fights just crossing a hallway.
- The combat doesn't really ever get that deep or difficult. Even the last boss I just had two people blast light magic while one healed and the last one threw mana potions all around. Was only around level 31.
- All the 3D models are pretty crude with few animations. Many of the buildings and objects have improper UV texture wrapping.
- The plot tried to set up a lot of stuff, but didn't feel like it really went anywhere. Gotta visit the shrines of the 4 cardinal direction beasts, then fight a bunch of Norse gods.

Good:
- The ability to move in both 2D and 3D is a nice touch! It's fun being able to gaze around the dungeons and world maps as you walk through.
- The enemy designs are kinda charming with how goofy they are honestly.
- Music's nice.
- There's several routes and endings if you end up wanting to go through that again. There's an included text file with the game with route hints.
- The different routes mean different chars can randomly die, which was a neat touch. Sad finding weapons for them after they perished.
- I liked the ice level and wandering into a pile of bone dragons at way too early of a level! Still survived and got to the teleporter, but was sad to see I couldn't do anything at that point in the game haha

Overall, I did enjoy playing this, though I wished it ended like 10 hours earlier honestly. I can't imagine myself going back for the other endings.

review:
I really, really wanted to like this game, but I cannot recommend it to other players...yet.  I'm a U.S. Navy veteran, a student of military history, a life long gamer and I have probably purchased every non-arcade, realistic type, naval video game released...even the terrible ones, so I have some understanding of the subject.  

I'll touch on the bad first.  After attempting for almost four hours just to learn the basics of how to play it, I largely failed.  The manual is minimal at best and is largely unhelpful.  The English needs major editing and redone in many areas.  There are numerous typos, incorrect use of words, poor selection of words to indicate what buttons are for, etc.  The controls are confusing and poorly designed, and I felt like I was actually fighting those  more than the enemy ships.  Same with the windows and how they operate within the game.  

This is a matter of taste, but, visually, I also dislike the blue, poorly imaged turrets and the huge round cannon balls.  This really detracts from an already visually limited game.  Much better, more accurate, representations of turrets can be accomplished at the resolution you are using.  I hope this is something that is just transitional, but we'll see.  There is more, but that's all I'll touch on at the moment.

Ok, for the good...well...it is a serious naval game that gives you both a strategic and a tactic component.  I did have some fun with the Battle of the River Platte inspired scenario, but struggled with the controls with even a single ship, so...   I think the game has serious potential, and with some work can become a very enjoyable game for us naval buffs, but it needs a lotta, lotta work.  It is currently still in it's alpha state imo, and really shouldn't have been released yet without more play testing and development.  I considered asking for a refund, but decided to stick it out and see how things develop.  

I'll offer my assistance to the developers, including editing of the English used, modification of game play, play testing, etc. (for free) if they are interested.

"Naval Battles Simulator is a real-time tactical simulation of World War II sea engagements. It models battleships, cruisers, destroyers, and submarines of several nations.
NBS puts the player in charge of a fleet controlling each ship's course, speed, and weapons. This way, the player detects and engages enemy fleets. What sets this game apart is its detailed model of weather, damage, and fire control. NBS models visibility based on weather, ship signature, and more. So spotting a submarine at night is much harder than spotting a battleship at day. Also, ships can hide in their own smokescreen.
NBS's graphics are basic. But it is a deep simulation of naval battles."

From myself, I can add a few more positive points of the game:
1. good value for money, hours of gameplay for £11.99
2. rare but regular updates
3. great in-game music and radio broadcasts
4. shipyard

Game is worth to support by buying it.

review: The more I play this game the more I see the potential but more the really bad failings.For those old enough to remember, this looks like a re-vamp of an old DOS Game, I think it was something like Great Pacific Sea Battles which was on Amiga and had about 5 different versions.This game reflects that in most ways with a modern twist.It is a slow time, strategy game where you put ships against each other. Its very basic but kind of addictive and will bring out the inner tactician in you.I wish I could give this a neutral review because the developer would appear not to be English, and the English is fairly poor - understandable, but for an English speaker it loses gloss.A lot of the controls are not perfected. For example, if you click on your own ship in the "Damage" screen with your right mouse button, you will either damage your own ship or flood it. Additionally, when you try to purposely flood parts of your ship, you can't stop the balance of water when it stops. It's little things like this that need to be tweaked as they are frustrating parts of gameplay.Additionally, if you choose a battle you can flick between the Axis and Allies - which takes away the fog of war element depending on which side you choose.The Campaign part is the most promising but also the most frustrating - the tutorial gives you a basic idea of how to operate your ship and this works well for the Battles only element. But the Campaign is just difficult to understand.I would love to work on the developers with the English and suggestions on how to make this game better and more usable. For the older generation who don't want all flashy graphics but the equivalent of a large tactical naval game of chess, this game has potential - but needs to be improved to give a solid thumbs up.In its current state its not worth the price tag due to poor English, buggy controls and lack of a Campaign tutorial. But the simplicity and playability of its game is worth investing in, if it was under 10 pounds.Good potential, not finished article yet.

review:
This is a brief update. Basically, I did not recommend this game originally because the AI was not very good and the move balance was not very good either. I have given the game another try after getting a notice from the developers which is appreciated. I tried arcade mode with Dre and found that the experience was much improved from the previous experience. The AI showed a good variety of pokes, zoning moves and anti-air abilities. Although the move barrage from the earlier version is finally gone, the difficulty is still more than sufficient to be considered a fair challenge. This still is very much an Early Access title, but after seeing the improvements made to the AI and effectiveness of the move sets, I think there is hope for this game to look something like a solid title once it makes it out of Early Access. 

Still needs to see improvements graphically and game feature wise. Characters seem to slide on the ground as the sync with the travel distance and walking animations are not quite right. Camera  dynamics are still a bit off. The camera jumps too much when the player 1 and player 2 are shifting around on the stage. Play like this too much and people will be vomiting excessively. Online needs to be a more solid option. Right now, there is some type of backdoor being offered in game but it does not resemble a proper netcode as you would see in other titles. All the characters would need to be completed and a proper intro/training mode made available. 4K is still needed. These things are considered the bare minimum for a fighting game title in 2019. Raise the price if you must. When it comes to fighting games, the FGC prioritizes quality over cheapness.

Original Review:

Needs work. I hope to update to a positive review later. Right now, there is not much of a game other than the cool intro video. Game mechanics and AI need massive overhaul. The AI does not appear to have any fighting game techniques programmed and instead just throws a bunch of random moves in a barrage at the player. No concept of zoning or anti-air or anything like that.  Also, player normals are not well balanced. For a character like Tonio, there is no point in trying to mix up punches and kicks as they are not effective in staggering opponents. 

Also, not sure why default resolution set maxes out at 1080p. Need full 4K support. 

Do I recommend the game? Not yet if you are fighting game fan. I think the idea is exciting as I would like to learn more about the world/Philippines through this game possibly, but it needs a lot of work.

review:
After playing the game for a few hours, i can say that i'm quickly becoming a fan, these characters make me want to go and learn about all of the Filipino icons they were derived from, and i believe that was the whole point of making the game.

As for the fighting system, i do see the potential this the combo system holds, and with a little bit of polish, it could be great.

The game feels like a mix of Marvel and street fighter. I like the idea that instead of 2 buttons being an EX move, you just have to press a special and a direction (diagonal forward if i remember correctly) to get the move to come out, that makes the game more accessible to people who may not be able to pull QCFs consistently, something more fighting games should do.

I have relatively few problems but they can be ironed out. Mostly, i have to set the SFX and Music volume back to zero every time i start the game, maybe that's just nitpicking. Another thing is that the game's AI is flawed at best, fighting the Leon bot is a nightmare because of the ways he uses his tools, he's practically teleporting across the stage. review: On paper, the premise is ideal: a combination of first person gameplay and RTS base-building. The RTSS (realtime strategy shooter) genre holds SO much potential, and it surprising nobody has made a spiritual successor to Battlezone 2 (which was lightyears ahead of its time). The main issue here is that controls are clunky at best, and combine this with the fact that this game is missing some generic RTS elements that would streamline gameplay. For instance, you can't assign groups of units to any sort of hotkey system (something like a rotary menu for unit management would be nice). review:
A short game, with a big flaw. 
I need to say that this game marked a certain part of my life (2020 Lockdown.). So i'll be a [i]little[/i] biased.

I first saw a Spanish YouTuber (Alexelcapo) playing this game, with a rather interesting thumbnail on his YouTube video. It was one night at 4 a.m., and I’m not going to lie — the game hooked me instantly. I pirated it right away, stopping the video at around the 20-minute mark, because the game is expensive and, well, I didn’t have any way to get money other than birthdays or certain special occasions. I enjoyed it so much that I ended up doing an any% deathless speedrun of the entire game (1:44 hrs), despite being a complete newbie to speedrunning. The game meant so much to me that it stuck with me for quite some time. It’s the only memory from 2020 that I can truly treasure.

Five years later, now I can buy my own games, I saw this game on sale on Steam — and you know what? It really caught my interest again. 2020 left a huge mark on me; it was a very different time, and I managed to find peace in the solitude of the things around me back then. So I decided to buy it, taking advantage of the sale, and well… I can’t say much else about it.

The game is quite short (~3–4 hours for a first playthrough, minimum). Right now, I’ve gotten all the achievements, including the extra capsules, just like I did back then. For a $10 game, it delivers a lot of quality in those 4 hours, even if for some people, “only” 4 hours for a first run feels like “a waste of money.” However, beyond its appeal as a “play as the villain-protagonist” kind of game, it has one MAJOR flaw — the cutscenes.

Whenever you perform an action (like pulling a lever) or kill a certain number of enemies required to progress, the game insists on taking away control of your character and shifting the camera to show you what has changed in the environment. And it does this EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. It’s VERY frustrating, YOU pulled a lever of a door that was in front of you? FORCED CAMERA CUT to show THE DAMN DOOR IN FRONT OF YOU.  I don’t remember this being such a big flaw during my first playthroughs — maybe because my memories of 2020 are blurry and I tend to only remember the “good” parts — but it’s something that can really HURT the experience, especially if you dislike losing control of your character.

Honestly, it’s still a gem, and something I’ll keep as one of the good memories 2020 left me.

TL;DR
Short, but great, Expect camera steals every time you do something. Buy if you can live with that. If not, wait for sales. lmao

I got it on sale and would have been very disappointed if I'd paid full price for it. It's not a long or difficult game.

The game strongly feels like it [i] should [/i] be a metroidvania. The cool, labyrinthine lab, the mutation upgrades, the different "zones" of the base. Except it just doesn't play that way. The game is incredibly linear, and will very often close pathways behind you meaning playing through this game felt less like exploring the world and more like being funneled through it. Maybe this design was intended to avoid the usual pitfalls of endless backtracking and aimless wandering in metroidvanias, but I personally felt like it robbed agency from the player. I wasn't making my own choices of where to go, what to investigate, what to attempt to solve. Whenever you encounter a puzzle you immediately solve it, because there is not really any other course of action or direction to take. There's no "aha" moments of using an ability in a new way in one area and realizing how that could be applied to a puzzle you encountered and couldn't solve earlier.

The other aspect I felt that was lacking was the combat. 9/10 times simply barreling into enemies and squishing them with tentacles as quickly as possible was more effective than trying to use any sort of strategy. [spoiler] Your abilities changing with your size/health [/spoiler] did provide some neat opportunities where you might change tactics mid-fight, and those were the combat encounters I enjoyed the most.

Here's a few other things that I found detracted from the game, some minor spoilers in here:
[spoiler] 1) The frontier 'overworld' has a number of one-way doors and passageways that end up locked, which made it a pain to navigate near the end of the game if you're going back to get missed containment units. Why make this difficult? Especially since the game has no map system.
2) The 'invisibility' ability seemed inconsistent, sometimes in combat I would try to use it only to have enemies track me regardless (I'm looking at you, copter drones). Why does it allow you pass by lasers but not the sensors for the latch-bombs? I understand that would break puzzles but it feels like poor design.
3) The upgrades to your electricity gauge felt largely pointless. Puzzles that required you to be invisible didn't need you to have a larger gauge, and as mentioned above the ability wasn't particularly useful in combat so having more juice didn't matter there as well. In big red form your keratin shield is mainly for the latch-bombs which drain your whole meter anyhow. Personally I found in combat I would drop from red mode to green mode so quickly I didn't get to use the yellow modes keratin spike ability all that much later in the game when I actually had gotten some of the electro upgrades.
4) Enemy variety also felt a little lacking, and this contributed to combat feeling underwhelming and repetitive. [/spoiler]

Positives: Art was excellent and visually the game was very easy to interpret. Movement of the creature was awesome [spoiler] although sometimes while in the large form I'd accidentally get sucked down a one-way tube I didn't intend to enter [/spoiler]. Concept was really cool, the idea of being the eldritch horror monstrosity that escapes the lab is quite a fun reversal.

I really wish I could recommend this game because I feel like it could've been awesome, but mainly because of the linear nature of the gameplay I just couldn't enjoy it as much as I would have wanted.

review: Imagine a laboratory where there have been made so many heinous and twisted experiments on a specific creature and our goal is to stop it before it destroys humani-... wait, what? Phobia Game Studio really wants me to be the monster? Well, now things got so much more interesting! CARRION is a Metroidvania genre game where you try to find your way out from this Godforsaken laboratory while optionally taking as many lives as you want with you. First things first, I need to say CARRION is my first Metroidvania game and it was definitely a decent time, but it overstayed its welcome real quick. You might want to ask something like: "Buddy, you finished both the main game and the DLC in 5 hours at best. How can you say something like it overstayed its welcome? It's not even that long!" I understand where you're coming from, so let me tell you why. When you begin the game and start learning how everything works, it feels like a really nice and smooth experience. Then it continues that way with a few new mechanics sprinkled around it. I feel like new features are not only very few, they could have been used a lot more than what we got and because of that, the game starts feeling dry and loses its charm real quick. I feel like the game could have finished 2 hours earlier and it would have felt much better. Yeah, I know it would be an extremely short game, but at least it wouldn't lose its charm like it did for me. So, the game having a lot fewer features than I expected, meanwhile still having a lot to do in it, made the end of my run feel extremely redundant. So, that's a con I can definitely bring up. Other than that, it was a decent time. I just think because of that con, I might never play this game again. Not just because it's bad or anything, just because game felt like a chore after some time. Other than that, I have seen some reviews mention they felt lost in the locations and they felt like this game needed a map, but I completely disagree. The entire time I played this game, I only felt like I got lost once and it was at the end of the game, other than that it was really easy to find my way out. Overall, it's definitely a pleasant game to give a shot at if you are looking for a simple and fun entry to the Metroidvania genre.

I gotta be real this chapter was... not as good. I feel like it messes with the pre-established lore of homestuck. 
-
(MAJOR SPOILERS FOR CHAPTER AND HOMESTUCK BELOW)
-
For starters, Karako. He is absolutely adorable, but the ending where he dies doesn't really make sense. The Dark Carnival was a fabrication made by Doc Scratch to get the purplebloods to further Lord English's goals. Washington D.C. was briefly renamed Dark Circus in the Alpha-kid timeline, and Vriska and Meenah eventually wandered into a dream bubble OF a carnival that they mused mighta been the place, but they almost immediately realize that's probably not the case and it's just some rando abandoned carnival (with a tatoo parlor). I mean yeah it was kinda funny but... eh. 

Secondly, It's weird that sea-dwellers are that strong. It's been stated before that Equis's strength is relatively unique to him. But the writing repeats at least 3 times in the space of maybe 5 minutes, "Damn, they're so tough." One guy literally get's gored by some sort of little shop of horrors plant knock-off and he just walks it off. It retroactively claims Polypa told you they were tough but, in her chapter, it was pretty implied that she just snuck up and ganked a guy, and any difficulty was in that sea-dwellers are well guarded and influential VIP's. Feferi got shot clean through and she DIED, and she's higher on the hemospectrum than they are. Granted it was a little different but... still.

Finally Marsti. I just... do not get what they're going for. She seems to imply she just cleans to clean but the second she sees Folykl it's like she's almost turned on. She seems genuinely fed up with you and your lack of awareness all the way to the end of the "good" route but is suddenly smiling with you like you're pals anyways. It almost feels like it's treating you as borderline unintentionally racist to lowbloods based off of assumptions you make so yeah, guilt-tripping. Fun.

The character designs and songs were great, as were the backgrounds. As far as art goes this chapter did maintain the quality. And, granted, I get the adventures of the MSPA reader are absolutely non-canon, and friendsim is here to tide the fanbase over until the next installment of the main game, but I was always under the impression the worldbuilding was accurate. Like everyone interested in the deeper dynamics of Alternian culture could finally get a peak. It feels like either 
A-
This is newly developed canon and we have to live with it, or 
B- 
I'm overthinking it. Which judging by the size of this review is quite possibly the case but we're 14 volumes in and this is the first hint of acanonness I've noticed.

Still eagerly awaiting the next one but coming off the last installment this chapter was a bit of a let down.

stepped back into the fight-tutorial just to proof myself that this game unfortunately got worse over the last couple of updates, not better... what i noticed so far are some bugs in the fight-tutorial ( enemys without shields dont give the same feedback when hit then the one with shields), and a confusion in the camera control description. i really dont know why you call the classic camera the "third person camera" (even tho both are third person cameras lol) and the new camera setting "classic camera". maybe this second option was viable to begin with, at this point i find it very hard to control, especially in biggger groups of people. the fighting overall feels buggier, maybe its just a feeling, maybe the very accurate control system cant handle moving arenas well, but you get a feeling of inconsistency with hitboxes, even tho im sure its consitend in itself and just gets buggy when you're too close to an enemy. Butm what itches me the most at the moment is an (appareantly) updated reputation system. Before some major updates, it was little to no problem to get all your patrons on a positive reputation and scaling. now, it wasnt possible for me to keep atleast one up on positive reputation when not solely focusing on one. i can imagine this was changed to make the game more harder and acutally give every patron a bit of exclusivity, since you need to decidide for which one you want to fight mainly. I really like the idea, but its frustrating to choose a patron for a fight and get punished by this exact patron, because you were in negative reputation with him. I think the biggest problems the game has atm are some fairly minor issues (like the inconsistency in combat at some pionts or the patron system) wich makes the game feels taxing at points where it really shouldnt be. i know the game is supposed to hard, but it shouldnt punish you for doing things "right". Getting a bad event with a patron because yopu ignored them too much or because you betrayed your favorite patron, totally legit. Getting a bad event with the patron you try to build up reputation with feels just.. not real. it somehow destroys the immersion in this over all very immersive and realistic feeling game.

That being said, i would give it time. the Idea is great, i actually like the fighting style once you get it. You will struggle with your character, being low on life at the end of a week still being forced to fight, which is probably the best for me personally, this feeling of immersion and unique-ness(?) of every run. Different classes and traits add really good into that, just like the new random events (getting robbed after a day of fighting for example is pretty neat if you win then against what you thought will be 1 men and ended up being 5).

If you are willing to get into the fighting system, definetly give it a try. But I personally really hope the developer will concentrate a bit more on smoothen the game and its features, instead of adding a ton of new ones at this moment.

review:
6/10, tournaments from mount&blade turned into own game. Alright for EA, but needs a lot more effort to be more than a one-shot game.

The game is currently extremely janky and unbalanced. Some of jank can be discarded as user error as the combat is supposed to be physics-based, and as a result is somewhat more complicated. However, I felt that a lot of the balancing steers the player away from the more fun ways to engage with this game.
First and foremost, the stamina is very restrictive. It runs out way too quick and takes way too long to recover. This is probably meant to limit how much you can attack, and force you into blocking/parrying, but what I ended up seeing is that most of the time I played I spent just awkwardly walking around the arena with enemies right at my heels, getting a few hits here and there when the opportunity arose. Rather than an exciting fighting game it ended up becoming an awkward herding puzzle. Most enemies can not deal with you simply walking away from them, with maybe the occasional "boss"-type guy being fast enough to catch up and get a cheeky hit in, but even that felt like undeserved jank rather than the game trying to punish me for playing "incorrectly".
There are a lot of different weapons to choose from (even if they are functionally mostly the same), but sadly the weapons come off as very underpowered due to the AI's obsession with shields. I had many instances where the enemy would stop fighting me just to run across the map into some random ditch to pick up a shield. Breaking these shields takes a lot of effort and feels very frustrating to work against. Admittedly, there is a factor of the game's fighting system being physics-based and needing some time to adjust, but flip-side is that this is very common even on low-level fights and as such might murder the motivation to learn this game.
Managerial game around the fighting feels very shallow.. There is a shop where you are meant to get equipment, but it is randomized, you get very limited inventory, and good stuff is prohibitively expensive, so I did not interact with it too much. It could be a bit more engaging, but maybe this is fine as it also gets out of your way very quickly to allow you to concentrate on the fights.
Controls feel very clunky and unpolished. For example, your character will drop their shield after you attack with your weapon requiring you to press the button again to get your shield up. Some attacks might come off weird, or not even occur at all due to characters' limbs getting stuck or something, I am not really sure. Level geometry might eat your attacks, especially if you are fighting with longer weapons (though, this may be okay if the game signals this properly). Dashes are very underpowered and I basically never used them.

Overall, "okay" for an EA, but needs a lot of effort to be more than one-shot experience.
At the current state it is maybe recommendable for fans of mount&blade-style sword fighting who can tolerate some jankiness.

review:
TLDR: A damnably good game, effectively functioning as the 28 weeks later of zombie strategy games. With the Large variety of units, variety of strategies to employ, open space for experimentation and civilian management, it really hits the feeling of 'Containment and Evacuation' it was built to represent.

NOW for the more detailed Review:

First thing I should mention is the Team itself. I had never met a team that will, upon hearing that a player is having a game breaking issue, sit down and work on a patch for that critical issue. And yet, the Cepheus team has does so, with issues I reported to make sure the game works. Not "We'll look into it and push an update eventually", instead pushing out a test version to make sure that the problem is solved. THAT is something truly special! 

As for the game itself, It has an impressive amount of variety for the rather direct concept of "End the infection, contain the threat." You can play as the saviour, Pushing infantry and trying to isolate the infection early on. Or if you want to, You can abandon the civilians and instead focus on fortifying and evacuating areas that you deem savagable. OR go full spec ops, using small elite teams to eliminate and cripple critical infected and slow it down.

You have an incredible amount of control over your forces, down to individual weapons, specialising troops into roles like CQC specialists with shotguns, Flame throwers and Barbed wire. You have Snipers, Machinegunners, Spec ops, Scientists that harvest information or check civilians, helicopters, defensive buildings and even MLRS and Artillery. It's so much fun!

Like RTS' of old, you can build massive and sprawling bases to support your endeavours, using them to facilitate you campaign against the infected. The best part in my opinion. Especially being able to set up FOB's in the enemy's territory and focusing their attention on you.

Alongside that is the infected themselves. They will swarm and harass you in turn, using special forms to burrow under and around you, traverse the waterways with swarms, and simply bash through your lines with juggernauts. And you can tweak them. Want a pure horde game mode? Remove the giants and ravens and purely deal with the teeming mass. OR want the beasts threatening you immediately? You can set them to do so. Tweak the enemy to your desires. 

Controls are classical RTS, which feels great and responsive. The camera can get RIGHT into the action, from nearly directly above your troops shoulders to see who they are shooting. It's great!

I love the game, and respect the hell out of the team.

HOWEVER, it's not perfect. The development team struggled with organising plans for content and sticking to them, but they do make regular progress and keep the community informed of their decisions. The AI, for the moment, is fairly basic and the infected don't do creative things intentionally. (Both being actively worked on and with plans to improve them in the coming months)

There's also the Limited map variety. There's two, featuring dense cityscapes, and that does result in the environments seeming VERY similar. I personally love cities in RTS, but this isn't for everyone I am aware.

And the last issue for me is the Slow spread of the infected themselves, which you can't really speed up. The infection can take a long time to spiral out of control, which can be exploited. With the coming updates, they are planning to improve this as well, and modding will eventually allow FAR greater changes for the game. But THAT isn't here yet, so what we have is what we get.

HOWEVER, That's not enough to ruin it for me. The game's fun, it's random, you can play it the way you want and be able to set it up in a way that you can enjoy. It feels like a proper 28 weeks later style game, and frankly that's something that I ADORE! 

It's a great game, and unique in both premise and execution. with a passionate and active dev team who have poured their soul into the project.

review:
I would love to leave a positive review of this game, because I really want the game it will be if it comes together. Many of the concepts are really great. Unfortunately the execution is currently not. I would love to change this review to positive if some of my feedback gets addressed.

=== Problems ===

I've checked back in with this game many times since purchasing it in 2021. Back then it was in a rough state, but the vision was clear and I enjoyed what was there. Performance and unit pathing were rough but it was early days.

Fast forward to 2025, and those issues feel worse now than in 2021. Layers of complexity have been added - for example the civilian & faction systems - and lots of mechanics have been reworked, but the beating heart of the game is unworkable; performance, unit pathing & UI all make it very tough to remain engaged for more than an hour or so.

Unit pathing is an unmitigated disaster. If you want to get your ground vehicles to even go down an unobstructed road, you will usually have to individually micromanage them down it to avoid them getting hung up on invisible obstacles or plowing into fences and buildings. With the additional problem of civilians now building encampments in the middle of roadways, the problem is worse now than ever. Your civilian evacuation buses will also get stuck and/or become orphaned if their parent building is destroyed, leaving them sitting around cluttering up the map in an irretrievable state.

If I play for an hour or more, it's almost guaranteed that multiple music tracks (calm vs combat) will start playing over the top of each other, which you have to fix by going into the main menu and changing the audio quality.

Unit controls have not improved since 2021. Without getting bogged down in UI design, I'll just say it's a very rough and fiddly experience, especially if you have mixed infantry squads with lots of toggleable abilities. There are also loads of little toggles and things you can twiddle with, most of which will either have absolutely no impact, or will have an impact but there's literally no reason not to always have them on one setting or the other, resulting in micromanagement busywork. I'm looking at you, weapon suppressors and flashlights. When I look at the UI in this game I simultaneously feel like there are a million unnecessary toggles, and yet also some very obviously missing toggles that would improve QoL for unit control.

All of this would be forgivable but for the performance. My *god* the performance. I have a strong PC, and it starts out fine, but the ambitious scale of the game quickly outreaches the ability to deliver it with performant code. By the mid-game - if you have even as little as 30-40 units and are battling hordes of infected - you can expect single digit frame rates once combat begins. It is effectively unplayable by the mid-game, making you just want to either rush a cheesy win rather than engage in any of the actual strategic fun the game tries to offer, or simply give up playing.

There will be infected units juddering across the screen unintelligibly, and your units will be getting obliterated by things you couldn't even see - either by range attacks with missing VFX or by smudge-like enemies moving across the screen at mach 7 at 3 fps, the icons for which the game has given up attempting to render half of. It is particularly miserable at night, where all you have to go on is a stuttering sea of icons. Lowering all settings to Low does nothing to mitigate this really, as most of those reduce GPU overhead - the problem is CPU performance.

I will also say that I think the attempt to include a 1st person shooter mode in the game was misguided. I love games that do it well, like the old Battlezone, but it's fundamentally not suited to a game with this pace of combat and with this much micromanagement and logistics required to stop your units dying in a flash, or just to get them from point A to point B frankly. As it stands the attempt to mesh these incompatible systems has done nothing but slow and dilute development in my view. Even if performance were good it wouldn't make sense with combat this swingy - with performance as it is, there's nothing in the world that would make me want to take 1st person control of an operative.


=== Suggestions ===

- Top priority: Identify the performance bottlenecks and work to optimise them. Cull features if necessary; none of it is usable in the current state. You can have the best mechanics in the world, it's no good if nobody can play them. Every time I come back to the game, various systems have been reworked or switched around, added and removed. But the performance has rendered this largely meaningless, as none of it is enjoyably playable once the infected build up in numbers.

- Second priority: Unit pathing. Ground vehicles above all else, though humanoid units could also use some work - they clump up and get confused frequently, or get hung up on buildings.

- Slow the pace of combat right down. I mean *right* down. Special infected unit movement is SO fast that it looks like a bug not a feature. Ranged attacks are almost undetectable visually. The game has extremely low visual clarity as a result. Right now engagements feel like a conveyor belt delivering hundreds of enemies per second into your firing line. Sounds great, and it would be if it were just zombies, but the volume of special infected that can come out of nowhere and deal enormous damage means you afford the player basically no agency to react or plan or understand what is happening on the screen. Re-balance speed, health and damage stats as necessary such that the combat doesn't exist on a nanosecond knife-edge and the player can get a feel for the impact of individual entities on the screen, react by retreating/repositioning/reinforcing, learn, and respond.

Slowing combat down would also serve to make 1st person much more tenable, though frankly I think that system should just be scrapped entirely unless vast improvements can be made to controls, unit autonomy and unit pathing.

- Make building feel better by providing a toggle for snap alignment. Right now you have to manually orient every single thing and it's a royal pain to build a nice base. It feels like wading through sludge to line things up nicely. Snap alignment (15 degree increments for example) would will speed up base building and improve flow.

- Reduce the negative impact of map clutter and obstructions by making scenery get destroyed by vehicles and explosions, removing their collision. I'm talking about trees, fences, random freight containers, whatever. As it stands, these things contribute very negatively to unit pathing, mostly affecting ground vehicles. Making ground vehicles able to simply roll over and destroy these things would be a huge improvement, rather than perpetually getting stuck on every collidable thing on the map. Nothing can be done about buildings, that will require improvements to pathing itself.

- A toggle for making transport helicopters automatically land / unload at their destination. It is surprisingly onerous to have to constantly send your helicopter from point A to point B, then wait for them to arrive, then have to tell them to land, then wait for them to land, then do whatever you need to do. It makes resupply annoying for attack helicopters too.

Focusing on QoL features like this would go a long way throughout. For example why not have a simple toggle to have units automatically turn on their lights at night time, and off at day time? I doubt many players want to have to babysit these rudimentary things.


=== Conclusion ===

This review probably seems harsh, but I wouldn't post it if I didn't think this game had great bones, and I really hope to see some of this addressed. There's clearly a lot of love put into this project, and I want to have the good time it keeps threatening me with.

+The art is good and the visuals are showcased well in the video trailer
+User friendly and easy to navigate and progress

-Have to do each level 5 times for both difficulties to 100% achievements
-Can't take Steam Screenshots in the game
-Steam broadcasting is not compatible with this game

Rather, the developers saw fit to have one decent sale and then make the game Free.

There are 21 levels total, with one hour-long play through all of them enough to 100% the achievements if that's what you're going for. I daresay earning three stars on all of the levels would be next to impossible though as cows love getting stuck on fences, then hopping over your horse and rocketing back the way they were just herded from. Later levels see a catapult function added, which if you're unlucky will drop all your cows on top of each other and cause the silly things to lock up until you ride a ways away from them.

I crashed out of Moo Moo four separate times, along with two lockups during level loading. Audio sometimes breaks for no apparent reason, and two levels contain weirdly loud bird chirping. Visuals and controls on the other hand are good, kind of surprising honestly. Closing the game though must be done via Task Manager as they couldn't be bothered to add an Exit button.

If you're curious, it's Free and an easy 100% although the confidence metric being left on the store page means this one will never count towards your completed games list.

I played the demo.  I liked the demo.  I purchased this game because of the demo and the "cool" looking graphics and style.

And then...  I quickly discovered a lesson I've learned long ago with games.  "Don't judge a book by its cover"
While this game seems to take its inspiration from the movie "World War Z" and it has frantic, fast, and relentless zombies... it quickly turns into nothing more than running in circles kiting the zombies over and over and over and over and over and over.  "Zombie Kiting 2020" would have been a much more fitting name for this game that in the end is about as shallow at that ditzy blonde we all knew in high school.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i4fgvOJtdLo&feature=youtu.be

I really did want to like this game.  But it just fades too fast and lacks any depth what-so-ever and this makes it lose it's initial luster very quickly.

- There are no power-ups, no different guns to buy or earn, no character upgrades of any kind, nothing to craft, no bosses, no real progression that makes you feel like you're advancing in any way.  Ugh.

- While I understand this is a zombie shooter, some kind of story and reason for why we are here would help

- Three maps and many different waves of zombies, but it doesn't matter what map or what wave you advance to, it's just the same thing as before.. run around in circles until all the zombies form a line behind you allowing you to stop and shoot, run and reload, stop and shoot, run and reload, stop and shoot, run and reload.. rise and repeat 1,000 times over.  Zzzzz.  It looks "cool" and the graphics are awesome, but it just quickly loses it's initial burst of appeal.. kinda like a cool firework that looks amazing for 3 seconds and then you're left looking into the cold night air.

- Another game that proves once again that we need to STOP judging games, movies, books, and people by what they look like at first glance and start searching deeper.  This game scored a perfect 10 out of 10 score from me in the "graphics" department, but because it's so damn shallow in gameplay and depth, it only mustered a total score of a 65%.

Not Recommended... unless the price drops to $3 or under OR the developer(s) adds substance to the game to keep it interesting and make it something other than running around in circles kiting the zombies over and over and over and over.

review:
[SHORT]

UNDERRATED... to an extent.

Yes if you play local. Best fighting game gameplay I've played for amateurs and pros! (But get it on discount)
No if you want content/progression/Online players. The typical Fighting Games problem...

Also, thanks for gate-keeping some extra stuffs, Square Enix... Not! (I will buy them if they're available forever, and yes I freaking like MAAB)

3/5 - Recommend: Apart from the gate-keep and lack of stuffs to do, I don't know.



[LONG]

  In a genre that's hard to even pick-up and play, with many, including veteran FGCs, not seeing the REAL issues with many devs trying to make them accessible but failed for many reasons (and I consider myself an amateur who played and struggled those "easy" FGs like DNF Duel and BlazBlue), MAAB might be one of THE best FGs that combines the best of accessible approach and professional satisfaction!
 And that's impressive considering this is a Fast-Pace Fighter, the one sub-genre I typically recommend avoiding for amateurs.

  Gameplay wise you look at it and say "This looks hard", but it isn't as bad as you think, and I'm telling you as an amateur. Choose a playable Character, 3 Assists, pay attention to the Element System and... go have fun! As simple as it sounds. Even motion inputs attacks aren't gruesome,typically it's just v->, Z and v-< for Assists, with some few <-v-> and 360 Motion inputs. (although v-v is more superior then Z motion input, I just hate to try to use a projectile only to somehow get a Z attack...)

 MAAB (or more precisely: Team Arcana) understands the issues of FGs even I didn't saw it coming. To picture an example: Combos and Damage Scaling.

 In many Fast-Pace FGs, you make a decent 10-ish combo you make moderate damage, but not good enough. 15-ish isn't even competitively viable while damage scaling "commence" and 20-ish is now competitive while damage scaling still isn't feeling like it's screwing you over until you make an absurd amount. It feels "reward the good players, gate-keep the n00bs" -or scrubs. Also, doing combos is typically hard, like VERY hard...
 In MAAB, 10-ish is considered very acceptable. 15-ish is actually competitive while feeling the damage scaling is really kicking in, and 20-ish is, I mean yeah, it's objectively good, but also have you seen the damage scaling??? It's literally saying "Woah, hey buddy that's cool, but I must do my job." Damage and damage scaling just feels right as how it should be without being to weirdly easy as GG Strive. Oh, and the combos are fun, not "impossible."

 "But practicing a Character and Assists to find its combo and all is boring..." NO. No it isn't for MAAB. Somehow, the sandbox is as fun and customizable as... Call of Duty! I'm serious.
 Choosing your Character is like choosing your weapon. Choosing the Assists is like choosing  equipments/attachments, and yes they're easy to use even in combos. It can even help cover a Character weakness like lack of projectile. And the Elements are like Perks!

 So the Elements comes as follows: Fire is the "I wanna do more damage by just contact" (Note: In Training it doesn't read the Fire damage, so if you thinks it's useless it's actually working), Ice makes your foe longer to move to make more Combos and Wind heals you (my favorite!). (Oh and there's a fourth one: N/A, which of course does nothing)
 Then there's Element Combo, which if attack again with the same Element it adds a multiplier of that attack, kinda countering the Damage Scaling (and even if you use a different Element it'll not cancel that other Element bonus, only if you drop the Combo) and Element Counter -Note: thankfully you're not at a disadvantage for choosing an Element Character and being attacked by the "strong versus this" Elements, a la RPG, but instead if you use an attack/Assist Elements after using a specific Element the foe will "freeze" longer (nice RPG reference!).

 The Characters are so cool and fun, and yes there's attractive ones but here's the thing: it's not just limited to Womans (Team Arcana are more inclusive then the Wokes???). There's even SE Crossovers, MA Protagonist outside of the main game (including a cancelled MA game), a unique, unplayable boss and SNK Legendary KoF Fighter: Iori Yagami (so make some noise!).


 Aaannnd then there's the negative.

 No content or progrresion. You can beat it in a couple of hours. What isn't new other then this outdated content? (I feel I got scam, like rather then having a full game I bought a demo!).
 No players Online plus uses the ol' delay-base netcode.

 That may look small, but look how many time I put. I want to play more but the game doesn't offer me that... How it isn't a small issue in the end?
 Now typically I would not recommend it, but this is the only Fighting Game so far that captured my heart, something many have failed or where close.

 Wait, I almost forgot: somehow doing a diagonal input (like doing a quarter forward circle) is hard to do because it's more strict/bugged? It's not impossible and can be understand, but that's weird.

To my Brain it's a 4/5, to my Heart a 5/5 gameplay wise, but an 3/5 in the end...

Also some gatekeep it because of an censorship to an assist? (And a character butt) Really? Like, don't get me wrong the end result is stupid, but also SE has nothing to do, apparently (It's not censored in Japan INCLUDING the PS4 version).
Don't let Million Arthur Arcana Blood be underrated!

review:
It hurts to give a negative review here, but this isn't an early access title: it is barely a tech demo. This is a very, very early alpha product that is very exciting for people who are into fencing, but will be very negatively received by people who are not. It is frankly irresponsible to even have this on the Steam store in this state. This is a demo only, and even by the standard of demos it is incomplete.

All that said, there is real gem in development here if it finishes. People of a particular age will remember an old Playstation series called Bushido Blade, and this has taken some pretty clear inspiration from it. This does lead to very frustrating exchanges where it is not clear why one blow was taken without apparent effect while another ends the round, though. The development team would do well to expose this information better, perhaps in the form of an abstracted paper doll if a traditional health bar is unacceptable. 
This issue is compounded by the core parrying system being fundamentally broken - the game relies on the traditional fencing principles of distance, proportion, and time and it sometimes captures these well, but it rests on a very shaky auto-block system where if you are not in an attack animation (or are holding backwards) you will parry. This system works inconsistently however, and leads to gameplay that is the antithesis of good fencing: it feels random and capricious.

All that said, this is an exciting project however, and though I *should* refund, I will not. I will instead warn other buyers that they wait until this is in a better state before purchasing, unless they are invested in the success of the project for other reasons beyond simply enjoying a game.

review: After transitioning from Half Sword to this game - Hellish Quart wipes the floor with Half Sword! Though some people might like the rubber-bandy, fast paced, and sometimes comical parts of Half Sword, I would rather play a game that takes itself seriously. I don't want this to be a compare and contrast of Half Sword and Hellish Quart, so I'll talk about some parts that make this game enjoyable; at least for me. Firstly, this game's realism is outstanding! From the way characters drop when wounded or injured, to the variety of techniques included within the move-sets of characters (that real HEMA experts use btw!), this game is amazing. Second, what I also love about this game is how much VARIATION this game holds. Several maps, dozens of characters each with their own backstories and traits, basically the types of characters you can play. From Turkish jannisary, to a Scottish Traveler, to bandits, drunkards, and straight-up duelists. Lastly, the different game-modes you can play are neat. Survival, a point-based mode where you see how long you can fight without losing (and you have ONE life), or a full story campaign with great voice acting and story-telling that immerses you into the world of 16th century Poland, or just a mode for training, whether you want to face an opponent in HEMA equipment, without any bloodshed or intense combat, or just a standing enemy to practice attack combos on. review:
Hellish Quart is a distinctive and ambitious fighting game developed by Kubold that seeks to revive and reimagine the art of classical European swordplay. Departing from the over-the-top combos and fantastical moves typical of many fighting games, Hellish Quart opts for a slower, more deliberate pace that emphasizes realistic fencing techniques and physics-based combat. This approach creates a deeply immersive and strategic experience that appeals not only to fighting game enthusiasts but also to history buffs and fans of martial arts simulation.

The game’s visual style is one of its most immediately striking features. Utilizing hand-painted character models and fluid animations captured through motion capture, Hellish Quart presents sword fighting in a way that feels both authentic and artistically beautiful. The character designs reflect historical accuracy, showcasing a variety of European warriors and duelists from the 17th and 18th centuries, each equipped with period-appropriate weapons and attire. The attention to detail in the movements—from parries and lunges to ripostes and footwork—is meticulous, emphasizing the weight and momentum of every strike and block. This level of authenticity lends a unique gravitas and elegance to each duel.

Gameplay in Hellish Quart is a masterclass in timing, positioning, and reading your opponent. Unlike traditional fighting games that rely on combos or flashy special moves, this title demands patience and tactical thinking. Combat is governed by realistic physics, meaning each strike follows believable trajectories and can be countered or redirected. The stamina system adds another layer of strategy, forcing players to manage their energy carefully and avoid reckless attacks. Matches can be intense psychological battles, where a single well-timed parry or feint can turn the tide. This makes the game rewarding but also challenging, with a steep learning curve that encourages players to study their opponents and improve their skills continually.

The single-player content includes a story-driven campaign that introduces players to the world and its characters, providing context and motivation for the duels. The narrative, though not the central focus, is engaging and grounded in historical and fictional elements that enrich the setting. Additionally, Hellish Quart offers training modes and tutorials that are invaluable for newcomers trying to grasp the complexities of classical sword fighting. The game also supports online multiplayer, which is where the true test of skill lies. Facing off against human opponents highlights the depth of the combat system and the need for adaptability and mental acuity.

Sound design and music contribute significantly to the immersive atmosphere. The clashing of blades, the subtle footfalls, and the rush of air from swinging swords are all rendered with crisp, realistic audio that enhances the tension and drama of each encounter. The soundtrack complements this with period-inspired compositions that underscore the game’s historical flavor without overwhelming the action.

While Hellish Quart excels in many areas, it’s worth noting that its focus on realism and technical combat may not appeal to everyone. The slow pacing and emphasis on precision over spectacle can feel less accessible to casual players or those accustomed to faster, more forgiving fighting games. The learning curve can be daunting, and matches may sometimes drag as players engage in cautious maneuvering. Additionally, the online player base is still growing, which can affect matchmaking and the availability of skilled opponents at times.

Visually, the game runs smoothly on a range of systems, and its stylized art direction helps it stand out from more graphically intense fighting games. The UI is clean and functional, designed to convey necessary combat information without cluttering the screen or detracting from the duel’s cinematic feel. Frequent updates and community feedback have helped the developers refine mechanics and add content, indicating a commitment to long-term support and improvement.

In summary, Hellish Quart is a refreshing and innovative fighting game that challenges conventional expectations of the genre by focusing on realistic swordsmanship and tactical depth. Its beautiful animation, meticulous attention to historical detail, and thoughtful gameplay mechanics create a unique and compelling experience for players willing to invest time and patience. While it may not be for those seeking fast-paced, flashy action, it stands out as a sophisticated and elegant title that celebrates the art and discipline of classical fencing. For anyone interested in a more thoughtful, skill-based fighting game with a historical twist, Hellish Quart is a rare gem worth exploring.

review:
[b]Battlestar Galactica Deadlock: Sin and Sacrifice[/b] is the newest expansion for Battlestar Galactica: Deadlock. It adds 2 new ships - Gorgon and Heracles gunship, a brand new campaign which picks up after Anabasis/TBA along with various gameplay adjustments as well as the Veterancy update. It is also the conclusion to the "First Season" of Deadlock's storyline. 

In the Sin and Sacrifice campaign, you continue fighting in the First Cylon war with either your old fleets (by importing saves) or by starting anew. This time around, there is more emphasis placed on the dozen campaign missions rather than combat encounters (although side missions are still around along with Cylon occupation). The story picks up where it left off with TBA/Anabasis, with you taking command of the fleet once again, this time trying to beat back a Cylon offensive. The new missions have much more work put into them when compared to TBA or main game, with focus on environments along with other aspects. This time around they feel more challenging, which I appreciate. The new campaign goes to interesting places, takes more risks and most often manages to pull them off. The only issues I had with them were minor bugs along with some really unnecessary hand holding in some missions. Either way, I found the direction that this expansion took to be quite interesting and playing through it was definitely worth it.

The new ships, Gorgon and Heracles, are neat additions as well. Gorgon is a Cylon support ship that seems to work nicely with fighter-centric fleets, buffing squadrons and working as a utility craft. The Heracles Gunship is somewhat of a successor to the Minotaur gunship - it has every inch decked out with guns along with flak ability, making it a force to be reckoned with in the battlefield. 

The Veterancy update also introduced some other features - a music player, fleet chatter and crew veterancy system along with some other minor tweaks or features. The in-game music player is a neat addition which lets you pick and play any of the in-game soundtracks. The fleet chatter is quite nice as well, adding some more life to your fleet and squadrons. You feel a lot more immersed with it. The crew veterancy system is also quite nice - as you win battles and keep your ships alive, you gain bonuses that improve your ships. Some of the bonuses are gimmicky, while others are more useful, e.g. firewall strength. I would have, however, preferred the exp gain to be faster or less demanding. 

Overall, I think the Sin and Sacrifice expansion is definitely worth picking up, thanks to the new missions, ships, fleshed out combat and the other tweaks. I felt a bit more interested in the storyline this time around, as well as found the new features to be quite neat. Also, the soundtrack is excellent (I can't stress this enough)! My only complaints would be some of the minor design choices (I would have preferred some leniency in certain missions) as well as a few glitches that didn't necessarily impact the experience.

Even though the days and nights pass in about a minute of real time, playing this LOW EFFORT UNITY TRASH for 100 minutes would be like stabbing your eyes with rusty nails for 100 minutes.  Ugh.

Watch my First Impressions Gameplay HERE:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gr5YKu_2_es&feature=youtu.be

You run around in a circle on a very small map with the same default buildings pasted over and over around while blank white and red boxes fall from the sky.  Collect them to add to your health and ammo respectively.  The "zombies" are really horrid looking flat sprites with no animation that slide at you and vanish into thin air when shot.

Rinse and Repeat for 100 minutes.  Ugh.  No thanks.

Absolute trash.  NOT RECOMMENDED.

My Score:  10%  (1 out of 10)

------------- UPDATE on May 9, 2019 ---------------

The developer's response shows me he is actually a legit developer who tried to make a "fun" game, but maybe lacks the experience and development time to have made this better.  He asked me what I thought could make this game better.. so here is my list of suggestions for this developer  (Take them or leave them, these are just my suggestions that I think would make this game better):

1) Learn how to make the AI "NOT" go thru walls to get to your X Y position
..This will be VERY important as you continue to develop games.  I'm sure there are tons of good AI videos on youtube for Unity so your enemies don't go thru walls.  Having enemies just move at ease right through walls and hit you/kill you feels cheap and cheap deaths make people rage.  

2) I'd change the health to either a bar that diminishes but preferably to a red heart shape that starts full and goes down as you lose health and just the % from 1 to 100 inside the heart
I'd also move your health to the left side

3) Put your day # and time both together in the upper right where your health is now like this:  Day 4:  2:15 PM (all together with just a couple of spaces between)

4) I'd put your ammo on the bottom left side, just feel like these locations im giving you are more standard positions for this kinda info in games.

5) Move your iron to bottom right where your ammo is now

These are just my suggestions, but most importantly... put your health in a heart shape or in a health bar.

6) I'd replace your current enemies.. with one of the following:
If you want them to float, fine.. make them more ghostly and make them animated as they move.. right now they look like stiff cardboard cut outs, and it just looks and comes off as "cheap" and "no effort"  
Maybe make one of them (instead of the see thru one). maybe make one a big floating clown head or something.. i see it with red hair and evil eyes make sure it animates tho, at least a little!

* I couldn't make assets like what I'd want in your game, if your game was mine, i'd probably find someone on fiver to make me what I wanted and pay them $20 per asset or whatever and promise to only sell it to me.. so that It would be only MY asset and not seen in 20 other Unity games on Steam
- Also with those assets, especially if you have them made... make sure the person making them gives you a death animation or an exploding animation where it gets shot and looks cool when it dies so it doesn't just disappear when shot.. that also feels cheap and unsatisfying when you play it

7) I actually like your boxes falling for health and ammo, that works just fine...
But maybe replace the white box with a super simple first aid kit instead, nothing fancy needed tho and if you do that, replace the red ammo box with something that actually looks like ammo.. maybe a dark green military ammo box?

8) Your current map is just fine but make sure your enemies don't spawn in mid air where they can be seen spawning... Making them spawn under ground and SLOW come up thru the earth in random locations would look and feel MUCH cooler imo.

9) Ohhhh, you need a SCORE!!  ..make SCORE be the thing in the top middle and make it bigger font!  Give players scores for each enemy type, the tougher the enemy, the more points he is worth.  Also give points for surviving a night perhaps and other actions as well.  A High score leaderboard for Steam would be cool too but not required.  However, learning how to make Steam leaderboards for your games is definitely something I'd learn how to do if you want to make more Steam games in the future.

I hope that helps or at least gives you some ideas.  =)

review:
While the game has alot of potential, if you're expecting something like plague inc, or pandemic but with gods this isn't it. This is a long haul game where you have to very carefully play exactly how the developers envisioned and if you don't you'll find yourself sitting at the screen for hours on end waiting for random events to show up that use RNG to determine success,. Even if you have 100% traits/rates, you can still fail. While the game is a very interesting concept, it lacks surfacing basic UI elements that most games would use to communicate instant feedback to the player, and instead of a "steady resource management" game as the videos try to make you believe it is, its a "pool of resources" strategy  game. 

If you make any mistakes, (by which I mean if RNG hates you, or you don't select the options the developers preordained as the 'good option') you get stuck and likely have to start over. Sure you could wait for random events, but you cannot even tab out of the game to wait for events to spawn, you have to sit there in real time and die of boredom for quite a while, and even then it's not likely you'll get anything meaningful out of the events.

Additionally, the game for some unknown reason has lot of far-left bias politics in it, even making mentions of "alt-right", and modern politics that really shouldn't have too much place in a typical god game, to an absurd degree.

I played this game on my friend's computer for two days when I visited him last weekend, and honestly, I had to reinstall Steam and buy this gem for myself because to me, it is such a great game with an affordable price, although there are still a few areas need improvements.

Pros:
1) Portraits are great, God's abilities are very well-written.
2) The music is calm and soothing.
3) The gameplay is challenging enough to keep me engaged and not discouraged. However, as some people mentioned, this might be too hard for them, so if there is an option to tune down the difficulty, it will be more helpful.
4) I really like how there is no perfect combination for Gods and Minor Gods. For example, take the benevolent route of Dionysus, he lacks of abilities to positively affect Education and Climate, and out of all the Minor Gods, only Thalassa can positively affect Climate, so both Dionysus and Thalassa combined are still not able to positively affect Education. 3) The skepticism penalty for choosing options should be less punishing, I once lost a game literally just by getting three +10% skepticism in a row (I was at 28% skepticism).

Again, thank you so much for this gem, developers! I am always a fan of Greek mythology and find your game is a valuable addition to this genre. I hope my feedback is helpful for you all. 

Again, great effort! Don't let negative reviews bring you down!

To other gamers, I understand your frustration but please be kind and polite and give the team some time to polish the game because this team is a very small team and they need constructive feedback to improve the game better. Please pardon me if I am asking too much.

All in all, it's a good idea and I like the game. The price seems about right to me.

review:
[h1]Little trap-dodger / shooter that's mostly a proof-of-concept[/h1]

[b]Concept:[/b] Flying a tiny spaceship through cramped levels, you find keys to open the door to the next area while avoiding hitting traps and occasional enemies. You can endure a couple of hits but the third will kill you and restart the level.

[i]5.84 Wing[/i] does not host a real story. Idea is simple: you can rotate quickly using pad or mouse (I used the latter) and only boost forward. Naturally, you retain momentum and get damaged by crashing too fast into walls. You also got a tiny turret, used to destroy certain walls and fight enemies and bosses.

There's three boss fights, inspired by [i]video games of olde[/i], each of which has at least two attack patterns or behaviours. They take a lot of shooting before they die. Killing bosses also grants an upgrade for your main weapon.

[h1]Some technicalities[/h1]

Using keyboard and mouse, spacebar is the boost key and left-click shoots. Just to mention, there's no rebinding options, though I found the controls adequate. The control scheme itself needs a bit of getting used to.

I encountered only one slight bug that when picking up the weapon upgrade the game slowed down for a sec: the upgrade should've been smooth.

[h1]Conclusions: It's got potential[/h1]

For a sub-$1 game (which even then I got on sale), it was alright: not great but not too bad either.

The main story lasted about 30 minutes, and there's a wave survival mode for some shooty action. All in all, it was fine if a bit forgettable experience with no real replay value.

I would like to see a bigger game using the same concept, perhaps even with more cramped levels and also some harder challenge levels.
