review: After playing and finishing the game after 18 hours here's my review. I never heard of this game until I looked up on a Steam curator of Sege Genesis games and this one caught my eye since I like playing JRPGs. I got it on a sale and the time I put to it was worth it. To begin the story takes place at a time where it's kind of middle age fantasy like setting with advanced technology. You do meet characters like Albert Einstein in the game who gives you a something to comunicate with him but he usually says things that you already know. You start off as a blue haired man named Tim who does a competition and something goes wrong and is banished from his village. When that happens you try to go around the world to prove your innocence. You have 5 party members in the game you meet in the game but you can only have 4 in the game to help you. The 5th party member comes near the end of the game and the 3rd party member is switched with someone else. Not gonna spoil who it is since it will spoil the story. The story isn't that memorable it's pretty cliche and is something you probably seen before in a JRPG so it's nothing special. The visauls in this game do look nice for a game that's in 1996 since it's the year since that playstation 1, Sega Saturn, and Nintendo 64 came out at this time. The music is alright but the music can be annoying when you hear it a bunch of times. There are different enemies in the game but most of them are the same but with different colors. There's enemies you probably seen before like slimes and dragons. Some of them are pretty goofy to me like a zombie like monster with a shotgun. When I first played this game I had no idea on what to do so I looked up a guide on YouTube on where to go and it helped me out a lot in this game. There are different areas in the game you go to like forest, snowy plains, deserts, industiral factories, and so on. Some of the bosses in the game can be tough when you fight them and can take a bit of trial and error but when you level up a lot in the game progress further in the game it gets pretty easy. Some bosses spells can one hit you which is pretty unfair at times also when you get further into the game the spells don't one hit you at all or do that much damage compared to past encounters. You do get exp and money in the game that are pretty useful. Everytime you level up it increase your stats like Health, MP, attack, defense, agility, and so on. For gold you use it to pay for things like for inns, weapons, shields, armor, healmets, and accesories that give different attributes depending on the one your using. You do get items that are useful like potions that heal your health, mp, or both. There are items that can help you fight against monsters but I never used them since I had spells to help me out. There are items that can heal certain things you got like poison, sleep, confusion, and so on. For spells you can either buy them from the store or get them from chest. Some spells in the chest are very useful like one where you get a spell thats much better than cure 2. When you get spells be wary because you can only carry a limited amount of spells so make sure you get rid of the ones you don't use very much. For spells you start off with basic spells to way more advanced spells that are more powerful than the last spells you have. You get spells like fire, ice, stone, cure, spells that increase attributes, spells that get rid of things like poison and many others that affect you, and spells that decrease and affect enemies like poison, slow, and many others. You can talk to people in this game that give you advice on where to go but some are pretty useless like one guy you meet in another town says he will give you advice but just scams you of your 100 gold. The final boss for me was so easy because I leveled up my character all the way up to nearly level 70. When I watched the walktrough the guy highest level in the game was like level 57 compared to mine since I was grinding a certain enemy that gave me a lot of exp for me and I put so much time trying to level up which helped me out a lot in the game and made things easy for me. There are a few things that were annoying like when you fight an enemy and one is near they can come after you after the battle and fight you before you have a chance to fight them. Also when I was done with a certain section I died to a point that I needed a break from the game then came back and got through it. The game does glitch a bit but it rarely happens so it's not a big deal for me. It's nothing game breaking it just makes the graphics not show on battles. Not the best JRPG I played but was pretty worth playing after a while. It kind of reminds me of Breath of Fire 2 on SNES when I played it on the Nintendo 3DS since I finished it before and because of the visuals of the game. I give this game a 6 out of 10. If you want to try it out and play it, get it when it goes on sale. I got for less than 4 euro which is pretty worth it compared to the time I put into it. I hope this review makes you think twice about getting or not getting the game. Thanks for reading my review and I hope you have a good day.

[h1]Original 2019 review[/h1]
Brave Battle Saga (also known as Barver Battle Saga) is a solid RPG. Just my kind of game.

Just to start off, this uses the Mednafen emulator, which works fine, though it had a few hitches. For some reason the emulator's "Pause" function doesn't work at all, and there were a couple of times where the audio desynced and the only fix I could find was to restart the emulator.

Although the preview images and videos show the image all stretched, it's actually far more reasonable, using the base 320x224 Genesis resolution (game looks chunkier at x1 or x2 scaling). The emulator allows up to 4x scaling with or without smoothing and it adds a neat little border when playing in full screen. The game only uses the ABC face buttons so configuring XYZ is not necessary. Steam overlay works fine. Now, into the game.

While the story's not exactly groundbreaking, it's got a couple moments that made me go "huh" in mild intrigue.

It's obvious the spritework and stuff was quite heavily influenced by games like Final Fantasy VI, but hey, they still look real nice.

The music is good, but the sound effects are kind of wonky. A lot of them are really quiet and certain events (getting hit, for example) produce no sounds at all which robs them of impact slightly. I don't know if this is an emulation quirk or if the game really was this way, but it definitely sounds off.

There are no random encounters, all encounters are portrayed as sprites in the world that initiate a battle when touched, though oddly most of the sprites have no correlation to what you'll be fighting, so I guess they're random in that aspect. One downside I'd note is that the screen uses this lazy scrolling where the you're always off-center when moving which annoys me a little, but it still leaves enough room to react to any potential enemies ahead.

Battles are in the standard turn-based style, which is totally fine by me, although I'll admit the fighting in this game boils down to only using Attack on the regular enemies and only using Spells to spam your strongest magic during boss fights since magic sucks against groups. The game has an option called Real Time Battles that essentially works like the ATB system (from Final Fantasy IV onwards). That option won't affect the pacing of fights much though, since it only "pauses" during submenu navigation if you have it set to Off.

The battle UI is a bit clunky, there's a Repeat command that performs the same move that character did the preceding turn, but it's useless because the battle cursor memorizes the last action you did and defaults to that on each turn. It's also a bit awkward to only be able to use left and right to navigate targets.

I didn't have to stop progress a single time to grind, but then again I engaged in a lot of battles voluntarily. I also didn't feel over-leveled except at one early point in the game, the overall balance felt pretty good.

In summary, this game definitely deserves my recommendation. Even though it is pretty derivative in some aspects, I still found it a very enjoyable experience through and through. Give it a shot if you're in the mood for an old school RPG.

review:
I'll recommend Brave Battle Saga, but only as a light recommendation for those who are looking for more old-school RPGs for their collection. It's reasonably priced, but the story and gameplay are fairly standard for those who have been around the RPG block.

Combat is turn-based, using an action bar that builds up to the respective party member's next turn (such as in Final Fantasy games). I oftentimes felt a little rushed trying to search through the Item and Spell lists in battle; there's a large quantity of items, gear, and spells you have to remember and keep in order. Spells in particular can get very messy, if you don't keep reorganizing each of your characters' menus (I didn't realize this was possible until midway through the game).

Enemy mobs are not random encounters: You can see them on the map and enter combat when you touch them. Knowing how tiring random encounters can get from other RPGs, this was very welcome at first. However, many of the mobs move very quickly, and they all immediately beeline after you if you get close enough to them. This became pretty frustrating, as much of the world features narrow canyons and corridors that prevent you from avoiding mobs. Foes also continue to move while you open chests or interact with the world. Sit too long, and all nearby enemies will be sitting on you, waiting to throw you into combat once that text box closes. I began to quickly tap to get through messages whenever I interacted with things, limiting my ability to tell what I actually picked up sometimes. The worst instances were finding chests containing unique magic spells, which require you to give the spell to a character after you pick it up; as a result, I'd either be swarmed by enemies ready to fight me once I finished assigning the spell, or I'd frantically slap it on the first available character and reorganize later.

...With those experiences in mind, I wonder if a random encounter system would have actually been preferable, given the high encounter rate and the way it punishes the player.

Two observations regarding combat I feel worth pointing out: First, magic spells seemed unreliable. While early spells aren't too MP-costly, subsequent tiers get very expensive. And there's a lot of spells out there. This is usually fine/expected in RPG magic systems, but the damage I was seeing didn't seem worth the cost--save for specific instances against magic-vulnerable foes or elemental weaknesses. Meanwhile, enemies' spells could be downright devastating and wipe characters instantly. More often than not, it was better to just stick with using physical attacks, even for the more magic-focused characters in the party. 

And that leads into my second combat observation: Critical hits seem incredibly common, and they are both your best friend and worst enemy. Why burn up your MP on attack spells for an extra bit of damage when your normal attacks have a high chance of going critical and multiplying damage several times over? It's better to keep the MP for healing and boost Spells, since items get pretty expensive (and there's plenty of things to buy otherwise). And watch out for enemies' critical hits--they can drain a character's whole HP bar in some instances.

Despite those shortcomings, Brave Battle Saga was still a fun RPG distraction. The low price definitely helped. But the gameplay and story might not be enough to keep some players invested.

review:
Hers was a white lie built on a grain of truth that snowballed as one lie after the other piled up. At first it was only hers, but then it became something that the two of them shared together – like a secret, a world upon which no other could encroach. He may have been “Friend A,” and she “the girl that loves my best friend,” but they were masquerading around a truth that neither one could openly admit because ultimately, the truth was much more painful.

Hentai Survive Island is a deceitfully masterful game that initially appears light-hearted and colorful, its palette boasting pastels that lend to the idea of it being another romantic game. Yet the moment we step past the disillusionment that it casts upon us by its false prefaces, we quickly realize that what we have immersed ourselves in is actually a tragedy in the making.

Tragic not because of a single element but because of all of its parts, and yet at the end of everything, this isn’t a game about tragedy. It is a game about learning to heal, learning to move on, and learning to accept the parts of ourselves that we’d rather pretend aren’t there. Part of that is accepting that sometimes we need a helping hand to take that first step. Part of it is learning to say goodbye when the time comes.

What is so compelling about the storyline is that it’s not merely an adventure into first love, it delves into the reality of post-traumatic stress disorder, childhood abuse, and chronic illness. It doesn’t paint any of these as artistic or tragically beautiful—they are horrible, they twist people, they ruin the best moments, and they have a long-lasting impact.

No one is completely black-and-white; everyone has their short-comings, fleshed out in full before our eyes. They have their hang-ups, their strengths, their struggles—and it’s in these characters that this game really takes off in full stride. It would be enough for them to be multifaceted with equal amounts of depth, but they take it a step further in painting the reality of youth.

Older game fans may critically analyze the game as an unrealistic approach to young teenagers, but that pessimism overlooks the reality of what it was like for us to be that age. We were all that point when we found our first love, when we thought it was forever, when we poured our passion into something that ultimately would not come to fruition or last. That’s what being young is about—and that’s what Hentai Survive Island gives us.

Granted that it may veer a bit over-dramatic at times in its representation of youth; there are moments of symbolism or hyperbole so overt that the cheesiness makes you shift a little uncomfortably in your seat (but I promise it’s not enough to gag you). Given that this is, however, a rather common trope that runs in games with heavier themes, it’s not necessarily a huge setback for an otherwise solid game. In the end, it is intended to be a fictional representation that conveys more than just what can be summarized in a few sentences or less.

The sound is completely on point, and the soundtrack artfully matches the emotions intended to be represented in each scene. From the actual classical music to the opening and ending, everything fits in like a jigsaw puzzle to give a full, satisfying final piece. When the characters analyze someone’s playing as harsh, rigid, and stilted, we can hear this—whether we are knowledgeable about music or not. Hentai Survive Island conveys emotion to us not just visually but aurally as well.

The animation is wonderful with bright, vibrant colors that bring the characters fully to life. There is an amazing, visually perceivable transition for the characters as time passes. It occasionally has some stilted moments but nothing outrageously noticeable to detract from the overall quality.

Ultimately, Hentai Survive Island is a story that starts out of the gates moving a bit slowly, but the pace matches the tone of the game. Structurally, it is a solid story of youth that dramatizes some aspects but never distracts from the intended message. On top of its other strong points, it’s aurally and visually a joy to the senses – and to anyone appreciative of a game willing to realistically approach the conflict of childhood abuse and the resulting trauma in a positive way. It’s not without a few setbacks, but in the end, Hentai Survive Island fashions itself to be a stand-out romance game that reminds us that while some relationships may be transient and brief, some people will come into our lives at just the right time for just long enough to touch us in a way we never thought possible.

review:
This is a fairly short HO game.  It took me 5.5 hours to play both main game and bonus chapter.  The devs have maintained the quality in this game but it was far too short and ended very quickly.  The bonus chapter was good and was full of twists and turns.
You are the leading expert on harmonium after all your travels.  A professor friend contacts you when a man from another world falls through her new portal.  He is ill and they don't know how to cure him.  Kraixx tell you that his world is on the brink of destruction because the harmonium there has become imbalanced.  It could affect Earth too.
You go back to his world and have to dodge the Watchers who arrest anyone with magical abilities.  As you travel Kraixx's world, you discover the backstory of his culture.
It is well done and the graphics are beautiful at times.  The music heightens the urgency of your quest.  There is a twist in the tale (which I saw coming).  There is a fair bit of backtracking, but you can fast travel through the map.  The map highlights where you can go next.
The HO scenes are varied which keep your interest.  You have a popper game as an option if you can't find an object.  The puzzles make you think, but are doable.  I didn't skip any.
There are owl collectables in every scene.  There are souvenirs too.  Both collectables can be found at the end of the game if you miss any.
I have been left with mixed feelings with this game.  Some things are done really well, like the puzzles, some of which were quite unique.  But I thought the game finished with a rush as if they ran out of ideas.  5 hours is very short for a HO game and especially at the asked price.
No bugs.  7.5/10

Let me just start out by saying i really wanted to like this game, its grafics are really nice and sound design is pretty solid aswell, and ive hear this being recomended by a lot of other people, but damn does it not market itself the way it should.

It is a rage game by design, and i like these type of games but you gotta be clear that you intend on being one. I mean seriously the tag on the store page says casual, and its literally the FARTHEST away from the truth. The "movement is not always easy" is also very misleading, it sounds like its refering to the actual obstacles themselves, and not the actual mechanics. But i would have let it slide if it didnt feel like there was a real oversight with the controls:

I did the first ~3 checkpoints with about 2 deaths, i was really enjoying the game, despite the fact that my "hands" were oriented wrong (it was about 90 degrees from how they should have been) and it used the trigger button instead of the grip button (it was really weird why they didnt just use the most natural "grabbing" button) (also, im using a rift s so maybe that isnt a problem for other headsets)

Then came this HellishWall™ climb with rocks falling down on you. You have to react, and FAST. It was then that i realized how off the actual trigger for grabbing stuff in my hand was, i needed to grab the air in front of the handles and not where it really should. It also really liked yeeting me off randomly (im guessing the game thought i was pushing myself away from the wall?) and there is also NO way to catch yourself after you fall, even if you try grabbing onto stuff on your way down it feels like the game deactivates you ability to do it. I died 58+ times (including an attempt where it spawned all 3 rocks at the same time where i was near the top) and finally got up to the top. Guess what? i needed to go all the way around to click a button, and for that i needed to go back onto the HellishWall™ to be able to click it. I died trying after the game yeeted me off for the 200th time.

For you to have a rage game, you have to be clear that whatever killed the player was the players fault, not of the game, so you gotta have consistent controls and mechanics, they must understand WHY they died. Otherwise it just feels like (or sometimes literally just is) a badly made game.

Overall, not recomended, at least until fixes to the contol bindings, collisions, and the weird hand rotation. I would refund this game if i didnt think it had potential, but it clearly does, just not right now, im hoping the devs polish this one up more.

review:
An Climber Game with an Abstract Art Style (and a Weird Title)
Not having played a climber-type game within the last 9-months (last one played was 'To The Top'), this game reminded me of why I enjoy them.

Pros:
- An abstract, minimalist art style that makes you feel like you are on a different world, without getting distracted by how next-gen the world looks.
- Some backgrounds remind me of a PS VR game I played called 'Bound', and those metallic hands you stand on scream out the movie 'Logan's Run' to myself for some reason.
- Gameplay is challenging at times; hard but fair.
- Saves points are reasonably spaced out (although the wimp in me would love to save anywhere)
- The pricing for this game almost makes purchasing the game a no-brainer (unless you're feeling extra cheap).
- Maybe I haven't gotten far enough into the game yet, but the game title would not have made me think about a climbing game. The title weirdly adds some appeal to myself.
Cons:
- Using Oculus Touch controllers, the hand orientation feels off by about 45 degrees.  The good news is that it is mostly a visual distraction, and has no tangible effect on gameplay.
- On occasion, I felt confused on what to do next (e.g., how to open those blue double doors? just touch them.  I tried jumping over the wall a few times before realizing that wasn't going to work).
- While the controls work well (grip, release), my own stupidity in forgetting to release one while grabbing the next gives me the false justification I need to list this as a Con.
- For how many times I've already died in this game, if I get one Achievement in this game, I'll be happy.

Overall (so far), a solid climbing game with responsive controls, a minimalist art style that accentuates its 'other worldliness', that is fun.

review:
To make a strange comparison, this is the Oddworld Abe's Oddysey of VR games. You are small, defenseless robot thing (?) trying to escape a cold, emotionless, mechanical beast of a world that wants to see you dead at every corner. Not for those afraid of heights, this will test your VR legs.

It's atmosphere is so rad. If you like dystopian science fiction, or just strange intriguing art styles this game will pull you in like nothing else. It's VERY minimalistic but it uses it heavily to it's advantage. Think Superhot, except take it soooo much further beyond white rooms. I want to know more about this world but that would ruin what makes it great. EVERY new section the game is throwing something entirely new at you and it never stops. It's suprisingly lengthy for such a cheap VR game too.

Also like Abe's Oddysey, I absolutely loved the experiance but I could never beat it again because FUCK is it hard. It is physically taxing, you will sweat, you will use every ounce of your energy attempting to clear a section, and you will die and fail anyway and have to try again. But god damn is nice when you succeed. I remember clearing a certain mid game section (the main reason I will never play this again) and grasping onto the balloon carrying on me for dear fucking life, terrified of having to do it again. Sometimes the challenge is just straight up endurance.

The controls are simple, and admittedly not as polished as some other VR climbing games but they get the job done. I did run into an animation glitch with Oculus touch controllers were the hands are always orientated wrong (apparently due to how the Vive controllers naturally rest verses the touch controllers) but as far as I could tell this was only cosmetic.

With Loneliness is a unique experiance I will never forget and something that could only be done in VR. Even though I can't go back to it, at least not for a good while, it's become one of my favorite VR games, hell, just video game I've ever played. At 7 bucks you really can't go wrong.

review:
ScourgeBringer is a one trick pony of a game with brutal difficulty, excellent combat, and absolutely nothing else. If you like the combat and the difficulty, you are in for a great time. If not, this game has nothing to offer you. Go into this expecting a roguelike with minimal variety between runs.

This review is being written after getting exactly one win. I turned adaptive difficulty off for my playthrough, so my playtime might be a bit inflated as a result. I did not do a second run with any difficulty modifiers enabled. I believe there is one final zone locked behind doing this.

Pros:
- Combat is excellent. Like extremely good. Seriously, this combat is absolutely fantastic if you like this combat system even a little bit, you will get something out of this game.
- Enemies, rooms, and bosses all feel fair and engaging to fight. The bosses felt surprisingly easy for how brutal the regular rooms and minibosses were.
- Stringing together attacks feels incredible.
- Each of the five main areas feels completely unique. Area 1 and 2 are fairly simple, area 3 and 4 add some gimmicky obstacles, and area 5 is pure chaos in the best possible way.
- Controls are very responsive and tight
- Graphics look really nice
- The music slaps

Neutral:
- The game at base difficulty is brutally hard. I have a few 5BC Dead Cells wins and find this to be nearly just as hard at base difficulty, though that could be due to lack of experience on my part.
- Health restoring items are rare and barely restore any HP
- Plenty of accessibility settings if you can't/don't enjoy dealing with the brutal difficulty

Cons:
- Build variety is basically nonexistent and feels incredibly lacking compared to basically... every other roguelike. Every enhancement offers minor stat boosts with the only exceptions being new guns and the one perk that makes the smash attack larger.
- The gun system is horribly unbalanced. You never have a reason to build a good weapon when a store will always offer you an awesome one (once you have a bit of the meta progression unlocked).
- Most of the gun mods are absolutely useless and offer 2.5 seconds of bonus sword damage against a specific enemy type. I always went for bouncing, piercing, and one of phasing or stun, no matter which gun I had.
- The meta progression is barebones and feels like padding. Essential game mechanics (reflecting shots, the dragon punch move, etc.) are locked behind collecting a currency that drops from bosses. These feel like base game mechanics that were locked behind meta progression at the last minute to add some form of replayability

review:
[h1] ScourgeBringer [/h1]
[h3] A brutally difficult yet rewarding rogue lite, with minor flaws [/h3]

This game has captured my attention in a way that I never would've expected, and I started loving the game the more I played it. But as great as ScourgeBringer is: it isn't perfect


[h3] What I love [/h3]

Each realm has clear themes and gorgeous pixel art that give every location a very unique look and feel, especially when paired with the music  of each location. Speaking of music, the game has unique tracks that play for when you're in combat, out of combat, or fighting a boss. All of those tracks change as you move through the various realms to fit their theme. The music mainly consists of metal, with some other sounds/genres mixed in, which I think is awesome. But if it's not your thing, you can always mute it and play your own music

The game's realms escalate in terms of hazards and different environmental changes. It gives each location a new gameplay gimmick that pairs well with the abilities of enemies that inhabit the realm. Each location also has small decorations like grass or vines that move when the player brushes past them or when enemies slam against the wall, shaking them all at once. These tiny details really add a ton of character and subtle interactability to the game

ScourgeBringer has never felt like an unfair game to me. It's brutal in its difficulty, yet the game makes sure to give you the tools to overcome it. There are always strategies you can organically learn for enemies or bosses when repeatedly facing them. It feels like the devs put a lot of thought into how the player interacts with the enemies and vice versa. Once you learn those enemy patterns and master your moveset, the game feels very satisfying as you fly from one enemy to the next! However, if the game remains too difficult, you can always turn down the bullet speed, game speed, increase health drops, or even turn on invincibility. The game has a ton of great accessibility features so that everyone can enjoy playing


[h3] Some critiques [/h3]

The game has a permanent currency you earn during every run called Judge Blood. It allows you to purchase new abilities, more health, and upgrades that are persistent through every future run. However, after a few hours, you'll earn enough Judge Blood to max out the available tree of upgrades, and Judge Blood very quickly becomes irrelevant, which is both a good thing and a bad thing. On the one hand, it allows the player to grasp the mechanics of the game before allowing them to upgrade existing abilities and acquire new ones. But on the other hand, beyond that, it doesn't have much use outside of 3 minor late game upgrades and 1 secret use that's completely optional

The game's enemies have clear patterns that can be learned and countered. They're tough but fair and feel incredibly rewarding when the flow of combat clicks. What I feel lacks in this area is the ability to practice against certain bosses/enemies, because once you reach a new area, you will have no idea what they do or how to deal with them. Oftentimes, you'll have to die repeatedly as you slowly learn the attacks of new enemies, which can be frustrating especially if you make it really far on a good run, beat a difficult boss, and immediately get cut down by new enemies you've never encountered before in the next realm. And if you die, you'll have to make your way back through the realms just to get another chance at facing them again. One easy solution to this would be to give the game's bestiary more functionality: if a player dies to or kills an enemy, they could unlock its entry in the bestiary and can fight it in a practice arena. That would soften the blow of repeatedly dying to new enemies and turn that death into new information for the player so they can go back to that realm with the knowledge they need to triumph


[h3] Closing thoughts [/h3]

I don't want you to come away from this review seeing all of the critiques I've levied at this game and think I hate it. On the contrary: at the time of writing this, it has the highest amount of time I've ever spent on a Steam game with just over 100 hours, and I've spent that time earning every achievement in the game without touching ScourgeBringer's accessibility features. It's been a rewarding challenge, and in my eyes: it shows just how much fun ScourgeBringer really is! It's tough yet fair and an absolute blast!

Who knew that going into a jungle and looking for treasure...  I mean your kids, would be such a snore?

I certainly "did" the "sokoban" one 4 times...  "Did"  Heh heh...  Because in all honesty...  The puzzles that repeat?  Which is like 80% of the game...  It's easier to just "skip" them then keep doing the same thing over...  And over...  And over again...

Granted they got better...  As I am familiar with the Publishers/Developers, but this.......

Can the plot save them?!

Well...  It was nice to play a Tomb Raider...  Minus the raiding and the enemy killing I suppose.  Then you get to the end and...  WHO IN THE HELL ARE THOSE PEOPLE?!  And the entire time she is sending letters to her husband...  Who is back at the police station...  HOW?!  TELEPORTING THEM INTO HIS HANDS?!  So she is hoping and "feels him" behind her...  Not an euphemism for something...  And then...  He hasn't moved from his spot at the police station.  Wot...?  Who in the hell did SHE FEEL?!

Oh and the story ends in a cliffhanger.  But seeing that there is NO JOAN JADE 2...  I'll tell you what happens next.  Ahem.  *Clear throat*:  Joan Jade goes into the temple to find the "treasure"...  Along with those bad guys from earlier...  Whoever they are.  They race against time and against one another to open that one door!  Then when they do...  Joan Jade will outwit them and find the "treasure"...  Which is too precious for the world to have.  So she decides to let it rest and seals the door, so that the next FAR SMARTER tomb raider shall acquire it!

Yes.  Yes THAT'S how bored you'll be during repeated puzzles that you'll actually write a damn part two!

Puzzle repetition is okay, but...  A little variation?  Maybe the fish could have spots!  Come on!  Use your imagination!

Anyway, I know it's useless to yell at an old game, and if this was their first project...  It would be passable...  But knowing that they went onto other H.O.G.s, they can remember this as a failure that got them through towards making even better games.

review:
This game is tons of fun. I don’t remember the last time a game made me laugh so much. I bought it because I wanted a classic turn-based RPG game with nice art and good story. It has all that and more. 

So, here are the good points.
The art is great. The Celestials are the best-looking characters ever.

The story is great and shines even through the bad translation. 

Lots of humor. The MC and other human warriors are the “brawn no brain” type and that leads to hilarious dialogues. Celestials are on a different level, they crack jokes intentionally. I loved Ishbel’s insolent sarcasm and Siegfried’s morbid jokes. Unfortunately, we only get about 40% of it, the rest is lost in the translation and the only way you could guess there was a joke is because the dialogue looks particularly awkward. Still, enough come through to make you laugh.

Characters. Again, they are on two different levels. Humans are very cliché, nothing to say about them. Celestials are intriguing, they have complex past stories and relationships that the main story only hints on. Wish I could know more. 

Autobattler!

It’s epic. It starts as a standard plot with the kids as main characters, but before you even get to the mid-game, you start recruiting the godlike Tetrarchs into your party. Next thing you know, you play with demi-god characters with abilities on par with their high stats. Yeah, I know, it’s all balanced and the enemies can thwart their efforts, but I don’t care, I just love to see Siegfrid use that insta-kill spell.

Not intentionally, translation bloopers make it hilarious. So do the outrageous stats. After they reached level 25, I found myself saying “my attack stat is WHAT now?” a lot. Really, when do you see your attack going over a thousand? It gets better, you have an achievement to do 3,000 in one blow. Once you do that, there is 10,000. Then 30,000. And yes, you can do all that. I couldn’t help laughing when I did it, it’s just so unusual, yet, so appropriate for having demi-gods in your party. 

Well, there are cons. The translation is very uneven and seems to be done by at least two different people, if not more. The worst part is the skill descriptions. The person who translated it had no idea what increase and decrease mean. Do not trust the descriptions, just try the skill out and see what it really does. It’s simple enough to figure out.

It’s easy to learn and easy to play. Some people may see it as not enough challenge. I love to tinker with the party composition and equipment, so I loved it, but that’s your primary challenge. If you are looking for something else, you may be disappointed.

In conclusion, yes, do buy this.

review:
You need to be a big Digimon fan to enjoy these games. Sadly they get very little right technically, mechanically and story-wise.

Starting off with the technical side: The port is horrible. Locked to 60 fps, can't change settings until you pick a game, said settings do not apply to the main menu of the game so you get blasted with the menu song at 100% volume every time you open the game, the control scheme is horrible and the mouse functionality is nonexistant (you can click to accept but your cursor won't select options).

Mechanically, battles are a slog. If you play on "normal" mode, you can clear most stuff with basic attacks (with some hp-sponge bosses from time to time), while hard mode is just hp sponge galore. Battle balance is awful, the mix of defense-penetrating attacks and high defense digimons renders most endgame mons useless because you'll be tickling bosses in lategame if you aren't using def-pen skills (you can download the Ultimate Digimon Pack mod for more variety i guess)

Finally, story-wise, it's fine, it touches some more mature themes like existential crisis, loss and some other stuff (sorry i forgot) but getting there is so PAINFUL. Story progression takes you from filler to filler to filler to some interesting story to filler to buying groceries for the cute digilab lady to filler and only starts picking up at around chapter 13~ out of 20 (cyber sleuth) or 18 (hacker's memory), you keep getting taken out of the story by useless fluff which makes you wonder if you really want to go on. The endings might gaslight you into thinking you played a mediocre at worst game but it's all an illusion, it's bad.

Eden metaverse design is pretty boring too, and the backtracking is insane. Hacker's memory adds some QoL stuff like a faster walking speed hack and a free return-to-entrance hack... which weren't ported to Cyber Sleuth for some reason (there is a mod for this too!).

All in all, this is a bad rpg being "carried" by a dying IP that can't quite get anything right (the more recent Digimon Survive sucked even more than these games!). Hopefully Time Stranger will be better, but honestly my expectations are really low.

Final Score: 4/10.

review:
10/10 Wonderful collection!

First of all, thank you so much for releasing this game for PC, Bandai Namco! 
Of all the Digimon games I've played on PC (well, there are only three at the moment), this one is the best.

I took a long break because I wanted to work through my pile of unplayed games by playing other games that don't take longer than 20 hours. 
However, when Digimon Story Time Stranger got announced, I was really excited. Before it comes out on October 3, 2025, I have to play through this game first, even though Time Stranger tells a completely new story.
I've already pre-ordered Time Stranger and am looking forward to playing the game. 

This collection is very extensive. The Main Story Mode takes about 30 to 50 hours per game. 

I love JRPGs with monster taming elements. This game is similar to the Persona games in terms of gameplay. If you're currently disappointed with Pokémon, please give Digimon a chance. You'll definitely love it. I guarantee it.


Digi evolution and de-evolution are pretty straightforward. Do it regularly to unlock new evolutions. Without doing so, you will have trouble advancing in the story.

__________________________________________________________________________________

Now I would like to rate Digimon Story Cyber Sleuth: Complete Edition. 
This collection includes two games: Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth and Digimon Story: Hacker's Memory.  

Digimon Story: Cyber Sleuth: The story mode is good, but not great. The level design, especially the dungeon, is monotonous and the story is dragged out.  The side quests, however, are interesting. And the soundtracks are fantastic. So I give it a 9/10.

Digimon Story: Hacker's Memory: This game fixed everything that Cyber Sleuth couldn't. The main story is fantastic, the characters are interesting, and the dungeon levels are unique. [spoiler] However, the ending is heartbreaking. I hope we'll see Hudiemon and other characters from both games in Time Stranger. [/spoiler] I give this game a 10/10.

__________________________________________________________________________________

I have to be honest. This game reminds me of Digimon Links, which was available for mobile devices. The more I play Digimon Story Cyber Sleuth: Complete Edition, the more I miss Digimon Links (and ReArise). I really hope that these mobile games will one day be re-released as offline premium games (€5-10 each) for mobile devices. It's great to have an official mobile game from Bandai Namco. Or a similar version of My Tamagotchi Forever, but with Digimon.

The only downside is that this game has some technical issues. It runs flawlessly on Windows. However, I continued playing on Linux (Bazzite) after a long break. Every hour, the performance dropped and it stuttered like crazy, even though I have a powerful PC. I have to restart Steam to fix the problem. This can be annoying, but at the moment I don't know how to fix it.

And the Steam Overlay does not work under Linux either. Therefore, it is not possible to take screenshots.


Totally and a question for Bandai Namco:
Overall, I'm thankful that this game exists on PC.
Now, I have a question (and I don't know where to ask it):

Could you please release more Digimon games for the PC, especially on GOG? I'd really like to see a remake of Digimon Adventure, which was released on the Playstation Portable.

review:
Cyber Sleuth is a game that's kind of contingent on you caring about Digimon. If you don't, you're better off just going to play SMT or Casette Beasts or something if you're looking for a good, standalone creature-focused RPG. That being said, as far as fanservice games go it could be VASTLY worse than Cyber Sleuth, and in many ways it still feels like a much more enjoyable experience that was more impactful to me than the obvious comparison in the room (Pokemon).

I'm not here to tell the story in these games is amazing. It is goofy, cliche, occasionally has some stupid or outright kind of gross character work (there are multiple all-but-confirmed gay characters whose existence seems to be a punchline), but by god does it have heart. A mixture of hilarious moments, this whole gonzo plotline in both games that features incredible amounts of rule of cool virtual reality insanity, and a couple of actually well-handled concepts like Erika and Ryuji's relationship in Hacker's Memory manage to just elevate this to a delightfully memorable mess, which is basically where I feel Digimon is at it's best.

The game's aesthetic rules when it's good. You could argue the vacuum-sealed-female-clothes are a bit trashy, but I find it fits well enough on a character like Nokia, and otherwise the game is ripe full of designs that are goofy yet instantly memorable, including an antagonistic force that manages to capture a kind of otherworldly and surreal vibe impressively well. They really look like abstract, physical manifestations of computer viruses or malware in a way I don't think I've seen media more worth classifying as "art" do nearly as well. Some areas, as well, look incredible. I think the physical spaces that get corrupted always look awesome, and for a handheld game it has an honestly awesome portrayal of Tokyo. The weaknesses are the nondescript and generic cyberspace settings, which are genuinely so boring to look at it's kind of painful. In comparison to how rich the game can feel when it does it's environment design well, the environments you spend >50% of the game in are so bland that I could barely believe it.

Gameplay is... mixed. It has enough to it that you kind of have to apply your brain, and I think the overall mechanics you have for raising/upgrading your Digimon are great. There's a very "let me cook" vibe to how much freedom you have to carry over skills and come up with silly ass combinations in your constant arms race against the game, and the tiers of Digimon really do feel like they accurately portray the power escalation from rookie to mega. In terms of serious analysis, though, very few fights really require you to think to beat them. A lot of bosses have no gimmicks or mechanics whatsoever, and devolve into either hitting the weakness or clicking the biggest damage move. It's laughably unbalanced - some digimon are cursed with signature moves almost less than worthless, while others (piercing attacks) are game-warpingly strong and easy to figure out. I don't think it's the worst RPG I've ever played, and if you're looking for a game where the digimon are fun to collect and level up, then you're getting that, but I really wish that these games would at least try and shoot for "good" instead of the same passable buff > attack > heal slop that defines so many mediocre JRPG combat systems.

Again, it all boils down to what you're looking for - if you think Digimon is cool and you want an enjoyable RPG with fun characters, good collection mechanics and a tone that feels simultaneously sillier yet more interesting than anything you'd get out of Pokemon, then go ahead. If you're just looking for a good RPG, go elsewhere.

review:
Warning: This review contains some spoilers that are related to some missions/mechanics found in the games, they are used specifically to clarify some points and that's all, so if you want to play the game fully blind just glance over them and most likely by the time you reach them in the game you will have forgotten them!

Welp, this is my first time writing a review for a game so don't expect much. To begin with, I'm a pretty huge fan of the game (as you can see me having played this game for around ~300 hours and that's excluding the time i played the original cyber sleuth back when it was originally released on ps4) but I'll be giving this review quite straight and objectively as well as reviewing both cyber sleuth and hackers memory combined (sometimes i will talk about them separately). I also Heavily Recommend to play Digimon Cyber Sleuth First and then Digimon Cyber Sleuth: Hacker's Memory because the game Digimon Cyber Sleuth: Hacker's Memory takes place in the background events of Digimon Cyber Sleuth.

Let's begin with the positives about the game:

1) Main Story and Side mission (NOT including ones you can get from researching in Digi-Farms) range from Amazing to good and can be as shallow or deep as you want to take them (as an example: from Cyber Sleuth main story wise, you will see Kyoko talking about alot of stuff that you can either straight up skip or learn a bunch of interesting theories/philosphies/Etc and from Hacker Memory side missions wise, you see missions that if you think about it deeply or take it seriously it talks about rather difficult or disputed topics such as the Fanbeemon case in which if you think about it deeply, it talks about animal experimentation for science.

2) Music wise i believe it to be quite good

3) In comparison to many other Digimon games and in general, Animations are pretty nice

4) As far as i play it [Didn't use any mods], there were no bugs or random glitches happening and extremely rare complaints from the internet about the bugs/glitches

5) You can Finish the game using any Digimon roster [Mega-wise] you choose on the easy/default mode

6) If you wish, for the vast majority of the game you can skip every single side case and just go through the main story [I personally wouldn't recommend it because of mainly side cases being mostly fun and that if you skip a very big amount of side cases you will have lower Exp than you should and would make battles harder for no reason...]

7) If you wanted to play the game casually [as most people usually do or should do, because in the end i personally believe that games should be played for self-enjoyment and not torture, unless it's your livelihood i guess], the combat system and menus that are most important are pretty much simple and straight forward to use

Negatives with the games:

1) It is near impossible to complete any of those 2 games on a blind playthrough in Hard Difficulty [Even after finishing the game and starting a new game plus in Hard difficulty, unless you have a VERY specific team, some cases ESPECIALLY MAIN CASE MAIN BOSSES are impossible/Extremely Tedious to beat], the only advantage of playing in hard mode rather than in normal mode is that you just get slightly more money (which by the way, can be farmed really easily upon getting a specific setup/ money isn't that important in the game [EXCEPT GETTING USBs/Extra final stats for digimon])

2) The game is an EXTREMELY HEAVY text dependant game and there is no way to skip text/cutscenes (other than by spamming the X or A button and that doesn't apply for cutscenes)

3) Majority of the time you have to go from one place to another manually (Sometimes the game teleport you to the destination but not much)

4) There are some key explanations/information that are not said/emphasized or sometimes explained at all [the attribute damage flowchart, You accepted a case and in the ginormous text summary they said where to go but you missed it/forgot it and it isn't shown in your case summary where to go, What is exactly CAM and ABI used for, Personality on Digi-Farms/stats that it increases....]

5) Farming Exp/Money it is EXTREMELY time consuming and annoying (to give you a preface about this point: 1) You need 9 Tactician/Billionaire USBs and in order to get them as fast and as most probable as possible, you need to: A) Fill out an entire farm with builders personality  B) Need to research using the correct money input  C) Save ~30 sec before building result comes out and Spam Restart the game from boot untill you get the item you want. 2) you NEED a specific 3 in battle Digimons for grinding and it's a champion digimon during the early to early mid game, a MEGA Digimon in late mid to late game. 3) Have to search online best spot to grind [it is available rather late in the game] and at that time you will also learn specific option settings that will make the grinding go faster such as battle animations set to short and to remove every single skill on the digimon and press the auto-battle mode.

6) Digimons are not balanced; i.e the only digimons that matter are the ones for grinding OR have an DEF/INT penetrating attack that will result in significant damage.

All in all, everything i wrote in this review comes from how much i love the games and not a place of spite. I can write many more points of what i like/dislike in the games but that won't affect your choice in whether you purchase/play the game so why bother writing it in the review. This digmon game as all other types of digimon games, favors a specific niche of players: If you are a person who likes a generic Turn based combat JRPGs with a heavy story, then is the game for you, but if it's not your type, you can try other Digimon games in the franchise because many entries in this franchise have extremely different play-styles, for example if you don't mind a tamagotchi  battle type of game, you can play Digimon World: Next Order or if you like a fun fighting co-op couch type of vibes you can play Digimon Rumble Arena 2 or if you like fighting games such as Tekken/Super Smash Bros you can download and play Project Digimon: Rumble Arena Remake (although it doesn't have online feature i believe), or if you like conventional JRPGs you can play Digimon World 3 and many other types of play-styles are there! Hope the review was in any way, shape or form usefull to you in your choice of purchasing or playing these 2 games. I will end this review with an inside reference joke: apparently i became just 6% of one of the Sacred Seven members as i am writing this review :)

If you thought Digimon World 4 was okay (despite all its flaws) and you have "some" fond memories of Digimon World DS/Dawn/Dusk, then this game will suit you just fine.

A far cry from the hours demanded by the World 4 and DS/Dawn/Dusk with actual story and some meaningful choices in Hacker's Memory.

This duology and a very special someone brought me back into the world of Digimon. 

I had been out of the series since after Tamers, I'd just fallen out, it wasn't even a "this isn't the Digimon I remembered." It was just a moving away point. 

Glad to say I'm back, Cyber Sleuth and Hackers Memory's stories aren't the most complex thing in the world, but they've got a whole lot of heart that captivated me especially in the latter game. I even got really emotional in the finale of Hacker's Memory! It's good but cruel. 

The mechanics are very in-depth and funnily enough you're more working for your post game than the main game, as it's rather easy. But it's incredibly satisfying to build your team and make your absolute death monsters. Tons of favorites and a lot of Digimon I didn't know since i'd been out for awhile are here. 

With Time Stranger on the horizon there isn't a better time to try out this duology, be it a returning, new or veteran fan. There is a lot to love here.

review:
Combat is Good. 

Story is Bad. (Long, Dull, Boring, takes away immersion constantly every step of the way) 

There isn't any quest markers or any pop up notifications that tells you make your way to (Specific Location) 

The map itself is utterly pointless because it's just a PNG, Kyoko and Mirei are supposed to provide helpful hints incase if you're ever lost or stuck. But 2/3rds of the time they pretty much say "Figure it out yourself" 

It felt like Chapter 10 - 13 was a big nothing burger in terms of progression  It honestly could of been 1 or 2 chapters instead of 4. Besides the fact that Nokia did practically nothing and was able to get War Graymon and Metal Garurumon, then almost immediately after Omnimon.  Again she ate a nothing burger and got Omnimon which did happen in the game.

 I was already working on obtaining Omnimon on my own, The game let's you command Nokia's Omnimon as well as it being in your party for a short period of time. It kinda took away that hype for me to obtain my own Omnimon. I only have Were Garurumon and Metal Greymon at the time Nokia had obtained her Omnimon.  Kinda lame.  

Expect to use a 3rd party guide more than half the time throughout the playthrough, even when you're paying attention to the games story. It creates very vague hints as to where you should be going. And other times the game will just instantly take you to the quests location.  

Unskipable cutscenes (if you even want to call it that) most of it is just characters gesturing and standing while a Dialogue box appears below. With no way to increase the speed, or to outright skip it entirely.  

I swear there was a cutscene that was probably at least 15 minutes long. And if you weren't going to read it. It was 10 whole minutes of you pressing the same button over and over. 

I don't mind reading. I play a lot!!! Of RPG's... But usually with Role Playing Games there is some sort of middle ground between combat and story, and character interactions.  

What could fix this game is Quest Markers, an interactive map with layers and the ability to see NPC's in the map and to see some sort of icon indicating they have a quest for you.  Reduced character dialogue with their personalities intact.  I feel like the entire cast of characters could lose at least several pages of dialogue in total and it would be a bit more tolerable.  Also could of included the option to skip dialogue.  

The Combat is the bread and butter of this game. However the story does it's very best to hinder that aspect as much as possible throughout the entire playthrough. 

I truly hope that TIME STRANGER will have some QOL improvements that are specific to the issues this game has.

review:
I rarely, if ever write reviews, but here goes.

This game is still in early access so take what I post with a grain of salt. 

To start, the game in it's current form, as of August of 2025, is a solid game in concept and it plays fairly smoothly. 

Pros:

1. It saves automatically quite often. I cannot express to you how absolutely useful and user friendly this is for gamers. Many games that should have auto save capability do not have it, and it's always a big reason why players lose interest once that first big mistake happens and they then lose hours, or sometimes an entire play through.

2. Buildings in this game can be moved instead of having to tear them down and reconstruct them. Many city builders seem to think that it is in the best interest of the game play to force players to lose resources AND time in tearing buildings down, only to then make them use more to build new ones. This is especially aggravating when it comes to upgraded buildings that require fully upgrading them over again. In FF, there is no such issue, you simply move the building to the desired location and it automatically repopulates and begins working as intended.

3. Most of the upgrading system for buildings is in a good place balance wise. There are a few notable black marks, but otherwise, the meat and potatoes of the game works well and each building upgrade seems to fit the need of the designed age or era in game play.

4. FF has multiple different map types and customizable difficulty levels that it allows you to control. The options to change your challenge levels are very in depth and provide massive replayability.

5. Upgraded buildings allow for automated resource gather for some of the most basic resources in the game once you have made it midway through a play through. This frees up time to focus on a larger city and not become overloaded. Many games do not handle this aspect well and become a slog by forcing players to endlessly pause the game just to continuously micro-manage even the most basic resources.


Cons:

1. Micro-management can become tedious at times, especially late game when your city becomes very large. Most city builders suffer from this so it is not a big surprise, and FF handles it fairly well, but it still becomes tedious nonetheless at city populations at or over 500.

2. Food resources are inconsistent in their use by villagers. The marketplace is supposed to supply dwellings with food, medicine, and basics like firewood and water. Unfortunately, I find that even with a fully upgraded marketplace and all villagers occupying it, they still cannot keep up with just 25 or so dwellings. I have witnessed behaviors where workers will take resources from one house, to another house, then back again, doing nothing but wasting time. 

3. Useless tasks added by developer. About 6 months ago, the developer, for some unknown reason decided to make workers go do things like "laundry", "sorting", and "cooking".... these actions might seem to make sense from a realism standpoint, but they only serve to take workers away from their appointed tasks. An example I recently encountered was a forager going to harvest berries, who picked about 10 berries, and abruptly dropped them to go do laundry. Then, when finished, they went to get more berries, and stopped halfway from the berries, then walked all the way back to their hut to cook. This cost over 2 months of in game time for that one worker, which represents about 25% of their entire available gathering period. All for nothing. This was not needed, and never should have been added to the game, as well as NO ONE asked for it.

4. Forager huts need to be fixed. Foragers were initially fairly useful, then were programmed to be so productive when upgraded that it made farming nearly useless. Then when they were patched to rebalance them, they were nerfed so badly that there is never a reason to have any more than 1 or 2 forager huts and NEVER to upgrade them at all. Upgraded forager huts need to be able to move any plant into their garden while simultaneously STILL being able to gather out from the wilderness. Currently, forager huts are unusable.

5. Terrain management needs to be upgraded so that we are not reliant on getting lucky just to find a plateau to place our town center on. If we can level terrain, then there is no reason we cannot raise or lower terrain. The current system requires hours of tedious point by point manipulation of terrain in order to get the desired result.


Overall, I DO recommend this game, however, I would say that it has a long way to go and the developers need to stop adding things into the game that drag villagers away from designated tasks. Realism is one thing, but functionality in games like this is far more important.

1. Visually appealing.  This is cosmetic, but the game feels good, and allows you to drift into the game.  
2. Control and Game Play.  It's relatively easy to control, somewhat self-explanatory, and in its current pre-release form, almost everything makes sense.  There's a few things that bug, such as controlling individuals and groups and such, but again, a work in progress - to be seen how it comes out in release.
3.  Depth of game.  Many of the resources intertwine with each other in terms of need, so even though there are not a 100 resources to boggle your mind, the 30 are all intertwined well.  The depth and interdependence makes the game challenging in a good way. 
 4.  Replayability.  Every map is different, and your cities will be different to adapt.   

Some of the annoying items are the combat and raids, predators, how much some buildings cost to maintain and such, but you have to remind yourself this game is close to release, so it is still a work in progress.  But the base of the game is great and challenging, and I recommend this game.

Overall, it's a great game.

Farthest Frontier is an incredibly immersive and enjoyable game that captures the magic of building a unique fantasy world from scratch. Set in a singular, fictional realm, this game offers players the opportunity to create and manage their own settlements within a vibrant, fantasy setting.

The game’s aesthetic is nothing short of stunning. The art style evokes a blend of whimsical fantasy elements with a touch of realism, creating a world that feels both familiar and otherworldly. Every building, from charming cottages to majestic cathedrals, is meticulously crafted with attention to detail. The environment also supports unique interactions—players can meet raiders who will attack you on sight!

As a colonials/simulator game, Farthest Frontier offers a deep and satisfying experience where you take control of your community. From deciding how to allocate resources to building settlements and fostering relationships with neighboring towns or mini-refugees, every decision can lead to significant changes in the growth and prosperity of your town. Whether you opt for a thriving city or a more laid-back village, the game provides ample opportunities to experiment and refine your approach.

The satisfaction of managing different aspects—such as handling disputes between raiders, ensuring the survival of your population, and adapting to unforeseen challenges—makes this game stand out. The ability to create unique buildings and structures not only enhances the visual appeal but also adds an extra layer of depth to the gameplay experience.

If you’re a fan of SimCity or enjoy building and managing colonies within fantasy worlds, Farthest Frontier is a must-play title that offers hours of engaging and satisfying gameplay. Its combination of fantasy setting and deep colonials/simulator mechanics ensures that every player can create their own unique story within this enchanting world.

In conclusion, Farthest Frontier is a standout game in its genre, offering a unique blend of fantasy aesthetics and strategic depth. Whether you’re ready to dive into building your ideal town or take on the role of an adventurous colonizer seeking to shape the future of your fictional realm, this game provides plenty of reason to explore its rich world and enjoy its charming gameplay mechanics.

review:
Farthest Frontier – The Ultimate “Ye Olde HOA” Simulator

If you’ve ever thought, “I’d like to build a lovely little medieval village, watch it thrive, and then see it all burn to the ground because I forgot to stock enough firewood for winter” — then congratulations, you’ve found your game.

You start with a few peasants, a wagon of hope, and a dream. Within an hour, you’ve either built a quaint, self-sustaining community… or created the Middle Ages’ worst tourist trap, complete with dysentery and wolves that seem to have unionized.

And then come the raiders. They don’t care about your feelings, your economy, or that you just finished putting up your cute new market square. They want your gold, your food, and probably your goats. They’ll tear through your lovingly placed palisade wall like it’s made of pretzel sticks. But hey—when you finally beat them back with your hastily armed militia, it’s one of the most satisfying “get off my lawn” moments in gaming history.

The graphics are gorgeous, the farming is oddly therapeutic, and watching your villagers go about their day is great—right up until they all die of scurvy because you forgot to plant a single fruit tree. review:
Unfortunately, this game just isn't up to scratch for a number of reasons.

Firstly, it looks like a game from 2005, with an ugly colour palette, low poly models, weird aliasing.. (and the list goes on). It has some serious performance issues, making my (very above specs) PC sound like a jet engine the whole time when playing. Simply moving the camera around is choppy/stuttery for no reason at all, even with high frame-rates, making the entire experience feel off.

Building your city and collecting resources is unnecessarily frustrating: at the beginning, you have to pick a spot where to start your main base to then expand from. However, you'll almost never find a position that has all materials needed, so if you pick a wrong spot you might find out later on to have NO ACCESS to vital resources. The solution is to either just restart the game and find a better spot, or to build another settlement far from your main one, which adds a lot of annoying travel time.

The cost of buildings is fine initially, but you'll soon be required to have absolute mountains of gold (a currency that you gain VERY slowly) even for basic small things like decorations. Same thing with some of the other resources. So get ready to sit there staring at the screen, while your required resources trickle up at a glacially slow pace just to afford some tiny decoration or one building (with the game at max speed).

Everything is on a grid, and while that isn't a problem per se as many other city builders are like that, it takes away from the naturalistic look and feel of the game. The (absolutely horrendous) road drawing tool allows you to draw curves, but nobody in their right mind should do that as it eats away squares from the grids and occupies vital building space. To add to this annoyance, any service building with an area of effect on surrounding ones has a HARD LIMIT on which areas it affects: If a building is even one square off the zone of influence, it receives NO service from the service building. And believe me, you'll need a LOT of service buildings and things of that nature, as this game has an absolute laundry list of micro-managerial tasks and annoyances to deal with (food spoilage, rats, diseases, temperature, beautification, religion, you name it).

The crop growing system is interesting, as it allows crop rotation over a few years, with certain crops having different weather or fertility requirements. The problem is that these requirements are represented by bars that are filled up to a certain point, but which are completely inconsistent with the results: I've had crops that claim to be resistant to certain climates be an absolute lie, and die with a minimal change of temperature.

The various threats that attack your settlement (wild animals, and eventually raiders) are a constant pain in the ass: since any form of defence is prohibitively expensive, get ready to watch your citizens get mauled to death by a random wandering wolf while you can do absolutely nothing about it until MUCH later on. Even a single defensive tower will cost you the equivalent of a bank loan and set you way back currency-wise.

I really tried liking this game but I just can't do it anymore. I sincerely hope it gets better during this early access period, but I've seen no substantial updates in a long time so I highly doubt it.

For any of the devs reading this: I'm sorry, I'm just being completely honest. I can feel the passion behind this, but at the same time the issues are too glaringly obvious. There is a gem hidden in this game somewhere, and I hope to see it shine one day.

If you don't make it in time to make your villagers happy, then you might as well start another game which makes you waste your time.

 I'm glad I did not pay for this.  It doesn't seem like a game that is being actively worked on since it's been in early access for many years.  If it is, then there's little money being thrown at it to hire devs.

I'm not talking about the "tutorial" they have with a pop up stating what a building does, but one that moves you through the mechanics.  This is how most games work.  They usually get your through the basic mechanics through the first level.  In this case, at least it should show you how to create a town center, shelter, how to harvest, how to tell a villager A to go harvest this and villager B to go harvest that.

Great potential here, but clearly this is an unfinished, seemingly abandoned game, hastily released to make a quick buck.

Unfortunately, several glitches have remained in game, unaddressed. Such as disappearing War Boxes, Objectives failing to update mid-stage, characters in the select screen being stuck in T pose, even Steam Achievements that fail to trigger. Also the character pics (top left) seem lazily copy pasted. Facial screenshots would have easily done the job, with minimal effort. These factors lead one to quickly realise that this game was initially created diligently, with care, and in good faith. But with the end result being a rushed-to-release title, with minimal fixes to critical issues.

The combat interface is solid, but the overall menu interface needs a lot of work. Good little timewaster. If fixes were in place for the aformentioned issues, this would easily be a $19.99 title, (more even, if paid content was available in game) instead of the $4.99 it's at now.

I have high hopes that this title is readdressed, and gets it's fixes. It would be a damn shame to see this game, with it's great potential, simply rot in the Steam Store, collecting nothing but dust.

review:
This is an amazingly fun item-arena brawler. The closest games I would compare it to are the Bomberman series and Killer Queen Black.  

Your character avatar has no impact on your move set, which consists of punching, grabbing/activating an item, and throwing an item. Your associated Ancient One cult (Cthulhu, Dagon, and Nyarlathotep right now) does have a slightly altered move set, which are fitting for the time-limited avatar transformations (similar to a Smash Bros. Smash Ball). The game moves at such a frantic, hilariously fast and fun pace that it doesn't need more than this.  

The maps are small king/queen-of-the-hill arenas, and your goal is to knock everyone off the map arena. The strategy element comes in from the weapon/item variety, which makes great use of rock-paper-scissors for the 5-second showdown fight. 

The single-player and cooperative content is there, but is still being worked on for a longer experience. What is there now is amazing and immersive. My only "complaint" as of July 9, '20 is that the story is short (note, this is early access). For Overcooked gamers, think of it as only having worlds 1-x and 2-x finalized for playing for the story campaign (there are more "worlds" being worked on). A solo gamer would enjoy this game as a fully released product. A solo gamer that likes the Cthulhu mythos would very likely enjoy the game now. There is no online cooperative element; it is currently local-coop only.

Competitive multiplayer matches are short and sweet. They're not quite as short as Mario Party or WarioWare games, and are closer to a Bomberman or Invisigun Heroes game experience. Each map is out to kill the players in a uniquely different way, so it's hard for a match to have a single person taking a huge lead. Regarding my earlier reference to Killer Queen Black, the Ancient One that your avatar worships and transforms into is very similar to the Soldier Bee mechanic. You have a limited experience in the "evolved state", and each transformation will alter your strategy.

review:
It's fairly basic for a game but fun still and a good value for the price.

The game has a number of different areas and holes and one thing I am not used to in the mini golf games I played in the past was being able to angle my ball up.  Being able to shoot your ball up at an angle makes for some interesting short cuts here and there if you dare try and take them.  The ball isn't confined to just the outline of the hole, so you can knock it up and over and I found that to be entertaining and a new concept compared to the mini golf games I played in the past (I admit I haven't played a lot of them so I don't know how common this is).

If it cost more I'd have an issue with one specific thing that I feel I need to let go for a game that is only $3.  There are camera angle issues that come up sometimes.  There are times where the camera should move positions but doesn't and there are a few just bad spots here and there because of the auto camera.  If we could move it a bit ourselves that issue would be taken care of (the courses are 3D, the camera has the ability to move all over the place, I'm not sure why they don't let us adjust it some ourselves when needed).

At first I thought there was no sound, but then I saw that my sound effects were set off by default for some reason and I quickly turned them on.  

The game is basically set in a single resolution so if you do set it to full screen, it doesn't look quite as pretty as the images stretch out to fit your full screen.

Like any game you have to play a bit to get used to the system, it is much more fun once you are used to how far the ball goes when hitting it at certain strengths and stuff.

In the end it's $3 (and goes on sale, so you may not even have to pay that).  So I have to let my camera issue go for that price.  It's basically fun to play through and especially interesting to see what I can do trying to make my own short cuts hitting the ball up and across different areas of the holes.

But inside a short game about taking your friend on a cruise are a couple of welcome, subtle ideas that make it especially worth a play and a bit of a gem.

You play as Barney, both a cartoon dog and one of the few blue collar gay protagonists I've seen in a game.  And Barney isn't just clad in overalls and hosting a rusting car on his yard.  The way he looks at the world and deals with people seems a bit harsh but it made sense from the perspective of a man who struggles with how he sees himself in society and how he feels about the guy he's sweet on.  He has his porn links on his desktop and uses public assistance to fund (in a roundabout way) a vacation with his one true love.  Barney's bad decisions anchor the game in a way that makes it much more about character than exploration, which I liked.  It's not an agenda game and the theme is in the periphery but I found that made it work very well over the course of its short runtime.  Plus a nice bit of theatrical misdirection involving a gun was amusing.

Pick it up if you have an hour and a half to spare over the weekend.  This game is the kind of little break we all need now and again.

review:
The original stood out with its unique blend of top-down stealth, co-op heists, and character-driven class abilities. With this sequel, the developer takes the concept further, experimenting with procedural generation and a new 3D presentation, while holding onto the chaotic charm that made the first game a favorite among co-op players.

The core idea remains the same: assemble a crew of specialists, infiltrate locations, and pull off daring heists while avoiding guards, cameras, and alarms. The shift to procedurally generated levels is the biggest change. Instead of hand-crafted maps, each mission is dynamically built, which boosts replayability but sacrifices some of the clever, puzzle-like design the first game was known for. The game retains the class system, with familiar roles like the Locksmith, Cleaner, and Hacker, each with distinct abilities that make teamwork essential. AI guards are smarter than before, responding more dynamically to noise, suspicious activity, and player mistakes, which adds intensity to each mission. [b]Monaco 2[/b] swaps the flat, colorful 2D aesthetic for a stylized 3D isometric look. While it loses a bit of the original’s minimalist clarity, the new style makes environments more detailed and immersive. Sound design is once again excellent, with reactive jazz music that ramps up as the action escalates. The frantic piano riffs returning mid-chase are a nostalgic highlight.

Just like its predecessor, co-op is the heart of the experience. Playing with friends, planning (or failing to plan) a perfect heist, and adapting to chaos on the fly is where [b]Monaco 2[/b] shines brightest. Solo play is possible, but without teammates, missions can feel more punishing and less entertaining.

[b]Monaco 2[/b] is both familiar and experimental: it captures the anarchic joy of botched heists with friends, but trades the original’s handcrafted brilliance for endless procedural variety. If you loved the chaos and camaraderie of [b]Monaco: What’s Yours is Mine[/b], the sequel is a worthy successor—though it may divide fans who preferred carefully designed levels over endless randomness.
