review:
Like Monaco 1, great game. The 3D perspective with semi-new classes is a great idea for a sequel.

Like Monaco 1, it takes a bit to get used to - it can be tricky to track coins in the new perspective. 

There is a planning stage at the beginning, and you can refer to your map at any time, but planning seems completely pointless at the beginning for everything but story atmosphere (which ends up being a negative - a bit of a "duhh let's just go" moment every level). The map works to find leftover coins later in the level which is great. For some reason, if your character is looking at the map and you're attacked or killed, you will not be warned or jolted out of the map - you'll just be none the wiser until you exit the map. I left feedback about this on discord 3.5 months before this review, and it's still in the game like this.

Like Monaco 1, you play as one of 4 classes in every level and these get mixed up depending on the level - love it, classic Monaco feels. This time around they get trinkets to further uniqueify them, and you unlock trinkets by playing levels with shorter times and more coins.

This progression falls over a bit here, and the most effective way to progress is a hard grind of the very easy first level using the new procedurally generated alternative seeds (which is very cool, albeit subtle). You get a new trinket with an alternative way to play your class at 1 gem, 2 gems, 5 gems and 10 gems, in that sequence. So to get the last skill-based trinket, you need to spend 19 gems per class, over 8 classes. The first level takes 3-10 minutes as a sort of tutorial level, and from about the third level onwards, you can expect to play for an hour or two depending on your speedrunning skill. I don't think the extra gems you get are worth the extra time and effort you spend on those much more difficult levels.

Importantly, the trinkets don't seem to get better with each tier - each character's trinkets are very hit and miss. Some you'll probably never want to use unless you want to challenge yourself, and those aren't the highest-level trinkets. It's not like you have a weaker trinket at tier 1 that you'll use until you unlock a better trinket at tier 2. What makes this stranger, is that every trinket has a health-based penalty, with higher tier trinkets costing as much or more health than the last tier. This would only make sense if the higher tier trinkets were always better.

There's multiple better ways to have done this, like just having the option to unlock any trinket at any point once you have enough gems (let's say 4 gems per tier). Then unlocking more trinkets would feel less like something you have to do and more like a bonus for experimenting as long as you like.

One character in particular seems to have no value at all. Her ability is a dash, but it barely moves you out of the way of whatever you're dashing away from or towards any faster than walking, and she has trinkets that are as expensive as any other character to do things you'd expect her dash to do - like dodge damage. Every other game has a dodge roll, why do I need to spend 19 gems to do that with this character? That ability should be free, and this highest-tier ability should be replaced with something else. Let me ricochet ranged attacks back to my attackers during dashes or something.

Probably the best thing about Monaco 2 is that (most of) the new classes feel a little overpowered in some cases, except that when you bring them into a game, you still feel like you're having fun with it and you still feel challenged by it. 

There is a particular issue, a victim of the 3D perspective I think, where usable items are placed too-close together, and only one becomes accessible at all. The prison level has a computer with a vent right next to it, and the computer is completely unusable because pressing E near it (in any position) triggers the windup to enter the vent instead. There's seemingly unavoidable situations like this all over the game anytime the pickaxe is used to create a new interactable.

Overall, the game could use some fine-tuning but I'm still regularly itching to play Monaco 2 just as much as I ever did with Monaco 1.

Started game up, it was extremely loud. Tried to find a menu to turn the game volume down, there was none. When I tried to play with a friend, I accidentally chose "Host Game" instead of join, and found there was no way back to the main menu that I could find, had to close the game and restart to get to the menu again.

Once actually in the game it was alright, but nothing special. It was very obscure what to do half the time, no indication of what objects are interactable and which are not. The area in which your hands have to be with an object to interact with it is extremely small. The ropes you climb were very inconsistent to grab because of it. Once you get into the main room it gets a little better, though the last room is really obscure and cluttered to the point that it's distracting and we spent over 10 minutes before we happened onto the mechanic the game was trying to have us perform.

There was also a lack of rotation options, snap rotation is something that should really be in any game where you're expected to rotate around consistently.

The lack of a real menu to adjust options, the lack of ability to go back to the starting screens, the lack of feedback from the game (pressing buttons doesn't make and visual or auditory effect to signal that it did something), lack of snap rotation, just made for a generally irritating experience.

Overall the game could use a lot of polish and better game design choices. The puzzles were simple and short, the game has little replayability other than trying to get the lowest score. It's not a bad game, I did get some fun out of it, just not enough for me to recommend, there were more painful moments in the game than enjoyable ones.

This being said, there weren't that many bugs, even if many mechanics felt stiff, unintuitive, or finicky. The game is only $3 at this point, so expectations weren't that high, so it was a closer call on whether to recommend or not. In the end, after playing it, I felt no desire to replay, thus my decision is not recommended.

review:
Ethanol in Dungeon is a casual game for a casual price. The controls are pretty awful...and that's perfectly fine.
It's one of those titles (like e.g. Octodad), where struggling with an unorthodox control scheme makes the backbone of the gameplay. It's called "Ethanol in Dungeon" because Reimu and Mystia have had too much liquor and must now fight Kedama and Fairies while being drunken zombies.
The girls will always walk forward no matter what and will even take damage when brushing the dungeon walls. You change direction on a click, but the direction you switch to is determined by timing your click with a pointer that's constantly rotating around you. Shooting is also done by clicking, but your weapon has a cooldown. Click when it's not ready and you'll just change direction. Under these rules, even the weakest, dumbest enemies are not to be taken lightly. There's a power-up system that allows you to improve your shots or reduce weapon cooldown, but get hit by an enemy and your power value drops in large jumps. For some levels, it's smart to stay out of trouble and find power icons before getting too close to the enemy clusters.
Reimu is the character for beginners, Mystia unlocks after clearing the third stage and is essentially hard mode, performing even worse than the hungover shrine maiden. Overall, it's a short but cute game that will amuse you as your initial performance will look so bumbling and confused, it's like you've never played a video game in your life.

** UPDATE ** at the bottom.

NOTE: I have only played this game for like 2-3 hours. I left it paused for a long time, so it says I played for like 8.

"Slight Yes" vote. It was fun for a couple hours, but is not very fun anymore.
 
This game has potential, but I see a couple issues that together severely limit it's replay value.

1) While the levels are technically different every time, it's still the same type of level with the same type of enemies. Level 1 is a dungeon and level 2 is a castle (I have not reached level 3 yet). This means that after I finish level 1 with skeletons, I am not surprised that level 2 is a castle with knights.

2) There are no save points and healing is limited. You only get 1 life and if you are almost dead by the time you get to the boss, there is nothing you can do but fight with low HP.

Each boss takes a couple attempts (I have tried the second boss 4 times now). Each time I die, I have to spend 20 minutes going through the dungeon and then the castle just to get to the second boss. This begins to feel grindy.

If I make it past the second boss, I will probably die soon after that and have to start over again. Each play through becomes exponentially longer, but is pretty much the same as the last - so there is not really any excitement getting back to the last point of death.

Imagine playing dark souls (or any other long multi-boss game) where you have to restart the entire game after each death.

If some or all of the following were added/changed, this would significantly boost the replay value:

* Randomizing the environment of each level (level 1 is not always a dungeon and level 2 is not always a castle). If I have to restart from the beginning, at least it feels like more of a new adventure.

* Save points after each level - so you don't have to start from the beginning again and again.

review:
Had a lot of fun with Moo Lander. This is a different kind of game than what I'm used to. I play a lot of Metroidvanias, and while this has elements of that genre, I wouldn't categorize it as one. It's more linear, with occasional offshoots, many of which are unfortunately missable. Go in one direction looking for a secret, and you could get locked into the next section of the main track before you know it, so just forge ahead and enjoy the experience. And that's totally fine! My FOMO faded quickly after this happened a couple times. You'll still get plenty of upgrade points, fun weapons, and encounter interesting and bizarre physics puzzles.

The bosses were fun challenges. While there was a fair amount of similarity between some boss battles, a couple in particular have unique mechanics that made them really stand out. The final boss was an absolute blast.

The sound design and visual style fit well and create a unique atmosphere consisting of several different biomes with unique mechanics, but you won't be backtracking through them like in a Metroidvania.

The story was fine. A little silly, with mostly consistently-paced plot developments to move you along. Many actual Metroidvania games are pretty light on plot, so it was nice to have one in place in Moo Lander, and having it be a self-aware plot lent a sense of levity that makes the experience unique from your run-of-the-mill Metroidvania where the world has been corrupted or infected and everything is dark and depressing. Not so in Moo Lander. While it wasn't as cheerful as Yoku's Island Express or Islets, it's definitely not a dark, harrowing experience overall, and won't drain your emotional energy.

This game was made by a small Bulgarian developer, and I'd like more people to play it to see the creativity on offer here. It's worth your money at the full price which is less than $20 USD, and does go on sale from time to time. Support small studios and play something completely unique! I look forward to The Sixth Hammer's next title.

review:
What a game. Going in, I wasn’t sure what to expect superhero games can be a hit or a miss. But this one surprised me in the best way. It’s funny, heartfelt, and packed with a story that works without leaning on the movies.

The story and characters are the real stars here. The banter between the Guardians is constant and often gave me a genuine chuckle, but it never feels like filler. Every character gets their moment, and some hit harder than I expected. [spoiler]Mantis stole the show for me with her weird, prophetic, almost “out of time” way of speaking. And Drax’ grief over his wife and daughter gave the game a weight I didn’t see coming, the way the Guardians supported him felt genuine.[/spoiler]

Gameplay was a mixed bag. Combat could feel repetitive at times, but the variety of Guardian abilities and the different ways to play as Star-Lord kept it engaging enough for one (maybe two) playthroughs. The real hook wasn’t the fighting anyway it was hearing the team’s interactions mid-battle or while exploring.

The presentation is top-notch. Every planet and location feels distinct and true to its story, and the visuals pop with color and personality. The licensed soundtrack is as good as you’d expect classic tracks paired with a strong original score that make even the downtime memorable.

The pacing hit the right spot for me. It’s a game that wants you to take your time, and it rewards you for it with dialogue and character moments. On a second playthrough, some areas dragged a little, but honestly, the sheer amount of banter made it easy to overlook.

As for replayability, it’s not really about making different choices the story feels more or less set. I’d probably revisit it years down the line, or even better, play it with a friend who hasn’t experienced it yet.

Overall, if you like character driven stories with humor, heart, and a killer soundtrack, you should absolutely give Guardians of the Galaxy a shot. It’s one of the few superhero games that feels less like a movie tie-in and more like its own complete adventure.

review:
[h2]Few games are ballsy enough to start with you listening to a 50 minute space metal album created specifically for the game itself.
The choice to stop listening and to continue the story... Is yours.[/h2]


I'll start by admitting that I haven't (Yet!) played Insomniac's Spider-Man games, so my knowledge of really good comic book inspired games is somewhat reduced.
Having said that, I think [b]Eidos Montreal's Guardians of the Galaxy is the best big budget, comic book based game I played since the Batman Arkham games.[/b]

When it comes to [b]the main cast[/b], there's just the right mix of familiarity with the MCU movies and the extended lore from the comics, all remixed into something just a bit different, enough to call its own.
They quip, they banter, they argue... Really, it's almost shocking just [b]HOW MUCH dialogue[/b] was written and recorded for this game. It's not just cutscenes and specific dialogue scenes, but also during gameplay, both in exploration and combat. While it's a subjective thing, I really believe the majority of it all is really well done, so I found it impossible to get tired of it, and it even seemed too eerily quiet when they just... shut up for a bit. More on that later.

Before the writing and dialogue, the thing that first jumps out at you (other than the aforementioned 50 minute music album) is just how [b]varied and amazing the art design is[/b]. There's just SO MUCH variety! Great use of colors, little to any reuse of materials and geometry... Every new place you go looks and feels completely different, in ways not often seen in video games. Even without Ray Traced reflections, the game really looks... [i]Marvelous[/i].

Exploration and combat are probably the least impressive parts of the game as a game, but they're not too bad:
During standard exploration you alternate between looking for collectibles, upgrade materials and listening to the ever-constant character banter. Sometimes you can find yourself just standing still and listening to the Guardians talk. It's fun stuff!

When thinking about the combat of the game, there can be a subjective feeling of a missed opportunity due to gameplay being entirely limited to just Star-Lord, as opposed to the possibility of playing as any Guardian. I get that, but I think [b]the choice to keep it strictly to Star-Lord worked out nicely[/b], because it feels more congruent with the game in general - you play as Star-Lord, the supposed "leader" of the Gardeners of the Galaxy (Wait, Gardeners? Must've been an administrative mistake on my part there. Blame Groot, heh), and throughout the game the character dynamics shift and change as new revelations and deeper connections are formed. I'd say more, but that would be a spoiler in and of itself.
When combat does happen, it's clear that as Star-Lord you're not meant be the main damage dealer of the team, but rather the LEADER of the team - the Guardians will listen to you when you tell them to use a specific combat ability, so it's entirely up to you to set up the right context for them to make the most of their abilities. The weak mobs that pepper the battlefield may not require any measure of concentration when dealing with them, so even just spamming melee attacks on them works out well enough, but when it comes to the mini-bosses... You HAVE to make the entire team work together, which means stacking up stagger multipliers by combining the right attack abilities coming from the whole team to set up special finishers. If this sounds a bit too tactical - no worries, even on the hard difficulty preset you can just get a feel for what works, spam it, and hope for the best.
If all else fails, when a specific bar fills up you can call the Guardians to huddle up, give them a pep talk and enjoy a few seconds of decreased cooldowns and damage buffs.
...Oh, and also a licensed song.

[b]Licensed Songs[/b] are an absolute highlight in Guardians of the Galaxy. The game features, both in cutscenes and in gameplay, some of the most popular and famous songs the western world jammed to in the 80s. They're used in every and any way that counts - as exclamation points during cutscenes, specific gameplay moments and even as ambient music in the Player's ship, the Milano.
Not to take anything away from the composed music for the game, however! It's not just the aforementioned album, there's also an entire score of music that fits well and works well for the game, so combined with some welcome advanced audio settings - the game really covers the audio part of audiovisual.

The part I'd like to talk about the least is the game's writing, and not because it's bad or wholly unimportant, rather the opposite - the game's writing, plot and character moments are surprisingly engaging and even deep at times in ways the casual MCU fan may not even realize. All I'll say is that the game tells a story that may have been told many times, but is as worth experiencing here as it's ever been.
As long as you're willing to welcome an entire game with the Guardians of the Galaxy, incessant banter and all, you'll get to experience what is arguably [b]their best depiction in any kind of audiovisual medium.[/b]

There's one thing worth lamenting now, years later - the possibly irreparable damage done to this game before it ever came out by the prior release and disappointment of the 2020 [i]Marvel's Avengers[/i] live-service game (also published by Square Enix). On the outside, both game seem similar - inspired by the success of the MCU, these games feature a cast that's obviously riffing off their MCU counterparts, both games are third person action games...
...And yet, they're just not the same at all! Whereas Marvel's Avengers was wholly and utterly compromised to its very core by its live-service trappings, Eidos Montreal's Guardians of the Galaxy was a game that was designed, written and produced to be exactly what it should've been - an action adventure game that is entirely single player, entirely story focused, and fully uncompromised.
If it wasn't for that failed Avengers game, GotG might've had the commercial success it deserved. Alas, it is likely to remain sequel-less.

I don't just recommend this game, I practically [b]urge[/b] you - if you even heard about it and thought it might be worth playing eventually: It IS. Play it. You'll likely not regret it.

review:
Absolutely great game! There are countless positives to experiencing Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy. 

For one, the combat is amazing. It has loads of variety, is engaging, and is honestly like no other combat i've experienced in any other game. No fight ever felt dragged or unpleasant, with the combat model and fights always offering a good challenge, and the need for strategy and consideration under pressure.

Also, the story was absolutely solid. It had all the components of (what I think) make a good, emotional and hard hitting story. One thing I found great was the inclusion plenty of comedy, which was never forced and felt natural to each scenario. However, there were also select moments that revealed how well written the story was, weather it was a simple lore dump on one of the characters, or a heartfelt moment in which you decide the outcome. I was also personally fond of the chapter model that the game used, making it really feel like I was experiencing a story, and it also provided fulfilment with the completion of each chapter. There were many points in the story where the player had a say in what occurred, which made the game feel even more immersive. 

On the topic of immersion - the characters and lore felt truly close to the Marvel Guardians of the Galaxy IPs. In the sense that each character always had the exact same vibe and demeanour seen in the 3 movies and Christmas special presented by Marvel. Compared to other games that are entirely based of pre-existing IPs, I would like to say this game did it perfectly.

Furthermore, there were plenty of fun and intrigueing aspects for collectors and completionists - with countless collectables, items that could initiate amusing chats with characters, pieces of lore scattered about, intricate outfits to collect for each character, and my favourite: the achievements! It was greatly enjoyable to keep track of achievements, and devising methods to get certain more difficult ones. 

Despite what many people say, I believe that the graphics were largely fine, with a consistent frame rate throughout my playthrough. The only gripe I would have with the presentation of the game was the morphing of objects and the odd glitch that made entities do silly (but funny) actions mid way through serious situations, e.g. walking through a counter during an intense argument. 

Overall, it was an unforgettable, satisfying, entertaining and (mostly) complete game! I would most definitely reccommend it to anybody who likes fighting games, story focused games, 'butterfly effect' games (as I like to call them) and generally those who love a good chapter based game backed by an undoubtedly strong IP.

A fantastic 8/10 for me. Try it out!

review:
[i]"Hello, Sidney - remember me?"[/i]

I don't usually review DLC, but here we go! Scream is iconic. Born in 1996 and an icon of horror cinema, this long running meta-slasher series has been an important part of the genre for some 30 plus years now. The story of determined Final Girl Sidney Prescott (now the Carpenter Sisters) and her stalker, the enigmatic, twisty, and stealthy Ghostface Killer in their many iterations, is truly one that is near and dear to many people's hearts. So it was a no-brainer that Dead by Daylight had to bring this slasher villain to the game in one way or another, even if they didn't get the Scream license. Here we are, almost 7 to 8 years into this game's release, and the Ghost Face chapter is still though early one of the most fun additions to the game - provided you can handle him, Blondie.

Of course the appeal of the Ghostface Killer is that they're an everyman - anyone can be under the mask, killing for whatever sick reason they find feasible. It's just a shame there's no Sidney Survivor or Macher House map to run around in like in Scream, but I get it. They could only get the mask... but you do get the option to get the classic robes, and even the option to swap masks as you see fit, just in case you wanted to, IDK, play the Scream VI iteration of Ghostie instead. This Ghostface is definitely not the same as any of the film iterations, he's his own thing - a serial killing mastermind that might be the sharpest version of this character yet. He's actually based directly on the same real-life horror that inspired Scream - the Gainesville Ripper case. While that murderous psycho was caught, this one never was - instead, he went on a spree of violence across the US, taking a job as a journalist even to cover up his crimes, using that to spread further paranoia about his murderous persona. Mild-mannered by day, monster by night - and who doesn't love a good true crime inspired serial killing masked madman, huh?

His lore is interesting but that's not the main draw - the draw is the gameplay, and the gameplay is pretty damn fun. Hard, but fun! His kit is built a little different from other Killers and it's a wall some people will bounce off of. While you do have no terror radius with him, you also don't have a lot of speed or map pressure, which can feel underwhelming. But for the right person playing him like he's Agent 47 or an evil Batman, you can have a hell of a lot of fun stalking and skulking around like a mastermind of paranoia. And of course, that's exactly what you do here with him - stealthy ambush jumpscares. He still has, all these years later, some of the best mindgame and jumpscare potential in the game, an important aspect of making DBD, well... scary again, and doesn't everyone love a good scary movie?

Unlike other characters in this game, Ghostie isn't a chasedown Killer. He's more of a wait and see approach, a passive style that is meant to cause tension in the Survivors. While this may not always work against the 1000+ hour squads at higher levels of play, it's still a grand old time, if you can get the stalks in and close the gaps. To this end you need to put on the right perks, just as a forewarning - his kit is decent, but not that good. I personally run my Ghostie as a high-info, high-gen-pressure build that keeps Survivors still long enough to be stalked, exposed, and downed in one hit. You also need to be precise and tactical because he's a bit like the knife he wields: if you are handling him well he can stomp, but if you handle him poorly you're only going to hurt yourself. He is not the strongest, no, but in the right hands, you can have loads of fun and do quite well. To do well, you have to learn the maps, the tiles, Survivor tactics, and how the game operates to really get good with him, and even then it can be a bit luck-dependent. Make no mistake, for an M1 Killer with a seemingly simple kit, he is deceptively tough to use well. But when you do get the good game, when you are able to keep Exposing people left and right, stalking and stealthing around, coming from corners for jumpscares and scattering them in a panic? Oh my God is it the most amazing feeling ever. No wonder at least six iterations of people in the films grew a bit... addicted to the feeling of being the Ghostface Killer. And what's even better is that because he's still a spookier character with a different kit, he's often just as fun and funny to go against as Survivor, too! Some of my favorite rounds in this game have been against Ghostfaces, and some of the scariest have been too.

If that isn't enough to sell you on this, maybe the fact you can crouch will. Oh yes, you can finally teabag those annoying Survivors back. Because of this you have a bit more expressiveness than the average Killer, leading to some super funny moments in rounds. Also, his Mori animation is hilarious - dude straight up stabs you four times and then takes a murder selfie. I might be slightly addicted to collecting these. Scratch that - I definitely am, and it's a problem I don't want help for. Playing the Ghostface is fun, often funny as hell, and really quite a different experience if you know what you are doing. If you like playing stealth games, grab this chapter. Why not take up the Buck 120 and don the mask of a legend in horror cinema with us? After all, "It's a fun game, Sidney..."

review:
Well, I shall be honest.
Ghostface is a really fun to play Killer, especially with his high jumpscare potential, just like Myers. His ability, Night Shroud, is one of the best stealth abilities in the game, almost as good as Myers with the Scratched Mirror. You can have zero terror radius and be able to stalk Survivors(either the usual way or by leaning from a corner) in order to get them Exposed, making them one shot for a good period of time. 45 seconds, to be exact. All these, as long as he is not revealed, either by a Survivor looking at him for too long or by him missing an attack or getting stunned. Also, he's the only Killer who can properly T-bag. So if you feel like humiliating an entitled Survivor who annoyed you for most of the match, there you go.
His perks though... are a mixed bag.  
-Thrilling Tremors is by far his best ability, allowing him to see if Survivors are working on gens or not while the other ones remain blocked for 16 seconds. May have a cooldown of 60 seconds at best, but it really helps with tracking down Survivors working on gens and buys you precious seconds. A really good anti-gen and tracking perk.
-Furtive Chase is pretty pointless. You can get up to 4 tokens that reduce your Terror Radius IN A CHASE by 4 meters every time you hook the obsession. Whoever unhooks the Obsession, becomes the Obsession. Pretty pointless, unless you play Scratched Mirror Myers or try to do a No Terror Radius build for spooky memes.
-I'm All Ears reveals the auras of Survivors that perform a rushed action within 48 meters, for 6 seconds. That sounds good, since it could help you with tracking. But who thought that giving this skill a cooldown was a good idea ? Yes, a cooldown. And the lowest you can get the cooldown is 40 seconds, which for me is just dumb. No wonder I almost never see this perk used, unless people are doing Adept Ghostface or have nothing better to choose. Unless Behavior remove the cooldown completely since not a lot of people will perform rushed actions anyway, it may become a bit more viable.

Overall, Ghostface is a really good Killer, if you play him right. Taking full advantage of Night Shroud is essential, since it helps you get closer to Survivors or have them be 1 shots for a good period of time if stalked long enough. But without it, he's a basic M1 Killer. And at high ranks, he will have trouble. Not to mention that he's pretty heavily reliant on add-ons, especially those that help him stalk faster and get Night Shroud faster since it has a cooldown of 30 seconds. Also, he is very map-reliant. Open and bright maps like Azarov, Coldwind or Crotus Prenn are his worst nightmare since he won't be able to properly sneak close to Survivors, risks getting revealed much easier and his scare factor is destroyed. However, smaller and darker maps like The Game, Midwich, Lerry's and even the new Badham Preschool ones... are where he truly shines. Dare I say he will be scary to go against on the visually updated Badham Preschool maps, just like Myers. So if you just wanna have fun spooking people, Ghostface is for you.

review:
The game has promise, but right now can be very frustrating.

Setting line-ups, positions and pitching roles is straight forward. The way to improve your team is through training points, free agents and trades. You have a minor league team, but NONE of the players are available to you unless you have demoted them from the major league roster. Yet, they generate a record, which is a headscratcher. Supposedly training points can be generated on the Training Screen by updating your training facility. I clicked on every color-coded button and searched for the three dot additional actions area in the upper right of the screen, but was never able to find out how to do an upgrade. It also wasn't in the Front Office screen or the the Ballpark screen.

You are allowed to make trades, but again I was never able to locate the "search" button in the Seasons Screen, so I had no way of seeing who I might want or who I'd want to trade away.

The actual game can be frustrating as well. As you watch the scroll and notice your pitcher getting hammered, quickly making a call to the bullpen doesn't get a reliever in the game until 3 batters later. Usually by then, the game is lost. Another problem is determining what secondary positions your players play. Their primary position is noted, but do all players in the infield play all infield positions? What about outfielders? DH's have no other position noted, so does that mean they are terrible at all positions? Same for pitchers. If you have a starter who is downright terrible, do you just move them to the bullpen and put a reliever in as a starter? What about stamina issues?

There is enough promise to not request a refund, but they need to work out these issues, along with others. The game probably should have been released as an Early Access title.

In its current state, I do not recommend the game.

Feels unfinished after playing for less than an hour so far.

The description of this game after playing for less than an hour seems to be the description for what it may become, which if it gets updated and fleshed out it could be a fun. Currently though it is irritating, though the ui and screens are wonderful, it looks nice.

The daily challenges at the is a cool little walk through, as far as i have gotten.Which isn't far since 2 of the challenges play for 5 days and use the search option under the season screen can't be completed. I went through 10 days with the play 5 days challenge up and it never updated, and then like the other user who commented capmjh I could not find the search option.

The players themselves are very striped down, each has 4 attributes and then their level in each is conveyed by the color of the box. Each time you open a players menu you have to close it to get to the next player, an option the would let you move to the next player would be helpful. Since without opening a players menu you can only see their name, position, current salary and current stats.

Minor league team has some issues, first its not actually a farm system in the normal sense of the word. Unless you demote players to it, there wont be any players on the team. It seems to be a resource generating aspect of the game, except there are 3 resources, its not explained (possible in the challenges which can't be advanced) how to generate them, you start getting popularity as you win games, which you spend to make your minor league stadium better which then generates more popularity.

Again as the other reviewer said the games play to fast, you can't pause them to change the pitcher before the inning is over. If you go to settings there is an option to slow it down, only you can't click it, there's also a option to change difficulty which you can't select. These could be place holders, or they could not be but if they are not working they shouldn't be on the screen. 

The number of available players in free agency is low, and again to learn about them besides that free agent dh wants 25 million a year you have to go into their menu then close out to get to the next one.

I could sadly keep nitpicking things about this game, but it feels unfinished for a pc game, should of been released as a early access game, as there does seem to be some good stuff here for a striped down, less intensive GM sports management game. Sadly i don't know if we will ever see it fulfilled as looking at the website it appears this game is actually meant for mobile devices. So in the end.

Despite being the latest entry in the series, this one was actually a disapointment.

The campaign wasn't as well put together in terms of story, and a lot of the scenes were put together a little lazily, with plenty of spaces obscured by assets that should have been hidden when viewing interiors. The use of features developed in earlier entries in the series was poorly done, with things like the weather/time of day changes only being used on a handful of maps, and without an easy way to see the previously found objects or replay levels.

With the same community creation tools, the game does still have potential - however being the newest in the series there is less quality content available than there is for other entries.

The game does have some interesting unique assets compared to other entries, however unless you or your family specifically have an interest in crime thrillers, classic monsters or aliens, I'd recommend giving this a pass.

If hidden object games are your thing, check out the original game or the Myths and Magic sequel. Only get this one if you are really keen on the unique themes this one features.

review:
[h1]Paint the whole level by visiting each tile[/h1]

[b]As other Nannings titles, [i]Voxel Bot[/i] has [url=https://www.newgrounds.com/portal/view/732270]a free version[/url] available on browser. Steam version has double the number of levels, with bigger ones in the mix but some repetitive aspects.[/b]

Taking the idea from [i]Hexa Path[/i] and taking it into its logical and casual finish line, [i]Voxel Bot[/i] requires you to simply visit each tile of the level, without caring about order. It's hardly even a puzzle game, leaning more towards casual action.

To make things more complicated, tiles may have timed spikes or have other simple mechanics like teleporters or forced movers.

Additionally, there are two kinds of enemies that roam the levels on marked tiles. Usually they just move once every few seconds. But in a couple of levels they move when you do, and since they tend towards you, these are the most puzzle-like levels in the game.

[h1]Technical improvements[/h1]

Graphics are cute voxels, played in isometric view. Controls have seen some progress: in addition to arrows and WASD, you can use diagonal numpad keys or keys 'UIJK', both of which are an improvement. No changing keybindings though, unfortunately.

Additionally, you can play with mouse, clicking each neighbouring tile to move there. I personally liked both mouse and numpad movement for this title.

[h1]An hour of okay[/h1]

Free version had 30 levels: Steam version has double that, 60 levels. My playthrough lasted a little over 1 hour.

The new Steam levels are a bit repetitive though, often with the same map but with different enemies or other features. There are bigger levels but not particularly more challenging. It's still as casual as the free version.

It's an okay game but quite easy and not worth to replay. At least wait for sale price.

I recommend this game, but understand going into it, that this game is not finished. 

Very literally, after going down a number of floors the game just stops, throwing you into a jarring black void with a text scroll and voice over telling you the remainder of the story. On the game's official discord, the dev noted it was meant to have several more floors and two more bosses, but the game didn't get enough following or interest so they just.... didn't. 

The gameplay that IS there is enjoyable, definitely. Took me 21 hours to complete, and I could still yet go back and try the hardcore mode. The fighting, while finicky, is enjoyable, the gear smithing is unique and a nice touch (although material drop rate is a bit annoying), and the bosses are all unique and many quite difficult. There's very little information in the form of guides or wikis or anything out right now about the game which forces the player to actually solve the puzzles and figure things out themselves. Which can be frustrating when, say, the game bugs out and generates a floor without a boss on it (happened several times in my playing), or when a boss clips through a wall never to be seen again and you have to leave and run that floor again. 

It's fun, essentially. Unfinished, but fun. I'd say worth the money.

review:
So I was waiting for them to release their free locomotion patch and they delivered in pretty short order so props on them for that… On the other hand, the game itself is in a pretty rough state.

I’ll admit I didn’t make it far enough into the dungeon to reach the next tileset, it was all cellar, but I’ll get to why that is. Despite that, within a couple floors I was running into some pretty obvious repetition in rooms, even on the same floor, which made navigating a bit of a tossup. Not that there’s much to navigate, the rooms are all pretty empty with the exception of an enemy here and there.

So the dungeon generation is pretty bad and repetitive, but at least you have the combat right? Well unfortunately it’s… well… A lot of people would argue they should use something similar to Blade and Sorcery/Gorn with their physics based combat, and while I can appreciate that, it does mean that you lose out on a lot of traditional gameplay mechanics and generally it’s hard to make high quality AI that put up a proper fight in that situation. That said, this combat doesn’t deliver. Generally the enemy will sit at exactly the range you can’t hit them, than do a prescripted attack routine (the same ones in the same orders) and when they are recovering after the routine you can hit them. It’s boring.

review:
I'm unfortunately having to refund this I'll briefly summarize below. This is based on the current offering at the current price and my opinion MAY change later as more updates, features and bug fixes are rolled out.
basically, there are good things that I like about this game, bad things I dont, and ugly things that are unacceptable; i'll be reviewing it like that. 

Good things:
     =Pseudo-random dungeon design. 
-Basically the game is assembled in blocks; these blocks are randomly pieced together in such a way as to ensure a long distance from the start and finish AND non linear directions/dead ends, making dungeoneering a skill, not a given.
     =Enemies of varying toughness that require different strategy to defeat.
-The first level is easy enough, although if you are careless you can easily die and the enemies have varying moves that are somewhat random, consisting of a random opener and random follow up attacks; the opener seems to be one of a handful and the follow ups seem much more plentiful. 

Neutral things:
     ="Crafting"
-I appreciate what the creator is trying to do, truly. The gamer culture is instant gratification; I come from a time where your loot      
-was hard wrought. Unfortunately, there is very little point to the system itself. The system simply exists as a time buffer/eyecandy. 
-Unlike normal rpg games where you find a mint condition, well oiled, laser sharpened death machine in a 200 year old dust laden 
-chest, this game requires you to find the blueprint for the weapon and craft it yourself. 
-Yes, this is cool, but it would be cooler if it did anything; If you could perhaps craft the perfect blade, or maybe a crappy blade if 
-you mess up; maybe reforging an existing weapon to give it better stats or something, or recycling old blades. nope, no such 
-thought. 

     =Hardcore & Leveling
-This game is indeed not an easy game. this is because enemies quickly become health sponges that deal massive damage. If 
-you neglect leveling your character in the "training" room, you will never get more health and you'll never get more damage 
-bonuses. However, statistics are predetermined. There is no magic or stealth that I can tell. Simply strength and "skill". Have not
-gotten far enough to comment on it. 

Bad things:
     =Random maps from a limited pool sucks, especially in the later longer layers.
-I love games that have random maps so long as there are multiple variations but sometimes the maps are funky. Take Daggerfall -for instance. Love the game to pieces... but a dungeon, EVEN WITH A MAP, was a nightmare to navigate. You would pass the 
-exact same stairs or room multiple times, and eventually you get deja' vu. This game doesn't even give you a map, so you're on
-your own to navigate the game. This really sucks hard. 
-The interaction in the levels is nill, so basically everything is eye candy,  with the same blotches of brown, generic swords, and 
-buckets. If you're lucky, you'll find a "loot" item lying around.  this "loot" is used for required upgrades in weapons and shields and such.

     =Combat "Lock", Weightless Weapons, Stupid High Strength Threshold
You will be forced to stand and fight an enemy, no matter how little sense the fighting ground is. Stairs for example cause the 
-enemy to swing under your feet or at them, and above is just as bad. And to get more than paltry damage, you have to practically
-swing your arm out of the socket. No responsiveness beyond a little vibration to hitting or blocking enemies, beyond sounds and 
-sparks, and occasionally a staggering enemy; This is in stark contrast to the many other things which have physics based 
-interactions, while combat is it's own thing entirely.  How people compare this to dark souls is beyond me. Take it from a hardcore
-Dark Souls fan - they are nothing alike. Not even superficially. 
     = Inventory and Items
-If you need to grab something, you have to put your sword in inventory. This is not cool, i really would rather put it on my hip than
-have to pull out my backpack and put it in a slot. Already have full slots? good luck trying to drop your weapon. Can't recycle the
-weapons that I can tell, so they just go on the ground or in the garbage so to speak.
-as far as variety it seems you simply get a bigger beat stick. No real stats other than "skill" and "strength" and related multipliers. 
-Most games give you an inventory belt for quick storage, but this game does not. 

Ugly things:
     =Hit detection and blocking is off.
-The game relies heavily on hitting and avoiding being hit, and if these interactions fail the game has a unacceptable bug. This is 
-the main event of the game, and it's buggy. 
     =My third weapon manufactured could neither be stored in inventory (couldnt drop my swords by pressing grip+trigger for 
-whatever reason even though it worked earlier) and WAS HELD SIDEWAYS! (FALCHION SWORD)
     =You can become hopelessly lost in dungeons beyond any sane level. 
-dont like it? tough shit. this is hardcore, remember?
     =This is developed by one guy. 
-And the history of these games ever being fixed or updated is beyond bad. So I would be very careful in expecting updates 
-beyond the most simple of things. There was a game I bought much like this called "Fadeholm" with many of the same type of 
-problems - single developer oversights, bad gameplay execution, and bugs. I have returned many VR games because of this 
-reason; I do try to give the benefit of the doubt by spending my money, but seeing lazy mistakes is where I start refunding things.
-This is nothing personal. I really do hope this gets better, but i'm seeing a common thread between the legions of other games i've -had problems with, and when a weapon is unusable/unplayable that is required to progress, there's no possible way you cant just 
-see something like that. Unless i'm entirely wrong and weapons are random too, this weapon is planned and unusable.
    =This is far from a true roguelike dungeoncrawler.
-There is no excuse to have roguelike in the name. Roguelikes have much more variety in items and player classes usually, and 
-many more complex statistics. If anyone has even played the original "Rogue, while weapons progress linearly and skills do, 
-there's tons of magic potions, staves, scrolls, enemies and secrets and other interesting tidbits. This game is nothing like that or any other game '-called a roguelike. It's linear, boring and uninspired. 
    =There are really stupid bugs. 
-to summarize, there are hands who's grip remain locked and cannot unlock, texture errors, items which are oriented incorrectly in 
-the hand and one that took a long time to build but was lost indefinitely and unable to store in inventory like other weapons, 
-enemy physics falls and hit detection. There's probably more, this is just one hour.

At the end of the day I cannot possibly fund this overpriced and underdeveloped game. I had hoped this would be fun, but It is not. I will reconsider buying this at a different time when things have been more developed.

review:
Let me just start out by acknowledging that yes, this is in early access and there are some things that could be better.  Presently locomotion is strictly by teleport, which could be a deal breaker for some.  Once when I exited the game the short sword I had smithed vanished - not a huge problem since the rusty one you get at the start is almost as good, but still an issue if it happens with other things.  Putting bugs and upcoming features aside, this is what I think of the game as it stands.

The good:  Swordplay can be pretty engaging, with opponents attacking from different angles or with different combinations of strikes that you'll need to block so you can get your own damage in on the counter.  Think of it as the Punch Out of rogue-likes.

The environments, while a little repetitive at times, look good and the dynamic lighting as you wave a torch around is pretty well done.  Occasionally you'll see a shadow under a candle that doesn't quite go away when the area is lit by your torch, but overall it's a good effect.

The bad:  Smithing is, frankly, boring.  You put a blueprint on a table, toss steel at it until you run out or have enough, then shove a bar of steel into the forge to wait until it heats up.  When that's done you beat on it any old way or place on the anvil and then move it vaguely back and forth on a grindstone.  For all the difference your efforts make it might as well give you the result once you have the blueprint and materials.

Also noteworthy:  As things stand, you really can't do much in a fight aside from wait for the enemy to attack you.  While I do enjoy the block and counter gameplay, sometimes an enemy is standing close enough to stab in the face, or simply dancing around without attacking, and it would be nice to have a way to take advantage of this kind of opening.

Due to the skill intensive combat, you will also never (at least in my experience) face multiple opponents.  Once I was beating on a goblin that had somehow or other lots its sword while retaining a shield and helmet.  Another goblin in the next room didn't join the battle until the first had died.  This makes me assume that two enemies at once simply can't happen - as stated, with the skill-based fighting it would be extremely hard to fight multiple opponents at once anyway, but it does seem a little off for a rogue-like.

Overall I feel this is worth playing already, and would recommend it to anyone who wants to do some serious swordplay.  Just don't get too upset if some bug does happen and your best weapon goes missing - I'm sure that in time that will be fixed.  In the meanwhile, it *may* show up again in the armory without simply vanishing from your hand as you enter the cellar like it did to me.

review:
It's hard for me to give this a Thumb's Down because even though it is fairly tight and competently made, it is ultimately a boring game with a very flat experience overall.

You start with a heavily-neutered set of powers and skills and as you proceed through the arenas (little planets), you gather chips which you may use for permanent upgrades. Every upgrade is MORE SOMETHING. So your basic gun sucks, and then you grind away to get upgrades to it's damage. Your jetpack sucks, and you grind away to get speed/fuel upgrades. Your speed is slow, and you grind to get speed upgrades. The core game does not have enough depth to keep a player interested enough to keep doing this and make it feel worthwhile. You're basically repeating the same dull arenas over and again with very little to keep you interested.

There are different weapons which randomly drop which are ostensibly there to help you tear through foes faster... but like other upgrade aspects of this game, those weapons are heavily-neutered to the point that your pop-gun is stronger so you have to grind to upgrade them to make them worthwhile. Even with all the weapons upgraded to MAX there's little difference in what any of them do... just different shooty graphics but really no mechanical differences. I honestly favored the basic pop-gun most of the time because picking up other weapons doesn't really seem to make much difference, and there's little risk/reward to gathering them when they drop.

Grind, grind, grind, grind for upgrades when the basic game just isn't all that fun. You could never in a million years beat this game on your first run, so it becomes an exercise in complete tedium. And with "upgrades" that don't feel meaningful and don't change the game mechanics in any way, it quickly becomes apparent how little depth there is here.

The other issue is unavoidable damage and loss of player control. There are times when you get forced into a lava pool which shoots you up in the air and back out. During this animation you lose the ability to control the player avatar and you can't use your jetpack to get you to safety, so you often end up being launched back into a pile of foes who then push you back into the lava. Which shoots you back up with no avatar control, lather rinse repeat. After a 15 minute run where you die this way, it makes you want to tear your hair out.

I guess you could get this on 80% sale or deeper discount if you really have to try it. But I feel like the mechanics of this game are so weak there's really no fun to be had. I'm giving up after my last fully-upgraded run ended with an unavoidable lava death. It is not worth it... there's so little here in terms of gameplay. Lots of window dressing, graphics, and animations to cover up a fundamentally boring game.

review:
One of these cases where I wish STEAM would have a sideways thumb or a 'MEH' option.
This game is fun for a while and is obviously a hommage to the excellent Super Stardust HD, with it's rotating spherical playfield. Unfortunately it ultimately falls flat compared to SS-HD. The game has okay graphics, fairly colorful and it never crashed during play. So thats a plus. 
Gameplay however gets VERY REPETITIVE, VERY QUICK. You drop onto a planet and then there is 4 stages where you have to either defuse bombs [stand next to a thing for couple of seconds] or kill everything/ survive 30 seconds, and eventually face off against a boss and move on to a Shop Planet to invest dropped money into permanent but very boring upgrades. You also get to choose a  perk upon completion of each planet. Typical 'Rogue Lite' fare. 
Suffers from most of the 'procedural generation ailments' you find in other games. Grindy nature, occasionally stupid placement of gameplay stuff like the bombs and that annoying repetition. There is planets which have 3 stages of bomb defusal in a row. Where SS-HD was a very fluid romp due to the endless nature of a spherical playfield. This game opts for barrires like rocks and lava pits which make fast movement a chore and comes with the obligatory collision issues. Rocks can be traveresed with the occasional jump pad [annoying] and pits can be jetpacked over. To fit the cool 3D rocks and pertrusions from the sphere, the playfield is actually very confined and there is tons of wasted screen estate at both sides. Enemies drop weapon pickups occassionally, which one rather avoids as they are, more often than not, less useful than the standard gun. 

Final verdict: Wish they woulda stuck CLOSER to the Super Stardust HD formula, instead of throwing all the worn out random generation, rogue lite stuff into the game. Random enemy respawn doesn't have any rhyme or reason, compared to the predictable nature of blasting Asteroids that Stardust relied upon and which made it so much fun.
It's probably okay on a sale, but then one might feel that they alreaady seen all of this in somewhat better games.
So yeah..it's a 'MEH'. Been there, done that.

review:
Gets boring pretty fast.
The game is very much carried by the visuals.

I only ever made it to the 3rd boss and the game was only really fun for the first 2-3 runs, after that it feels very "samey". The "rougelite" perk selection is very generic and most of them you hardly notice any difference. There is virtually no learning process at all and every run feels very much like the same thing from start to finish only with gradually increased difficulty and more instances of unavoidable damage

Also, the permanent upgrades that carry over between runs feel very much like a mandatory grind in order to progress rather than a nice helpful bonus. I can't imagine it would be possible to complete a fresh save file run of this game just because of how mandatory the mobility, health, and damage upgrades are in order to survive. Which should not be the case in a rougelite IMO, the barrier to completing a run should be knowledge/skill, not grinding.

Its a well made game, but there just isn't nearly enough variety in between "runs" in order to keep the game interesting or justify the 1 life rougelite design.

If you like classic arcade score attack games you might enjoy this, but at that point I would just recommend "Geometry wars 3" as a much better alternative to this game (purely for gameplay not aesthetic). If you're looking for a rougelite for the rougelite elements, I would suggest any of the games they listed as being inspired by in the "about this game" section of the store page.

review:
First of all, let me tell you that this game is not for flat earthers, we can definitely see that the small planets in this game are all round so beware!

Joke aside, I bought the game during the last Halloween sale and it's a lot of fun! You like top-down rogue-like wave shooters and rotating around small planets and shooting everything that is moving sounds good to you? Then yes, you might enjoy this one. I was a bit concerned that I would not enjoy or simply bear the gameplay about fighting on a very small rotating planets with top-down view but now that I tested it, I find it really cool.

You can unlock temporary perks for the run that are lost upon death, there is also a small shop that you will visit every 5 waves in which you can buy permanent cybernetics implants to improve your characters, weapons or the support items that you can use during combat with a cooldown but infinite use. Talking about the characters, you start with 1 and can unlock 2 others knowing they have different passive stats and use of the jetpack.

One concern though is that I faced few issues already (played almost an hour so far) that I reported [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/1099170/discussions/0/3004424478075996467/]here[/url] as well by email to the support address provided on Steam but I don't have much hope for any help, one of the issues that I found a workaround for, was already reported more than a year ago so I doubt it's going to be addressed but at least it's not game breaking, not to mention that the developers don’t seem active on the Steam forum at least.

Another point is that the game doesn't seem to offer much content and customization so the goal is to beat the last wave, which is wave 50, unlock the two other characters, max them and that should be it but the game is really enjoyable so I don't mind.

Anyway, I really like the game, very smooth gameplay, I found that fighting enemy waves on small planets that you rotate as you move around was really enjoyable and unique, the game has both permanent and temporary progression and I know I’m going to spend a few more hours in that one so I recommend it.

LONGER:  been looking for a fun lil mouse and keyboard top down shooter roguelite(u can buy upgrades that carry over to your future runs and eventually become a beast) thats fun and fast AND HERE IT IS.
 i hate playing an hour straight to pass a level in shooters but this game is the remedy for that as some runs go for a few minutes if you are bad/unlucky and other runs can go on far longer...but this game has breaks between the action which makes it perfect for fun fast top down action fun with no grind involved.  I bought to coop but  have only had the chance to try solo and it's super fun.  I love twin stick shooters with cool weapons and features and this is a fun unique game. it controls great with wasd to move/mouse aim n shoot but has full controller support for traditional twinstick play.

Good: game has short fun fast levels. game is a roguelite and therefore you can upgrade your characters on runs that you dont think you did well but when you get that cash for a permanent upgrade that forever is for all your characters future runs such as more health/ammo/speed etc.... so as game gets harder in later levels after buying post match upgrades you can make your next run a little smoother. so game difficulty scales as you get stronger in a way. 
It's a fun top down shooter with an interesting ideas that you are running around spherical planets and you  kite enemies but also must risk your life to stand in an area close enough to diffuse a bomb at the saame time you are fighting enemies and it gets fun and frantic.  also there are multiple guns that are all fun to use. even the starter setup is fun.  running around the round world and figuring out how to aim around this world takes a little while to adjust, but it doesnt take long to get the feel for running around the planet and accurately aiming after a few rounds.  also you have a jetpack that adds some additional mobility to your moves.  Fun stuff.

Overall... I HIGHLY RECOMMEND THIS GAME... esp if you are a top down shooter/ bullet hell/ shmup  fan if you are looking for a fun roguelite game that is different  that the others.... in a good way.  Plan to play coop but tried 1 player and it was a blast so this game is a win for me. thx devs for a game i actually like as im super picky and own a ton of trash games(behold my profile) ..but this game is hidden gem for sure and im glad i took  a chance on it. i hope u guys/devs keep adding 2 game like more weapons in the future.. but game as it stands is great as is. review:
I think this important to precise what you buy here if you do.
This is a bullets hell shooter and a real rogue like on a timer. You have one life, you progress as much as you can, you buy gears upgrades that you will keep the next time you play. You die, you start all over again but powered up.
Maps arrives randomly at least for a certain level of difficulty.
Schema is always the same. 1 phase is a bomb defuse game. So on timer under hordes of enemies. Second phase is just hordes. Third phase is bomb defuse again with generally more bombs. Fourth and last phase is a boss. Then you stop at a shop, gear up and repeat on another planet.
You can unlock 2 more characters that you will need to upgrade as well. They have their own specialties.
The design is interesting.  Maps are not spherical, this is a fish eye effect. It is more like a rugby ball that you see spherical. 

Visuals are ok. The sound could be better, louder but that is also ok. Action is also ok. 
The overall is nothing tremendous but all ok or just ok.
I bought it at 75% off or something. At this price I do not regret anything and I will play a couple of hour with it. But I could not recommend it at full price.

However, I wonder if somebody finished it except perhaps the peoples who made it. 
By essence, roguelikes are repetitive. But this one I feel it more than some other. 
I can see in the reviews some have played it till more than 25h. Most are at 5h. Which I believe will be more my case.
Records I have seen on some other roguelikes are ++1 600h and not only for one player. When myself, if I passe the 40h, that means the game is very good in its genre.

review:
Not a bad game per se, but I also think it has enough weaknesses to justify both either a good or bad review and since i'm such an hipster I wanna leave the only negative review of this game so far.

So what's the problem actually?

The game itself does nothing innovative and I suppose that was never the main draw. It's basically just a collection of tons of different puzzles, you've seen in eons of 2D games. Mostly Sokoban based but the mechanics never hold back to not introduce any cliché of a puzzle that someone ever has done in a videogame before.

Sometimes the different elements get combined, but often times they just introduce one (well known) concept after another and the execution of that... well it varies greatly depending on the level.

My favorite idea was the inclusion of portals simply because they did it consistently throughout the game, you can push blocks through portals, there is an projectile weapon to create new ones, you can extend pistons indefinitely and since they don't move together with pushables blocks once you set them, they could work both ways. This is used in the best way imaginable in a lots of way and it turns the thinking to a lot of these drawn out concepts upside-down, steering it in interesting ways. However this idea that could basically justify a whole game (I mean it has obviously) is mainly used for the third world, after that it's rarely used again.

This is the single best feature the game included, the rest isn't too bad either don't get me wrong, but it feels uninspired purely methodical, as if the developers just check boxes of what they haven't done before.

And the structure of the levels doesn't help with that. There are fixed chapters with an open area you can explore by your own leisure, there is usually a super short critical path, sometimes you can just run through the exit, while there tons of forks that lead to various collectibles that are indicated in the game. My problem with that structure is that there is no real build up of mechanics, levels vaguely focus on a specific mechanic, but after 3 puzzles there is now another new one, none of them are connected they are just self-contained. Sometimes levels utilize their openess for some "secrets" but at 95% of the time you're just doing self-contained puzzles, which you tick off one after another. 

This can get as tiresome as it is predictable since there is like previously stated rarely a "magic trick", something where you have to think outside of the box that makes you feel smart. It feels like drawing by numbers, it doesn't help that the difficulty curve seems static and especially world 4,5 and 6 nearly half of the game are easier than everything that came before, as it just introduces new concept without upping the difficulty of existing ones. Levels aren't interesting that way as it reiterates though the same structure time and time again.

Yet the game shows sometimes how it could be better.
Levels like "A-Maze-ing Forest" have a magical crossroad, that changes the next screen depending on which order you run through circles which is great as it included navigation inside the level, it doesn't feel like just another hub, so later on you approach rooms from several directions, such ideas are remakable expections which I wish there could've been more of.

The quality of levels feels all over the place sometimes, like the last egypt level has a green pyramid that is supposed to be the great finale, then the "puzzle" is just walking through the goal in an small uninspired labyrinth, something that is trivial as you can see all of it on the screen. It feels unfinished in this regard, just like the castle you can buy, basically the ending of the game. It was never fully implemented as well as several game modes. I don't think it should be indicated inside the game if it never gets finished anyway.

Collectibles also lose their value very very quickly, so you're just doing the puzzles as an end in itself. Like the main goal is collecting 999 gems, something which you can reach after 3 worlds already. If you collected them all at this point, afterwards, asides from an achievement, they become useless.

Gold ingots are used for bonus puzzles which are mostly very easy but surprisingly diverting I think focussing on just single puzzles makes up a better "pick up & play" dynamic as for the big levels, usually you want to finish at least one for a session.
Anyway... the requirements for the bonus puzzles (you unlock them in "puzzle packs") are laughably low, so low that quickly this ressource loses its value as well. And that could've been easily prevented by making the ingots unlock single puzzles, not everything in packs, makes it easier to play them along the line with the main campaign and doesn't spoiler mechanics.

The last ressource are "Crystal Hearts" and well they basically have no purpose over all, besides the corresponding achievements just another redundant collectible.
Also there is a dog to pet and feed in every level, which is yeah I admit kinda cute, so no problem with that. But it shows the whole game is very checklist orientated, with the things you're collecting having next to no extrinsic value, this makes the game feel kinda "empty" toward the later half. As you're doing it for a percentage number going up, but there is no "main story" that could come to an conclusion, no higher purpose, so after you finished the last level, the game is just bringing you unceremonial back to the level select. So its just all for the feel you've done everything - busywork, but nothing remains you will remember in hindsight after you're done with it. 

This is some kind of "fastfood" design I especially criticize in puzzles games, but all of that still wouldn't make me give this game a negative review wouldn't it be for one additional decision.

Sacrificing the integrity of your puzzles for comfort - I fucking hate this in videogames and sometimes I call puzzle games the last bastion of elegant game design, as it's basically the premise that you can't break, bribe or rationalize them.
 
Well Princess Castle Quest has a fast travel system across all kind of different points on the map, where you also restart a puzzle. The problem is, the puzzle doesn't restart if you use it. 
This allows you to easily break a majority of the game. I haven't done it, but it's easy and temping to exploit and sometimes you don't even know if its actually intended, as the first thing you're doing in the tutorial is using the fast travel system to cross an river you couldn't cross otherwise. so if there is something unclear, you can't be too sure if you actually should use the feature that easily allows you to skip most of the brainwork. There are several badly communicated moments (like blocks you can push together although it never was indicated in world 7, or a laser generator that can still be activated asides from the point where the receiver is pointed)

The developer were aware of that, but they stated in the forum that they priotize the handiness of quick traveling, over cheesing the puzzles. So that's actually a philosphy I strongly disagree with, since it could've been so easy to prevent. Just make the puzzle restart on fast travel and remove the upgrades the player possess. This just speaks to me like the developers don't care about their handcrafted levels or it wasn't important enough for them to find a solution to that. For me this is one of the biggest, if not THE biggest mistake a linear puzzle game could do. Usually cheesy and exploitable behaviour like this is getting fixed, with leaving it in they just damage the premise of their game.

So yeah i'm running out of lines here. To bring this to an conclusion, this game is pretty much coded in habits I usually strongly dislike in modern games and this is a shame since the core even if a bit uninspired has potential I think this could've been a real gem with a stronger and more focused direction.

review:
Dave-Man is kinda like if Pac-Man had RPG elements… but not like that actual Pac-Man RPG… this is more like classic arcade style maze dot collecting, or in this case, coffee bean collecting, mixed with that sort of quirky, self aware humor and sincerity you’d find in the Mother series.

Dave is a simple guy. He wakes up late for work every day, and prioritizes getting a fresh cup of coffee over everything else. To get that cup of coffee, Dave has to avoid annoying co-workers.

If he succeeds, he performs well at his job and takes home some pay. If he fails, his work suffers, and he goes home without any pay. Dave needs money to buy stuff, because he’s thirty days away from retirement and doesn’t want to be bored for the rest of his life.

He spends a lot of time online shopping, but he has to be careful with his purchases. His wife is going to get rid of the computer once Dave retires, so he needs to buy everything he wants while he still has time.

The audio and visuals feel like a cross between the Gameboy and the NES, with some really charming and finely crafted pixel art all throughout the game.

I could forgive someone for mistakenly writing this off as some overly simplistic retro throwback indie game, but there’s really a lot more going on here if you take the time to dig in.

There’s a thing that I’ve seen in some indie games where the game itself is almost more like a zine or chapbook accompanied by a familiar or relatively simple gameplay mechanic. That gameplay mechanic helps the title fulfill its role as a “game”, but the real meat in these sorts of projects is in the writing and presentation. There is a ton of really fun, creative writing all throughout this game, and in order to read it, you need to interact with the world and complete objectives. The desire to explore the creativity on display in Dave-Man is what drives you to succeed at the Pac-Man style gameplay found between these reading sessions.

While you do try to avoid your annoying co-workers, some co-workers can be found at the water cooler, and approaching them allows you to safely engage in conversation. You can shoot the shit, learn about new websites to order new stuff from, or trade quest items. Yes, there are some quests in the game. How you treat people and how you spend your time and money in Dave-Man all gets recapped at the end of the game, which kinda reminded me of the endings for Fallout 1 and 2.

There’s something surprisingly powerful about taking on the role of a person trudging through the mundanity of their final month of work, faced with the unknown of retirement and the looming threat of death, and responding to all that with doing as much online shopping as possible. It’s funny, but it’s sad. I had Dave-Man on my Steam Wishlist for a while before finally picking it up, but I’m really glad I finally did. You can play through the story mode in about 90 minutes, but there’s definitely  a whole lot more to explore on subsequent playthroughs  if you enjoy the writing, tone, and visual stuff.

[b]Who knew a story about one of my favourite fruits could be so meaningful? *munches pink lady apple*[/b]

I do not recall how I came across this but this is one of my best discoveries in 2019. This is a fantastic effort by one person. It’s a genuine shame that this has very little reviews and has not been played by more people.

Playing as plucky imp Ringo, he is happily living his life in Applewood with his friends. One day he investigates a rumble. Ringo with the support of friends old and new starts his journey to Mt Durian to pursue the legend of the first apple…

This pixel art game may not be the most aesthetically pleasing game but has dollops of uncomplicated charm and strong engagement. Take your time to enjoy the dialogue of the cute characters: they may give you wise words of wisdom, some light laughs, clues or just say sweet things.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1914549342

Game play consists of creative problem solving by placing items in the right place to open doors for the next section. This gets progressively more complex as new elements are introduced. Enemies cannot be directly killed so you have to use other resources. There items to collect such as gold berries to purchase items and hats.

The game is very generous with lives and plenty of save points. You do not need twitch reflexes to complete this game. However, there is a longer end game difficulty spike. Controls were smooth and tight with X to throw, A to jump/hover and the D-pad or left stick to move Ringo. Ringo can barely swim and can just skim the water by hovering. Do not jump in deep water!

I personally experienced technical issues with this game. It crashed on me several times. In two major fights I got an error message and was forced to close the game which is discussed in a thread here. I also experienced a bug at one of these when hitting an enemy. All the characters subsequently froze except for Ringo.

https://steamcommunity.com/app/1107470/discussions/0/3166519278510402949/

Despite my enthusiasm this may not be a game for everyone. Despite its slower pace, due to game design, if you have any issues with aiming because of poor co-ordination this may be a frustrating experience. If you are currently looking for a more hardcore or run n gun experience this is not your game.

Applewood is a truly charming puzzle-platformer that pulls you in with its cute characters, clever dialogue, and fun gameplay, and then really grabs hold with some good old-fashioned emotional content. The controls are easy enough to pick up, though it took me most of the game to get the hang of throwing items quickly and accurately. Those who don't play many platformers (like me) should be aware that the endgame might seem overwhelmingly tough at first. Don't panic, keep on trying, and the game will forgive your mistakes with generous checkpoints. Whenever I died - which I did, a lot - I never felt like I had to redo too much. And it's not hard to want to keep trying, because the story and characters are so compelling! It's 100% worth the effort.

2) I completed the game 100%. The average playtime is probably more like 8 hours.

Applewood is a game with lovable characters, fun mechanics, and a catchy soundtrack. It isn't insanely hard (except for a certain optional dungeon) and provides a decent challenge for any level gamer. 

Now while all of that is awesome, there is much more to this game than meets the eye...

I'm not saying the game will make you cry (this isn't the Hallmark Channel), but it will get you invested. It deals with heavy themes and makes you care about the characters.

The beginning of the game is humble. Yet, it is the ending which sets it apart.

It is reminiscent of Undertale, but has a better story. You can see similarities in the intro story, as well as in the ending.

I sincerely hope this game gets the popularity it deserves some day. But until then, I will cherish it as a private gem. Thanks Garrett. 

Godspeed,
Burton
