review:
Okay right out of the gate, yes, I did like this game. But it is a labor of love to get through.

The game is lucky the story is so compelling to keep you going through some frustrating choices. And also, if I hadn't played Automata first, I am not sure I would have kept going on an original run.

The game features multiple endings, and to get many of them you have to repeat a good chunk of the game. There is a few things different, but my god it is a labor to just go through the same areas and the same fights over and over again. To say nothing of how combat is very shallow and not difficult. At times I got a headache having to redo parts I wasn't a fan of the first time. 

But then you get to ending E which is new with this version. It is kind of crazy how about one hour of a game makes up for all of that. I have replayed Automata multiple times. I can't say if I will be as dedicated to this game as that one. But it was a journey I am glad I took.

And it is very good that Automata takes lessons from this game and fixes them. This game is rough. But great characters and a very good story push you through. But if I never have to go in to the Junk Heap again, you won't see me complaining.

review:
I’ve completed Automata before playing this, and I’m gonna say that I might’ve enjoyed this even more than Automata. I made this game my personal goal to earn completionist before Dying Light: The Beast gets released on 09/19/2025, and I’m glad I was able to complete it before that date. Another reason why I decided to try this game out after completing Automata is so I can watch the anime, in hopes of enjoying it even more.

Users who have complained how very grindy this game was, were absolutely correct. The grinding process was very tedious. It took me a few hours to get the needed number of a certain material needed, with the Subdued Bracelet being the least enjoyable one for example. Even getting 100% on side quests was bad also as it takes away from the main focus of the story, and instead you’d have to worry about other NPC’s issues just for the sake of missing anything important, especially if you’re going for all achievements. I’d also recommend doing all 100% side quests if you’re aiming for completionist so you could gather enough gold, materials, knowledge, fishes, etc to help make completionist easier. This makes it way different from Automata, since most people would just buy the achievements and not suffer through the tedious grinding. Personally, I didn’t buy any of the achievements in Automata because I want to experience them myself.

Although this game holds its flaws, it doesn’t compare well enough for my personal enjoyment of this game. Even from all the tedious grinding, sidequests, etc, I’ve absolutely enjoyed the process and I’m glad to experience it. After dealing with the grindy achievements, such as maxing out all weapons, catching all fishes, completing all 100% side quests, etc, it was very rewarding and relieving to go back to playing the main story. Though I’m disappointed in giving myself minor spoilers of reading the descriptions of locked achievements to plan how I’ll get them, like fighting Popola and Devola.

What I’ve absolutely enjoyed the most about this game is the amazing soundtracks. The remix concept in The World of Recycled Vessel was an epic experience. I also liked the fact while fighting Popola and Devola, Popola dances along with the soundtrack, surprisingly in sync. Details like these were fun to acknowledge.

I hope I'll get a chance to play the Gestalt version some time in the future when it gets released on Steam. Though, I don’t have high hopes it will be released on Steam.

review:
Beware potential minor spoilers.

I will start by saying the shorter version, is it good? Yes, is it worth 60 euros? absolutely not, i'm giving it a do not recommend only because there isn't a "meh" button on steam, but if you find this game on a heavy discount (20 euro or lower) i would say do pick it up as it's an interesting game in its own way.

Now for the long version, why thumbs down instead of thumbs up despite being meh and still recommending it when discounted? well a few factors.
First of all it's the gameplay; aside boss battles, it's like eating unsalted gluten free crackers. An infinite amount of fetch quests and "Go here go there" on a map that doesn't see fast travel after midgame.
Second issue is how the game hides some important mechanics or upgrades behind meaningless and voidlike subquests, i bet many people don't even know there is a mount in the game that is hidden behind a stupid sidequest at the start of the game THAT COULD BECOME AN UNCOMPLETABLE QUEST EVEN ON A "NEW GAME+", simply because most likely they didn't even bother doing it from how boring they are.
Third, and worst of all in my opinion, is that you don't get to see around 50% of the game until you beat it and PLAY IT AGAIN. With this i mean full on cutscenes, character stories and interactions between characters and between enemies that are simply not shown during the ENTIRE FIRST PLAYTHROUGH. When i did my first run i had literally zero attachment to ANY of the characters, and the various big reveals at the end felt like nothing due to the game literally showing NOTHING, you can play it again and get the full experience sure but now you already know how it ends and it literally spoils the whole story, missing emotions that otherwise would've been present the first run, so it doesn't matter how many times you play it, it'll still feel like total emptiness. 

I genuinely feel like i have been robbed of an amazing game if only Yoko Taru didn't have a kink with leaving things in the dark.

Despite the huge flaws though the game isn't all bad, the music is a banger, the bossfights are a banger and there are some gameplay mechanics that are unique, but those are few and far between. Graphics wise it's okay for a remaster/remake and the character models are super cool, but that's about it for the positives.

As for the conclusions, if you're unsure between getting automata or replicant, just get automata, buy replicant only if you want a minor elucidation on past events and only if you see it on a heavy discount.

review:
REPLICANT SIDE OF THE REVIEW!!!

I gathered my things. Disconnecting my stuff from the living room TV. I went back to my room and placed it all over my bed. I had returned everything to my room and it was just me and the silence. I felt nothing in that moment. I walked towards my door. The door to my room expecting my next actions to be opening it and moving forward. 

I expected my life to continue as normal, but I fell. I fell to my knees and I lost it. My entire body flung to the ground as tears flowed out of me. I couldn’t breathe I couldn’t think I just I just I just I just I just i couldn’t it was all. All I could do was cry. I broke down onto the ground and for 20 minutes I let go of my ego and my body. I let it all out sputtering like a baby my sense of self shattered as I yelled out. “It’s beautiful!” “MASTERPIECE!” And “ART!” 

I can’t lie. I was actually so happy in that moment, a melancholic happiness that nier gave me. I fell to my knees and broke down into nothing of the person I once was. I cried and yelled and shouted at the end of it all. And I truly never ever. We’ll ever. I just. 

Stop it. You’re lying again. Just take a second. Take a deep breath. And tell the truth. 

I was finally alive. Given purpose, by Art. Art is my purpose it’s what I strive to bring to this world one way or another. I live for it now. It’s all thanks to Nier;Automata. And Yoko Taro. 

I had been broken and battered by this world, beliving that the ideals of others were all I could ever strive for and even then I could never live up to them. But it was all lies. Humanity as a whole, their ideals and dreams. Hopes beyond belief are just the precipice of them, I have a hard time understanding myself even now. But nier automata is a deconstruction of humanity and its dreams. Of War, Peace, Love, Hate, Emotion, Emptiness, Life, and Death. It’s the same as me, the same as all of us. It is Art. And it is my dream. 

It truly feels like an honor to have written this. I feel like this world that Mr. Taro created is not simply his own. Well he has his own likes and dislikes, but humanity was the catalyst for the nier games in the purest forms we are the reason for its existence and the inspiration behind every turned page. Our species is wholly flawed and our actions do have consequences, but in the end the actions that we take aren’t all in vain. 

Thx Nier Automata, for breaking me and putting me together again. This is more of a confession than a review if anything. It’s crazy I went beyond the steam review letter limit I didn’t even know that was a thing. But yeah. Good game everyone you should definitely check it out. Also nier replicant if you want, might actually be cooler so you can get lore for the flowers along with Devola and Popola. I’m sure there’s more than just that. 

Jeez, P.S.
I’m only writing this now because things in my life have changed and I feel comfortable with myself more and feel confident to tell my own truth. There is no greater feeling than being comfortable in your own skin I can tell you that and it sometimes feels like a risk to do so, but it’s always worth the effort.

P.P.S. I actually really liked nier replicant too, but the emotional response was nowhere near as intense as Automata so uh yeah this is taking up my space for a nier replicant review spot oops…

P.P.P.S. Also if ur wondering why this is such a weird looking review then you’d be right about that, but also this is only half of the review from one on Nier automata so don’t get the wrong idea I just made a super long review for my own sake.

Anyways bye!

-Angel Waffles

Having played Nier Replicant after thoroughly enjoying Nier Automata about half a year ago I do have to admit that even though Replicant didn't seem to have the impact Automata had on me it's still without a doubt which I can't even call special because that would be a plain insult to Replicant. The story does take a little to unfold, but it is one of the most gut wrenching and real ones I've had the pleasure of experiencing. Replicant's characters feel like genuine people, they have issues and don't always get to properly deal with them. The game's story about family and friendship is a one of a kind which I'd highly recommend you to experience without any further research, please, trust me, it's absolutely worth it. To make things even better, I do think Replicant's OST is one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard - some of the motiffs are probably never going to leave my head, at least I hope they won't.

On a final note, don't bother with side quests, except for the three you need to do to see Ending C and D. They are tedious at best and not really worth your time, unless you are into repetitive sidequests. Besides them, Nier Replicant is at least a solid 9 to me, so go and play it already!

review:
NieR:Replicant feels like a weird stage play of a video game. The parts are there, the characters emote, there is things that make it look like a game and there is a story. But everything is just weirdly off, and not in a very interesting way. Top that with a crazy 60€ price tag for an okay port of a really old game.

The whole first act feels like an eerie hommage to Zelda, complete with the animation when the Prince receives the item, almost like a jab at the generic fantasy RPG village beginnings. The neverending back-and-forth for insanely dull main and side quests feels like some kind of subversive critique of bland gameplay. 
Characters join your party, you do one thing together and suddenly there is a huge dramatic scene where emotions overflow and the characters swear eternal allegiance to each other in the name of their unbreakable friendship. As if the script writer just tossed the whole intermittent part between beginning and end of the act out the window, which seems like some kind of parody of video game plots. The game's story beats and character reactions outside of the side quests seem so exaggerated to the point where you suspect this is leading up to some kind of plot relevant twist.
However, after hours of running back and forth on the same maps, killing the same few enemies by mashing buttons, and hearing the same generic dialogue from side NPCs I gave up trying to figure out if there is some grand point to be made and whether or not those things actually lead up to something.

There is nothing to get invested in to make me want to see it through to the end, because all you are given is the game telling you that the characters have deep connections with each other, but you never really see any of this. Side quests are aggravatingly generic in the variety of "Kill X wolves until you get their drop Y times", "Bring the item to NPC Z" or "Deliver this item but you cannot dodge or get hit or you have to try again". If you force yourself through these torturously laborious side quests you are rewarded with world building insights among the lines of "Thank you!". No interesting bits about the world or characters, no interesting philosophical conundrums like in Automata. Just a forgettable sentence of a forgettable NPC in a generic world.

There is some decent writing in there somewhere. The text wall segment in the forest was really well written and some of the dialogues are very pleasing to listen to, aided by the very strong voice acting.

But ultimately the game is so insanely flat and sterile and just feels like it's wasting your time with every bit of gameplay that stands in the way of the next bit of story that may or may not be interesting that I cannot be bothered. And I definitely don't want to slog through it multiple times for multiple endings. I'll just look up a story summary online.

review:
You know, I at first considered giving this game a numeric rating of 7/10 due to how tedious the route is just to reach the true ending. But after a careful month-long reflection, I think I’ll give it a rating of 8.75/10. Let me explain why.

Don’t get me wrong. NieR: Replicant ver. sqrt(1.5) is definitely grindy and repetitive especially when compared to its successor NieR: Automata. Not only do you have to repeat the second half of the story twice as the same character, but you also have to collect all 33 weapons or else you won’t be able to unlock Endings C, D, and E. And that involves doing a series of very boring back-and-forth fetch quests that can understandably frustrate the player. But hey after all, this is a **remaster** (note: not a remake) of the original Replicant from 2010, so it’s only natural for it to reflect video game design trends of that era.

But looking back aside from the combat (which to be honest isn’t really that awful but still pretty mediocre compared to Automata) and what I just described above, Replicant excels at pretty much everything else that I think makes it worth your time and money to play if you’re a Drakengard/NieR fan. The music is spectacular, the story is compelling, and it comes with emotional arcs for several characters, both major and minor. There are even references to Replicant in Automata that link both of them together. I would definitely go back and replay some parts of the game just to experience it all again (sadly there isn’t any Chapter Select like there is in Automata so you can only replay from your last save which is right before reaching the end). 

And finally, once you’ve reached Ending E and if you’re anything like me, you’re definitely going to spend the next few days watching a couple lore videos on YouTube trying to make sense of the story but honestly? That just makes it all the more fun in my opinion.

This game is a junky mess.
I'll rate this game as a 2021 game (meaning I expect it to meet 2021 game standards), not a 2010 one.

The story is acceptable enough that it kept me playing and forced me to play and get the ABCDE endings.

And the story is the only positive thing about this game; everything else is mediocre/horrible.

- Combat - junky, tedious, repetitive. Sometimes I just ran past enemies because I didn't feel like fighting them.
- Side-Quests - absolutely horrible, boring, snooze-fest. Most of them are fetch-quests that add nothing to the game.
- Fast Travel System - should be much better, not this crap with boats where you have four places to travel and usually it's faster to get somewhere else by just running there
- Bosses - most of them were tragic, boring, and too long. Lots of gimmick bosses, multiple phases. The culmination of the bosses' tragedy was a boar that had to be killed 15 times (I counted) in many places to progress.
- The structure of this game is poor. The gameplay should be structured so that you play once and discover everything in that single playthrough, instead of everything being divided up so that in route A you get almost nothing, in route B you get a few more cutscenes, and in route C you get a few more dialogue lines. And you play for hours just to get one more line of dialogue. All of this should be in one playthrough, not forcing the player to repeat everything multiple times to get the "context" of what we've done.

I am not sure in what kind of war I got myself into, but I am armed with guns killing guys who mostly run around with sticks, while stealing pirate treasure from them. 

Unfortunately, the game has several issues that hinder the experience. Guns have no sound, the minimap is terrible and weird, and the camera is way too close to the character, making it hard to see anything. I often found myself asking, "Why did all colors decide to gang up against blue? Why am I alone in the war? What happened to the other blues? What kind of war is this?"

Most of the time, I don't know where I am shooting. I have to rely on the minimap because I can barely see anything else. New weapons come with literally 1-2 bullets, and there are no bullets to pick up on maps. Enemies clip through walls, which is never a good sign. You can't shoot through grass, and my desktop mouse is visible even after restarting the game, which is quite distracting. Additionally, Steam achievements only pop up when you exit the game.

I don't like writing negative reviews, especially since I know how much time and effort goes into creating a game, but Alone in the War needs a lot more polishing before it becomes shelf-ready. When you open the map, it always says "Level 4," no matter which level you are on. The controls are confusing, with '+' for zooming out and '-' for zooming in. If enemies get close to you, you shoot past them, and the aim sometimes snaps to objects if you go near them. If you go to the edge of the map, the crosshair snaps to it. The rifle is okay, but you get so little ammo that you won't use it much. You can sprint for exactly 1 second every 10 seconds.

Overall, Alone in the War could have potential, especially since I have seen the developer being active, but it requires significant improvements to deliver a satisfying gaming experience.

[b]I am the Dirt – for Art by Scum Studio (PC 2019)[/b]

This is a Chinese visual novel with 3 suggestive scenes. None of which are overly explicit and can be further controlled by customising the dress up character by choosing what it wears or doesn’t wear manually. I guess similar in a way a barbie doll works. You play the role of an overly inappropriate hormonal Japanese student whose banter always revolves around sex and which doesn’t translate at all that well from Chinese to English.

An example of this is a section where the main protagonist, I assume is trying to say something like,

“I would like to rub your chest…”

Instead, the game translates it from Chinese to English as,

“I would like to rub your grandmother…”

In which she replies in a tonal expression ‘Oh how sweet!’

The visual novel has 8 chapters in total which all play out in an abandoned classroom which a student has repurposed as a painting studio. The painter (AKA Predecessor) has really set up the studio so that he can encourage local women to model for him and try and groom them for his own selfish gratification purposes, making him scum. 

There are 2 models/victims he is entertaining to bed. One is a fellow student named Cecily who he has known for 3 years and though he is not interested in pursuing a long-term meaningful relationship with her, he is aware that she has a crush on him and would make an easy target. He is also aware that pursuing a shallow love interest with her, will most likely destroy the friendship they have, but doesn’t really care. He is more interested in having her as a trophy, more than anything else and is rather selfish and shallow enough not to care what emotional damage it might cause.

The second is Nancy Armani Ming Ming who already has a boyfriend, is sexually like-minded like himself and is not satisfied with her current jealous, over protective lover.

Each chapter simply requires you to pick 3 out of 4 items to talk about in the studio with the person featured in that chapter (Cecily or Armani). While your presented with multiple statements you can make with each item, they all do the exact same thing and simply push the story forward. There is NO, I repeat, NO wrong choice. All statements, no matter what you choose, lead to the same consequence. This makes the time spent playing the visual novel, extremely meaningless.

Another thing that makes this visual novel completely meaningless, is that there is no noble message in its conclusion. There are some comical scenes such as the awkward kiss, the fire scenes and the odd silly translation, but nothing saves this from being anything more than a lazy template design with a quick sex sells gimmick. 

Each chapter concludes with you being able to paint the model featured for that day with whatever they are wearing and then you suggesting they wear more revealing clothes at their next appointment.

I find this game's title is so deceiving. The game has these glimmering moments where every element in the game artfully aligns. But unlike art that is truly an escape, I found myself bored through the overwhelming majority of the game.

It's a essentially a walking sim. There is a painfully easy guitar minigame that there is no punishment for losing, but overall, it's a walking sim. 

I go into a walking sim expecting strong story because there is no gameplay, but the story isn't interesting. The main character is a pathetic musician who's in the shadow of his uncle, but suddenly halfway through the story, he flips on a dime and becomes 99% confident. I don't blame him for becoming super confident either, because he goes on this journey to realize that he a good musician without his uncle and every place he performs calls him the god of music. 

All of this is extra ironic since the music in this game gets stale REALLY QUICK. Like, there is a button to dash, and it also makes you shred on your guitar. There are all these elements in the game that react to you playing your guitar, and I never really engaged with them because I got sick of the guitar so fast.

The visuals also really get stale. Everything really falls into the bucket of "blob-y purple alien, maybe with yellow".

And yet there are these moments. There is a pretty strong story beat at the end of the game that the "captain" supports really well. There will be 10 seconds of music that I find really appealing. The visuals in the level transition are really cool (the first time). Nothing consistent over the whole game.

Are these moments worth it? No. You should artfully escape from this steam page and play something else.

[b]Everspace 2: A Great Game Missing Its True Potential Without VR[/b]

Everspace 2 is a well-crafted game with gorgeous visuals, engaging combat, and plenty of exploration. It certainly works, and there's a lot to enjoy about it. In many ways, I think this game would have been even more successful if it had been released a decade or two ago, it has that classic space shooter charm.

However, one of the biggest missed opportunities here is the lack of VR support. The first Everspace embraced VR, and it was a key part of the immersion for many players. Without it, Everspace 2 feels like it’s missing that extra layer of magic that could have made it truly exceptional. As a result, it’s a solid game, but it doesn’t quite reach the heights it could have.

review:
I bought this game shortly after I bought myself a gaming PC, 2 years ago, having spent 25 years as a console player using controllers. With hindsight trying to get used to M&K with this game was a mistake and I bounced off it for that reason alone.

On a whim I decided to try playing it again and decided I'd use my controller this time and this game is so good - the story is good, the exploration is amazing fun, the weapons and progression feel meaningful, hell even getting the ship colour upgrades from defeating enemies feels satisfying, even if it is just another shade of grey :)

Anyway, I'm only 12 hours in but damn this game is enjoyable. I know I'd have more fine control with a m&k but I'm having a blast playing and that's what it's all about. The weapons are impactful and hearing a missile smash into an asteroid or another ship is never not satisfying, the different guns also feel and sound fairly unique and have that thump or bite. review:
[b]🚀 Everspace 2 – A Loot Shooter Trapped in Space, Without the Depth to Match[/b]

If I had to sum this one up, it’s:

[i]“The first ten minutes of combat... is the rest of the game.”[/i]

That’s not me being cheeky. That’s me staring at my ship, ten hours in, wondering why nothing has evolved except the enemy health bars and the number of lasers I have to dodge.

[b]🔬 Systems Breakdown[/b]

[b]• Space Combat?[/b]  
Yeah, it’s slick. Tight controls, flashy dodges, lots of pew-pew. The problem? That’s it. You’ve played 80% of the combat in the first 30 minutes. Bigger battles come later, sure. You get more weapons, abilities, and a few new tricks. But the way you [i]engage[/i] never really changes. There’s no transformation. No escalation. Just stat inflation and more visual clutter.

[b]• Ship Variety?[/b]  
There are multiple ships, yes. But don’t get excited—they’re sidegrades, not actual upgrades. You’re not building toward a heavy frigate, a stealth recon build, or squad command. You're just choosing which flavor of the same loop you want. Stats shift, abilities rotate, but nothing fundamentally reinvents your experience.

[b]• Upgrade System?[/b]  
It’s wrapped in the illusion of depth. You contribute resources to vendors or characters, unlocking perks that mostly amount to [i]+2% to something you won’t notice.[/i] You’ll pick up junk, donate it, and tick boxes, but it rarely feels like you're progressing—it just feels like you’re maintaining.

[b]• Exploration?[/b]  
Technically yes. Spiritually? Nah. The world looks great, but what you [i]do[/i] in it doesn’t justify the beauty. It’s mostly linear point-to-point traversal with flavor text and loot chests. The wonder wears off fast, and what’s left is a pretty loop of sameness.

[b]• Progression Curve?[/b]  
Flatlined. You start strong, plateau early, and coast. You don’t become something [i]more[/i], just something [i]repeated[/i]. No ship evolution, no strategic turning point, just more of what you already had.

[b]✅ Pros:[/b]
• Combat feels great (for the first few hours).  
• Visually stunning. The environments are AAA-tier screenshot bait.  
• Good “shut-your-brain-off” game in short bursts.  
• Solid performance and polish. It’s technically well-made.

[b]❌ Cons:[/b]
• Combat loop plateaus almost immediately.  
• Ships are mostly sidegrades—variety without transformation.  
• Upgrade paths are shallow; progression is mostly cosmetic or statistical.  
• Exploration lacks depth and payoff.  
• Not built for long sessions; the fun burns out quickly.

[b]🎯 Do I recommend this game?[/b]  
Kind of. If you want arcade dogfighting and some sci-fi loot polish, it’ll scratch the itch. But if you’re chasing systems depth, evolving builds, or that “climb from scrappy pilot to galactic legend” fantasy—this ain’t it.

[b]Score: 6/10[/b]  
[i](7/10 if you go in knowing exactly what you're getting: short bursts, light systems, big explosions)[/i]

review:
Everspace 2 is a game whose shortcomings are noticeable but ultimately forgiven, thanks to everything it gets right.

If you like excellent graphics, space combat, dogfights, adventure, upgrading, customizing, a little humor, lots of action, and an open world that lets you feel a sense of challenge while also feeling the power of your latest ship upgrades, this game will be the perfect answer for you.

With Diablo-like looting, the game has a decent-sized story (most estimates placed it around 40 hours from what I've seen), but the game can easily be played for hundreds and hundreds of hours, if you like completing side quests and getting all the best gear.

I would say the areas it comes up short are in the limited resources spent on developing cut scenes. Some folks may like the indie style. But for me, I am a sucker for a game that invests in great storytelling and special effects. So The cut scenes were fine for me, but I did find myself wishing there was a bit more invested in these scenes.

I also found the game's core content to just overall be a bit lacking, in the way that you basically have a single playthrough of the main story, and then you're running rifts and spamming loot drops until you get bored. I do like that the zones level up to stay current with you for the first part of the game, though.

But I think the biggest shortcoming is just the linear nature of the story - despite the open world vibes and expansive realm to explore, you ultimately are on a railroad with the story, where nothing you do has any impact on the end result and you are given zero choices about how to get to the end.

For many who may be drawn to the more open-world elements of space-faring games like this, a story that you have zero say over may feel disappointing. But as I mentioned, with everything this game doesn't have, it's loaded with fun overall gameplay itself that will keep you entertained for a long time.

So, while it seems that the genre is sorely lacking in a "perfect" game, one where the budget and vision allowed them to give you the best of everything, Everspace 2 is by far the best looking game with the level of depth it offers. 

While some other space games have a lot more complexity, story, and depth, most of those games are sadly very dated looking. So if you're wanting to enjoy a solid entry into the genre that can also wow you visually, I have not yet found an alternative that can rival Everspace 2.

P.S. I did not get the expansion packs, as there's just way too much cost for a few extra hours of content (at least, according to several reviews stating as much), so this review is for the base game only.

review:
A surprisingly good game!  

Movement is quite well done.  Your ship always has the ability to move in any direction (up down forward back strafe left and right, boost and spin) so you have full control while flying in all environments.  Flying around feels pretty good and pointing and shooting with the mouse is easy.  The physics are not realistic in the slightest - if you stop accelerating then your ship slowly glides to a stop, which is not at all what would happen in space, but the less realistic mechanics feel better to move with.  Most impressive is when your ship has to go into enclosed spaces, you can really squeeze into some tight areas without a problem and the camera is shockingly good at staying behind you.  You can smash your ship into walls at a pretty high speed and only take shield damage so total precision isn't required.

It's a space shooter but really more of an RPG.  There's an impressive amount of exploration and treasure hunting in the many locations you visit.  While you may not think there can be puzzles in space, the game is packed full of them.  Pressing buttons, finding passwords, hidden containers, flipping switches, powering generators, opening doors, moving energy balls to locks, there's just a ton of things to do and stuff to find.  There's a lot of sidequests and many are interesting.  There's randomly generated side jobs you can do for cash.  There's random encounters on the world map.  It plays a lot like an RPG just...in space.

Combat feels pretty good too.  You have two primary weapons that recharge if you're not shooting, so you fire with one until it runs out of power and switch to the other and back again.  You have subsystems, devices which refresh on cooldown, and sub weapons which are limited.  Depending on what kind of ship you use your strategy might change a lot.  I played a long range sniper type, but everything seems viable.  Some weapons are much better close up.

Your weapons shield scanners boosters and other equipment have rarities, levels, and modifiers and enemy ships have levels too so while you can overcome things with skill you aren't gonna get far without improving your gear.  A lot of enemy ships have hitscan type attacks if they get close enough so you can't avoid ALL damage.  Boosting and juking wildly shakes off missiles and most shots but then it's hard to aim and fire back while doing so.  You get the same interesting problem that's been present in most space shooters from way back in the X-Wing/Tie Fighter games where you deal the most damage to each other while flying into attack range because you're driving straight at them and can't really see them firing at you, but also all your shots are gonna land too because the enemy isn't dodging either.  

There's a very nice amount of aim assist in the game too which is very necessary.  For your weapons that hitscan, pointing into a little circle around each enemy ship will usually guarantee the shot lands, and for weapons that shoot a projectile you instead aim at a projected path circle in FRONT of the enemy, and if you shoot in that circle your shots bend and land.  It's a nice system.

The main story is decent overall.  Voice acting quality is hit or miss but the VAs of your main character and his ship AI are the best and they're the ones you hear most often.

The one downside with the game is that is has level scaling and leans into it too much.  Everything you pick up is scaled to your level so you get the infamous problem of "I shouldn't open that chest because it'll have better stuff if I come back later" and which is something that should never happen in an RPG.  You also have the "I leveled up and got weaker" problem because enemies upgrade but you don't because most of your power comes from equipment, and you need to find or upgrade pieces to your current level to see improvements.

Graphics and weapon effects aren't amazing but look good enough.

I was really impressed by this game.  It has an impressive amount of content and will keep you occupied for a while.

review:
Everspace 2 is a good looking space shooter looter game. Still it is an arcade style game. There is no combat skill involved. No maneuver. To survive, just need shield, armor, hull and high damage output destroy the enemy as fast as you can, because there are too many of them in High Risk Areas and Rifts. You can't dodge anything, the roll is useless. The boost is slower than the enemies. 

The crafting system seems appealing, but not better than the drops, so is quite useless. You think you can upgrade your favorite gear? You can't upgrade legendaries. Don't bother with the Ancient Altar upgrade. It is a tiny upgrade after fighting the ancients each time.

What good are the rifts? Enemies with huge health and damage, circle you and shoot you down in no time.  I have 100K shield still is no better than 50K. Is pretty useless at Luancy more than 500. The rift does not allow breaks to charge shield.  There is a timer. Is tough just to use nanobots. Once you notice armor is gone, your ship is destroyed before you try to use nanobots. That is the amount of incoming damage. Just ridiculous.

The game is good for some arcade action. The end-game rift is really bad. There are lots of guns but most of them is useless here, especially the sniper and slow firing ones. The lunacy level does not show the real difficulty because there are modifiers you must choose in each 4 stages of the rift. You can't get any better by repeating the rift. The drop chance is so low, and no better gear drops. I can't really say the game is a RPG. There is only level 30 and that is the limit. what good is  that? There is only a tiny percentage of players pass 500 or 1000 lunacy.

[h3]Grand Duke[/h3]
THE demolition derby car, so good that the real-life equivalent has been banned from quite a few competitions.  Shaped like a brick, handles like a brick, and hits like a brick, the Grand Duke is a force to be feared in the derby arena.  It's got some mean-looking customization options too, and is surprisingly quick if given enough time and distance to accelerate.  Watch out.

[h3]Little Thrasher[/h3]
Basically the MudDigger's little brother, this truck is a bit lighter, a bit smaller, and a bit less powerful.  Still rather top-heavy even on moderate suspension settings, the Little Thrasher is pretty good at anything that you'd want to use the MudDigger for if it wasn't so big... whatever that might be.  Bonus points for some good customization, as well as the fact that the Goofy Roofs teddy bear sits nicely in the bed instead of on the roof.  Not a super common pick, but it can hold its own.

[h3]Wildking[/h3]
The default appearance is a bit silly, but the Wildking has enough range with its customization to go between that level of crazy and something more sensible without difficulty.  It doesn't have any "racing" paint styles unfortunately, but there's some cool sheet metal ones that make up for that.  It's lighter and more balanced than most of the American muscle cars, meaning that it's a lot more grippy through corners and gives you the chance to pull off some cool overtakes once you get the hang of it.  Starting out though, it can tend to feel a bit floaty when entering a corner because of how different it is compared to something like the Starbeast or Roadslayer; it doesn't have the raw power but can put what it does have to more effective use. What Vault of the Void has up on a lot of other similar games in the genre is the difficulty. Slay the Spire, Monster Train, and a other similar titles are fun, but once you've really figured out how to play deckbuilders as a whole, they get pretty easy pretty fast. VotV is much more difficult, and you'll actually have to use your brain for (most) of the archetypes you play into. And without spoiling too much, you are richly rewarded for completing runs with a lot of cool stuff to make future runs more interesting, challenging, or both.

Also helps that the devs are a transparent studio of awesome people.

If you enjoy deckbuilders, buy it. If you like a challenge, buy it. If you're on the fence, guess what - buy it. Trust me, you won't regret it.

review:
Ultimate Fishing® Simulator 2 builds upon the foundations of its predecessor to deliver a highly immersive and detailed fishing experience that appeals both to seasoned anglers and newcomers curious about the sport. Developed by Bit Golem and published by Ultimate Games, this sequel aims to blend realism with accessibility, providing players with a wide variety of fishing environments, techniques, and gear. Unlike many arcade-style fishing games, Ultimate Fishing® Simulator 2 takes a more simulation-heavy approach, focusing on the nuances of bait selection, casting mechanics, and fish behavior to create a genuinely engaging and sometimes challenging experience.

One of the first things that stands out about the game is the sheer breadth of fishing locations and species available. From tranquil freshwater lakes to vast coastal waters, the game features a diverse array of environments, each meticulously recreated with attention to ecological detail and aesthetic appeal. Locations range from serene mountain lakes to large, open ocean settings, providing distinct challenges depending on the terrain and the species inhabiting it. The developers have included dozens of fish species, each with its own behavior patterns, feeding times, and preferred habitats, which adds layers of strategy to each fishing expedition. This diversity ensures that the game rarely feels repetitive, as every outing requires adaptation and planning.

The gameplay mechanics in Ultimate Fishing® Simulator 2 are impressively nuanced. Casting requires skill and timing, with factors like wind, rod type, and reel choice influencing the accuracy and distance. Players must consider water depth, temperature, and time of day to maximize their chances of attracting specific fish. The bait system is equally intricate, offering live bait, lures, and artificial options that behave differently depending on conditions. This level of detail rewards players who take time to learn and experiment, while still allowing casual players to jump in and enjoy the core fishing experience without feeling overwhelmed. The tension in the fishing line, the struggle during a catch, and the visual feedback of the fish’s movements all contribute to a satisfying and immersive fishing simulation.

Graphically, the game makes a solid impression. The water effects, weather conditions, and natural environments are rendered with care, creating a relaxing yet visually engaging atmosphere. Dynamic day-night cycles and weather changes not only enhance immersion but also affect fish behavior, reinforcing the game’s emphasis on realism. The sound design complements this beautifully; ambient noises such as birdsong, water lapping, and reel spinning add layers of authenticity, making the player feel truly present by the water’s edge. Although the visuals may not push the limits of modern hardware, the overall presentation is polished and effective in conveying the serene yet exciting nature of fishing.

Customization and progression systems also play an important role in Ultimate Fishing® Simulator 2. Players start with basic equipment but can gradually upgrade rods, reels, lines, and tackle to suit different fishing styles or target species. The variety of gear reflects real-world fishing choices and encourages strategic planning. Additionally, the game features multiple modes, including a career mode with various fishing tournaments and challenges, as well as a free-roam mode where players can explore locations and fish at their own pace. These options cater to different playstyles and provide longevity, whether one prefers structured goals or relaxed exploration.

While the game excels in many areas, it’s not without minor issues. The learning curve can be steep for some, especially given the level of simulation detail. Early gameplay might feel slow or technical to those unfamiliar with fishing mechanics, and the user interface, while functional, could be more intuitive in helping new players understand the numerous variables at play. Occasional bugs or glitches related to fish AI or physics have been reported, though developers have been relatively active in addressing these through patches. These minor flaws don’t detract significantly from the overall experience but may be worth noting for players seeking a more casual or flawless outing.

Ultimately, Ultimate Fishing® Simulator 2 is a compelling and authentic fishing game that succeeds in delivering depth and realism without becoming inaccessible. It’s a thoughtful blend of simulation and enjoyment, inviting players to learn the intricacies of fishing while immersing themselves in beautifully crafted aquatic environments. For fans of fishing or simulation games, it offers a rewarding challenge and a peaceful escape into nature. Its commitment to detail, variety of locations and species, and satisfying gameplay mechanics make it one of the most complete fishing simulators currently available on Steam, well worth the time of anyone looking to experience the subtle art and excitement of the sport from the comfort of their own home.

review:
Review based on VR version - using original HTC Vive.

Having played The Persistence quite a bit on PSVR a year or two back, it was an instant purchase for me on Steam, in the hope of getting a perfect version of the game at last.  As with most PSVR titles, while still a top notch game and visually impressive - the graphics could feel a little blurry on the PS4 and wasn't quite reaching its potential.  I haven't had a chance to play much tonight but I've played the original enough to confidently review this already and can already see some of its shortcomings.

The Good:  The Persistence is a fantastic stealth horror action game with some light rogue-like elements in regards to character upgrades over multiple plays/deaths - and some randomisation to the specific decks/levels you visit.  While there are lots of comparisons to be made to System Shock, Alien Isolation and Dead Space, its definitely its own unique title.  While definitely firmly in the stealth horror camp, it feels more arcadey (in a good way) than other titles in that genre, so I find it quite a fun "one more go" kinda gameplay - rather than outright terrifying :D  The combat can feel simplistic (and at times totally OP if you're having a great run and stocked up on items/weapons along the way) - but it can also be incredibly punishing, especially in the early game when you're learning the ropes and more prone to panicking when a creature jumps out at ya!  Oh and draining the enemy of their precious genetic code is always totally satisfying ^^

The Meh:  Unfortunately at this time (launch day on Steam) the game doesn't seem to have altered much from the original PSVR release.  It should only be played seated, and ideally with a joypad, i'm using an old x360 controller without issues there.  The majority of actions in-game such as interacting with buttons and picking up items are done by staring at the item in question (Gaze interactions) - as such there is permanently an icon in the dead centre of your vision so the game knows what you are looking directly at. 

  Motion controls unfortunately are not supported (even using the joypad style controls on them) and neither is room scale movement - making it one of the more inanimate VR titles to release in 2020 :)  Now thats not necessarily a bad thing as sometimes you want a great VR game to play without needing the energy to run a metaphorical mile - but it does feel like the Devs have missed a trick by not updating the engine to support actual motion controls - picking up items by hand, using weapons directly etc.  The level of immersion would be increased dramatically and it would help declutter some of the UI in-game (for example item names could appear over the item in your hand rather than popping up whenever you look at it in the world).

  Graphics options in-game are entirely missing - no way to increase textures, supersampling isn't making a noticeable difference and theres a heavy level of antialiasing which muddies the visuals giving it that PSVR look.

Final Thoughts:  It might look like the cons outweigh the pros above - but bear in mind the majority of these are just additions to the existing game I would have hoped to see in the PC version.  The fact is that the base game, even if directly ported across from PSVR, is really tight and a whole lotta fun...I'm just glad its even got a PC release so that more people get a chance to try it for themselves :)  I can highly recommend it, just know what you're buying into controls-wise.

  Hopefully the Devs can still make some significant updates that could improve some of the above issues.  While I really REALLY hope they can eventually bring out support for tracked motion controls, I wouldn't buy into this expecting that to happen - the entire game was constructed around seated joypad control and the Gaze based interactions so it would require significant reworking of the entire games systems to support that.  Hopefully graphics options are added to the game soon so we can boost the visuals, with that i'll be more than satisfied with the purchase :)

review:
Review for the non-VR mode:

The Persistence is a first person roguelike with some survival horror elements mixed in, originally the game was released as a PSVR title and the VR game design shows throughout the game - some of the things translate pretty well outside of VR but unfortunately some of the control/interaction mechanics feel a little out of place and more importantly the horror atmosphere doesn't adapt that well to non-VR mode.

My run though the campaign took roughly 5.5 hours (with 21 deaths) and I got what seems to be the best ending, although the game has some replay value with different modes, unlocks/leveling and the campaign maps being generated from a tileset every time you die - I have absolutely no desire to play the game again.

Campaign has the player tackle a few objectives that are split between 4 decks of the ship you're on board of, along with a small area for the grand finale. During the first portion of the game, my impressions were reasonably positive - despite some minor issues.

However during the latter portions of deck 3, the repetitive nature of the game was starting to take its toll and during deck 4, it became obvious that rather than introducing new challenges - the last portion of the game was padded out to extend the campaign length in the worst possible way: Add lot, a whole lot more of the same enemies while being a lot more stingy with giving the players the opportunity to craft the actually functional weapons.

Rather than being an enjoyable challenge, the 4th deck became an annoyance - one that ultimately started to highlight the flaws of the game. Minor things such as the lack of environment & visual variety (as you might expect from a starship), automatically switching to a weapon each time you pick one up and giving you the same introductory voice line about it (making you go back to menu to select your actual main weapon again), some enemies being able to spin 180 degrees in a split second when you teleport behind them, some of them lacking any sort of hit reaction when hit by some of the weaker weapons - became more and more annoying.

Along with some more major issues like the clear lack of balance between weapons and equipment as some of them are far superior to others - and too bad if you upgraded ones that are next to useless in the "endgame", I guess you could grind out more resources to upgrade the worthwhile ones.

Would I recommend the game? No, definitely not at a full price, there are much better roguelike games out there. For the fans of the genre, I'd recommend waiting for a sale or if the dev team patches out some of the issues and takes a look at the weapon/equipment balance in general.

review:
UPDATE 17 DEC:
Just completed the Main Campaign. I found the campaign to be well-balanced; it often took various attempts to get through each level, but the game fortunately saved major accomplishments as you went through the level, so you never had to replay too much of the current level.  Ultimately,there was a steady sense of progression as you played the game, with the only exception being the final part of the game where you had only a single life left (HINT: Use the Captain's DNA to double your health).
Even though rogue-like games have a certain amount of repitition the longer you play them, this game did better than most where the randomly-generated levels left 'just different enough. Even the enemies seemed to be randomly generated  enough to where I never felt like I could predict exactly what i would be getting into.

This game would benefit a great deal if motion controls schemes used in most modern FPS shooters were applied here

It was a joy to play, and I'm currently trying to go through the Challenges.
Although the game has GAME+ modes, and a Perma Death Mode, I can't say I would go through the campaign again if I had to start over from ground zero.
================================================ 

A Wonderful Premise With Some Outdated Control Implementation (played on a Valve Index, i7-8700, 16GB RAM, GTX 1070Ti).

This is a rogue-based space shooter that has influences in Dead Space, Dead Effect 2 VR, and Alien: Isolation. I could see this as being the outer space equivalent of 'In Death'. You have a decent level of narrative in the form of a story to give you a goal to strive, you have grinding/leveling up to build up stats/attributes to better your character (and the improvements stay with you even when you die), and the rogue-based level design that gives you different pathways to the next objectives.

Where the game falters slightly is in the control implementation.  Not being a fan of keyboard/mouse for a VR game, all that was available was a gamepad.  The gamepad default controls work reasonably well for myself, but I have two issues: (1) Gamepad controls are not configurable (As far as I can tell), and (2) no VR controller implementation.  My beef with (2) is based on recently completing Alien: Isolation using the Index Controller, which helps immersion slightly, but more importantly, allows you to look one way where your smooth locomotion that you in another (trying this in The Persistence makes me feel like I'm going diagonal instead of straight).
I don't know what the level of effort would be to convert to control like that for Lone Echo, or Dead Effect 2 VR,but it would be something to see.

The concept of the game is straight-forward, and it's goals are clear.  The leveling up of your stats is helped by the different level structure each time you play, which keeps it relatively fresh.  The environment has a good sci-fi feel.  The gamepad controls are acceptable, but updating them to today's standard might increase commercial appeal (especially in the days of Oculus Quest 2).

As long as there is a tangible sense of progression (in both skills and narrative), I see myself as continuing to play this game.  For an older game, this is a pleasureable find.

review:
This is a cool sci-fi horror rogue-lite with some really elegant UI/UX design, sort of reminiscent of Dead Space, and a fun clone conceit to contextualise your infinite respawns. There's a lot of resource collection/management and lots of equipment and genetic upgrade trees to level up, and exploration involves quite a bit of sneaking and some slow-ish paced, deliberate combat - this definitely isn't a run 'n' gun action game, much more like an immersive sim. The visuals are nice and clean and the audio adds a lot of atmosphere (the voice actor for your companion/guide isn't annoying, which is a relief as she talks to you quite a bit with objectives, tips after deaths etc.).

The original PSVR version is a few years old now and this shows a bit in the port, mainly with the lack of Oculus Touch (or equivalent) controller support - it's gamepad only in VR mode, which may be a turn-off for some. Aside from that though, the VR features are good, with lots of customisable comfort options and a slick 'look-at-to-interact-with' UI/UX system. This port adds a non-VR mode though, which I actually prefer: the UI system translates very smoothly to non-VR, and I find it a lot easier to play for longer stretches (I'm very prone to VR sickness even with comfort options, and VR headsets are heavy and sweaty).

Overall, a solid game with some cool ideas and satisfying gameplay. Would recommend.

review:
What a great surprise is The Persistance VR !
Is too early to give a definitive review but so far I want to give this game a big thumb up !
I Recommend this for VR players.
So far the game is an 8/10 for me.

Here is a good gameplay video that shows different mechanics: https://youtu.be/fwtger58dyw

And here is an updated video of the new ENHANCED version in VR and RT: 
https://youtu.be/BxrN8KHK16o

The game has a main story where the player is embodied on clones that can evolve in stats, and the player can unlock blueprints of new weapons and features. With those premises the game generates a procedural level with the current objective of the campaign. 
The levels are BIG, full of surprises, resources, blueprints, weapons, or machines that allow to invest resources to pull specific weapons or tools that were previously discovered. The catch is that the roguelike factor plays with each life, recreating the level with a new life but retaining stats and blueprints unlocked, but you will need to get the guns and tools in the new generated level again.

The gameplay itself in VR is handled by the gamepad but the view of the player in VR is blended with these controls, so you can aim with your view, pick things with your view, open doors, etc.
The gameplay uses a First Person view and a similar slow pace like Alien Isolation, but here you have some weapons to have good shooting parts mixed with melee combat + shield that covers brief instants and you have to time correctly.
 The player as a result can use different tactics, starting from stealth ones that have additional rewards for silently taking enemies, or using guns (so far I unlocked 3 of them), grenades with different effects or some exotic ones, or evolve the melee approach. But there is more options that I do not want to reveal yet as I have still plenty more to unlock.

There 2 things that I think the game could probably have in the future that will make this a much better game
1) Full VR controls support instead of gamepad + VR View. The game was created with gamepad in mind, not sure if this was because it was also for PS4. Do not get me wrong, I got used to the controls just fine and enjoying the game seated a lot, but It is clear that if developers in the future add full VR Controls the game would be uber amazing jejejej

2) There are no Video Options to configure at all. The game looks great, has great visuals, but I think I would always prefer to have a way to disable AA and adjust other options, once again this could be because it was in PS4 as well? not sure.

I understand now why some Non-VR players are not enjoying this so much as I'm, because clearly the VR way to view naturally improves the gameplay a lot.

Bonus: The game allows some assymetric couch multiplayer where the 2nd player can download a mobile phone client called Solex App to assist the player that is playing, I will update this soon with more detais.

review:
[i] My Experience [/i]

I was pleasantly surprised by Hope; or How We Survived. I had recently played and [i]mostly[/i] enjoyed a game called Zombo Buster Rising, and this game reminded me of it, only with the addition of some dialogue.

There are really two parts to the game, and each has its highs and lows. I found the shooting sections to be somewhat challenging and tense, especially the horde section towards the end. However, I would recommend just sticking to the rifle that you start with. It seems to have a balance of power and clip size that is ideal. From what I could tell from trying them out, the clip size on the shotgun is a bit too small and the firepower of the revolver is a bit lacking.

The writing was actually quite good during the dialogue sections - the writer has a solid degree of self-awareness and the comments made seemed authentic. Unfortunately, you often can't tell what your guard will say based on the options you're given. You might be given three words to choose between, but each word is then extrapolated into a sentence. There were a few times where I communicated something I didn't really intend. In addition, the noises that the game uses to represent speech are obnoxious. Perhaps the mask worn by the guard muffled his voice, but I felt that the otherwise solid "tone" was compromised a bit through the silly noises.

I liked this little "slice-of-life" game. I thought the "rules" of the settlement were a nice touch that made sense given the circumstances. You can indeed imagine a settlement waiting to admit a wanderer with unknown infection status, even if we were talking about a mysterious deadly pathogen instead of a zombie outbreak. Hope attempts to answer the question, "what would happen in the meantime?"

Although I'm likely reading too much into the experience, I found it interesting to contemplate while playing the ways that we create boundaries to protect ourselves in relationships. Do we need to know someone's name, interests, or history to care for them? Or is there a basic human decency that exists nonetheless?

review:
The White Door is a uniquely stylized point-and-click puzzle adventure from the creators of the Rusty Lake series. It carries the signature surrealism, psychological tension, and narrative ambiguity that fans of the studio have come to expect, yet it also carves its own distinct identity within that universe. Taking place in a mental health facility, the game follows Robert Hill, a man suffering from memory loss and depression, as he experiences the monotony of institutional life while slowly unraveling the events that led him there. The story is told through daily routines—brushing teeth, eating breakfast, doing cognitive tests—but beneath this ordinary surface is an unsettling and often heartbreaking exploration of trauma, memory, and loss.

What immediately sets The White Door apart is its presentation. The game is split into two panels: the left side represents Robert’s actions and the right shows his thoughts, memories, or sometimes just another angle of the scene. This dual-panel interface serves both as a narrative device and gameplay mechanic, challenging players to engage with two perspectives simultaneously. The minimalist black-and-white art style, with occasional splashes of color used to denote emotional or narrative significance, reinforces the sense of detachment and mental fragility. It's a simple yet effective aesthetic that suits the sterile, quiet atmosphere of the clinic, while also emphasizing the stark contrast between reality and memory.

Gameplay in The White Door is relatively light on traditional puzzles, especially compared to other Rusty Lake titles. Most of the interactions are rooted in following Robert's strict daily regimen: wake up, shower, eat, complete simple tests, go to sleep. Yet, as the days progress, subtle anomalies begin to appear—objects shift, time loops, and brief flashes of color or distorted memories hint at something more buried beneath the routine. These moments gradually peel away the layers of Robert’s psychological state. When the puzzles do come, they are clever and emotionally resonant, focusing less on complexity and more on symbolism and progression. Instead of testing logic, they often test observation and emotional engagement, aligning the player's experience closely with Robert’s.

Narratively, the game is linear but deeply atmospheric. Through sparse voice-over and environmental storytelling, players slowly uncover the tragic events that led Robert to the institution. Without spoiling too much, the themes deal with heartbreak, guilt, and disassociation, handled in a way that is both surreal and grounded. The pacing is deliberate and melancholic, moving from the sterile monotony of the clinic to increasingly abstract sequences as Robert’s memories resurface. This emotional arc is where the game truly shines. Though short—roughly two to three hours—it manages to build a meaningful sense of empathy and introspection, drawing players into Robert’s internal struggle without relying on overt exposition.

The White Door is also subtly connected to the broader Rusty Lake universe, offering small nods to fans of the series while remaining fully self-contained for newcomers. These connections add an extra layer of depth for those familiar with the lore, but they never overshadow the central narrative. The game’s ending, while somewhat ambiguous, is emotionally satisfying and ties together its thematic threads in a way that encourages reflection. It’s not a game that answers every question, but rather one that invites interpretation and emotional resonance—hallmarks of the Rusty Lake style.

Technically, the game runs smoothly, with clean interfaces and responsive controls. It’s accessible on multiple platforms, and its point-and-click mechanics are intuitive, even for those unfamiliar with the genre. The sound design is subtle but powerful, with quiet ambient music and minimal effects that reinforce the game’s meditative tone. The voice acting, while sparse, is impactful, helping to convey the protagonist’s state of mind with restraint and authenticity.

Ultimately, The White Door is a short, thoughtful, and artistically cohesive experience. It’s less about solving puzzles and more about stepping into the fractured psyche of a grieving man, piecing together his story one small interaction at a time. It won’t appeal to players looking for complex mechanics or high-stakes gameplay, but for those who appreciate narrative-driven games with emotional depth and atmospheric storytelling, it offers a memorable and haunting journey. It’s a quiet game, one that stays with you not because of what it says, but because of how it makes you feel.

Rating: 9/10

For full clarity: I did the steam trailer for this game but I still bought it on my own in 2021's Summer Steam Sale.

Brother Brother is a unique experience as the game is able to get so much out of it's simple control scheme of WASD to move and Arrow keys to use your weapon, as the game goes on you unlock greater weapons and abilities that add to your versatility but still stays true to it's simple control scheme.

I feel like Brother Brother's greatest strength is it's world, every area of the land is so densely populated that at no point do you feel like an area is filler or padding, each area has a purpose and a puzzle to it, whether self contained or hints to a grand scale puzzle that'll take you across the map to hunt powerful foes.

For me at least, the game's weakest points are a few of the boss fights. These fights in particular are about dodging projectiles in a game with only one form of movement so it becomes easy to get beaten down quickly.

I would easily recommend this game for it's charm alone but throw in a densely packed and enjoyable world, plenty of goods to collect, and a super simple yet enjoyable combat system- it easily becomes my go-to recommendation for if you want to spend your afternoon on an adventure.

I look forward to Brothers Apart when it comes out!

review:
To say I was disappointed with this game would be an understatement. I have played other games by this same developer and thought this game would be similar. It's not. I am just glad I bought it on sale for 59 cents.

- On the positive side, the controls are fairly standard: left click to mark a square solid (green) to denote solution, right click to mark a pirate-y themed X for not solution.
- The puzzles were pirate and sea themed. Yup, it had fish, sharks, boats, (really creepy looking) pirates and mermaids...

- There was no story. None. They had pirates and didn't do any story! The only time the pirates "speak" is during the incredibly long tutorial. The description lied to me about pirates and sea monsters and sailing.
- They cross out the numbers as you logically fill in the green squares, but (in my opinion) they can get a bit overzealous and make leaps in logic without you. It would be better if I could mark the number off as I used it rather than them doing it for me. Or just leave it and I can count/match the squares with the numbers.
- The music was boring. And the sounds when you clicked were really annoying. I muted it.
- You only get 2 mistakes per level. Which is rude. Oh, misclick? Sorry! No stars for you! It makes levels more difficult because I can't just put an X in to mark where the end would be when I'm counting, no, I've got to remember where they all end for 5 different numbers across 25 squares. Ugh.
- The pictures were awful. You get seconds to stare at your finished green blob and try to decipher what it was supposed to be before it brings up the stars/time/etc page. The only way to tell what this was supposed to be is to click map and check their drawing, which does not even match. Previous games would fade the pictures into color and you had time to feel proud of your puzzle prowess.
- The puzzles are small. Being so small they are really simple. The most time I spent on a level was 15 minutes. Logical? Yes. Hard? No. The entire game felt more like a World 1 difficulty. If people have trouble, there are hints. Every green square you fill in gives coins which can be used to immediately "purchase" a new hint. You have to use 15 hints for the achievement.
- I spent 20 hours on this game and was done; even with the achievements. It was short and not very sweet.

I guess I'll just go replay the Red Riding Hood picross series.

"Griddlers Legend Of The Pirates" is a basic Nonogram game... for those who never played one, it's a kind of grid-deduction-puzzle game, not unlike Minesweeper or Sudoku.  You're given a grid and a number of numerical clues.  You must deduce where the safe places to click are.  In a Nonogram, the correct clicks will reveal a small, obviously low resolution image or pattern.  Yay, what fun.  This is why top of the line gaming PCs costs thousands of dollars, right?

The developer, Creobit, has copy + pasted this game an insane FOURTY ONE TIMES... why cash in on one asset if you can cash in on multiple copies of the same game?  Asset flipping begins at home!

Here's a list of the asset flips of this game that the Russian "developer" is polluting Steam with:

[/list]

[i][b]These are all reskins of exactly the same game![/b][/i]

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features extremely lazy, minimalist "art", of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with crappy "wings" to pad out the space).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

"Griddlers Legend Of The Pirates" has the gamer gouging price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

review: I love this game, I remember playing the 2020 demo my first year of college and I knew it would amaze me when it would release. I've had it in my Wishlist since then and only now played it. It's a beautiful story that gives you lots of freedom to explore, find secrets, tinker with the puzzles, and reward you with fun cameos and achievements. There are moments that made me hold back tears and moments that made me feel hopeful in my own life. All in all, this is not just a game but an interactive story, and those who feel a connection to it will be put through an emotional journey. I highly recommend this game to people who enjoy pixel art games like Locomotive, If On A Winter's Night, Backbone (Tail's Noir), etc, or games with deep/heavy story aspects intertwined with their puzzles like Night in the Woods, CrossCode, Disco Elysium, Lucifer Within Us, Universe For Sale, etc. In summary, its a wonderful, mostly calm, challenging but rewarding game meant for everyone, but those with a deep relationship with indie games will feel the fullest weight of the story.

This game was really a mixed bag.  The  main game was decent enough for a HOG.  It has an odd, somewhat confusing story in which you play a detective trying to catch the phantom terrorizing the theater.  Nothing is overly difficult; the HO scenes and mini-games are fun and pretty easy, an enjoyable way to pass the time.  As with most HOGs, it has a silly story, but it was decent and I enjoyed the gameplay.

Then I finished the main game and started the bonus game and suddenly all conventions went straight out the window.  Mini-games suddenly have no logic no clues, and incomplete or incomprehensible instructions, forcing you to guess what you're supposed to do and then brute-force and/or guess your way to the solution (or use the built-in guide to look up the solution). 
 I had no problem with the main game, but I couldn't solve even the first mini-game in the bonus game.  For the life of me, I cannot figure out how the developer could make a decent main game but then make the worst bonus game I've ever seen.
