[h3]Disclaimer[/h3]
First and foremost, XIII has mouse acceleration & saving issues with possible audio issues, all of these can be fixed by player input & guides shared on steam.

In regards to saving you can remedy it by manually saving in the menu & also using the auto save key (F5) throughout the level, however you must be aware that the saves only restore you to the latest checkpoint not to where you saved. In some cases there are long gaps without checkpoints that can be extremely frustrating.

XIII also has [b]Unskippable cut scenes & sequences that halt player movement/interactions[/b]. This is not a problem on its own but in conjuction with the poor checkpoint system & boss fights utilising them, it can lead to frustration as you seem them multiple times after dying or failing the mission guidelines.[i] One level in particular "infiltrate, disable generators & save hostage" can set you back minutes.[/i]

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
XIII is a PS2 era first person shooter forged out of comic book stylization based on a European graphic novel series. It features stealth mechanics from the time alongside finer gameplay elements like grappling hooks & interactable objects like glass shards, bricks, chairs etc. that can be used to take down targets. 

It utilises displays of onomatopoeia where applicable as movement indicators alongside comic panel cut-outs that overlay the screen during specific stealth related sequences or upon landing headshots. Despite the game running in odd resolutions the XIII’s graphics and art style alongside the aforementioned hold up to this day with only a few instances of obvious aging.

The item interactions are engaging and satisfying. Blunt objects like chairs, brooms, bricks and ash trays can be used to knock out targets while lighter objects like glass can be used to create distractions, the latter of which can be gained by destroying windows. 

While stealth is fun, the same can't be said for gunplay & combat (outside of the crossbow & throwing knives). Weapons are inaccurate with huge bullet spread that makes mid-long range encounters a pain to clear. That being said, combat feels janky & realistic in that shots to the head eliminate NPCs swiftly while shots elsewhere stagger targets depending on their armour (armour of which you can steal if left undamaged from your assault.

Bosses on the other hand are awful & do not reflect the basic gameplay, they are bullet sponges, have high mobility and increased damage. The final boss in particular has an interesting loop tied to damaging him but it's poorly implemented and leaves the player wasting ammo & thought on inconsistent movement & untelegraphed strikes. These bosses might not be a problem on their own but they also have the aforementioned Unskippable cut scenes and movement restrictions throughout that you'll experience numerous times on reset.

Level design is on par with other titles of the 6th console generation & the variety of their biome is welcome even if short. You’ll go from the beachside, city rooftops, hotel rooms to snowy mountains, docks & military complexes. XIII in a way evolves as you progress & gain access to more weapons & utility. The latter involves a grappling hook that sees use in preset locations to access the next section of levels, secrets & vantage points. The former has less appearances in comparison and offers little 

[h3]Story[/h3]
XIII is a spy thriller about a conspiratorial plot to overthrow the United States government by unknown individuals that use Roman numerals to mask their real identities. It's a competent video game story for the time but it lacks a conclusion and opted for a cliffhanger ending. The mystery can also be lost if you've engaged with any media in the genre before alongside a majority of the canal having no presence or showcase throughout the 30 levels.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
XIII is a near perfect 6th console generation video game in that it has love, charm & variety however due to the time of its release it also lacks quality of life improvements that some in the modern day may prefer in a shooter. Bosses are awful compared to other targets, checkpoint gaps are frustrating, saving can be inconsistent, guns are inaccurate, the story ends on a cliffhanger & the game requires external editing to remove mouse acceleration & to possibly restore audio or increase the resolution.

That being said the comic art style that forms the gameplay like stealth with its onomatopoeia & panel cutouts are unique, the headshot panel killcams are satisfying, the grappling hook while limited is fun, crossbow/throwing knives are a blast during stealth sections, the story despite its cliffhanger & predictability is intriguing, the 30+ levels have variety & there is a vast amount of weapons available across the levels; all of the aforementioned make XIII a unique experience that I have not seen since its release that despite the flaws & frustrations I have to recommend the title.

[b]It’s $18.50 but during sales it drops to $1.50AUD and for that price XIII is definitely worth playing for the unique experience alone.[/b]

review:
The Magician's Workshop is a really interesting game with a few really glaring flaws. The writing is enjoyable, I like how the addition of magic doesn't change much about Renaissance-era Italy, and it ends up being a fun setting to play around in. The main path through the game is fairly linear, but a LOT of the side stories, descriptions and dialog changes significantly based on who you've befriended, what projects you work on, what magic you specialize in. I've done a few playthroughs and I get the sense there's a lot I still haven't seen.

That, however, leads to the big negative. There are so many stats and reputations to try to keep track of that even playthroughs where you you focus on a handful of stats, you'll still be presented with several choices that your character seems woefully unprepared for. I'm more or less fine with this (it's realistic after all), but I feel like the execution in the gameplay is a little clumsy. This is especially evident in the romance options, where if you misread or fail checks at the beginning of the game, you lock yourself out of them entirely. Either way, it feels like a bit of a struggle/slog to build a character that's better than OK at more than a couple of skills.

Pros:

+ Fun setting
+ Well written story
+ Really fun to see how many different combinations of skills/reputations/projects create unique scenes and dialog

Cons:

- Huge array of skills and reputation bars can be a bit much to manage and feel somewhat arbitrary
- Epilogues don't really stick the landing

Overall: This is a really interesting concept with a lot of fun minor and major variations to scenes based on your choices. That said, it lacks a bit of focus and is a min/max nightmare.

I also don't like how the multiple plots resolve, I feel like the writer had a grand idea for how these intricate plot threads would coalesce, but in reality they fell flat for me. I wouldn't be so bothered, but I genuinely can't see the choices I missed on the road to get the outcome I need. Here are some examples.

I kept no secrets from my rivals, and told them off the bat I believed in a triumvurate. Despite this, one of them felt like I was out to stab them in the back (I don't think I made one choice that involved lying, but ok). I tried to empathise with the apprentices in the workshop, and let them democratically choose their teams, but they preferred the other two to me. I led and completed three commissions, two of which were good enough to earn a tip, but that didn't factor in at all to the choice of next master.

In conclusion, high ambitions but faltering execution.

Highly recommended.

review:
TL;DR - 8/10 - Cute little family-friendly single-player exploration/collectathon game. Adorable and mostly non-violent, should be appropriate for all ages. Not a must-play, but enjoyable.

And now... a "little" more.
...
Do you see what I did there?
...
Do... do you see what I did there?
...
Do you see----

ADORABLE AND WHOLESOME
This game caught my eye after I finished [i]Untitled Goose Game[/i] with a friend as being something in the same vein, and I was not disappointed, though I enjoyed goose mischief ever so slightly more. [i]Little Kitty, Big City[/i] is cute, enjoyable, and wholesome. Little Kitty can't die (I tried, because I'm a psychopath). Violence in the game is limited to Little Kitty accidentally (or intentionally) tripping people in the street and causing many of them to fall flat on their face (which I did... repeatedly, because... again... psychopath). Unlike [i]Untitled Goose Game[/i], there is dialogue between the animals. It's all pretty adorable. I had to reach to try to make any of it sound dirty. The worst I got was a dog talking about its lost balls. It's talking about tennis balls, but of course... I got creative with photo mode... (What part of psychopath didn't you understand?)

GAMEPLAY
In all seriousness, though... the developers advertise this as a wholesome, adorable, chill cat exploration/collectathon, and they delivered on a wholesome, adorable, chill cat exploration/collectathon. You wander around the map completing a to-do list (quests) and challenges and you gain new abilities and in-game features (like photo mode, which you can use to make double entendres like a 12-year-old when a certain dog talks about his lost tennis balls). Challenges consist of completing specific tasks, like making someone trip over a banana peel or recycling 100 cans. It's all very chill and non-strenuous. The weirdest bit is that the game introduces a fast-travel network, and while it's cute and fun... the map is really too small to warrant a fast-travel network. Traveling between one point and another will take you literally an extra minute (after you unlock running) so there's really no reason to use it aside from achievement hunting. Platforming and cat-movement is very cat-like, though there is just the tiniest bit of artisan jank.

GLITCHES AND JANK
The most egregious glitch I encountered was after digging through a particular trash can. I went to pick up my items, and Little Kitty suddenly flew up into the air and landed on an invisible wall above the railroad tracks. It was amusing, but it was clearly a case of artisan jank. I was able to jump down, though, and Little Kitty cannot die, so his guts were NOT splattered around the pavement when I did so (I told you I tested it). Pedestrians have a tendency to materialize in the distance or disappear so that you just see a floating bagel and then, suddenly, they decloak. Birds appear to be able to fly through walls and no clip frequently through buildings. There is also one spot on a high building where a texture doesn't appear to be complete.

That said, most of these are just nitpicks as the game runs pretty smoothly and I didn't have any major crashes or game breaking issues with it. All of the achievements worked for me, and I was able to do them in under 7 hours. 

OVERALL
This game is exactly what it says it is: a cute little family-friendly single-player exploration/collectathon. It's not a must-play, but I do give it a strong recommendation, especially for kids, cat lovers, and people looking to destress. 8/10

review:
The game is very fun, albeit short, and many of the puzzles are quite creative and enjoyable to solve. However, there are some issues with the game, mostly bugs, and while there is no 'neutral' rating on Steam, I would still lean toward a yes on this game despite playing other games with similar problems that I rated negatively. But without further ado:

Pros:
-The graphics are very nice. Colorful, but not hard on the eyes.
-If it wasn't obvious already, the game has similar vibes to Untitled Goose Game, down to a To-Do list where your quests and random cat shenanigans are including hidden ones. This game has actual animal NPCs to talk to, however, with their own little side stories as you play. The dialogue is fun, as it feels like real animals in their own bubbles chatting to you about what was on their mind, but it's not super childish either.
-The game's soundtrack is just a very laid-back piano tune, which is quite fitting even with the cat chaos going on. Calming, pleasant little melody as you leg-swipe every human and stash their phones in your den.
-As of the Picture Purrfect update, you can now customize your kitty, and it's a very robust tool as well. You can layer stripes on a tuxedo pattern as an example, change the pupil size, heterochromia, paw bean color, whisker color, you name it. I don't know if there's a layer limit, but if so it's a generous one.

Cons:
-The game is very vague in certain scenarios, especially the achievements. There are many hidden achievements in your To-Do list, but the game gives absolutely no hints for them, so most you will either find by accident or by throwing stuff at the wall until it sticks. A lot of them are mostly just rewarded for doing funni cat things, but some can be kind of obscure. [spoiler]Like one where you have to trip an NPC with a banana peel[/spoiler]
-The controls are a little wonky sometimes. The cat controls fine for the most part, but precise movements are tricky and falling off ledges is common. Ivy climbing is very clunky depending on what angle you started at, and despite doing the big climb multiple times, I never trust that my cat will land on this one tiny ledge at the start to recharge climbing stamina.
-The game is very, VERY buggy. Nothing truly heinous like save corruption as far as I can tell, but quests straight up not working is common. I did not encounter any major issues (at first), but I know many people did have quests break. One bug at launch was that the emote wheel straight up didn't work on keyboard, so my poor kitty couldn't make biscuits until they fixed it. As of Picture Purrfect, there's even more bugs, but to the devs' credit they fixed many bugs before this update. One thing that broke in the update was the tracker for collecting hats in your To-Do list, where it completely resets upon collecting the new hats and as of me writing this, the only way to fix it is with save editing. Something that cannot be fixed with save editing is the save file now reads with -1 hat despite no hat being missing, and it reverts back to the incorrect number even after editing.
-Picture Purrfect is even vaguer than the base game. It's only been out for 3-4 days while I'm writing this, but despite seemingly doing all it had to offer, my previously completed save file still says 87%. I just recently learned what the second hidden achievement was, so unless I'm missing something, no NPC has anything to tell me anymore and I am very lost lol.

At the end of the day, this is a sandbox kitty physics simulator. It has a light story of your kitty getting back home after falling out of their apartment window, but generally once you finish the story, the game expects you to get most of your entertainment from doing cat things. If that's your thing, you'll love this game. Tbh one of my favorite moments was collecting 15 phones and bringing each one up to my lair, took like 2 hours but it was worth it. Although stolen items don't save so, phooey. I wouldn't say the game is worth $25, so if you want to do cat things, snatch it while it's on sale. Embrace the kitty empire

review:
An incredibly charming exploration game that's just brimming with personality. It kinda gives "The Untitled Goose Game" vibes if you've played that, except this has more of a narrative and platforming focus. 

You're a cute little kitty who has fallen off of their favorite napping spot near the top of an apartment building and need to find your way back up to the top. Along the way you meet several animal friends who will all need your help in different ways. You collect "shinies" throughout the city as a form of money to pay to your crow friend, and there's a plethora of challenges spread around the city to do. As you do this you're also able to interact with NPCs by tripping them over, stealing their food, stealing their phones, being a nuisance to shopkeepers, etc. You can even bait and catch birds, which is pretty fun and allows you to fast travel.

Honestly the only gripe I have is the length compared to the price. If you went out of your way to collect every single hat and complete every single objective, then that'll maybe get you around 8 hours, but this is for most people around a 3-4 hour game, or as little as an hour if you rush things. Now I loved every second of playing this game, and don't regret buying it in the slightest, but that may be worth considering due to the fairly steep $25 price tag.

If its on sale or if you have a spare $25 you don't mind spending, Little Kitty Big City is a wonderful game to play over a weekend and I do recommend you buy it. It's obvious from the care put into it that this was a passion project of the development studio, which doesn't feel all too common nowadays.

review:
I am a huge fan of crazy eights.. I grew up with it, and as an adult, I play it whenever I get the chance.. so I was so excited to see this game in the works..  Ive been literally checking the status of this game once a week (or more) for the past 2 months in eager anticipation.. I finally saw it was released... but now.. I wish the team would have waited longer.. I'm not sure how this got out the door.. just in the first 5 minutes I encountered a ton of bugs and issue.. but let me first talk about the good parts :)
1. ) The on screen 3D graphics are very nice.. the table, the cards.. the scene in the background, all top notch.
2. ) Animations are great, the flow of the card play feels very natural and organic.
3. ) The options of card backs, and card "fronts" is done very well and look exactly as you'd expect
4. ) The music.. is.. a good attempt :) I would honestly rather they utilized more meditative, relaxing music that was less pop'y, or at least fit the setting to which you are playing, but all in all, is fine.

So Now the Cons...
1. ) First of all.. resolution.. I have a large monitor that uses a 3840x2160 size.. first of all the game didn't suggest using it, so i pushed it up anyways.. once applied I could only see about 30% of the screen and the rest was off the screen AND the cursor didn't line up with the buttons so I had to drift in magic space and wait for the game to highlight what my mouse was over to get things back to normal (no "did these settings apply correctly.. resetting in 30 seconds").. So I went back to what the game recommended. The game play space was locked to the lower left portion of the screen but worked.. So then I decided Ill switch to "windowed mode" hoping it would get things back in line.. which it did.. roughly.. but the game doesn't use a true "windowed" mode.. its a mini full screen that you have to use the in-game "move" function to move the window.. O.o   ... serious?
2. ) Card type... So for some reason.. the card type defaults to an UNO style card face.. Maybe I've been out of the crazy eights community too long to know what the norm is., but in my crazy eights was played with regular cards.. but lets put all that aside., my personal preference is to use regular cards.. so thankfully in the settings you can choose to set this back to normal cards.. HOWEVER.. after a round is completed.. the cards revert BACK to UNO cards.. so in essence.. every time you start a match you have to go back to setting and reset.. super frustrating..
3. ) Crazy Jacks.. This may be another result of me not keeping up with the crazy eights community.. but last I checked.. the game was called crazy eights.. to my understanding that means when someone plays an eight you get to choose a new suit for the group to play on.. HOWEVER.. in this version of crazy EIGHTS.. apparently the Jack is crazy instead.. maybe I'm just picking the wrong game type.. so this may just be me.. idk.

All in all., a nice step forward towards a great crazy eights game., but this feel VERY premature.. idk what testers they have, but there is a TON of basic things that seem to have been missed for the first release.. I truly hope the team will continue to  make this experience the best it can be. I will definitely be waiting excitedly to see what it can become.

review:
Hasfax is a low-budget indie horror game with a very shallow story, and even more depth-challenged gameplay. You play as a nameless man, and wake up with no memory of where you are or how you got there. Through vague clues, you realize that you've been kidnapped. To get out of the abandoned warehouse that you find yourself in, you must find a way to escape; although that ends up being simply wandering in and out of room after room, pixel-hunting keys until you're led to the end of the campaign.

Yes, this is yet another key finding simulator masquerading around as a horror game. The gameplay is particularly awful in this reiteration of the worn out mechanics, the keys themselves tiny and hard to see since they blend in well to the surfaces that they're laid on. They all have the same name and model as well, being therefore impossible to distinguish from one another, leading you to try every key in your inventory on every door until one finally works. Even adding some nameplates and tags to both the doors and keys would've been a leap of an improvement to this nearly Alpha-state title, but that would've made the sub-hour campaign closer to 15-20 minutes in length instead.

You may end up thinking that you're going to get chased, or at the very least jump-scared, by a masked man in Hasfax due to the appearance of such a character in screenshots, the trailer, and the banner. However, the best you're going to get is some eerie background music and a couple of stagnant hallucinations. There is huge wasted potential in this game, and it's a shame since the foundation is surprisingly really well done; the flickering lights, dismal atmosphere, and genuinely creepy OST all work well together. Unfortunately, the developer squandered this fantastic base by just throwing in a bunch of rooms, teeny-tiny keys, and vague notes and called it a day. Not worth the full price, not worth the sale price... it's a "full release" that never truly left alpha.

review:
Solid! This was a tough game to complete because I had a heck of a time finding the right book for one of the puzzles. I'll upload a screenshot of it once I'm finished writing this up for anyone else who is stuck. <3

As far as graphics and atmosphere go, Hasfax is dead on. True, it is a walking simulator, so you will never be in any danger. So if you're looking for a creepy place to explore without having to worry about being constantly chased or pursued, this may be right up your alley. 

This is a game that you need sharp eyes for. Check every surface because it may have a key. Collect the keys and unlock the doors until you eventually get to the exit. Win!

The story was a little hard to follow until the end. I kinda wish that there were more documents or that the documents that were there had more writing. 

The book puzzle is an interesting conundrum. It's hard to make it much more obvious without making it too obvious, but it's a little too hard to find as it is. I wish that I had a better suggestion to make this easier while maintaining the integrity of the puzzle itself. Hopefully the Devs can find a happy medium. 

I have two complaints. First, your character is suffering from a headache and so their default standing position is to sway and bob a lot. Yikes for my motion sickness sensitivity. I managed to muddle through without getting too queasy, but others may not be so lucky. 

My second complaint is that the big scares are simply a stationary image of the masked man that you're looking for. Even if they are just phantoms that do no damage, it would be nice if they could swing at you or something to create the illusion of danger rather than just an illusion. 

That's it! I enjoyed this game and I feel like it's worth the full price.

ZELDA: MAJORA'S MASK
Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask
The Legend of Zelda continues. Could it be as glorious and perfect as The Ocarina of Time? Find out.
Fran Mirabella III
BY FRAN MIRABELLA III
UPDATED: DEC 13, 2018 4:32 AM
POSTED: OCT 26, 2000 2:00 AM
Shortly after Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time was released and subsequently conquered by gamers around the world, many began to wonder if they would see another Zelda game within the next five years. Historically, Nintendo has taken anywhere from three to six years to deliver sequels to its hit Zelda franchise. The six year wait from A Link to the Past (1992) to The Ocarina of Time (1998) was almost unbearable. In the end, though, Nintendo immaculately transformed the 2D world of Hyrule into the defining 3D utopia it proved to be. Everything about The Ocarina of Time was something in which all future games could learn from.
Nintendo sold millions upon millions of those precious gold carts regardless of the N64's inadequate user-base. The question was would Nintendo deliver N64 owners one more blissful Zelda experience before the console faded away? There was the secretive Ura-Zelda title for the 64DD, but it didn't look like that would find its way to America and on top of that it was merely just an expansion of The Ocarina of Time's world. In May of 1999 IGN64 brought you the news that Nintendo was underway with a sequel that would hit the N64 in a big way with a whole new world and set of temples to explore. The follow-up title was promised to run on the acclaimed Ocarina of Time game engine, and would even be enhanced by use of the 4MB expansion pak. That game turned out to be what was temporarily called Zelda: Gaiden, which was then briefly named Zelda: Mask of Majora, and finally the title Zelda: Majora's Mask was set in stone. And so the legend continues as Link sets out on another quest to defend all that is good from the evil that lurks.

Features

Brand-new expansive 3D world outside of Hyrule called Termina
Real-time night/day sequences
Three different days
Play as young Link
Gain new swords, weapons, and spells
Gain masks to change form and get different character interaction
Capitalizes on the acclaimed Ocarina of Time engine
Utilizes the 4MB expansion pak for bigger worlds and better graphics
The Story
Link's new journey begins where The Ocarina of Time left off. After he rid Hyrule of evil he decided to set out on a quest that would benefit him. He went searching for an adored friend whom he set apart from when his legacy turned legendary. In the middle of this journey Link stumbles into a mysterious new land named, Termina (Note: Termina appears to be based off the word "Terminus", which denotes a limit or ending point). Through word of mouth, Link hears that Termina is in peril because the moon is unmercifully crashing down towards the earth leaving only a matter of days before the land breaths its last breath. On this new territory Link is riding his young steed through a thick forest, when two fairies scare his horse throwing him to the ground leaving him unconscious. It turns out the two fairies are working at the hand of an evil masked thief and all-around troublemaker. Link awakens angered to find them toying with his Ocarina of Time, which was given to him by Princess Zelda. This masked villain steals Link's horse and eventually curses Link himself. This is where the story begins and just three days -- 72 Hours-- later it will end if you don't halt the moons death march towards the land of Termina. Link isn't sure where this disguised troublemaker fits in, but the end of the world awaits if he doesn't vow to help these people.

Gameplay
Like the Ocarina of Time before it Majora's Mask opens up with an exquisite cut-scene that is visually dramatic with moody lighting, fog, and flawless animation. It pulls you into the world of Termina swiftly by inflaming your rage for this masked character that stole your Ocarina of Time and your horse too. Nintendo has done an amazing job of immersing you in the story right away. If you've played The Ocarina of Time the story will prove to be more intimate to you, but even as a newcomer to this franchise anyone will find pleasure with the story line. In fact, one might go as far to say that you don't even need to have played the previous Zeldas to feel like a part of the game. That's not to say you won't feel the nostalgia pouring in, but the storyline is one that doesn't really rely on the Zelda franchise to pull you in. This is truly a testament to the skills of Nintendo's team. Through Majora's Mask they've proved they haven't been forced to rehash gameplay and storylines to create a good piece of software.

The object of Majora's Mask revolves around two things: masks and time. Without spoiling the game too much, the masks stem from the owner of the Happy Mask Shop. The villain introduced to you in the beginning has stole one of the shopkeeper's most important masks. The Happy Mask Shop owner offers to lift the curse that was cast upon you if you agree to get his mask back. In lifting the curse you receive a mask that gives you the ability to transform into a different creature when you put it on. With that said, know that more masks come as you progress through the story. As Link you have three days to save the world from destruction, and in the midst of your quest you gain masks which you need to use to accomplish certain tasks or advance the storyline. The masks play such an integral part to the game you actually can't do many of the things without finding certain masks. There are a total of 24 masks to find, and each of them will aid you in a different way.

At the heart of Termina lies Clock Town, and surrounding it are four lands, each unique in their own way; swamps, snow-covered mountains, beaches, and deserts lie at each corner of the land. In these four areas lie the temples which have been cursed by the masked marauder. The boss figure that protects each temple has also been cursed. The object is to relieve the cursed creatures of their masked suffering

review:
Cover Your Eyes is a strange but very good RPG Maker horror game, so what is the story. A retired police officer Chloe is not having a very good day, not only she has to work a dead end 9 to 5 job after retiring from the police force because of the Emoji killer incident and raising two kids, but she finds out her husband is having an affair. So deciding to follow her husband and confront him she soon discovers her beloved town of Verwood is under attack by horrible monsters, now Chloe must find her husband and get him and their two children out of town, but with her fragile mental state, the ghosts of her past and the horrible monsters, the mother of two is in for a hell of a fight.

Alright then let’s get into the likes, the story is really good with plenty of great twists, turns and some heartfelt moments, it also has plenty of fourth wall breaks, it can be a bit confusing at first but once you get to the end it starts to make sense. The graphics are very good for an RPGmaker with a good use of colors, designs and background that makes you want to just look at it a bit. The levels are good with a nice use of scenery and little odds and ends that also ties into the story and makes a lot of sense on why everything is so strange, especially in the buildings.

The gameplay is good basically explore and kill monsters while solving some light puzzles that do not feel too hard and the combat’s fair, there are some enemies that are a pain though, there’s also a little bit of strategy involved in picking which monsters to kill and which to just ignore. The puzzles were okay nothing too complicated mostly involved picking up an item and using it on something. The enemies and bosses are very good they have the right balance of goofy and disturbing, like some being goofy and lol to others being downright horrifying and disturbing. 

The characters are good, each one is well written I really liked Chloe as you could definitely feel her struggle and you want to see her escape with her children, her children are good they don't feel like annoying little kids that are in some video games, they have the right balance of cute and kiddish without coming off as annoying.

The music was okay it can feel off and kind of bizarre, but it does fit a bizarre game like this. The atmosphere was good nice and spooky without being too spooky as you wander around the first few levels dreading early on, on what could be behind the next door.  The price for the game is also very fair.

Now is this game scary, sometimes it does have some good jumpscares, but it's more psychological horror than regular horror.

Alright then let’s get into the dislikes, there are some frustrating parts in the game like certain enemies can be a real pain in the ass to fight, the worst probably being the fetus monsters that just move sporadically and there is one puzzle in the game that is a real pain and it’s in the Vernwood News Corp as it was just trial and error and just really frustrating. First off, the game has great visuals and music, plus there's lots of cool '80s references (mainly movies and cartoons). Unfortunately that's not enough to make a good game though, but if you're just looking to kill some time I guess it might be alright. Still, I think there are better alternatives out there.

[b]Below some of the issues I have with the game:[/b]
Enemies glitch out way too often. Every fifth run or so I've run into enemies that behave in ways they shouldn't (especially "Hammers"), and it can make them extremely unpredictable, which can end a good run just like that.

The upgrades you can buy are almost exclusively extended time for the various powerups, which isn't that interesting.

Unlocking everything is way more time-consuming than it has any right to be, especially since you'll just be doing the same thing for hours on end, with very little variation to keep things interesting.

Missions are too often dependent on luck (getting 3 of a specific powerup in a run for instance), and you only ever have three active missions at a time, meaning you will only be able to make progress for those three missions until you get new ones (with a few exceptions).

The "buddy time" minigame activates on its own, and can make you miss a mission critical boss or powerup. Also, if you activate a friend's ability just as the minigame starts, the game will glitch out completely. Only pausing and then unpausing made it go back to normal, except the controls stopped working until the run ended.

As good as the music is, there's not enough of it, which soon made it repetitive.

The store page says "Level up and customize your 80’s room", which is a bit misleading since you don't get to choose the furniture yourself, instead it's just automatically placed when you obtain something for the apartment.

The "floor is lava" sections feel oddly balanced, and can sometimes be nearly impossible due to the "floaty" jumps. You can press down while in the air in order to descend faster, but this can arbitrarily make you go down through platforms and in this case into the lava. It seems to just happen randomly.

More control of the jumps (holding the button for higher jumps) would alleviate the above issue. Double jumping also sometimes (somewhat rarely) doesn't work even if you've touched ground between jumps.

The bouncy platforms are just annoying.

review:
Top Run is a fairly standard runner that doesn't really do anything to set itself apart from other runners but is decent fun if you like this type of game. The main selling point is the 80s aesthetic, with lots of neon and cheesy synth rock and pop culture references. For the most part I think the game looks pretty good, although until you get used to it some platforms don't stand out and tend to blend into the background. Also, you occasionally trigger "buddy time" where you control your dog companion for a chance to acquire more pixels (the game's currency) and those scenes are almost offensively ugly.

I often found myself getting frustrated at first, such as when "the floor is lava" is triggered while I'm in mid-jump and can't possibly get to safe ground, or when I'm about to kill an enemy that counts towards a mission goal only to have "buddy time" trigger before my projectile hits the enemy. Like most runners, though, I eventually got a "feel" for when these events are likely to be triggered and was able to avoid repeating those scenarios.

Speaking of missions, you can get XP and raise your character's level by accomplishing tons of missions with simple goals like "Kill X amount of Y enemy" or "Rescue X friend Y times". I appreciate mission systems like this as they force me to use certain strategies during my runs, and they certainly get more challenging as you progress. They are finite, though, so you will eventually reach your max level with some patience. The pixels you earn during gameplay can be spent on skins for you and your dog (in a nice touch, your skins come with different buffs), extending the effective time of powerups, and allowing you to trigger pixels being worth double (and eventually triple) after a certain distance is run. You also unlock a more difficult mode (where all pixels are worth double), a mode where you get infinite projectiles (that normally recharge very slowly), and a couple of different backgrounds (the vaporware one is the least cluttered and easiest to navigate, in my opinion).

To me, a good runner needs to have the following:
- A reason to play repeatedly (unlockables, stat boosts, etc).
- The sense that it's cheap and unfair at first, until you learn the game's nuances and use its systems to your advantage.

Top Run has both of these. I enjoyed the consistent sense of progress I felt as I unlocked features and buffs (and in another nice touch, kept adding stuff to my apartment until it was downright luxurious), and it was satisfying to learn strategies to use against certain enemy types and hold on to certain friends to use against the Prism. It doesn't reinvent the wheel, but I had enough fun with Top Run to stick with it for all the achievements. If you like runners, you can get this one cheap when it's on sale and have some fun with it.

review:
Nexomon: Extinction is a love letter to classic monster-catching RPGs, but with a sharp edge, self-awareness, and a surprising amount of narrative depth. Developed by VEWO Interactive, the game proudly wears its Pokémon inspirations on its sleeve, but quickly sets itself apart with a bolder tone, a massive roster of unique creatures, and a world that isn’t afraid to confront darker, more mature themes. Released on Steam and various other platforms, it arrives as both a nostalgic throwback and a genuine attempt to modernize the genre’s formula. What starts as a seemingly lighthearted journey into monster taming soon reveals itself to be a layered story about survival, rebellion, and the ethics of power.

The game opens in the wake of a great catastrophe—the fall of humanity’s once-thriving civilization due to the rise of powerful Nexomon tyrants. You step into the shoes of an orphan in a world where the balance between humans and Nexomon is fragile at best. Within minutes, you’re thrown into danger, conscripted into the Tamer’s Guild, and swept into a plot that is far more ambitious than typical genre entries. What stands out immediately is the tone: while it retains the whimsical charm of colorful creatures and fantastical locales, the writing is packed with dry humor, biting sarcasm, and fourth-wall-breaking commentary. Characters constantly poke fun at tropes, question your decisions, and comment on the absurdity of certain mechanics. This self-awareness adds levity, but also helps the game stand apart from the very franchise it emulates.

The monster designs themselves are a highlight. With over 380 Nexomon to capture, the game offers an impressive range of elemental creatures, from the adorable to the intimidating. Unlike some of its genre peers, Nexomon: Extinction avoids the issue of filler creatures—most designs are memorable, creative, and feel like they belong to the same artistic universe. Evolution is handled through traditional leveling, and each Nexomon comes with a tight move pool that makes combat feel more strategic than it initially appears. Elemental weaknesses are more complex than the typical rock-paper-scissors approach, and battles often require you to think several turns ahead. Stamina replaces the traditional PP system, and managing it becomes a key tactical decision—especially in longer fights, where even your strongest creatures can exhaust themselves quickly if used without restraint.

Combat is fast-paced and challenging, especially compared to similar games that tend to handhold or pad difficulty with grinding. You’re encouraged to swap Nexomon frequently, use status effects, and take advantage of terrain bonuses. Boss fights—particularly against the powerful Tyrant Nexomon—are legitimate tests of skill, not just level checks. What’s more, the game has no shortage of content. There’s a robust main story, dozens of side quests, hidden vaults, legendary creatures to hunt, and dynamic world events. Wild Nexomon scale in difficulty based on your progress, which keeps exploration relevant and engaging throughout the entire playthrough. This design choice does away with the traditional early-game “trash encounters” and makes the world feel more cohesive and alive.

Visually, the game is bright, crisp, and charming. Its 2D sprite art and colorful environments are reminiscent of handheld RPGs from the Game Boy Advance era, but polished for modern systems. The animations during combat are clean and snappy, while the world map is diverse and beautifully illustrated. From volcanic wastelands to snowy peaks and deep forests, each zone has its own biome and Nexomon pool, encouraging exploration. The soundtrack complements the world well—catchy battle themes, ambient town music, and tense Tyrant encounters all heighten the atmosphere without overpowering it. While it doesn’t boast cutting-edge visuals, the art style is cohesive and packed with personality.

The narrative is a genuine standout. While it begins with a fairly typical “young hero joins an organization to save the world” premise, it quickly deepens with themes of betrayal, systemic corruption, moral ambiguity, and personal growth. The supporting cast—particularly your snarky sidekick, Coco the talking cat—is entertaining and often hilarious, but also capable of delivering weightier moments. Your decisions don’t drastically change the story’s outcome, but the game constantly offers small moments of choice, sarcasm, or rebellion that make your protagonist feel less like a silent observer and more like a grounded character in a chaotic world. The story doesn’t shy away from showing the cost of war between humans and Nexomon, nor does it ignore the darker implications of taming powerful beings to impose order.

There are a few rough edges. While the game is challenging, the lack of a traditional experience share can make level grinding tedious, especially if you prefer to rotate a full team. There are moments where difficulty spikes unexpectedly, particularly in boss fights that seem overtuned unless you’ve over-leveled. Additionally, although most side content is engaging, some fetch quests feel like padding, and there’s room for improvement in the pacing of certain mid-game segments. Still, these flaws are minor in the context of the overall experience, and most players will find the challenge rewarding rather than discouraging.

Nexomon: Extinction is more than a clone—it’s a reimagination. It takes the foundation laid by monster-taming classics and injects it with personality, humor, and modern design sensibilities. With a rich world, clever writing, satisfying combat, and a genuinely compelling story, it stands tall as one of the best indie entries in the genre. It may not have the name recognition of the giants it draws from, but in many ways, it succeeds where they’ve grown complacent. Whether you’re a nostalgic fan of old-school monster-catching games or someone looking for a sharper, smarter twist on the formula, this is one extinction event well worth surviving.

still these flaws are minor in the context of the overall experience and most players will find the challenge rewarding rather than discouraging nexomon extinction is more than a clone it s a I love pinball games; apart from break outs and 2D space shmup's and maybe tower defense games  they are  among my  favourite arcade games. If I had my way and had enough money I'd open up a pinball parlour with real pinball machines liberally sprinkled with all the famous  cabinet games like Space Invaders, Star Wars, Asteroids and, not forgetting  Donkey Kong etc and create an environment on the lines of Flynn' s Arcade from the movie TRON.  Sadly, that will never happen as I don't have the resources or the space.  So, I've settled for digital pinball games, of which I have many,  having bought most of the big name  pinball collections and single titled games  via Steam, some via GOG, several hard copies and  some  abandonware titles like 3-D Ultra Pinball: Creep Night and it's compatriots (Thrillride & The Lost Continent).   When I saw that Pinball Universe was on sale for 90% off  I bought it without a though.  Considering  Zaccarina Pinball,  Malzbie's Pinball Collection , Pinball FX 2 & 3,  Pinball Arcade and it's companion Stern Pinball Arcade ALL include at least one or two free tables and  their DLC content  most of the collections price their  extra tables   is cheap enough to purchase   three to five excellent pinball tables (depending on which collection you are buying for) and double that when they are on sale for  the price of this game, I think  it's appalling that the developer is asking £15.49 for just two mediocre,  but functional tables.  They are reasonably constructed, the ball physics are okay and the odd   animation is okay;  but,  its still not good enough for the price.  

Plus, there are other collections  such as Pinball HD Collection (despite its odd keyboard bindings and is oddly by  the same developer of   Pinball Universe) is the same price as this title when not on sale but has fifteen far superior tables.   For that alone, I really cannot recommend Pinball Universe at its present price point.    Game play wise its sub par to any of the ones I've mentioned above despite the  positives I've previously mention  (e.g. ball physics etc), including  the developers better HD collection of fifteen excellent tables.  That said,  the tables  are functional even though on my first attempt my first three balls  went straight down the drain  without ever hitting  any flippers; though I soon realised I needed to actually move the flippers when the ball was approaching to just about kiss the ball and thus keep it in  play. Once I'd done that I was able to keep the ball in play until I got fed up and ended the game.  Several more short attempts  felt as lack lustre as the first time I played, so again it's not a game I'd recommend.

That said, if it's on a good discount, like  it was when I purchased it at 90%, then it's  just about middle of the road and 'maybe' worth buying. I'd say it's a good starter pinball game for  novices only and is the reason I didn't give it a thumbs down.  If there was a third  neutral option that's where I'd actually  put my vote.  Sorry OOO Gameprom this is so  poor compared to your  Pinball HD collection, both games were released on the same day back in 2016.  I don't understand why you would release this for the same price as your much superior  HD collection that includes 15 decent pinball tables?

Mini Countries is a transport game like Industry Giant or Transport Tycoon in a form of logical puzzle game. You need to transport various goods to towns or factories, but each town, factory or warehouse have only a limited number of connections. Mini Countries presents this in a nice simple, but completely sufficient graphics. Variety of loggical transport puzzles are presented in the form of mini countries, which adds to charm.

Under normal circumstances, this would be a great game. However, Mini Countries is as much a logical game as it is a clicker game. You don't just connect everything in a logical grid, you need to transport goods to a places that are not directly connected. This is done in a purely manual manner, you need to click every single good and select destination every time you want to transport anything. And you will be doing this a LOT due to the very limited number of connections. And the more cities are on the map, the more goods you need to transport into factories, the more clicking you need to do. Mini Countries does not keep me busy thinking about my grid, it keeps me busy by having to click on goods before cities revolt due to lack of a supply.

Dev seems to realize this issue and there is a roadmap with (unspecified) automatization. So put this into watchlist and wait.

This game ends up being more about micromanagement than strategy.

I wanted to like this, as a fan of Mini Metro and similar games. The concept is good: connect cities and resources together so that everyone gets what they need. Unfortunately, the strategy of placing buildings and connecting things doesn't seem to have that much depth. As long as every town is connected to each resource with some path, it can work. The difficulty comes in actually sending the resources where they need to go, which needs to be done manually whenever a resource isn't directly connected to a town.

Since the limited connections prevent you from giving each town a direct connection to all resources, you inevitably have to send things between the towns and storage buildings to get them where they need to go, and it's frankly tedious. It's easy enough to pause when there's a lot of demand and direct everything as needed, without much danger. But that isn't really fun.

Worse, towns have limited storage, and when they are full, they won't accept anything, even the resource they're currently demanding. Paris needs one wheat? Well you can't send them any because they already have cows, sugar, wood, and stone. So you need to send all of the wood away so it can receive that single wheat. And then it asks for wood.

It sounds like there are plans to make the sending of resources less tedious in a future update, but as is, I don't really enjoy this game, as much as I hoped to.

I really wanted to like this game. I found the concept and the visuals to be very appealing. I thought that this would be a nice, relaxing game with a small amount of challenge.
Unfortunately, the gameplay is quite frustrating. Before the first updates, the game's difficulty quickly surged after a few levels, an issue that the developer announced would be soon adjusted. Unfortunately, even after these updates (v1.1), the game continues to be too difficult - impossible, really - to progress.
First, once multiple connections are made to various cities, storage facilities, etc., the routes get very tangled and confusing. It becomes very difficult to identify which roads connect to which places and when there are precious seconds to get resources to a city, time cannot be wasted thru trial-and-error to remember which routes to get items to their needed destinations. 
Second, even in easy mode, it is still quite difficult to advance through the countries. Although easy mode adds a plethora of roads, storage, etc., these do no good when a city demands nothing but a single resource (fish, grapes) that is not being produced because it is out of season. This issue becomes exacerbated once factories unlock and the out of season raw materials are also needed to make luxury goods. There is nothing one can do but watch the scenario fail because the item(s) simply cannot be produced before the timer runs out. review:
Its clear where this goes.
It is a Mini Metro with economy building by distributing resources instead of people.
Pretty much exactly what Train Valley does.

[u][b]Introduction[/b][/u]
There is a campaign with different levels that ramp up in difficulty by gaining more complex distribution needs and more cities as you go.

It looks solid if you like the style, gameplay mechanics are well refined, but it lacks content, replayability and longevity.
Im coming to that in the next paragraph, [u]so take this positive review with a grain of salt and consider me standing yet undecided.[/u]

[u][b] The core problem[/b][/u]
My main gripe with it is the lack of modes and thus longevity or replayability.
Basically if you played a level, there is no need to replay it.
Where Mini Metro shines with tons of interesting modes and difficulty levels, this one is completely barren in that regard.
No highscore hunt, no endless mode, no reverse mode or anything the like.
Due to the similarities the developer could easily transfer mode ideas from Mini Metro, tweaking it a bit here and there so it works with the mechanics and then implement it.

Otherwise i see not enough content at all right now.
Since it has a limited amount of levels and no random map generator, its content is severely lacking.

[u][b]I suggest two things to do:[/b][/u]
1.) Implement more open modes into the game like highscore hunting (howm any citizens can you gain before your distribution fails), endless mode or anything mong those lines.
This would need the levels to get open access to buildings and techs, but this shouldnt be too much of a problem.

2.) A random map generator, where an algorithm creates a map randomly with a preselected set of starting resources (or automatically selected) and you play on that map with open access to all buildings and techs.
Basically highscore mode with random maps.
This would ask for more implementation effort but create infinite replayability.


In that term, this game functions a lot like Train Valley 1 or 2.
However, Train Valley offers a lot more replayability and expansive gameplay to offer longevity, as does Mini Metro.

Of the 14 offered levels in Mini Countries it took me 15 Minutes to complete 4.
And i wont replay those levels because they only take you that long to complete and there is no difference to be had.
I ask, why would i replay them? To gain a higher score? Not possible because the level outright stops when i reach the goal (like 500 citizens).
To play differently? How? I am only getting the same buildings and resources for that level and the same amount of cities.
The only difference when replaying a level is where cities spawn.



Later levels become more expansive and offer deeper gameplay. 
However because every level has a preset condition on what can occur, what buildings will occur for me to build and so on, it is the same experience no matter how often i would play that level.
With alternative gamemodes that are open and allow me to scorehunt and see how long i can manage to do it, this would already change.
But the above two suggestions are a must to provide any content, as i am not seeing how more levels with the current limitation is in any way interesting.
It would just artificially stretch content for a limited time, but then still stops.
Where i come back to games like Mini Metro to play a few hours on only one level for a better score, i dont do this with Mini Countries.

[u][b]Conclusion[/b][/u]
Therefor, this remains a sceptical review and recommendation. 
Im yet undecided on whether to refund for now and see where this goes or keeping it and...well also see where it goes, for better or worse.

Keep in mind that it is severely limited in content, replayability and longevity and does not offer any other mode besides a prescripted campaign.
A shame, as the gameplay concept is actually really good.

But if you look at my playtime and think "why is that person already creating a review", then my answer would be: 
"Because with that playtime of roughly 15-20 minutes i already finished 1/3 of the game, didnt get any challenge and that 1/3 of the game wont be ever replayed by me because there is no reason to do so, there are no other modes giving me an incentive, there are no difficulty levels to choose from making those levels harder or more complex on my next try and there is nothing giving me an incentive to retry later levels as well."

I was actually surprised to see it pop up as a released game and feel like it would be rather a fit for early access, as it feels like it is not ready or finished.

I will play around a bit later and find out whether it ramps up enough to provide enough for me to keep it. 
As i keep promising games normally.

Surprising I stumbled upon this page by going down a rabbit hole looking for a puzzle game that could entertain me without requiring me to spend most of my time trying to figure out the puzzle/strategy in order for me to complete it. I bought this game purely based on first looks and watching the developer play a bit of it on his live stream before I decided to just jump in and try in on my own. 

Honestly, I was surprised by the way it looked first right off the bat and how the music and design were clean and refreshing from the start. Reminded me of the puzzle game The Witness on the first loading screen of just the background and music drawing you in before thrusting you in a game where you use your wits to figure out what to do. Though, this game did start with instructions which made it easier to understand on certain parts. Even with the Instructions I got, it was neat to learn things that the instructions didn't go over completely (like the fact that you can connect storage units to each other). However, I thought from the first levels it would be a repetitive process until I hit later levels where cities would pop up more and more mechanics were added. Nearly lost my mind trying to find a new strategy for different levels. 

So far I'm halfway through the game and I love it a lot. It's a nice game to make my brain think but not to much where I hurt myself and I can unwind after work. Though it might not be for everyone, I would recommend giving it a try to see what you can come up with and see the clean and refreshing indie design that you don't get to see often with most strategy games. 

Though I am do want to see if the developer will branch of to other continents in the future which would be interesting to see, especially since it's a one-man operation making me respect the man a lot and I hope he will continue making games while still taking care of his older ones. Honestly want to see another Eric Barone in the making.

Inquisition is a labor of love, and it shows. However....

I have so many gripes with this game that i'm litterally grinding my teeth about it. The begining of this game took 15 hours longer than it should have, by the sole fact that the EA store app has forced its way to be a REQUIREMENT to play the game, and as with everything EA touches, it is a massive pile of shit. Over at LEAST 70 crashes total. Corrupted save files. Infinite loading screens. Skipped dialog. Missing Essential NPCs. the list could go on for hours.

Then we get to the gameplay. Holy shit. WHY AM I ONLY ABLE TO HAVE 8 ABILITIES?! one of my favorite aspects of the last two games (besides the story and allies) was my ability to mix and match my spells to be extremely dynamic. instead im forced to choose 8 favorites instead of building combos out of spell interactions and ability clashes. because of this, i slowly came to hate playing my build due to the strictness of allowed abilities. speaking of being dynamicly lacking! the camera oh my GODDD. the first two games had a better camera and they came out nearly a decade before. i know that with making maps more vertical you have to change how the camera works, but i cant belive how clunky it is. and verticality? inquisition,  i know your happy with yourselves for introduciing a jump button, but you really REALLY arent a platformer, stop trying to be a platformer, it makes me want to tear out my eyeballs. if i have to turn the camera around to make my character walk in a direction and youre wanting me to balance on a beam and then hop on an uneven surface that will make my inquisitor glitch halfway into the floor, all to find out that the chest at the end of the room only has a common hat and a chantry candle stub, it makes me want to throw my PC into a river.

on the topic of story, there were a lot of beats i liked, some that made me stew in rage, but overall i liked the inquisitors arc. the villains are unbeliveably dumb and mustache twirly tho. I'm not the best at reviewing stories, but in the end, a lot about the lore developments didnt sit right with me. especially with how they handled the Qunari.

the best part of this game for me has to be the characters, i love the main cast. their characters are endlessly charming, especially when the bicker like Varric and Cassandra. The romance was fun, but i feel like they fell a bit flat.

To conclude. Good game with too many hang ups for me to fully recommend to newcomers to the series. if you want to get into dragon age, don not start with this one. start with origins. i know its rough going back to older games, but its worth it.

review:
This is a tough one because it's not terrible but there was SOOOO much that it needed to be better. Played this game years ago on console and at first I was like "This is awesome" mainly because I figured the avenue of player choices both in this game and from previous games would be large.

In reality however it's completely different, a lot of the choices from Dragon Age Keep, where you are able to craft the story you want, have little to no effect outside of MINOR dialgoue about said character and or events. I remember I created two completely different imports and it felt like I got the same one both times, the only actually differences were end game results of origins and DA2.

And then you have the Frost engine EA forced them to use. GOOD GOD. This is absolute garbage bro. I mean literally. It's the engine they use or used for games like fifa, madden, 2k, etc. It's not designed for large scale open world rpgs with so many moving parts. It stops the majority of modding outside of simple things like changing variable for fetch quests or so on. 

Gameplay is fine, they learned a little more with action rpg fighting and it feels a little better. Kinda bummed at the lack of customization you have when it comes to skills and the fact that the ability trees feel so empty just doesn't fit the vibe of the past two games. It's just boring in all honesty. Later you get access to specializations, it's only 3 per class this time. Not terrible but again it's only doing so much to help the already bare bones leveling system. Even your companions don't have custom specializations anymore which I thought was lame.

The war table aspect was also just poorly done. You have 3 main advisors who do stuff for you, and you can aquire agents to help their time to completion shortened. Cool. What I think would have been better is being able to attach say a companion or a special ally you gain like say Isabella and you get better results or some kind of buff to it. It felt very limited for a function that's essentially you telling your forces what to do.

Companions also feel like they could have done more. Some scenes that specifically play out in romances, such as Blackwall bringing the inquisitor to where he took his identity and finds the Warden Constable's badge, felt like they could have been used in high friendship scenes than just romance. Another example is Josephine only being able to get a small ship with her house sigil on it as a romance gift. The other part of it is I feel like we could have had MORE companion options. For instance your telling me Varric is keeping tabs on his friends from Kirkwall but doesn't think they would be of use to the Inquisition fighting the world? Your telling me if Allistair was king, he wouldn't be a more prominent figure in the story than just a war table action and brief cameo at Redcliffe.

That is essentially what you can expect from Inquisition. It starts great, you get into it, and then you start thinking "Wait why didn't they do this or that." for the rest of the time you play.

review:
This review is long overdue, for many reasons. 
For a sequel continuing an overarching story spread out across different regions and entirely new characters- it stands strongly enough on its own to be a solid launching point into the series, like it was for me. I initially played this game when it first came out on the ps4- about a decade ago. 
I was immersed in the massive maps of secrets and quests to find and complete, the cast of characters you can recruit to your cause and potentially romance- this game has a good balance between action, strategy, and a decent enough story. 
I was both impressed with- and annoyed by- the romanceable characters having their own preferences to who they can be romantically entangled with( Dorian, I'm looking RIGHT AT YOU). It did make it feel unique, playing as an elf that is into, well, everyone, anddddd most of the characters finding my character about as appealing as a wet paper sack in a rainstorm meant to carry potatoes- in other words, no appeal whatsoever. I don't think any other game has successfully made 2D rejection sting quite as much as trying to romance the dashing, sassy mage, only to be firmly rejected because of what ISN'T between my legs. 
That being said and all jokes aside- romance is done right in this installment. 
You get to learn more about the characters and if you're careful with your words and choices, you can easily befriend or alienate your rag-tag team members. 
The banter between some of the characters while roaming around the map is- without a doubt- highly entertaining. If you haven't put together a party of characters who can hardly stand each other just to see what shit they talk to each other, you're playing wrong. 
The story overall is decent. If you happen to play a lot of rpgs, its fairly easy to predict what will happen- but even i wasn't prepared- mentally or emotionally- for the betrayal that came with FINALLY securing the ONE romance I cared about. That betrayal cut me so deeply, I STILL remember it, a decade later. I may have gotten the most recent installment JUST for closure from this one particular nasty, festering wound of distrust and downright rage for the end of this game. Justice will be mine, Solas, one way or another, you pompous little shit. (The game is literally a decade old- if you're just now jumping on the bandwagon, welcome, but i am ultimately doing you a favor here, trust me)
In short, if you like combat, engaging storylines and characters that you love but also want to throttle a little- dive on in. There's more waiting in the next installment, and I'm sure you'll see a review for that one much, much sooner than a decade after the release- at least from me. 
P.S. Solas, you may have broken my heart, but I will break your face in the next one.

review:
So my review is more geared towards players interested in her play style. As far as looks go we can all tell she looks pretty like the rest of the DOA female cast so I'm just going to skip any reviews on her appearance. If you were also extra interested in her because of her Aikido style and thought she might play like Aoi from VF then read on my friend. 

As a fan of the Virtua Fighter series I was definitely interested when this DLC character was revealed to also be an Aikido user. Aoi was one of my favorite characters from VF so naturally I was interested, as Aoi was also an Aikido-practitioner. After some thinking I finally gave in and shelled out the cash to get her. Now after about 20 minutes of going through her command list and doing some fights against the AI in versus I have the following impressions:

The Good:
She really does play somewhat like Aoi which was a pleasant surprise for me. A lot of her basic punch and kick strings are very similar to Aoi's basic punch and kick strings from Virtua Fighter 5 Final Showdown. The following attacks looks particularly similar to Aoi's with the same input commands:
- P, K
- P, P, P
- her down + forward diagonal kick (3K)
- K, K
- 2k (down kick)
She also has a unique throw move that can be tagged on to the end of some strings. For example if you input 
6P, 6T(forward + punch followed by forward + throw ) she does a punch followed by a throw which can apparently beat out a lot of other attacks and can catch opponents off guard. Now moving on...

The bad:
Okay so I got her because I was hoping for a fighter similar to Aoi, and in some ways I got exactly that. However, to my disappointment, she also feels simpler than the version of Aoi in VF5 Final Showdown. She essentially got some more flashy DOA-like moves but lacks some of the versatility tools of Aoi that made Aoi feel special in VF.

First of all, she does not have access to a kick after the third punch. So this means she does not have a P, P, P, K  or a P, P, P, 2K. In VF Aoi's P, P, P, 2K could be cancelled by holding guard right before the kick command's animation executes completely (I don't have the frame data but the idea is you hold guard at the start of the leg sweep animation). That I thought was an interesting mechanic as basing on whether you hit confirmed with the first attack you can decide to follow through with the full string or cancel at the last second. So the idea is that if your opponent blocks the first attack and continues to block all subsequent attacks up to the final kick, then the final kick is unsafe, meaning the opponent has guaranteed punishment if he/she executes properly. However if you do cancel the final kick then you are safe from retaliation and the game goes back to a somewhat neutral advantage state. This added some level of skill to playing Aoi.

This leads us to the next tool kit that Aoi has which Tamaki is missing: cancel-able attacks. Aoi has quite a few other moves that has this cancelling property besides the one mentioned above, namely 6P, P~ (2nd P cancelled by holding guard before it's initial animation ends), 66P (dash punch, an elbow strike which can be cancelled), P, P, 6P, P (last punch can be cancelled). Aoi always had these moves, but in VF5 FS additional movesets were added which allowed Aoi to follow up her cancel animation with 2 attacks: a throw or a kick. None of this is possible with Tamaki as she has no cancels in her moveset. 

Tamaki is also lacking quite a few of Aoi's P+K attacks. A few of Aoi's most recognizable attacks come from her P+K inputs, namely her forward low palm strike (43 P+K), her double palm strike (46 P+K), and finally her feint into a sideways palm strike to the opponents head (44 P+K). All of the above three moves can deal massive damage when landed as a counter, and is useful for the start up of damaging strings. Sadly none of these moves aside from the double palm strike is present in Tamaki's movelist (Tamaki's double palm strike is done by 7P if I remember correctly)

Finally Aoi also has a unique parry stance that can be entered by pressing back + all 3 commands in VF (4 P+K+G). This stance has a few interesting properties and can be used both offensively and defensively. Sadly Tamaki also does not have this.

So in conclusion, while I'm mostly happy with what I got, as Tamaki is still fun to play with and her moves are still graceful as expected of an Aikido user, I am a little disappointed that Team Ninja couldn't bring more of Aoi's tools into Tamaki's moveset considering their similarities as they are both practitioners of Aikido. I understand Tamaki is not Aoi, but I just feel like Team Ninja missed a chance at making Tamaki more interesting. I personally am happy with her, but I believe the price is a little high for a somewhat simple character. If you were attracted by her style than I would suggest waiting for a sale.

TLDR: Character looks nice and plays somewhat like Aoi from VF, which is a plus. Sadly Tamaki's moveset lacks some of the best parts of Aoi's moveset.

edit: After a little more time with her fighting against the AI she is actually pretty fun. Everything I said above still stands, and I still wish there was more to her kit, but her moveset is pretty fun in DOA's system. Still think she is a bit expensive, but I like her.

review:
I was really looking forward to [b]krystopia: nova's journey[/b] because [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/dohi64/recommended/1172170]krystopia: a puzzle adventure[/url] from last year was a lot of fun. I didn't have high expectations, just wanted more of the same, and while the two games are very similar indeed, I still ended up being disappointed, partly because it's a buggy mess and costs twice as much as the original for about the same amount of content, plus some other issues.

[b]it can be played on its own[/b] and it's basically the same thing gameplay-wise with the same puzzle types (mostly light redirecting, often with some timing, plus various symbols), and a few new ones thrown in for good measure. sadly, [b]they did away with the awesome diorama-like levels[/b] and it plays like your average 3rd-person point & click adventure now.

along with the dioramas [b]the solitary mood is gone as well[/b]. while the first game was mostly a puzzler with some narrative injected here and there, this is more of an adventure with an actual plot and characters. after finding your companion, you can [b]switch between the two of you at any time[/b], but it's only necessary in a handful of situations. there are also a bunch of npcs to talk to, so [b]the world is more lively[/b], but I preferred the 'solo explorer in an unknown world' setup, especially because [b]the characters are not great[/b].

the graphics still look good and the voiceover lady did a great job once again, but only during cutscenes and relic descriptions, as [b]none of the dialog is voiced[/b], only annoying grunts and random noises during [b]conversations that were clearly written by a 5-year-old[/b]. and here's another lazy thing: [b]there is zero difference between the two endings[/b]. same cutscene, same epilogue, no matter who you side with at the end.

collectibles (relics) for more lore and breakable pots for stress relief are present once again, and [b]rotating stuff works better now, plus right click can be used to zoom out[/b]. these are the only two improvements compared to the first game, and even right click can bug out. [b]saving anytime is still possible[/b], only by going back to the menu though, and some stuff (pots, half-solved puzzles) resets next time you continue, plus cutscenes have to be skipped every time. unfortunately, it's still better than most games where lazy and/or incompetent devs can't be bothered to provide a proper save system or at least frequent enough checkpoints.

not that these guys are flawless, far from it. the game is [b]a lot buggier than the first[/b] and there are still no separate volume settings and toggles, so one could mute annoying gibberish and maybe hear what little voiceover there is without the overpowering music. right click should also put away the currently examined object, a hotspot indicater wouldn't go amiss either, and x/y axis flip would be handy for camera controls, though panning around is 100% useless and unnecessary, so I guess there's not much point.

while it's mostly more of the same, including the [b]roughly 3-hour playtime[/b], it's also less in many ways and [b]definitely not worth full price, even half would be too much[/b]. make sure to wait for a major sale before picking it up and play the first game in the meantime, it's a lot better even at full price, but can be had for peanuts during sales.

This game is a continuation of Nova's adventure from the Puzzle Journey. Nova's character has expanded a lot more in here, and her conversations with her companions are so fun that I often check if there's more dialogue. The puzzles still revolve around the same mechanics from the first game, but there are a lot of variations in them that you never feel that you are doing the same exact puzzle. Interacting with the objects are so interesting because you're never really sure how they will react and what some of them are used for. You have to really think and use your imagination in playing this game because the puzzles are so creatively made in how they are supposed to be solved. Solving them actually gave me a sense of fulfillment. For a casual game it's so highly entertaining and immersive.
