review:
Pipe Mania is an ancient game from 2008.  It's a whopping 16 years old at the time of this review.  The game lacks support for the typical features of modern gaming PCs, hasn't been modernised or updated to run smoothly on contemporary machines.  The game looks and feels dated.  Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an old game.  This seems to have be lingering on Steam with an inflated price to try profit from abandonware.

This is a re-hash of 1989's Amiga game, Pipe Dream/Pipe Mania, but it's not copyright infringement, it looks like Empire Interactive are a valid copyright holder for it, so that's something.  That doesn't mean this is a great game... Pipe Dream has been rehashed so many times (heck, it's the hacking minigame in Bioshock), and this teenaged rehash isn't a winner.  You get some different skins/game modes etc but is that really what was needed to make a smash hit out of something that would today be more fitting as a Flash game?  Nope.  And I'm never going to tell gamers on Steam to spend money on glorified Flash games.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks.  There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display.  There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio, due to the age of the game, it predates the 16:9 widescreen gaming standard established back in 2006.  It's possible they're marketing this towards people using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game is being specifically marketed towards people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.  It's obviously not going to look right on a modern 16:9 gaming display.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 100,000 games for gamers to choose from, the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Pipe Mania is relatively expensive for an abandonware nostalgia gouge, at $4 USD, and it's not worth it.  The game is just too old, hasn't been modernised.  And as the old saying goes, you can't go home again.  This is also competing with over 11,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this paid product.

[b]3/10[/b]

Snake for two!

[b]What is it:[/b] A turn-based snake-inspired game, in which you play with two water snakes trying to collect all the pies. The snakes can grow and shrink, keeping their tail part in one spot, and they can also switch between two levels, above and below water. There are 4 different worlds, one with just the snakes and obstacles in their way, with focus on finding paths without colliding, one with fish that also try to eat the cakes, so you must hurry and block their path first, one with water spouts that automatically push you up from under water, if there isn't already a snake above, and one with ice that blocks you from switching levels. Also, the game is supposed to have co-op play, but I don't think it actually works.

The mechanics are interesting, and could make a great game, but this game is really bad.

[b]How hard is it:[/b] Very easy to easy.

[b]How long is it:[/b] 20 levels, 5 in each of the 4 worlds, for less than 30 minutes of playtime. Levels need to be played in order.

[b]Level design:[/b] Meh, none impressed me, seems like obvious designs showcasing the mechanics.

[b]Quality:[/b] Very bad. Non-configurable ZXC + arrows controls, with Z as reset right next to the main action buttons. No undo. No cloud saves, no achievements. Too few levels. One fixed resolution. Almost no other settings, just a sound toggle. Bad/inconsistent keyboard navigation. 45deg view forcing me to play with my head tilted. After I turned fullscreen on, the game always crashed on the Steam Deck, rendering it unplayable.

[b]Worth the price:[/b] No.

[b]Most positive aspect for me:[/b] Interesting mechanics.

[b]Most negative aspect for me:[/b] Everything.

Although I've only accumulated about an hour of playtime, I've put two separate play sesssions into [b]Loch Mess[/b] with two separate co-op partners. Both of these instances left me underwhelmed. We'd make marginal progress until we randomly happened upon a solution.

While other players might find a way to be more intentional about solving these puzzles, this didn't come naturally to myself or either of my co-op partners. Rather than feeling satisfaction about finding a solution, I usually just felt relief that the level in question was over.

review:
This is a small, polished football game that has a clear focus on fun, and succeeds right out of the gate. While most modern football games strive for more and more realism, Ballsy! goes the complete opposite way and throws out anything that would detract from the fun for realism's sake - and I'm very thankful for that.

This commitment is visible throughout the whole gameplay design: Matches are played by teams of 7 players on a field with no side-lines (similar to indoor soccer), no offside rule and no referee - resulting in an uninterrupted gameplay flow until a goal is scored. Menus are responsive and fast, there's no loading screens and no unskippable intros, so getting into a game is a matter of seconds.

The content is similarly lean, with 30+ national teams of varying football skill, but no player names (I'm not even sure if there's skill differences between the players). The two game modes are either a friendly, or the World Cup where a team progresses in knock-out phases towards the final. The simplicity is also reflected in the graphics, which is a throwback to older, arcade games (but runs so much smoother).

The big plus of the game is, of course, its gameplay. Controls are tight and fast to pick-up, yet take some time to master - but thankfully not because of their complexity (they have been trimmed down to only the core actions). There's not too many parameters like in modern football sims, but anything that's there is configurable. The AI is surprisingly well-made, both the opponent's and the one controlling the other members of the team that are off-ball. The opponent AI especially offers a decent challenge, with five different difficulty levels.

All these aspects make for a very fun, fast-paced arcadey game, with virtually no down-time. In more "realistic" football games I am met with constant small segments of downtime - intro, game loading, foul, players reacting, replay, substitution, and that's without all the gameplay-related downtime where possession of the ball changes much more slowly. Ballsy has none of that. And while commitment to realism and technical progress is admirable, I'm very happy that there's also games like this one that do away with all the cruft and focus on being a fun game without trying to also be a good simulation.

Technically, the game runs very smooth. I didn't notice any bugs, glitches or framerate slowdown whatsoever on Linux, even on a weaker machine. It gives a concentrated and polished impression - it knows what it wants to do, focuses on it and does it well. I recommend it to anyone looking for a fast-paced, fun football game and doesn't mind the lack of realism.

review:
I didn't play the game much before it died off, but looking through a lot of these replies, I don't see a specific issue mentioned much, if at all. 

The reason MMORPGS work in the first place is large player bases that can interact and play together. From making towns feel more lively, to allowing for raid dungeons, to building a sense of genuine player community, a large number of players helps these types of games IMMENSELY, if not makes them functional in the first place. review:
I don't have much experience with the genre to compare it to, as it hit its peak well before I started gaming, to talk about the gameplay in-depth. So, there's no need to focus too much on that. It's a lot like other classic platformers with a focus on perfection and figuring out the correct path. You're on a fairly strict timer that can be added to with oxygen tanks. I didn't feel there was a lot of time to take it in, because you dive into a frantic blitz to get through it before you run out of air, but that's in line with the difficulty-increasing tactics the genre's known for. 


The impressive part for me was the presentation and dedication to accurately recreating the experience it's inspired by. 

Once the game boots up, you're treated to a start screen and initial menu that is ripped right out of the 80s. From the color palette, to the sounds as you navigate, it all comes together look like something you'd have brought home and slammed into an early console. 

That theme sticks with it, too. As the level loads and transitions into the actual gameplay, it feels very "80s AAA". The environment takes a limited color palette and manages to make all the details pop and feel a lot more complex than what it actually is. Just like Pitfall, a little bit goes a long way in making the environment more than just an assortment of blocky pillars and switches. A testament to old school game design. 

The sound is phenomenal. Even as someone who isn't really into the genre, it was one of my favorite bits, and it felt exactly like something I'd expect to hear if I had a time machine and went back to a simpler time. 

This ties into gameplay, but the controls and movements are presented as accurately as anyone could get to an old school experience. You have four directions and two buttons to play around with, the astronaut moves with a sense of agility and floatiness that you'd expect from a certain plumber, and the level design makes the most out of the limited input options you have to make you feel like you're genuinely in control. 

Overall, I'm not into the tight time limit and what feels to be near-pixel-perfect path finding, but I'm not the target audience. It's a nostalgia dive that actually manages to properly recreate the experience and mirrors the handful of titles I actually have played from the 80s. That's not common. Many of the attempted recreations of past console generations nail some areas and completely miss the mark in others whether due to poor design or trying to insert modern concepts to widen the appeal. This attempt to recreate the early gaming experience actually nails it. 

If you're an older gamer who misses simpler times, it's great. If you're just curious, it's an accurate depiction of the era that inspired it. You won't feel cheated or as if you need to hunt down yellowing hardware and random cartridges to get the real thing.

review:
This is yet another in a long series of asset flip type amateur hour VR productions.  It's titled like it's some historical Jerusalem biblical stuff, but looks more like the american Southwest circa 1965 or something.  This seems par for the course with the rest of this guy's cheeseball titles.  

It looks to me like he grabbed some background asset packs off of unity's store or something, and then paired it up with 4 minigames that don't even belong together much less in the same title as "historical journey to Jerusalem", and then he copy pasted the exact same base "game" with a dozen or so scenery packs.  TA DA!  When do the big bucks start rolling in?  Do I get trading cards? I hear those are big bucks with the asset flip crowd! DIgital Homocide? Illusive Team?  You guys wanna hook a brotha up?

Anyway, this is garbage... I'm not even going to bother reviewing each title separately because they're all pretty much identical except for some of the scenery.  You get a handful of scenery to teleport around in but you can't interact with anything.  There's no quality control on the way stuff interacts with each other even so you get plants growing through walls, and you can easily teleport out of bounds and see unfinished stuff all over the place.  

Just about the most polished part of this are the minigames.  

There's a "Snake fighting" game which has nothing to with fighting, and yeah, there's a snake in it but it's not even as good as the mobile game from your old Nokia phone.  It looks to me like it was meant to be some kind of therapy program for doctors to use to help people exercise their necks after an injury (and it says "for neck exercise" on it when you start it up).  

There's another crappy hunting game with the worst bow and arrow mechanics you can imagine.  Think of the worst Bow and Arrow game from 2016 and then make it worse than that.  It's bad.  For some reason you're shooting deer in ancient Japan amidst sakura and bamboo.  

Related to this game is a fishing game in the same forest (but there's a nearby pond) and you have to spear the fish with this comically large trident like spear.  I've never seen anything quite like this but it's probably from a cheap unity asset pack.  

There was another "Snake football" game but I didn't bother with it.  It's probably another neck exercise game where you have to roll your neck around in circles to get the snake to move a ball somewhere.  I don't know, it's really not worth trying (though if I get bored maybe I'll come back and edit this).

So the tl:dr is this:  You're paying for a crappy asset flip that's not even fun OR educational.  Maybe the mingames would entertain a 5 year old while she sings "baby shark doo doo doodoo doodoo" or plays with her Elsa and Spiderman dolls.

Don't waste your money

review:
Fun little rogue-lite game. You try and escape a prison to go kill the king, finding the keys in the dungeons to rescue your men who join your party along the way. Certain sections have a lot of enemies and you will need their help. You will level up with experience along the way as you fight through enemy knights, but should you die, you lose your weapons and gained experience up to that point. You keep your money and levels though, making your next attempt that bit easier. The game map is random every time, ensuring endless re-playability. There are shops to buy weapons, and there are a couple of traps as well. Also you can co-op multiplayer.

Now the cons:
 
The game lacks a lot of polish. The game's combat tries to ape Dark Souls but ends up being floaty and spammy more than strategic. More work needed here to make the combat feel good with appropriate sound effects and to prevent the player from locking on and yet swing past an enemy. Critical backstabs and stealth works well, but the enemies can do that to you too, cutting short your game very quickly.
Map replayability is nice, but it also ensures that you get hopelessly lost with each new game. It displays where items are, to cut down on frustration - but you can't scroll through parts of the map off the window. It also often shows floors above you over the top of the map, obscuring your view and it also makes it look ugly and useless in places.
Additionally the random map generation sometimes places you in impossible situations from the start room (e.g. three knights and no weapons around to fight them), so some attempts are just doomed to go nowhere - which wastes the player's time.
Picking items up is a pain, as you often have to tap a few times and you pick up the wrong thing when items are bunched together more often than not.
Also there are glitches, particularly with your team just getting stuck. I had a large squad, and then an enemy glitched into a wall nearby. This confused my squad's AI until I could kill the enemy in the wall - and since I couldn't see him and my squad were useless - he killed me and ended my game prematurely.
There needs to be a toggle to control squad AI from aggressive to passive, as my attempts at being stealthy with a backstab were often thwarted by a team member who just went in all aggro.
The inventory screen is full of glitches.
Support for resolutions above 1080p is also lacking and the screen display may not fit properly on your monitor.
The game is also a bit short. You'll complete it in about 5 hours or less.

Hard to believe that the release version has so many bugs really. The game needs a lot of work to polish up the ugly bits, but there is a fun little game here if you can deal with the initial jank. I hope it all gets fixed as my first two hours were quite entertaining. The developer seems pretty active and open to suggestions.

Also reminiscent of "Koma" in terms of length, style and concept, just without the performance issues.

Another thing to point out, the developers were very friendly and responsive in the forums.
Black Chapter is not an RPG maker game, but made in Unity, for anyone who cares about this.

I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys games like the "Strange Men" series.

review:
Riding Seas is a simple racing game on boats, however the only way it really makes use of the water, seems to be that you need to dive below obstacles sometimes. You can/need to jump too sometimes, because of the way courses are built or to be able to take shortcuts. Otherwise it is a bit floaty, but not enough of a difference to really feel like its much different from normal street racers.

The game itself starts off without the option to change the resolution or turn on a windowed more or anything. Huge downside for me, I like my window and hate fullscreen.

Secondly the games audio is all sorts of wonkey. SFX changes all kinds of things, however even if you turn it all the way up, you barely hear any motorsounds, while the menu will blast your ears off. Incredibly unbalanced audio at that. So to be able to enjoy this without giving damage to your ears in the menu, you will drive a motorboat, without hearing any motornoises.

The game also seems like it would want to be a funracer, without actually being a funracer. There are no items, which makes it pretty weird to play, because it only uses a boost based system, which doesn't really need much input from the player. It also starts of waaaaaaay too easy, which makes it boring without any items until you get to the harder levels. The later cups get pretty hard, but mostly because you won't have enough money to buy better ships if you rushed through all the cups first try. Though I will say, that the last 3 cups are more of a challenge, even with a fully upgraded and bought boat.

So all in all, the game doesn't let you customize, is mute, boring to play, since there isn't that much going on aside from some traps. And while it looks and feels like a funracer, its a racer without any additional powerups or "fun" mechanics added to the monotone driving through the easy tracks. The later tracks are better, but also have these instakill traps that waste sooo much time that it simply says "get hit by it once and you need to restart to get first" that makes it harder, but really only feels annoying imo. 

Its also got camera glitches if you drive near walls, which is very disorienting sometimes and because you need to dive below bridges in some levels, you can't see whats coming in front of you until after you've passed it.

I can't really recommend it, I quickly did all the cups, farmed a bit of money inbetween to get the better ships and have no desire to keep on playing it after that.

review:
Turing Complete, available on Steam and developed by Levelhead Studio, is an ambitious and intellectually rigorous game that dares to teach the inner workings of computers not through lectures or text, but through actual hands-on construction and logic design. At first glance, it might resemble a puzzle game, but beneath the surface it’s a full-fledged educational simulator disguised as entertainment. For anyone curious about how computers truly work—from simple switches to a fully functional CPU—Turing Complete provides a comprehensive, interactive experience that is as challenging as it is rewarding.

The premise is simple but effective: you play as a small robot who awakens in a mysterious, abandoned alien facility where computers once reigned supreme. Rather than rely on exposition-heavy storytelling, the game introduces its narrative quietly, through environment design and small interactions, allowing the player to focus on the primary objective—learning how to build computing systems from the ground up. The robot acts as both protagonist and proxy learner, reflecting your own journey from digital novice to master logic architect. The story is largely minimalist, but the setting creates a curious backdrop that gives context and purpose to the increasingly complex tasks you're assigned.

Where Turing Complete truly shines is in its gradual yet uncompromising approach to teaching computational concepts. The game starts with basic digital logic gates—AND, OR, NOT—and quickly progresses to more complex circuitry, including multiplexers, decoders, registers, memory systems, and eventually a full CPU. Every component you construct must follow the real-world principles of digital electronics, and nothing is abstracted or dumbed down. As a result, players aren't simply memorizing how things work—they're building it and seeing it in action. You learn how to represent numbers in binary, how to simulate clock cycles, and how to move data through buses and address lines, all within a sleek, sandbox-like interface.

The design philosophy behind Turing Complete respects the player’s intelligence. It assumes that you’re willing to fail, retry, and explore. The puzzles don’t offer hints or simplified solutions; instead, they provide a goal—build a component that performs a function—and leave the how entirely up to you. This open-ended design leads to genuine problem solving and the same kind of creative satisfaction found in games like Zachtronics titles or SpaceChem. Yet, Turing Complete distinguishes itself by staying rooted in real computer science. When you build an adder or construct RAM, you’re not just completing a puzzle—you’re learning actual engineering principles applicable in both software and hardware contexts.

The interface deserves particular praise. It’s clean, intuitive, and surprisingly elegant considering the complexity of what it's managing. Visual cues clearly indicate the flow of electricity, the state of individual bits, and the behavior of circuits over time. The built-in tools for debugging, simulating clock speeds, and visualizing data flow are powerful and user-friendly, making even the most complex systems manageable with enough patience. Players can save and re-use their own components, leading to a layered design experience where you’re not just building solutions, but building tools to build solutions.

One of the most striking aspects of Turing Complete is the sense of empowerment it fosters. Many people use computers every day without the slightest idea of what happens beneath the surface. This game pulls back the curtain in a way that’s rarely attempted in mainstream media. You don’t just learn what a CPU does—you build one. And by the end, you understand why modern computing is both miraculous and incredibly logical. It’s not flashy, and it doesn’t rely on spectacle. The “aha” moments come from intellectual discovery—when a custom-built program finally runs correctly or a complicated memory circuit performs flawlessly, the satisfaction is immense.

However, it’s worth acknowledging that Turing Complete is not for everyone. The learning curve is steep, and there’s no traditional “gameplay loop” with immediate gratification. There’s no combat, no narrative twists, no flashy rewards. The satisfaction comes from understanding, not spectacle. Players looking for a relaxed or guided experience may find themselves overwhelmed or frustrated, especially as the game expects a level of persistence and focus that rivals real-world engineering studies. But for those who relish systems-based learning or who’ve always wanted to understand how their computer actually thinks, the game is a revelation.

In terms of replayability, Turing Complete offers a near-infinite sandbox. Once you've mastered the built-in challenges, the game provides a canvas for experimentation. You can build your own machines, design your own architectures, or attempt to optimize existing systems for speed and efficiency. There’s even a community-driven sharing system that allows you to see how others solved the same problems, offering new insights and design philosophies. This gives the game an extended life beyond its core curriculum, turning it into a kind of computational playground.

In conclusion, Turing Complete is a brilliant, meticulously designed educational experience that transforms the intimidating world of digital logic into something interactive, engaging, and deeply rewarding. It’s a niche title, to be sure, but within that niche it excels to a degree few games can match. It doesn’t just simulate computing—it demystifies it. For the curious, the patient, and the intellectually adventurous, this game is not just entertainment; it’s a transformative tool for understanding the foundation of modern technology.

review:
You have been abducted by aliens and now have to prove your intelligence to not get eaten. So you go on the awe-inspiring journey of constructing your own working computer from the fundamental building block of computing: the NAND gate.

Actually, you build two different 8-bit architectures: the very rudimentary "Overture," which compresses operations and operands into a single byte. And the much more flexible and powerful "LEG" that can process 4 bytes (1 operation, 3 operands) at once.

You then define your own assembly language to program your computer so it can solve various puzzle tasks, including the classic Towers of Hanoi. Some of the programming levels are arguably harder than any circuit construction level.

How the levels build onto each other is mostly well-thought-out didactically, but the learning curve is still steep sometimes, and the game's explanations can be very terse.

⚠️  I beat the game without prior knowledge of CPU design, only following in-game explanations - but with a firm grasp on logic and number theory (which definitely helped with two's complement). But if you go into this game with even less, you might have to read some additional explanations elsewhere.

Now, while Turing Complete is absolutely fantastic as an educational tool, as an indie video game it leaves [b]a lot[/b] to be desired. E.g., a puzzle/programming game like Opus Magnum by Zachtronics has a unique look and feel, a distinct aesthetic, and a great story that all fit together with the overall theme to create an immersive experience. Turing Complete is nothing like that at all and is instead [b]extremely[/b] bare-bones. It doesn't have to be overly fancy, but a few improvements (e.g., some interactive dialogue or different reaction portraits of our alien tutor) would already make a difference!

The game could also benefit from some quality-of-life improvements: many functions are only accessible via shortcuts, and corresponding UI elements are missing. This is very unfortunate and, IMHO, violates basic UI design principles (you first don't even know that those shortcuts exist!). Also, I sometimes broke my working solutions, which was frustrating. It would be very nice if one could easily reset to the last correct design without having saved the circuit before.

I’ve spent hours playing Hentai Furry 2 on Steam, and within that span, it managed to leave a strong impression. At its core, the game is a memory-based puzzle title that gradually increases in difficulty, presenting a surprisingly addictive challenge. As the levels become more complex, the incentive to push forward remains constant—driven in no small part by the provocative artwork that reveals more with each stage. It’s structured to reward progress with escalating visual content, transitioning from fully clothed characters to progressively more revealing images, culminating in full nudity. This progression system, while simple, cleverly ties gameplay completion to visual motivation.

The game features 40 levels in total, with the first half showcasing the characters in various outfits and the latter half stripping them down layer by layer. Despite the risqué premise, the puzzle mechanics themselves are solid. Completing each stage feels satisfying, not only because of the visual reward but also due to the inclusion of a built-in speedrun timer. After finishing a level, you're shown how long it took, which subtly encourages you to replay and improve your completion time. It's a basic but effective system that adds a layer of replayability.

One of the most surprising aspects of Hentai Furry is its price point. At just a cheap price, it delivers a level of engagement and polish that exceeds expectations for a title in its category. While clearly targeted at a niche audience, the game doesn’t pretend to be more than it is. It blends casual puzzle gameplay with adult-themed content in a way that’s straightforward, unpretentious, and—for those who enjoy both elements—oddly compelling.

TL;DR: Beginner friendly organic 3D modelling that's quick to learn. Only let down by no key rebind option.

Positives
+++ Extremely easy to use & understand. I'm an experienced 3D modeller and was right at home instantly, but I believe even beginners would also be up to speed quickly.
++ Great for very fast easy organic shapes.
+ Imports & Exports in OBJ for near universal compatibility with other 3D tools. Also imports SVGs, which is very useful.
+ Seems quite undemanding of hardware, so I'd be confident in running it on older hardware, maybe even laptops.

Negatives
--- [BASIC MAJOR FAILING] Default keybinds are bad, counter to some common popular 3D programs, and there is no key rebind option! There is no excuse for this. ***Please add rebind key options for ALL keys AND mouse operations*** (Missing Rebind options almost made this review a negative)
- Less suitable for mechanical shapes, though not impossible (SVG import helps) but I doubt most modellers would use this tool for that purpose.
- As a fairly niche tool video tutorials are few and far between, although the few that exist to a decent enough job explaining the basics.

Summary
If you like modelling organic shapes quickly with minimum fuss in a quick to learn program then this is for you. I'd say it's ideal for beginners to organic 3D modelling (excluding the lack of key rebinds). For experienced 3D modellers it's likely the quickest, easiest organic shape maker available at this low price.

It's also a fun tool for creative play to just launch and draw something quickly.

review:
My main experience of Marble Parkour was with the Switch release, as it runs better on there.
The better performance wasn't the game's saving grace, though. In-fact, it didn't even get a saving grace.

Pros:
-Music. Surprisingly, this game's OST is great...but not fire. The music sounds like those placeholder-type songs you would easily find within 30 seconds using Unity.
-Inspired by Marble Blast and Marble Madness. The style that the game creator were trying to go for is similar to Marble Blast.(Considering Marble Blast was based upon Marble Madness, I listed it) When making something like Marble Blast, it either results in a masterpiece (like Marble Skies), gets something or a few things right, or a fail. The Marble Platformer Formula is a hard style to work with.
-This Game Had Potential. If Marble Parkour got more time in the oven(and more play testers), it could have been a great game.

Cons:
-Physics. The marble falls a bit too slow and deaccelerates if you fall too far, and the jump height needs to be increased a bit.
-Level Design. There are too many tornados in one area and most of the time, it halts any progress. There's a heck of a lot of bumpers, actually, scratch that, MOVING BUMPERS?! The levels are too short.(In my opinion, anyways) The level design doesn't really reward quick players due to so much going on at once. (The tornados make it difficult to speedrun)
-Game Length. Just like the levels, this game is too short. If you're skilled, you can beat the entire game in an hour and still have enough playtime to receive your refund(Only applies if you played on the Steam release) If more difficult levels are added(or more levels in general), then the overall playtime of this game will certainly increase.

review:
Triversal is a super satisfying puzzle experience.  The music, visuals, and fx draw you in.  It reminds me of Tetris Effect, taking a uniquely simple yet complex puzzle idea and doing it in this chilled out style.  

You can just zone out playing this game, but the puzzles are still naturally satisfying to solve because of how they are designed.  They have a great tie to what I would consider real world physics so solving them is super satisfying because you kind of have an innate knowledge of what might and might not work as soon as a puzzle is presented to you.  Triversal ties into our seemingly uniquely human love to classify and explain numerical and angle phenomenon throughout our physical reality using mathematics, physics, and science. I view these elements as constructs we developed to make sense of the universe essentially.  I think it is a uniquely satisfying puzzle game because it ties in so heavily to that sort of built in knowledge but still presents a challenge to solve.  

They also have a cool mechanic where you collect coins as you solve the puzzles so it becomes a challenge of collecting all the coins while still solving the puzzle in as few moves as possible.  All these elements really work well together and create an awesome, immersive experience that you can just get lost in.

A fun little puzzle game, simple to understand and a lovely clean interface.  Click on up to three tether points to suspend your glow ball over the black hole.  Most levels are fairly straightforward, but then you hit one that stumps you for a few minutes as you try one combination after another.

I try to do the daily puzzle every morning, then one of the packs later in the day, and if I have some time on my hands there are the endurance modes for (potentially) infinite play.

There's a free demo available to try before you pay, so why not give it a go?

Edit: May 2024

The game has had a significant update a month or so ago, which has considerably increased the complexity of the puzzles.  For me, that's made it less fun - your mileage will vary.  Honestly, I would have preferred it if the new version had been released as a separate game - I would have bought it, tried it and probably decided I preferred the original and stuck to playing that.  As it is, I can't go back to the old version, and I've basically stopped playing.  I still recommend that you try it out though and see if it suits you.

review:
I've seen the first stream of this route and immediately saw too many bugs. I would have hoped the devs would have listened to feedback ( mine included ) from the Twitch live stream or the Train Sim Community Discord. Then again, I probably should have written my feedback over the DTG forums as it is the official place to provide feedback, I guess. I don't really feel that it would make a difference, but who knows.

Anyway, I'll start with the positive things I've seen on this DLC:

+ The route itself looks pretty nice. It is nicely detailed, generally quite a nice ambient to it, looks good.
+ The train services are rather appealing as there can be quite a bit of traffic at least not far from Hamburg. Had an RE service overtaking an RB at some point, that was quite cool really.
+ Good to see a freight-vocational Taurus, that's definitely a welcome addition. But don't fall for this just yet... see the negative part of it.

Unfortunately, I believe that's about it all for positives.

Negatives:

- BR 112:
1 - a great loco that I looked forward to see. Unfortunately, the major disappointment of this DLC. The exterior model outside looks quite OK. Some people pointed out it looks a bit strange, but maybe that is because most people are used to how a BR 143 looks like. I can be wrong about this, though. It looks OK to me at least.

2 - Sounds are a mess. They are completely unrealistic. Maybe I would be willing to accept it if at least the ventilator sounds were as loud and as accurate as the real one. The ventilators are possibly the most evident sound that one can hear on a BR 112 ( and even the BR 143, which suffers the exact same problem - sounds recycled? ) 

3 - The cab instruments are off proportions. The needle gauges for traction effort and speed are not accurate. The main pressure brake gauge is also smaller than it should. The train brake lever is too small ( the ball at the end of it is also too small ). The same with the locomotive brake handle. Please do make an investigation of what a cab of a BR 112 looks like. Even better, you could even take virtualRailroads' cab as an example! 

4 - The ammeter needle is not working properly. One power notch increases from 0 to 500 AMP. It should NOT do that. The same behaviour happens when using the dynamic brakes...

5 - Speaking of dynamic brakes, those are not even deployed unless you apply full train brakes. The 112 uses a blended dynamic brake with the train brakes, so the loco uses both dynamic and air brakes right from the 1st notch of train brake. 

6 - Passenger information screens are not manually adjustable like we can do on the BR 146 and some other rolling stock. Why is there a missing quality consistency on most of your work? I just can't understand it.

7 - Why doesn't the Ebula screen work for this loco? Again another lack of quality consistency... Yeah they are sort of useless at this stage, but the community already found a way to use it. At least make it working properly just like all other locos...

8 - The engine temperature is not simulated ( or is it? ) and thus the temperature indicator in the cab is not working.

9 - There's some more other minor bugs that should be looked into.

Now for the Taurus...

1 - Recycled horrible sounds. Sorry guys, at first try I get it, but at second try? No excuse. The Taurus tone sounds are very unique. Yours sound very fake, synthesised. 

2 - The traction effort display is in the incorrect display. It should be on the right side of the loco, where you've placed the Ebula.

3 - The AFB can get broken if you deactivate it while having the AFB lever at some position. The AFB needle remains on the position where you turned it off and it won't move from there anymore. The AFB needle should be reset to 0 km/h as soon as you turn off the system, or at least that's how I believe it works. 

4 - Not exactly sure if this is related to the Taurus but the car transporting freight wagons do not have tail markers when I drove a service with the Taurus leading. 

5 - There's possibly even more things I haven't looked around because for me, the loco is still not good enough to enjoy driving. Just like the first DB 182. A shame, really. The exterior model looks pretty good.

For a final note on this DLC: 

The included rolling stock is what really kills the experience on this. There's of course some silly bugs on the route but that happens, they aren't anything game breaking really ( unless of course there are some which can be game breaking, but I haven't found any... )

I would enjoy driving this route if the rolling stock provided would have at least some decent sounds and would have a good quality consistency like the previously released DB BR 101 - that loco really raised the quality bar to something you couldn't deliver on this DLC. Sad. Unless bugs are fixed, I won't be repurchasing this again. Refunded for now.

review:
This would be a great route. If it were done with a bit more care!

I am from Hamburg and I feel at home on this route. The stations look great and the buildings and landscape along the track are fine.
The scenarios are fun and the timetable mode provides a good variety including the BR101, although I would have liked to see an ICE around Germany`s busiest train station.

But there is this giant BUT

Besides a number of bugs that will hopefully get fixed sooner rather than later, like for example the BR112 constantly derailing when the emergency brake is applied (hardly avoidable when trying to master the PZB), the passengers and player having difficulty using the front door on the DoSto steering cab at Hamburg Hbf, the cab lights being reversed at the beginning of a drive and so on, the route is just absolutely dead.

It`s the worst at Hamburg Hbf, the biggest train station in Germany by Passenger numbers, that regularly has two trains behind each other at the same platform to cope with these numbers (which is actually simulated).
On most scenarios and timetable drives, my train was the only one in the entire station and there were maybe 20 to 30 NPC`s on all platforms combined. This is just ridiculous. Even in Scenario planner there are only 3 platforms available to fill with trains to make it a bit more bearable. Why cant you have some random AI trains at the unused platforms? I wouldn`t even care if they were completely stationary. Do anything to make it feel like this is an actual, real place with traffic...
And it`s not much better at the other stations along the line. Lübeck is a lot smaller but there should still be atleast one or two different trains visible.
Also there are way too few passengers. It`s not as bad or noticable as on the Bakerloo Line (where the station being entirely empty at Picadilly Circus at 5:30pm is apparently to be normal) but still I had runs with literally bot a single passenger boarding the train on the entire journey.

How can you waste so much work and potential like this? Its just sad that DTG managed to kill any kind of immersion like this...

review:
Lets start with the positives:
The route itself is decent, has some nice scenic areas with the usual sorts of details such as working PIS as well as some rather quirky easter eggs at Hamburg. Lengthwise is also fairly decent being 64km (38 miles) it's adequate for a moderate run.

The scenarios included are meh, but as with any other route released by DTG, I haven't really found any that exciting or challenging,  but that's about as much as I can positively say about it.

The negatives:
The DB 112 which is supposedly the new loco for this route is mediocre. Whilst the modelling itself isn't too bad, it's not the greatest that we have seen from DTG before. Whilst it is ok to drive, the overall sounds (which are taken straight from the 143) completely ruin the immersion for me, it feels dreary and very disconjointed.

The DOSTOS have absolutely NOTHING new about them. Whilst now we do have first class in the intermediate carriages they are the same old boring Gen 4 ones which have been used FAR too much within the German side of TSW content, DTG seriously need to stop using these and actually come up with something new and different for once. Lastly, the type used are NOT prototypically accurate for the route they run on. Complete and utter laziness is all I have to say about them.

The 182, nothing new about it apart from a different livery. Still feels awful to drive, poor acceleration physics and has really dodgy motor sounds. Again, was this the best DTG could do?


The freight wagons, still the same boring old Habbins, Laaers, Roos and Sggmrss we have seen before, nothing new or remotely interesting about them in any way.

The performance:

For the most part I was getting a good solid 60FPS, however the Hamburg area was stuttering really badly for me, and according to others, they also have the same issue too.


In conclusion is this worth £24.99?

Absolutely not


Is it worth buying it on sale?

Depends on what the discount is


Is it better than it's TS1 predecessor?

No

What's my verdict all round?

A decent route lacking any form of commitment towards new rolling stock.

review:
It's okay; it is a pretty route with many choices of trains to run services with, but there are some big flaws. The number one issue I have is that PZB is broken: 500Hz magnets do not work, and I have had the emergency brakes tripped while approaching a stop aspect even while adhering to the standard O-mode speed restrictions. This is to me unacceptable, as this should be implemented correctly in every German route they put out. Also, there seems to be some optimization issues when you are within 15km or so of Hamburg. During their showcase stream this was apparent, although they blamed it on poor stream quality, but for me on my machine it performs exactly as was showcased during their two preview streams of the route. 1001 Jigsaw Home Sweet Home Wedding Ceremony is a basic browser/Flash/mobile-app like jigsaw puzzle game.  Solve various jigsaw puzzles made up from images that the "developer" stole off the Internet and used without crediting the actual creators, making this plagiarism, as well as an asset flip and a cash grab.

An example of the stolen, uncredited/plagiarised artwork is [url=https://www.alamy.com/diamond-engagement-inside-of-a-heart-shaped-box-of-chocolate-truffles-with-red-roses-selective-focus-on-diamond-ring-with-soft-blurred-background-image273912394.html]"Diamond Engagement Inside Of a Heart Shaped Box"[/url], stolen and used without any apparent permissions or rights from Alamy/YAY Media AS.  Sure, the image rights may allow some stock images to be used without credit (although there's no reason to believe so in this case), and claiming credit for the work of others, as is happening here, is unethical, and the creative and intellectual bankruptcy going on here is unacceptable.

So what we have here is a basic jigsaw puzzle engine that's been skinned with a bunch of photos stolen off the internet and used without attribution.  The icing on the cake is the "developer" here has copy + pasted + reskinned this same asset onto Steam [i]a lot[/i]. 

The developer, Creobit/8Floor, has copy + pasted this game an insane SEVENTY SIX TIMES onto Steam with minor reskins... why cash in on one asset if you can cash in on multiple copies of the same game? Asset flipping begins at home! Here's a list of Creobit's copy + pastes of this asset:

There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players. Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

review:
As a fan of wayforward games, this feels like a cross between shantae and mighty switch force. 

it's first and foremost a puzzle platformer. You solve puzzle rooms using your hair whip and dash abilities. There are a few enemies, but they're really not a threat until much later levels, and even then they aren't really. The stage hazards are much more likely to kill you than enemies.

The game has 7 areas, of which 6 are playable right now. each area has 4 stages and a boss stage. Our protagonist, Repunzel is an android super battery or something, and for some reason has some sort of prehensile hair, like shantae from wayforward. You use your hair to grab enemies and throw thing, along with grabbing little boost icons, that will fling you in a direction. you also have a dash move that can be performed once in the air, and has a cool down on the ground. during the dash, you're invulnerable and damage whatever you touch. 

Throughout levels you collect little balls and memory disks. the balls increase your max health once you've accumulated enough of them, and the memory disks will give you a lore related image when you collect all 5 in each stage.

collecting memory disks is very easy, and most of the stages are really easy, with a few interesting stages here and there. the boss battles are where this game shines, aside from the second boss, kinda a snorefest. 

This is primarily a korean game by a korean dev, so the english translations will be a little rough here and there, and the voice acting is all in korean. I'm studying korean, so that's kinda why I got the game, one of the few steam games with actual korean voice acting, and a good amount of it too, though it seems like the 6th area doesn't have voice acting yet.

it's a fun puzzle game like mighty switch force, but without the switch gimmick and instead you focus on launching yourself around stages.

review:
Well... this game was surprisingly very nice.
For a while, Galaxy Tales: Story of Rapunzel was just another game in my Steam backlog. I thought it looked good and snatched it on sale when it got out of early access, but never got around to playing it. Now that I have played it though, I cannot believe how good it is.

Just like another reviewer on the game's store page, I also believe this game to be a mixture of Shantae and Mighty Switch Force, only with speedrun-esque features thrown in it. Galaxy Tales is mostly a puzzle platformer, with heavy emphasis on traversing through platforming hazards rather than fighting with enemies. In fact, it is very much encouraged to avoid unnecessary combat and focus on getting to the next checkpoint; unless for when you get to a bossfight of course.
While the game is fun, I do believe the basic gameplay principles get a bit repetitive if you play the game for long periods of time, especially since the game really overuses some mechanics. While Galaxy Tales keeps adding new hazards and enemies to keep the experience fresh through its 4~5 hour story mode, there's no denying that the main thing you're supposed to do stays the same: solve some puzzles, traverse hazards using the main character's abilities and get to the end. Though I do believe that by playing the game as fast as you can, like speedrunning it by skipping stuff or damage boosting through hazards, you'll have a much more fun experience. I recommend playing it in short bursts as well to avoid getting burnt out.

I also find the post-game content to be quite lackluster. While the idea of having a hard mode with modified, more challenging level layouts is pretty interesting, the game gives you no incentives to try and finish it. The main game has extra collectibles (golden disks) that unlock art explaining the events before the game starts, yet the very same collectibles have no value in hard mode other than raising your score. Not only that, there are no hard mode achievements either so you feel you don't really have a reason for playing this mode.
As for the minigames... there are no minigames. The levels in this mode only consist of chases where one death equals restarting from the beginning. Although the game does offer an achievement for beating all of them, it is not much encouragement.

Presentation-wise, Galaxy Tales looks great. Not only the art is simple yet beautiful (the main character being the highlight), but the animations are also oozing with love and care. You just have to pay attention to Rapunzel's action to see how the devs put a lot of work into them: From her idle animation to her facial expressions changing after doing certain actions. The music is also pleasant to listen to; although they can get a bit repetitive. Unfortunately, the number of music tracks in the game is very limited; to the point all of the cutscenes and special chase sections use the normal level tracks. This is very unfortunate as it damages the game experience to a degree.
The most surprising thing though, is that all of the cutscenes are fully voice acted in Korean. And not of the "so bad it's good" kind; the voice acting we have here is actually well-done. Complimenting the voice acting is the rather well English translation that only has a handful of roughness here and there. A look through the community screenshots section shows a lot of the usual jank of eastern games present in the early access version, so good on the devs for taking feedback seriously and fixing the English translation.



It is clear to me that a lot of love has gone into making this game. Despite some flaws, I ultimately found Galaxy Tales quite fun to play by going fast and trying to bypass hazards as much as I could. Your mileage may vary though, as the game doesn't feel very hard.

Elylah is tired of life. She and her bestie, Kathleen enjoy sucking off men. For reasons unknown, their clients haven't been receptive to their advances. She has stolen her father's "mystic keys", keys that'll grant them the ability to leave their island, and explore new realms -- perhaps, if her father's guard doesn't catch them first, get to the bottom of the Dreamers' absence.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
If it wasn't for the horrible "Caution" box, I'd call the titlescreen a work of art -- it features a wonderful, romantic painting. From "Preferences", you are able to adjust audio and display settings. "Help" brings up a written guide to the game's controls. The artwork is something to behold -- apparently, it was rendered using "Acrylics, watercolors and rough pastels." The artwork fumes with style, but it isn't nearly as clean or refined as typical, digital artwork. [b]Symphony of Delights[/b] boasts a wonderful selection of art, but some people may find it "crude" or undesirable. I think it's nice to see a novel not joining the hentai bandwagon. I feel as though I'm viewing pieces that belong in a retro RPG, or some dirty mag' from the 90s. The animations are jerky sometimes, but again the artwork is very high-quality. There's BDSM, tentacles and juicy cumshots. . . not bad a mix indeed!

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Sure, I recommend this game! As long as the artwork appeals to you, it's definitely worth checking out [b]Symphony of Delights[/b]. I sincerely hope Enygmage continues to produce titles in the same vein as this game, complete "Fully hand-drawn" artwork.

review:
Symphony of Delights is part of a series made by the same developer. This is the 1st game in the series and, although it feels a bit rough around the edges, it is the natural starting point. Playing it I felt kind of like I was watching an episode from a series and should've known more about the world and its characters, but accepting that not all of my questions will be answered in this game was easy and let me enjoy the mysteries, learning more alongside the game's characters.

In my personal opinion, the "Delights" series by Enygmage has three big hooks to pull you in. Its art style, at least in my experience, is unique, and I really appreciate the time and effort necessary to create every image we see in the game, of which there are quite a few. Next are the charming characters, both brave and playful so the art can showcase them in all their beauty. And third but certainly not least, the world of dreams and how it fits together into the big picture, I must say looking at humans as 'dreamers', outsiders lost in the world of dreams, is a refreshing take that holds a lot of novelty.

The games are quite short overall, you can reach all the endings and get every achievement in slightly over an hour, depending on how fast you read and how much time you spend appreciating the artwork. Not that it's a bad thing, that makes these bite-sized adventures perfect for a short gaming session, and if you like one then the others will probably suit you too. The fact they provide lots of checkpoints to return to should you hit a dead end helps keep the game moving, so you never really get stuck; even when RNG makes a battle go poorly, you have a good chance to pass it next time with average or better luck.

The first three games in the series share save files. That doesn't mean you can play all three in one game, as loading a save from one game in another is likely to get you an error, but it is something to keep in mind. I just kept their saves on different pages to not get them mixed up, and focused on each game in its own right.

Now focusing more on Symphony of Delights in particular, I must admit this game has the most lore and exposition in it. Some of it is setting the tone and theme for the story, some of it is brought in tales that characters can share at various points, but it is a lot to process in one go - I wasn't confused at any point, but some details didn't 'fall into place' until I played the later games and they answered some of my questions. Some characters are merely mentioned or namedropped without showing up, and you might even forget them until later, but that's okay - I found that encountering a character and realizing 'oh, so That's the One they talked about earlier' was more of a welcome surprise than a problem.

As the first game in the series, Symphony also feels the most linear too. Sometimes your options give you a different dialogue, sometimes some unique art, and sometimes they hit a dead end and bring you back to your checkpoint. You can't really get stuck though, and reaching the end you get the sense that this is just one step in Elylah's great journey, which is a nice springboard to jump right into the other games in this series.

review:
A good start, however definitely lacking polish and including a few bugs. 
The general concept is spawn into the world, find power stations to turn on and the codes to open the doors, all the while avoiding velociraptors. Once you've got enough power you turn on the radio and get to the choppa! 

Pros:
- Dual-wield chairs and smash your way through dinos Jackie Chan style
- Run from dinosaurs in a pitch black forest with your friends
- The velociraptor is pretty scary when face to face, or chasing you through tall grass
- It feels fun trying to navigate your way around the map using only clues
- A decent amount of human customization through achievements
- You can fiddle with all of the knobs on the radio
- Lots of neat landmarks around the map to navigate by

Cons:
- Whenever you pick up a note, it'll toggle a quest marker in the form of a green laser beam pointing down from the sky. I like having a sense of direction but it makes finding some spots too easy.
- The raptor AI can be pretty dumb. We skirted around one who was just hanging out on a cliffside and it just sat there barking and sniffing dirt.
- In my group, we got to the helicopter without finding a single torch, are they rare or are we unlucky?
- Doors sometimes get stuck on the stuff in your hands. The metal shield was slightly problematic.
- No extra ammo for guns!

It's a fun game for the price, and I'm looking forward to seeing where it goes.

review:
Overall, this game is a good play the 1st and 2nd time around to get both the painter and thinner paths. I did about 4 runs to try and get everything because some are well hidden and others really depend on the combination of choices you make, which can cause more runs if you mess it up. I never played the original so I don't know the comparison there, but the graphics are nice, decent mechanics and the game isn't overly difficult. It is simple fun and a decently long game to give you something to burn through for a few days. The missions are fun and add a lot of extra material to do besides the main story, but there can be a lot of fetching and bringing stuff back. 

I do have a small handful of complaints. This game can easily become extremely irritating, annoying and rage baiting. It also can be buggy and glitchy. Trying to get all the pins (regular and special), concept art, reels and Gremlins is extremely tedious. I used a wonderful guide on the community page that laid out everything pretty well to help find what I have missed. 

I had 1 special pin that is given after defeating the Bloticles on Mean Street that never wanted to spawn. I got every other special pin but wasn't able to 100% that set of collectibles over a glitch that is pretty common per Reddit. Theorectically, you have to start a whole new save (not New Game+) and it might spawn then, but I didn't feel trying that. I also wasn't able to get the last concept art which is The Spawner, which is literally inside one of the machines for the Mad Doctor's Attic battle. I did a previous run where I released Jarvis which makes it undoable because he disables that machine for you. So, I did a speed run after that, never saw the art and thinned the red circle above which blocks you being able to get it there too. I am not doing a 5th run for that stupid art. I think it is in a really shitty spot and should have never been placed there.

Continuing with the issue of doing 1 thing and your run can be ruined, thinning out the supports to the platform to jump to a certain Gremlin after taking the submarine to the next section of TomorrowLand really pissed me off. By the time I saw him up there it was too late. I tried so hard to make the jump and eventually did, but I was ready to give up and never come back to this game. To get him, you have to be on the very right edge of the platform, run and then dash off the end, quickly long press for a higher jump, double jump and spin attack to be able to make the distance and the height to get up there. Thank you to the people in the discussions who also had the same issue and told me it was possible.

I got all Steam achievements, all gold, silver, and bronze pins, reels and Gremlins. Just missed 1 special pin (bugged) and 1 concept art for it being in a stupid spot that easily locks you out. So I am considering this a 100% completion. I will probably delay playing the 2nd game because I don't feel like torturing myself right now.

review:
'Cosplaying' vampire challenged by a demon to a game with a castle at stake. Should you try this product or just buy some garlic instead?

The story places you in the shoes of a female vampire, who just returned home, only to be met with a new design and owner. Now to get your castle back, you'll need to go through a number of puzzles and enemies. There is only one ending, so one playthrough is sufficient to see all events. It sure ain't an epic, world-saving tale, but that also ain't the main focus of this game. Puzzles and scuffles are where this product affirms its merit.
While this rpg was made in the RPG Maker, it does have some fairly unique combat mechanics, making it stand out a little bit within the endless sea of RPG Maker games. Your attack options and stats depend on the state of your body. Transformations of body parts, either imposed by enemy attacks or through crystals, will modify skills dependent on the particular part: head, torso, arms, crotch,and legs. The type of attack (melee, ranged, or magic), effects, and number of skill changes. Also, stats are modified per every transformed part.
Additionally, the location (front or back) during battle also impacts which skills to use. You can move with specific skills, so the location is yours to decide. 
Puzzles are tied to body transformations. To find hidden items or unblock passages, will require you to use particular transformations. Most are easy to solve, but a few can pose a more serious challenge.
There is also a shop where you can obtain potions, upgrades, and accessories. There are no level ups here so the only way to get stronger is through item upgrades; initially they are pretty costly, so some grinding will be required but near the end it gets more affordable. 
The difficulty is moderate, but since there are no game overs, you can just pick yourself up by your bootstraps and resume the fight. Ending all trials and tribulations can be done in less than 10h. There is an option of new game+ in case you feel like replaying the adventure. I was happy enough with one run. 

The character art of this title does not suit my tastes much; I judge it at most average. Some body transformations were rather weird, but who am I to judge if some like them. 'Tis but my subjective feeling. Dungeons are rather compact and uninspired. Even considering the low price more could be done. Maybe the brevity is a positive aspect, though. The h-scenes are presented with text, only; they're brief and basic. Overall, visuals have a budget feel, indeed.

Music is average at best, too. Nothing was memorable or catchy, but at least none of the tracks irritated my sound receptors. Sound effects are of similar standard as well.

Several times my screen froze while playing. I could still act, but not see. Game restart was required every time. I recommend saving frequently.

Overall, a very much short, budget rpg, with a silly story, uncommon battle mechanics, and average art and music. I can't say I disliked it very much, but I can only give positive recommendation when on serious sale: 4.8/10

Here's the thing.
I get that the list of TF games were quite limited a few and more years ago, and I probably could compliment this one for trying, but no.
Despite the rather interesting idea and some kind of a story, it is simply not interesting to play. Yes, the main feature here is the possibility of transforming body parts and try different combinations which will affect your skills. Even though the actual look is random and awkward - I kinda like it, it's like an enemy you fight with is infecting and turning your body into something like her own. Plus, quite interesting to try different "builds".
However, the implementation of an adult genre like this is simply lame. I doubt that putting more emphasis on the explicit visuals or the depth of the plot would've saved it from my disappointment, but at least it would be justified to have NSFW in the tags and would raise interest to the game itself. 
Ah yes, the grind that needed for advancing through the story - my favorite. The reason I was able to get to the maids location, when VB finally lost me after a few tries; hucows are meh - very sad boring looking; and the only okayish part for me personally was the bimbo area, which is literally the start of the game.

Overall, I think it's unjustified that this game costs so much even in the region with the lowest price possible. Today you can find much more complex, catchy games with, God forgive me, juicy shots, good visual and interesting plot and characters. And all that for the same or even lower price on itch.io or any similar website/marketplace for independent creators. Which are also not made exclusively on a RPG maker from its bare assets, just for the sake of chibi-walking and the same type of screen battles.
And judging by the following projects of this dev, which he releases to this day, I don't see any difference between them, neither much point in buying them to try.

If I recommended something instead, it would be Latex Dungeon (also in Steam). Of course, there are problems in it too, but for exactly the same price you will get a lot more joy, both from a variety of high-quality hand-drawn explicit arts, animations, combat, characters and visual effects.

review:
Gorilla Tag is easily one of the most fun and unique VR games I’ve ever played. The movement system is simple but so genius — no joysticks, no teleporting, just using your arms to run, climb, and swing like an actual gorilla. It feels natural and surprisingly immersive, and it gets you moving in a way that no other VR game really does.

What makes it even better is the community. Every lobby feels different — sometimes it’s competitive, sometimes it’s hilarious, and sometimes it feels like a giant game of tag on the playground. The maps are creative and constantly updated, and the devs put a lot of love into adding new cosmetics, seasonal events, and content that keeps the game fresh.

I’ve laughed, I’ve screamed, I’ve gotten exercise without even realizing it, and I’ve made memories with friends that I’ll never forget. Whether you’re playing casually or sweating it out in competitive lobbies, Gorilla Tag is just pure fun.

If you own a VR headset, this game is a must-have.

"Christmas Griddlers Journey to Santa" is a basic Nonogram game... for those who never played one, it's a kind of grid-deduction-puzzle game, not unlike Minecraft or Sudoku.  You're given a grid and a number of numerical clues.  You must deduce where the safe places to click are.  In a Nonogram, the correct clicks will reveal a small, obviously low resolution image or pattern.  Yay, what fun.  This is why top of the line gaming PCs costs thousands of dollars, right?

The developer, Creobit, has copy + pasted this game an insane FOURTY ONE TIMES... why cash in on one asset if you can cash in on multiple copies of the same game?  Asset flipping begins at home!

Here's a list of the asset flips of this game that the Russian "developer" is polluting Steam with:

[*] Riddle of the mask
[*] Royal Riddles
[*] Santa's Toy Factory Nonograms
[*] Thanksgiving Day Griddlers
[*] Valentine's Day Griddlers 1 + 2
[/list]

[i][b]These are all reskins of exactly the same game![/b][/i]

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game features extremely lazy, minimalist "art", of the type you normally expect to see in low effort Flash/browser games and mobile apps.  Considering this is being evaluated as a PC game, having the graphics phoned in like this isn't going to result in a high quality, visually impressive game that PC gamers are used to seeing.

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with crappy "wings" to pad out the space).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

The controls can't be customised because the game has such a dumbed down, simplified interface that it's just iPhone screen tapping stuff.  The fact that the interface is this dumbed down might be seen as a problem in itself, however... this is a fairly shallow experience if you're the kind of gamer that likes to play games with deep, rich control schemes and interaction.  You'll get none of that here.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 4 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 110,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 11,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

"Fill And Cross Christmas Riddles" has the gamer gouging price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

review:
Although it says my game time is 27+ hours, that's only because I left the PC on with the game open for a day or so.  

I'm about 2 hours in so far and finding this very hard work.

The dialogue is far too much - to the extent where I'm not even reading it anymore, just mindlessly clicking through conversations so that I can continue the game.   It's excessive for the sake of being excessive.  I'm not averse to reading text - I grew up in the age of the text adventure, but this is just over the top and prevents the game from flowing well.   Why use 3,000 words to make a point, when 100 will do?

The script isn't great - a lot of the time it feels very unnatural.  Almost like it's been run through Google Translate.

The acting is worse than the scripting - it's cringe-worthy in many place.  It doesn't help that the English actors are clearly reading the script verbatim (including errors), and they seem to lack any particular acting skills.

There are some strange inconsistencies.  One example - the game is clearly set in England, yet there are references to money as 'bucks' and images of dollar signs on the map and at the mansion, and then Alfredo and Bob asking for Euros. 

The game has potential, for sure, the story is nice enough and there seem to be plenty of locations and some decent puzzles so far.

I will *try* and continue with the game, and maybe I'll find myself updating my review later, but at this moment in time I can't recommend it.

-------------

UPDATE #1
2 days after my initial review, I'm still trying to get through this game, but it's becoming more and more painful. The whole Police Quest 1 dialogue was especially torturous.

It's also bothering me that the screen just goes black during certain key sections when there probably should be an animation. Instead you get a black screen with (more) dialogue, describing what's happening.  

I'm going to finish the game with the walkthrough as I just don't have time to sit through all of this.

I really cannot recommend this game.  I apologise to the developers, as it's clearly a project with a lot of love in it - but as a game, it just feels like a chore to play.

----------------

UPDATE  #2
Having finally finished the game (using a walkthrough and skipping all dialogue), my feelings haven't really changed.  The story is nice and has a sweet sentiment to it which I liked.  The graphics are pleasant - nothing to complain about and the music is decent enough.  However, the endless reams of dialogue made me really dislike the game which is a shame, because I love PnC games and really wanted to enjoy this one. The script and English voice acting was also really quite bad.

I'm sure there will be many people who bought this game and who will disagree with my thoughts.  There are probably many people who have yet to buy it and who will love it.  It just wasn't for me , sadly.
