review:
Sword and Fairy: Together Forever is a visually stunning and emotionally resonant action RPG that blends Chinese mythology, character-driven drama, and fast-paced combat into a richly realized adventure. As part of the long-running Sword and Fairy franchise, this installment serves both as a standalone story and a gateway into a larger universe that many players in the West may be encountering for the first time. The narrative follows a group of characters drawn together by fate, as they navigate the tensions between the human and deity realms. The plot steadily unfolds through themes of sacrifice, honor, destiny, and love, all set within a world steeped in ancient folklore and spiritual symbolism.

The story is one of the game’s strongest features, offering a uniquely Chinese narrative voice that stands apart from typical Western or Japanese RPG storytelling. It’s not just about good versus evil or heroism in the traditional sense. Instead, it delves into morally complex situations, internal conflicts, and mystical traditions drawn from Taoist and Buddhist influences. The dialogue—while occasionally stilted due to localization—reflects a poetic and philosophical tone that enhances the overall atmosphere. Over time, the characters evolve meaningfully, and relationships among them—particularly the romantic and familial ones—are given room to breathe and deepen. This allows players to invest in more than just the combat or exploration; there’s a genuine emotional core to the experience.

Gameplay in Sword and Fairy: Together Forever blends real-time action with party-based strategy, allowing you to control multiple characters with distinct combat styles. You can switch between party members on the fly, chaining together abilities and managing their cooldowns in a way that feels fluid and engaging. Although the mechanics don’t demand the level of precision or depth seen in more hardcore action RPGs, they remain satisfying thanks to polished animations and powerful visual effects. Special attacks and ultimate abilities feel impactful, and enemy encounters—especially bosses—require enough strategy to stay interesting without being punishing. Combat difficulty is balanced to appeal to a wide range of players, making it accessible for newcomers while offering more advanced playstyles for veterans.

Beyond combat, the game offers a variety of features that help flesh out its world and systems. Side quests, mini-games, and character interactions provide welcome distractions from the main story and add flavor to the experience. Activities such as cooking meals, exploring hidden areas, or taking on optional challenges make the world feel alive, even if some of these elements are relatively light in complexity. The game also includes collectibles, lore entries, and bestiary information, which help expand the player’s understanding of the mythological context while rewarding curiosity and exploration.

Visually, the game is a standout achievement. The environments are lush, atmospheric, and diverse, ranging from ethereal mountain temples to tranquil lakesides and bustling villages. Attention to detail is evident in the architecture, costume design, and natural landscapes, all of which reinforce the game’s strong cultural identity. Whether you're admiring the lantern-lit streets of a traditional town or watching sakura petals drift across the screen in a quiet forest, the artistic direction is consistently breathtaking. The soundtrack complements this beautifully, featuring orchestral and traditional Chinese instrumentals that evoke emotion, tension, and wonder throughout the journey.

That said, the game isn’t without its rough edges. The English localization can feel uneven, with some awkward phrasing and grammar issues that occasionally detract from the otherwise lyrical tone of the story. The pacing, particularly in the early chapters, can be slow, with long stretches of dialogue and exposition that may challenge the patience of players eager to dive into action. Some technical hiccups—like frame drops during crowded scenes or audio sync issues in cutscenes—also remind you that this isn’t a big-budget AAA production. However, these issues rarely overshadow the experience as a whole, especially for players who value narrative and artistic ambition.

Sword and Fairy: Together Forever ultimately succeeds as a thoughtful and heartfelt RPG that stands out because of its unique cultural roots and narrative focus. It doesn’t try to imitate Western fantasy tropes or action-heavy RPG formulas—instead, it tells a story grounded in Chinese spiritualism, filled with poetic melancholy and moments of quiet beauty. Its characters are memorable, its world is immersive, and its blend of gameplay and story is both engaging and refreshing. For players looking to experience a different flavor of fantasy—one shaped by centuries of myth and guided by sincerity rather than spectacle—this game is well worth your time.

Rating: 9/10

This game could be a lot better, and could be a lot worse. 

The cursor is Very Cute, and I like the sprite of a little wizard man casting spells, however I don't know how you managed to make a cursor that is confusing. It is quite literally one of the most basic things about a computer, and this cursor made me feel strange and unusual. I cannot tell if the tip of the sprite is the clicky part, or the Big Targeting Diamond Thing. My best bet was just hovering the entire cursor over what i wanted and hoping. Which sucked for the menu buttons because in the game, the menu buttons are Small. 

Yes, the visuals are very cute, but not good for a puzzle game. There are pieces that are entirely one solid color with no defining features to them, which makes them hard to place unless you accidentally fit them in or guess when you have an outline of a shape. 
All the Puzzle Pieces are kindof that Dog-Bone shape (at least as far as I got), which also adds to the boringness. 
Also of note, For some reason the cursor defaults to picking up pieces that are at the bottom of a stack? Very Cool to not pick up the piece you are clicking on, and instead sorting through maybe 4 or 5 pieces that are solid brown.

The Music Loop is infuriating and grating to the nerves. It's a few seconds long and i immediately had to almost mute the sounds it was making. [url=https://pernyblom.github.io/abundant-music/index.html]Here's a link to a website that generates music for you[/url]! you will probably make nicer sounding Sounds than the maybe 4 second loop this game drools out. 

If you'll allow me a quick gripe, it says "Hold down H to skip to next puzzle". You do not have to hold down H, I pressed it on accident and it skipped right on by the gameplay. I feel as though there is a difference between Pressing a key and Holding Down a key. 

Overall, it is a cute [i]looking[/i] game, but I do not think that this is a great puzzle game. A kid might enjoy it, You could get little Timothy to get all the steam achievements, but I don't know man. I would suggest you just go to a dollar store and get a cheap puzzle. Paint the front side white, get your kid to draw a picture/story on it, and boom. You have a family activity that you can then keep in a box for memories sake.

review:
Tehachapi Loop is a pretty well-designed route. In fact, little was disappointing aside from the locomotives. I’ll get to that in a moment. This is why I’m giving a positive review. The scenarios all worked properly and it was fun to drive even if I was forced to use some questionable locomotives. Also it was only $3.33. I bought it with TSC on sale and got 3 routes I did not have for $10. It’s hard to go wrong for that price!

Short version: 

+ Route design wasn’t bad. The grades can be challenging, especially as the corners are long and create drag on long trains.
+ Plenty of things to do if you want to make your own scenarios.
+ All six of the included scenarios work perfectly without having to play funny games to get points to work or achievements to pop. They’re also adequate examples of running the route overall.
+ The scenarios all start with 1000 points and ding you if you screw up. This is much more relaxing than trying to stick to an unrealistic time table for a huge freight train running a mountain pass! 

- Four of the six included locomotives have issues
- A couple of small graphics glitches described below. Not major, but they’re still sloppy

+/- Now this is questionable. There appear to be 9 achievements which is odd. As most of you will know DTG routes usually have 10. Also, I’m quite certain one of these 9 was triggered by a different route/event. My log shows it was triggered in Feb 2022 when I did not own this route. So good luck with that… But the other 8 did work properly. 

Additional nit-picking and commentary: 

I found only two minor complaints about the overall design. The first: Near one end of the track, the electrical wires actually curved around a corner between the poles instead of just running a straight line between poles. Not sure how that happened! Also, there was one tunnel entrance showing ground covering it as you enter it. A common problem with TSC routes. Of course, it doesn’t obstruct the train – it just looks pretty poor. The rest was very well designed in my opinion. 

The locomotives are a bit of a different story. It does come with more than most routes, but that’s probably because none are new, most are old, and several have serious quality issues. 

UP ES44AC: Mostly a minor issue, but when you use dynamic brakes, the HUD doesn’t display the negative power at all. Also, the tractive effort doesn’t show correctly on the main screen display. 

BNSF ES44AC: This one came from Marias Pass. It’s easy to tell because one of the windshield wipers doesn’t work. The one from Stevens pass works fine, so why not use that one? Shows how much they pay attn I guess… Same problems as above too – tractive effort doesn’t work properly on the display and no negative power on the HUD when you use the dynamic brakes. 

AC4400CW: I think this one was ok… At least I don’t recall an issue at this moment. 

GP40-2: This is a pretty decent locomotive. I think it’s from the GP40-2 pack. 

SD70Ace: A terrible locomotive that was pretty bad when it was released originally many years ago. The display is extremely basic and looks poor. The ONLY thing that works at all is the speedometer and it doesn’t show the correct speed. It does look decent from the outside which is probably why it was included. For AI traffic. 

Some said they had issues with brakes releasing or not releasing depending on the locomotive. I had none of these issues. As far as physics go, they all worked. I had no errors at all and good FPS throughout. I’d recommend it on sale only. If they want full price, they need to include NEW locomotives that look new and work properly. This rehashing of old content is getting old. Literally.

ENG: 

A nice route leading from Bakersfield over Tehachapi Pass to the town of Mohave. There is a double-track non-electrified line from Bakersfield to Caliente, where the line speed is 40 - 60 mph. After Caliente, the single-track section begins a steep climb, with the track split at several points to accommodate crossing oncoming trains. A challenging climb brings the train to the legendary Tehachapi Loop, from which the climb continues to Tehachapi. At Tehachapi, the train climbs onto a plateau and the track is doubled here, with line speeds reaching up to 60mph. It then descends to the town of Mojave.  

Overall, this is a challenging track, with track speeds climbing to 23mph and trains vulture hard up the steep grade (up to 2.2%), or have to brake very carefully on the descent.  

The locomotives included in the package are types ES44AC, ES44DC, SD70ACe, AC4400CW and GP40-2. In most of the missions you will be driving very heavy freight trains over a pass, some missions are marshalling. There are two more paid DLCs with 20 missions and a number of fan missions.  

Overall, I rate it 7/10. The track is very nice, albeit with occasional bugs, the character is that of a semi-desert area, as you climb the pass you gain bushes and trees only to have the train drop back down into arid and treeless areas. Especially in the morning or evening the scenery is very pretty.

review:
TLDR:  Route is good, and new AC4400 is nice, but I'd wait for a sale.


Introduction/general information:

The legendary loop finally comes to TS.


Scenery quality: 3/5 [Grade C]

Scenery quality seems pretty average for DTG's in-house routes: not super great, but not terrible either. 

 Like most of DTG's routes, there are recycled assets aplenty (not nearly as bad as Granger Heartland though), but some new ones were created for the more recognizable areas of the route (Bakersfield Amtrak station, the old SP depot in Tehachapi and it's companion water tower, at least).

The pass itself seems fairly detailed, however, there are some areas (namely from about Bena to Bowen) where the scenery is fairly sparse, and the ground textures seem too bright.  From Bowen east to Mojave, the scenery becomes more dense and more dulled down.  

(I thought I read that there were two development teams that were working on the textures for the route, and that the team working on the west end of the route ran out of time or something?  Don't take my word for it, though).

One... somewhat annoying... issue I noticed regarding the scenery is that some areas of distant terrain look unfinished, like the terrain wasn't downloaded for that particular area.  Additionally, I spotted (at least) two areas where some of the scenery is floating (a floating signal head on an industrial siding just east of Bakersfield, and a missing control point shed at CP Cable).

One more thing that kind of bothers me is the somewhat over-reliance of 2D trees in some areas of the route.  They work fine on flat areas, where closer, more detailed assets can sort of hide them from direct viewing, but that illusion falls apart on mountainsides, where one can see the ground behind the tree.  Not a complete suspension-of-disbelief destroyer, but it's something I just thought I would note.

Scenery gets a 3 out of 5.


Route length: 3/5 [Grade C]

The route is ~70 miles from Mojave to Bakersfield.  Not a super long distance, but it seems like it would take a little under 3 hours to drive end-to-end.

3 out of 5 here, as well.


Performance: 3/5 [Grade C]

The route performs fairly well for me, with most of the route getting ~80 FPS on my machine.  However (at night, probably faster during the day), Bakersfield was running at ~40 FPS, and the Amtrak station dropped caused my game to drop to ~20 FPs (as stated earlier, at night).

Performance gets a 3/5 from me (would have been 4, save for the extremely-slow night lighting).


Functionality: 4/5 [Grade B]

It seems like some of the in-route speed limits don't match what is displayed on the HUD, with some limits being enacted earlier than expected, and some not changing until the train is well-clear of the restriction.

Most of the whistle boards on the route are displayed on the HUD, which is nice, however some of them don't show up there.

4 out of 5 on functionality.


Versatility: 2/5 [Grade D]

The route seems more geared towards mainline, a-to-b freights, however there are a handful of industries along the route that could local trains could serve.  Switching opportunities seem somewhat limited; outside of the yards in Bakersfield and Mojave, and maybe some of the "larger" industrial areas, there's not much you can really do in that regard.

Passenger service is nonexistent, save for the rare Coast Starlight detour over the pass.

The route seems to be set in the modern era (circa 2021), but I believe that it could also serve the previous 20 years or so fairly well.

Versatility gets a 2 out of 5.


Extra credit and nitpicks:

(I'm covering the rolling stock here, since they're not the main focus of the route; it's just thrown in so that you have something to drive the route with.)

The rolling stock (except for the AC4400CW) is just copy/pasted from other routes and rolling stock packs.  The Gevos, GP40-2s, and SD70ACes aren't any different from what they were copied from (except for the brakes on, at least, the BNSF Gevos).

The only new thing included is the AC4400CW, which, while your average Dovetail-quality, is quite a nice addition.  The model and texture work was done by Reppo, and it certainly shows (in a good way).  The sounds aren't anything special; they're ripped straight from the CSX AC6000.

The physics seem alright, except that the dynamic brakes seem kind of weak (during the scenario I tested them with, I had to supplement with some air to keep the train from running away).

+1 extra credit for the AC44.


Final grade and closing remarks: 

Final grade of 16/25 [Grade B-].

While the AC4400 is a nice addition to the U.S Train Sim fleet, I wouldn't buy the route just for it (either buy and reskin Searchlight's AC44, or wait until they release their UP AC44, if you're just interested in the locomotive, and don't care about the route).

review:
[h1]Experienced on the Oculus Quest 2[/h1]

You can view my review & gameplay here: https://youtu.be/487Fw1M2iM0

So this game has a lot of similarities to Phasmophobia, but it nowhere near as good as Phasmo. It's basically a single-player Phasmophobia and you're playing on the school map. There's also a bit of a story here where you're an occult investigator and you're trying to find out what happened to a missing girl. 

You have 4 tools that you can use: a cube that reacts whenever a demon / revenant is nearby, a stun light grenade that stuns & then slows the demon, CCTV cameras, & tesla shock coils that can trap an area. You also have a tablet that can give you case information or that you can use to take UV photos. You'll see clues using the UV and you can also use it to damage revenants with magic photos. 

Game is running on the Unity Engine. On high graphical settings, the game was running at a steady 90 fps on my RTX 3080. You have full locomotion as well as smooth and snap turning (along with degree of turn or how fast you smooth turn). You also have head directed or hand directed movement, along with a comfort option. You can play the game seated as there is a crouch button, but I did find that I was a bit too low to the ground by default so I played standing.

Overall, this game is budget priced at only $13 USD normal price (I paid 10% off release sale price). For that reason, I can recommend it even though it is lacking in the depth to the gameplay. I think the biggest weakness (compared to Phasmo) is the sound design / sound mix. It's not very good in this game and there were long stretches of game time where there was absolutely no sound. I also think the game could use a lot more depth to the gameplay. I was never really scared like I was in Phasmophobia. It is in Early Access though and it is a nice start to EA (just not a nice of a start as was the case in Phasmo).

[b]Rate 6/10.[/b]

Revenants first off, is a very immersive VR gaming experience. It will scare you, wear your brown pants. In the game we play a Occult investigator, that collects evidence of demonic forces, then hunts them down. We have a range of high tech toys to work with. We are on a cold case called Spirt & Mind, its a old case of a missing school girl. We will be exploring a creepy old school, where we must investigate and collect evidence of demonic forces, then try to survive and hunt them down. This game gives me strong vibes of the TV show Supernatural, with the Winchester brothers Sam & Dean. Unlike Sam & Dean though, I was not as brave, and the hair on my arms actually stood up at times.

The game world is dark and scary, and will send chills down your spine. From the spooky looking dark school we explore to the great sounds and background music, you will feel like you are in a horror movie / show. Supernatural made this job look easy and fun. It was challenging and terrifying instead. I went into this think, hey I'm going to hunt down some demonic forces, I am going to be a tough guy like Sam & Dean or at least like a Ghostbuster. But no, I felt like I was the one being hunted, and dreaded what was behind the next door. I am a 70s baby and grew up on horror movies, played a ton of horror games and though this will be a cake walk. No this game scared the crap out of me a few times and was far from a cake walk. 

You only have the light from your tablet to see in this dark school of creepy sounds. You may have some high tech toys to help you, but it will do nothing to keep the fear away. I really love the horror genre, and had an amazing scary time in this game. This is an amazing VR experience, and horror buffs are going to want to dive into this one. review:
Initially, I wasn't planning on going too hard on this game and its developers. But after spending few hours trying to figure out performance issues that this game has and figuring out the source of the softlock in the tutorial level (which I have informed the developer about) and then spending good few hours playing the game trying to see how many other issues are in this game and if there is a chance it is ever getting patched, I have come decided otherwise. So here goes...

THIS GAME IS NOT RELEASE READY! IT IS NOT EVEN EARLY ACCESS READY! And to pretend it otherwise is absurd! Furthermore, I highly doubt there was any QA done by the publisher - if there was, someone would have caught the softlock issue in the tutorial. It is literally in the first 10 min of the game. It's not even something that is easily missed in test environments (like improper character coding in system paths for example is). All you need is one person from a region, which uses a comma as a decimal separator and you have your softlock and there are loads of them (see: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimal_separator#Countries_using_decimal_comma). No - there just wasn't QA done, and all we're dealing with is an attempt to pass a game that would barely classify as an alpha build as a full release, in a sickening attempt to recoup some losses by either a publisher, developer or both. Again, I was originally planning on not being too harsh, but ultimately, after seeing the state this game is in, the abysmal performance and that is with the ridiculous hacks that developers have implemented (like disabling shadow casting for almost all surfaces and setting a far plane for the camera to distance of something less than 100m), I just can't, cause at the end of the day, I am a game developer myself, I work with Unity and because of games like this I then have to deal with people constantly nagging "why Unity when you could use X,Y,Z", while in reality Unity - in the right hands - is perfectly capable of handling a game like this and much more. Essentially because of games like this, my professional life gets harder and I have to put even more effort into what I do, to convince people that now have a biased against games using Unity, that the choice of Unity as the core of the project wasn't the wrong one.

Right. Haven't even managed to get to what this game essentially is and what it is, is a stealth game with some randomization (call it rouge-lite if you must). Problem is, the entire level generator is a gigantic mess that is unlikely to ever get fixed (and that is even if additional months of development get magically funded), as it is simply incapable of doing even basic stuff like connecting floors with one another without bugging out in a way that it leaves a gigantic hole in geometry in the place where the wall is supposed to be or putting a tiny room out of nowhere in the middle of the staircase with only inside faces of that room being present. It's a miracle if it even manages to spawn required objectives, as I had cases where I was supposed to disable X security systems and then the moment I loaded, it turned out that objective said 0 out of 0. I have had cameras spawn above the ceiling, ceilings spawning below where they should be and lacking collisions, I have had rooms without walls or doors on one of the ends that just lead into the void, where there wasn't any level anymore. I have had failed connections between rooms. I have had flowers being planted outside the ground, objects floating in mid-air and I literally NEVER had a single level that was generated as intended.

It's just one gigantic mess and from the looks of it - it is never getting fixed and you should certainly NOT buy it in hopes it gets fixed one day - cause the likelihood of that happening is almost zero.

Oh, and as for fixing the softlock, since I got no response being nicely ignored and there doesn't seem to be any movement on even the developer's branch, here is how much code has to be added to have that fixed, so if it doesn't get fixed soon - you might as well call this a scam project:
[code]CultureInfo EnforcedCulture = new CultureInfo("en-GB");
CultureInfo.CurrentCulture = EnforcedCulture;
CultureInfo.DefaultThreadCurrentCulture = EnforcedCulture;[/code]

This should be executed once at the start-up of the program.
Good day!

-- EDIT --
Patch has dropped, sadly despite the notes saying a softlock in tutorial was removed - the softlock is still a thing.

review:
This game is for freaks only.

Are you a Thief freak? Someone who will play anything that even remotely resembles the Thief games? If you said yes then this game is for you. Otherwise you might just get angry.

Abermore has personality. Like the climbing system that I haven't come across anywhere else. Or the Gutter and its inhabitants, I just love the game's random NPC generator's tendency to create the most hipster looking individuals. All the environments are quite charming. The writing is generally nice and at times really good! A definite highlight of the whole game. The small nuggets of story and worldbuilding paint a picture of a magic realist place. It's clear the developers love immersive sims and their worlds.

I had to download a Unity debug tool so I could access the game's files on runtime and save myself from situations that were game breaking. I had to rely on this tool more than once. Actually pretty often. This would be my recommended way of experiencing the game. It is not the way games should be played I know, but as someone who makes games I had fun exploring the files and seeing how I can untangle the mess the game world was in. Now if that is not immersive simulation I don't know what is!

Abermore has its own style,  a thing I think should not be taken as granted. The developers had a vision and that shows. Making video games is hard and making immersive sims is even harder. So I applaud the devs for making one and giving us a glimpse of a world with personality and quirkiness.

review:
Okay, listen, we need to talk. There are at least 5 achievements that are definitely broken, probably 6 unless I can figure out who the heck Aevon Gardott is. I've written a bit of a guide that details what they are, and maybe I'll finish that up and complete what I can.

After 20 hours, I feel I've given Abermore a fair shake. Though I cannot speak to its state at launch, it is far more playable than most of these reviews would have you believe. I have not once encountered a level geometry that is truly unplayable, though I've certainly encountered some ridiculous layouts and oddly placed walls. I've also encountered several times where the game hangs, especially in cut scenes, and some missions that seem pretty broken. Yes, there are some ugly seams and rough edges to point and laugh at, but I think everybody else has beat that to death.

There is a fun game in Abermore. It is far from perfect, but it is fun. Should you buy it? I don't know your finances, but I picked it up when it went on sale for less than $2, and if it does that again, then sure, why not. If you're here, looking at these reviews, then I can only imagine you're waist deep in an immersive sim binge, and you've seen this mentioned offhand in a video or two. If that's you, and you're curious, add this to your wishlist and wait for the next sale.

I genuinely really enjoy the writing in this game. I think they've painted a setting worth exploring, and it's hard to see when things break down. I really wish this game would get a little more support. I would happily offer my services as a Unity dev, at least just to fix those achievements and some poor data handling in the inventory grids. But I suppose that's a problem, that it's hard to say something good about Abermore without also admitting its faults in the same breath.

Thing is, I don't think a lot of these reviews have even given it a chance. Maybe you bought it on the first day, and maybe it was significantly more broken at that point. I understand. That hurts. But here's the thing: reviews are weapons. You cannot call a game a scam and expect it to get fixed. If the developers had any intention of continuing support for this game, which, I don't know, not gonna hold my breath, but if they had any intention of doing so, getting overwhelmingly negative reviews would absolutely kill any desire to continue development.

Is it more important for you, as a consumer, to be part of a collective of consumers, or would you like to engage in a constructive dialogue with the creators? Because that's what reviews can be. Despite what some grumpy fictional swamp goblin might say, there is no do, there is only trying and occasionally succeeding. Though Abermore has some clear misses, with a little more trying, I for one believe it can hit the right spot. If you did give it a chance and truly found no redeeming qualities hidden within, I can understand, but luckily there are so many other games to play.

I love Abermore. Sometimes it does things that I hate, sometimes it aggravates and disappoints, but it has a raw flawed beauty that I truly adore. I cannot, in good faith, recommend it to just anyone out there, but I do think, if you're here, reading this, that you should give it a try. Try to see past its ugliness. Try to appreciate the writing, notwithstanding the occasional misspellings. Try to be kind. Because for all its faults, I can't stand seeing a game like this get nothing but hate.

I am enjoying the pieces of what Abermore could have been, but that takes patience, imagination, and a whole lot of forgiveness. This game is much too broken to be released to paying audiences like this. It starts with bad framerates and slows down over the course of a mission to an unplayable slideshow of 5fps. Level geometry is missing walls and ceilings. Clipping out of the level is commonplace. Lights dont work. AIs fail at pathfinding. I had the Y axis of my mouselook go wild and then eventually lock up. The UI is plagued with constant full screen flashes of broken polygons. I havent had a single session that wasnt deeply broken.

But in among all that, and despite the stealth systems being rudimentary to the point of bad, there is something at the core of this game. I am enjoying the light touch weird worldbuilding in the quests and npcs, and in the moments between the game's brokenness I find myself liking what they were going for. Not what they actually produced, mind you, just what I can see in it.

TLDR: has potential, but wait for bug-fixes/updates before purchasing.

I can tell a lot of effort has gone into making this game, but it's not ready for commercial release yet. I've played the tutorial, and one and a half levels. I like the concept, had a couple fun moments, and am interested in some of the features that were introduced, but it needs bug fixes and polish. There is a game breaking bug where the camera gets locked on an NPC you just killed. I think it may have been intended to be some sort of combat lock/targeting system, but it's broken and after a couple minutes of trying to unlock it I had to exit the game (also it broke the inventory system, may have had something to do with my knife breaking at the same time though). Another issue is that the camera sways (not just the tutorial level) when moving even after setting the "head bob" setting to 0. The setting seems to only reduce head bobbing from walking/running, but doesn't reduce the camera sway from looking around and changing direction of movement. I get motion sick easily and don't want to get nauseated from simply looking around the environment. Furthermore, the procedural map making algorithm still produces disjoint looking building interiors (honestly, handcrafted maps might be better anyway. The algorithm was making mazes without any character), I believe this was with the day 1 hot fix patch already in place.

This game is obviously a love letter to the dishonored series, and I would love to see "Abermore" succeed as it appears to bring new ideas to the table. I'm going to keep an eye on it and try it again after some time has passed.

EDIT: the ominous foot step sound on the hound/knight guys was cool.

As loathe as I am to submit this (because there's a great game here!), I can't recommend this based on bugs alone.

- The inventory system barely works; items keep covering up other items in the inventory, then dragging them around causes all sorts of weirdness.
- Every level I played had massive gaping holes in the geometry, specifically around stairs with not a single set of them appearing without an issue.
- I was bumped out of the level geometry while crawling through a vent. I was able to get back inside in that case though.
- I finished a quest but the person refused to acknowledge that I'd finished the quest so I couldn't progress their mission, because the level wasn't selectable again (as I'd already finished it!).
- A dude pushed me out of the level geometry and into a cupboard, leaving me to be stuck while they sounded an alarm and I could do nothing but sit there waiting for the timer to go down.

With all the above problems, it really does pain me to say "don't buy it just yet". It's so much fun and would be brilliant if it weren't so broken. I was willing to push through all the bugs and weirdness because I was having a great time stealing stuff, knocking people out, sneaking about and selling my ill-gotten goods, but one thing after another wore me down. The playground here is fun, the abilities are a nice twist, the moment-to-moment gameplay is satisfying, but it's just so broken.

I will happily amend this review to a positive if some fixes come out, but until then I can't recommend it.

review:
Disappointing.

The unique style of the game, as well as the lore of the setting, and the cool mechanics that were promised really had me hyped for this game. I was prepared for some bugs, and willing to excuse those. Other reviews have mentioned them already and I will not retread the topic here. What I want to focus on is how hard it is to actually play this game. Instead, I felt like someone tricked me into reading their hacked together fantasy novel.

The game fails at the most basic piece of writing advice: rather than showing instead of telling,  the game starts with a long info dump about its world's lore. Contrivance after contrivance occurs to set up the point where you can actually play. I spent my time in Abermore reading in an awkward dialogue interface. The little bit of gameplay felt nice, but the tedious and poorly written fantasy novel worth of exposition is not worth it.

Aside from the game being info-dumpy. its plot isn't even well written. Why would the king himself show up on some random boat to grab a wanted criminal? Why would he torture the crew to threaten said criminal? Why would the criminals wife let some random guy join their heist?

The aesthetic of the world and the general ideas are great, but the details of the story are absolute garbage and I cannot deal with that when all I want is some tense immersive sim thieving in a magitech setting. I quit when I had to go through two completely empty "corridor" areas, each with their own loading screen before entering them, before I could start getting to any sort of gameplay after dealing with a ten page prologue with maybe a minute worth of gameplay that should have been a skipable tutorial.

I hope they rework the game into something worth playing eventually. As it stands, I could have probably come up with a better script.

I was actually hoping this game would be great fun with lots of repeatability with the randomly generated worlds you must thieve in. 


It began with my first run, i quickly got the hang of the game and ran through the tutorial with no issues. The next mission went by quickly too, it was an easy stealth run. The next run was where it began. I started in an underground area, it looks like the minecart track you ride off on. Its easy to find the room with several lockers but with no markers i got stuck and was unable to progress (turns out theres little vent holes in the walls you can use! the tutorial didn't really cover these.) 

I learned quickly. I started using those vents and tunnels to get around NPCs and get behind cameras. THEN, it happened. I was crawling through and then poof! I'm now above the map. It allowed me to see through walls and simply walking backwards pushed me back into the world. Easy fix. However, after this mission my game would crash and I would lose the save file.

My second run was much more successful. I had ran through all the missions. I have completed relationships with everyone in the guild. But according to the game I have 2 days until the final mission, where you rob the castle, and no missions left. You must be thinking "great! He can go on to the finale and finish the game!" Wrong. Even if you fill all the slots and reduce the risk of the mission to low, you are unable to start it because the game says theres 2 days left until you can run it. I guess you aren't supposed to complete all the missions with such speed. 

TLDR: Game good, some bugs occur but 99% are easy to fix and don't break the game (the crash issue was fixed in the day 1 patch). Don't try to finish all the tasks too quickly or it'll bug and you wont be able to progress.

review:
Worse game I have ever played.

The graphics and art direction are all over the place. Makes you think it's either an asset flip, or made by people who weren't actually paid to do any artwork. Some of the more grotesque characters and character animations you'll ever see. To the point you have to question if child workers were employed in the creation of it.

The story seems sketchy at best, there's no voice acting at all, which considering this is a wannabe Theif replacement is a real let down. Even the first Thief had narration ffs.

The gameplay is Ok-ish. I still wonder how much of it is litetallly just an asset flip right from the unity marketplace.

The predictive animation is OK/surprisingly nice. And it seems to be just about the only thing that this game completed.

The premise is downright retarded though - you incapacitate people, and if you don't hide their bodies on something like a chair (Which isn't hiding anything) they will eventually wake up.

It's unfinished as fuck.
To the point there's no keyboard bindings option, no way to know what buttons to press at all. No way to quit the game. No way to save the game. You get the point.
If the artwork had me worried about the age of those producing assets, the UI has me worried about the company that produced this as a whole. 
It's not love the game was released in "early access", this is supposedly a finished fucking product.

Sure. For $15 wtf do you expect? That's really the only redeeming quality here. I feel like the money wasn't *completely* thrown into the trash - which realistically it was.

The only thing that resembleds Thief is how low fucking poly shit is.
Seriously. It's 2022 for fuck sake. Any graphics card out there, even that 1060 potato that Steam reports as being owned by "everyone" can handle much higher details than this game has.

The random room generation is wierd. Doesn't even seem random at times.
Still, I guess it works. Even if for whatever fucking reason if you access a random quest you end up getting stuff from some other random fucking event you triggered into the quest itself.

Gear has no purpose. And 90% of it doesn't even work.
Blow gun? Sleep dart? I didn't even try the gun or the crossbow since the goddman point of the game is not to kill anyway. Whatever the fuck where they thinking when they added deadly weapons anyway? Who knows.
Maybe further in the story they could serve a purpose.

Considering the current state, I doubt I'll find out.

The proper pricing for this is probably around $0.99 in case you are wondering.
Anything above that is wasted money in its current state.

You ask me, it's got no potential. Or reason to exist futher really.

Having a new Thief game, that was a nice thought. This isn't it and will never be.

[h1]Not ready[/h1]

[b]Abermore[/b] is the story of a thief, dreaming of building up his reputation to the status of Legend in a world that is not without reminding you of Dishonored. By joining one big heist, you will get to learn about the fate of the Hanged Man and your subsequent adventures to rescue her and potentially establish yourself as a famous thief.

Graphically speaking, while it is certainly its own, the level design and the main city are definitely inspired by the Dishonored series. The gameplay integrates some interesting elements like tarot cards that give your character special abilities or crafting from the items you loot in-game and food to eat to replenish your stamina.
 
Sadly, while the concept and ideas for the game are interesting, Abermore is a thieving game that will just effectively steal your time, patience, and money as of today, release day.

This game presents an unique "twist" in guidance-path type puzzles where you are guiding a kitty kat from an entrance door, through a small dungeon laced with dropping floor panels (both controlled and random), tripping floor panels that open doors, teleporting floor panels, and panels that when stepped on will rotate the entire dungeon 90-degrees counter-clockwise.  All of this to get the cat from the entrance door to the exit door in order to move to the next level.  Each floor may/may not have special "pillars" with a symbol on top ("torches", "sheilds", "swords") that cause the four adjacent floor panels to drop in a predefined pattern as determined in a parchment paper pasted on the level.

Using these characteristics, this game is a family-friendly puzzle where it teaches the concepts of "planning ahead" and plotting your course to meet the objective.  It progresses in difficulty during the game but never reaches the point of frustration where you feel the need to "cheat" yet, it still tests your thought ability.  This is a really good casual-style game where you can stop, walk away, and come back to play more...I would recommend this game...going on to play the second game in the series which should prove to be a little more difficult and frustrating...have fun! review:
When I first saw Blood West, it looked really interesting. It had some unique concepts with a heavy emphasis on "old school stealth" and "eldritch horror". This really captivated me but, I heard that it was riddled with bugs and issues when it first came out, so, I done what I usually do - wishlist it and wait till it gets some love poured into it.

Here I am, in 2025 FINALLY playing Blood West... 2 years after it came out. I am not sure if I got this in a Humble Bundle or got it gifted by a friend but, I can say this with all due respect - I had so much fun exploring this world. Learning about the creatures and just downright sneaking around with a pair of bear fists killing everything!

[h1][b] Pro's [/b][/h1] 
⚫I loved the stealth aspect of the game because it felt rewarding. You can almost 1 hit kill anything in stealth with a headshot, melee and range. You also get a little bar at the bottom letting you know your "stealth" and 2 icons - an eye and ear symbol indicating seen and hearing. I am also going to mention this one in con's for a specific reason. 
⚫The combat #1 - MELEE - Personally the melee combat is exceptional in my opinion, especially when you stealth. There is plenty of unique melee weapons to choose from ranging from - knives, spears, axe's and a good few more! 
⚫The combat #2 - RANGED - Ranged for me was a hit or a miss. Especially because of the long reload times, sometimes the "hit reg" (more about this in cons) but there was plenty of ranged weapons to use. Lever action rifles, buffalo rifles, bow and arrows, crossbows, revolvers... a "CHAIN PISTOL" which I fell in love with using FANNING!! but, I used melee mainly. 
⚫Exploration was really fun. Going building to building looking for some ammo, medical supplies or goodies to sell so I can buy that coveted legendary weapon I want (or a larger backpack). The map's (yes, maps) are not "HUGE" but they are pretty large for a game like this. Making my way into a church, finding a hidden basement, going down it and then resorting to running away from a mass army of cultist cannibals wanting to skin and eat me alive... oh boy... 
⚫The atmosphere at times was just absolutely spot on. A decrepit burial site with eerie noises, cobweb infested holes and the pained grunting of the cultists waiting behind those nasty corners, if not that... an elevator that goes down 3 levels into an almost pitch black mine... with an evil secret at the bottom waiting to be explored!!!
⚫The inventory management was rather great in my opinion. Slowly collecting items to sell to buy a backpack, then a large backpack then to be able to carry more - once full, use a raven skull to go back to the "safe zone", sell your items (don't worry, enemies won't respawn unless you die or rest) and then set back out in the world, repeat. I thought this was great because most games FORCE you to run back with "carry weight" or no option to teleport.
⚫Having tonnes of different artifacts for different types of build was really cool. Being able to add resistances to acid, fire or increase HP, stamina or increasing ranged, melee damage or - you see where I am going. There are tonnes of different setups you can play around with - EACH - to your own playstyle!! 
⚫The enemy design is pretty damn good also. Rather threatening and menacing looking, some of them anyway... meanwhile others have HUGE BAHONGADAHONGS and carry a double barrel shotgun ready to shove it down your throat. I thought the design of these enemies were spot on - totally not distracted for a moment: 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3543729846 
⚫The little RPG skill system was rather fun to play around with. Increasing my stamina, melee damage and booze tolerance was like... the first thing I done. After that, I had fun playing around with my skillpoints. If you are worried about spending them - don't worry - there's a horse called "ALVARO" that will give you like... 69 skill points haha! Not even kidding, look yourself:
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3545119114 

[h1][b] Con's [/b][/h1] 
⚫Now, about the "STEALTH" - I feel like they invested WAY to much into stealth. If you don't stealth it can get tough because you can get rushed by everything and it can be a little unforgiving at times. Especially if you bleed, get shot at, get set on fire and spat at all at the same time... while managing your stamina (or missing shots).
⚫RANGED COMBAT - this was very temperamental for me. Reloading a weapon takes... a long time without proper setup. Not only that, if you miss a shot it can be unforgiving. Sometimes when you go to "shoot an enemy" you will miss... why? the hit reg I am going to assume. All I can say is this - Ranged for me, I did not like compared to melee. Not only that... ranged damage has a severe range falloff. A lever action is like 25 metres which just ruins the point.
⚫Using the raven skulls to teleport to a safe zone always teleported me to the VERY FIRST bed in the zone (imagine just spawning in, thats where it always teleported me to) which forced me to run back to the NPC to hand in my quest. I wish there was a SET TELEPORT option on the bed. I am not sure if this is intentional or a bug.
⚫You take "deathly" fall damage from a 4-5ft drop. This somewhat ruined the pace of the game because I was scared to jump off the top of a building or slightly fall down some ladders to avoid danger/getting hurt.
⚫Enemies can see through shadows and bushes... why even let us know we are "hiding" in the bushes with that little icon if enemies will just detect you almost at the same speed they usually do. No in-depth stealth system sadly.

[h1][b] Dead Man's Promise DLC [/b][/h1] 
This DLC was worth every penny. It took Blood West to a whole new level of enjoyment, especially with weapons and enemies. 

You are a "SHAMAN" in this DLC. You can find staffs that fire skulls, heal you and more. My personal favourite was the raven staff that let me fire skulls because it was a ranged weapon and melee... and if you done the skeleteon guys quest he opens his chest and gives you a book (trinket) that adds damage, a lot of damage to these ranged skulls. (P.S - think I'm getting my staffs mixed up).

THEN - YOU CAN GET YOUR OWN DEATHLY SUMMONS:

review:
I don't usually do in depth reviews or reviews at all, but I was honestly pretty disappointed with Blood West. I got it because I really enjoyed Gloomwood and wanted more stealth games like it. Blood West is a stealth game but I feel it's very similar to souls like games as you will be dying a lot, especially in Chapter 3. I just wanted to note down the things that make me somewhat dislike this overall good game.

1. You know how in FPS games the sniper always sways back and forth? Yeah that's every gun, and it will usually make you not miss shots whenever you get caught and chased. The reason that's such an issue is my other problem.

2. Headshots are practically required unless you like using shotguns. Most pistols require 3 to 4 shots to the body to kill your average enemy, which isn't too bad cause you'd just headshot for extra damage but the sway makes it near impossible to do that.

3. Healing items are mostly useless since you can get equipment that passively gives you health. Not only that but by the time you get towards the end of Chapter 2 and anywhere in Chapter 3, enemies usually will have you dead as soon as your caught which makes healing items extra useless.

4. The bosses of each Chapter are ok in concept but are mostly annoying or confusing. As you can expect putting an FPS game boss in a stealth game doesn't always fit, especially when ammo is limited and bosses can be extra tanky. Chapter 1 seemed promising with the second path to break cysts on the roots to lower the health for the actual fight through a stealth section, but the other bosses don't seem to have this. Maybe something to give us infinite stamina and ammo drops if we run out would make it a little more enjoyable, but I don't think I'll ever look forward to the bosses.

The last thing that disappointed me is just personal and isn't causing any issues to the game itself but when I bought this game, I got it a day or 2 before the sale. By the time the sale came out it was already too late to refund the game and get it at a lower price. Overall I wouldn't recommend people to buy the game but I wouldn't tell anybody to not buy it if they're interested, It's a good game just not what I expected. Just keep in mind this game gets very hard very quickly as you progress from Chapter to Chapter. It definitely should be considered more of a Souls like.

review:
An excellent horror shooter featuring exploration, stealth and desperate combat.

Blood West has a deliciously bleak setting with a haunting atmosphere. The highly addictive gameplay loop has the player exploring large, highly detailed open maps packed with secrets, dying to something gruesome, reviving and resuming their quest. (Death comes with a price: curses. These debuffs can be removed by using specific items or completing tasks, such as landing a set number of stealth kills.) You'll constantly weigh your remaining ammo, potions, and gear as you decide when to fight or flee. On the other hand, scavenging the lands for resources is part of the fun!

Each chapter keeps things fresh by having a distinct setting, new allies and unique enemies (ranging from undead bandits to eldritch horrors). There is a large variety of weapons, as well as a level progression system that unlocks a set of well-conceived passive skills. The pacing kept me engaged throughout; not once did the game (or its story) feel dull, and I felt the game had earned its conclusion by the end of the final battle.

review:
TLDR: 
Pretty fun retro stealth shooter "soulslike". 
If you like what you see in the trailer you will likely enjoy the game.

Story and setting:
The story is is as bare bones as the the hundreds of skeletons you will come across. 
However the "cursed western" vibes are immaculate and all the dialogue is a joy to listen to, from the different NPCs to the constant quips and commentary of your own undead gunslinger.

Gameplay:
You can either carefully sneak around, picking of enemies one by one, or you can chose the fast option and go in guns blazing (and likely die unless you have those twitch reflexes), both approaches are generally super satisfying.

There is a ton of enemy variety as well as a bunch of different weapons, trinkets and consumables to find allowing you to customize your play style.
This, paired with limited inventory space, the fact that the game does not pause on the inventory screen [spoiler]Unless you find and use a specific trinket[/spoiler] and a pretty short time to kill (for you as well as most enemies) requires you to carefully consider how you equip yourself and approach fights. 

All of that gives the game that "easy to learn, hard to master" feeling (although i was drowning in ammo, potions and cash by the end).

Over my 29 hours of playtime i didn't experience a single bug 
and i had only one crash (during death/respawn with no progress lost)

Summary:
Very good, i did enjoy my time a lot (and i also died a lot, especially in the second area)

review:
I was super excited to play this. As a huge fan of Deus Ex, Thief, and Dishonored, I figured this game would be right up my alley. Well... I was wrong. 

Blood West's base gameplay mechanics are atrocious, full stop. I can't remember the last time I played an action game with such transparently cumbersome movement and inconsistent shooting mechanics. Is it supposed to be inconsistent? Who knows? I do know that it feels like garbage. I'm having trouble understanding where the enjoyment is going to come from when the gameplay is janky unpolished trash. It feels clunkier than the famously clunky OG Thief from 1998 when polygonal games were new. That is unacceptable. Furthermore, the stealth system from Thief is dramatically better than what is offered here. Oftentimes, the stealth meter will be increasing and you have no idea why. They can also hear you sneaking in unrealistic scenarios and to compound the issue, the game might have the slowest sneaking in video game history. Sprinkling trinkets throughout the game to give you +15% sneak speed and +10% health does not make up for the horrid gameplay. 

This game, purportedly about free-form, creative, experimental combat, also punishes death severely and there is no manual saving. When you die you respawn with a "permanent" debuff. You have to spend the money that you tediously grinded out to fix it. This death mechanic is so poorly conceived it makes me question if the devs actually like immersive sim and stealth style games. It's almost as if the devs thought they were making a first person souls-like. Punishing the player for experimenting in this kind of game is stunningly misguided. Especially when you already have a hardcore one-death mode. Totally brain dead game design. What is also brain dead is the ai. There is, transparently, only one ai mode for every enemy and it is set to "annoy the player ". There is also essentially nothing to interact with. I don't think I saw a single door, just empty archways.  FFS, there are open windows, with no glass, that you cannot jump through. Because it is not an Immersive sim in any conceivable way. That would be a dishonest description.  

The tutorial takes less than 5 minutes if you don't die, yet 30% of players drop this game before the tutorial is done. That is truly remarkable, and I don't think I've ever seen anything like it. I can't help but think that this is because of the transparently awful base game mechanics. Only 28% of the people who bought this game have completed the first chapter. I think that that speaks for itself, TBH. If 72% of people who paid money for a game drop it before the first chapter is complete, we have something close to an objectively bad game. The devs should be straight up ashamed of this effort. It is an unpolished clunky mess of a game that still feels like it is in Alpha. I know that I will totally avoid any games from this dev in the future. 

All in all, this is one of the worst games I have ever played. Unenjoyable from the first second of gameplay until I decided to drop it. I just played through the 2023 remake of System Shock and it blows away this disaster is every single aspect. Go play that instead.

review:
[b][u]TL;DR:[/u][/b] Cool artbook and map, and a way to say thankyou to the indie developers of Trials of Fire.


[b][u]Full review[/u][/b]

The artbook is lavish. Not just a few concept art pictures, but 91 pages of high-res, super material, from the enlarged versions of the card art, concept pictures, intermediate illustrations and icons. And there is a fair amount of text that explains the rationale, and the style and motivation of the character classes. It talks about the NPCs and enemies and has a lot of pictures and material on the items, equipment and weapons from the game. If you are a fan of the Trials of Fire concept, the realm of Ashe or are just looking for some cool content to inspire your next table-top role-playing game, then this is definitely recommended.

And then there is the map. It is described as 4k, but it is actually a 5893 x 4535 image in 24-bit PNG format (40 Mbytes). This reveals the land of Ashe, the layout of the continent the various different features. While a nicety to look at, I actually found it useful for the Beacon of Hope campaign in the game, as it allowed me to figure out where I was, and note where on the map a set of "merchant scales" was, that I had to leave behind and move on, but later needed to come back for and recover to complete the mission. It is also useful if you are trying to systematically find all the landmarks, because you are completionist, like me.


[b][u]Access[/u][/b]

In case it helps anyone, to access the content, go to your Steam Library, then right-click on Trials of Fire in your Library. From there, select Manage --> Browse local files, and you will find the content in the "Extras" folder.


[b][u]Conclusion[/u][/b]

So, both items (book + map) are nice, but this is really a supporter pack to help the indie developers. For the price of a cup of café coffee, you get to say thanks to them for them making such a cool game. Definitely worth it, in my opinion.

review:
Absolutely fantastic game right here. Tinykin is basically Pikmin, but it's a 3D platformer.
There's no combat, only exploring and puzzle solving if that's your thing.

The levels are huge and filled to the brim with stuff to collect. 
What this game does exceptionally well is that each area has plenty of characters to make the world feel alive.
Your character has a soapboard which allows him to move around very quickly, and you can use your Tinykin to create shortcuts.

The speed, weight and feel of the controls are borderline perfect.
As for the Tinykin themselves, you don't have to worry about babysitting them as they always keep up with you.
Each of the types have their time to shine, although I wish yellows got used a bit more.

The only real complaint I have with this game is that getting all of the collectibles can be a pain.
There's no radar to locate what you're missing, so it can become frustrating trying to figure out where you haven't looked.
To clarify, you only need to complete the main objective of each area. The collectibles are just there for people who want to get them.

I'll be glad if this review convinces people to check out Tinykin. It deserves more love, and I hope we get a sequel or DLC for the first game.

Solitaire Game Halloween 2 is a basic mobile-app like solitaire puzzle game.  Solve various puzzle levels using Klondike style card moving and matching.  It's been done a million times before, for free, and free on mobile app stores too... yet this one has a hefty price tag on it.  Who knew you can just charge $5 for mobile trash?  I guess Creobit does. 

The developer, Creobit/8Floor, has copy + pasted this game an insane SEVENTY TWO TIMES onto Steam with minor reskins... why cash in on one asset if you can cash in on multiple copies of the same game? Asset flipping begins at home! Here's a list of Creobit's copy + pastes of this asset:

[list]

[*] Solitaire Victorian Picnic 1 + 2
[*] Strike Solitaire 1-3
[*] Sweet Solitaire: School Witch 1-3
[*] True Detective Solitaire 1 + 2 
[/list]

[i]These are all reskins of exactly the same game![/i]  What value is there in this spam/pollution glutting the Steam store for gamers?

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with some lazy "wings" to fill the pillar).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes Solitaire Game Halloween 2 might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

Solitaire Game Halloween 2 has the farcical price of around $5 USD, it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

review:
I love this game. There are genuinely many things about this that I loved and think show the passion and effort put into this game.

Game-play wise, I believe the game plays really great! The controls are pretty tight, Jimmy goes where you want him to go when you want him too and his jumps are pretty fluid, making the platforming feel fun. Combat is also fun too, however, I usually found myself using the throw attack a lot, but this didn't detract from my enjoyment. I like the time element of the levels too, I found an extra challenge in trying to go through levels as quickly as I could to beat my record and mixing attacks up between fork and bounce attacks to keep my momentum going, adding to the fluidity of the gameplay.

Visually the game is really fun too, I love the 8-bit style for all of the characters, levels and the musics, the Pasta Master Victory Dance is by far my favourite little visual element. The levels especially had pretty good variety with terrain ranging from creating bridges from destructible pillars to changing gravity with intractable items. I especially loved the design of the Pastomination, the music for that level mixed with the design gave of an almost alien like vibe which was cool. The boss fight being a 3 phase fight split across the level also made it an interesting final boss, with each phase increasing in difficulty. The story itself is also very charming too, with Pizza King's backstory being comically serious and sad making me chuckle.

In terms of improvements, I feel the game is pretty short, but for a £1.99 price tag for a game that has obviously had a lot of effort and passion put in by a single developer, you absolutely cannot grumble for the length. I also feel the level end screen comes in too quickly, meaning the Pasta Master Victory Dance is cut off a bit short at the end. I also felt that for some of the platforming sections, the camera changes can be a bit jarring, where it suddenly changes so you cannot see the platform you are standing on, however, this only really occurred twice throughout the whole game.

All in all this is a really great game that I would highly recommend. I can't wait to see what else there is to come for Pasta Master in the future :)

review:
I think the game is very enjoyable on a first playthrough when you are looking for all of the secret areas and just enjoying the world, you can get about 90 minutes of exploration out of it, but the character is effectively immortal because he respawns where he died, you lose some currency for cosmetic unlocks but it's not a significant amount. If you don't care for collection you can casually complete the game in 1 hour or less. The death only matters if you are doing a speedrun, which you do need to do for some unlocks like the songs, granted they are not challenging and if you want those achievements it will not be very time consuming (I got all the time-attack challenges with no practice, it's not that difficult). The hard mode has 1 less heart which in a practical sense, makes no difference because you are not losing any more progress. To be clear, I don't mind easy games, but in a long run, I think it makes the replay value for this game less appealing, and I think the hard mode should have been different, maybe the death would respawn you at the start of the stage, and I think it would need a few new enemies with ranged attacks. 

The music was actually the most enjoyable part of the game for me, it's pretty awesome and the game even comes with a music player, but you will need to unlock the songs by doing the challenges. In addition to the adventure mode with multiple save slots, you can unlock the arcade mode with limited time, and the time-attack mode that just puts a timer on your playthrough with an option to enable your ghosts. I actually didn't enjoy the first 2 areas in the game, but the level design and the visuals improved later in the game, if you are nostalgic for the 8-bit aesthetic I think you will enjoy it overall. The game has a TON of filters in a form of color palettes, and you can switch between them at any point if they are unlocked. In addition, there are a few other cosmetic options such as hats and lenses. 

Even though the secrets in this game are not very difficult, I think the level design is enjoyable and it's fun to look for those hidden walls and obscured paths. I don't have much to say in terms of platforming timing, it's pretty solid for what it is, but the game does not add much to change it. I will say I didn't like that character could not swing on some of the objects once they stopped. After I completed the game it would not allow me to go back and get all of the collectibles and I was only a few short of the achievement. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) If you do like that 8-bit aesthetic, the game has a relatively enjoyable level design (depending on the area), a lot of color palettes, cosmetic hats, and lenses. The stage design also has a lot of hidden walls so it's fun to navigate the game, at least the first time you play it. For the most part, the platforming timing is very tight, I don't have much to say there.

(+) Music was really the highlight of the game for me, I hope it's unique to this game because it was exceptionally good. You can also use the music player in the menu and unlock the songs for it.

(+) After you beat the game you can try other modes like arcade and the time-attack. You can also do various challenges to unlock more music and some colors if I am not mistaken. Good achievement support. 

Apparently, there are some host-based multiplayer mechanics too,  but I don't really have anyone to test what they do exactly.

[h1] FeedBack: [/h1]

[u] Nitpicks [/u] - I wish you could swing on those chandeliers even when they stopped, like left to right. You should ask the player at the end of the game if they want to go back and finish exploring, I was at like 98% and now I am not going to replay it.

[u] Hard Mode [/u] - right now it's the same as normal mode, having 2 hearts makes no difference because you still respawn where you die. Hard mode, should be a hard mode, not immortal mode. Maybe 3 lives, I also felt like the game needed more enemy variety, perhaps a few ranged enemies, at least for hard mode. The boss fights were pretty underwhelming. I mean feel free to disagree, but I don't see the point of a hard mode right now, might as well not even have it. 

[u] Optional Widescreen [/u] - I understand that you don't want to stretch it, but some of us have very big screens, I had to move my head closer to PC the entire run. If possible to do it, keep the map somewhere too.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 8/10 [/b]

Personally, I wanted the game to be a little more challenging toward the end, but if you want to play it one time and just enjoy the music and look for secrets, it's still very fun for 90 minutes or so. There are various unlocks, but I don't know, the game is just too easy for me to care and replay it. Anyway, still better than I expected, I think the music by itself was worth it.

I absolutely recommend anyone with even a slight interest in psychotherapy to try this game out, not because it'll blow your mind or because Leary was some kind of genius, but because it's a solid example of what I believe to be a therapy-oriented game.

Somewhere between interactive fiction and gestalt therapy (not mention the weird words and "archetypes"), this program is for all I have read basically a reproduction of Leary's PhD thesis. It might well have been a facebook quiz if it was written two decades later! It's not particularly avant-garde or exceptionally brilliant as far as I'm concerned, but it's neat to play through.

As far as LSD's legacy goes, it's worth remembering that one of the reasons Leary and others picked the drug up and started popularizing it, was that they believed it could be a tool to transform the way we think, but as anyone who's tried psychedelics (and isn't a numbskull) will tell you, drugs themselves are not a sole magical gateway to an "expanded" mind. Creative explorations of thought is very much what Timothy Leary's software intends here, and while the game aspect is pretty "meh", it's worth a playthrough. Not "because Leary", but because it's an interesting concept.

It's a decent management game, but it seems to have gotten harder than when I first tried it.  On the lowest difficulty setting, you cannot get off the ground with your own creations, you have to use franchises.

It also crashes on me a lot. It didn't at first, but something is making it worse over time. I had it loaded on 3 different computers, and they all did the same thing... the longer the same game goes on, the more prone it is to crashing.  Start a new game, and it works fine for a while.
Which brings up another point, no cloud saves! Which means if you play the game on a different device, you have to start all over again.
  It could use some more features too, like a simple spreadsheet to show who's working on what.  When you open an employee's window too, it should show which comics they are currently working on. 
  Overall though, I have fun playing it.  You need to pour a ton of money into recruiting in order to get good staff, and when you do, pay attention to the target audience.  Even if you get a good artist numbers, if they don't appeal to your audience, they're not going to be well-received.

review:
A decent enough hex crawler exploration game through a nicely designed desert planet, but unpolished and not a particularly deep experience.

Aesthetically, I like this game very much. And this look of things ties into the actual gameplay. When one thinks of a desert wasteland adventure, they might get the idea of barren featureless lands with nothing in them- Sandwalkers is more of a thriving world of deserts and oases, just with too much sun exposure and out of control weather for the populace. Your task is to revive the great tree that once brought life and shade to the world and navigate the wilderness to find fragments. These turns it into a survival simulator (at least in concept) where you need to weigh resource scavenging, plot out routes for the most efficient travel, and so on. This kind of falls off after the first few caravans (you make a new group if the old one gets wiped out, but keep progress) when you get a handle on things and unlock some perks to make the next playthrough more doable. 

Each character plays a role based on their species and they're all reasonably different. I don't think I found any outright bad options, although some didn't fit into my group synergies. It was also unusual to figure out who was a tank type at first. The Protector elephant was obvious, but he's slow enough to entirely miss the first round of defending against attacks. Meanwhile, the tornado casting mage had high shields and could go first, making him the better meat shield for the front line, for example. You can also load up on a few support people, including some individuals trapped in mirrors underground... who you can have multiple versions of? Actually, let's get into that.

Sandwalkers is not a polished game. Items can have negative amounts and it can cost you to sell them off. Preset walking paths just cancel midway for no reason that I can determine. My bard party member would randomly gain Exalted status instead of doing damage with his weakening attack on an enemy, etc etc. These aren't breaking bugs, as the game is not that hard by the 3rd or 4th caravan run (my 4th steamrolled 75% of the remaining game) but they're a reminder that there's loose nuts and bolts banging around under the hood of the car, even if it otherwise runs.

Storywise, it's so-so. There's decent world building lore to be had and world specific terms have hypertext like pop-ups that explain them- when they work and aren't spewing broken code. But much of the resolution to story events and the memory orbs you collect come off as broken abstract snippets that don't seem relevant or lack emotional weight. I kind of wish we started to bypass this aspect in modern gaming of gathering vague notes to compose the story, because they come off as scattershot or just lacking.

Unfortunately, Sandwalkers has a 'vast as an ocean, shallow as a puddle' feel to the world. Sure, there's a lot of hexes to cross, resources to find, etc- but it all just repeats very fast. You'll almost never see anything out in the world you haven't seen dozens of times. Same handful of regional enemies, same generic resources, and so on. Very few times will you come across any small locations with lore, secret treasure (very samey loot throughout the game), or anything else of note. The only real exception I had to this was while walking through a stretch of the desert near the end, I was accosted with a riddle challenge from storm spirits. This was unusual and interesting. Unfortunately, even if you fail at a riddle, you just get hit with a basic enemy encounter and the sequence ultimately wasn't a big deal despite how out of left field it came.

I'm not going to say I didn't enjoy my time playing, but most of the game is on an endless repeat of whatever you saw in the first few hours. Even the end game itself is very linear and to the point. This is a very 6/10 type of experience that could have been so much more.

review:
Its not BAD game but its far from a good one. Every change from PW1 is basically a straight downgrade:

- The biggest issue is the level design or lack thereof. A lot of the maps feel randomly generated rather than made with any sense of direction or purpose. Theres a few standouts (the train, the old west town) but most level design is 80% bland sprawling 'rocky area' or 'blocky urban something' made of featureless corridors and empty space. Each chapter has a theme of sorts but in the first two only a couple of maps in each seem to bother adhering to it, the rest being pretty interchangeable. 

- Whilst the gun play is fine the arsenal is all over the place, some weapons/upgrades/spells are very powerful while others are either utterly useless or just overshadowed by other options and feel unnecessary.
