review:
Project Warlock 1, while it had some flaws and design choices I didn't fully agree with, is a game I still think back to from time to time. When I heard there was a sequel, I had high hopes that they would take their experience from the first game to elevate it to the status of the best kitchen sink fantasy shooter out there.

Sadly, it seems no lessons were learned. Project Warlock 2 is worse than the previous in almost every way. It's not just that I don't agree with their design decisions, but that the sequel does nothing the first game didn't already do. It has the same flaws but worse, the performance is worse, levels are just easier to get lost in without really being innovative, and the quality tapers off the longer you play it. Several reworks throughout early access have done little to help it stand out against other games like it.

The gameplay is Nu-Doom with some light RPG mechanics. Killing enemies gives you health and cools down your abilities to kill enemies faster, and most encounters after the first few levels take place in arenas that enemies spawn into. The game is separated into three chapters with each having a unique character that can be remixed after beating it. There's secret hunting, boss levels, variable difficulties. Everything is really on the tin for these kinds of games, and this one is no exception. Compared to the first game, levels are bigger and more detailed, feeling more like Build or GZDoom, and the game is overall a bit harder and has more complex rpg mechanics.

Personally, I rarely care for psuedo-rpg mechanics in shooters. Tight design always triumphs over invisible math, and I think Project Warlock 1 and 2 both run into the same pitfalls there. However, balance is always just a nitpick for me.

The biggest problem I have is that the game looks bad. The first game had a distinct visual style, and the levels, while primitive in gameplay, invoked a kind of pseudo-retro shooter feel that not many games try to replicate. You could see enemy sprites clearly and appreciate what was going on. In Project Warlock 2, enemy sprites are muddy, and half of the time I can't even tell what I'm supposed to be looking at when a new enemy type shows up. It's overly stylized, and without the same level design, it just feels like just another inauthentic throwback.

Just like the first game, the weapon upgrade system is largely unwelcome to me. Some upgrades are blatantly overpowered, while others are sidegrades, tradeoffs, or entirely ineffectual. I can't speak for every machine, but larger maps chug along for me, whereas the first game ran perfectly (likely due to its simpler design). I've had plenty of clipping, out-of-bounds, and stuck spots. Encounters can be overly cheap monster spawns or entirely ineffectual mobs running in a straight line, whereas I only felt truly disadvantaged once in the first game and never felt like an enemy was poorly placed. Making new characters and a fresh start for each chapter should have been a smart idea, but somehow it still feels like a slog.

If this was the only game in the series, it would be a "meh" for me and I wouldn't be writing this. The problem is that it stacks up against it's own previous iteration and falls short. If you wanted a weird fantasy shooter thing, I recommend Hedon or Nightmare Reaper. If you want shooter rpgs, I would stick with things like System Shock 2, Peripeteia, or Sonar Shock. There might still be people who would enjoy this for what it is, but it would take so much visual and level overhauling to not say I'm disappointed in this.

review:
Creature of Havoc, originally a gamebook from late 1986, is perhaps the best Fighting Fantasy adventure, with a few close seconds, so I was really pleased to see that Tin Man had added it to their library of virtual FF gamebooks. I suppose I must remember the path through the book well enough and it's a tough one, easy to miss important knowledge and items, but I beat the book without too many dead ends. 

Originally it took me ages to find my way out of the dungeons, because I didn't understand the instructions for decoding the human speech and text, which you, as a monster, don't understand at first. I realised that the code wasn't quite as it appeared, leading to decodes the didn't make sense, but at length I realized what was actually meant and that within some of the speech or text were hidden reference numbers that you should turn to, to show you understand, leading to new choices. Of course that problem is removed here, once you find the vapour of tongues all foreign text is translated for you and you are given the extra choices. Admittedly there was something exciting about decoding the text yourself and discovering the hidden choices, but it wouldn't make much sense to have this in a computer controlled version of the book. It's such a relief to finally make it out of the dungeons with all their horror. 

There's obviously a lot more "backstory" to read through before starting than in any other FF gamebook, but it's quite enjoyable, just like Steve Jackson's FF novel, The Trolltooth Wars, which concerns similar events to those of Creature of Havoc. You could say Creature of Havoc is the most ambitious of the original gamebooks and the concept succeeded well. There are other parts where I think the computer game loses something that the book had. The best example is probably the part where you are supposedly killed by Toadmen. In the game it doesn't seem so much like the end, because under the right circumstances a way out will appear. In the book there is a way out too, but you may not spot it. That's something that made Creature of Havoc such an exciting challenge, very hard to cheat at and unique from the other books.

As the "Creature of Havoc" you're forced by your nature to kill many innocents early on and behave in cruel selfish ways, but of course you gradually develop more control over your actions. You find an unlikely and invaluable companion outside the dungeons, you're helped by trecherous witches who are concerned about maintaining a sort of good and evil balance. The evil necromancer who is threatening this balance, Zharradan Marr, is strange, he appears to be part orc or goblin. You come to learn that he's manipulating your path from afar and things get really interesting when you finally meet him.

review:
[h1] if you gaze long into Chaos, Chaos also gazes into you[/h1]

This adventure was written by Steve Jackson, the co-creator of the series as well as the most adventurous of the pair, adding magic, space, horror, super heroes in his various books. This one is a back to the roots and is often ranked highly in "best Fighting Fantasy" lists so it should be great, right? Right?

First of all, Tin Man Games did an excellent job as usual to make this book in the ebook format, it's also including very good improvements as automatically adapting the text or choices according to your inventory/skills.
This is very important as the original book was very difficult and its difficulty ranked up as you needed to read between the lines/decipher a weird language to advance in the story but here it's done more or less automatically for you.

Its very high difficulty is actually why it's loved so much, as well as the very intriguing story of playing a monster for once. The background part of the story is also very long and full of lore.
The first times, you will suffer, like in the author's House of Hell but hopefully, after you beat it once (and even the cheat modes available in the app's "free read" mode won't help you!), you can finally come to understand that it was almost like a huge epic. 

In conclusion, it's indeed a masterpiece, but it's also probably the most difficult book in the whole collection right now. Think of it as the "last boss" book and don't try this one first!

Surprisingly, there is no support whatsoever for user maps.

Overall, a disappointment.

review:
Maptroid: Worlds is a 2D metroidvania with a rather unique twist: the entire game takes place in what appears to be a traditional map screen that you'd find within a full-fledged metroidvania. Despite its (very) short length, it provides an entertaining jaunt for those of us obsessed with the explore/collect/explore loop offered by games of the genre.

The presentation here is spartan, but it perfectly suits both the core conceit and gameplay itself. The appearance of the game world will instantly look familiar to anyone who's played a Metroid game, making gathering your bearings a breeze. A small panel atop the screen displays your powerups, keycards, and even a small side-view representation of what the portion of the game world you're currently in "would" look like in a traditional metroidvania. Nice touch.

Special callout here for the music: the soundtrack is gorgeous and I found myself revisiting planets just to hear their particular tunes.

You won't find any combat or puzzles here, really - it truly is about navigating a grid, finding stuff, and then returning to navigating more of the grid. It's peaceful and relaxed, aside from a segment or two I won't spoil here.

If you're a freak for metroidvanias and looking for something new and low-stress, you can't go wrong here. Snag it for a few bucks and see how it hits you.

Preface: I am recommending this game with the caveat that this is indeed an earlier work from the creator. As such it has quirks; your actions have limited consequences compared to their newer titles. The work itself is a bit quieter and toned down comparatively, but it does lean into the more lighthearted genre and I think that it's meant to be this way. While there is some mystery and intrigue interconnected within the games lore itself its rudamentary, however I'm grading it based on how it would appear as someone playing it back during its release rather than in comparison to their current games (which I have now played VtM: Night City which this pales in comparison by).

However, I would still wholeheartedly recommend this as a Text Based RPG. Why? Because it's light, it's fluffy and gentle. It has an air of gentle romance that I think is nice and can be seen more as a means of light reading similar to a "light novel" genre as opposed to an "epic fantasy" that VtM provides in their more recent works. If you're looking for something that leans into that category to dip your toes into Text Based RPGs then I would recommend giving this a try as it won't impede your enjoyment if you make the wrong decision, and it's short enough that you're not parsing through several hundred thousand words to get to where you need to "fix" your story line. That being said what I do like the most about this game is the fact that it IS simple, and allows those new to the genre to learn by giving them simplified stats to work off of. It was a breath of fresh air and that's something that I think is needed when epics exist in the space that can be daunting and hard to handle. There's nothing more that I love than being able to sit down after a stressful day of work, and just romance a silly little buffoon in my dazzling little outfit and play out silly fantasies of theatrical Renaissance while uncovering more lore and mysteries hidden around the game itself.

review:
[h1]Overview:[/h1]
'[i]Magic gems[/i]' is a color collecting game where the objective is to collect as many colored tiles as you can in as few moves as possible to meet the amount needed to finish the level. On the surface it seems casual and innocent enough but soon enough you realize the flaw behind the game and I'll explain that later. There are 11 levels in total and all of them play the same. No new features or mechanics are introduced, it's quite literally just clicking on the gems with the most connected pieces.

The game itself is done very poorly and appears to have been developed by one person rushing to push out a cheap product that lacks even the most basic of quality. There's no story, no introduction, no tutorials and not even an ending for all your troubles. Absolutely nothing. There aren't even achievements despite the game stating that there are, that's false advertising at its finest. In addition to that, the reviews on the store page are as believable as a casino telling you that you're gonna win the next big one. This is essentially [i]Steam's[/i] version of a cheap dollar store clearance toy and it can be completed in less than 20 minutes.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
'[i]Magic gems[/i]' advertises itself as a (and I quote) "[i]three in a row[/i]" game but is nothing like that. What the game [i]actually[/i] is is a game where you can essentially click anything you want, even single gems can be collected and counts as a move. The whole "three in a row" premise is thrown out the window because you aren't trying to create a row of at least 3 gems of the same type, you're just clicking them (preferably in large clusters). That is [i]not[/i] "three in a row". So if you're a fan of those types of games like the developer suggests, avoid '[i]Magic gems[/i]' as it isn't that at all. Even then avoid it as it has more red flags than an Olympic downhill skiing event.

Digressing from that, the game (as simple as it is) becomes surprisingly difficult in later stages as the moves provided to the player are too small to be able to complete a stage at a reasonable level. More than half of the levels give the player 20 moves which for the most part is more than enough to meet quota required to beat the level but once you hit the later levels it comes down to luck to beat them. You begin having to rely on the randomly generated levels to form large clusters in your favor or else beating the stage becomes impossible. For the most part you're only able to find clusters of 4 or less gems when you require more than 100, and you only have 20 moves to get there, do the math. Only in the stages near the end of the game does the game finally have some mercy and give you an extra 5 moves and even then it doesn't help a lot as the gems required to beat [i]those[/i] levels scale up even higher.

Another thing that's confusing is the sprites used to represent quota and moves. The game uses a red diamond shaped gem to represent the players' quota. Coincidentally, there's a red diamond shaped gem in the game. So imagine my confusion when I was only trying to collect the red gems thinking that's what the game requested when in fact, I could just get any gem I wanted. Why use a sprite of a gem almost identical to one of the gems on the playing area when you aren't asking for that particular gem?

Not only that but the moves are represented by what looks like a circular yellow gem. And low and behold, one of the gems on the board is [b][i]also[/i][/b] a circular yellow gem! Once again, I believed I needed both red and yellow so you could imagine my dismay when the numbers weren't adding up when I started collecting them. It's just baffling how you could mess something up that bad. You'd have to [b]try[/b] to screw something like that up. Honestly, it would've been better to just have numbers with words rather than pictures. At least that would eliminate any form of confusion.

[h1]Controls:[/h1]
Just click on the largest clusters and hope to god that you meet the required number to complete the level.

[h1]Graphics:[/h1]
Appears very cheaply made with just a few game sprites here and there with a basic game board with basic sprites. The background also looks like something you can literally recreate in [i]Microsoft Paint[/i] and holds no decent quality whatsoever.

[h1]Audio:[/h1]
The game has no sound effects but it [i]does[/i] have rather crappy music with a terrible loop. Trust me, within a minute, the music becomes gruelling to say the least and guess what? There's no option to turn it off, what a treat.

[h1]Conclusion/TL;DR:[/h1]
'[i]Magic gems[/i]' is a color collecting game where you collect gems as efficiently as possible with the given moves. It does [i]not[/i] play like a "three in a row" or "match-3" game as many potential buyers might think. You just click the biggest cluster of gems of the same color. The gameplay is simple, straightforward and offers no new mechanics whatsoever and gets old fast on top of looking very cheaply made and being riddled with fake/paid for reviews. Even with 11 levels and gameplay based on luck, the game can still be finished in under 20 minutes. It gives absolutely nothing to the player (even an ending/credits screen) for beating the game and for a price of CDN$ 14.49, that's criminal. Avoid at all costs.

Rent's Due Is An Indie Made Platformer That Really Ended Up Enjoying It. It Does Have It's Pros And Cons (Which I Will Get Into Shortly), But Knowing That This Game Was Created By A One Man Team Who Not Only Listens To Criticism, But Also Continuously Works On New Content AND Fixing Any Bugs That Get Found Truly Impresses Me; So I Do In Fact Let A Few "Cons" Pass Knowing All This.

That Being Said, After Two Hours Of Running Through 22 Levels, I Was Really Enthralled With The Landscapes Created Through The Unreal Engine While Finding Fun Little Easter Eggs Through Some Of The Levels. The Platforming Had A Perfect Level Of Difficulty In My Opinion. Not Too Easy, Not Too Hard (However, I'm Not Brave Enough To Face The Permadeath Mode). Now There Were A Few Levels That Left Me A Little Frustrated Towards The End Of The Game, However I Was Playing At 5am With A Lack Of Sleep So I Don't Judge Too Harshly.

With All That Being Said, There Were A Few Things That Got A Little Bit Of A Negative Reaction From. First Came Around Level 6. I Was Unaware That If You Double Tapped The Jump Button Twice VERY Quickly, You Get The Maximum Amount Of Momentum And Jump Even Higher. Maybe I Just Missed That Tutorial, But I Actually Had To Message The Dev Because I Was So Lost And Though It Was A Wall Jumping Bug. Later In The Game I Discovered That The Hitbox Is A Little... Larger Than Expected. I Spent A Long While Getting Murdered By Laser Beams, But With Enough Resolve I Was Able To Get Through. The Only Other Thing I COULD Complain About Is The Lack Of Story In The Actual Game, But As I Said Earlier, I Can Give That A Pass Since It Was All Being Done By One Guy.

Overall This Is A Very Fun Platformer That I Recommend (ESPECIALLY FOR ONLY $3!!!) Can't Wait To Experience The Free DLC The Dev Has Mentioned And I'm Excited To See What Else This Guy Brings Us In The Future!

review:
This is another horror run & hide game with a few cheap jump scares, and it seems heavily influenced by '[b]Outlast[/b]'.  The main antagonist who chases you for the first two or three sections of the game is a huge beast of a man.  He's tall, overweight, bald, and shirtless... which looks way too much like Chris Walker.

This guy doesn't speak though.  He wears a gas mask, and makes noises through it like a snorting pig.  When you hear a noise that sounds like a chainsaw being fired up, you only got two or three seconds to start running.  I don't understand why there's a chainsaw sound, cause this guy just kills you with his bare hands.

The other antagonists in the game are called both "[i]zombies[/i]" and "[i]mutants[/i]".  But again, coincidentally, all of those guys look like they auditioned for roles as "[i]variants[/i]" in '[b]Outlast[/b]'.  Some of them even have all their skin flayed off.  One of them, a bigger one who stands out from the rest, is totally naked.

The story is so shallow that it's practically non-existant.  Your brother went to Chernobyl to take some photos, but once he entered a building he got trapped and couldn't get back out the way he came in.  Before his phone battery died, he managed to get a message to you asking for help.  So you go to rescue him.

However, when you enter, you also get trapped the same way he did.  Your goal is to find your brother, and/or a way out.  This maze of a cinder block building is littered with rusty 55-gallon drums and debris.  You wander back and forth through hallways, up and down stairs, and across metal catwalks.

You have to find generators and power them up in order to unlock several doors.  You only have a flashlight on you, but the environment is sometimes too dark for the flashlight to be of any help.  Unfortunately, there are no game settings to brighten your view either.

Without any defense capabilities, your only choice is to run and hide when being attacked.  This almost always means navigating quickly through this combination of obstacle course and labyrinth, looking for either a small hole in the wall, or a tunnel the size of an industrial air vent shaft, that you can crouch and crawl into.

Throughout the game you'll see dead females with short black hair, dressed in what looks like hospital gowns.  Sometimes you'll see a lone body, and sometimes you'll see a pile of them, like it's a serial killer's dump site.  Also, once in a while you'll see a zombie munching on one of them.  However, there is no explanation as to who these females are, or why they all look alike, or why they are all dressed alike.

There are no manual saves.  When you die, or leave the game and come back later, you will restart back at the last checkpoint.  The checkpoints divide the game up into seven sections, with one save for each section.  At each checkpoint, you'll find a short scribbled note of useless information from your brother.

For a game made in 2022, the graphics are way below average. Many things look "[i]blocky[/i]", and crudely detailed.  The ending was disappointingly anti-climatic, and very unsatisfying.  The game did run perfectly fine though, which is the best thing I can say about it.  I personally experienced no glitches at all.

It should only take you 2.5 to 3.5 hours to complete, depending on your pace of exploration, your sense of direction in the dark, and how many times you die.  In summary, this game rates a big "[i]No[/i]" from me.  There is no fear, no surprises, no story, no trading cards, no achievements, no replayability, and no fun.

review:
Castle of Delights is part of a series made by the same developer. This is the 2nd game in the series and probably my recommended starting point. While you meet a lot of characters that already know each other and have to catch up on how they are related to one another, the story itself is easy to follow, it presents two compelling goals (Vulpes and Zamora looking for the liquer for their own reasons) and manages to resolve them both to bring events to a satisfying conclusion.

In my personal opinion, the "Delights" series by Enygmage has three big hooks to pull you in. Its art style, at least in my experience, is unique, and I really appreciate the time and effort necessary to create every image we see in the game, of which there are quite a few. Next are the charming characters, both brave and playful so the art can showcase them in all their beauty. And third but certainly not least, the world of dreams and how it fits together into the big picture, I must say looking at humans as 'dreamers', outsiders lost in the world of dreams, is a refreshing take that holds a lot of novelty.

The games are quite short overall, you can reach all the endings and get every achievement in slightly over an hour, depending on how fast you read and how much time you spend appreciating the artwork. Not that it's a bad thing, that makes these bite-sized adventures perfect for a short gaming session, and if you like one then the others will probably suit you too. The fact they provide lots of checkpoints to return to should you hit a dead end helps keep the game moving, so you never really get stuck; even when RNG makes a battle go poorly, you have a good chance to pass it next time with average or better luck.

The first three games in the series share save files. That doesn't mean you can play all three in one game, as loading a save from one game in another is likely to get you an error, but it is something to keep in mind. I just kept their saves on different pages to not get them mixed up, and focused on each game in its own right.

As far as Castle of Delights in particular, this game has to deliver a lot of information about the characters and the world they inhabit, but the messaging is more subtle and natural. Some information is shared for Zamora's sake, as she is a Dreamer who lost her way in the dream world, but some of it is told through events and the behaviours of certain characters, like how Morpheus treats Zamora, or how Elylah, Vulpes and Nostalgia think and feel about each other. The more the game sticks to the 'show, don't tell' method of storytelling, the more freedom it gives the player to form their own opinions about these characters, and that is a freedom I appreciate, it proves the author put in a lot of work and forethought when creating this game.

Beyond that, Castle is also a lot less linear than the previous game. Although the game still goes through a few key beats on the way to one of a few endings, you can reach those endings through very different paths, each featuring unique artwork. That's what draws me to games with branching storylines, and I must say it was a pleasure to explore every path, including the last section when you are exploring the castle at leisure, with all three characters - Elylah, Vulpes and Zamora. The fact the castle has a gallery full of artwork is another bonus! They even show glimpses of characters the player hasn't met yet, foreshadowing future events, but as far as this game goes, the endings do a good job wrapping up the story and resolving Zamora's and Vulpes' search with a -very- satisfying conclusion.

Inevitable Excess - played a bit, it went wild and hard from the getgo ("random" mechanics to combat "anomalies") which with level 20 commander fighting for his dear life was not what i expected from mook combat. Dropped and may revisit later. Didnt like it too much, story about closing paradoxical rifts sounds alright enough, but it doesnt feel great. Feels like rushed something they wanted to put into the main story, and its start from before the last battle of the campaign doesnt feel great.

Through the Ashes - new mechanics, interesting concept of low level fight for every stone and healing potion, but its focus around fighting encounters or spending valuable resources to bypass doesnt sit exactly where it wants to be. Environmental interaction is janky and not allways clear what you will get out of it. + Why cant my cleric just cast lesser restoration on the "hireling" and i must spend a potion of the same spell to lessen hirelings "(un)health" status. I feel it would fare far better at BG III engine/setup, but they gave it a good shot nonetheless.

The Treasure of the Midnight Isles - What i wanted was 1-20 rogue lite mode with maybe 1-10 mythic progression to test builds for the main campaign via combat arenas. We got... Something close, i dont recall the max level, maybe its 20, mythic is not at 10 tho. You have to choose from different paths on the islands, sacrificing the rest. Sometimes you need to not rest again so you pick lower difficulty, or you want piece of a treasure map, or extra exp/mythic rank for next time so you sacrifice the other options. Not great. The undertows are also random and very bad (have a party of mages when every spell is nat1 from kiling your run) - random buff/debuffs for the entire island. Tailwinds are nice, but not nice enough - permanent boosts for one run. Treasure is nice enough, vendors have good enough selection of gear and you have after each main boss to reequip + you earn loot at the islands proper as well. Difficulty curve is very wonky (one island low threat is easy peasy, another at medium difficulty wipes you), early elemental pillar islands are very hard. And you dont get to squad up 4 people from the start, and starting with 6 is borderline not a thing, investing to merks is expensive and you get like 1 per recruit island per boss island voyage. Getting a squad of 6 is way too late, instead of being and option from the start/after first boss. I hoped for random battle arenas with random enemy types and encounters, instead its themed islands. And getting shadows/wights/undead when you dont have death ward/restoration online yet, or island full of air elementals with permanent vortex xdx dmg each round + concentration + ranged attack penalties is death sentence for otherwise a good party composition. Running dhampir only has been surprisingly easy mode...

all in all, if this gets cheap, might be worth it, the treasures add some nice items and side story for commander, but it was not great bunch of dlc

I genuinely love Starfield. The world-building, the freedom, the ships, the outposts  it’s everything I wanted in a Bethesda space RPG. I’ve sunk hundreds of hours into one character, pushing them well beyond level 300, and I still find new things to do.
But here’s the problem: Bethesda designed Starfield as a long-haul game, not a short replayable one.
Outposts are built to expand, link resources, and grow over time.
Ship building is a massive time investment, meant to evolve with your character.
The whole premise is that your universe grows with you.
And yet… the engine can’t sustain it.
Without a proper save file cleaner, the game slowly chokes itself with leftover data  ghost scripts, orphaned quests, broken references. Eventually your once-great save risks crashing, bloating, or stuttering until you’re told the only “solution” is to restart.
Restarting is fine in Skyrim or Fallout where each playthrough can feel fresh. But in Starfield? Restarting means deleting years of investment in outposts, ships, and character progression. That’s not replay value  that’s punishment for long-term players.
Yes, modders have stepped in with experimental save cleaners, but this should not be left to unpaid volunteers. Bethesda knows this problem has existed since Skyrim. If Starfield is truly meant to be “a game you can play forever,” then we need official tools to keep forever saves stable.

review:
Starfield is one of those games that I really want to love.

I'm a big fan of Bethesda's work, first being introduced to them through Morrowind. But Starfield is the first game from Bethesda that I can't recommend, and I keep trying to find that same feeling Morrowind gave me.

Starfield has a lot going for it. Ship battles and customization can be fun. The same kind of Fallout-esque first person shooter style fun with a lot of loot to sort through. By all accounts this SHOULD be a hit.

The issues where this games struggles, and where I see several space type games failing, is the transition between space and planets. So much of this game is loading screens because you load to travel to a planet, you load to land, you briefly load to get out of your ship, and if you're real lucky, you'll load again to enter a building. And then you'll spend a brief time in that area and end up doing that all again just to sell off your loot.

While I get the attempt to make a more realistic space game, I'm furious that every person you speak with is human... if you're going to make a space game without aliens, you need to make me care about the different factions in the story, and to be honest, they're pretty lame. The only faction that made me care was the UC sysdef, and that's because I really want to kill their leader everytime I accidentally get caught with contraband I didn't even know was on this ship I'm trying to register...

Setting up outposts, researching, making weapon and armor mods, these should all be less painful systems. I try my best to utilize those systems because that's such a big chunk of getting the weapons you want, but it is such a time suck.

EDIT: Another point I thought of that absolutely drives me crazy is how the best stories in this game are the things you heard about that happened in the past, or that you find through writing. I understand that lore and world building is a key point for Bethesda games, but if you're offering me the choice between a time where I have to listen to an ultra-wealthy man and a priest argue about whether a space rock was sent from god or not, or a time where there are interplanetary battles taking place with xenowarfare and mechs, I'm going to choose the latter... there are also so many points in the game where they could have leaned further into the space horror or cosmic horror of the game, and they don't. Basically what I'm saying is this is the unseasoned chicken of games, and I know for a fact there's a whole spice rack that could have been used...

----SPOILERS BELOW!!!!----

While I love the endgame idea of kind of restarting the whole thing from the beginning, and letting you choose how you approach that restart, there's not enough in the game to make me care about that.

Ultimately, I'll keep coming back to this game from time to time, but it'll never be quite what I'm looking for.

There are a lot of great things in this game: ship builder, outpost building, manufacturing, excellent faction stories. Like REALLY good stories. This game is one of the best scifi themed games. But all of these pointless because game systems are badly interconnected. You have the best ship builder game, but space exploration and space battles are meh. So your ideas and vision of the perfect ship wont matter that much. There are good outpost and industry systems, but the whole usefulness of it is just plain money printing which you wont need anyway. The story lines. Yeah, stories is extremely good and this game has a lore heavy as we used to see from bethesda games. The side stories alone carrying this game. But, it is just not enough for me because i need to go through bad UI and load screens to get things done. This is simply not uneven story pacing due to technical limitations. 
Yes, and then there are technical issues. I really struggled to put all the technical things in place to have a smooth playthrough. TBH, technical side of things is just not acceptable in the modern game industry. 
Overall, this game is just a sort of good wrapper but bad filling. 
Still, ill keep my eye on the development and future updates and have a plan to give it another shot because there are some things that are just so incredibly good.
TBH, leaving this game a downvote is just a sad moment for me. :(

review:
[h1]Bethesda Gave Me the Stars… Then took away the sky [/h1]

I was walking in New Atlantis, just there wandering, alone, thinking about how this city looks big but feels small at the same time, that's where I stumbled upon it, 'TerraBrew' i went there, maybe to get some latte or just black coffee with no sugar, the employees were arguing with someone, so i thought I'd help myself, went to one of the tables, and took a sip from the latte left there, the next thing i knew is UC security all over the place, weapons all drawn at me, and they telling me that i am under arrest, I thought okay, maybe I'd pay a fine or get a lawyer or something, but nooooo. Blackout, i wake up in jail, somewhere in space, and Commander Ikande is there telling me that I have the qualifications to work for space government (i really wish getting a job in real life was this easy) and infiltrate the Crimson fleet as a spy. This where I realized that Bethesda don't make games, they make fever dreams with budget.
And that's basically Starfield, a Space RPG in space, where logic is optional and your ship is real but your freedom is mostly a 'Suggestion'.

You see a planet there, you like it? you think am gonna fly there and live the space exploration dream, Nope, you basically open a menu, go to map, then get out of planet click again to get out of system, click on that system to enter, click on that planet to travel to, and maybe you start to think this is it... but again nope... loading screen appears. you reach that planet and now times to land and yes you guessed it again, open that google map thing and click where to land and again loading SCREEN, you think OK at least i will fly inside the planet exploring and all, but again no, you only land and walk from there, and even if you want to change the spot you landed at, you again open map and click on different spot and land, A PROCESS THAT KILLS THE IMMERSION!!!! OF YOUR EXPERIENCE.
 It feels like if i gave you a Lamborghini car, you set there very happy, can't believe yourself. Now let's have a ride, but nope the steering wheel is locked instead am gonna show you [b]A POWERPOINT SLIDESHOW OF YOUR DREAMS BEING SHATTERED!.[/b] They build an entire galaxy then taped a fast travel system to it, and called it immersive, it's a very disappointing experience that has zero seamless space to planet flighting, it completely ruins the space exploration experience and every time you get that excitement feeling it just gets shutdown by that process.

Now to be fair there's always the bad and good, and Oh boy, this game makes up for those dream shattering moments in some way.

[h3]SHIP BUILDING:[/h3]
This is the best thing in the game, it feels like Lego but for adults with interior design trauma, you want to build a war machine?? yeah you can. you would like a comfy mobile home? or maybe an IKEA showroom that you can decorate and make it yours, yes you can do all that(You can even put a toilet with toilet paper in the cockpit, for some reason). this is something I've put many hours into and every time i feel to do more and more building non stop, it's therapy.

[h3]World details:[/h3]
I’ve never seen a game in my life that is this detailed. Bethesda’s art team went feral, every single item, sandwich, object, every lab or deserted outpost there are details everywhere, in every corner around the galaxy. I think someone personally hand placed them during a 3 AM breakdown. i am amazed, Many times I would just walk around, staring at objects like a creep, because the level of detail is insane. you can tell someone’s soul went into decorating these spaces. Heck, there’s more storytelling in an open closet or lab than in the story itself. BUT.... then you leave those handcrafted areas and land on a random moon or a planet, and the magic is just gone, yes there are breathtaking views and very cool alien skies, but the details are gone, it's just an empty copy pasted layout on every planet to the point where exploring becomes very boring and has no value, i do understand that this is what space in reality would look like, empty and vast but still, we need something to keep the player engaged, not to find abandoned facility with the same layout on all moons and planets.

[h3]Story:[/h3]
yeah the main story is there, you touch some rock, see a vision, float a bit, tbh i didn't care, it felt as if they were trying to be deep and mysterious, but to me it felt shallow and forgettable, However...all the real magic went into the side quest, especially the faction storylines, those are where the game comes alive, I've enjoyed all of them, they'er not top tier, but they are solid enough to keep you engaged and interested.

[h3]Companions:[/h3]
I was never this disappointed with this kind of companions. It was a disastrous experience. They don’t feel like your companions, they feel like some company HR interns but in space. you commit a very tiny mistake and they’re like, “I don’t think that aligns with our mission values” Especially Sarah Morgan. I HATE YOU.
Sometimes they feel very dumb. for example, Andreja will keep asking me, “Can we talk for a moment?” while I am engaging in combat and fighting for my life, and it happened not one time or two, but many times, at the end i just preferred to travel alone with no companions.

[h3]Gameplay:[/h3]
I'd say it's okay, typical Bethesda gameplay, I did really enjoy the guns in this game, the combat and shooting mechanics where okay i guess, also the ship battles where fun sometimes, the most fun time i had is when i hijacked others ship and enter them and steal the ship and kill all it's crew. also there are many guns in this game, i loved them, they are detailed, you can customize them, put a silencer, but for nothing since the stealth in this game is garbage. 

[h3]Photomode:[/h3]
I am really amazed here. While nothing particularly special, the game is damn pretty that you could accidentally create a masterpiece. there’s so much to capture, alien moons, space sunsets, giant gas planets, it’s a straight desktop wallpaper factory, the depth of field is also really good in this game.

finally i would rate this game a 6/10 for building a dream world and hold it all together with loading screens, 10/10 for ship building alone, maybe 8/10 for that coffee theft to spy career shift, AND -999 FOR PRETENDING FAST TRAVEL IS THE SAME AS FLYING!!!

Dear Bethesda,
You made something huge. Something packed with tons of details, art, ambition, and almost feels handcrafted (the planets are not though). But then you sat me down and said:
“You see that planet? You can’t actually go there. But here’s a loading screen.”

You gave me a spaceship and told me I could explore the stars...
Then made me teleport every single time and open that damn Google Maps in space.

You handed me the keys to a galaxy,
and then locked the steering wheel.

WHY?

We didn’t want loading screens.
We wanted to feel control.
I wanted to feel the journey.
To live like the real thing.

I would say only buy this game if you really enjoy space, or you are just like me who like to stare maybe for long times, at objects, views, spaceship interior, or love to take screenshots, because photomode is decent. it's not worth full price unless you truly understand what you are getting. tbh there's much more to talk about but i feel this is enough for now.

review: This game, even after so many hours, just feels empty. The only aspect of this game that really sucked me in was the shipbuilding (an amazingly designed system with a few hiccups). The story? Lame and disjointed. The worldbuilding? Nonexistent compared to TES or Fallout. The gameplay? It was fine but not a huge improvement over anything else Bethesda has made. The RPG elements? Horrid. The dialogue? Awful. The graphics? A horribly mixed bag with some elements (like space) looking beautiful with others (the NPCs in cities) looking terrible. Map design and exploration? Cities are just as small as ever and the world feels empty and devoid of reasons to explore. Everything is procedural generation and I found ONE interesting quest on a random planet. If you like endless repeated dungeons across planets that are supposed to be barren yet have dozens of abandoned outposts with a maddeningly poorly written story and world with no depth, this game is for you. If you like quality, go elsewhere in Bethesda's catalog or just anywhere else on Steam. I regret my purchase.

review:
This is going to be one of the most painful reviews I've done. I have, regrettably, 300+ hours in this game. For the love of god, don't do that to yourself. I am clearly NOT WELL and easily susceptible to delusions. I tried so hard to believe I was playing a good game in those 300 hours. At first I thought it was misunderstood. Then I thought it was uniquely for me. Then I thought it had potential, and that I could fix it, so I downloaded the creation kit. Then I finally beat the game, and it hit me, this wasn't good. 

It's issues:
1. Plots bad. Quite boring and stale. Being "starborn" is so absurd I can't believe it's real. The ending twists and reveals are lackluster or eye-roll worthy. About the only interesting reveal was what happened to Earth and that's mildly interesting.
2. Some of the side quest lines are interesting like the Crimson Fleet and UC Vanguard but they still feel held back a bit. The other side quests just lack meat to their stories. 
3. I think a lot of the world building and aesthetics are decently handled, but just not in depth enough, especially given this is the first entry in a new, original IP.
4. Exploration is absolutely killed. I know I'm beating a dead horse here but the random points of interest on a randomly generated square of land is not fun, and the vehicles they added barely helped. 
5. Space is practically pointless considering you can't fly to different planets, everything is fast travel essentially. As a result, the cool ship customization ultimately feels a little pointless. 
6. Underwhelming main cities. New Atlantis is impressive for Bethesda but is unbelievable as a CAPITOL CITY for the majority of what is left of humanity. I literally drew up plans for an expanded New Atlantis because I just wanted it to be good SO BAD. Neon makes sense size wise but i still feel it should be much bigger or at the least not split up with loading screens. And Akila City is just kind of pathetic. Could've had a bunch of smaller towns outside of it giving it kind of a mini Skyrim feel to match it's Whiterun feel. 

And so many other minor things that just add up. It's a shame because i thoroughly enjoy it's semi-grounded approach to future space travel and aesthetic. I really like the ship building but i am the type of person that spent time in the gummy ship editor in KH I am not normal. Base building is similarly fine, I'm just definitely willing to put up with bad base building because I enjoy it so much. I like the design of the ship parts and interiors and the lore and purpose of all of the different ship manufacturers.

But most importantly, the reason I kept playing is i LOVE space. I love the idea of space travel and I like that this fictional vision was near future instead of waaaay in the future. I was so locked in on the idea that I could design my ship, interior layout and exterior, decorate it, fly it (barely), and fight with it. It's like Star Citizen, but i can customize my ship. It's like No Man's Sky, but I can customize and walk around my ship. Except it's not like those games all. This game has the one thing those 2 games lack, an actual story, and it's not even good. At least it's SOMETHING compared to those games, and if I could have the perfect mixture of those 3 games, I'd probably never play anything else again.

But this is NOT. THAT. GAME. 

This is what feels like the final nail in the coffin for Bethesda. Conceptually flawed, this seems unsalvageable. Creation Kit modders seem to want nothing to do with it, except the ones utilizing the creation club, which is going to cost you even more money. Bethesda publishing their own stuff on there at the cost of MORE MONEY when the game is horrendously lackluster on launch is such a kick in the nuts. I have yet to play the actual DLC expansion, but I hear it's not helping very much. I don't think this game can pull a No Man's Sky, no matter how badly I wanted it to. 

3/10

review:
Good, relaxing space sim. Nothing too special but I like it 7/10

Technical:
-A little unoptimised and the game save can get bloated within only a couple hundred hours (increases loading time)
-Most stable Bethesda game. Ignore those viral "clips" of the game. Dig deeper and you'll find that those are out-of-context clips from people messing around with console commands

Story:
-It's alright. Think of a space sci-fi movie trope and Starfield will probably fit any of them, with a space fantasy-esque twist in the middle
-Though it has RPG elements and choices do matter, it doesn't seem to be the main focus as the writing is a bit flat and outdated

Gameplay:
-Combat is better than one would expect out of a game like this. You can take it slow and fire potshots from cover or you can charge in, use sword and magic to manipulate the entire battlefield and fulfil that Jedi (or Sith) fantasy
-Dialogue choices are quite good and cover most moral stances, allowing us to roleplay as good/ evil as we want
-Ship and base building in this game are great. It's easy enough for someone new to it to make something viable for even endgame gameplay but also allows plenty of freedom for those who are interested in making complex designs

review:
The game is as empty as people say. I struggled to find a reason to continue playing. I am now testing some mods again to see if it improves. I installed the mod collection Gate to Stars from nexusmods and it truly improves almost every aspect of the game. But vanilla Starfield still is not the game it was said to be prior to release.

The game is basically space fallout but with a less interesting story and even less interesting characters. The world building is not good. I have seen some reviewers, even critical reviewers, claim the world building is good. It is not. This is supposed to be a large part of the galaxy that has been explored, inhabited, for something like a couple hundred years. It amounts to 2,000 empty planets. 

Even the planets that have what should be large populations, major cities, are tiny insignificant and bland locales. The game is not a space exploration game. The planets have nothing of interest besides resources you need to gather that are never in one planet so youll be planet hopping across systems just to go through the tedious process of upgrading one of the many terrible weapons.

It is a fast travel and loading screen simulator. Often times when i play an MMO or multiplayer RPG game, i think "i wish this were a single player game". But with this game its the opposite. this would be a fantastic multiplayer game. But that is one of the many things Bethesda has been on record of definitely not doing. Along with all of their other "definite nos" when creating this game and responding to the feedback. They seem to love disappointing people and making the game as poorly as possible.

But this is nothing new. A lot of people have talked about this. But I have given this game a lot of hours without paying attention to the critics because I wanted to get an idea of it on my own before really paying attention to the same complaints I had.

So the game is worse than the fallout games in story, environment, etc. But that doesnt mean it is absolute trash. It still was entertaining enough. I also dont agree with people who claim a game must have 150-1000 hours of gameplay to make it worth the 60 dollar price tag. If you play for 60 hours, thats 1 dollar per hour. Is that really not worth it? Even if it is a disappointing experience, you still spent 60 hours for some reason. I recognize that, and because of that I really cannot say I regret playing it. It had aspects that are really cool and fun. Just because something isnt as good as something else doesnt mean it is worthless. I love the movie Alien and Aliens, and find Alien 3, 4 etc to be awful compared but i still enjoy them and will watch them all together every so many years when I binge the series again. Even the Alien VS Predator movies find their way in and those are pretty bad movies.

But Bethesda should not be making the equivalent of B movies when making their games. Starfield is not 1:1 the equivalent of Alien Vs Predator when looking at things that came before... but it is not much better.

I love it now that the modders have made it brilliant. And I hate that Bethesda gets rewarded by the work of the modders (due to people buying their game, and playing it only due to modders making it worth playing). But thats why we need to support indie game creators more. They are truly making interesting content.

If you really dont care that Bethesda made a subpar game and lied about what they were making prior to release, then buy it and get mods and youll probably enjoy it a lot. But the average gamer isnt going to install most of these mods. A lot of them may still like it.. especially if you didnt expect it to be what they said it would be prior to release.

During my time with the game during the few day early access period, I did enjoy quite a bit of the game, and that's what Starfield does do well, is makes you think you've got a lot of depth to the game, when really, once you dig into that apple pie, you learn that most of the pie is 99.9% crust, and 0.1% filling. I really did enjoy the new character customization options  such as pronoun control and even a few in depth options like walking style and I was hyped for the whole traits and backgrounds system, but it really ended up all falling flat for me. It took Bethesda nearly a full year to release mod support, and by then, the game was dead in the water. Shattered Space came and went, and at least for me, the modding community has nothing interesting to offer to keep me interested in the game. Take this as a lesson. Never pre-order a game out of hype. Especially never Bethesda. Nostalgia can be a drug. If you're looking for a good spaceship simulator, go to Elite Dangerous. You want RPG elements with modern-ish graphics? Fallout 4 has infinitely more content and even a thriving modding community for you that is sure to give you HUNDREDS of more hours of actual enjoyment than Starfield, while being cheaper. I just cannot recommend this game in it's current state.

What a waste of money and time this game was. You'd be better off playing The Outer Worlds (seriously, even better than this) for a space travel story, or No Man's Sky for space exploration instead. Those two games would fill in any shortcomings Starfield has.

review:
After 421 hours, I finished my first playthrough. I explored so much, scouring the Milky Way for as much content as I could find, and even having completed so much of the story and the side missions, I was still hesitant to let it come to and end. 

It is shocking to me how mixed the reviews are. So much thought has gone into the game. There are differences between this and the other Bethesda games, but I find that it is usually pretty beneficial for every game to not be, you know, the exact same game. Starfield contains so much depth and beauty to the world; the designs of the cities, the scenery from so many of the planets. Even the barren rocky moons that so many people complain about; listening to this fantastic score while sitting in a crater-speckled valley as the sun rises over the horizon and casts long shadows over the mottled landscape was a truly pleasant experience for me. 

I won't pretend it was a flawless experience. There are systems layered on systems layered on systems. I have a liquid-cooled PC, and had to replace sections of tubing that had warped or cracked from the stress of running so hot for so long whole playing the game a half dozen times or so. It crashed at least once per play session. The inventory and resource management system is so janky that not only was it frustrating, but they added a button to "transfer all resources" and it was a 50/50 chance that this button would not only crash the game, but the computer itself. That said, this was also the crunchiest any bethesda game has been. The act of spending your meager upgrade points means going through a collegiate process (oh, you want a 300-level skill? Sorry, you need to spend at least 2 more point-hours in 100 or 200-level courses before you have the science background to handle that skill. You want to improve your Botany level? Looks like you have not yet finished the assignment from your last Botany class, to demonstrate you actually learned the skills you were shown). As someone who loves a road-trip, an experience where you have vast expanses of nothing, dotted with small settlements peopled with strangers whose names you don't know, and who may need help, or may outright hate you; that isn't just feel accurate to Space travel, it feels accurate to driving across most of the country. And then every once in a while, there is a vibrant, unique, packed city filled with people and stores and things to do. It just feels good. 

Fortunately, the New Game+ is baked into the story itself, so I did just keep right on playing. 13 hours into a new game, and so far I am finding so much new dialogue, a lot of new experiences. However imperfect it may be, this game is unlike anything I have ever played. So much thought, love, and detail went into making an experience that fits me so well that after all these hours, I still don't really want to leave.

A MOBA 3D brawler with a lock on  fighting system of Dark Souls? Yea suprised me as I never played the demo and I thought I was getting just a 3D arena type fighting game. Cool. It has RPG leveling elements so you can upgrade your poise, health, or power. Like it. Also upgrade your moveset and your weapons. Nice. 
The graphics are fresh, the gameplay - button mashing until I upgraded my moveset - is pretty fun (against AI), but the characters are borderline bland but remind me so much of Battle Arena Toshinden IDGAF! 
I'm keeping it and you will see my time go up more as I get to know the game as I have barely scratched the surface here. Wish there was a tutorial also.
After playing a handful of vs. AI matches I wish there were humans to play against. This is fun! Its an arcade like mash up of  PvP and PvE while trying to destroy the other teams cores. Like a Dark Souls, weapon based, 3D multiplayer fighting game MOBA. Flanking another human would probably be way more difficult but way more fun. Getting your combo off feels pretty satisfying. Hit multiple opponents at once if they are bunched up. You can be collateral damage if you are bunched up too. Don't get caught missing your combo or the AI will take advantage and make you pay after your whiffed you attack. I can imagine I would even have a smile on my face if I got combo'd or parried then counter combo'd by a human because its just fun. The music probably has something to do with that too. It's got catchy riffs that make it difficult to be upset at things not going your way in-game.  The controls are responsive (I'm on an Xbox controller) and navigating around the 3D maps takes a little getting used to but when in combat they are good. Knowing when to engage and disengage is key or you will be flanked and combo'd.  
Solo dev too. Custom game engine is a good one! Keep it up Handmade Games. Hoping that Guardians gets more exposure!

review:
One of the things I appreciate most about Last Vanguard is that it starts players with a double jump. Where most Metroidvanias feel restrictive at the beginning, this one immediately gives movement a smooth and satisfying flow. The game is also truly open—players can head to any area from the start. Combat feels equally good, with the option to move and fire or stay stationary and aim. Different guns with unique firing patterns provide variety, and I especially liked the inclusion of a healing bot. It charges from melee strikes on enemies, creating a loop of ranged combat, close-up strikes, and healing that kept me engaged. Enemy and boss variety is also strong, with distinct patterns to learn and overcome.

Unfortunately, the writing is not on the same level. Dialogue often boils down to “We’re going to fight because you’re here,” without meaningful context. Worse, it can’t be skipped cleanly—pauses in the text force you to sit through it, making the weak story even harder to ignore.

The reconnaissance bot is another major low point. Controlling it feels awful, requiring constant jump taps to elevate while navigating to boxes to use electricity to activate switches. These sections are explained poorly, break up the action, and play out like a frustrating Flappy Bird minigame. They’re not only unfun, but used repeatedly, and they single-handedly make replaying the game unappealing. I’m baffled these weren’t scrapped.

Navigation is also an issue. The map doesn’t feel intuitive, forcing you to zoom in to see detail. Pinning locations is clunky, and the map often opens centered on a previous area rather than your current position. It feels uniquely unhelpful for getting around.

Bosses, while well-designed in concept, suffer from excessive health pools. Their telegraphs are clear and their mechanics interesting, but the drawn-out length of each fight tests patience more than skill. Beating them wasn’t difficult—usually within a try or two—but enduring minutes of repeated dodges and attacks dulled the excitement. They end up being both a highlight and a disappointment.

Other frustrations include poorly communicated mechanics—like melee switches hidden in the environment that I only discovered by accident—and oddly picky NPC interactions that require standing in the exact right spot to press up. These aren’t game-breaking, but they add friction.

Technical issues, however, were harder to ignore. I encountered a boss that refused to move or attack, another that sank into the floor, and a chase sequence where the camera failed to pan properly, forcing reloads. Reloading itself is a chore, as you must exit the game and trek back from the nearest save point. On top of that, my PS4 controller wasn’t recognized at all, even though the game claims it supports it.

Despite these problems, I’m still recommending Last Vanguard thanks to its excellent core combat loop, satisfying movement, and strong enemy variety. But the reconnaissance bot sections, bloated boss health, clumsy map, and technical issues keep it from greatness. As a first project from this team, it shows real promise, and I hope future titles refine the foundation laid here.

review:
This game reminds me of flash games, which I used to play a lot when I was little. The game's relatively small, containing 5 stages, and three playable characters each with 2 items you can choose from. The controls are nice and tight, and from what I can tell the hit boxes seem fine too (although your character bobbing up and down while stationary can cause some issues), and the Items function as they should.
 The game doesn't ask much of you when it comes to dodging, because the main objective of this game is scoring, which is an interesting concept, but the falling tea makes it feel too random to me, so I don't know how competition for this game would look like.
 One thing I do know however, is the best character in the game, Lacey. she's the fastest character, which in a game about screen control is super important, and she has the best ability in the game, which is to turn all the tea cups large for, I think 20 seconds. while having an overpowered character is fine, I wish it wasn't so apparent how much better she is, although I do realize that is just a personal issue.

review:
Incredibly engrossing. 

This is resource management at its finest, wrapped in an intricate stat-driven RPG and a lovingly crafted pixel art aesthetic. Think (plot focused) The Escapists meets (light) Disco Elysium meets Blacksad.

The strength of the game is its cleverness in refreshing constant short, mid and long term goals, through the use of time-limited exploration areas. Each zone of the prison is accessible during a set part of the day, meaning you'll need to plan in advance *what* to do, *when* and *where*, depending on your available resources (mainly stamina, focus, money and items along a few others secondary ones such as satiety/digestion).

The game is a constant juggle of inventory management (what gifts to carry to get rapport with fellow inmates to unlock their skills?), quest imperatives (what to do, how long will it take, how much energy do you need for your objectives?) and exploration, both character and location driven (what do people want, how do you get it for them, and where can you go that you're not supposed to be?). The barriers of the game slowly fade as you expand your roaming radius and discover its many, many options as to tackle any given problems (several of which aren't stated outright and need paying attention to dialog, eavesdropping on conversations, scrounging for info in unlikely places, etc).

Both characters released (so far) broadly share similar mechanics, but have a different playstyle insofar their starting skills and stats tailor them for specific approaches. Their plotlines are also very different, both thematically and mechanically.

All in all: this is a gem of a "seemingly short scope, but actually bigger than you think" RPG that encourages replay through New Game+, multiple characters, multiple difficulty modes and many achievements to unlock reflecting the many different ways you can attempt to escape (or fail to). An amazing new reference, and I can't wait for the third character to be released.

review:
This game is awesome.

I had my eye on this for a while since it was shown in a next-fest, but it released early access and I wanted to wait for 1.0 before diving into any sort of story game. It was worth waiting for.

Fundamentally, the game can be divided into two main parts: Surviving your day-to-day prison life, and progressing your character's stories (as well as additional plotlines that you might start to see unravel inside the prison). and of course, these are connected as getting to new areas will require skills or connections, and there are often multiple ways to solve an objective.

The prison simulator aspect is actually quite fun; there is a lot of choice in how you can develope you character. Want to be prison boss who solves things with fist? You can, and join the boxing club for some cash. Want to be a goody-two shoes and work with the guards to live a more comfortable life? you can. Rather use a silver tongue to make friends with everyone, bluff through card bets, and accumulate lots of wealth? Yep, you can. 

Further, I like the balance in requiring both 'know-how' and actual character skills. My character is much stronger now than at the beginning of the game of course, but a lot of thriving in prison is simply knowing where to look, whose palms to grease, where the best work assignments are, etc.. and I've gone from struggling to even get enough food to survive a day to a pimped out cell I almost don't want to leave!

The story is pretty interesting too. I chose Thomas for my first playthough, and have been enjoying conversing with my lawyer Reed through letters, calls, and visitations, each of us on one side of the law working to stop the corrupt mayor from being elected. You can't dally in prison forever, there is a time limit of course to enact justice, which might put some people off. Personally, while the time pressure does keep your main objective at the front of your mind, I did not feel it was overly punishing, offering a lot of time to explore the prison and get to know your fellow prisoners. 

I am just about finished with my first playthrough with one character, and am excited to continue with the other character after a break.

While the game is not obscure, I do feel it's a bit of an underrated gem, filled with story, fun, and polish. Recommended.

review:
I came across this game randomly when browsing steam trying to cure my boredom and want-to-play-games-but-all-my-games-sound-boring limbo. I'm not usually much of a fan of pixel-art games, but this game genuinely has some amazing art and the overall style is a treat. What I especially enjoy are the segments that blend 3-D elements with the 2-D sprites. The environments have so much attention to detail with very pleasing color palettes and structure. 
My very first play through was of course with Thomas the fox, but if I had to go back and tell myself something, it would be to know I will fail. I was admittedly frustrated the first time around because I felt as if I didn't have enough time do do the things I needed for the ending I wanted. I now realize that there are multiple endings, some probably easier to achieve than others, but I ended up getting the worst one and I felt like the hours I put into the run were for nothing. I do appreciate how the game isn't completely heartless- you keep the bonds with other inmates on your next run, and on top of that you know a lot more anyway by default of playing it all before. Now that I realize I'm past most learning opportunities, I'm more confident in achieving a better ending for Thomas. Without getting into spoilers, the segments for his story in particular really had me hooked, and I fell in love with Reed's character (if you know, you know). 
I'm starting a new run with Bob, and I really like how his perspective is quite different from Thomas' which I look forward too with the rest of the playable cast. When I first started the game, I found that resource management was very difficult for me and I seemed to not be able to keep my health or mind up, but now that I have ample experience, I have nearly no problems in doing so. I think the biggest thing is to have patience, but the narrative the game tells is very worth the effort I feel, even if you do end up getting a bad ending. 
One thing I think I would love to see more of are the conversations you have with the other inmates. After befriending them, you're able to choose the prompt "chat" which raises their relationship with you. However, I wish the other inmates had more of these conversations to offer as it seems most only have one, then you must resort to giving them gifts if you want to raise their relationship further. I would love to chat with the other inmates more than once, and I think it would be a good reward for spending time with them. In my play through, I found it somewhat difficult to raise the relationships of multiple inmates at a time especially with juggling everything else. Their items for purchasing above a certain relationship threshold was useless to me since I never got that far with them, anyway. I could definitely see more dialogue with the inmates a future update from the Devs.
Most negative reviews I see about this game is the 21 day limit until the end. While I understand these gripes, I do think 21 days is ample time for an ending on a second playthough, but perhaps not the first. I can see how this is annoying during a initial run since getting a good ending would require you to have more experience with the game first.

***SPOLIERS BELOW OF ENDING***


So when I played the first time with Thomas, I ended up going through with the escape ending via the sewage pipes in the laundry room. Getting around the sewers and unlocking the doors took many days which I have no issue with, but I was totally flabbergasted when after DIGGING into the pipe room from the laundry room, then using my pathetic dice rolls to crawl through the pipes, I was expected to fight a huge spider with little health (because of the crawling). There was just no way I was getting past the spider, and it was also the 21st day of my sentence meaning it was all or nothing, so in the end I was forced to go with the nothing route. I built Thomas as more of a charismatic and intelligent inmate as it goes hand-in-hand with his past of being a journalist. I was heavily punished for this, it seems, because I lacked the agility and strength to fight that spider which costed me everything. I wished I would've went with a different ending, but at the time I wasn't aware of the different ones I could achieve. I had already dedicated so much time to the pipe escape ending that starting another route wouldn't work either. Honestly, I think I would've liked it much more if that spider creature was scrapped entirely. The shock factor of seeing other dead inmates down in the sewer would've been enough for the narrative, and the section where Thomas crawls though the pipes to the outside would've been much more satisfying instead of being jumped with a spider and being screwed if you're not built for fighting. 
In conclusion, I would rate this game a 7/10 at the moment which could be subject to change with future updates. I can enjoy playing the game much more since I don't feel stressed about all the learning curves like I did the first time around. I'm really looking forward to other stories we will see of the playable characters and I think despite my own gripes with this game, the pros outweigh the cons and I'm very glad I played it (and still am playing it).

This is a nice experience.  It's kind of like a screen saver you can interact with.  

I enjoy having it on while I'm working, or otherwise occupied.  It's neat to check in and see civilizations in their infancy, or massive empires destroyed by earthquakes.  How the natives must tremble as meteors rain down upon them; how such grand armies perish beneath clouds of volcanic ash.
Just as the world recovers from such violent upheaval, an elegant rainbow illuminates under the cool oceanic rain.

There's an astonishing amount of depth.  The inhabitants of the world appear to be governed by a need for space and food.  They plant crops and expand their territories through exploration and conquest, and each individual being has their own needs.  They have mothers and fathers.  They eat, sleep, age, reproduce and die under the eyes of the great, perception-less, omnipresent being they may call their God; whom we would know as ourselves.

Precipitation and thunderstorms follow what could be interpreted as fronts, as they wrap their way around pressure systems created by the warmth of the sun and the cool of the night; the clouds perceptively generated by moist air from evaporated seas and lakes.

It's pretty neat.  I recommend it.

You do have to use your imagination, as the graphics are very primitive.  This doesn't hurt the experience, but rather pushes you further into observation of this charming application.  It MUST be observed to be fully appreciated.

Also the dev is still working on it and responds to things well......that's always good.

review:
Draft Day Sports Pro Football is a promising American Football Simulation game that I really hope continues to advance and enhance.

Like many other sports gamers, I am desperately looking for a real franchise sim since Madden has chased the MUT money and left the rest of us behind. It is my hope that this game finds support from the franchise/sim community to enable the developer the resources and market to continue to evolve this game.

I believe DDSPF aims to be the OOTP of American Football which would be amazing. It is not there yet but I do believe the potential is there. 

The game is not without its issues this year. The UI can use some quality of life improvements (sorting, league wide editing), there are some bugs (safeties are far too common, QB rushing is off and some stats totals are bugged) and the on field play execution is a bit janky (players not lining up correctly, plays not always representing the outcome) and not as smooth or accurate as it needs to be given the lack of visuals.
 
It is important here to note that this game does not have or NEED fancy play execution visuals to be a top notch product (see OOTP Baseball). The Xs and Os on field display will be perfectly adequate once it becomes smooth and accurate.

If you are looking for a Madden clone, this is not it. 

If you are looking for a GM/Franchise Sim then this game has the potential to be a go to product. 

So while the game is not perfect I definitely can recommend this as a buy to support the genre and is an enjoyable product even with its flaws. Hopefully the developer keeps iterating each year to focus enhancements in areas EA has forgotten. 

My wish list for 2023 includes:

- More commissioner mode support

- Impact player roles/tendencies (game-breaker, scrambler, strong arm, deep threat, fan favorite, fumbler, sack specialist, power back, injury prone, shutdown corner, big hitter, road blocker, etc - similar to Madden 08 PS2) This would allow more diversity among player types.

- Watch a college "all-star" game with incoming draft class rookies as a scouting tool

- Pregame show (screen) with key players, stats, predictions

In closing, the game has improved every year and I hope those on the fence will throw support and a few bucks behind this game to further broaden the market and allow these amazing independent/Not EA developers to create a game that can meet or even surpass what OOTP has done for baseball.

I want to love this, I really do, and I do not necessarily resent spending the money if it leads for them to have the budget to further develop the game in newer incarnations. As it is right now though? God damn it is awful.

I cannot and do not really intend to comment on the engine and the logic of how the game runs because in reality I cannot get past my roster without throwing my hands up in utter despair at the level this game is pitched it.

So, why do I consider it so fundamentally bad ? It is the interplay between stats and positions, or simply, the lack thereof.

Every single player in the fame only has a few stats Strength, Agility, Intelligence, Arm, Accuracy, Tackling, Speeds, Hands, Endurance, Pass Blocking, Run Blocking, Kick Accuracy and Kick Distance... that is it... In this stat block it in some way defines what a good receiver is? A good CB? A good anything? Essentially stats and a "good" player is defined by how high these numbers are overall, not really weighted toward positional needs.

Then we get to positions, they are pathetically basic. You have the basic positions in any NFL roster but that is it. DO you have outside, slot, possession receivers? Nope. Do you have man, press, outside corners? Nope. Linebackers, you do not even have the definition between and ILB and an OLB. Pass rushers are they power, or speed, do they specialise in setting the edge, who knows? This goes on and on for every position.

So let's step back a second, you have a horrifically basic stat block and a very simplified position tree, what are you left with? Well I was left with the suggestion that, apparently, my best Nickel Corner was T.J Watt.....

The game really needs a redesign at the basic level of stats and positions, this is a very, very simplistic change though it will of course add a lot more complexity and subtlety to the game, right now it is just "trololol big numbers go brrrrr" and thats about it.

They need to do some basic research of a game like Football Manager, look how they set out their stats, physical, mental, skill and then work out which particular skills lean toward being a good positional player and viola, you have a much, much better game.

There are other basic issues such as a pretty horrifically designed and unintuitive UI, laggy as hell despite being a small game and (probably because of my earlier complaints on stats) a weird setup where OL seems to be the easiest position to play in football as every half decent or average (in real life) lineman is rated about 90+

Despite this I will actually continue to buy it, for the sake of £20 I wont miss that and hopefully the game will continue to develop with more money but right now, as damning as this may sound, you get more complexity in Madden Franchise mode.
