No Power, No Chaos. 


I firstly want to say I love The Tribe and the show has been a big part of my childhood. So when the talks about a game and sneak peeks of the art started popping up, I could not be unexcited about it.
But now here I am. Few minutes less 14 hours start to finish, in two sittings, and even that was pretty generous amount of stalling. 

Positives - the art is beautiful and captures the characters true and with love, the dialogue and interactions loyal to the show and humour in it.

Negatives - Firstly, the controls are horrible. I had to exit once or twice completely right at the start, because I couldn't progress or see what I was doing with the game. If you have any accessibility issues you will struggle from the get go. The first thing I usually do when starting a new game, is go over audio options etc. But without info on the clunky controls at first, I couldn't change anything. Which should not be a thing in 2022. Eventually after changing some audio settings, not all sounds actually complied to them, and I had deafening seagulls screech at me every time I went to the beach. 
Despite the game being so simple and having bad controls, the absence of proper tutorial going over basics was striking, yet ironically (without spoiling) when you get used to the gameplay, the game decides to hold your hand and repeat things over and over and over until the end. 
Adding to bad controls/lack of, the game looks old, in every possible way, and not a release of 2022.
The game itself is very simple, and could've used more time and love. The skills level up and cap out in no time and have no real weight in progress. At no point was I given actual choice to do or decline in something meaningful (like joining a tribe), only dialogue, which again did not have any effect on the outcome. Sometimes, the game would take over so hard, you'd miss areas to see and things to gather completely. At no point was I actually given the chance to explore and loot ie the front of the Mall. 

Only the battles I found to be somewhat challenging and change of pace - to a point.
The plot also follows very closely to the show, but gets abruptly cut off and "the end" screen pops up.


I really really waited for this game and did not want to be mean or negative in any way. But as a big The Tribe fan I am disappointed. I can not see a newcomer to the series or game, to get anything out of this and fully enjoy it. I can not see a veteran Tribe member to be satisfied either. A demo, early access or any other effort with fans would've surely helped with development and ironing out controls/ideas and other. This game could've been a proper length group project, with lots to do and see. Alas, my time part of the Mall Rats was short lived.

For what the game is right now and what I personally got out of it, I can not recommend it or justify the price. Honestly, I would've rather spent the money on a part of The Tribe physical release instead.

review:
Acutally, I am torn about this game. I don't want to give it a thumbs down, but it's not exactly a masterpiece. So lets break it down a little:

pro: 
-for fans of the show this is pure nostalgia
-it is really nice to be able to interact with the characters of the show
-the artwork is gorgeous
-the music is well picked
-the story is near enough to the show so you roughly know where you are in the story, even though its not all in chronological order. but we want to experience something new, not replay the show, so this is perfectly fine.
-the fight system is alright, kinda like an old „final fantasy“ or „breath of fire 3“

Con:
-you can't pick the games resolution
-the german translation is not very well, there are grammar errors and sometimes words are just missing from sentences. 
-it says you can pick between english and german but I didn't find an option to change the language anywhere ingame and wasn't asked when installing which language I want.
-it's still kinda buggy... i.e. If you accidentally look into a mirror you have to change your appearance (or at least pick the same options you had selected before) you cant just quit the process. Or you can't end a day on purpose by going to bed. you wake up and its still night and you can't really continue the story etc.
-the games engine is not programmed to well, i.e. you cant pick any controls you like, which would be alright if you could at least look up the controls, but there is no „help“ option. For changeing furniture colors I had to ask the support on facebook. Granted, they answered fast, but there is no way to find out how to do it besides trial and error ( it's page up/page down in case anyone was wondering) etc.
-farming process is very tedious
-It's completely infuriating to me that you walk past a dozen forageable items in cutscenes but get no chance to pick them up because you cant go back to get them. Just don't show the sparkle in the cutscenes then.
-You can pick you answers when interacting with people. Now this should be a positive, but the answeres are mostly saying the same thing, just formulated a little differently. It's not like you get a choice, when Lex is flirty with you that you can choose to flirt back or insult him or something. The game gives you 2 answers to choose from that both basically say, no thanks. At that point there is no need to even give us a choice.

-but what bugs me the most is this: you can't just decide not to play the story, go exploring and meet people. You get teleported places you need to go and forage a few maps at the time and talk to the people that are there, but you can't leave there until you have found your objective. Sometimes you have farmed the whole area and have to wait for respawn, and when you have what you need, you can't decide to stay in the location. The story teleports you to the next area you need to find stuff.

In conclusion:
I was very excited for this game. But even though my expectations weren't to high, because I knew the developers are new to the gameing scene I am a little disappointed. Nostalgia and storywise its a great experience, but gaming wise it has alot of room for improvement. I hope they keep working on it and learn a little from titles like stardew valley. I will finish playing the story, and maybe my biggest complain will vanish later in the game. We will see. I will edit if something changes :) KTDA

review:
This game, is aesthetically pleasing, but when you can't get past the character creation screen because the image keeps freezing so you have no idea how to progress, well I wouldn't consider that a good game. And not having accessability options like full screen mode, etc is a bit strange. And the audio, you don't know which audio setting is for what audio. And when you change the audio settings, it doesn't reflect the actual in game audio either. If there's something I always start by doing, it's lower the volume so it's comfortable for me wearing headphones. And full screen the game. Here neither of those worked. I wished this game was better, because I watched the tribe, and have been a fan for like two decades already. 
I wish I could give it a better review, but I couldn't even get past the character creation screen, and not for a lack of trying. Not even remapping keys helped. 
The fact that there's also no way of exiting the game, doesn't help. 
From the video and screenshots it looks like a cute game, and aesthetically pleasing. But when it's unplayable, well I can't do anything except ask for a refund for it. Because with how it currently sits, it's not worth its full price. 
I might get it in the future if it recieves updates to fix its issues. But until then, I'm going to hold off, and I recommend you all to hold up until it has had patches, if it ever will get them.

And to respond to the devs, all of my drivers are always up to date. I've been gaming for over 20 years, it's the first thing I check when I game doesn't work.

So a friend of mine, gifted me this game outside of steam. And I still have the same issue, but I managed to get past it, and could play for like an hour before it crashed again and stopped working. And the worst part, it didn't save any progress. But I did get it back running and it worked better the second time around, but still have issues with the character creation screen not wanting to progress.
But from what I did play, It's a nice looking game, I'll give it that. And since I have gamed as much as I have, I could figure out the controls without having a tutorial for it.

Speaking of tutorial, there should be a proper tutorial in the beginning, to teach you which buttons to use for what, and how to do things. I shouldn't have to go into the settings and check the controls to know how to play it. 

Another thing, I know you can make the game full screen by pressing f4, but there should be an option that allows you to do that in settings, along with better audio settings. Then in the menu for settings, there should be a button that allows you to exit to desktop. You shouldn't have to force quit the game to turn it off. 

The story is all right, considering it follows season one. And the art is beautiful. I don't mind that it was made in rpg maker. Everyone starts somewhere. It's a good start for an indie rpg that has developers that might not have worked on many games before, if any. 

There are still a lot of bugs, like it crashes, you get stuck in places when trying to forage. And having to reboot the game. And for me when I was crafting it would break and I would have to stop crafting and reboot. The game glitches when trying to click through the text, and I wish there was a skip button for the text, because I don't always want to read it. 

It'd be nice of the actual skills do anything for you in the game. Like I get that the farming skill gives you more crops etc, but it'd be fun if they did more than just that. And that you didn't max out the level for them in like ten minutes of doing said skill. It gets a bit boring. 

For me, this game still gets a no recommend. Because for it's price, and where the game sits, it's not worth the full prize. And I hope it gets updates and gets improvements, and most of all, quality of life updates, as some other here have suggested.

Overall this was a fun, relaxing game with an engaging narrative well worth giving a go.

Maybe it's part the sheer nostalgia of the series, which has and always will have my deep unyielding love, but I will simply say that this has the soul of The Tribe in it. 

I'd hope that it's issues - the crashes and at time the mapping are dealt with by the dev team in time as I'd expect, but the romanticist in me still adores the visuals and the music - above all the music, which is an uplifting triumph and homage to the old in the new. 

I would say that anyone whose lives have been touched since childhood from this series will be well rewarded, and that all who hold this work accountable to the metric of comparable games  with compassion view this as what it is - as the recollection, lament and revival of an old song. 

For all it's imperfections this, beyond everything else I have ever encountered associated with it, is the continuation of something profound. Is the poetry which we were gifted in our youth. Is the rightful and lauded heir to the old sagas, and like all songs of the singers who lose something in their repetition nonetheless contains something deep. I can say without reservation that this game raises it's voice to what The Tribe was for all of us, and for those who have longed in our remembrance it will not disappoint - for you who never experienced it in it's time, look no further than here.

It is saga and it is vision - it is a beautiful thing, and a telling of old tales in new voice. That's all of it I can or need tell - and damn anyone for who that is not enough.

I'm having such a great time playing this! I have watched The Tribe series countless times, and it has played a big part in my life, so this feels like hanging out with old friends! Very nostalgic. I always wanted to explore the set and be a part of the Mall Rats when I watched the show, so it was like a dream creating my own character and exploring the Mall! Everything about it makes me feel so warm and happy, like watching the show. Only now, I get to be a part of it! I'm only part way through the game. When I started, I told myself I would only play for a little while, but I feel like I want to stay in the story! There is a lot to gather and collect. I may or may not have gotten a bit obsessed with farming... 

I love the art so much! Seeing the characters like this was so cool. I think the artists did a great job at capturing the essence of the characters. The same can be said for the writing and story as well! I think they captured all the characters very well and without spoiling anything, there are lots of things I didn't expect! Also, there are lots of background characters from the show that I recognised who get fleshed out more! It's really exciting to see the world of The Tribe expand in a different way to the series. It was also really nice to hear the music. For some reason, when I think of the show, I can always hear the music playing in my head, so it made me really happy to listen to it! 

I also think this would be a great introduction to The Tribe for people who haven't seen or heard of the series before. I would definitely recommend it and I can't wait to play more!

review:
I ultimately can't recommend this game, despite thinking it's not essentially a bad game. It could hit right for certain people, but I don't see most playing for a long time for a roguelite.

The main problem with the game is that it doesn't feel tactical enough, contrary to what the previews suggest. Most of the gameplay boils down to moving your mechs close to the enemy and watching as they attack. The mechs move too slowly and don't fire when moving, so there's no real reason to move them while in active combat. You'd only lose hp by doing so. The whole game just feels like you need to hope for the best, as there's not much you can do to increase your chances of winning.

The mechs do have 1 active ability each, but they barely make a difference in the way you'd play. The most useful is with the first mech, allowing you to jump to a farther tile. The mobility can be helpful, but ultimately doesn't make a difference if you're only taking out one enemy, then it immediately goes back to just watching again.

The game mostly played itself, so it's more of an autobattler than anything, which is a real shame. From the visuals, this would have been a lot more fun as a standard turn-based tactics game where you get to upgrade mechs and strategically fire off artillery based on enemy positions. Or the devs could have committed to an autobattler instead of trying to mix the two and failing to do so. The ideas they were trying to mix just didn't come together due to the execution.

review:
Grit and Valor – 1949 is a compact, fast-paced roguelite tactics game that reimagines post–World War II Europe through a dieselpunk lens. Rather than retelling history, the game constructs a fictional alternate 1949 where the war never truly ended. In this world, the remnants of fascist powers have entrenched themselves behind walls of steel and fire, and you command a small squad of resistance-controlled mechs in a last-ditch effort to liberate occupied zones. The game wastes no time getting you into the action, but behind its punchy presentation is a layered, strategic core that balances real-time combat, resource management, and risk-versus-reward decision-making in satisfying rhythm.

At its heart, the gameplay is structured around brief tactical missions that combine the strategic positioning of classic turn-based titles with the time pressure of real-time decision-making. Each map drops your squad into a confined battlefield where you must hold out against increasingly overwhelming enemy waves. Your goal is to protect a central command unit while managing cooldowns, pilot abilities, terrain advantages, and a limited pool of action time. Fortunately, you can pause or slow down time to plan out moves, adding a layer of accessibility that helps bridge the gap between reactive skill and thoughtful planning. It creates a tense, puzzle-like flow where each decision matters, especially as enemy types escalate in complexity.

The combat system is underpinned by a rock-paper-scissors mechanic—fire beats bombs, bombs beat bullets, bullets beat fire—that encourages variety in squad composition and thoughtful matchup exploitation. This foundation is bolstered by mech customization, pilot progression, and a growing arsenal of tech that evolves between runs. Every mech can be upgraded with modules that tweak stats or provide active abilities, and your pilots can level up to unlock tactical skills such as airstrikes, smoke grenades, and powerful overdrive maneuvers. These systems are easy to understand but rich enough to support experimentation, and the roguelite progression—accruing scrap and valor to unlock upgrades, new pilot archetypes, and loadout options—gives each failed run a sense of purpose.

What gives Grit and Valor – 1949 its unique flair is the setting. The alternate-history dieselpunk aesthetic is more than just a coat of paint; it informs everything from enemy design to environmental hazards. Battlefields are scattered across a fictionalized Europe, with each region introducing new challenges: bombing runs that periodically hammer the field, urban environments with tight alleyways and overwatch traps, or countryside maps with unpredictable terrain modifiers. The visual style is clean and utilitarian, with an art direction that leans into sharp silhouettes, bold animations, and comic book flair. There’s just enough personality in the visuals and audio to sell the world without slowing the pace, and the minimal UI keeps your focus on the battlefield rather than on parsing stats.

Narratively, the game is deliberately light. There’s no deep campaign or intricate lore—just a handful of briefings and radio chatter to introduce you to new bosses or biome mechanics. Villains like the mustache-twirling General Harmsworth or the mad scientist Doctor Z fit the tone of the game perfectly: over-the-top, archetypal, and designed to serve as stylish obstacles more than emotionally resonant characters. The story’s main function is to provide momentum between missions and a sense of escalation, which it accomplishes with decent effect. Still, players hoping for a deep or morally complex narrative won’t find one here. This is a game more concerned with tone and tactical pacing than worldbuilding or introspection.

Despite the smooth moment-to-moment gameplay, Grit and Valor – 1949 does suffer from a few noticeable limitations. Some maps begin to feel repetitive after several runs, particularly when environmental variety is underutilized. The early game progression can also feel slow, with core upgrades locked behind several rounds of grinding for scrap or valor. While this steady ramp-up works to extend the game’s lifespan, it can cause some early frustration when your squad lacks the tools to adapt to certain challenges. Additionally, interface clarity—especially around ability ranges, cooldown indicators, and terrain effects—is an area that could benefit from further refinement. These issues are not game-breaking, but they do slightly undermine the otherwise slick presentation.

The game is at its best when you’re deep into a run, juggling pilot cooldowns, terrain positions, and mission modifiers while trying to keep your squad intact. Every move has weight, every mistake feels recoverable but costly, and victories feel genuinely earned. There’s a sense of mounting tension as you push deeper into enemy territory, facing off against progressively absurd bosses with unpredictable behaviors and area-denying weapons. When your team finally triumphs over a daunting general or survives a multi-phase assault with a sliver of health, the sense of accomplishment is undeniable. The way the game compresses a full tactical arc into bite-sized battles gives it a rhythm that’s hard to put down.

Overall, Grit and Valor – 1949 is a tightly crafted strategy experience that knows exactly what kind of game it wants to be. It’s stylish, replayable, and welcoming to both newcomers and veterans of tactical roguelites. While it doesn’t reinvent the genre, it successfully blends real-time tactics and grid-based strategy into a distinctive package that rewards smart decision-making and flexible thinking. Its brisk pace and upgrade loops make it an excellent game for quick sessions, yet its progression system and mech variety give it the longevity to stick with you over time. For players seeking strategic depth without the time investment of more traditional tactics titles, this dieselpunk skirmisher is well worth the fight.

Rating: 7/10

Chinese Train Trip: A Journey of Culture, Strategy, and Adventure

Chinese Train Trip is an immersive and uniquely engaging board game that beautifully blends Chinese culture with strategic gameplay. It’s a game that invites players to embark on a cross-country adventure aboard China’s iconic trains, with each step revealing new destinations, challenges, and opportunities.

Gameplay
The game is centered around traveling through China via train, where players must manage their routes, resources, and decisions to reach various cities. The gameplay is a combination of strategy, luck, and decision-making, with each player's path offering a different experience. Players collect and use tickets, navigate the train schedules, and even encounter random events, such as delays and train accidents, that affect their progress.

The game does a fantastic job of weaving in cultural elements, from Chinese landmarks and cities to the inclusion of local cuisine and traditions. As you travel from Beijing to Shanghai, or head into the remote mountains of Tibet, you'll find yourself learning about China’s diverse landscapes and rich heritage, making the experience both educational and fun.

Strategic Depth
Chinese Train Trip is not just about getting from point A to point B. Players must consider factors like train speed, passenger satisfaction, and the best routes to take, all while managing a limited supply of resources. Timing is crucial—too many delays can set you back, while quick, smart decisions can put you ahead of your competition.

The game also offers multiple routes, giving players room for creative strategies. Do you take the scenic path, slowing you down but offering potential rewards, or do you stick to the fast and reliable options, playing it safe? The variety of choices ensures that no two games are the same, adding replayability.

Visuals & Presentation
The artwork in Chinese Train Trip is stunning. The colorful, detailed maps and illustrations of the cities, landscapes, and trains bring the game to life, offering a visually rich experience. Each city is represented with beautiful art that highlights the unique characteristics of that area, making the game feel like a virtual tour of China. The train pieces and tokens are also well-designed, adding a tactile dimension to the game that enhances the overall experience.

Learning Experience
One of the most enjoyable aspects of Chinese Train Trip is its educational value. Players are not only competing to be the fastest or most efficient traveler—they’re also gaining insights into Chinese culture, geography, and history. Whether it’s learning about the Great Wall of China or the bustling metropolis of Hong Kong, the game gives players a deeper appreciation for the country’s rich cultural tapestry.

Final Thoughts
Chinese Train Trip is a captivating blend of strategy, adventure, and education. Its cultural depth, strategic gameplay, and beautiful presentation make it a standout title for board game enthusiasts, particularly those who enjoy games with a learning component. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or just looking for something fun and engaging, Chinese Train Trip offers a delightful journey that you won’t soon forget.

10/10

EDIT: So the developer has made some crucial changes, and I can confidently say they've greatly improved the overall experience. The addition of colors is small enough to keep the game's minimalist look intact, but makes a huge difference in the moment to moment gameplay. Being able to easily identify different enemy types based on their colors means the combat is much more readable. Red guys are melee chargers, green guys shoot pistols, etc. Now I can not only notice but also appreciate the enemy types and how they spice up the gameplay. I can not stress enough how much better the colors and redone sprites have made the experience.

The game overall feels much better to play and easier to understand, which allows me to better focus on the core gameplay. The tutorial is also a welcome addition that further helps players understand the mechanics. Auto aim feels very OP, but I do appreciate it as a way to allow players who otherwise wouldn't be able to keep up with the frenetic pace a way of enjoying it regardless.

Progression feels a bit rough, with not enough cash coming in to allow upgrades to be bought at anything above a snail's pace, but it's very nice being able to slowly get more powerful. It's a nice balance of player skill and in-game progression

However, I still don't feel this game is really worth 3.00 USD. It feels more like a proof of concept showing the developer's skill at making fast and fun twinstick shooter combat. The fundamentals are rock solid, but ultimately it just doesn't feel like a product worth paying for. If the developer were to use this combat system and implement it into a much larger game, I'd likely be down to pay for it. I understand this is probably the most subjective part of the whole review, and I'm sure there will be people out there who think it's well worth the three bucks, but this is just my opinion on the matter.

I hope the developer continues to improve their craft, because they're on the right track towards making something really special, whether that be an intensively updated and revised version of Quoin or a new game altogether. My previous review was a thumbs down, but I'm giving a thumbs up this time not only because of the improvements in the game, but because the developer cared enough to listen to feedback and use it to craft a better experience. I'll leave my original review below for context, but this here is my current thoughts on Quoin. Very interested to see what the dev does next.

ORIGINAL REVIEW

The combat feels nice and punchy. The music's good as well, though the sudden n-word in one of the tracks was a little jarring for a game this simplistic and cute. The main problem I have is that, in the pretty chaotic combat, it's a little hard to figure out what exactly is happening. All the enemies look just a little too similar, and it's not easy to tell what's an enemy drop and what's just effects from their death. It led to some frustrating deaths where I really wasn't sure what I was looking at.

Ultimately, this is a fun little game, but I can't recommend it because honestly it feels like it should be free. There's just not enough here to justify a price tag when it feels more like a Newgrounds game than a paid release.

I love mystery games. I like being able to deduce an answer, and actually have to think about why that is the answer. It's fun, it's satisfying, and it brings me joy. This is not that. Oh lord, is this not that. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3547319274 

Between Horizons is a sci-fi detective story set aboard an interstellar spaceship. You play as Stella, the head of security, as she investigates increasingly disruptive activities which threaten to derail the ship's journey to a new planet and a new home for those on board. 

As a result of the game being a 2.5D projection, the vast majority of its puzzles are word games, asking players to look at a series of phrases and sus out the solution. While I took very few screenshots so as not to spoil solutions for later players, one example of this style of word puzzle might be that, given four numbers that equal 18, with each of the two sets of numbers having an equal sum as the other set, find the four numbers. Others are like the puzzle depicted in the above screenshot - they require a bit of attention, but once the question being asked is clear, so is the solution. Puzzling and tricksy, these ain't. 

This makes the third style of puzzle feel frustrating in comparison. Stella is, as previously mentioned, a detective, and part of how she solves mysteries is through interrogating witnesses and gathering evidence. Various pieces of evidence from around the ship can be shown to certain characters, prompting them to tell Stella what she needs to know. Despite this being a narrative game, however, and despite there being an active attempt to undermine ship leadership and Stella herself, this process of evidence gathering is never particularly difficult. Everyone, when confronted with a random pill bottle or an observation about their mother, will immediately spill their guts about the ship's resistance movement. No one lies. No one obfuscates. Evidence is clearly labelled as important and the context within which it's important. The hardest part of the game is remembering where the person Stella is meant to show the evidence to is, and which of the little faces in the evidence book is them. 

Between Horizons is a mystery game, yes, but the mystery isn't the ship sabotage. The mystery is instead why so much of this game seems to be apologia for autocracy, and especially the abuse of power by police.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3547320115 

One of the key elements of Between Horizons is that the choices Stella makes throughout the story are meaningful and shape its outcome. This ranges from consequences if Stella solves a case incorrectly to story moments where Stella can choose how to respond. 

This is not a new system, and there are many, many narrative games to the point that, short of walking simulators, I'd argue there's an expectation on the part of the players that they be able to shape the narrative. It allows for better immersion, and for the players to feel as if their actions are more broadly meaningful rather than meaningful solely to them. However, for this choices matter element to feel effective, the choices need to be actual choices, meaning the player has to feel as if they have shaped the character in such a way that a choice is reasonable. There must be RPG elements, however small, for choices to actually matter. 

Between Horizons faces two fundamental problems with making a choices matter system work. The first is that some of its choices are based on how the game's puzzles are solved. Given that they are very simple puzzles, inputting any solution except the right one is the result of an active choice on the part of the player. That there are achievements for consistently providing the correct solution disincentivises answering the puzzles wrong, but more generally, the point of a mystery game is to solve the mystery. Asking the player to not solve the mystery when mysteries are the heart of the game fundamentally misunderstands what draws people to the genre in the first place. 

That said, players could still make the choice to intentionally provide an incorrect solution. The problem here is that there's no reason to do so. As much as the game advertises that players have a choice, the reality is that, short of self-sabotage, there's no reason to ever make these choices. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3547320476 

While I don't generally comment on the length of a game, since how each player experiences that time varies widely, in the case of Between Horizons, the length is very much indicative of the general lack of development of the narrative. Over the course of three hours, the player is introduced to a setting and its context, dozens of characters, a bivvy of locations, and a story about trying to undermine everything the player just learned. It's a dizzying amount of information to convey, and the consequence of trying to do so is that none of it gets anywhere near the development it needs to actually be compelling. Each of the characters the player meets are barely more than faces on a screen. Locations never become familiar, instead being navigable solely as spaces on a map. Characters are constantly moving between story beats, making the world feel fundamentally inaccessible and alien. The only characters with whom Stella interacts are those that she can find or that actively tell her to talk to them, which, given that one of the parties is actively hiding from her, means the only position she's ever really given a chance to interact with is the status quo of the autocratic regime. 

When a choice springs up two hours into the game, then, Stella hasn't developed as a character. No one has. While the incentive to overturn the status quo may be obvious to me as an outside observer, within the world of the ship, it's even more obvious the harm doing so would cause. There is no incentive for the choice to actually be a choice - there is a right answer and a wrong answer, and nothing more. 

And while the game makes it clear the player should choose democracy, that's not the reality the game's story is telling. While characters players barely know yell about democracy, everything in their actions and the greater context shows that ultimately, the correct answer is autocracy. 

Between Horizons wants to be a narrative game, but asks the player to do all the legwork in making its narrative satisfying. It wants to be a mystery game, but provides mysteries that are trivial while also asking the player to botch their solutions just to see what different ending they get. It wants to be a game of depth and meaning, when ultimately, most of its playtime is spent scouring rooms to find the one person you're meant to show the one clue to to actually progress the story. 

There's so much here that could have been good. The setting is excellent, and the look and feel of the game are good fits for that setting. It's in its execution, however, that Between Horizons utterly misunderstands how to achieve what it's trying to achieve and be an actual story. It wants players to make decisions about the future of humanity, while offering no incentive for them to ever do so.

I feel bad leaving a negative review, but this game does not feel finished.

I completed the first mission, and I encountered:
- Spelling errors in a few of the tutorial prompts
- Tutorial prompts that don't dismiss properly
- No melee attack that I could figure out from the controls
- Getting stuck behind/inside a door when I open it
- When I completed a mission objective by hacking a terminal, my camera was stuck facing that terminal, and I had to complete the rest of the mission facing that direction.

I won't be refunding it - part of me enjoying the janky nature of some of it, and it does seem like a project of passion by a small team (or maybe even a single developer), but it'll need a significant amount of basic polish before I'd turn this to a recommend.

- Major tweaks to  movement and climbing.

It's clear that this is the passion product of a single developer. The game has charm. It took a few tries for me to understand that it isn't a SC clone. Killing is not an option, and melee is not an option (well, minus a few things I figured out by accident). You are expected to complete your tasks with the tools you are given.

After the first level the game becomes far less linear. Trading hallways for large spaces you can traverse however you see fit.

review:
My review is a recommend, but there are some very important things I want to bring up.

There's no mistaking this game is heavily inspired by Splinter Cell, and many of SC's fundamentals are there. For a small indie project, this is a fantastic game. It's fully complete (woah!), and the art style is just astounding (I may have came close to edging a few times at certain parts because the lighting and shadows were just too good). I want to really emphasize, I love the graphics and art style. I took a lot of photos at the cost of a few lives here and there lol I love hard shadows.

First, the game is very janky and needs a lot of polish.
The guard AI is all over the place. The states of awareness (such as "heard something" or "hunting you down" modes) are so inconsistent. In one of the levels, as soon as I started moving, a guard from another room heard me and immediately goes into hunt mode and kicks down a door and starts looking for me. I manage to hide, but now the guard is constantly looking for me despite having never seen me. 
Another issue with the guards is that they sometimes teeter between not being alerted and hunt mode, and they will become schizophrenic beings that will jump at their own shadows and alert THEMSELVES, causing them to resume hunt mode and will somehow home in on you to shoot your loser ass who thinks hiding behind a single crate and some pipes will maybe protect you. I found this to be really funny, though it did make me lose a few runs lol. I liked to bully the guards by shooting them with my gun endlessly.

There is a lack of a (quick) save system, and as an avid save scummer, I found this to be a bit frustrating. After playing the game, I found that there's not really a reason to have mid-level saves. The levels are quite small, and you can easily learn them after one or two retries. I learned alternative routes and memorized the hacking locations and could stun and run past the guards and finish the levels.

A small note, having all the graphics set to Epic for the last level results in huge frame rate drops. I have to lower everything down to Low to get it to an acceptable frame rate. I moved Shadows to High and it was laggy, then moved it to Medium and the frames got better. It could be just the Shadows option affecting everything, not sure.

The one thing I absolutely did not like at all is the controls for using the gun. I don't like how it's a toggle (though I haven't checked the settings, so that might be on me), and I really do not like how aiming with the pistol is not with a stationary cursor in the middle. You have to use the laser pointer attached to the gun, which means it's insanely hard to shoot and stun enemies while running away like a bitch because your laser pointer feels like it wants to be on the other side of the screen for a tropical vacation. This is probably my biggest gripe with the game. I've died a lot because I was unable to shoot and stun nearby enemies and escape just because I couldn't aim properly.
Grenades have the complete opposite problem, you have to hold down the grenade button and then click to throw. The action of throwing also takes a long time for whatever reason. It's hard to run at the same time as throwing a grenade because I have to weirdly hold down W and G at the same time, then aim my mouse to throw. By the time I throw it, I'm already at half health and my grenade was thrown too far ahead of my enemies and does nothing lmao oopsies.

The sound mechanic is kind of weird. Enemies can easily hear your normal crouch walking. I have to say that this might have been a personal problem, because I like to crouch and roll everywhere. I'm not entirely sure about the sound mechanic. I think guards can hear you just a little too well, though.

The camera is a little finicky, as being too close to objects or having too many things surrounding you can mess up your camera.
Doors are also a bit finicky, as if you're too close when opening one and it opens towards you, the door will smack you and physically move you as it opens. In certain areas, it can actually trap you because the door closes you in against some nearby objects, and you have to close the door to move again.

Cloak & Dagger has everything in place to be a fantastic game, but the only thing it's lacking is just polish and maybe a few control and UI tweaks. Typos are also scattered around in the first level tutorial. 
I think it is a very good sign if I enjoyed a game despite its rough edges. I know I wrote an entire essay that seems to have more bad than good, but please know it's because I care! I liked the game, but the cons are things I thought were very important to discuss.

As I finished up my review, the 1.1 patch came out and fixed some of the things I brought up, so my review is a tiny bit outdated.

Thanks for a fun game!

review: EDIT: I decided to reinstall it after the last couple updates and I was able to finish the final level. Don't get me wrong. There are still some bugs. The AI bugs out and often stay alert no matter how much time has passed. That said, I did enjoy my time with it. Splinter Cell Chaos Theory is my favorite stealth game ever and this game brought back those memories. This is one of only a handful of games I've played to have sound masking. The ability to use environmental ambiance  to mask the noise your making is a brilliant concept that few games have explored. It reminds me most of the awesome spies vs. mercs multiplayer since you can't kill the soldiers, but you can use the many tools at your disposal to stun, distract, and blind your enemies. There's no saving mid-level. You got one shot, but you can recover health from the med station in each level. Level design isn't huge. There are only a few missions and they won't take long to complete, unless you suck at Splinter Cell. It did feel good to ghost missions with no alerts or knockouts. The graphics are nothing special, but the dynamic lighting adds to the atmosphere. Death comes swiftly if you're caught, so missions are pretty tense. The oil rig mission was my personal favorite. I've always loved this type of level in tactical shooters and this one is the most expansive non-linear stage in the game. The dev has been good about rolling out updates and fixing issues. If you're into classic Splinter Cell or just love stealth games like me, you take what you can get. This genre is niche and will likely never be a trendsetter, so if it takes indie devs to get a decent stealth experience, then I'll take it. It's decent and worth the small price. 6/10

review:
Ok Look! I feel hurt to give it a negative review but i have to unfortunately as this game needs more work to feel or get the positive review.

But let me be a good guy and tell the good things about this.

First of all:
- I can clearly see the motivation, passion and love the solo developer have for this game. I respect and love his passion to make a game which is inspired by the Original Splinter Cell ( which have a special place in my heart ). Huge respect and salute for the passion you have on this game

-  Also i am really impressed by the amount of stuff this game have ESPECIALLY made by 1 single developer. The style is beautiful, the game runs pretty well, the mechanics that are there works well, the 1990s setting is interesting. the good old sound and seen icon gave me original nostalgia. From a single developer, it is really impressive here and well done on what you have done

- The levels are well designed ( not counting tutorial one ). From the first mission you have this open level to get to objective however you can, avoiding or moving however you want ( through ground or above ) and leave. Well done on that

BUT unfortunately this game have a lot of issues and missing features which i would love to have in it:

- First thing i noticed is no melee or take downs which immediately turned me off from this game, i know this game is to sneak around, avoid enemies, get objective done and leave BUT i always respect and love when games give you multiple ways to do them. so for me for example i would love to take down enemies from behind and move around freely than wait until he moves, do what i need to do and hide again before he comes back

- And it gets worse from not so well made AI sadly, in the first level i triggered the alarm and every enemy ran into the building i was in and than just stayed there till mission complete. I thankfully got the objective done or there would be no way i got it in that building after seeing 5+ enemies standing there.

- This game is super janky and needs polish

- The Sound design is also not great, i played it with headphones but did not heard any footsteps from the enemies which for a game like this, footsteps is critical mechanic to have ( original Splinter Cell have it ). Enemies sometimes heard me even when i did not made any sound and something did not heard me when i jumped from a glass window. It needs a redo

- No Map ( or one that i saw ) so i blindly had to search every building while avoiding the enemies which i can't take down to find a green light to get to to do the objective

- No quick save system which again i can understand if it was not made to make game harder and make you to finish mission on 1 try or restart but i died from small jump from a crate and that really pissed me off when that happened and made me wish the game had save system. Again, i would love if this game gives you option to play and choose what to use however you want so make it a difficulty thingy for example. have quick save system available for easy or medium difficulty and on hard no quick save or takedown like i mentioned.

- I didn't like the control of gun too. simple and small thing that would have made it better would be to have a aim icon when aiming down sight to make you know where you aiming that a light 

- Stun animation are short IMO. i felt like i shot a camera or guard 5+ times before i could move to where i want.

- Same objective of hacking computer and exiting. I wish there was at least some variety to it

LOOK! Cloak & Dagger can be a super fun, short game to bring back Original Splinter Cell Nostalgia to people but it will only be after a lot of work is done into it and OH BOY! it needs a lot of work. I won't refund this game to support the dev and i have respect for a solo dev to make a game this level all by himself but it needs added features, polish and few tweaks. 

And word of motivation to the dev, Don't give up on this game. Make the changes we are asking for and we will always have huge respect to you and the game will become super fun and nostalgia filled advanture.

Please keep up the great work you are doing and i hope some gaming company hires you cause you have a skill and a really good one. Until than i will keep my eye out on this game and will surely return when the things needed gets added/fixed. Thanks for a fun game!

review:
Cloak & Dagger is a short stealth game heavily inspired by old Splinter Cell titles. The game features 5 levels (though one of them is a tutorial and only has 2 enemies), with the main challenge being avoiding the guards that cannot be killed or taken out in any way. While developer did add an option to knock guards out from behind, it can be very clunky to use and enemies only stay down for a very limited period of time, so it's best to avoid confrontation entirely if you can help it.

Our spy is equipped with 4 weapons to help him deal with the enemies: a EMP gun that can be used to shock enemies or disable lights and cameras, which is completely silent, or you can charge up a powerful shot that will destroy the lights completely (though not the cameras), but that can be heard by enemies who will arrive to investigate the commotion. The other 3 weapons are all different types of grenades: EMP grenade, the most useful of the bunch, can disable every light source in the environment, though in my experience it doesn't always disable cameras, and I'm unsure if it's a bug or not. Next we have a flashbang, which disables enemies for a limited time, and finally a noisemaker. Frankly, in my playthrough I only ever used the EMP grenade.

Levels in the game are very short, if one were to look on youtube you can easily find walkthroughs of the full game that can take less than 30 minutes overall. However, they aren't without their charm, the Oil Rig level in particular was a pretty big difficulty spike due to cramped environments and confusing layout. Despite their small size, the levels often provide the player with different ways of approaching their objective, such as breakable windows or vents that can sometimes be used to circumvent a large part of the level.

The game can be pretty buggy, particularly during climbing animations, which a few times resulted in me getting completely stuck and unable to move. The final level also had noticeable framerate dips, though overall it was playable and the game never crashed on me. The AI can sometimes bug out and end up stuck on in an alert state, standing in the same spot, which I assume happens because guards are unable to reach the source of the sound and end up stuck in place. 

Despite its issues, I did enjoy Cloak & Dagger, and my main issue with it isn't even the price, which isn't all that high, but rather the length. Game is very short, and while, to my knowledge, the dev is currently working on a new title, I wish he made an update or DLC for Shadow Operations with a few new levels. Even with how short they are, if the title had at least twice as many levels I could've easily recommended it, but as it stands this is a very cautious recommend that mostly applies to the fans of the genre, or those willing to support indie devs interested in providing us with the style of game that AAA publishers are not invested in these days.

The Camera zoom  when it's registering there's a wall behind the character  is oriented to the way the character is facing, not the positioning of the camera, forcing it to zoom into the players body no matter what angle the character is at when against walls, at least half the time I noticed it, distinctly on the second and third level.  

The stun animations are way to short almost negligable, basically slapping you on the wrist for even trying to  use stun features along with the fact the guards instantly come out of it and on alert.

The crawling section under the trailer/house at the second level where the terminal is, has invisible walls under it locking you in there. 

There isn't any sort of melee or grapple system to disarm guards as a alternative or follow up for the stun, only making the idea even more hampering.

The crouch walking is painfully slower then simply crawling, which shouldn't be the case, especially with the noise level you generate simply crouching, I think it should be faster, and the noise level should be reduced for noiser surfaces, 

sometimes climbing objects, especially the tilted barrels, near walls will clip you right into and through the wall, I got locked in the third level climbing something by the wall and just had to quit out. Along with climbing the barrels by the window on the second level, clipped me through into the building. 

The cone vision is a bit to blaring obstructive, It's funny to compare it to old games where they have vision cones, but they should be reduced to simply using the flash light on the ground as a indicator to their cone of vision. 

last thing to suggest, the grenades fall into the same issue as the weapon, the emp grenades don't give close to enough time, the stun grenades don't let you do anything, and the noise maker probably isn't loud enough. It didn't work for me all that well at least. 

I strongly thing that there should be a way to get physical to reward players for getting close enough to a guard unseen, but also, I think there should be a point system for never disturbing the guards, that being said, They seem extremely sensitive and just break out of any stuns to easy.

review:
Up front I feel that far too many early access reviews do everyone a disservice: the Indie Developer, the would-be curious Fan wondering if they should buy the game and the Reviewer's credibility.

Reviewing an early access game should be treated like something pre-alpha, proof of concept, proof or feature implementation -- so, if the game is only as far along as some very limited design goal, you're reviewing that, not what isn't there yet, or may never be offered.

By far most games in early access on Steam are very small teams, sometimes just a one man show projects that are looking for a few basic things:

· is what they're offering appealing
· are people interested in this kind of game implementation
· does it work properly on many machines
· are people willing to pay for it
· is there enough of any the above to continue development

If you're paying for an early access game, you are almost never buying anything remotely resembling a finished game, it may even be a game that's NEVER finished.

Early access game may have almost zero fun factor, i.e. it may just be a test of various features and systems, to see if they work properly and smoothly -- and unless you like game engines and exploring this kind of thing there may be nothing to occupy your interest. Or it may be a brilliant implantation of high concept game design that's horrifically bug ridden and virtually unplayable.

In the opinion of this reviewer you should not buy an early access game for the same reasons you buy a big commercially developed titles from a large publisher, i.e. something that that's a known quantity, a known kind of fun, and has certain reasonable expectations and disappointments attached to it.

The reasons you should buy an early access game are, or should include: you like the genre, you like the Developer's ideas or content, the genre is poorly represented and anything that has hope of going in a good direction needs your support, there is enough of a game there at the price that you're happy to pay for it regardless of limitations.

Of course, if development continues, and you support the game you may have some input in the direction development takes, and this can be a lot of fun and a very constructive positive experience for Fans and the Developer.

So 捍卫SafeGuard, is a very bare bones game at this stage, what it does offer on the six PCs I have run it on is rock solid everything, no crashing, hitching, or flaky everything. This imho, is how games SHOULD be developed -- features are added, refined till the work flawlessly, then new features can be added or a level of aesthetic polish can be added.

So very bare-bones game, but all the systems are there for what could evolve into a very compelling and well-built game: good net code, weapons configuration systems, terrain maps!, and decent looking art assets.

Where 捍卫SafeGuard goes from here remains to be seen, but if the Developer continues this could be a real sleeper that becomes one of those hidden gems. Until then you can support it like I did buy buying it, but you're not putting money down for a game with much in the way of compelling game design yet, but a very solid foundation for what could be a good tactical realism game.

"Pineapple pizza" and some sort of variant of "OMGLOL" were among the unlocks. Very "lol so randum XD" type stuff.

Avoid. Not even worth it if it's on sale.

Play it if you're new to the genre, but don't bother if you've played these for a while.

review:
No Anglerfish is a quirky puzzle adventure. Much like the Witness, you are exploring a chain of islands with computer screens scattered around, and you need to solve the logic puzzles on the screens to progress in the overworld. Usually the puzzles are self contained, but there are cool moments where the environment affects the puzzles, and where the puzzles affect the environment (like the Witness). 

This game was made entirely in Python by a teenager. This means there is not much polish, and several UI and control-related frustrations. The doodle art style and offbeat dialogue gives the light story a very stream-of-consciousness feel. I found the whole exprerience to be delightful and refreshing. With so many games trying to create epic cinematic experiences and heart-wrenching tragic stories, its nice to play a light-hearted game with silly moments and no message. 

The puzzles are sokoban-style with some extra elements thrown in, like multi-push and conveyor belts. Trust me when I say this is a unique take on the sokoban genre, and that the puzzles do a good job of exploring the most interesting concepts in the possibility space. Each puzzle also has an optimization challenge, where you need to solve in a target number of moves, awarding a token when you do. I thought the optimization was fun, but in case that is not your thing, you can be assured that you do not need to do the optimization in order to progress the story (though there are some secrets which require tokens).

It doesn't feel like the average mobile game-esque vibe that many current year tower defense takes up; It more so feels like a classic flash game which is always an appreciated style in my opinion. It's a simple game, you buy peasants and you give them weapons both bought and crafted. It's an original idea, and I can appreciate some intuitive design in what is otherwise a genre full of copycats of whatever's popular.

However, I do have some criticisms here. 
1. It'd be preferable to be able to see the remaining amount of rounds, I may have missed it, but if it's there then it's not visible enough.
2. The balancing is pretty great, but I think to be able to actually tell what tower is doing and firing what some visual indicators of things like slow down and burning would be ideal. 
3. Generally the particles should be more distinctly visible for the sake of clarity. This could be achieved by brightening the colors or even making the sprites more complex: For example making fire have a range of red, orange, and yellow bits inside the particle's sprite instead of one orangish pixel. 

Overall, I like this game's beginning and I hope it goes farther! Great job.

review:
I've completed 4 of the game types (the 3 Spider Solitaire variants and Simple Simon) and was trying the game type Scorpion before review. There's a lot of luck involved in the hand you get dealt. 

In the Scorpion mode I noticed that a certain move was impossible for me to make, but it had to be made to be able to win. The cards were dealt unlucky from the get go: an 8 of Clubs lay on a Queen of Diamonds and a Jack of Diamonds lay on a 9 of Clubs; I could only place the 8 on the 9 and could only place the Jack on the Queen, there was no other valid place to place these cards on, because empty rows may only be filled with a king and you may only place same suits on eachother where the cards follow directly (e.g. a 9 of Clubs needs to be followed by an 8 of Clubs).

Because of this luck needed to be involved, most of these game modes seem to me as a huge waste of time. Games are already a waste of time but games with an unobtainable goal are the worst of the bunch. 

Also, the double click to move a stack didn't always make the smartest move, it was annoying to use here, in comparison to the Freecell Collection. 

Of the game modes I tried, Simple Simon looked like the most replayable. Because you can see all the cards from the start, you're able to check if the goal is even achievable to begin with and to set up a strategy. Spider Solitaire with 1 and 2 suits were very achievable but less interesting than Simple Simon.

Spider solitaire with 4 suits and Scorpion were, imo, frustrating because of the hidden cards, on top of the luck of the deal you need to even be able to win.

If you want to invest in a collection of cool solitaire card games, I would rather suggest the Freecell Collection. It's still mind-bending but achievable. I even think each freecell game is even winnable if you play your cards right but the collection doesn't have the option to replay a deal, so the only way to find out if you can win a deal you lost is by doing a bunch of undo's until you're at the start again.

To recap: imo, Spider Solitaire isn't worth your time because a lot of the deals are unwinnable from the start, not (just) because your strategy was bad, and you'll only find out after you've invested a bunch of time in it.

Maybe I'll try the other game modes later. Maybe I'll update this rambling review some day.

review:
Alright. [i]8/8/88 Needle AL[/i] is done and dusted. I don't know if I bought this at some point or if it was always free to play and I happened to claim it randomly, but I tried playing this previously on my Steam Deck and it was not functional, so I thought I'd give it another go on my desktop. And I'm happy(?) to report that it did in fact function fine on desktop with k/m controls. Anyway, let's dive in:

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319130851

First off, I want to talk a little about the title itself. In numerology, this is known as [i]Repetition of 8[/i], which is when the number 8 appears multiple times. Its influence is amplified. The date 8/8/88 has four eights, which can be seen as a strong indicator of prosperity and significant positive changes. The number eight represents wealth and success, and when eights are linked together, they are known as [i]angel numbers[/i], whereby, allegedly, they are very powerful messages from your guardian angels telling you that something big is coming soon. [b]I already knew about the number eight in numerology, but I compiled the rest of this via internet searches.[/b] Now, I am very definitely not religious, nor do I give credence to the idea of angels, but this game absolutely does. However, it takes the approach that you should always be careful of what you wish for, lest you actually get the thing you were seeking. And that the positive change you were hoping for might actually be the opposite of what you were seeking.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319130611

With that out of the way, this is not a fun game. It's actually very serious and very very dark. It features all the things you hope to never witness or experience in life. Rape, torture, pedophilia, murder, being eaten alive, watching your children die, slavery, racism, religious cults, the elite stealing everything from you, and so on. It's all in this game. [b]In fact, I would advise seriously considering this when you are deciding whether or not you would like to play this.[/b] You will not feel good after playing this. And those rewards I mentioned when talking about numerology. Those were doled out to the people in charge, who also took everything from the people who they governed/employed/enslaved. And the punishment for getting what you seek was also meted out amongst the people who had to deal with them. As such, nobody really wins (actually, one character did kind of win by managing to escape, but otherwise, not so much).

As far as the gameplay itself, the game is presented mostly via aged, filtered light photographs with random interactable objects that each advance the story in some way. You play as a brain damaged middle aged to old (this is not exactly specified) janitor who has the hots for a 12-year-old girl and finds himself alone in this town of Needle, Alabama; wondering where everybody went and wandering about trying to find the rest of the townspeople. As he triggers memories (via those random interactable objects), he slowly begins to unlock the mystery of the town. It is implied that other people did manage to leave the town, but not many. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3319130632

Anyway, that is the game. It takes about an hour and twenty minutes to complete, and you probably will wish you hadn't played it for all the sick shit that is presented within. However, the saving grace is that this game does not condone any of these activities. It functions more as a lens by which you can view what life was like in small Southern towns after the Civil War in America, and how people struggled to deal with the integration of black people and the dissolution of legal slavery. Interestingly enough, that does parallel the far-right movement in the U.S. today, where said people struggle with and rail against the integration of women, minorities, secularism, and gender identity in a world that has moved on without them. And for that reason, this game does actually have a strong message about the folly of clinging to hate and divisiveness, despite my warnings about the actual content. And there is merit in experiencing it. You just need to be aware of the incredibly dark content before deciding to do so.

review:
I love the 3D photographs, and the effects overlaid upon them (e.g. the fog, dust specs, lens flare etc). The audio is ok (I did use headphones).

However, the story does nothing for me. I realise this is alpha, however it seems more like a virtual tour as opposed to even the beginnings of a game. 

As for the areas the devs want feedback on, here goes:

1) Narrator's voice and dialect: I didn't have any narration, it was all just subtitles, I could hear the sound effects, didn't know there was supposed to be narration until after I finished the 2 chapters.

2) Pacing: It didn't intrigue nor engage me. It was a fairly interesting tour of an abandoned prison, but there was nothing that compelled me to explore, I just wanted to get to the end of it,

3) Storyline arc: I disliked the story, it was very vague and I wasn't keen on the subject matter. The hotspots had nothing to do with the story, they just served to make me admire the setting, but I felt the entire experience was completely devoid of a storyline beyond the snippets of info hidden behind the hotspots

4) Atmosphere: The atmosphere generated by the imagery and audio was good, however it really didn't add anything to the story, as above I felt it was little more than a tour of an abandoned prison, with some randomly placed hotspots that had nothing to do with the text.

Reading the other reviews I am wondering if I played a different game to everyone else.

I hate to leave such a negative review, and while this isn't for me it may be for some people. What I will reiterate is the 3D photography, setting and atmosphere these specific items generate is beautiful. 

Good luck to the devs, I hope it is a success when it comes out! 👍

review:
Sadly this is a big step down from the developers' first game, Wardwell House (which I enjoyed a lot).

The basic game mechanic consists of clicking through 360-degree photo environments; it may seem simplistic, but the environments are usually creepy enough that the atmosphere is great. These locations are just fantastically eerie.

The problem is that there's essentially nothing worthwhile beyond the cool 360 photos. The game's plot initially seems promising, but it goes nowhere; it basically devolves into clicking through lame stories (about prisoners being tortured or the activities of a creepy cult). The game is completely lacking the sense of dread and suspense that fueled the experience in the developer's previous game.

There's no suspense or fear here at all. Just wandering through creepy 360-degree photos and clicking through stories. That's it.

Like other reviewers have mentioned, it also feels like this was a low-effort project (beyond the story and text). There are obvious elements in the 360-degree photos that are modern and not period-appropriate, but they haven't been removed. I wouldn't mind this too much except that the experience as a whole is just so yawn-inducing and boring.

Simply not worth it, even at a sale price.

review:
The good part of the game is the gameplay: The gameplay is really interesting. The whole reason I bought it was based on the idea of a panoramic horror-exploration game. I was hoping exploration would be more incentivized though: This is more of a visual novel. The only way to progress is by clicking on the blue dots in each area then clicking on the arrow that pops up to move to the next scene. The panoramic camera shots, though, were amazing and I often found myself spinning around and admiring the scenery. It's not 100% period accurate: some things from modern times bleed through into the shots, but I didn't have a problem suspending my disbelief over those little details. Obviously the pictures weren't taken in the 1800s.

But unfortunately I'm not gonna pull punches with the bad, I'm just gonna swing the whole hammer: The story has a lot of racist undertones, and in chapter 2 that switches to overtones with a splash of p*d*philia to boot. This really caught me off guard: Somehow even after reading (let's be honest, skimming) the short blurb synopsis, I still expected the game to take place in 1988 and not 1888. The thing that gave it away to me wasn't the locales but the way African-American people are referenced throughout the first chapter. 

Overall the details are way over the top and gratuitous, and it takes way too long to get to the part where the racist p*d*phile cult leaders get razed and dragged to hell. That's just what I HOPE happens at the end of this. There are 3 chapters and I stopped at what I assume was near the end of Chapter 2, right after the note where a judge begins staging a race riot and simultaneously asks for a 14 year old girl to be sent his way. I imagine that's just typical 2 birds, one stone behavior in this community. 

This just felt so empty that I feel like I became less of a person playing it. You can do better.

[b]TLDR: Don't try to play this on stream like I did: uncovering what this game truly is makes for a very, VERY uncomfortable experience. [/b]

And a note to ALL horror writers since I've seen this bleak and edgy style becoming more prevalent in the genre: There's a point where you're supposed to stop dogpiling the viewer with THE BAD and let something [i]good[/i] happen. These reprieves are what drive the story forwards. Inevitably you're gonna run out of likable characters, and then... why is the viewer even here?

review:
IMO, this should be marked as BETA. It has a lot of bugs. It's not beginner friendly, either. If you know nothing of programming, you would probably find it hard to follow and learn. It doesn't really have an audience: It's too buggy for professional development, yet too complicated for beginners, IMO. 

"Programming Without Coding" sounds like a misnomer, too. It's not like SCRATCH, for instance. You can't just build the code like building blocks, per se. You need to understand the semantics of RING to program with it. For instance, you need to know the syntax of conditionals, strings, etc. 

It says I used it for 12.5 hours, but that's a lie, lol. I left the program open overnight :) I used it for maybe a couple of hours, exploring what it was about, but I keep running into bugs. 

For example, it will crash out of no where, then you lose all your unsaved code. If I run into it again, I will describe what happened.

There are other areas that don't make sense, like you can't move blocks of code through drag and drop or between branches. Let's say you want to enclose an area into a loop that you already created... Well, you have to copy, cut, paste it into the new area. You can't just relocate it. 

Another annoying area is how the console popup works: When you run code for console mode, a CMD prompt pops up, which is fine, but you can't reuse that popup and put it into a split screen. The popup takes forever to come up on my computer, then each debugging requires a new popup, which isn't on top of the screen, so you have to navigate to it through the task bar. 

If you try to use the program in split screen, the program crashes for some strange reason. Like if I put the CMD prompt on one side and this on the other, it will crash and freeze. 

There is no way to put the CMD prompt into the development area, either, so it's aggravating. When I was looking online, I came across RING Notepad, which does have input in the development, too. 

Some of the decisions seem weird, like the Switch statement: It has cases for the individual cases, yet in the RING Notepad, a lot of examples uses ON, so that's a weird change. I noticed that you could use multiple things for the same thing, like PRINT versus SEE versus PUT. I don't know the language enough, but the documentation uses SEE a lot, so it's weird that this uses PRINT everywhere. It's just confusing if you are following the RING documentation. 

I could see the developer is passionate, and I support that, but I can't recommend it outside BETA. Thus, I will go with not recommended for that reason. If it was in BETA, I would recommend it.

review:
PWCT is a refreshing entry into the field of easier to use products for conceptualizing an idea into an actual working application. PWCT should be considered an easier transition into the world of understanding what it is to develop an application. With its visual approach to programming it makes the understanding of what is required and how to apply it less of a burden on people who want to create applications. 
How does it do this? It provides a list of many of the building pieces called components in PWCT that allow you to apply everything from declaring variables to interfacing with files or databases. Does this require you to understand the concepts of developing applications? Yes, it does but the learning curve to gain this knowledge is made easier by PWCT’s visual approach to putting the application together. 
It closely resembles the idea put forth by Legos the popular toys that provide a way to build anything you can imagine. Although Legos will allow you to build complex building structures it does require you to understand building principles to accomplish that goal. However, like Legos there is little, or no knowledge required to get started and begin to build something that works and bring you satisfaction that it is indeed possible to take an idea from concept to reality with the right tools. 
PWCT is supported by a team of dedicated professionals who are very responsive to the questions and needs of their community. Each  day a new tutorial is being created to help new users of this product to create something that works while learning programming concepts at the same time. The community is strong as well for a new product with some of its members providing tutorials based on the learning they are doing of PWCT to assist others who might be helped by a different perspective; that of someone learning the product as they are. 
The price point to dive into this development environment is very inexpensive currently compared to other integrated development environments or tools. What can you develop with it, really anything you can imagine. A personal application, something that would be sold commercially, or even a game as it supports many gaming libraries as well. As you progress your knowledge of the development process will improve. That learning process is required to have an understanding of the pieces needed to create a larger more complex application. 
Achieving this though is made easier by PWCT’s approach to it. I as an owner of the tool and end-user still learning, encourage others to jump into this environment. What do you have to lose, a few dollars and a little time if it doesn’t work for you. What do you have to gain, a broader world where you now can create applications that serve your needs and allow you to gain some important skills in the world of development.

The Dev's are also quite active and are quick to fix bugs and are open to user feedback. For example, there was an issue with the application not resizing correctly (or at all) and within a day they had resolved the issue and put out an update. There seems to be quite a bit of work planned and so far it seems the dev's are up for the challenge!

For anyone looking to get into a base line of coding and get a feel as to how coding works and the logic behind it, this is a great first step! The dev's have released a few video tutorials to help get you started in the steam discussions as there's currently no implemented tutorial but that seems like it will be added in a future update.

For the price of the program including the current sale price, it's worth getting it and trying it out for yourself!

review:
If you get frustrated easily, this is not the game for you.

Star Lodge is as advertised - a solitaire-esque game featuring 3DCG art on the cards. Unfortunately, there is no explanation on how to play. The main menu gives you an option to play a game...that's it. A card gallery would be a nice touch, but you'll have to make your own.

You are tasked with unlocking the full deck of cards to play with (you start with 25 of 50 already available to you) with those unlocked cards being able to be used in future games. You have resources to accumulate and spend on cards to help in your progress towards a win. Research, Biology, Technology, Health and %(?)Progress are what you will be seeing on your starting cards. I won my first game after 30 minutes which unlocked a Coin card, but I have no clue what Coins are for at this point, but there is a counter for them on the main game page. Resources are tracked in the lower right corner of the game screen and can be used to "purchase" better cards (possibly) from the next rotation of Pick-3. Get to 100% progress to win the current game and unlock a new card.

There seems to be a level of RNG involved with what you receive, even if you are saving up your resources for the better cards. Quite frustrating when you go 111 rounds to be left with a choice of -75 Health|-100 Health|-75 Health. I would categorize this as a time waster where you could maybe unlock all the cards after 12-15 hours of gameplay with seemingly little in the way of rewards (the renders on the cards are decent). I would definitely say get this on heavy sale as the base price of $4 seems high for what is being offered. I'd probably give it a neutral if I could, but the negatives seem to outweigh the positives on this one.

TL;DR - Overpriced, frustrating time waster. Buyers beware.

Highly recommended! Fantasy Fighters has been a fun ride and so easy to jump into.

In this game you have the choice of 4 classes (elf, dwarf, paladin and Rogue) my personal favourite was the elf class. All the character animations are nicely animated and all the character designs are well thought out. The backgrounds are also nicely varied with forests, deserts, snow and castles.

The combat is easy to get into and fun to play. You will have different weapons depending on class but you will have some archers and a healer to back you up. There is also a choice of using a shield or a special attack. I recommend doing the special arrow attack as its honestly so satisfying.

Another thing that's satisfying is the sound design, the victory jingle is really rewarding and fun to hear. The sound of people being hit by your special attack really packs a punch.
