The system requirements in this game are incredibly misleading, the store page states that it only requires a GTX 770 and a "3rd gen i5", with 2gb of RAM on Windows Vista. First and foremost, the Vista requirement is very misleading as Steam ended support for operating systems older than Windows 10 on January 1st. So despite what the system requirements say, this game would not run on Windows Vista. 

Next off, the GPU stated in the requirements is a GTX 770 which only has 2gb of VRAM...As this game runs off of the DirectX12 API and uses UE5. 2gb of VRAM in this game will simply not cut it, I am testing this game on my rig with a Radeon RX 7900XT (20 gb's of VRAM) and will report that at 1440p Default settings (This game has no graphical options) The game uses 2.5 gb's of VRAM, higher than the 2gb on the GTX 770 and that's not even accounting for background tasks running on your card. 

Which also brings me into my issue with the system RAM requirements, this game lists 2gb of RAM enough to run the game. Considering that Windows 10 itself will hardly run off of 2gb of RAM, this is false. If we are going to revisit the GPU (GTX 770) with 2gb of VRAM and the game itself using as much 2.5 gb of VRAM. Then this means that we are going to have a memory leak where the game will leak into system memory because of the lack of VRAM. Leaving your system with only 1.5 gb of system RAM, not accounting for the 500mb of System RAM the game already utilizes. Leaving you with a total of 1 gb, obviously Windows 10 cannot function on a single gigabyte of system RAM. So this will likely result in the game being unplayable or just a flat out crash. 

This game seemed very promising but this just ruined it for me and I can't recommend it.

review:
Dicefolk is a unique and charming blend of roguelike and dice-based mechanics that offers a fresh take on dungeon crawling and tactical decision-making. From the outset, the game grabs your attention with its quirky premise and engaging gameplay loop, where every move hinges on the roll of dice. This core mechanic adds a layer of unpredictability and strategy that keeps each run feeling different and full of tension. The combination of chance and choice is handled deftly, striking a satisfying balance between luck and skill that rewards thoughtful planning without ever feeling unfair.

At its heart, Dicefolk invites players to manage a small tribe of dice creatures navigating dangerous dungeons filled with enemies, traps, and treasure. Each dice character has unique abilities linked to their numbers and suits, creating a surprising depth of strategy in how you build your team and approach each encounter. Combat and exploration revolve around rolling dice, with outcomes influencing your success in battle or the discovery of secrets. This system encourages players to weigh risk versus reward constantly, deciding when to press forward, when to retreat, or how to optimize their dice combinations for maximum effect.

Visually, Dicefolk stands out with a delightful pixel-art style that manages to be both retro and whimsical. The colorful, hand-crafted environments and character designs give the game a warm, inviting personality that contrasts nicely with the tension of dungeon exploration. The UI is clean and functional, helping players keep track of their dice stats, abilities, and health without overwhelming the screen. Accompanying the visuals is a catchy, upbeat soundtrack that complements the game’s playful tone while maintaining a steady rhythm that keeps the gameplay flowing.

One of the most impressive aspects of Dicefolk is its replayability. The procedural generation of dungeons means that no two runs are the same, with randomized layouts, enemy placements, and loot drops ensuring fresh challenges with every attempt. This unpredictability, combined with the dice mechanics, creates an exciting dynamic where adapting on the fly is essential. The game also features meaningful progression systems that unlock new dice characters, abilities, and upgrades over time, providing a sense of growth and motivation to keep coming back even after tough losses.

While Dicefolk excels in many areas, it is not without some minor flaws. The learning curve can be steep at times, especially for players unfamiliar with dice mechanics or roguelikes. Early runs might feel punishing due to the randomness inherent in dice rolls, and some encounters can feel disproportionately difficult without the right strategy or luck. Additionally, the pacing can sometimes slow down during longer dungeon stretches, which may challenge players looking for a faster, more action-oriented experience. However, these issues are relatively minor compared to the overall enjoyment and depth the game provides.

In conclusion, Dicefolk is an inventive and engaging roguelike that successfully combines dice-based gameplay with tactical dungeon exploration. Its charming art style, thoughtful mechanics, and high replay value make it a standout title for fans of strategy and chance-based games alike. Whether you’re drawn in by its unique concept or the challenge of mastering its systems, Dicefolk offers a rich and rewarding experience that keeps you thinking—and rolling—through every twist and turn.

Rating: 8/10

review:
TLDR: Movement shooter with nice gameplay but limited level & enemy design.
————————————————————————————————————————–  
Nice movement shooter with tracking aim as the first class citizen, since the weapons with the highest uptime are the fast-firing automatics. Each weapon felt reasonably distinct and useful in some way.

The gameplay feels reasonably good and polished. Pretty nice UI, nice sounds, sufficiently good animations. Your movement is pretty nice. You can get to decently fast speeds, but with limited air accel, BUT you have a dash that redirects your velocity (e.g., Diabotical et al.). Tracking feels pretty comfy since the movement acceleration of you and enemies is pretty soft.


This game does streamline the ammo mechanics compared to other games in this genre by forgoing ammo pickups and having regenerating ammo instead. You still feel reasonably encouraged to swap around your weapons despite technically infinite ammo since the regeneration is slow and there's some incentive to swap to other weapons to speed up the regeneration of others.

Some weapons have low uptime because of their slow regeneration and max ammo.
For example, the rocket launcher only has 3 rockets and regenerates each rocket reaaallly slowly, making it a fairly conditional weapon. Enemies killed by it do have higher shield/health drop chance, so they make use of its low uptime by giving that nice spice.

No ammo pickups also means it's much less visual clutter. All-in-all, I like the ammo system and how certain weapons are limited. The numbers on them also feel reasonably tuned. But I do like tracking aim, so I'm heavily biased in this regard.


Now, let's get into what I didn't like about the game. I mainly didn't enjoy fighting some enemies, and I think the enemy & level design is a bit limited in scope.

For enemies, there are two main annoying offenders—the spheres that shoot lasers and the venators.

The spheres that shoot lasers will track you perfectly up to a certain speed, and you need to be decently close and bhopping around them in order to avoid their laser. It's not inherently a bad thing, but they get spammed quite a lot. Fortunately, they're not terribly tanky for the most part. E.g., you can railgun the weaker ones once and then punch them. The stronger ones are rare enough and large enough that I can DPS them down with the plasmagun and/or hide from them until you have opportunities to dink them. Still, it annoyed me. I wish they had an angular acceleration limit and/or a small time-delay, but maybe that would make them too easy, depending on the numbers on those.
I mainly have an unpleasant memory from one level without too much cover where I had to DPS check them on a second run through the level after my first atttempt ended up with me getting lasered to death.

Venators are enemies with an attack that shoot projectiles towards where you will be. What makes this attack annoying is the combination of how much damage it deals and how tanky Venators are in general. They feel oppressive to the point where I avoid them and snipe them from a distance, which feels wrong but felt like the only consistent strategy because they move too much for my other weapons.

But, there's one level where the entirety of it is spent fighting two elite Venators, and there are two challenges where you take less than 2000 damage and kill them before you waste too much time, so I assume there's a better way to deal with them that I haven't figured out. Probably just weaving left and right to bait their predictive projectiles and then orb + plasma.

There's one enemy that teeters on the point of being annoying because they have an invincible dash of sorts that they use when attacked too much, and they can chain this dash right after using it once, so predicting where they will be occasionally fails. But they are reasonably easy to avoid, they usually stay in place enough to get value from an orb, and the gameplay loop of shooting other enemies & sniping them when they're in sight (and not dashing) is enjoyable enough to offset my distaste for these aspects of them.

The caveat to my complaints is that I am rather bad at kiting and movement in games. I also actively avoid improving my movement for a certain insane reason. So, there's my bias and pecularity that makes these enemies particularly annoying to me.


Now, what do I mean by "limited enemy & level design"? I mean that the variety of enemies and levels is not as much as it could be.

I don't want to extend the length of this review too much, some of my thoughts are too vague, and it will definitely be some heavy dev backseating, so I will just remark on parkour stuff. The parkour sections are relatively sparse, and the sections that exist are also pretty short. Could've probably thrown in some more parkour stuff and had more objectives to do that weren't just shooting plasma fuses. Have some shooty objectives with less health, smaller, etc. 


Something that I hated was the final boss. I will just say that I did not enjoy the lava mechanic, and the boss fight did not feel particularly engaging.

Smaller nitpicks:
	• I wish weapon swapping was faster by default, but you had to wait until after a weapon was finished firing until the swap happened. E.g., Quake.
	• Energy dmg type/shield type didn't feel particularly relevant or something that I had to think about too much since enemies that can gain shields are also enemies that I was usually using the plasmagun on. 
	• I wish the sensitivity could go down lower, but I'm an insane person who prefers to use 25600 DPI for an admittedly stupid reason, so it is what it is, and I can just lower my DPI.
	• I wish the hacked timer was closer to your crosshair rather than being in the upper right. Also, it's weird that you can be hacked multiples times but being hacked is an idempotent debuff as far as I can tell.
	• The score display should probably be on by default. I glanced over the option because I didn't realize it also showed your combo multis and all that, and I don't think it's not too much clutter. Though, I'm not the type of player who pays attention to scores, speaking from my experience of having played Ultrakill, so I'm speaking for a supposed group that I'm not a part of.
	• The tutorials could be a bit slower. The game mainly explains a gun's mechanics in a text box when you pick it up (though you can read them again in a menu), and I think it would've been nice to have sections that force players to use a gun's mechanics before they can move on.
	• Enemies can sometimes stay behind cover and take a slight amount of effort to find when they're the last alive.
	• Not a fan of how you can still pick stuff up even if you're full on that resource.
	• It was sometimes slightly unclear what you're supposed to do. There's one mission where a jump pad opens up after a fight, but it wasn't obvious to me until I accidentally took it and got launched into the path forward. For the fights with the elite venators, it took me a bit to realize that I should be shooting the plasma fuses to drop their green shield, and I had to get a hint from the challenge to realize it.

review:
While this route is definitely one of the more iconic to come for the series, there is one major glaring issue that makes this pretty much unplayable: controlling long distance trains downhill reasonably.

In the ES44AC, the dynamic braking application is very much all-or-nothing as opposed to the ranged power that is supposed to work in practice and is implemented in all the EMD units as well as the other GE products.  Going from set-up to B3 goes from no braking force to full braking force, and similarly to reduce braking power from above B3, one has to drop all the way to B1.  This causes players to have to constantly adjust dynamic levels and brake line reductions to avoid runaways, especially dropping down from Gallitzin to Altoona over the 1.8% gradient.

Additionally, this is an issue that actually has carryover effect onto other maps by identically affecting the dynamic braking application on the AC4400's on both Sand Patch and Cane Creek.  Uninstalling this DLC also does not fix this particular issue with the AC4400's.  Perhaps an oversight, but I do not see these getting fixed.

During Aegis’s time to take down the tyrannical clockwork tyrant the resistance tells her that one of its members have disappeared and all signs point to the somewhat abandoned Hôpital Saint Louis, an almost abandoned hospital with many a dark rumor, a place that the twisted Cagliostro operates from, so Aegis must explore this twisted place and save one of the resistance members, but that's easier said than done for what horror will Aegis face in Caliostro's lair.

The likes, the levels is very good like I said this is a good DLC as we get to explore a whole new area, the hospital is definitely creepy with some good environmental storytelling. The new enemies and boss are good, they have some interesting looks and killing these new enemies is a good way to help in grinding a lot of XP, the boss of that area is also pretty interesting it has a nice design and I like the quill sword it has.

The story was good as we get to find a little bit more about Caliostro and the things he was doing. The characters were good like I said in the review of the main game it uses real life historical figures in an alternative history setting which is quite interesting as you get to learn a little bit of real life historical facts about them.

And two I do wish they kind of went a little bit further with the horrors of Cagliostro's Secrets, I mean this is the place where he conducts his dark rituals I don't know I feel like they could up the horror factor a bit maybe even include another boss, maybe one made up of mechanical and human parts like a legion type creature, but that's just me personally.

Now that I told you this Steelrising - Cagliostro's Secrets is actually a good DLC, and this is a step in the right direction for DLC, as it introduces a new area, new enemies and new boss, I just wish they expanded it a bit more in the horror factor, but I recommend this. But I also recommend that you buy this when it’s on sale, maybe along with the two other DLCs if you want.

review:
Feels like a mobile to PC port (since it is exactly that). Physics works well, the boats act like they normally would, but there isn't as wide a range of content as i thought would come with a simulator that costs £2 or 3$. It makes sense that is isn't the most technical simulator out there, as it is only £2, but it does seem a bit basic, especially with the controls. The whole thing is controlled by a mouse, meaning that you can focus on one specific thing at a time, which means that you have to try and switch fast between the sheet and tiller controls. In a real life sailboat, especially the Laser dinghy, you would have hold of both the main sheet and the tiller at the same time, which therefore means that you can control both at the same time, and in this game, you cannot.

Don't get me wrong here, it is great if you want a chill sailing sim, but if you want to get the proper feel of a sailing yacht or dinghy, you should find another, likely more expensive sim, such as eSail. This is a budget option - has all of the basics, but isn't the most detailed. It is good, but not great.

I finally finished the game on Hard difficulty
PROS
The game itself is really fun and does what it sets out to do well. On their own, most enemies felt fun to have to dodge their projectiles, especially cultists, their bulllets were just slow enough to be able to dodge out of the way if you were careful

CONS
The more I played it though, it quickly turned into a major slog. Especially in the 2nd and 3rd chapters, everything began to seriously overstay its welcome. Everything from the greater daemon fights to the sorcerer to every single different type of enemy, just was repeated over and over again until killing them felt like annoying chores. At some point in Chapter 2, I started saving in the middle of fights so that I wouldn't need to go back if I died - I feel like that's a sign that the game is too much of a slog. review:
Boltgun is a good game for most of the time you spend playing it. The combat is really satisfying and the movement feels great, and it's very authentic to the Warhammer 40k experience, but the deeper you get into the campaign (if you're playing on hard difficulty like I was) the more you start to see the seams come apart with bad bossfight arenas and gimmicks instead of challenges.

I bought 40k Boltgun + the expansion pack on sale and I'd recommend the whole thing when it does go on sale. Auroch Digital & Focus Entertainment are pretty generous with the discount and for $14 you can't really go wrong with Boltgun.

[h1]Extended thoughts[/h1]

I can't stress enough how good it feels to just do basic FPS things in Boltgun. There's some decent airstrafing you can do and dashjumping feels good for crossing distances, and it feels very in-line with how superhuman space marines in 40k are. There are some tricks you can do with dashjump + airstrafe + homing melee attacks that add a really nice level of movement skill to the gameplay. The game gives us all of the 40k fan favorite weapons plus some more niche ones; the bolter and heavy bolter have really satisfying sound + animation, the homebrewed imperium shotbolter is a nice take on a shotgun, the rocket launcher has truly big explosions, etc.

I think the armor ratings do a disservice to the flexibility of the weapon pool. It's the same kind of system that DOOM Eternal used where instead of doing simon says with weapon colors, you have to use a weapon that has a damage rating that's greater than or equal to the armor rating of the enemy. Playing on hard difficulty, this translates to a lot of "wtf that did almost nothing" moments when you're experimenting with weapons to see what will let you conserve ammo for big threats. Additionally, this is really all the game has going for it to separate itself from the original DOOM. This is a double-edge sword in that this is a great facet if you haven't played a lot of DOOM but sucks if you have and also played other DOOM inspired games or even custom .WAD levels.

Each chapter starts out really well and has a bunch of really cool and challenging levels, but you can tell that the dev team was cooking hard for the beginning and middle and then couldn't tie it up that well for each chapter's end. I think one of my favorite levels was the [spoiler]Grand Elevator[/spoiler] and it's a truly incredible arena. Some of my least favorite levels are in Forges of Corruption, one thing that stood out to me was that levels became a lot more cramped and hallway-ish with designated "box" arenas as I went through the campaign.

I will say that it was really damn cool to fight a [spoiler]Lord of Change[/spoiler] for the first time and then just have it be a common mini-boss for the rest of the game, same with the [spoiler]Great Unclean One[/spoiler]. Talked with fellow 40k fans as I played through Boltgun and the consensus we've come to is that while having Nurgle and Tzeentch team up is a neat pairing gameplay wise, it's weird lore-wise. The game doesn't leverage traitor marines and traitor guard for Nurgle at all which is a bummer. 

I think they got pretty close with the basic enemies in Boltgun but there are a lot of annoying nits. For instance, the traitor champions having plasma gun blasts is kinda stupid because they're based off of the pinky demon from DOOM, but the whole reason the pinky demon is balanced is because it's a useless dip that's a walking target when engaged at range. The traitor champion being able to resurrect should be enough of a challenge to deal with. Conversely, I really like the way they implemented Terminators in Boltgun because they have a ranged and melee version, and the melee version is a teleporting pinky demon which is a crazy good take on modifying a DOOM enemy.

The fights against [spoiler]the sorcerer[/spoiler] honestly sucked past the first. I think the very first fight where you have to [spoiler]ascend the arena and make use of portals and ledges to snipe him[/spoiler] are cool, but with an action-driven game like Boltgun where you get to truly go fast and get into the fighting instantly, I'd say having some form of the infamous "yellow paint" would have actually been a good application of it. The fights against him get progressively less fun. The last mission in Forges of Corruption is the cheesiest and least-fun level I've played since the all-blue level in DUSK, just constantly respawning enemies without any kind of tact.

All that said, I'll likely buy Boltgun 2 when it goes on sale. There's just enough that makes Boltgun 1 fun that would keep me interested and the bangin soundtrack helps mask some of the issues while playing, but after dealing with some of the later levels in Boltgun 1, I'd rather wait.

review:
This game is just boring.
Unless you are some turbo fan of the warhammer 40k series, skip.

It is rather unfortunate to leave a negative review here, as this game does have the correct fundamentals.
The visuals are very good, and with the combination of SFX and subtle animations they have really sold the feeling of being in a heavy space marine suit.

However, this game really struggles to engage the player.
Weapons feel rather underwhelming in damage which leads to a lot of the enemies feeling rather tanky.
I guess on the flip side means that the titular boltgun is rather decent.
Of the seven weapons I have seen, only like 3 felt decent, and one of them was severely crippled by its ammo count.
Being crippled by ammo count is a running theme for most weapons, most of them have rather low capacity and rather rare ammo, especially ones that are actually good.
The combination of enemies being rather tanky and you being significantly limited by ammo turns this into a rather methodical shooter, which, imo, completely ruins the whole premise of being a space marine on a glorious conquest.
I feel like I am legally obligated to give the shotgun a shoutout for being impressively underwhelming, and the rocket launcher for being very annoying.
Not only is the rocket launcher damaging you on prolonged use (negligible damage, but still), it has a rather lengthy cool off animation during which you can not switch off of it.
Level design, mechanically, is rather dull - it is long "fetch quests for keys" to open doors impeding your progress, with arena fights sprinkled in-between.
Arena fights are really annoying as they just spawn enemies in waves, and the spawn locations do not care where you are - you can have enemies spawn behind you for an easy ambush, and you can have a melee-oriented berserker spawn right in front of you and immediately hit you.
Even on normal difficulty enemies deal a surprising amount of damage, not enough to make you die, but enough to make you feel like you are wearing heavy chinesium rather than tons of emperor-sanctified steel.
Most levels have secrets but even those are the most uninspired thing ever - it is just a bunch of repeating "bonuses" (3? types of a singular magazine of powerful ammo, mild weapon upgrade that persists for a level, temporary damage up, extra armor, strong grenade, and a full ammo refill).
It does not even give you an early weapon as a secret, ever.
There is a rather low enemy variety.
At the start you slowly get introduced to the enemies and it is rather interesting to look at them, but then these same enemies are just the staple of the game going forward.
That would have been fine, and really, I would have commended the game for not being afraid of throwing fodder at you as it helps with making you feel powerful, but it reuses some of the bosses quite consistently for future arena fights, also.
It is one thing to fight a rather tanky boss when he is the challenge at the end of the chapter, completely another when he is just thrown repeatedly into a generic arena fight, while feeling just as tanky (can't even make an excuse of showing that your arsenal got stronger), for no reason whatsoever.

I do not think I am alone in this sentiment.
This game consists of 3 chapters, and according to the steam achievement stats at the time of writing, the completion rates for those are <32%, <17%, <13%.
Even if you discard the 32% clear rate for the first chapter (maybe a significant portion of owners have not played the game at all), of the players who have gotten through the first chapter, only ~42% (13/31) actually bother to finish the game.
Overall, I would suggest looking elsewhere, despite the rather positive rating this game is rather dull.
At best you would be looking at a coin flip for a mediocre experience.

I relied heavily on it and wouldn't recommend the game without it, because looking for the right keyhole kills the pacing.

Overall, it's a flawed boomer shooter, which gets repetitive, unbalanced, and boring at times. I got through it in 9 hours on medium difficulty, playing 1 or 2 levels at a time. Play it if you like the original DOOM.

review:
It's a Warhammer 40,000 Boomer Shooter. Nothing more really needs to be said. The plot is simple and straightforward (Kill heretics and daemons invading Graia), the weapons are all loud and punchy and turn your enemies into pixelated giblets (Shout out to the Heavy Bolter, my goat), and there are many, many hordes of enemies just lining up to be obliterated by the one Space Marine in their way (We probably kill an entire Black Crusade's worth of Black Legion over the course of the game). 

It's fun. Not perfect, but my complaints are minor. Base game isn't extremely difficult, though the DLC chapter ramps up the challenge. The environments will largely look the same (Varieties of factory, smelter, lab, and bigger factory), with the exception of some areas that get Warped around. Like many Boomer Shooters, getting lost in samey corridors can and will happen, though the devs added in an optional navigation toggle post launch to remedy that. Sometimes enemies will teleport into the arena directly on top of you, leading to some unfortunate deaths. 

All in all, if you like the genre and/or setting, Boltgun can be a good time. There's nothing that really stands out about it, but it accomplishes everything a game like it should. You run and jump and kill a lot. Plus, there's a dedicated taunt button. Recommended.

review:
In the grim darkness of the 41st millennium there are only boomer shooters. 

Boltgun is a FPS set in the over the top insanity that is the Warhammer 40k universe. A universe that is known for running entirely on the rule of cool and a healthy dose of madness. And this game knows how to best capture that: by pretending it's still 1996 and running with it. 

Boltgun happily advertises itself as a game that takes after shooters from the 90s. Maze-like level design, hyper fast movement and carrying a veritable arsenal of guns in your back pocket. The comparison to Doom is easily made, but I find it compares more to Build engine games like Duke Nukem 3D and Blood. In both visual style and gameplay. And that's not a bad thing, as those games are excellent sources of inspiration. 

And then there's the Warhammer angle here. The locals are full of skulls, the enemies are bloodcrazed cultists serving thirsting eldritch gods and you play a 2 meter tall augmented space monk preaching the righteousness of humanity with a fully automatic rocket launcher firing explosive Red Bull cans. Oh and you can taunt your opponents with the press of a button. 

It all feels awesome and faithfully captures a past era of gaming. Even without knowledge of the universe the game is set in, it is an adrenaline filled ride of fun. 

And if this is your first taste of the insanity that is Warhammer 40k: welcome aboard!

review:
I always enjoyed it for about 30 minutes per sitting. Any duration after that got repetitive and often annoying, despite how great the presentation was. Don't pay full price.

[h1]The Good[/h1]
+Skippable splash screens
+Four difficulties
+Horde mode (survive waves of enemies and bosses)
+Tons of options, can rebind everything, adjust UI etc
+Display options to increase or decrease pixelation
+Accessibility options to include invincibility
+Surprisingly colorful, for the most part
+Rare cutscenes are well drawn
+Good music
+Sound is excellent. Love the thumping of movement and bolt weapons.
+Autosaves, quicksaves, and manual saves available
+Squishy enemies in all levels for power trip
+The servoskull has some rare but funny dialog
+You can hear when a bolter magazine is nearly empty

[h1]YMMV[/h1]
~EULA
~The story makes no sense unless you're familiar with Warhammer
~10-12 hours for a single playthrough
~Servoskull can be distracting, even when set to low duration
~Shotgun's kinda garbage...and it's not bound to #3
~No map
~HP, armor, weapon powerup, ammo capacity reset after each level
~The rare areas with unexpected instant death mechanics are annoying
~Many combat areas don't provide enough room to dodge well
~Falling in most pits just teleports you to nearest platform
~The angled elevator in chapter 3 was very buggy for me
~The melee attack is needlessly complicated and rather useless
~The dash doesn't work if you're on any kind of incline
~The taunt is great for RP, but pointless otherwise. This, the melee attack, and dash (if it worked on anything other than flat terrain) should have given some kind of buff or health/armor regen if used successfully.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]
-Gets repetitive quickly, especially the first and third chapters
-Game doesn't explain quirks of some weapons
-More fog than Turok on the N64. Some can be turned off, but not all
-The two charging enemies do ridiculous damage
-The two charging enemies are usually unavoidable. Seriously. F those Aspirants.
-Bosses are repeated over and over and over and over
-Many bosses have infinite annoying trash spawns
-Vortex grenades should have their own hotkey
-Servoskull's directions are often wrong (deadend, old objective, etc)
-One boss had a wall-of-text dialog that there was no chance to read in the middle of combat

Played on:
Win11Pro, i7-14700K, RTX5060 Ti 16GB, 32GB DDR5-6000 @ 1920x1080
using KB&M
Normal difficulty

review:
Extremely cute! Unfortunately I can't say there's much beyond what you can see in the video previews/trailers. The description saying there's no objectives or points isn't exactly true; you have to unlock furniture by inviting gourdlets and waiting until they grow flowers until they fill a bar, which I assume is coded with a numerical value which... well, [i]I[/i] would call those points.
But it's a sandbox game, so you make your own goals. Except I made a goal to build a theme park, but realised there was a ferris wheel and nothing else. I made a goal to build a market, but got as far as some tables and umbrellas before finding there was barely anything I could put on them. I tried to make a forest camping ground, a beach, a bakery, a farmer's store, an arcade, but all of the decorations were so sparse and disjointed without even including the fact that sometimes I'd have to wait an hour before randomly unlocking the next one. It didn't feel like there were no objectives because I was free to do what I wanted, it felt like there were no objectives because I couldn't finish anything at all.

It's not even that I want "more" decorations, it's that the categories/ideas seemed almost entirely random and unfinished. Like, there's a vampire haunted mansion looking thing in the otherwise entirely euro-townhouse style options. There's a swingset, but no slide or carousel. There are picnic blankets but no picnic baskets. There's a bunch of gigantic pottery clearly from the pre-gourdlet era. There's one single, glowing mushroom.

Three especially minor things that bugged me since I have to justify giving a bad review to a cute, cheap indie game;

-The lack of counters/benches/desks. I know some of the tables are meant to [i]look[/i] like counters, but they're gigantic and clunky-looking and if you want to put down things like a cash register or display products, that's half of your already limited space gone. I'm also going to include in this that there's nothing in the outside category that can serve as a market stall - making a city builder without a way to make lemonade stands, ticket counters, coffee stations etc. is crazy to me.

-There are two main colour palettes for objects, one pastel and one saturated. The range/choice of colours is extremely limited and, to me, just as disjointed and random as everything else. There was no consistency in which objects had which palette, which also changed depending what pattern the object had (particularly the walls/floors) and it was tedious going through the menu trying to check them all. The yellow, orange and red were often indistinguishably ugly (sometimes pink included) and the default BSOD blue was always completely out of place. The lack of a neutral brown especially annoyed me because something as simple as a wooden floor was a chore to make.

-My playtime would probably be cut in half if not for that random grind achievement they hit you with at the very end. The combination of gourdlet flowers not being collected passively, the ridiculously slow amount of time it takes for them to grow and the fact it's tied into getting the rest of the items (most of which you probably don't even want) means you end the game on a very bad note. It's fine, I just trapped them in an eternal maze-prison of hedges like everybody else and took a nap.

review:
LONESTAR is a slick, inventive blend of roguelike deckbuilder and tactical spaceship combat that takes familiar mechanics and reframes them in a way that feels fresh, deeply strategic, and packed with style. Developed by Math Tide and released into full version in April 2025 after a strong early access period, LONESTAR casts you as a lone bounty hunter navigating a universe of criminals, relics, and unpredictable interstellar chaos. It borrows from classics like Slay the Spire and FTL but carves out a distinct identity with a battle system that feels more like chess with lasers than cards and dice. The result is a game that excels at moment-to-moment decision-making while offering long-term progression and build variety that can easily suck you into one more run.

At the heart of LONESTAR is its unique tactical combat system. Rather than relying on the usual energy-costed cards or real-time ship combat, the game introduces a system built around energy “pigments,” weapon lanes, and the careful management of offensive and defensive modules. Each ship has three lanes, and in every battle you must charge one up with collected energy to try to overpower the enemy’s aligned lane. If you win that lane clash, you deal damage; if not, you take a hit. It’s a system that seems simple at first but becomes surprisingly deep as you add weapons that pull energy from other lanes, install relics that change how power is generated, and unlock talents that synergize with specific actions or timing. Defensively, you can dodge attacks by shifting your ship out of a targeted lane, but doing so costs precious fuel, creating an ongoing tension between mobility and endurance.

Every run in LONESTAR begins with a choice of pilot and ship, and each pairing dramatically changes how you’ll approach battles. Pilots have unique talents and quirks, and ships vary in their energy systems and lane configurations. Over time, you unlock new pilots, ships, and modules—more than 50 pilots and 200 components by the full release—which gives the game staggering build variety. Some pilots lean into shield play, others boost energy production, while certain ships are clearly designed to set up late-game combos that can melt even the hardest enemies in a few turns. As you progress through a run, defeating bounties and choosing routes across the galaxy, you’ll earn relics and new modules that further specialize your build. Some synergies can be so powerful they feel almost broken—but the path to discovering them is a huge part of the fun.

Between bounty hunts, the game introduces a novel twist: vacation segments. These intermissions give your bounty hunter time to relax, recover, and explore optional narrative choices that can result in treasure, new talents, or weird outcomes. These brief breaks from combat add a surprising layer of storytelling and character to a game that might otherwise be all tactics and numbers. They also affect your next bounty contract, giving each run a narrative rhythm that elevates it beyond pure repetition. The writing in these segments is humorous and sometimes surreal, which complements the quirky tone of the game’s art style and worldbuilding.

Visually, LONESTAR opts for a clean, cartoon-inspired aesthetic that emphasizes clarity over spectacle. Ships are modular and colorful, UI elements are sharp and highly readable, and each new relic or pilot feels distinct and easy to understand. Though the game’s art isn’t technically flashy, it nails the presentation required for a systems-heavy strategy title, ensuring that information is never lost in visual noise. What really stands out is the UI’s commitment to transparency—hovering over components and actions shows exact outcomes and predictions, making the game’s inner workings feel intuitive and fair. There are no hidden dice rolls or behind-the-scenes trickery; LONESTAR wants you to understand every move you make.

The full version includes a final boss, The Endbringer, and a series of difficulty modifiers called Bounty Levels that ramp up the challenge significantly. At higher levels, enemy behaviors change, damage scaling becomes punishing, and decision-making becomes even more critical. These endgame challenges cater to hardcore players, and while they do occasionally result in difficulty spikes that feel unfair, they also reward experimentation and mastery. However, not everything lands perfectly. Some players may find that later runs begin to blur together due to repetitive event design or familiar treasure options. Additionally, the tutorial remains minimal even in version 1.0, making it harder for new players to grasp the deeper mechanics without some trial-and-error. A glossary or expanded onboarding system would go a long way toward easing that learning curve.

Despite a few rough edges, LONESTAR more than delivers on its promise of strategic depth and replayability. Runs are tightly paced—most lasting under an hour—and the sheer number of pilot, ship, and module combinations means that no two journeys feel quite the same. Steam Workshop support also allows for custom ships, relics, and pilots, opening the door for community-made content and even more variety. For players who enjoy carefully constructed synergies, tactical positioning, and creative problem-solving, this game is a goldmine. It doesn’t reinvent the roguelike formula, but it reshapes it with smart mechanics, rich customization, and a tone that’s equal parts cool and weird.

In a crowded field of roguelike deckbuilders, LONESTAR finds its footing by doing something unmistakably its own. It’s not just about building a deck—it’s about mastering space as a battlefield, managing energy as both weapon and lifeline, and pushing your build to survive a gauntlet of beautifully constructed challenges. The loop of combat, customization, and strange little space vacations creates a compelling rhythm that’s hard to put down. For strategy fans, roguelike enthusiasts, or anyone who’s ever wanted a little more tactics in their deckbuilding, LONESTAR is an easy recommendation—and a game that will likely stick around in the genre’s conversation for some time.

Rating: 9/10

review:
This is currently my favorite DCS campaign. It's a prequel to the Raven One book and you play as their protagonist, Jim "Flip" Wilson earlier in his career aboard the Valley Forge. Most DCS campaigns challenge comes from purely combat related tasks, but this campaign smartly gives the player a broad spectrum of tasks that test your knowledge of the Hornet and carrier ops. 

I'd highly recommend it to anyone seeing a more realistic campaign and has a fair amount of Hornet flight hours under their belt. You'll definitely want to read the kneeboards a few times before attempting a mission as the objectives aren't reiterated mid-flight as pilots would be expected to know them. You'll spent a fair amount of time hopping radio frequencies and cross-referencing daily code word changes which will challenge your ability to multitask in a way other campaigns do not. 

Pros: 

- Interesting and challenging mission objectives.
- High quality VO with known members of the community, including custom AWACS and Carrier comms.
- Baltic Dragon constantly updates his campaigns to work with new DCS updates/features/bugs.
- Having a tie-in book series makes the story content inherently more interesting.
- Extremely detailed kneeboards that are critical to your success.

Cons:

- Not the creator's fault, but the Syria map is a known performance hog, especially on longer missions (Which peak around 2.5 hours near the end of the campaign).

review:
I wouldn't normally review this but I do have a bit of feedback that I'd like the dev to see

I like this game, it's neat and does some playful stuff with it's transformation mechanic; I've seen a few games experiment with tf fetishes and they're neat though they don't always push things in mechanically interesting ways
latex dungeon which was a recent, more popular, one for instance has tf and stuff, but does very little with it outside of using it as a means to make you grind tasks that are kind of boring

the tf in this though IS mechanically interesting; having both your form and your abilities constantly altered based on who is attacking you is a solid mechanic and in isolation from the rest of the game's design, it's good enough that if you removed all of the sexual elements, you would still have an interesting game to fool around with

it is only good in theory though
you see, the tf mechanic is very dependent on *who* is attacking you; it's very cool when you have enemies pushing and pulling you in different directions, 
but you need multiple enemy types for that to work,
and unfortunately there is generally only one style of enemy tf per every area, so it rarely happens outside of your initial few minutes of exploration.

since you can't really fend of the tf forever, you ultimately always end up being stuck with a single form, regardless of what you brought into the area,
when this happens, the game just sort of goes back to being a standard rpg maker game, except worse because mechanics like swapable equipment had to be nixed to make the tf mechanic function the way it does

this is a kinda sad, cause it straight up nullifies the game's best aspect.

I'm not sure what would be the best way for the dev to solve this, they could try and have it so there's a bit of cross pollination between areas with you dealing with multiple enemy archetypes in each zone so you are tfing more constantly
or they could add more tfs per zone so one sub enemy type tries to turn you into one thing whilst another tries to turn you into the other (as an example in the first area, one enemy type could try to turn you into the bunny sub as seen in game and the other could try to turn you into a counter bunny domme with very different abilities)

I honestly don't know how they should go about it, but it is an issue that needs to be fixed in order for this to be as fun as it could be

review:
[i]Note: Played the game for dozens of hours over on the Quest so don't mind my low hour-count on here. But here are my thoughts as a somewhat veteran of the game:). SPOILER:[/i] [spoiler]It's great, get it!:)[/spoiler]

[h1]A VR Sports-Trainer Done Right![/h1]
The concept of Rezzil Player is as simple and straight forward as it can get: [i]"Play elements of real-life-sports in VR".[/i]
However, in my years of VR experience so far, i have yet to find another game that manages to translate motions like heading a ball or throwing a Football into VR as accurately and seemlessly as this one. The inevitable lack of an object's weight is being compensated by a close to perfect and predicable physics engine which elevates this game to the forefront of all Coordination Trainers and Sports Simulation Games in VR. I keep having to remind myself that I am in fact not hitting physical object but a virtual one.
The wholesome and communicative team of developers have been working together with top athletes from a variety of fields, ranging from professional Soccer Players, to NFL player or even Race drivers to try and deliver the ultimate training experience in VR and it shows - I have to attribute a lot of my physical fitness, as well as recent gains in hand-eye coordination to this game!
But before I briefly cover the individual modes:

[h1]Yes, the Challenges are real and there is thousands of dollars in cash up for grabs, monthly![/h1]
The team curates special challenges in form of the Pentathlon (a combination of all modes with a huge prize pool), famous goal recreations and several other themed challenges every month.
Now that that's covered, lets have quick look at the different modes available in the game:

[h1]Headers[/h1]
As the company "Rezzil" itself is deeply rooted in Football (or soccer for the Non-English), it makes sense that the game's signature and pretty much main gamemode revolves around heading balls around.
This is where the superb physics come into clutch, as the player can choose test their skills in 4 different modes of headers - Traditional goal-shooting, passing, clearing and ball control. Every one of these modes features several dozens of levels that range from easy to INCREDIBLY DIFFICULT so every player is guaranteed to find a suitable challenge (Same applies for the other gamemodes). As is the case with any mode, there is both leaderboards for players to place themselves on in pursuit of that coveted rank #1 and modifiers that allow players to spice up their gameplay (invisible balls are brutal).

[h1]Reaction Wall[/h1]
While the headers modes are geared more towards full-body coordination and accuracy, the Reaction Wall drill is guaranteed to bring anyone's sweats on by testing their speed, reaction time and hand-eye coordination. The principle is simple: Hit the lights in front of you as fast as possible and try to get into the zone. I personally view this drill as a concentration exercise even, as you really have to focus completely on the task at hand if you want to do well.

[h1]Hoops[/h1]
Hoops is the rhythm game portion of the game where you lead a basketball through oncoming rings. The same concept as with any rhythm game applies here too: Looks easy and simple but turns out to become eshausting really quick. Thus, view this as the cardio portion and leg workout of the game.

[h1]Field General[/h1]
Field general turns you into an NFL quarterback by putting an american football into your hands with the mission to throw that thing far and hard. Same as with the headers mode, you are able to work your way through an assortment of levels and difficulties where the game strikes a healthy balance of force needed to throw and "throw assist".

[h1]... Closing Words[/h1]
Would I say this game is for anyone? Pretty much, yes. - While I surely won't recommend Rezzil Player as an essential pick to someone that's looking for action or shooter games, I still think that everyone is able to get something out of the game, no matter if they are a full-on athlete or my grandma. Be it the gamified cardio, serious training capabilities, raw challenge or physics appreciation, Rezzil Player will be an awesome bang for your buck!

I hope this little insight could help with determining if this is a buy for you:)... Hoping to catch you on the leaderboards then!;)

Finally the legendary BR 103 arrived!

Bugs!
There are some bugs or things that seem unfinished I found:
- The Speedometer on the 103 isn't entirely accurate! It is accurate up until 90km/h and then creeps out of sync, usually displaying a speed 1-3km/h below your actual speed, so beware when wanting those gold medals!
- Trees are plopping in quite visibly, especially when playing in Winter without snow in the vicinity, as the distant LODs will still show snow on the trees.
- The HUD sometimes shows incorrect upcoming speed limits. The signage is correct, so that's a good chance to learn to drive without HUD assistance ;) (f.e. a Lf7 showing "Expect 100", the HUD saying "Expect 120" and the actual speed limit both posted and game-internal are 100km/h)

The most important question:
Did they fuck up the BR103?
No! It is great. It really feels like the beast that it is, drives and sounds just amazing and I'm really glad we got this addition - hoping we will see more of it in the future and it won't be confined to a single route!

Route is set in 1990s and my personal opinion is that is one of the better routes provided by DTG, really enjoyable if you are player enjoying older locomotives. 

Gameplay: 
In base game you can find Two locomotives and one control car: 
DB BR 103 - jevel of this route, really nice loco
DB BR 110 - known from Bremen route, really like this one, at least here comes with different livery for vagons
Bnrdzf 463.0 control vagon for BR 110 passenger setups
Those locos came with passengers only for BR 103 as high speed train, and local passenger with more stops for BR 110 in mint livery vagons and with freight versions of BR 110 pulling two types of cargo wagons. It is mixed passenger and freight route which is good. I consider that type of routes best from TSW. 

Scenarios and timetables: 
There are 6 scenarios for base game, 2x for BR 110, 3x for BR 103 and one mixed for both locomotives, thumbs up there was good idea from dovetail (maybe last by the state of latest DLC´s).
If you own Niedertalbahn and Kassel - Wurzburg routes there are 301 timetables: 
- 113 for BR 103
- 188 for BR 110 passenger and freight
- 39 for control vagon
- from Niedertahlbahn there is DB BR 628.2 diesel multiple unit with 49 timetables, nice to see in traffic and sitting in yards
- from Kassel - Wurzburg TSW3 base route is BR 401 old ICE running only in 2 timetables. But guaranteed you will enjoy sipping coffe while riding on AFB with this one! (Becouse those old locos are more like playing piano on this route - here accept, here sifa, here brake a bit, here power to slight incline and so on :D ). Sadly nothing more as layer, as in my knowledge now. 

Scenery: 
Route looks really nice by DTG standart. Maybe they took something from Niedertahlbahn reviews? Anyway, you drive pretty nice and long route, in two thirds of lengt by the river, rest in suburban and urban area as closing to terminal station. Water looks really nice. Right now I was enjoying autumn sceneries. Do not expect miracles - road cars are discusting as ever, on some stations there are people stuck in station only head can be seen out of concrete floor... Still looks good in comparison to others. 

Pros:
+ scenery
+ diversity of trains in base game
+ mixed freight and passenger route
+ set in 1990s

Cons:
- stuttering! lag! still present (october 2023)
- locomotives moving without pantograph raised (for example in last scenario - BR 103)
- no layers from older german routes (only from Niedertahlbahn and Kassel-Wurzburg), dangerous precedens
- BR 103 can NOT be played on any other german route, and this is sad

As whole pack I recommend this route. Is really good for players who likes old locomotives. Nice change from germans everywhere present push-pull passenger setups. With nice scenery and multiple trains is always something to choose and play. Control vagon Bnrdzf 463.0 should be something for experienced players, new players may find it too difficult to enjoy, but for experienced players is really nice gamplay! My only concern is fact that there are many locomotives in my library which of none is usable in this route, and that is sad. Players should not be locked from gameplay just becouse "out of period" excuse from DTG.

review:
Ladies and gentlemen, buckle up and prepare for a wild ride as we review Train Sim World® 3: Linke Rheinstrecke: Mainz - Koblenz Route Add-On. This add-on is the talk of the town, and by "talk," I mean people are discussing its uncanny ability to disappoint at every turn. If you love bugs, graphical glitches, and errors, then boy, do we have a treat for you!

Starting off with a bang, or should I say a screech, the 110's brakes are as broken as my New Year's resolutions. In fact, they're so broken that the 103 decided to join the party too! This brake fiasco is so much fun that it makes you wonder why anyone would bother fixing it. I mean, who doesn't want to go from 160km/h to a dead stop in a matter of seconds?

But wait, there's more! The scenery is like a buffet of glitches, from catenary masts standing in walls to black areas and awkwardly simple boat models on the river. It's like a game of "spot the anachronism" with wrong cars and buses from various time periods thrown into the mix. The only thing missing is a dinosaur waiting for a train at the station. Speaking of stations, good luck finding out when your train will arrive since the PIS system is entirely absent. Who needs to know arrival times anyway, right?

Now, if you're a fan of abstract art, you'll love the trees that appear as white lines against the horizon. It's like Mother Nature herself decided to dabble in minimalist painting. And if you thought the Oldenburg DLC was a bit lackluster, hold onto your conductor's hat because this new route takes it to a whole new level of emptiness.

The cries of "Please Dovetail Games, fix your stuff!" echo through the forums, but it seems like these issues continue to go unnoticed. The golden days of Train Sim World 2 German routes are long gone, replaced by the sheer hilarity of this trainwreck of a release.

You might ask yourself, will they fix the Oldenburg route? The answer, my friends, is a giant question mark looming over the train sim world like a missing catenary mast. Perhaps we'll have to wait for the mythical "special projects team" to bless us with a working PIS system, or maybe we'll just have to enjoy the chaotic mess that is Train Sim World® 3: Linke Rheinstrecke: Mainz - Koblenz Route Add-On.

This DLC is a masterpiece of comedy, featuring poorly textured buildings, recycled sounds, broken brakes, and mysteriously disappearing water. If you're looking for a laugh, this is the perfect addition to your collection. After all, who wouldn't want to pay for the privilege of being utterly baffled and frustrated by the sheer lack of quality in a game? So, hop on board this crazy train and enjoy the ride!

So, all aboard the Disappointment Express; our final destination: Facepalm Central!

review: one of the only nazzombies like i have played to truly feel like its atmospherically embracing the horror genre. the visuals are beautiful, moody, stylistic, and entrancing. the contrast of color choices and the way dithering and film grain are used is flawless. the way the map design mimics the best part of simple zombies maps but maintains aspects of bo1 zombies with the added perks and certain other features of later zombies is peak. the music is so fun, and the camo grind is fun too. most of all though, the movement in this game is great fun, and because everything is intentionally staggered, navigating and weaving between enemies and gaining distance works much better than traditional trains here -- especially with the expensiveness of the games resources causing the need for extra careful execution of early round strategies and i fucking love it. even late in the game the knife can be used for tactical point kills, the gunplay is so much fun and punchy and requires high precision to progress and not be overwhelmed. the exploration and constant progress upgrades of weapons and perks is so much fun and i frankly feel like even for a game that seems somewhat small ive barely scratched the surface. i fucking love this game and it is absolutely one of the best and most unique takes on the zombies formula ive seen. the closest thing i can think of to how this game wants to embody the horror energy of its genre is if we took the horror of sker ritual and condenscened it almost entirely to the use of tense atmospheric resource management, and it is still the same sort of vibe as nach der untoten. i love it, its great, if you like nazzombies like shooters you should absolutely get it as it is a blast and once you get used to it, the intensity and tactical decisions of a slower zombies experience gets to be quite a tense thrill. amazing game, get it full price even and you wont be disappointed. the only thing i really need to report is there are a few weird bugs, sometimes the game gets overwhelmed and crashes, or the melee stops working for the duration the game is running if you do not rebind the key (it stops afterwards though) otherwise -- reddoor is a spectacular, and deeply strategically atmospheric experience, and if you like the genre you will love this game.

review:
Compared to the infamous 40$ RE3R (originally 60$), this 10$ DLC offers the same playtime of around 5 hours with more content along with a lot more good puzzles than 3r (which had like 1 or 2 trivial puzzles in total xd). It also offers some well-distributed merchant quests whose completion is rewarded with [spoiler] the indestructible Elite Knife [/spoiler].

      [h2] Development: [/h2] Content-wise, it can be pointed out that the main campaign and the DLC were in development at the same time. For instance, in the base game you look at some inaccessible areas (like the high wooden rafters in the village) and think it's only for aesthetic purposes, then you find yourself playing at these areas in the DLC which released 6 days after its announcement and 6 months after the release of its base game, indicating this DLC was undertook along with RE4R parallelly since the earliest concepts of the game.
      [h2] Ada's hookshot [/h2] is now essential in combat and boss fights, moving around rooftops, wooden platforms and even getting around the hostile garden maze. The merchant has new voice lines in separate ways.

      [h2] Missing OG content / DLC Quality: [/h2] Rest assured, everything that haters said was omitted in the remake is, not only back in the DLC (which, again, is inseparable from the base game) , but also better presented and more enjoyable than the OG.
      We're talking about the good and iconic content here, not the lava room (ts is ridiculous and looks like it's from some zelda game).
[list]
    [*]The second village El Gigante you don't face as Leon.
    [*]The second Garrador (though isn't in a cage, the cage itself is present in a new beautiful grand hall)
    [*]Gandola ride (yay!)
    [*]The spinning spikes trap.
    [*]Novistadors sewers.
    [*]The iconic Laser Room is back with one of the best cinematic moments in the series.
    [*]Dropping pillars trap is back.
    [*]Not from 4 OG but def worth pointing out that chapter end music is remade off Ada's music in 1998's RE2!
[/list]

      That being said, Separate Ways doesn't mainly rely on said returning content. No. Something I appreciate about Separate Ways is how it gradually ramps up both the interactivity and tension, efficiently preventing monotony for those (like me) who already spent a hundred hours in base game. You get to experience RE4R for the first time again in a concentrated form with new content. At first, I was just going along with it not expecting more than what I saw in the main campaign or the OG — but I got hooked (no pun intended). That steady buildup keeps it from ever feeling repetitive. You would think that you don't need another boring El Gigante encounter, hoho man you won't believe how fun it was as Ada. Even the island, though only 2 chapters, is surprisingly more enjoyable in the DLC. 
 

      [h2] Ada's character [/h2] Ada's character design is fine, but the voice acting is definitely overhated. Yes, her one‑liners come off as dry rather than playful or mysterious, distancing her from her OG iconic [i] femme fatale [/i] voice/persona, lacking the early typical charisma and seductive undertones, and yes there is dissonance when comparing Ada to the other outstanding performances. So here ya go, maybe a bit lackluster but overhated considering the VA deactivated her socials for a while.

      [h2] Story/Next remake [/h2] is further expanded upon here it's not even comparable to the OG. Changes were made for the sake of story integrity and keeping things fresh. Salazar doesn't merge with his other [i] hand [/i] (aka The Black Robe) but is rather reintroduced as -surprisingly- [spoiler] U3/It [/spoiler] which serves as a main antagonist haunting Ada throughout the DLC creating multiple encounters. I respect how Krauser doesn't work for Wesker in the remake (probably never met the guy) and Ada not being there to help Leon out in the knife duel. I don't think Krauser ever met Ada, nor did Saddler (not until the end). This all (gratefully) eradicates the motive that led to Krauser fighting Ada in the OG, because it didn't make any sense. Separate Ways ends with a strong implication that the next remake is not Code Veronica, but RE5R. Wesker's character design, script, and voice acting is best we got arguably since RE1 but people love 5's Wesker as a supervillain and I wish this remains the case with RE5R, my man exudes class and grandeur in every aspect. Resident Evil is living its best days rn. It's not a matter of whether we're getting a 5R or CV remake, but only a matter of when.


      [h2] Pricing [/h2] Regarding complaints about charging ten bucks for the extra 6 hours you get: Dude 2005's low quality cheesy Separate Ways shouldn't even be put in comparison to its 2023 counterpart that is considered one of the best DLCs in gaming generally. If anyone were to return to the OG separate ways after the remake, they will realize how half-assed it was to justify the full price tag for the PS2 port a year after release, meaning we still indirectly paid for Separate Ways in the OG. Fighting Krauser again? rly?


 Separate Ways had to be remade, and this iteration of Separate Ways DELIVERED.
10$ quality DLC >>>> Superfluous not-so-free DLC

I say 2023 Separate Ways should be the gold-standard of how companies create DLCs, and a slap in the face to haters who still live in the past, blinded by nostalgia. 

Hands down the best DLC in the franchise with no contender.

review:
Worthwhile addition to "Resident Evil 4: Remake (RE4R)." If you liked RE4R, you'll like this.

"Separate Ways" (SE) is a pastiche of some of the best set-pieces from the base game, which you'll revisit as Ada Wong. Playing as Ada, you'll access these various areas through different means than did Leon (different caves, across the beams of a ceiling in the castle, etc). Sometimes you'll even play them in reverse (such as in the first two chapters).

Gameplay as Ada is noticeably different; she has no armor, a different (in some ways diminished) kit and a neat, if underutilized, new toy: her grapple gun. The grapple gun provides an illusion of mobility which was shattered for me during my Professional play through. Yes, it's fast enough to use in combat, but its applications in combat are limited. So much so that even with the arena set up for its use, its still just a gimmick.

The DLC is shorter than the base game, which is to be expected: RE4R contains 16 chapters while SE has 7. SE mirrors RE4Rs difficulty options: Assist and Standard are available right out of the gate, with Hardcore and Professional unlocking after a complete play through on one of the aforementioned difficulties. Those difficulty options play out similarly in both games, which is to say Assist is fairly easy, Standard is pretty normal, Hardcore seems to be the sweet spot between tough and fun, and Professional is an absolute slog. Achievement hunting in SE is more slog-like than it would be in its comparable difficulty in RE4R. To this end, I don't recommend folks do a lot of it... unless you're OCD about achievements (like yours truly) or a game wizard (unlike yours truly).

Recommend for: fans of RE4R; fans of the RE remakes in general; lovers of survival horror; those who appreciate visually stunning over-the-shoulder shooters that focus on the grotesque. Give it a play on Standard, then maybe Hardcore and leave it as a 'one and done'. That first pass through the old stomping grounds is a lot of fun and feels pretty different. Leave the Professional play through and achievement hunting to the pro's and possibly the sadists, though. Two thumbs up and probably an 8/10 for a single pass, but this extra episode might get long in the tooth for players before they've completed even the their first run.

review:
There's a core of a reasonable incremental game here, marred by two significant problems.

1. The game appears to be too simple. Perhaps there's some further depth to it, but I wasn't able to find it in nearly 3h30m of gameplay. Mechanically speaking, there's not a whole lot to strategise.

2. The controls and UI are.. well, they're pretty bad. After the very early game of each planet, your efficiency is based on how quickly you can wangle your mouse around, rather than your upgrades. Managing your upgrades and such in the overworld/hub area is awkward, with the menus being automatically opened and closed based on proximity to their.. building? Thing? This means that walking past the different utilities at your disposal makes you lose sight of your character. These menus also hide important UI elements, like the money you have to spend in the shop that's open.

The solution to the UI and control problems is fairly trivial, but the game mechanic issues may require a significant overhaul. 

For £1.70? Yeah, it's not bad. I don't regret getting it. But I wouldn't call it "good". It simply lacks the depth required to be engaging for more than a small time.

review:
I set up a "residents wanted!" sign on my town.  I spend gold to hire a maid NPC before going to town and buying a pig from an animal tamer.  Coming back, I set the pig to do my cleaning and the maid to be livestock because the game has no programming to recognize the difference between humans, animals, and monsters - they all have the same stats, hobbies, jobs, and even dialogue.  (Nothing like a pig shouting "The time has come for us humans to prosper!") The game also doesn't understand what gender is, either, because the maid is a male and as livestock is laying eggs so I can have a fresh maid egg omelette every morning, which boosts my learning potential so I can read more eldritch arcane tomes and finally learn the meteor spell so I can speed-fry more eggs.  If getting eggs from males bothers you, don't worry, the local drug dealer sells hormone drugs that you can toss at people to instantly change their gender, sometimes to the mysterious "???" gender.  Male Loytel was annoying, but as a modded blushing girl avatar, is much easier to tolerate.  Some eggs are fertilized, and using the gene machine, I can splice the maid eggs with the DNA I took from an eldritch horror to turn them into the ultimate maid lifeform.

Welcome to Elin, the roguelike with no sanity checks.  Please leave your common sense at the door.

Elin is prequel to the free (VERY) Japanese roguelike Elona, setting up the events in Elona nobody who speaks English cares about because the way it was written made the story cutscene translations non-functional.  Fortunately, Elona is a sandbox, so you just did whatever you wanted until you got bored and played something else as the plot of the game, anyway.  The main draw being that it's "Single-player Runescape with no level cap."  Feel free to grind the Abyss where there are infinite floors and infinitely-scaling enemies until you hit the point that the monsters are moving twenty times to every one of your turns and kills you instantly with the shockwaves of their footsteps before even noticing you exist.

Elona, in turn, was based on ADoM, a classic roguelike game that is available (in a version with an actual graphical interface) on Steam if you wanted to check it out.  This helps explain some of the otherwise inexplicable design choices, such as random mutations and the first dungeon being a puppy cave, that were "inspired" by ADoM.

Compared to Elona's quest to grind more stats, Elin has a much better-developed set of side mechanics centered upon owning your own lands and crafting, to the point that the game feels like it's bleeding into the Survival Craft genre.  Both are fleshed out enough that you can play either, but it's really designed for you to flip between the two, with the laid-back base management stuff being a breather to the high-tension dungeon combat.

Speaking of dungeon combat, you may be in for a bad time if you refuse to adopt any strategy other than basic fighter in platemail running straight at the enemy.  Similar to other roguelikes, the game is built around gaining random items that inflict status effects that the enemies have scaling resistances to.  Every thread in the forums about how they're hitting a wall unable to progress is a guy who refuses to use allies or summons, refuses to learn magic, refuses to use items, and just melee mashes until up against an enemy that can just lightning bolt him from range and then teleport away if he survives to reach melee range.  An actual brain is required, and the system for allies leveling up through using skills is the same as yours, so it's often best to leave meatheaded bull charges to the dumb AI scripts of your pets (which can be human or monster) while you use your brain to come up with tactics like throwing a silence potion at the teleporting wizard to stop that nonsense or casting the elemental resistance spell to stop taking instant death damage from the lightning.

The game has "classes," but this is a pure train-through-use game, so they mostly just give a bonus to how fast you gain experience in a few skills.  You can play a farmer class and, through the power of selectively bred mushrooms that boost magic potential, become a better wizard than the wizard class.  "Sticking to your class" is purely a self-imposed handicap, and almost impossible if you play the non-combat classes like pianist that scream to just use the tips you get from performances to buy spellbooks and learn magic for your actual dungeon-delving.

Elin's new expanded crafting system is clearly based upon the Atelier games from Gust, now KoeiTecmo, except now with the patented no sanity checks of Elin.  People leave bags of garbage out in my town.  I smash the garbage with a hammer to turn trashbags into plastic fiber.  I weave these into plastic shoes, then smash the shoes to get plastic ore.  I smelt ore to make plastic ingots, and then use plastic to make objects that are supposed to be made of metal, like a plastic cauldron that weighs 1/4th as much so I can put my kitchen inside my tent and carry all my food prep tools with me everywhere in my back pocket.

Add to this that this is a game with a lot of references and in-jokes.  Many of these are ported directly from the nearly-two-decade-old Elona, so enjoy a reference to "crawling in my skin" played by the bards some of you are too young to even know about. You can play as a tourist, a joke class that was a reference to Discworld back in NetHack where it first showed up, but is now a reference to a reference to a reference to NetHack.  If you're a chaos shape class, you mutate more limbs as you level up, but lose health unless you suck [Adam] out of [Little Sisters] gained by killing a [[Big Daddy]] in clear reference to BioShock.  Do not confuse a [Little Sister] for a younger sister, which is a de-facto mascot character of the game gained by reading a younger sister diary in reference to the now fairly old manga Chokkoto Sister (Notebook Sister) where a boy got a younger sister from santa like he wished for ten years ago.  (It wasn't an incest series in case you're wondering, he goes out with the landlady he gets to babysit for his magic ex nihilo younger sister.)

It also features content requested by a Kickstarter campaign, with the sort of Japanese NEET who spends hundreds of thousands of their parents' yen on a indie pixel art game with no sanity checks choosing what was added.  They chose an "Older Younger Sister" NPC (who is an older woman not biologically related to you that has never met you before who claims to have hidden a kitchen knife in your bedroom who wants to be your younger sister, for you to pay her 10,000 gp in "allowance," and is definitely not a crazy stalker you should run away from,) Melilith, a necromancer who continually summons zombie younger sisters, a shark younger sister and a younger sister shark, (the former being a younger sister wearing a shark hoodie like Guwa Gura and the latter being an actual shark that has a younger sister-shaped "lure" for a tongue,) an all-female cast of waifu unique rival adventurers that can be recruited, the option to play as [i]two different flavors[/i] of fox girl (two people paid ~$5000 and asked for the same thing) with their own fox girl village added to the game plus their own fox deities and fox girl maids that will join as an ally, the ability to play as a succubus race adventurer that gains power by crawling into bed with ANY sleeping creature, the NPC "mother" that is a nun ("mother superior") but is also a succubus with the class "predator" and will teleport to anyone sleeping to ravage them - one works in the orphanage that also seems to be a backer reward and a mother applied to be a member of my town with the stats "age 37 male, job: personal pleasure, hobby: nursing"... and several more still being implemented!  (There's also some other backer rewards like the punch-with-magic sword sage and edgy executioner class, but those aren't quite as funny.)

review:
Serious potential but it's not there yet.
Elin is an amazing idea for a game with great character customisation options. However there's only 1 really viable strategy in the entire game and if you aren't doing some variation of that strategy you won't be able to keep up with the end game.

The strategy is basically: Pick farmer, make money fishing and making wine. Level up crops to max out your stats.

Now I really don't want to see them nerf this strat, I think a lot of the end game content assumes you're running this strat. What I want to see is different strats being buffed to become as strong as this strat.
Like a monster breeding strat where you breed two monsters with high stats together to increase the base stats of the child. Making an army of high stat monsters of any kind eventually.
I adore that farming seed levelling systems, it takes me back to the early days of 7 days to die. But there needs to be more ways to raise your stats as viably as eating.

This game basically feels like this: You go into a playthrough after handcrafting a strategy you think could be viable, like level maxing a certain spell (Won't help you survive being hit), picking succubus and recruiting companions you can use to buff every stat (Potential levels degrade on level up), or investing heavily in crafting in the hopes to make an overpowered weapon (Crafted weapons are never stronger than dropped weapons, which are free).
Only to discover no strategy works other than, farmer, fishing, sell wine, eat high level food.

Hopefully the devs buff everything other than farming and leave farming as it is, if we could get like 7 different ways to play the game that isn't just farm-fish-sell wine-drink, it'd probably be a recommendation from me. Right now it's not quite there yet, which sucks because this game has serious "Game of the year" potential.

P.S. One other gripe is the devs seem adamant on nerfing your ability to get love pots, which are how you get monster eggs to recruit monsters. Other than high level monster balls which are pretty rare. If anything they should be encouraging players to recruit more monsters not punishing that playstyle.
