review:
the best game you *probably* haven't played

thanks to sseth it's getting the love it truly deserves. it's... hard to describe this game. REALLY hard. this is one of the very few games i have ever looked at the steam page of and thought to my self "genuinely what is this game about?"

to cut it 'somewhat' short - it's a mix of stardew-esque affection systems, farming & fishing, rimworld base management, procedurally generated roguelike dungeons, runescape-esque leveling (albeit infinite and less grindy) and many, many more. this game doesn't really do just one thing - it does EVERYTHING. the crafting, cooking, smithing etc systems are incredibly elaborate and are more akin to material alchemy than traditional crafting.

graphically, the game is isometric top-down with beautifully drawn pixel art. seriously, for all the things people praise this game for, pixel/vfx art doesn't get enough love. sure, it's basic, there aren't many animations and companions just kinda float behind you. but man does it look amazing sometimes, in its own way! lighting can be done REALLY well too if you got a knack for base building.

speaking of... this game is paradise for anyone who loves automation and in-depth base management/building. not only can you make things look extremely pretty but you can also automate production, the sale of goods, cooking/brewing, etc... down to the very minutest of details by filtering out specific keywords in chests so on and so forth. it's magical.

this is quite personal but one of my favourite things in this game is the fact that you can make almost ANYONE your compaion/resident. there are only very few exceptions (guild leaders and a couple other npcs i forget) that are excluded from this. other than that - monster ball any cool enemy you see, affection your way up with the king and have him farm crops for you. because why the fuck not? as someone who LOVES companions in video games, this is a dream come true.

all of this is a very short description of what the game has to offer. perfecting your livestock through gene mutations and various other bizzarre systems, an in-built sprite changer that is extremely simple & convenient to use, amazing mod support, VERY active development (the man doesn't sleep) and a great community to back it up. 

the only "criticism" i have of this game is that.. with the powers given to you to do whatever you want, some scenarios might get a little weird. you're not blocked from doing anything, the game doesn't wag any imaginary finger in front of you and say "no-no, that's messed up!" if you can think of it - you can do it. which can lead to odd results, so keep that in mind.

if you're someone who can get past the fact that his game isn't some graphical AAA masterpiece - get it & play it. chances are if you've come here from sseth and got somewhat intrigued by the concept of it you're gonna love it and drop 100 hours in a week. the fact that this game is in EA, offers you hundreds upon hundreds of hours of entertainment, has an extremely passionate, reliable & active developer.. AND ONLY costs 20$ is a fucking crime. it's less than most dlcs in modern day AAA slop.

review:
Reviewing Elin is a difficult one. Mostly, because there are simply not that many games around that are like this game. It's a very unique game, thats for sure.

Playing it, feels like being part of the Gintama Universe, there is so much absurdity everywhere you look. And honestly? That's one of the things that build the charme of this game the most. It is so hilarious sometimes, so many unexpected things can happen. And then you notice how deep this game actually is. Almost anything you think of, is possible in this game, almost anything can happen. The more you play it, the more hilarious and funny things you discover and the more you notice, that this game is almost as deep and offers that much of a sandbox, as Dwarf Fortress. The difference? You actually play a character and go on great adventures! 

The game basically lets you build your own town, recruit NPCs to live there, or even to join your party, or to just go onto adventures, find gear and things to sell in dungeons, get stronger and eventually become as strong as a god. Whatever suits your playstyle, everything is viable. There is no right or wrong way to play the game. There is a 'unfinished' story right now, but this game is mostly a sandbox! You decide what your goals are and you decide what you want to do. You can build a farm and make wine and become rich in the process or you go out onto adventures, getting stronger and stronger and dive into dungeons, which get harder and harder as well. You can also go catch monsters and make them your companions ... or livestock! You can do the same with normal NPCs as well! ... and lots more!

The possibilities are almost endless. Playing Elin makes you feel as if you live in some kind of cursed, silly isekai fantasy world. There are so many things possible in this game, way more than you could think of! Getting into the game is a bit difficult though. The intention behind that is: that the game just wants you to go out and try things. Experiment. Find out what you can do. And you'll most likely die a lot of times, but thats okay, because you learn like everyone did when they started the game.

I highly recommend this one for sandbox game enthusiasts. It's very fun but definitely difficult to get into.

review:
Going to start with the game's biggest downside first. This is a *very* complicated game with tons of systems and not a lot of explanation or help. In other words, you *need* to be willing to look stuff up practically constantly, and have to be okay with a lot of the game's documentation either not existing or being hard to understand.

Having said that as my disclaimer, this game is exceptionally fun. You can be a roaming wizard who uses fireballs, a warrior with a shining spear to pierce the heavens, a musician who is an expert at evasion so they can dodge incoming rocks, a fisherman who harvests whales worth the combined GDP of Europe, a farmer with a harem of body pillows, and really just about anything else you can think of being in a high fantasy setting. The freedom this game allows is amazing, and that's *before* considering the fact that it is heavily moddable with Steam Workshop access!

As far as the worldbuilding goes, it's pretty solid. The world is interesting, with a mix of both randomly generated AND unique NPCs so that there's both a consistent cast of important characters, but you'll still encounter other characters that exist only in your game from time to time. You can also name the random ones, change just about everything about them, and even use custom skins and portraits just by placing appropriately sized images into a specific folder.

The story so far at least is excellent, with a good mix of intrigue, unique characters, and just barely enough explained to get you theorizing without spelling out what will happen next. I'll hold off on explaining more though due to spoilers, as I'd rather not ruin the game for ya'll like some reviewers do.

Ultimately, the game is very fun. You really can do whatever you want in it pretty much, and there's mods for anything you can't. As SsethTzeentach(the youtuber who reviewed the game and got me to play it) said, "For as many turbo-level hypersweats at level 3 billion in the void, there's just as many who haven't even left their own base. So rest assured that, no matter where you're at, there's some guy who spent his entire playthrough cultivating mushrooms, and who has more money than the entire economy."

10/10, and I will probably play at least another 200 hours before I even know what I'm doing. lol

review:
Yep. It's Elona.
I say that in the most affectionate possible way; it's Elona, but it's also everything I never knew I wanted Elona to be, which means this game is going to destroy my life. It even still has that insane tonal jankness to it, so I don't have to leave my comfort zone. My comfort zone got *upgraded*.

For the uninitiated, this game and its predecessor are mystery dungeon-style open-ended RPG games consisting of a living hell of nigh-endless, punishing, and yet constantly satisfying grinding. Everything has a number and you can make it go up. There are ways to make the numbers go up faster that themselves grind numbers. You grind numbers to get to new places to get new numbers to grind, until eventually you have all the numbers and the only thing to do is make numbers go up higher, faster (and nuke Palmia but that's later). The only number the game's missing is a Getting-Kicked-In-The-Junk skill, because you need to become incredible at tanking nut-shots (if applicable) to be able to withstand some of the complete nonsense the RNG of this game will throw at you while you're trying to find rocks and books to sell to pay your endlessly scaling taxes.
And now, there's friggin'... *actual base-building*. Before you had a house that only existed to put fancy stuff and merchants in so you get tax breaks and don't have to go places to sell stuff. Now you can kind of delegate boring tasks to people, if you plan it right. The resources for crafting aren't just piles of crap you find on the ground anymore, they actually come from somewhere and you have to find them and carry them. The game's also a lot nicer to look at and listen to and many of the old tracks were remade; some others replaced, for better as far as I'm concerned. What I'm really all about is all the new combat effects. Makes fighting a lot more interesting and keeps me off autopilot. That and the obvious dedication put into a lot of the sprites — the tiles, especially, and how many of them have winter variants, more than impressed me. Game loves its details.

Generally, it's a solid upgrade and a solid game overall so far (I haven't moved beyond level 4 dungeons in like 40 hours because I keep getting new pets =v=). More than worth 20 bucks. The only downsides I can pick out are the perspective occasionally blinding me (mostly in cities so it's nbd really), and the fact that I have to play almost exclusively with my mouse now. I do miss the ridiculous number of keybinds a little, but I can't deny this new control scheme is pretty intuitive once you've gotten familiar with it, so maybe that's just a me problem.

As for the machine translation, who cares, like, at all. Keep the AI hate to the art sphere, folks; it does, surprisingly, have actual uses outside of grifting. Even if it's best for grifting. It's kinda like baking soda, sometimes you use it to make pastries, sometimes you use it to rig a trap behind your friend (or enemy)'s front door that'll cause a giant explosive mess when they walk in.
I'm sure that simile carried.

Anyway! My work here is done. I rambled publicly about a video game. It's a good one. Buy it if you like grinding, insanity, and pain.
Time to go back to my cave.
See you all when I'm 60.

review:
There aren't words in the English language to adequately describe this game, but I'm going to try.

Elin is... something, alright. Take your standard sandbox, grind its bones into powder and feed them to an RPG, then make cake with that RPG and an Isekai anime. Now assume that your third cousins are Kenshi and Dwarf Fortress. 

The game runs about 90% on normal game logic. Stuff like "do thing, get better at thing." Or "Plant seeds to grow crops so you can eat." Normal, established game logic. That last ten percent is unhinged, psychotic 90s/00s internet humor that ranges from silly and weird(often with nods to various online/IRL stuff) to lolrandomXD nonsense. 

This leads to it feeling like you're an Isekai character. Not necessarily the protagonist, though you can be, but a character in a semi-realistic world that also has a drunk cracked out narrator. You can open a tourist trap bar, or play music, or commit war crimes, or sell your body, or sell other people's bodies, or just be a hermit in the middle of nowhere selling flowers. 

The game is wildly broad, and frighteningly esoteric. The humor is unhinged, and sometimes concerning. I still do not know what I am doing, I'm just winging it. I also feel like I'm on drugs when I play, which you can make/do in the game for that matter.

I highly suggest this if you like old internet humor, total freedom, and an overall solid RPG. Now, time for me to get back to trying to catching fish for a catgirl that is regressing to cat...

review:
Um. Yes!

I can best describe Elin as Stardew Valley with a huge dose of schizophrenia. It pretends to be a dungeon crawler, town manager, farming sim, survival game, and a bunch of other things in one oddly synergistic package.

One thing that stands out in particular is the game's material-based system - almost any item can be made out of any material and that creates wholly bizarre experiences like making hats out of sand, swords out of paper, bricks of meat, and scepters of grass. All of these material-item matchups have real mechanical significance so it leads to bouts of experimentation where you attempt to wrangle items and materials to fit your bidding.

Also, it's super duper easy to die so try not to take that seriously and prepare for that in advance.
I highly recommend this game!

review:
This game is absolutely unhinged. I enjoy the base building aspect, the sandbox nature of the game, the freeform character builds that don't pigeonhole you into specific playstyles, the zany and intricate sandbox and immersive sim elements, and the number of ridiculous ways one can die in the game. Here are just a few of mine in the short time I've had to play:

>Crushed to death by my own hubris and heresy trying to make off with a holy altar to a goddess. I didn't know it was so heavy, and promptly ignored the action log telling me I was too heavy to move and being squashed by my own backpack's crushing weight. I kept trying to move until I was slowly crushed to death by sacrilege. 

>Drank an unidentified potion, which instantly killed me because I unwittingly drank a bottle of sulfuric acid.

>Mauled to death by a god damn turkey because it was, apparently, some kind of godlike enchanted mutation of a normal turkey.

>Drank another unidentified potion, which spawned several shadows around me. Confused as to what they actually did, I continued my adventure with my shadowy pals trailing behind. Upon seeing an enemy near me, one of them proceeded to make a beeline for it and exploded, killing it and me instantly. Shadows are good friends so long as your definition of friendship is "roleplays as dynamite and doesn't understand the frailty of the mortal flesh". 

>Accidentally hanged myself on a gallows by misclicking, which caused my pet to beat the everloving fuck out of me until dead.

>Mauled to death by a hermit crab. There's nothing extraordinary about this death, I just found it amusing.

This game is ridiculous, and after 15 hours, I can strongly recommend anyone who hasn't played it pick it up. It's tough, it's unfair at times, but it's delightful and I can't wait to see how much more absurd it can get.

review:
SRPGs are some of my favourite games. From Shining Force, Vandal Hearts, to the Fire Emblem franchise; these games always put a smile on my face on how they tackle the subgenre. Redemption Reapers piqued my interest once news was getting around about it. Outside of the game itself, hearing a veteran from Fire Emblem, Masayuki Horikawa, was involved made me even more interested. And with that, I dove in to see what this project had to offer.

For one is the music which is truly stunning. I never found myself distracted by the music and thought it helped assist in the mood the game was going for. Whether a more bombastic song in the adventures of the Ashen Hawks or, further in, some much more melancholic, these tracks throughout all aid in the game throughout one's journey. Even outside of the game, the songs hold up well.

The visuals are not bad. In-game, I think they're actually fairly well done. Each Mort you run into are quite distinct from one another, with the exceptions of upgraded Mort. The game is dreary and the visuals do a good enough job conveying this. The game is darker in colours, too, but I do enjoy how they balance that throughout the game. 
With that said, the cutscenes throughout could have used some more work. While not standing out as bad, they just have this uncanny nature to them. Some of the models will look over to the side several times when it doesn't make sense why they're looping the animation. The hair on many of the models, while not bad, just doesn't look right sometimes. Just some examples, but they do add up to make the cutscenes, which should be an experience and show to reach, be just a little strange to look at.

The gameplay is a mixed bag. This game focuses heavily on being just a small band fighting against impossible odds. With that said, the game only has 5 units to use. This severely diminishes a lot of strategy that other games in the genre have. Whether it be in a plethora of spells to use, many classes to play around with, or a game brimming with mechanics; Redemption Reapers is lacking in that department.
However, to say there is none is false. I found myself pulled in and found it fun to piece together how this rag tag group could manage their way out of a bad looking situation. How to manage one's AP in case you would need to unleash a bigger move next turn. Or how the defend command halved all damage, but you had to determine whether sacrificing your counter attack was worth it.
Redemption Reapers is a game with plenty of hidden depth, though due to the lack of options, some options are the best thing to do. However, this game does feel familiar to play, and with a veteran of Fire Emblem in board, a lot of the mechanics feel adjacent to the popular franchise.

The biggest flaw in this game is the story. Without going into spoilers, the issue here is there really isn't a goal. The characters only react and go from mission-to-mission. The lore and characters try to build up this world, but I never once found myself wanting to explore more and see how these characters fit in. Learning more about the group, I just kept asking for more, wanting more than what was being provided.
[spoiler]     The game attempts to have a narrative note of desolation and fighting against impossible odds. The ending, itself, lends to this as how doomed this whole situation is. And yet because your group never has a goal or clear mission except 'Kill the Mort', it makes it hard to follow along and root for them. The story is something that can work, but since this game doesn't give the characters a more attainable goal, you just play the game solely for gameplay and end up seeing the story as an annoying roadblock you reach.[/spoiler]

Redemption Reapers is not perfect. The package sounds amazing and the visuals, while good, could have used some additional work. The gameplay is lacking in options and makes a lot of situations play out the same. But, I found it kept pulling me back in and, in doing so, showing the depth it was secretly hiding. But the hardest pill is the story. A lacking piece of writing which makes you realize the missed opportunity it was.

The game's price went down to $25. For those who love SRPGs, I would recommend giving this a playthrough. Maybe catch it on sale, if you can, but certainly give it a playthrough. It's an interesting take on the formula, especially with such a limited cast. If you're interested and haven't played much in the genre, try to catch it on sale. However, for those who are on the fence, maybe play something else in the genre first. See if you like the gameplay and come back. This game is a lovely experience, but surely is geared more towards those who have played through these games before.

A flawed gem, this game. I enjoyed my time through it. I hope others can look past it's shortcomings and come to enjoy the game just as much.

review:
Redemption Reapers is an ambitious and atmospheric action RPG that immerses players in a dark, gothic world where themes of redemption, loss, and morality intertwine. The game invites players to step into the shoes of a reaper tasked with guiding lost souls toward their ultimate fate, blending intense combat mechanics with a richly layered narrative that unfolds through exploration and choice. What sets Redemption Reapers apart is its commitment to creating a moody, immersive experience that balances challenging gameplay with a deep, thought-provoking storyline.

The core gameplay revolves around fast-paced, skill-based combat that requires precision, timing, and strategic use of abilities. Players have access to a versatile arsenal of weapons and supernatural powers, each offering distinct combat styles that can be tailored to personal preference. Whether it’s swift melee strikes, ranged magic attacks, or powerful area-of-effect abilities, the combat system encourages experimentation and adaptability. Enemies are varied and often unforgiving, demanding players to learn their patterns and weaknesses. This makes every encounter feel intense and rewarding, especially when players successfully chain combos or evade deadly attacks.

Exploration plays a significant role in Redemption Reapers, with the game world designed as a sprawling, interconnected gothic landscape filled with secrets, hidden paths, and environmental storytelling. Players traverse eerie cathedrals, haunted forests, and desolate ruins, each area rich in atmosphere and detail. The world design is supported by hauntingly beautiful visuals and a melancholic soundtrack that reinforces the game’s somber tone. The environments not only provide a backdrop for combat but also serve to deepen the narrative, revealing fragments of the characters’ histories and the lore that shapes their fates.

Narrative choice is a key element in Redemption Reapers, with decisions made during interactions influencing both the story’s direction and the player’s alignment. The game explores complex themes such as forgiveness, justice, and the consequences of one’s actions, pushing players to reflect on the moral weight of their choices. Character development is nuanced, with a cast of intriguing NPCs whose stories intertwine with the player’s journey. These interactions add emotional depth and encourage multiple playthroughs to uncover all narrative branches and endings.

One of the standout features of Redemption Reapers is its art style, which combines dark fantasy aesthetics with gothic horror influences. The character designs are striking, and the animation is fluid, lending a sense of weight and realism to combat. The soundtrack complements the visuals perfectly, blending haunting melodies with intense battle themes to create an immersive audio-visual experience. The attention to detail in the world-building and presentation significantly elevates the game beyond typical action RPG fare.

While Redemption Reapers offers a compelling and richly textured experience, it is not without its challenges. Some players might find the difficulty curve steep, especially during boss fights that require mastering complex mechanics. Additionally, the game’s pacing occasionally slows during exploration segments, which might not appeal to those who prefer a more streamlined experience. There are also minor technical hiccups, such as occasional frame drops or input lag, which can disrupt the otherwise smooth gameplay flow. However, these issues are relatively minor in the context of the overall experience.

In conclusion, Redemption Reapers is a captivating action RPG that combines challenging combat, atmospheric world-building, and a thought-provoking narrative to create a memorable journey through a dark, gothic realm. Its emphasis on moral choices and character development adds depth to the traditional hack-and-slash formula, encouraging players to engage both intellectually and emotionally. While it demands patience and skill, the rewards come in the form of a richly crafted world and a story that lingers long after the final battle. For fans of dark fantasy and action RPGs seeking a mature, immersive adventure, Redemption Reapers is a title well worth exploring.

Rating: 7/10

Also, this is pretty much the only game I can think of that has weapon durability as something that actually matters for your decisions instead of it just being an annoying, pointless mechanic.

I hope we eventually get an improved sequel. At a reasonable price.

A very good foundation for this Early Access bullet heaven title. The stylized 3D urban sci-fi vibe and look works out well, with an already polished and fun gameplay and a good power progression. It's a bit closer to those slow bullet heaven titles where the player is outgunned early on, but the movement speed and health levels mean it's feasible to properly crowd control large amounts of enemies with the correct weapons and perks. The game only launched today, at the time of this writing, and while there's various characters, ultimate abilities and levels to unlock and use, the latter even in harder Horde and Night modes, the variety of enemies, weapons and visuals is ultimately not too high, and even the permanent upgrades are playing it safe. In short, DEFCON: Xenos won't quite set the world on fire for originality and still has to finetune a couple aspects, but it's certainly one of the most enjoyable bullet heaven titles already and I'm excited about its future.

The game has full controller support, too.

review:
Before you read this, it should be noted that I left a negative review for the first game, and only recommended it under heavy discount. Not because I didn't enjoy it, but because I didn't recommend that experience for the price. 

Bad Blood is nothing like that. Not only is it cheaper, but it is a larger game, witch more options and more varied environments. Instead of facing off with a certain vampire in each shorter route, you interact with them all, with a saved history from the previous game with various details you can change. There are only two endings, the "good" and the "not good" ending, with a small change depending on which of the three you end up with, if you do. Despite the lack of endings comparitively, this has 4 CGs, like the other game. 

The steam store says choices with a heart will not be penalised, but on the other side of that, you're not penalised for staying asexual and approaching the game without looking to bang one of them, which is nice. My one "real" complaint about this dlc was that I wish it didn't have a CG locked behind being physically intimate, however. It doesn't matter to me, but I know when it's marketed and even just giving the options for polyamory and asexual players - it might upset players to know some of the content isn't able to be 100%'d without that aspect. It's fine for me, and I'm honestly grateful for the smut, but it's something you might personally care about. 

Other than that, it feels a shame to even call this DLC. This could've been an entirely new game, and I would've enjoyed it as one, too. And it honestly feels like it's at a detriment to call it DLC, because it is a feature length game that some might be inclined to skip thinking it's only 20 minutes or something. It's not - it asks you to launch a wholly different game, and takes about 5 hours to complete all routes. That's a significant amount of content, and worth considering if you enjoyed the series. Because that's what this DLC has turned First Bite into - a series. 

And despite my negative review of the first game, I remember enjoying it fondly. This is more of the same, peppered with the same dumb humour that made me laugh like the first game. Technically, it's identical, with less dead ends, and the same voices and mostly full voice acting and stunning art. Only thing I'd even hesitate to mention is that the overall quality of the CGs is different, but I didn't see it as lacking - just different.

review:
Jumping into New Cycle on normal difficulty feels both familiar and different if you have played other survival city-builders. The setup is classic, with humanity clawing back from collapse and you taking responsibility for organizing the first sparks of civilization, where every decision matters.

The opening focuses on survival by securing food, wood, and housing while constantly juggling limited workers between gathering and construction. On normal mode, the difficulty feels fair because mistakes such as expanding housing too quickly before stabilizing food supplies are noticeable but not devastating.

The atmosphere stands out as one of the strongest elements. The bleak post-apocalyptic setting and detailed visuals make it rewarding to watch a small camp slowly grow into a functioning village. Some mechanics feel unclear at first, and the resource loop can become repetitive as you shift workers around to keep production moving.

Unexpected events also keep things interesting, like when a worker at the soup kitchen died in a fire, forcing you to adapt quickly. Compared to easy mode, normal is far more engaging. On easy, resources are abundant, setbacks are mild, and events rarely disrupt your plans, so the challenge and tension are almost absent. I would recommend playing on normal since it strikes a better balance between survival pressure and steady progress, making victories feel earned rather than handed to you.

Still, the game would feel smoother if the population were not so demanding. Right now, everyone seems to want something different at the same time: one person asks for a shack, another demands better health care, and someone else expects improved worker morale. Meeting all of these requests in the same time frame feels overwhelming and at times unrealistic, which makes progression more frustrating than it needs to be.

Overall, New Cycle already delivers a solid foundation with its atmosphere, resource management, and survival tension. With future updates and development, it has the potential to become something even more polished and enjoyable

review:
Get creative making your own dioramas using a whole host of settings and objects or create your own custom furniture from scratch. 

[h2][u]Settings & Extras[/u][/h2]

Settings & extras include; resolution & screen mode options, quality options, interface scale, audio controls, language, cursor type, selection appearance, grid and default object sizing. 

[h2][u]The Gameplay & Tips[/u][/h2]

The game has an optional tutorial that is broken down into 10 mini room objectives to complete that get you used to scaling, size, colouring and mechanics. I did find some things were not covered in the tutorial and learned though just by trying everything. Here are some tips from my time trying things out. 

[u]Tips[/u]

🔹 You can change the look of the floor and walls by clicking on them (three icons will pop up). The first is to change the floor size and shape (templates are provided but limited). The second icon is colour and the third icon is finishes (wood, tile, etc). Sadly if you pick a patterned wallpaper you cannot colour it different colours (like stripes). At least I did not find a way.
🔹 Remember to save your rooms manually. Go to settings and Save. There are plenty of save slots. 
🔹 To dup an item just hold down shift after creating the first one (like string lights), to string them in a row. 
🔹 When you place a fake wall you put items up against it but not on it (like artwork or a mirror). 
🔹 When you move an item, a table for example. Items you placed on it will NOT move with it. Just keep placement in mind when putting down items before you start going crazy with the small details. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3544188952

[u]Wishlist[/u]

🔸 I wish we could do multi-level or multi-room layouts. At this time you can only do single rooms but change the shapes of walls and the floor above. You can also allude to an upper floor or other rooms by using doors, stairs and putting in walls. 
🔸 Item snapping for things like kitchen cupboards and cabinets to line them up easily.
🔸 More lighting, especially wall lights like sconces. 
🔸 Allow us to colour patterned flooring and wallpapers. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3544198829

[h2][u]Overall Experience[/u][/h2]

I am enjoying this creative game and the developer has stated they have free updates and more content planned for the future. There are certainly things I would love to see but what is present and for the price makes for an enjoyable time.

You can also create your own furniture (I still have yet to really get into this part of the game). The game also supports mod creations through Steam so you can share and download items the community has created. This keeps the game fresh and some people in the community are very talented and create some amazing things (as a big House Flipper fan I can attest to this). A wholesome game that gets your creative juices flowing and fun for all ages to enjoy. ✨

review:
[b]MakeRoom[/b] is a cute low-poly decorating game with a bite-sized campaign, a solid collection of colorful items, and [i]super fiddly[/i] controls.  I didn't vibe with it at first, but Kenney's latest title ultimately won me over with charming level themes... and also cats. 

[h3]What's a Kenney?[/h3]
If you enjoy indie games, then you've bumped into at least one of the 40,000+ high-quality [i]free[/i] assets Kenney has released since 2014. On the flip side, if you've ever dabbled in asset creation, you've probably looked into Kenney's Asset Forge.  Basically, Kenney is awesome for indie devs.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
[b]Controls.[/b]  There are keyboard shortcuts, but the game can be played using only a mouse: left click to select, scrollwheel to rotate.  Technically works with an X-Box Controller, but it's [i]infinitely[/i] more fiddly.

[b]Modes.[/b]  Freely decorate in a sandbox-style "Create" mode, or "Play" the campaign: 13 themed levels with short lists of objectives.  Finishing all levels scores an achievement and takes ~30 minutes of focused play. 

[h3]What Works For Me[/h3]
✅ [b]Art + Assets.[/b]  There's a decent selection of adorable low-poly furniture, decorations, plants, and more to mix and match.  While not the trendiest catalog, everything looks like it belongs in the same game. 

✅ [b]Cats![/b]  Special shout-out for cat models and cat-themed furniture.  There are dogs and fish, too, but I can't stop laughing at the number of scratching posts and cat shelves.

✅ [b]Flexibility.[/b]  All items can be re-colored (including a "random color" option), rotated, re-sized, duplicated, and freely placed.  There's no grid snap, which is a little annoying when placing shelves, wall panels, sectional couches, or countertops, but also gives you more freedom to create cluttered rooms.   

✅ [b]Camera Mode.[/b]  In-game camera includes a variety of options and filters, and saves photos directly to Steam's screenshot folder for easier sharing.

✅ [b]Object Maker + Workshop Support.[/b] Create your own furniture in the object maker and upload the results to the Steam workshop!  The object maker is intimidating at first glance, and doesn't include a way to compare the scale of your items to in-game assets, but it's kind of like [i]My Fisher-Price's First Asset Forge[/i].  

[h3]What Doesn't Work For Me[/h3]
❎ [b]Fiddly.[/b]  If you select an asset from the menu, you need to place it or select another item; you can't right-click to delete it (click-click).  Once an item is placed, click to open the modification menu and then click the hand to move the item or a modification button (click-click).  If you stock up a bookshelf and decide to move it two inches to the left, you need to move the bookshelf and every item on it one-by-one (click-click-drag).  There's no autosave.  You can only exit to the menu, not to the map. The UI as a whole is clunky and fiddly and clicky. 

❎ [b]Limited Colors + Art.[/b]  Every item uses some combination of the same 41 colors, and there's only a few patterns available to use as framed "art."  It's strangely restrictive, especially if you have a bone-deep aversion to highly saturated colors or deep love for wood furniture.

❎ [b]"Campaign."[/b]  The campaign sounds cool in theory: Go to unique locations, fulfill customer requests, unlock new stuff.  In practice, it's annoying and a tad uninspired.  The themes are fun, but the little house dude tells you to clean up a bit, add a few items of furniture, and -- bam!  Level complete in 5 minutes or less.    

[h3]Final Thoughts + Recommendation[/h3]
To be honest, I almost returned this after the agonizingly slow tutorial showcased a lot of click-click-clicking.  And then after I forgot to manually save the first room.   But I stuck with it, and was eventually charmed by themed levels like "spy headquarters" and cat rooms.  

Overall, it's clunky, but it's also easy to pick up/put down and nice to chill with while watching TV.  There's plenty of player freedom and potential to create unique rooms, and this purchase supports a staple of the indie game dev community.  If that sounds cozy, then I recommend this!

If you're looking for more realistic art, a more meaningful campaign, and/or better controls, then I'd steer you toward [i][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/3151380/Small_Spaces/?curator_clanid=45365863]Small Spaces[/url][/i] instead.

This is cute! Here's a few thought tho:

Pros
- it looks nice, I do enjoy the low poly look
- you can change the room size, floor plan, walls and shape it's cool I like it
- chill gameplay for anyone who likes decorating
- controls are very easy but there's also a help icon in case you struggle
- you can scale items which is really cool
- you can BUILD and save your own furniture with premade parts - this is awesome

General feedback:

- I wish for more camera movement, if I am placing a shelf at the front wall I can't put decoration in it because the camera doesn't swing around. Yes technically you can't see it but it's just something I would enjoy to do

- also the angle you can rotate in feels very claustrophobic to me, I can't even get a straight on view from the North or West "wall" side at all, this is an issue if I am trying to align furniture pieces, the camera just feels very limiting for no good reason

- if you are zoomed out all the way you can not move the cam to the left or right anymore you can only rotate the angle, this is a problem especially for longer rooms

- I don't see a good reason why the color palette is so limited, the colors are nice but you should get to pick any color and save your favorites into the color menu directly

- autosave, i have not experienced any crashes but I almost went back into the menu without saving

review:
[i]Make Room[/i] is pretty great.

Look, this is no [i]House Flipper[/i]. The number of items, the palette, the room shapes are limited, and you might not be able to make everything *exactly* the way you picture it... right away. Because with a little patience and a bit of elbow grease, you can still make a surprising variety of things. Having basic shapes to play with, and a specific item maker, is a huuuge help. The fact that the game is relatively light weight is also a big win.

Now... yes, it could use a little refining. Some quality of life polishing would make it perfect: an undo button, a way to align windows, the freedom to rotate or stick any sort of objects to wall... But I would still recommend it in its current state! If you are the sort of person who likes this sort of game, craves coziness and doesn't mind a bit of thinking outside the box, it will fit right into your library. 

tldr: lightweight cozy room maker with surprising adaptability, would and will Make Room again

review:
Not far in so far, but already not really enjoying it. What I also don't enjoy is being harsh to someone's labour and creativity, but sadly, here we are.


The requests seem to be the main idea of the game, but feel more like an afterthought. Now, if you played the Sims, or the glorious Unpacking, or Animal Crossing, or Tiny Glade, or Enshrouded, or any kind of these sort of games, you will notice how limited the selection of furniture is. And it seems to hit you in the face right away.

Let me explain:

I started with the 'Garage to Home Theatre' request. So far so good. Cleaning it up, finding some nice low-table, big screen, two chairs with foot-rests... but ... where's the remote? There's none? Why? Where's a box that even sort of resembles a subwoofer? There is none? Where's the option to have a beamer and projection screen? No? Okay. DVD boxes? No? Popcorn anyone? Ah well...

Picture frames are white, with a paspartout that can't be white, what's up with that? Why not have a few dozen presets for the content of those pictures, anyway? Oh,, it's hidden in one of the sub-menus, never mind the content. Or the TV screen for that matter. Not even some kind of stylized movie posters?

Am I being too needy or expecting too much here? Aren't these kind of things sort of the basics tho? What your mind immediately goes to when you think of the topic at hand? The game actively suggests a home theatre, but doesn't deliver on anything to support that.


How about something a bit more general? Separatators or dividers? Half-high walls? If you lower both of the rear walls, there's a visual bug in the corner, btw.

I also think that the diorama thing is a limiting factor - being able to see and use all four walls would be such an improvement to have things look cozy. I know that that's not the point of the game, but not being able to move the camera around a bit more feels so restrictive.


Snapping needs to be a lot more intelligent. The mesh would benefit from an even finer option, so things don't have to be pixel perfect and frustrating. Maybe also if you have two of the same items, they will notice that and line up with one another, maybe as an option.

Also, it would be nice, if related items would snap to one another. For example, right now, I'm working on the backyard garden task, and I want to move that flowerbed. Oh, it's several pieces which I now have to pixel-perfect shift around to a different spot where I want it to have.

That being said, being able to mark several things and move or shrink/grow them equally would help a lot with otherwise frustrating edits like that.

Also, spinning items dont support the angle that the cornered floor offers. Frustrating when you want to add a fence around your garden plot in front....


Back to the items at hand. There's too little selection, and they aren't really fitting in with each other. There seems to not be an overall style to things - eveyrthing seems individually designed, not as part of a group or style.


Where we are at designing. I just briefly glimpsed into the Custom item maker and.... what's that supposed to be? That's not even how the devs made all the items, right? It can't be. There are a handful groups with a few things in them, it feels like an afterthought, not remotely like what I thought it would be - the core system of the game. You can put some flower magnets on some shapes, okay.

Maybe there's more to this, but it again feels very unintuitive.


General UI issues and bothers:

The menu selection for items is too small, it wastes so much real-estate. The items would benefit from being sorted in logical groups and sub-groups. Display their names please, on mouse-hover or something. Searching for something comes up with a ton of unrelated things, just like modern search engines do, and that is not helpful. Also, it's a wild guessing game.

Controls would benefit if everything could be done with just the mouse - not holding shift or ctrl or whatever else to use functions of the game, like snap-to-grid. Have on-screen toggle buttons for these functions - after al, there is tons of real-estate there. See Tiny Glade's menu for example.

Camera position is way too close to the scene if you extend the floor shape. Automatically snapping back a bit would help a lot in those cases, or add a way to move the camera position.


Colours in general: Why have presets, across two pages to boot, when you could have a more intuitive option there. Or at least try to keep it to one page.

Update: Colour wheel, thumbs up!

Also, the main colour should always be the main colour for every item - Case in point: Chair with two colour options, changed the main one to red. Copy colour scheme. Change to different chair. Paste colour scheme - but the new chair isn't red, because it pastes 'red' into whatever the third option now is. This would greatly benefit from being unified across all items - and with that I mean that the first colour is always the main / body colour, not sometimes the third or the second one.


Photo mode: The filters aren't named. I have to guess what each one does. The tilt shift is just 'on or off'. And I don't understand what Orthographic is supposed to do other than ... - is it bugged? I mean, it looks weird - it squishes what's close and widens what's far. Is that supposed to be what that mode is going for?


But the worst bit so far is this: It does not keep your room as you made them. Not from the Requests menu, that is.

Also, saving a request mid-progress and then loading that basically softlocks you from any progress in that plot. You gotta start again. So, just to unlock all those rainbow items (thanks for locking a watering can behind that, btw), you better just rush through it, eliminating the entire point or momentum that the little house mascot could have ever generated with you. What's the point of going back in and actually working on a plot when you already "satisfied" the mascot's wants?

Also, please. You couldn't add even just a flame to the candles when they're on? You do have a flame effect, but they don't come with it? Weird.


There is no flourish to anything either. No little simplified toon going like "oh wow, this looks so nice~" or anything like that. Some sort of gratification as a player, you know? Or even just automatically loading the last saved / active / auto-saved room when you re-enter a house you already worked on. Re-setting the entire quest should not be the default, imho.


Also, please work on the music. The tracks are way too short, and too generic. Are they AI generated, or just samples? Please don't. I know that music is very subjective, but something that's keeping a certain mood for 5 minutes would greatly help with that players can lose themselves in the fun of this game.


All in all....

Am I having fun? So far, the first hour left a rather disappointing impression. Everything that this game sets out to be seems unfinished, or subpar, or barely functional. There is no polish, at least not what you'd expect from a full 1.0 release these days.

I wouldn't be so harsh if this were still in early access.

That's why I can't in good faith upvote this game.

I am not going to refund this though. There's a framework going on, but  here is hope they keep working on it. There's so much that feels unfinished or missing here.

I'll give this some more time to breathe - maybe the weird item unlock function reveals something awesome later on (I hope there aren't any crucial items locked behind following 5 step requests ten times tho). Maybe in a couple of months, this game earns itself a thumbs up.

review:
Overall: Cute game, but at least for me, not really worth it. The gameplay feels more tedious than fun for me, and there's no real extrinsic motivation. Intrinsic motivation drains with how finicky and clunky decorating feels. But hey, if you enjoy something relaxing with nice music and hyper-customization decorative pieces I'd say it'd be fun for you. 

Positive thoughts:
Relaxing music, and the artstyle is cute. Each item is reasonably customizable, with color swatches, resizing, and angling furniture. Also you can pet the house guy. 

Negative thoughts:
But UI is a bit annoying to navigate. While there's no single massive annoyance, there are small things that can add up. I got through the Tutorial, Garden area, and started the Gaming room. I found the rooms rather small, with the default items in room quite large, and difficult to fit unless you go to each item to shrink it down. When entering a new 'level' of sorts, you're still automatically put on the last category you had from before. Certain items, like a bed is separated into 3 different items (pillow, main bedframe/mattress, and the blanket), so if you need or want to move or edit size/orientation it you'll have to do it for each piece. While it can be great for more customization, it's also annoying that this isn't just automatically grouped together. clicking on things in the garden is a bit finicky as there are a bunch of small items super close together, and for recoloring things, there is swatches. Not a RGB color picker. Finally, there is no story, which honestly  I thought wouldn't be a problem. Yet the game is tiny, and there's nothing connecting the different areas what-so-ever and the first time you click on an area you need to fulfill the little house guy's demands before it goes into proper sandbox. These demands are the closest thing to a 'story' you get. 

TLDR: Relaxing music and cute artstyle. But can be finnicky and tedious to decorate too small rooms. There is no story what-so-ever.

review:
If your looking for a space to just decorate then I think its a fine game. However it lacks items - or clusters of items - to create clusters you have to tediously place them all and the layering is objectively frustrating to work with. The having to shift items multiple times to achieve a layered look is frustrating and can only be viewed from a single angle as the perspective warps placement and I found items hovering where before they were not. 

The undo button does not work properly - I'm almost never undoing my last action but an action from three movements or items ago. The creative space is also just as tedious to try to build in because a shift in perspective ruins everything and attempting to rotate items or resize is a disaster of undoing your own work or placement extending too far so the item you were trying to achieve is just not possible. As long as you keep it very simple you can probably create something passable but the layering and perspective often left items hovering where they should not. It was also frustrating to not be able to select clusters of item for movement so if I decided to rearrange a space I was left recreating the clutter I had created as well.

I think this game is a fine though faulty experience, I would recommend as a casual experience EXCEPT because of how bad the undo button is and the inability to select clusters of items making it too tedious. If you are a very particular individual who likes to detail excessively I would not recommend either. With the implementation of a working undo button and more items this game would be fine for casual play.

[h3]MakeRoom is [b]PERFECT[/b]![/h3]

The idea of the game is simple and super relaxing, perfect if you’re looking for something creative and stress free.
[b]Creativity is the key[/b] here. The possibilities are endless, and it’s not just about building rooms. You can create anything you want, starting with different types of grounds, walls… and even a van!

The game comes with [b]1000+ decoration pieces[/b], which is impressive for a project developed by just [b]one person[/b]. And I say “+” because the [b]Object Creator[/b] is amazing and very easy to use, even if you’ve never modelled anything before.
Imagine you want a specific plate, a wall decoration, a console or even a car that isn’t in the base game. [b]You can create it and use it in your diorama[/b]!

And the best part? [b]Steam Workshop![/b]
You can share and download objects and dioramas from other players. It’s not just about creating, it’s about sharing your hobby, your art, and your creative side with the community.

[b]Photo Mode[/b] is spectacular! I love the filters, they don’t just change the colors but also add different lighting effects on some of them - [i]specially filter 12, it's perfect for Vintage Vibes ;)[/i]. The zoom and focus option are amazing for capturing close-up shots of objects!

The concept is fantastic, the UI feels calm, and the music + sound effects are great.

Of course, there are a few tweaks and minor bugs to fix, but nothing that ruins the experience. They’re small visual issues, and [b]Kenney[/b] (the single dev) is already working on solving them.

[b]Overall: a perfect game to relax and unleash your imagination with cuttie visuals.[/b]

review:
I bought it yesterday and I have been loving it! Furniture wise, there's a great variety to me (i've seen people say that it lacks things but I think it's moreso that they're sometimes oddly organized) but if you don't find what you're looking for, you can make it yourself with the Object mode or download it. I love the game's look and the atmosphere really nails that cozy vibe. I did a little review for you.

Here are some good points:
-it has a really reasonable price: under 10€, about 9€ right now since it's on sale(really worth it imo)
-surprisingly good music, was not expecting it!
-I haven't experienced any bugs, the game feels really stable to me. I also think it's well optimised, I noticed the loading times were really short on steamdeck and everything just feels smooth
-object mode is powerful and lets you be really creative with what you can make
-steam workshop integration, if you don't want to make items yourself, you can always download others'! The game's only been out for a day but there is already some awesome creations there.
-Really great low poly models, they all look cohesive together and I think this game has such a cute and cozy charm to it
-you can make interiors, exteriors and van designs!
-you can change the room's size and dispositon (this works for interiors and exteriors, sadly vans aren't customizable). You can make the room bigger, make it an L shape, ect.. there aren't THAT many options but the few there is (16 options) are all great.
-In the construction menu, there are floors and walls which will match the wallpaper and flooring you have, making it really easy to change how the room feels. There are also stairs, pillars and other things you can experiment with.
-Resize anything!! I think this is the most awesome feature this game has. Seriously!
-I found the controls to be much more intuitive than the other games of this genre that I've played (I played on steamdeck and PC). Another plus, if you play on Steamdeck, there's a setting to enlarge the UI, so if you're on a small screen or need this accessibility setting, it's there.
-There is a "campaign" mode, that's essentially 11 levels that are designed with a goal in mind, so if you like guidance you'll love them!
-possibly the BEST thing is that the developper plans on supporting the game for a while and will add more items and features as time goes on. This is awesome and you can tell he's a perfectionnist which is a great thing because he will inplement what we'll ask for! The discord is very active, and I recommend you join it if you want to share anything about the game!
-you can change the look of some UI elements, this is such a small detail but i really appreciated it, you can tell this game is really polished
-Kenny made it. We have to give props to this person who gave so much to the gaming community throughout the years and I personnally wish that this game pops off in the cozy decorating game niche because it deserves it. It's my favourite decorating game I've played!

There are many more qualities but this is getting long so i'll talk about the flaws now.
Some things that might draw you back are:
-very limited color palette (i found this to be okay because the colors are really well chosen and harmonious together so no matter what you pick it'll look cool)
-no undo feature (hard to implement)
-when you put items on another item, when moving the bottom one, the one on top doesn't follow. It just stays there, floating. There should be a way to move tables with items on it without having to put everything back together again.

But as stated earlier, Kenny will support the game for a little while, and as I can see on the game's discord, they are already hard at work fixing bugs and adding items! I am so happy that a game like this exists, and even happier that Kenny made it.

review:
Make Room is a great game to relax with and revisit for some calm down time if you love creating. Not only can you decorate with provided pieces but if you want something different, click the 'Objects' button on the main screen to design your own completely unique piece and share it on Steam Workshop for others to also admire and use. 

[b]Overview of main screen options: [/b]
[list][*]'Create' - A blank canvas inside a Room, Camper, Garden. 
[*]'Open' - Sample diorama's to configure & your subscribed items from Steam Workshop. 
[*]'Play' - Some scenario requests which all give an unlocked decor item. 
[*]'Objects' - Let creative freedom fly. Design your own completely unique item/diorama. [/list]

[h1]Inside a diorama[/h1]
At the bottom of the screen you can change the color and the low poly background behind the diorama with the first two options, and the next two options work to change the lighting inside the diorama and the ambient noise which also change the weather in some cases. Snowflake will give you some snow fall and umbrella some rain drops for example. 

[b]Floor Size[/b][list]
[*]The Room diorama starts as a small square. You can click the floor and the first option looking like a diamond (3d room) lets you increase to a larger square, rectangles, L shapes and various clipped edge shapes for the flow that feels right. 
Walls can be tweaked with the clipped shapes. 
[*]The Garden diorama also starts as a small square with no walls. The floor space can be changed to a circle, the larger squares, and various rectangles. [/list]

[b]Customize[/b]
Each thing you click has it's own menu to change that piece. 
[list]
[*]Change colors of floor, walls and decor pieces, including the pets! 
[i]Would be nice to see this as a color picker in the future.[/i]
[*]Change/add a pattern to floor and walls. 
[*]Resize pieces, great for versatility. Take a plant from a big floor plant to a small table plant. 
[*]Duplicate the item. Handy for placement of multiple items, especially if you resized it just right already.[/list]

review:
For a dollar and some change? I suppose I can recommend it. I think the audio needs some work as the generic banshee screeching doesn't really seem to fit the idea of a world where a super natural motorcycle is chasing you, even in in this case that seems to mean the "motorcycle" in question is an electric moped that makes no noise other then the screeching noises as it chases you through a few different venues that most horror game enthusiast will likely recognize. I will admit to not completing each area myself, but I respect the work that's gone in so far.

Things I'd love to see, 
1.) Change the audio, replace the generic heartbeat system and banshee screeching, instead replace it with the low distant rumble of a large motorcycle engine prowling, picking up and gaining as it spots and begins to chase you, I feel like that alone would improve atmosphere a lot. 
2.) Try and acquire a motorcycle model instead of the moped, though I will admit to the silliness factor of a vespa chasing you.
3.) Work on the lighting just a bit, right now the heavy darkness isn't inherently bad, however it is clear (especially on the first park map) that it is relied on a lot to hide the somewhat lower end map, it ends up making the main struggle of the game, not running from the motorcycle but rather just trying to figure out where the heck you are.

review:
Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 isn’t just a strategy game—it’s a timeless classic that continues to win hearts decades after its original release. Few titles have managed to capture the perfect balance of fun, depth, and sheer personality the way Red Alert 2 does.

From the moment the game begins, you are immersed in its wonderfully over-the-top alternate history storyline, complete with charismatic acting, campy yet brilliant cutscenes, and a setting that perfectly blends serious conflicts with tongue-in-cheek humor. The factions are distinct and memorable, each offering unique units and playstyles that keep every match fresh and exciting. Whether you’re summoning giant squids as the Soviets or deploying the mighty Prism Tanks as the Allies, the diversity and creativity in the arsenal never fail to delight.

Strategically, RA2 hits the sweet spot—it’s accessible enough for newcomers yet robust and challenging for veterans. Base-building, resource management, and tactical unit control are all finely tuned, allowing players to develop multiple approaches and playstyles. The pacing feels just right, with battles escalating into thrilling large-scale clashes that test both planning and quick decision-making.

Beyond gameplay, the art style, sound design, and music deserve special praise. The colorful, slightly exaggerated visuals give the game an enduring charm, while Frank Klepacki’s legendary soundtrack keeps the adrenaline pumping throughout every mission.

What truly sets Red Alert 2 apart is its replayability. The gripping single-player campaigns offer variety and memorable scenarios, while skirmishes and multiplayer battles provide endless hours of fun. Even today, with community mods and online play still alive, the game manages to stay relevant and loved by fans around the world.

In short, Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 is more than just a strategy title—it’s an experience, a piece of gaming history that continues to inspire and entertain. It represents the golden era of RTS gaming and remains one of the finest examples of the genre.

review:
Kill The Climbers is a very simplistic, old school, pick-up and play style of game with mechanics that are a little rough around the edges. As the game is in early access, it would be best to address these concerns while building upon what makes the game fun. I will attempt to illuminate my experience to the masses so that they may continue to build on my feedback.

Pros:

Progression: The game is built around the idea of meta progression. You are very unlikely to complete level 1 on your first attempt and will likely take a number of tries to even see the boss until you have purchased upgrades using coins earned from playing the levels. I consider this a good thing, as it adds a sense of satisfaction to getting just a little bit further than you did on previous attempts and pads out the experience while rewarding you for each attempt. Better yet is that the upgrades are both optional and you personally get to choose what to upgrade. I would argue this is the best part of the game.

Enemies: You will encounter a variety of climbers each attempting to reach the mountain peak. Some are basic who take very little damage and climb slowly while others are just upgrades to the basic climbers. Where the game gets really interesting is just how many varieties of climbers you will encounter who specialize in certain aspects of climbing. Like being very fast but die in a single hit or ones that are significantly bulkier but climb at a snails pace. Everything to your average joe to literally flying supermen. The devs put in solid work to make each individual climber unique.

Art: You have to have an appreciation for 8-bit art and that can be tough unless you grew up in the 90's. But there is a charm that is absolutely unrivaled by these kinds of sprites. This is more of a bias than anything but the sprites are all very charming and full of life.

Cons:

The Yeti: For being the face of the game, I regret to inform that the Yeti is useless... If it's not, then I don't know what I was doing wrong. It should be automated the moment it is summoned and it should be an absolute terror, tearing apart every climber it comes across as opposed to chucking snowballs. Worst mechanic in the game.

Controls: I has some assistance learning the games controls. With that being said, I have always had trouble following directions and generally follow a trial and error way of learning video games. One important critique is adding some kind of slow down effect after upgrading in the middle of the level. Those few seconds of being thrown back into the game can cost you. Once you know what you're doing, it's fine... Until you realize that most of what you're doing is...

Learning Automation: This is hands down the worst part of the experience. Once it becomes obvious that all you have to do is hold your mouse at the peak and let it rain rocks on everything and occasionally cause an avalanche in order to win. The game becomes much more tedious and tiresome. The game will try to convince you it values strategy and quick wits, but it doesn't. I believe this could be remedied by changing the way some of its mechanics are handled or even add in new mechanics.

EX: 
- Making the wind sweep from one side of the screen to the other. 
- Adding cool downs or limitations to all attacks. 
- Having the options to purchase additional traps for a more tower defense like experience.
- Adding additional peaks to defend.

Automation can be a necessary and good choice mechanic at times, but the more something is automatic, the less I'm actually required to play and therefore the less I want to play. This needs more work than anything.

Overall a decent experience but I encourage you to try the game for yourself and give your own feedback so that the developers can work to make the game better.

review:
So I'm pretty mixed on this game, but I would say I overall enjoyed it but there are certainly some faults with it.

The game is obviously very inspired by Starfox games, particularly 64 which is totally fine, I love those games. But how well does this game compare. 

I'll start with the things I enjoyed. Firstly the controls felt very fluid, it never felt like I was against the game which is great. Like if you are wanting a more modern Starfox Game, then controls wise this has gotten a good feel. 

There are also a lot of set pieces within this game that are really cool. Some of these have spoilers so I will tag them [spoiler] But I love the part where you are running away from the big boss and your teammate Kiro beats the boss. And the flip on the controls in the one boss was fun, I also love the glitchy asthetic of the levels once it gets into that. [/spoiler] A really fun twist on a classic formula. And also visually I enjoyed it, very Snythwave and simplistic but it works well

But let's talk about the negatives. The biggest one for me is the cast and there is a couple issues with it. The first one is I don't like the lack of voice acting. In the options there is an option for voices, which is genuinely a great option to have, but I was disappointed to learn that the "voices" in question are akin to that of Animalese from Animal Crossing and not actually Voice Acting. I think this is especially a problem because the visuals in this game are so vidid and arguably a lot, that I can't read what the characters are saying most of the time. 
The other issue I have is just writing wise they come off as a bit bland unfortunately. They are clearly inspired by Fox, Falco and Slippy respectively but they lack the charm that the originals come with. It almost seems unfair to compare the two given how different they are. While both games have the same sort of atmosphere and cryptic storytelling Me && MORY is [i]much[/i] smaller in it's scope, essentially just being a short sokoban game with talking boxes. 

That's not to say that what the boxes (or "sticky data") have to say isn't interesting, their ability to paint a picture of a world in only a few sentences between them and leave me wanting to know more is an achievement in of itself but that only makes it all the more disappointing when they start repeating lines towards the end of the game. 

On it's own merit I'd say that Me && MORY has a bit of trouble standing alone without the larger and more intricate world of LAMBDA end THEORY behind it, and I would definitely not recommend playing Me && MORY if you haven't played LAMBDA end THEORY. If you [i]have[/i] played LAMBDA end THEORY this definitely doesn't feel like a proper follow up, think of it more like a bite sized snack to tide you over for now. If nothing else though this does make me excited to see what's coming in the next volume of the DATA + STARS saga.

review:
Its hard for me to write about how much I absolutely love Raw Metal (not that you can tell from how long this review is). Everyone who plays games a lot will occasionally reach the point where it feels like its impossible for a new game to really grab you and you are just going through the motions trying to reignite that spark, and this absolutely did reignite it for me. While I will not claim it necessarily the best thing I have ever played, there was undeniable heart put into the game from the voice actors putting in fantastic performances to easter eggs like the Power Rangers rip off playing on one of the TVs. I truly believe that alone makes it worth your time to at least try the demo (and we should always applaud developers for giving us demos to try before we buy). The developers have also spent a year regularly tweaking and balancing the game based on issues that the community has raised, and while I didn't play at release, it looks like it has been massively improved.

The combat is really impactful, with everyone and everything having a real sense of weight that makes most attacks feel incredibly powerful. The voice acting is also great, from guards and audio logs all the way up to the bosses. I would like to draw special attention the the first boss, who absolutely gave me chills the first time I heard his[spoiler]phase transition and phase 2[/spoiler]dialogue. The visual style of the game worked really well for me, the neons help accentuate the important aspects of the environment (and also allow you to have an awesome silhouette). Not sure if it was intentional, but there are definitely some anime influences throughout the game. The maps are static with a few set random doors, which I liked as it allowed me to still learn the maps, but forced a little bit of flexibility into my routing. The guard attack patterns are a little samey in the base game, but in NG+ helps with that by changing how one of the guards work and modifying the health of the guards, allowing the different guard types to feel more distinct. 

My only major complaint is the fight camera. Its not the worst I've seen, but I definitely lost some fights because I was at war with it. The biggest issue was that the camera would "respect" the walls of the room during fights and that could often lead to it getting suck in a corner as it tries to focus on me and my opponent(s), blinding me in the process. While there are attack indicators, which help somewhat, it was still a very distracting issue. If the camera could phase through walls and instead tried to keep a constant distance, I think that would be a massive improvement.

Besides the camera, my only other issues were that the dodge and stealth were generally less useful during combat. Regarding the dodge, even when I used a full gear set to build into it, I still found it more useful to parry than to dodge. The lack of the heat reset and the end lag on it made it harder to capitalize on openings created by it. Similarly, I found that using stealth during combat was generally inferior to maintaining the pressure on my opponents via juggling and wall-splats. It would have been nice if it was maybe possible to do a finisher from stealth in the middle of combat for massive damage or an immediate KO.

The 100% experience is really simple due to the difficulty settings not restricting achievements. While I did everything on the default difficulty settings, sans some resource farming to max out one copy of every gear piece (not needed for an achievement, I just wanted to), The lower difficulty settings can trivialize most of the achievements. It is up to you to make the 100% experience as simple or challenging as you want, which I really appreciate.

It took me ~9 hours to beat the game and I estimate it took me an additional 5 hours to complete the remaining achievements.

I've had this game wish listed for awhile because it looked interesting and I wanted to play it. I have unfortunately requested a refund after a short play time. 

A few issues I ran into.

Mouse lag: When moving the mouse the on screen cursor would move noticeably later than when you moved your mouse.

Frame rate: The frame rate would get some what choppy throughout playing.

Character Stuck: I was sneaking around a group of zombies and I hit an invisible wall where the player cannot pass. I turned around to go back another way only to find that I was stuck in place and had to restart the game. After restarting the camera was stuck to just above ground level for a short while before returning to normal.

Zombies: Upon returning to the area where you encounter the first zombie, the zombie was not present and then just appeared in the middle of the camp ground. I walked right by him and he simply did not react to my presence.

Second Zombie encounter: Upon returning to the area where I got stuck and restarted the game the zombies there did react to my presence and chased me. When I hit the area that crosses you over into the next zone I got stuck in a loading screen that lasted upwards of 5 minutes.

I know that the game was developed by a single person and they have clearly put in a lot of work with the game but with just this I have experienced the game in it's current state is unplayable, again in my experience. I definitely wish the developer luck and I hope that the game gets some updates to fix these issues. If and when that happens I'd love to try it again because it does seem genuinely interesting. 

TLDR: In its current state based on my experience I do not recommend getting the game.

review:
First level had promise but it goes severely downhill from there.
The warehouse level requiring you to crouch to avoid the monster becomes extremely tedious while you search for the key card. The key card can also vary its position depending on player POV.
The pipe dreams level is extremely long for no good reason. While backroom levels being extremely long is lore accurate, it still makes for awful game-play.
The chase level gives you moments after spawning to run, combine that with player collision, you tend to die before you can get your bearings. However, the death trigger is insanely loud, and can repeatedly spam on the same person, requiring us to turn the game down.

The office level is okay-ish, the doors do take the piss though. Having a door swing towards you when it opens can be so annoying while you're being chased. The parkour is so janky, sometimes you slide off the object you're jumping to, nearby players who fail the jump can somehow suck you into the hole with them. You can also survive the fall, softlocking the game and having to start again.

The hotel level is also just okay. The doors here are even heavier and require you to sprint into them to get them to open, and monsters path in and out of the rooms, opening up the chance you die without actually seeing what happened. You can also walk up again the walls to look through them rather than go through the door.

The water level is the last one we attempted. So many sections of this area had spots where water hadn't been placed, so you have these hard cuts at the edge of the water. There are parts of the map that simply do not have walls, as if they had been forgotten to implement, there are also tiny gaps in the floor that can cause you to fall out of the map. There is no death, so you once again get softlocked.

Overall, this game feels like it wasn't tested for potential problems that can arise and levels were rushed out and made excessively long to make it feel bigger and more fleshed out than it is.

review:
Good concept but lacking in execution. I got to level 11. The game's earliest levels offer some good level design but things start to crumble fast when pseudorandom elements like the spiral enemies and projectiles enter the mix. Being given unwieldy controls to manage movement in a game as punishing as a precision platformer is a recipe for disaster.

If I could offer some tips on how the game might be improved, I would start with polish. Some collisions especially involving the clocks (rings with moving "hands" in them) and timers were inconsistent. Then I would consider making the pseudorandom elements deterministic such that every time you respawn, things come from the same position at the same time. This can help foster the speedrun playstyle you seem to be incentivizing. But with random elements strewn around and awkward controls (can't change rotation direction without moving) this is more frustrating than rewarding.  

The art direction was nice and minimalistic, and the music was nice. It was cool that the music's tempo was set to the rhythm of how you would have to tap to move in a straight line.

If your core audience was masochistic speedrunners, I think this game misses the mark for them too because of the lack of precision and consistency and readability. But again with polish I think you can get there. I hope you can expand or rework this idea to make for a more enjoyable experience for at least the core audience. But as it is, I can't recommend it to them.
