review:
o---o is a unique arcade-style precision platformer that utilizes a very intriguing baseline mechanic in its brain-twisting linear rotation movement controlled by a singular button, but is withheld by poor and non-complementary level design that demands uncanny execution, consistency, and patience that will cater to a very limited audience.

Difficult video games usually have satisfying payoffs once one attains mastery of the gameplay mechanics, but this game brews frustration and anguish over the deliberately crude hazard and enemy cycles, made worse when coupled with an unforgiving implementation of checkpoints and lives. 

The game in its current state demands practice that resembles that of a speedrunner's regimen, where levels must be started over from the beginning once all lives are lost, regardless of the checkpoint progress within that level. With the plethora of "knowledge checks" around corners in several levels, and the lack of a practice or training mode in which to improve in the game mechanics or nail these "knowledge check" sections, it is an unfulfilling, tedious, and eventually fatiguing process to learn and clear a level. There were even a few instances where it was implied by the game that the center circle had landed in a safe spot outside of the bounds of a clock, but moments later after landing, it still triggered a death.

For that matter, the clocks and spinning blades are among the most exceptionally frustrating hazards/enemies in the game, and both are introduced rather early into the game. Namely, as the clock hands are about to rotate, they telegraph themselves by an abrupt backwards snap before rotating forward, along with which its collision box/hitbox moves as well. This seemingly exists to make the game more difficult for difficulty's sake, and is not very intuitive or profound. As for the spinning blades, since their durability is very high, and they infinitely/semi-randomly respawn on an unpredictable cycle (and later on even shoot pre-aimed projectiles!), it makes them feel like a proxy for a timer, as if to say, "move fast or else", as opposed to "clear these enemies and move thoughtfully".

Also, the breakable walls in the game are unrelenting, in that they are often times placed in tight spaces guarded by approaching hazards or enemies, and while the remaining durability persists between deaths, it feels like dying a few times while destroying them is inevitable. This kind of level design does not do well to prop up the basic gameplay.

As such, while the core mechanic of the game is compelling and has lots of potential, the level design needs to succeed at supporting the foundation, and the game presently does not accomplish this. Not only could the level design use more polish at bring out the fullness of the basic movement, but also the lack of a proper options menu for adjusting the music/sound volume, the screen resolution, the singular button of control, and the like unfortunately reflects poorly on the experience of playing the game overall.

Regarding the aesthetic and presentation of the game, I will commend the developer for achieving a distinctly appealing style that kept me immersed in the mysterious world that [b]o---o[/b] exists in. It's cool that the beats of measure of the music align with the period of [b]o---o[/b]'s rotation. The game's environment leads to its being self-explanatory, not requiring explicit tutorials, and concepts are onboarded at a steady pace over the course of the levels.

If the player is content with the frustrations that come with not only learning a tricky gimmick, but also engaging with quarter-muncher-esque obstacles scattered across the levels, in a manner that essentially asks you to learn like a speedrunner, then this game might be of interest. However, there are several other arcade-style games out there of comparable difficulty that can provide more fulfillment for mastering the mechanics than this game.

review:
So at face value, this game appears to be quite simple. And in fact, it is. But that said, it is absolutely worth the price. In my first play through, I spent 2 hours scouring the heavens for any sign of a habitable world. Unfortunately, I was unable to save humanity. But I feel that my 2 hours were well spent, and I'll gladly play again the next time I get the itch. Even the somewhat-clunky UI elements can be forgiven, because at the end of it all, it's still a fun game for science nerds like myself.

Now, I do have a couple of gripes. 

First is in regards to the transit view minimum zoom level. Some of these systems are very large, and because of that, even at the minimum zoom level the outer planets orbit so wide that they completely leave your field of view, leaving you entirely unsure of where they are or when they might return. Scaling this minimum zoom back to that it is certain that all planets would remain in the bounds of the screen would be a great help.

Second is time compression. When scanning systems to capture planet transits, many of them have very large orbits with long orbital periods. Which means if you miss these transits, you have an extremely long wait until that planet might pass by the star again. It would be lovely if there were some way to speed up time beyond what the current controls allow.

That brings me to gripe number 3. The game FEELS like a mad rush. There's not enough time to get a sufficient number of planets scanned and analyzed before the inevitable doom to planet Earth occurs. If there were some way to allow time compression in the planet transit tool, and also extend the total amount of time before the "big event", then I'd give this a glowing review. Maybe 2 years instead of just one before the game ends?

And finally, we need to be able to save and reload the game. It's unrealistic to expect people to be able to play a game, every time, for 2.2 hours straight (that's about how long the game takes before you "die").

All in all, if you are a space nerd, love science, or have dreamed of extra-solar habitable worlds, just get it. You'll be glad you did.

review:
Okay, against some of the bad reviews I bought the game and played it on the Index... Seemed to be a brave decision reading all the feedback. But it was not as bad as I thought it might be. I even give it a good review now though it still has some "problems".

First of all: Yes, the hand orientation is wrong for Index players, the usual "approx 45° misalignment" we see in some games, I am astonished THIS repeating misalignment is still a thing.
It would be nice the devs would simply adjust this instead of giving a calibration feature, BUT the calibration feature is not as bad and as complicated as some think and wrote about. You do not even have to "reach" the virtual hands or put your hands into them, just stay in your position and hold your hands up into the air in the orientation shown before you and press the trigger, done. It was no problem playing the game with this calibration change. Though the calibration does not get saved, you need to do this again after a complete restart, but that was just done in like 10 seconds.

Gameplay and content wise I did not expect anything and I did not read, much as usual. The game has some jump scares, but the "horror" aspect was not too strong for me. I really loved, after understanding it, the gameplay mechanic when you encounter Michael, but I am not going to talk about that further to prevent spoilers.
Most of the game is a big riddle escape room... Find stuff, think about what to do with it, where it belongs and solve them to proceed. Apart from 1-2 situations, that got me a bit frustrated at first, I pretty much ran through them as they are not too complicated and no real issue for people with puzzle game experience (then rather on the easy side). All in all, thinking back about the game after finishing, it was mostly logical, but I see (and experienced myself) some issues with giving too much room without a hint system.

Including 2 passages where I took a bit longer I beat the game in about 4 hours and 15 minutes (while streaming, so it probably it would have taken even less time). I wish it would have been a bit longer.
The save points are fair, also if in doubt just save in between and run to a save point near you if you want to make sure you don't want to redo things in case you fail. The difficulty is probably medium to lower as I do not see myself as the best player and had no real struggle to complete it.

The biggest issue of the game could be the lack of hints, as sometimes the player might not know if you need to proceed in the current location or if you need to head to somewhere else - WHEREVER THAT MIGHT BE... And then that could end in running around for hours if you do not have the brilliant idea all the sudden. Adding hint systems do not hurt, but could really help - players that do not need it just do not have to use it then :).

From a technical standpoint we already have stated the hand orientation on Index. Also for the developer I like to add that streaming the game was a bit hard as it ignores when I change my playspace (s I turn around 180 degree for story game streaming to face the camera, while my usual playspace is for Mixed Reality and my back towards the camera).
The game orientates at the initial playspace of SteamVR and ignores changes, but streamers might rotate their playspace dynamically, so it would be nice if the game rotates with the playspace as well. This is only the second amongst hundreds of games I streamed now, that ignores a change of playspace. I even tried to change my playspace first and then starting the game, but it was again wrongly aligned.
Also the "first time grabbing" of objects seem to be a bit odd and the collision points to walls are a bit far so I got pushed back a lot of times when I just wanted to look at something a bit closer.

So all in all I liked it, I just wish it would have had more content. But I am glad I decided to buy and play it - I had "fun".

Game does not work with Index controllers - hands are totally misaligned - but there is a tool in the game to change hand alignment, and you have to do this every time you start the game. Devs should fix this. There is no Index finger tracking. Also Index controllers lack a menu button. 

The game also feels too dark for lcd - feels like a game optimized for oled. Maybe a great game for Rift CV1 users.... If you can accept these shortcomigs, the game is not bad, even if also not great. More like a 5-6/10 rating. 

EDIT: I just dusted off the great old Rift CV1, and with that hmd the game works flawlessly. I can see so many things I could not with lcd - and controllers and menu buttons now work perfectly. The game supports Meta OpenXR, so performance is optimal with Rift CV1. I do wonder if this game has been in development for so long that the devs originally used oled hmds (orig Vive, Vive Pro, Rift CV1 and Quest 1) - or maybe they optimized the game for PSVR2, which also uses oled. Many of the textures do look dated (slightly low-res) with lcd like Index, but look more high-end thanks to the SDE using Rift CV1. I'm staying with the Rift CV1 for this game - the game looks great forcing ss 2.5 (27 mill pixels per frame combining both eyes). Coming from MADiSON, OVRDark kinda feels like a walk in the park... But I'm far from having completed the game. First puzzles do feel dated and simple too - kinda feels like a game having been in development for more than 5-6 years...

My current ratings:

Index: 5/10
Rift CV1: 7.5/10

My rig: RTX 3090, i9 10900K (10cores and 20threads, 5.3Ghz), 32GB 3200MHz, Win10 Pro.

review:
This game is very similar to the "Ori and the blind forest" series, in terms of gameplay (Plateformers/metroidvania).
It is... okay. If I had to put a mark, I would say it is about a 6.5/10.
If you really liked Ori and are still waiting for a similar title (keufkeuf Silksongkeufkeuf), then I would recommend having a look at it (despites its issues). If you are not a strong fan of the genre, pass your way.

Positive:
+ The graphisms/environnements are good.
+ The music is good.
+ It is rare to have a game using African mythology, and that was one of the arguments that have motivated me to give this game a try.

Neutral:
o Nothing that innovative
o No hard puzzles. The difficulty is coming from (optionals) combat challenges or plateforming sections.
o There is some slight backtracking, but the map is made such that it is very easy to know in which section the missing element is.

Negative:
- This is one of the kind of game where the look of a level was prioritized over its design. I am thinking about spike positionning, in particular in the corner of some plateforms, or some small steps that do not make sense in term of gameplay (but does because there is a mecanism on top) and triggers the wall jump (in the middle of a challenge section). This is especially an issue on the chase section at the end of act 2.

- The camera movement: is improvable. Globally, they are fine (the lag introduced by the time the camera needs to follow our position is sometimes impractical, but this is minor). For example, in a certain challenge where you are gliding toward the bottom (while navigating a corridor of spike), or when we want to dive in a chasm and want to see what is below, putting the character at the middle of the screen (instead of the top of the screen) is not a good thing.

- By far, the controls.
  I am playing on PC, and the keys are not remappable. For the two first acts, this is not an issue (the keys chosen are natural). However, there comes an ability in act 3 (to burst blocks/doors), that is mapped... using a combination of previous keys.

And here is the issue: in a certain challenge, you need to move mid air (surrounding by stuffs that one-shot you), thus you are using part of the "WASD" touch to direct + Space (if you need to glide). Then suddently, you need to use E + [move the mouse to target a direction, with no pause] + Shift.
The issue is that, in the game, the "E" key does not register on a keyboard if one of the WASD key is already held. Plus "shift" is already used for the dash, thus if E is not registered, you end up in the surrounding spikes.
That makes a certain challenge of act 3 at the level of difficulty of "Path of Pain" of Hollow Knight, which is probably not the intension of the developpers.
So:
1) Please do NOT overload the keys on a keyboard (it works on a controller, not for all keys in a keyboard).
2) To correct that, I would recommend either (i) to introduce a "mid air pause" (similar to the sun lance ability) when holding the "E" (note that Ori has a similar ability, which does exactly that), or (ii) introduce an auto-door targetting to this act 3 ability or (iii) Instead of E+Shift, just gives us the option of putting it on another key.

- For both the character and the enemies, the knockback distance when getting a hit is too large (if the character is 1m50 of height, it's about 5m). This makes it too easy to throw all kind of enemies in pits that one-shot them, and that makes it too punitive for us to take a hit in certain arena section with a dangerous floor. That also makes our "sun dive-hit" ability overpowered.

- The smoke of the "combat section" of the boss of act 2 is badly designed. It is way too easy to end up in a part of the arena with absolutely not way out and the smoke closing in (the smoke one-shot the player). This makes this fight almost purely RNG, since the heart position decides if the player end up dying of bu****it or not. I would recommend either making this smoke poisonous (instead of one-shoting the player) or arranging the arena so that getting stuck with no way out is not possible.


I will temperate this whole review by saying that I am still trying to 100% this game (which is not that hard) and I did not have to force myself to finish it. However, there were still some very frustrating moments. Thus, the 6.5/10.

review:
As a gamer that played a lot of DRG and survivor games, I can say that this one is one of the worst in the genre.

I was having fun being DRG, but the gameplay loop quickly becomes boring and stupidly grindy, for a meta progression that feels incredibly slow and not rewarding. First of all, 95% of upgrades are just +% of a stat. That by itself is pretty boring. You are way too much pressured by time with the amount of side objective + resources you have to farm, that will impact your run and meta progression. 

Then the systems that exist for the meta progression... They feel so grindy, such a drag and not rewarding at all. What do you mean I have to do a ~30min somewhat hard run for a permanent +5% damage on a weapon? This multiplied by 5 times per weapon (I think we currently have 41 weapons, so that would be 205 runs if you can complete them 1st try to have all the weapons upgrades with + really small % of some stat)... Its just way too much of the same gameplay loop for a reward that I will barely notice.  

I have to say that the mining for resources and being able to create pathways on the map is the best feature of this game and is very fresh within survivor genre. But other than that, the game fails to deliver the fun that you'd expect on a survivor game. Will revisit on 1.0 to see how the new systems change this, but at this state, I can't recommend it

review:
I love Deep Rock Galactic and Roguelite bullet hell games, so I had to try this game. It has potential, but is not recommended to play at least in the Early Access. I'll explain:

The gameplay loop is fun, but the variety of builds, enemies and map variety in each run is small and the developer is really slow at adding in new stuff. On top of this the "bullet hell" never really becomes a bullet hell - the scaling is slow and you never get a crazy amount of distruction. This results in the experience quickly becoming stale. A successful early access will add in new content at a consistent pace unless they already have enough content, and Funday Games fail at both. Thus, if you start playing this game in early access, you may quickly lose interest. It is more value for the money than going to the cinema and if that's all you need then by all means go ahead, BUT it might leave a sour taste in your mouth when you come back months later and little has changed.

review:
Its a fun game, but the balance is ridiculously bad. (I have 166 hours in this game. I have over 1000 hours on DRG.) If not balance, its the learning curve. Some classes or weapons you can lollygag on Hazard 5 with terrible RNG but others you are sweating buckets and not getting anything done. I'm told this is because you need to spec a certain way. But how am I supposed to know that? The game doesn't teach you anything. It doesn't give you much of any hints as to the best practices are. It just throws you in front of an alien bear and expects you know what to do against it.

Trying to get mastery 5 maintenance worker (Engineer) is the reason I uninstalled this game. Seriously, you play out of your mind and you barely dent the bugs health in a map smaller than your broom closet.

I tried, I tried, I tried very very very hard and many many many times. The game seriously hates you. There's absolutely no way the game teaches you the best ways to spec. And you end up frustrated a billion times over trying to figure it out.

There is no fun times trying to figure it out. Because you have no idea what you're doing wrong. Zero.

I'm serious that one weapon or class makes it look like you're Son Goku about to destroy the whole galaxy, the next you feel like you're an ant trying to kill an elephant.

Complete opposite of DRG (the coop FPS this game is based on) balance. In DRG you can play random weapon / class / overclocks and be decent at Hazard 5. Mind you, you can figure out good builds on your own in DRG within just a few missions. And even with what is considered as bad builds, you can still do a fairly good job at Haz 5.

In this game it won't even be your fault but you'll be using a water gun on a star destroyer if you just happen to not know the one specific focus you need to have in your RNG upgrades. And there are like hundreds of upgrades and literal millions of combinations of them so you can't really test them all out in a healthy amount of time.

Literally the hardest Dark Souls boss is a cakewalk compared to some missions in this game not because of skill, but because of this. Or as the high level players say, "need to read guides to know which spec to use." Meaning you can't learn this game aside from guides or doing 1000 runs of pure frustration.

Concept is fun. Balance or learning curve is negative 1 billion. Steam only lets you say recommend or not. I'll say recommend but only until you reach around Haz 3-4. But yes, I'm giving it a downvote. I'm told you need to spec certain things that you have absolutely no way to figure out unless you look up a guide or experiment 1000 times.

Anything higher Haz is a practice in futility and its not even your fault.

Frustration is not fun. It isn't good. Game needs a lot of work to teach players so they don't get frustrated.

review:
A  dungeon crawler RPG game with some quite reasonable elements and some not so good elements. It takes an hour or so to get use to the mechanics and quirks of the game and its game play. The atmosphere and sound effects and exploration are quite good,  and the character progression system is basic but OK. The combat system is just  about adequate. The "puzzles" are simple.

The reason I gave the game "Not Recommended" is that it became unplayable due to serious software bugs around Level 4. No matter what I tried I kept floating off the floor or falling through the floor - like being in an uncontrollable flight simulator -  to  be  delivered completely outside of the dungeon area !!!  I think this is due to the game having serious programming errors and  not being corrected / patched by the developer. 

I do not think it is my computer (Windows 11) causing the problem as a few other people seem to  have had similar  problems. However, on the plus side the game is very cheap and it gave me about 8 hours of game play, which in general was OK, before it become unplayable.

UPDATE
Since my earlier review I have played an additional 10 hours and by re-loading saved games have managed to get past the dungeon level 4 where I repeatedly either fell through the floor or floated upwards through the ceiling !!!

Despite all its problems this is a reasonable dungeon crawler with some fairly decent role playing elements and I actually started to enjoy the game after getting passed the above mentioned dungeon level. However, there are quite a few software bugs including critical items (keys) that disappear from your inventory forcing you to re-load a saved game. (It is best to save the game once you start a new level and do not overwrite until you have completed the level.)

I can understand why this game has received quite a few negative reviews !

review:
I feel like the game had a good foundation for a compelling world-building, I was almost salivating to get that lore injection, reminds me a bit of Tamashii with its erotic themes, but it never really happened. The world looks interesting, and I want to learn more about it, but there is just so little context to it, and the very little visual storytelling that I got didn't explain much of anything. I am not always a fan of forcing the dialogue into games, but you probably could have at least put a few characters into it just to give you an idea of what I am looking at.

At first, I was a little confused by the style of animation, it didn't look great in the trailer, but now that you mention Oddworld as the source of inspiration, it makes more sense, I can see that you almost imitating that feel, kind of like intentionally using old prerendered models, so given the context, it looks better than I initially thought. My personal experience with cinematic platformers is more from the Flashback side, but this game is not really going for those momentum controls, and to be honest it does not feel very cinematic, with the exception of a few 2.5D effects. It seems there are more basic puzzles in this game than the actual experience that you would associate with a game like this, and that is why I think I feel the disconnect. 

The game can be completed in about 60 to 90 minutes, mostly simple puzzles and some basic platforming, with some combat that only starts maybe half-way into the game. My first impression was really bad, I think the animation feels extremely clunky, especially when you change direction, and exiting the slide as well, it kinda has a delay feel to it, and I think you should remove it completely, just make it constant or almost the same speed. See once I got the blades I didn't mind the animation as much, the attack frames are much faster than any interaction so I am like, wtf, now the game feels better, why could you not do the same for movement. 

Visually I felt the game had a very bad consistency with the effort that you would put into decorating the areas. Many segments of the game felt cheap, while some rooms had very complex structures with patterns and nice light effects, almost reminds me of the dev that goes by ArkHouse, so like, I kinda wish you did that level of quality across the entire game and not just some rooms. 

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

(+) I will say the visuals and the level design were not consistently good, whenever you would go out of your way to create those patterns on the walls and actually put some clear light effects against the images, I thought the game looked a lot better. There are many other effects that I was not a fan of though, like the blurry lights and fog spam.

(+) The combat system really didn't have much to it, but at least compared to regular movement the attack animations were a lot faster and more responsive. I do like that some enemies would have multiple attack animations, I kinda wish you took the game further into that direction and maybe make of a metroidvania style of game.

(+) Interesting world, except well, you kind of left me with nothing to work with, it's okay to keep it vague, but give me something you know, maybe a few characters that would talk to you.

[h1] Feedback: [/h1]

- So the attack animations have really fast frames, but why everything else feels so slow. I think that turning speed and animation recovery between movement should be more consistent compared to your walking speed, if you can do that I think the game will feel better. Also maybe speed up that chain climb and swing momentum. The direction speed change has such a big delay, it almost feels like the game is lagging, even though it's just bad animation speed.

- I was waiting for you to toss me that world-building bone, but you never really gave it to me. Even when it comes to visual storytelling you not really elaborating on anything that I see, I get it has some erotic metaphors, but for what. I kinda wish there were maybe a few characters that would talk to you, give a little bit of a background.

- Some parts of the game really didn't look that great. The game looks better when you create those wall patterns and designs that I can somehow associate with this strange world, I wish you kept that look of the game consistently across the experience. Some light effects, especially those that are clear look a lot better than blurry fog and static. 

- Maybe mid-air attack should cleave down a bit, cuz it goes straight, so you can easily hit over things 

- Perhaps for immersion's sake, instead of having Loading between every segment, put something world related, some animations perhaps.

- The ending felt too abrupt, a little context would help.

[b] Overall Thoughts: 5/10 [/b]

I finished the game mainly out of curiosity, I was waiting for the game to give some lore injections but it never really happened, I was interested in the world, but you didn't explain any of it really, it's erotic in nature, something about lust and submission, that is about as much as I can see. A lot of it comes down to the game not having the best pacing and overall experience, some parts are a bit more thought-provoking, others feel like you doing another generic puzzle. Needed a bit more world-building and perhaps a little more exploration, cool idea, but came out feeling a bit underdeveloped.

review:
I ended up enjoying it more than I expected.

Just like the description says, very easy to see the inspirations in Oddworld and Limbo, given the heavy focus on the environment and the "fast to die/respawn" kind of puzzles. It never felt annoying or too complicated, but the 2D (with 3D elements) perspective and overall brightness does make it a little hard to see the platforms.
The mechanical body horror of the world and characters are very well made, gruesome and detailed (especially some of the death scenes). Some imagery and zones are incredible, really add up to the dark and oppressive atmosphere.

It's an interesting experience, maybe a bit too short and bizarre, with some bits of jankyness, but it's memorable and intriguing on itself, it's worth playing.

review:
Metal ape is bit of a rough one. On one hand you have these amazing surreal visuals and setpieces that are really intrigueing but on the other hand they lack consistency to tell a story. The whole game is a bit of a fever dream but it's hard to make sense of it all. The only place for context is the 4 achievements and their description, not enough to tell a coherent story. This makes the game feel a bit aimless. The gameplay is also quite basic, but most games in this genre are so i cannot hold that against it. What i can hold against it is the mediocre sound design and lack of music for most of the game. It's featured in a select few scenes to make those have more impact but i still would have liked a soundscape or ambience for the rest of the levels as they feel too quiet. I get that this gives off more of an eerie atmosphere but INSIDE for example had stellar sound design and has one of the best atmospheres in gaming. 

Still though the visuals do a good enough job of setting the tone and there's some creepy moments sprinkled throughout the short runtime. As you can see by my platime the game can be over in the blink of an eye but luckily it's very cheap. While the ending was abrupt it also did not overstay its welcome this way. Generally these types of games should be anywhere in the 2-4 hours mark to be short but memorable experiences. Not that this is a particularly memorable experience, i can name many games in this vein that are better. But if you're out of those and still want more then i can recommend this one. If only because it is so cheap and looks pretty damn good. Everything else is adequate to mediocre but the game is functional (despite long initial load times).

review: The game has a number of issues that make the game effectively unplayable. Dodging's invincibility frames are effectively meaningless as they exist for such a small part of movement that hitting them is effectively RNG. The sanity restoration mechanic that stops the screen from being filled with random bullshit is possibly RNG as it requires you to spam the U button until you restore a section, and if it isn't RNG it means that it sometimes just doesn't work on if you are able to restore sanity. If you don't restore sanity you are going to have various images spawn covering the screen, have a reduced field of vision that gives you pretty much no time to run away from the monster, have your dodges stop working (This also happens at low health), and are going to be inundated with even more noise then is already caused by the cacophonous background noise that is way too loud even when you reduce the sound of it. Furthermore, blocking is next to useless as if you block you are guaranteed to take more damage then you would take from running away due to blocking removing the knockback. All of these issues caused by the monster wouldn't be such an issue if it didn't spawn within roughly ten seconds of you actually managing to remove it. And, if you do go through the trouble of removing it you get stuck on a black screen that you can't leave for roughly 5 seconds and sometimes even longer then that even if you're pressing the button to leave. The end result is a game that the best way to deal with it's mechanics is to pray that the monster which causes the worst of them doesn't appear, and to use dodges to move between doors as fast as possible in the areas where doing this will prevent you from taking a hit. If your sanity is too low to allow for consistent dodge spam, only then do you jump into a closet to lose the monster and then you have to pray that you'll recover sanity in time to spam dodges again so that you can avoid dealing with the monster. Part of me wants to like the game, the aesthetics have their own charm to them, the dialouge is bad in a way that can be funny, and the couple of scenarios such as killing classmates and bossfights are cheesy in a way that might make it enjoyably bad if the game itself wasn't so awful to play. It would feel dissapointing if free, but the cost for this is way too much to find any enjoyment in it.

review:
This game is not good, but i can see some good in it. It was made by a new-ish solo dev, so i won't be too harsh. 

Let's get the negatives out of the way:

The gameplay is very clunky, it's buggy (i got stuck twice and it required resets), the dialogue is bad (expected, writing is hard) but it's also full of typos wich make it feel like it's a low effort game and i don't think that's the case, and the animation is very limited. 

Now with the positives:

I think the sprites look nice.
I respect the ambition the dev had for the gameplay. This could have been a simple "hide and seek" horror game but they decided to give it boss battles, blocking and punishing, a dodge roll, a sanity meter. None of it is well executed but i admire them for trying.
The music is good, a few times i found myself thinking "that's a nice tune". 
The Willow Man himself is a cool character and a good concept for a monster, i like him.

Unfortunately, i can't recommend this game for it's price. if it was a free game (or a lot cheaper) i would have recommended it so the dev gets more feedback. 
There's potential here and i'm interested to see the dev improve, they have some good concepts but are lacking in execution. While i can't say it's good, i can say i enjoyed its ideas and my friends enjoyed watching me endure the jank on stream.

review:
If you're looking for an old school ARPG, I'd recommend picking up the original Diablo from back in the 90's over this one.  It's $10 on GoG (the Good Old Games program) or $10 on the Blizzard store (for the more up-to-date version), vs the $15 for this game.  Diablo is also fully fleshed out with dialogue, quests, and better overall design.

This game is entirely too reliant on RNG.  Healing is minimal and hit/miss chance for attacks is extremely unpredictable.  ToK is NOT a rogue-like.  You have to manually save the game, no quick saves, manually going into the game menu and saving there.  When you die, you will have to reload your manual save, losing ALL progress between your last save and your death.  This all adds up to a lot of deaths and a lot of wasted time due to poor RNG mechanics.

That being said, ToK doesn't have a story.  There are no friendly NPCs, vendors, or mechanics outside of killing enemies until you die due to bad balancing, so you're not missing much by skipping this one.  The developer has also made it perfectly clear on the forums that they don't care if this game sells or not because they're not trying to make money, so they don't plan to make changes to the game in response to feedback.  In short, don't buy this expecting it to improve in the future.

Remember all the things that made Diablo 1 great, like a town that you could return to to get rid of your junk and possibly get better items to equip yourself with? Like wandering around the dungeon and slowly regaining health and mana? Feeling your stat increases actually having an affect on your character and feeling confident facing the lower levels? Well, toss all that fun stuff out the window and prepare yourself for a miserable time in "Tower of Kalemonvo". The game starts off fine with reasonable balance, but a massive difficulty spike and suddenly impossible leveling around the 4th floor brings the game to a grinding halt. I thought maybe my luck was bad on this run, so I started over, and tried allocating my attribute points differently and being more careful with the potions....I didn't make it much further the second time through. 

I'm a huge fan of ARPG's....the first two Diablo games, Grim Dawn, Victor Vran, and the Van Helsing series I've sunk a combined several hundred hours in. "Kalemonvo" plays more like a roguelike, and if that's your thing, maybe you'll like this. But if you're looking for a true Diablo experience... just play the original.

[i]These are all reskins of exactly the same game![/i]  What value is there in this spam/pollution glutting the Steam store for gamers?

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.

There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings.  There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.  There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. 

The game only displays in 4:3 pillarboxed aspect ratio (with some lazy "wings" to fill the pillar).  It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, or this game has been specifically designed for people gaming on PC's from 1995... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes this might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.  At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players.  This is a remarkably low number, and now, the only player activity occurs once or twice a month, presumably someone loading it up to see what it is then quickly uninstalling it.  Considering there's over 120 million gamers on Steam and well over 50,000 games for gamers to choose from (over 9,000 completely free titles), the overwhelming lack of interest in this low quality game is to be expected.

"Mystery Solitaire Cthulhu Mythos 2" has the scam price of around $5 USD (for other people's work), it's not worth it given the defects and shortcomings with the product, especially considering the sheer number of completely free, much higher quality games on Steam.

review:
I like these rouge games that you play, die, upgrade, get better, try again and repeat.
This game does that.

What I liked:
- The graphics
- Solid 144 fps, even when a lot happened on screen at the same time
- Sound made it feel impactful
- Interesting upgrade system. Thin at the beginning but after one has finished or died, you can upgrade to include more stuff to upgrade.
- The "!" events are a nice addition as it makes the player have to move in order to not take damage. It starts easy but the events are increasing in as the time goes on.

Things I think can be worked on:
- after about 10 minutes (first round playing) I felt too overpowered. I one-shot anything and leveling up wasn't something I wished to happen anymore. It became very much less interesting.
- There are no volume sliders when you are in-game when pressing 'esc'. Would be nice to have.

My ideas on what could make the game more fun/interesting:
- Almost every upgrade I came across has a trade-off - according to me it shouldn't be for the majority of the upgrades. Having a trade-off should be that IF you have a typical play-style in mind that should be in the upgrades. Let me make it clear what I mean:
Let say you have a character that wants a speedy-character. There should be upgrades doing that. The trade-off should be something that seems "reasonable". A speedy character is hard to hit, so trade-off could be, less defense. Why? Well, someone wearing a heavy armor isn't really a fast person, right.

After the first level-up I felt a big change in the upgrades. This is what every upgrade should feel like. Enemies should either be more in numbers or more hp. To counter that one should yearn for the next upgrade. Feel powerful for a moment because you made a though tout decision and then it should increasingly feel thougher.

Maybe have an event on screen where a shop appears where you could buy the parts for guns instead of having them in a level-up. You could have two parts. One for upgrading your characters status like health, speed, crits, defense etc. and a GunShop where you could buy gadgets, parts for guns.

Maybe player could have other effects like, shooting out fire or maybe lightning from his arse xD every 30 second. With an option to upgrade that intensity or damage or frequency.

Maybe have parts that instead of just numbers, maybe have rare, unique and legendary upgrades. Each gunpart has a specific charateristic effect. Bouncing bullets, piercing bullets, exploding bullets, electric bullets, fiery bullets, splitting bullets.

Conclusion:
Upgrades should matter.
You have a good base for a game. But as of now, it feels uninspiring.

I will give you a thumbs up because of:
- Low price
- Intersting "!" mechanics
- The screenshake is done right!
- I have a feeling you want to do better as a developer ;)

review:
A superb tribute to the metroidvania-style action rpg genre made by a team who knows these kinds of games from back to front. Not merely an imitation of the classics, Chronicles of the Wolf strives to improve upon the formula that made Castlevania a 2D titan, avoiding the all-too-common pitfall of replicating the older games' flaws without understanding why.

Excellent 2D pixel artwork, background, and music design are all included in this fairly substantial game about a knight hunting a demonic werewolf cult in the French countryside. I'm finishing this off with 21 hours and only about two of those were me getting stuck or not knowing where to go. I found the game to be on the very easy side for the first half of the game, which is what I usually expect: A lot well-designed but mostly insubstantial enemies and some light platforming. Then, you get to the second act and the kid gloves come off. Enemies are dangerous without late-game gear, and there are death traps everywhere. At that point it was clear to me the devs weren't messing around.

The big thing I appreciate is it does away with ridiculous power creep and grinding. No getting a game-breaking sword from a goofy trash mob and instantly killing the final boss. No grinding the same enemy 20 times for a rare ingredient you need for a quest or an upgrade. You're always on the hunt and not having to constantly stop to check a guide. When these games forget the "action" part of being an action rpg, they often flunk for me, and I am glad to say the devs did not miss here.

There's a lot of adhering to old design philosophies in this game, and while I can appreciate it, I'm sure it's not for everyone. Stiff jumping, slow movement speed, bosses that are tough to intuit, and some lackluster system options may pull people away. It's also a shame that the post-game crossover is the worst part by far. Still, I'd encourage patience.

Chronicles of the Wolf is almost must-buy material for me. If you weren't a big fan of Iga's Castlevania action rpgs, I'd still encourage giving this one a try because it does away with what probably annoyed you in that game. If you're a retro only Castlevania fan, harkening back to the original 4, this one does not disappoint with its steady pace and gameplay that rewards skillful maneuvering over numbers crunch. If you're interested in the aesthetic, there isn't really a whole lot else out there treats 'Baroque/Gothic' this well without becoming pompous or indulging in anime tropes. If you're a veteran of metroidvania-style games, you need this. Highly recommended.

review:
[i] My Experience [/i]

I found [b]Shadow of the Treasure[/b] while dredging Steam for games with the "card game" tag. Although it's not a deckbuilder (probably the most popular type of card game), it is a card game nonetheless. At the same time, I've enjoyed some strategic card games that aren't strictly deckbuilders (like [b]Spectromancer[/b]). I thought it was cool that developer Teleport Games Bt created [b]Shadow of the Treasure[/b] as part of the universe for his previous game [b]Tortured Hearts[/b]. It's sort of a [b]Witcher 3[/b] and [b]Gwent[/b] situation. Although the text-only story was a bit dull, I always appreciate a fresh take on the card game genre.

[b]Shadow of the Treasure[/b] takes you through 15 scenarios, each having different goals that you're looking to reach. You'll reach these goals by activating the cards you're presented with in an advantageous order. Cards can often feature trade-offs. For instance, you might spend gold to activate a card that provides experience. However, if the scenario in question has an experience goal but not a gold goal, this could be an important card to help you get there. However, you might need to activate a card beforehand to get a bit of extra gold. Some cards require your character to have reached a certain stat score to activate, and other cards can increase your stat scores.

I think that where the game lost me was in the sheer variety of choices you have on any given scenario. You can start by picking any of 16 cards (that you meet the requirements for) to activate. The card deal itself seems to be random, which sends a signal that there could be many ways to work your way to the goal. Rather than feeling exacting and tactical, the game felt rather freeform. There's also a lack of feedback for the player as you are working your way to a certain goal - if you end up failing, it's hard to figure out exactly where you went wrong.

Maybe I was looking for more of a puzzle game? I don't know if there's a midpoint between having the card choices be as freeform as they are and having one set solution to each scenario, but I think that this midpoint is perhaps what I would like the game to be. Perhaps fewer choices on the board at any given time? A set card layout for each scenario? Either way, I ended up bouncing off of [b]Shadow of the Treasure[/b]. If you like the concept of the game but have a similar reaction, perhaps try [b]Spectromancer[/b] instead.

review:
I love Balatro, which is why I picked up this game, but after 15 hours of trying really hard to like it I just can't recommend it barring a major rebalance.

What makes a roguelite deckbuilder good tends to be its balance and the player's ability to cultivate a winning deck over the course of a run. Slay the Spire, for example, is so well-balanced that you can win a run with just about any card in your deck if played right, and StS gives you plenty of opportunities to craft a winning deck through card removal, card upgrades, card copying, etc. 

Dungeons and Degenerate Gamblers doesn't really do any of this in a way I would consider satisfying. There are plenty of opportunities to add cards from a random selection of 3-4 after every encounter in addition to shops, but there are so many cards that are either bad enough to never want to take, or so good that you will always take them when presented. The same could be said for the passive chips that you get at the start of the game which grant a consumable called advantage that can be used to play additional cards or use a card's effect. Conversely, card removal is incredibly hard to come by, especially after the starting area (on another note, each run from start to finish is way too long in my opinion). This leads to a tendency to play every run the exact same way, taking the same types of cards and the same chips every time, which leads to runs feeling very samey and unsatisfying. But even good cards aren't enough in many cases, because you usually can only play one card at a time that you can't see before playing (this is blackjack, after all), so the wrong card played at the wrong time means that sometimes you just straight up lose. And losing can take a very long time because shielding and healing exists for both sides, so you might as well restart when you get to this point (very frustrating when you're really deep into a run!)

After the umpteenth time of basically softlocking myself by drawing the wrong card at the wrong time, I've decided to call it quits and uninstall, at least until a major rebalance happens (if ever). I think almost every card needs to be looked over, and the devs should probably rethink the advantage system as it exists right now as well. Barring that, I can't recommend this even as someone who really wants to like it, as a fan of both blackjack and roguelite deckbuilders.

Above all, D&DG nails the general atmosphere. To me, this is the highlight. The tavern where the game takes place is quirky, seedy, and all sorts of bizarre at once, with music and artwork fully supporting the vibe conjuration process. There's no proper story to speak of, but I don't believe its presence would've done the game much (if any) good anyway.

The gameplay is on the level, with decks and individual cards being varied enough to keep the game fresh for a good amount of time. Blackjack isn't exactly the most intricate of games, but I'd say the game has succeeded in reforging the concept into something that's obviously blackjack-adjacent, yet also full of its own strengths and charm.

Overall, I'm having a good time, and I intend to keep going for a while longer.

Other than that, no real complaints for the first game.
I would recommend buying this game on sale, but nonetheless, if you liked the Phoenix Wright trilogy, you will absolutely adore this one. 

I would still consider this game an absolute gem. If you like ace attorney, and are looking to play more of it, you will enjoy this collection, no question.

review:
110 levels of puzzle-M3 fusion which are more challenging than some of the recent Cursed House games.  The goal in every level is to collect all the coins, which charge up the Amulet that slowly removes the curse from the house.  The puzzles seem to be more well-thought out this time in that the solutions aren't as repetitive as a recent other game this developer released.  Most of the puzzles have 7 or 8 steps, so aren't baby easy, but not impossibly difficult if you spend some time studying the levels to see what you can do next.

There are still an awful lot of minigames which appear every few levels.  Most of them (25) are Sokoban "push the box" (in this case, gems), but also a mix of one-up one-down solitaire (15), hidden object scenes (2), and spot the difference (8) scenes.  Not only is this rather excessive IMO, but the order in which the minigame types appear doesn't seem that well executed because sometimes you get 2 Sokoban games almost on top of each other, and other times it's like there's nothing but solitaire or spot the difference.

The way the house gets "un-cursed" near the end of the game makes me wonder if extra levels were thrown in just to extend the game more.  I'd have been happy with less levels and definitely less minigames.  But otherwise, doesn't disappoint for the Cursed House series.

[h1] OH LOOK, A NEW HOUSE ON THE MARKET! [/h1]

I've been trying to exorcize the demons from this house for 13 years...maybe 13 will be my lucky number!?! Perhaps this time, I will be able to banish this evil and send it back to the bowels of He[insert double L's] I've got to make a quick trip to Walmart to stock up on supplies. Wooden Stakes are sold in the garden center, right?

This is one of my favorite Match 3 games of all time because it requires tasks to be completed in a specific order; it's a thinking kind of game! Thanks, Igore, for including a Hint button, lol. You can play in a Relaxed Mode, a Limited Time Mode, or a Limited Moves Mode, and this is one of the few games that I play in Limited Moves Mode versus Limited-Time because of the Strategy involved; it just makes more sense to be able to plot your next move.

A Match 4 will give you Dynamite, and a Match 5, 6, and 7 will give you a Morphing Power-up (just click when it's on the desired power-up) The Morphing Power-up choices include a TNT Barrel, Lightning which removes all of one kind of tile (whatever it is swapped with), or a Rocket which targets objects from most important to least important depending on what obstacles remain. The chosen morph can be canceled within 10 seconds by right-clicking. Power-ups are usually a critical component because most coins are blocked by obstacles that require a power-up to destroy them, and most often by a specific power-up.

Collecting Coins is always the goal, and there are several different types of Coins that can be collected with an adjacent match, but they are usually blocked by an obstacle that requires a specific power-up:

$~Gold Coins: adjacent match
$~Dust Coins: adjacent match twice
$~Frozen Coins: direct Fire to melt
$~Trunk Coins: adjacent match (collect all to open Trunks)
$~Locked Coins: move the key to the lock$~Coin Molds: move gold drops to fill the molds.
$~Half Coins: clear a path between halves until they adjoin.$~Bug Coins: destroy the bugs to unlock the coin.
$~Cursed Coins: destroy with light.
$NEW-Coins & Cursed Coins that drop and are invulnerable to Rockets!

There are Obstacles that require using strategies to overcome. Lots and lots of Obstacles, some old, some new, but always challenging:

☆~Magnets: will magnetize all rocket power-ups and lightning
☆~Bombs: requires an adjacent match, Lightning, or Cannons to detonate.☆~Darkness: requires a direct ray of light (light is reflected by mirrors, etc.)
☆~Trunks: collect all Trunk Coins then make an adjacent match near Trunk to open.
☆~Crates: adjacent match or power-up.☆~Shielded Crates: adjacent match near unshielded sides or power-up.
☆~Cannon: adjacent match next to the wick.
☆~Shields: place shields in front of cannonball fire to ricochet the ball (shields have directional arrows showing the direction the ball will travel)
☆~Bugs: use power-ups or cannons to destroy them.
☆~Vials: move liquid drops to fill vials that block areas.
☆~Papyrus: make matches in the sequence shown on the papyrus to remove it.
☆~Ground Tiles: make an adjacent match.
☆~Lava Stones: use power-ups or cannons to destroy them.
☆~Fog: adjacent match or cannons.
☆~Ice: make a match with the tile inside the Ice.
☆~Snow: adjacent match or fire
☆~Chains: adjacent match or cannons.
☆~Crests: remove the required number of specified tiles shown inside the bubble.
☆~Red & Green Cells: adjacent matches or power-ups.
☆~Red & Green Hot Stones: remove all Red & Green Cells.
☆~Locks: create a path for the Key towards the Lock.
☆~Electricity Emitters: create a continuous path of Blue tiles from Emitter to Bulb. (single adjacent electricity tiles can be moved into place)

After playing a few Match 3 levels, you can play a Mini-Game that does include a Skip feature & can be replayed. My personal favorites are the Spot The Differences scenes; in my opinion, nobody does a better job with this mini-game because they do an incredible job of making the obvious not-so-obvious. I love the Diamond Push game, where you use a ladybug to push diamonds into place, hopefully without getting stuck in a corner. The Hidden Object Scenes have incredibly well-blended objects as well.

review:
After finishing all the main quests, side quests, collectibles, and the Burning Shores DLC in over 114 hours of gameplay, I just want to share my personal thoughts. Just as a note, I’ve already played Horizon Zero Dawn before, so this is coming from that experience.

I feel like a lot of things have been improved compared to the previous game. I don’t even need to talk about the visuals—obviously, with a 4-year gap, the graphics and visual quality are absolutely stunning.
One of the improvements I noticed is that Coils and Weaves can now be stacked in your inventory, making it way more spacious and easier to manage. Weapon upgrades are now more progressive, the world feels more alive, and you can even randomly talk to some NPCs now (even if they only say generic lines).

In this sequel, we get tons of new features like the Shieldwing, Pullcaster, diving gear, and a more flexible climbing system that makes exploration much easier. We also get to face new, more brutal and aggressive machines, plus some new mounts to ride.

There are a bunch of new activities too—like machine races, colosseum battles with machines, and many more. Oh, and don’t forget, you can find some cool easter eggs from other PlayStation games here. Thanks to these new activities, you won’t just be going from one mission to another in a repetitive loop, especially in the mid-to-late game where it could otherwise start to feel really boring. But then again, I think that’s just how most AAA games are these days.

review:
Spoiler free review.

After thoroughly enjoying the first game I wish I never started playing the sequel. Even though I waited months for it to be sold on PC.

The moment I started playing I noticed just how bad the audio is. I honestly thought my PC had issues processing audio - I use external DAC and a headset and no game so far had any issues with this setup but I was still sceptical. After watching videos online I had my confirmation that in fact it was the sound design that was sub-par to say the least. It feels as if sometimes half of audio is absent but that's just how it is.

Never mind, I ploughed through, maybe this will change. Next thing was infuriating controls e.g. double arrow tap means dive and roll. I dove off many cliffs until I finally changed the controls. Talking about cliffs - the climbing mechanics are outright annoying. I don't enjoy them, nor I found them useful, might as well not have them in game. Felt half baked, bit like audio.

Next onto the foes. I would fight a number of enemies, turn around, go 100m, fight one enemy, return - all enemies are back and well. Considering there's only a handful of characters in a square km surely it won't be much of a hassle to code this in. Especially as most of them follow a scripted path.

Graphics are OK. Coming from Death Stranding - not great but OK. Different look I guess. However, when standing on top of a higher platform I noticed a lot of tiling issues with textures. Sort of thing you'd expect in much older game. Performance overall is nothing to write home about, I get 144 fps maxed out on 5080 and 9800X3D with up-scaling.
One problem graphics wise is power usage. Even when paused or in map view game runs at 99% GPU usage. Most games would drop it to 10-20% but not this... To me it matters, if not for energy costs, for PC longevity and heat output which is very noticeable in warmer months.

So far I'm 40 hours in and things are not getting any better so I am unsure if I should continue since I paid for the game or just abandon it altogether. I am noticing another unwelcome trend - "political correctness", kind of thing Disney is in hot water for now. It is subtle for sure but you notice it - some NPC character design, certain cosmetics for main character and other subtle hints. I won't go further into story as I don't want to spoil anything for those enjoying the game, I just found it a bit unnecessary.

Overall - I am far too late in game for a refund and far too annoyed to continue. I hope this will help some players but I wouldn't hold breath that the developer improves on this. To me this hints of problems within the company and it's management.

review:
This no recommendation is only to tell you to avoid ultra hard; My game time played is also not indicative of real-time played as I left the game running for weeks while not playing.

Horizon Forbidden West – Final Score: 2.7 / 5

✅ Fun: 1.5/3**
✅ Graphical Fidelity: 0.5/0.5
✅ Mechanics: 0.5/1
❌ Story & Music: 0.2/.5

👎 Combat, Difficulty & AI

Ultra Hard vs Very Hard:** Ultra Hard is punishing with inflated numbers; Very Hard becomes trivial after getting purple gear. No mechanical variance—just stat bloat.

Final Boss:** Regenerates plating, not health—only viable tactic is spamming explosive spikes. Gear upgrades aren’t worth the grind.

Enemy AI & Boundaries:** Invisible barriers break immersion—pull agro and drag machines unrealistically far.

Environmental Hazards:** Terrain often kills you via forced climbing, bouncing, or getting stuck.

Knockdown Recovery:** Leads directly into death; no i-frames or counterplay.

Status Effects:** Irrelevant on higher difficulties. Warrior bows? Useless past Normal. Melee? Too risky to use.

Slide-and-Shoot:** Cool idea, ruined by enemy AI with perfect aim tracking.

👎 Story, World Design, and Believability

Main Story:** Short (5 hrs if rushed), emotionally flat, heavily reliant on scanning → walk → exposition loops. Supporting cast is one-note.

Factions:** Rebels seem to have won—most terrain is under their control. Yet the game acts like they’re "a threat," not the de facto rulers.

Towns:** Look like abstract puzzle boxes, not livable places. E.g., Plainsong's design is impractical; The Bulwark is a joke defense-wise.

Major Lore Errors:** Nearly all world datapoints are entertainment-based, which wouldn’t survive a millennium. Pipes and tanks made of zinc alloy steel surviving 1,000 years? Not credible.

Quest Design Flaws:** In "The Wound in the Sand," no one thought to check for the massive** pipe buried inches under the surface. Player handholding is constant—Aloy autocompletes puzzles aloud before you even think.

👎 Machine Strike (Board Game)

1/5 quality overall.
Exploitable: Only the longest-range, highest-HP units matter. Using 1 unit (like Frostclaw) lets you attack twice per turn, breaking the game.
Glitches:**

  Clicking during a move causes unintentional movement from the previous piece.
  Saved piece sets become grayed out and unusable unless deleted and remade manually.

👎 Technical Problems
 HUD & UI:**

  Hotbar constantly reshuffles without consent.
  Data Points have no map markers.

Cutscene Skip Crashes:**
 Skipping several in a row, or just major ones, causes full game crashes—pointing to a memory leak or cinematic deallocation fault.

Textures:** Overuse of shiny materials makes characters look plasticky.
Machine Strike UI Bugs:** Game keeps focus on last selected piece; misclicking moves it unintentionally.

 👍 Small Wins

Upgradeable items are listed first.
Stealth detection is slightly better than Skyrim (not exactly a high bar).

Verdict:** The game’s stunning visuals can’t mask shallow systems, narrative emptiness, broken mechanics, and critical immersion failures. With countless bugs, especially in its board game and cinematic systems, *Horizon Forbidden West* feels like an inflated expansion, not a true sequel. Stylish, but hollow.

There are no big pushes for microtransactions, you don't feel shorted, and the expansion pack is a nice addition that brings a new environment to the game.

review:
Horizon Forbidden West Complete Edition – Steam Review (6/10)

I would buy this only on sale, not worth the full amount. The story is Good, but the PC port is terrible. If you have the money to spend on the full price, just get a game like Cyberpunk  2077 instead they keep giving steady updates compared to the whatever this slop is . I would not recommend this at full price until the game has been patched.

The base game of Horizon Forbidden West earns an 8/10 for its engaging gameplay and a good story, with the flyable Sunwing mount and Shieldwing gliding as standout features that make exploration a thrill, i liked the concept of companions . The pacing at the start is also painfully slow, nearly losing me early on.

The upgrade system is decent, but the ammo and upgrade resource management is a major downgrade from Zero Dawn. I loved how the original let players flexibly balance resources to prioritize either upgrades or ammo as needed, but Forbidden West limits all resources, making it harder to manage both effectively and breaking the strategic flow. Speaking of Zero Dawn, its remastered map, with vibrant cities like Meridian, blows Forbidden West’s map out of the water. NPCs here feel flat, lacking the lively spark of the original’s world.

Optimization in the base game isn’t great, especially on NVIDIA cards. I hit artifacting issues on character faces during cutscenes with NVIDIA Reflex enabled—not a driver issue, as no other games had this problem. Texture optimization is also terrible, dragging down the experience. On my 1440p ultrawide monitor, I averaged 80 FPS on high textures with DLSS Quality in the base game, which is decent and I can live with it, but the game still needs serious polish.

The Burning Shores DLC is disappointing, earning a generous 4/10. Performance stutters so badly it makes a PowerPoint presentation look smooth. Even on low textures and DLSS Performance, I dropped to a pathetic 25 FPS in the DLC map. It’s unacceptable that, over a year after release, there’s no fix. You need a NASA-tier PC to run it properly. The DLC story is good but doesn’t match the depth of The Frozen Wilds DLC from Zero Dawn, largely because Seyka’s character needed more development to shine.

Compared to Zero Dawn Remastered, which had optimization issues but nothing this severe, Forbidden West’s Complete Edition disappoints. The slow start, restrictive resource system, and DLC’s technical flaws drag down the strong base game, resulting in an overall 6/10. I want to like this game, but it’s hard for me. I’d recommend picking up the base game on sale for its gameplay and exploration, but steer clear of the DLC unless you have a high-end PC and don’t mind its flaws.

RIP Lance Reddick – your presence as Sylens will be missed.

review:
Unfortunately, very glitchy. The sound of dialog drops very often and is followed by a loss of use of the map. Once that problems appears, the game will soon freeze once we enter the menu. The game has to be restarted each time to avoid the freeze or has to be crashed with the task manager if it actually froze. This glitch happens very often (every 30min or more often). Other times, the game just lags a lot or get almost frozen during an action from Aloy (gathering ressource, interacting with objects in the environnement). After that glitch, the game will suddenly close itself without any warning.

For the gameplay itself, I am still in the early game (20 hours or so), but some skills that I loved and used really a lot in Horizon Zero Dawn has been removed and changes a lot the gameplay in my personal situation (attack from above, attack from below, dismount attack, advanced skill of calling a mount even when none is overriden at the moment). Many new skills and skill tree have been introduced, but I wasn't expecting to loose many of the Zero Dawn skills since this game seem to be like a continuity of the first one.

Also, unlike Zero Dawn, Forbidden West has a lot of "going back on your footstep" situation (ex: blocked path that you have to acquire tools or other things to be able to open). Since the load of the fast travel is kind of long, I can see that it will become irritating eventually if you want to explore the whole map because you will have to constanly go back on your footsteps. Some side quest can also be started and in the middle you realize that you encountered a blocked path and cannot complete the side quest before unlocking that ability.

A big big plus of this game is that it is very very customizable. This game seems overall harder than Zero Dawn with the new machine, complexity of combat, new elements, skill tree, etc... but the fact that it is so customizable really makes up for it. There is different difficulty available, but the is also "custom difficulty" which allows you to adjust everything to your liking (ex: you want less damage, but you want to keep the more advanced mechanic of parts harvesting). Underwater exploration is now possible and there is even an option for Thalassophobia that removes the time pressure of "oxygen". Also, all the controls are customizable to link with the keys you want of the keyboard (there seem to be a glitch to change the use of the "X" key, but otherwise ok). To the developpers: thank you very much for all that customizable options, it is really awesome, wow!

If the game was not as glitchy as it is, I might have been interested to play longer and my recommentation might have been different, but unfortunately, it really killed the fun since it prevents you from getting immersed in the universe they built and make you fear and anticipate the crashes. Also, I did some research on those glitches and they seem to be known, but are still not corrected 3 years after the release date. So, sadly, I cannot recommend this game.

Oh, and don't you DARE take on a mission above your level. If an enemy is 1 level above you you could nuke him and he'll barely notice and he'll accidentally kill you by breaking wind. (slight exaggeration, but only slight....)

Advice for people wanting to speedrun:
- download all the colour+inusuku+bonus content mods, there is a guide for this posted elsewhere.

- 10x adventure books every weekend

- Make sure you spend all your free time reading books and using "talk->blow on" to keep your motivation high.

- make sure that unless your weekly meeting policy is "lunchbox life" you go to bed with at lease 20 stamina

- prioritise attack/defence training throughout the weekdays, and do special training if nothing else is available

- weekends do your trip to the town's bookstore on on day, then part time on the other. Then "individual training -> go for a run" to finish off the day portions

review:
I had the amazing opportunity to both play the demo for gaming expos and playtest the game. Big thank you to Danny for that!

Let’s start with the positives. The pixel art is very well crafted and implemented. The level aesthetics are beautiful; taking the player through verdant forests to glacial lakes to volcanoes and more. The animation of certain details such as waves in the water elevate the game from other pixel art games that just have static backgrounds. It is clear to me that a lot of time was spent on making sure all of the sprites fit with the aesthetic. Nothing feels out of place visually.  

The soundtrack fits the mood of each level very well. Whilst I do agree with others that have reviewed the game and wanted more variation, I think that the instrumentation for each level creates a fitting atmosphere. I would say this is especially the case for level two and five. An additional shout out must be made to the final boss theme composed by a friend of the developer. It is easily the best track in the game and makes getting to the end of the game feel even more rewarding.

From a control perspective, the ability to play this game on both keyboard and controller provides another layer of customisation and allows you to play in whichever way is more comfortable for you.

This game does a very good job in the exploration department. In each level there are often branching routes that you can take where you can encounter different enemies or optional resources. If you love finding hidden areas then you will be in for a treat (especially if you love hidden lore). However, I would say that in some of the levels the branching paths merge leading to a singular path to progress. This does lower the sense of exploration a little bit as in some levels you will emerge at the same place no matter what path you took.

Speaking of resources, the main mechanic other than swinging your sword is the potion crafting system. This is an incredible inclusion to the game and elevates the experience significantly. There are various berries you can collect in the levels that, if you combine them, provide potions that heal, shield, buff and even one that highlights the aggro range of enemies. The combinations are vast and allow each player to create a unique potion to solve a problem. Need healing whilst dealing more damage? You can do that. In certain areas you can also exchange berries of one colour for another. This is great game design as it allows the player to make the potion they want even if they didn’t get the berries they wanted. This is easily the best feature of the game and makes finding berries feel like a big reward. I would note however that as you progress, the threshold for the amount of berries needed to craft a potion increases therefore there may be times where you have four berries but need five to craft a potion and therefore have to venture through that area without a potion until you can find more. There will be ‘dry spots’ where berries are rare and therefore you will need to be comfortable in getting past enemies without the use of potions.

The story is very simple but effective. Finding hidden areas expands your connection to the characters but it is not required to experience the main story beats. There are alternate endings which provide replay value. 

That being said, this game is [b] not [/b] for a casual audience. This is a challenging game that will test your reaction time, positioning and resource management skills. Don’t let the Zelda-esque visuals fool you as this game is a lot more about combat than Zelda. This game demands a lot of patience and trial and error. Each enemy has its own abilities and movement patterns. Mastering how to deal with each enemy type is crucial as, in many areas, you will be outnumbered by a lot. Combine this with the fact that Novi (the player character) stops when you swing the sword and it can be easy to become surrounded on all sides. Novi can only swing in the direction that they are facing (unless you have certain potions) making them very vulnerable to attack from behind. Positioning and spacing are the most important things in combat as enemies will try to get as close to you as they can and, once they are up close, they are extremely difficult to deal with. There will also be enemies placed off screen but their aggro range will extend into the screen. Using the green berry will make this very apparent and help warn you of upcoming danger but it is limited time wise.

Health management is also highly important as from level one certain enemies will out DPS you meaning that trading blows is not an option. I would say the biggest spike in difficulty is from level one to two as two contains a lot more of the harder enemy types in the game. Once you’re over this difficulty spike though, the game takes on a more standard difficulty curve. I would even say that some of the later levels are easier than the middle ones.

There are also certain levels that require you to take environmental damage to progress, meaning that you can’t get away with being on low health constantly. It’s also important to manage health as there are no checkpoints in this game. If you die you go straight back to the beginning of the level regardless of if you died 20% or 99% of the way through. This can become very frustrating in later levels where there are many more enemies guarding the exit to the level. You do however get to save after each level so you don’t have to play the game all in one sitting unlike some other games.

Overall, this is a game that has been made with a lot of love and visually and sonically you can feel that. However it is a game that will challenge you more than most games of a similar style. If you enjoy overcoming difficult enemies and mastering the mechanics of the games you play then you will love this game. This game will provide about 4 hours of gameplay depending on skill level or if you want to explore everything it has to offer. However, it has been designed with a lot of speed running features allowing veterans to breeze through levels. There is also an achievement one can gain if they beat the game without using potions if you really want to test your skills. If you attempt this, I wish you good luck and I hope you succeed.

If you like games where RNG is king and you’re always chasing “just one more run,” this one’s worth it.

The gameplay is very flat.  

In this style of game you'd really like to see a degree of progression or improvement of the things you're playing with (e.g. add/remove/improve your cards), but nothing really ever changes.  The result is that you're just playing whatever cards add the type of resource you're currently missing the most, coupled with with some basic discussion ahead of time about what your teammate(s) should prioritize.

The "don't talk to your teammate when picking cards" thing is just kinda meh.  It's not the worst thing ever, but it's also not engaging.  I'd rather they dump that and come up with something else.

There's not a lot of strategy.  There's very little depth.  There's just not much going on in general.

It's a shame, because the game could be a lot more appealing if there was actually deckbuilding or similar progression that was interesting.  It doesn't seem like any mechanics like that are part of the future, so I'd say this is a game to skip.

This feels like a really unique deck building game and has a lot of potential. It revolves around resource management, positioning yourself well in the loop, and then finally planning for a killing blow on demons. 

It's more of a story-driven game where your deck is constantly re-made, rather than being a roguelike where each run features one growing deck.

Each card has 3 uses: movement around the loop, played effect, or discarded for its Knowledge. I love multi-use cards and Knowledge especially is a cool mechanic:

If I discard for Knowledge, I am able to learn a new card from the Codex DURING the encounter and it goes into my discard pile. The Codex is basically a shop that usually starts empty, but cards can be added to it during a scenario. 

I can access the Codex at any point on my turn, giving a lot of flexibility in when I take cards into my deck. As far as I know this isn't a very common mechanic in deckbuilders and it has a lot of depth and decision making involved here.

I recommend this if you want a deckbuilder that is NOT a roguelike and that explores more mechanics outside of pure combat.
