"Demon Loop" was far from what I expected. It is not the deckbuilding-powered boardgame with high replayability, but a descent puzzle game with intelligently-made scenarios to solve. The twist with the board definitely lets "Demon Loop" stand out. You have to wallk around the board, using buildings, getting powered up, and - unfortunately - run intro dead ends that make winning the scenario impossible. The mechanics within the game are very complex, with influence, honor, codex-learning, knowledge-spending, dice-placing taking a lot to think about. It all depends on what cards you choose and use to beat enemies that easily overpower you (think of a dagger or bow doing 1-3 damage points maximum, but the enemy needing a six to be rolled - impossible). In between the scenarios you upgrade your base, giving you important power-ups. To round it up, the scenarios are interconnected with a visual-novel-style story that - well - might not be the most thrilling experience, but at least binds the puzzles together. With a lovely graphic style, this game sure has the potential to become a stand-out game when leaving early access. What I wish for the future:

- adding a bit more stuff to play in between the scenarios, meaning like quests to earn crystals so that you can improve the character to better compete during the main quest
-an option to increase font size and contrast text to beackground - that might be a puzzling wish, but since I'm using barrier-free options within computer-use frequently, it would make some effect for me

A good game I will return to soon! All the best!

review:
Clever optimization deck-builder from Alexander Pfister. Can be very challenging, which may put off new players, particularly those not accustomed to Pfister's other games similar to this (notably, Blackout: Hong Kong). I think this works well as a digital app, perhaps more so than it would as a physical game, with gradually-revealed hidden terrain and custom decks per level. May feel like more of a puzzle than a game, but this is one of the appealing aspects to me. Can be very frustrating, particularly when you realize you've made a mistake, and there is no way to restart the turn.

I experienced only a few minor glitches during gameplay, and there are some minor language errors, but nothing game-breaking or preventing understanding, though be sure to take note of the warning during startup that this is still Early Access and save-game data may be lost/unusable after an update (which may prompt some people considering the purchase to wait until official release).

review:
This game is so addictive that it's hard to find time to come up for air to make a review!

I never played the first game, but I am quite pleased with this one. It is easy to learn, fast-paced yet long. It can appeal to anyone, but especially minimalistic number crunching nerds who like tediousness. 

It requires a little micromanagement in the beginning as you are learning. Once you learn how to set not only priorities on actions but also the number of times a day an action occurs, it begins to run on its own.

While the game isn't "pretty" like the Sims, the roleplay is very much alive in this game. 

In the beginning, I was fired from multiple jobs and expelled several times before I learned how it worked.

Tips:

- Look for a bigger apartment and move before June 2025. You are going to need the space. Ordering pizza all the time is expensive and bad for your health. You'll want a heating surface (IE stove), a fridge, and cooking ingredients. Press SHIFT when you click on cooking ingredients to have it automatically renew when you are low.

- Enroll in school early as the interest rates are lower at the start of the game.

- Don't try to have a full time job when going to school. Once you graduate, get a job for 160 hours or two part time jobs that equal around that. 

- Always set work and school priority to 1. It defaults to 2. 

- Pay off student loans as soon as you can. Sorry, no student loan forgiveness here! Trade school is cheap. University loans take longer.

- If you get burnout while you are going to school and working, take a short vacation at the start of the month. You typically have enough time to take the vacation, go to work, go to school during the month. 

- Don't have children until you have a decent amount of savings AND have your monthly needs worked out. 

- Nannies are expensive! Take in a "close friend" into your household. I use a nanny for the first 200 hours of the month while everyone is at work. Then between the husband, wife, and close friend, the baby's needs are taken care of. 

- Put money in savings or CDs often. If stocks are your thing, proceed at your own risk. 

That's all for now. This game is definitely worth adding to your collection if you enjoy life sim games.

review:
If you've ever played The Sims and wished it had less silly poses and deeper mechanics - like long-term stress and health management, or game-defining traits, or a way deeper economic simulation which doesn't make it trivial to top out at making money - this is the game for you. It's a lovely sandbox that's as deep as you want it to be.

You can simply roleplay a person living a normal life - get an education, a family, a mortgage, work 9 to 5, and find ways to juggle your money, time, mental state and health. Raise children. Retire.

Or you might pursue a passion to rob a bank, struggle to pay the bills while planning the heist, and discover it actually takes a lot to pull it off - and that if you don't, you can get thrown in jail - for *years* of in-game time.

Or try to become a billionaire, get into running businesses - and discover a surprisingly deep economic model that makes it very satisfying to actually keep a profitable business empire.

Or you can tune up the character's - very powerful! - traits, and become a hobo monk, living in a tent and meditating on a bench, perfectly happy to NOT be bothered by the glamour and prestige of the riches.

And while the game makes time fly, it's (mostly) very respectful of your time, with nice enough priority-based automation and a way to speed things WAY up. The only thing I found time-consuming was to manage contracts across multiple businesses - but that, again, is not mandatory - and rather adds to the immersion of running a business.

Overall, it's great fun. Go get it!

review:
TLDR: This is a great game, but does have a few flaws. But after some trial and error, it's great. Almost like an idle, 2D Sims. 

EDIT: I haven't actually closed the game, it's been suspending on my Steam deck in between sessions so I guess it says I haven't played any hours. Really it's been 10-15.

Okay, so there's a lot of positive reviews and some negative ones. Let me start by saying I love this game. It plays really well on the Steam Deck. However, like most Sim games, I did start over twice as I learned things that made everything easier. This wasn't necessary, but it's something I do with most Sim games, so I wasn't surprised.

First off, I played on the Steam Deck and as of right now it's only "Playable" but I had zero issues. There is a lot of text (duh), so some of it is by nature, smaller, but it really plays well on the couch with the GF where I can not be afraid to let it play out a month without me watching as it'll pause at month-end.

The negative reviews do touch on some minor things. Stocks probably should be in the financial overview, and it doesn't always include all lines like dividends, unless they were paid out in the last three months. Most businesses you can run aren't hand-held on setup. That could be more touched upon in the tutorial. However, the tutorial does go over the basics of setting up a business. I would mention here that with a lot of businesses, they take A WHILE to be profitable. However, there's three ways this happens:

1) Direct monthly revenue - pretty obvious, you make more each month than you pay. This scales over time, but isn't that much honestly.
2) Contracts - some businesses allow you to have contracts for specific time periods (6 month increments) and these pay out set disbursements every 6 months if you fulfill the work hours. These can be VERY lucrative and can give you large money dumps routinely. Some businesses can have like 7 contracts, so potentially each month has a payout or some have massive ones. Not all businesses have contracts. Some businesses will ONLY make money off contracts. Security something was one such, and costs like 100k/mo to run, with 7 contracts all for like 120-150k every six months. As you can see, it is profitable, but at the same time the contracts each have different employee type requirements so does require handholding as it isn't static, and requires a heavy investment until 6mos in when the first few contracts pay out.
3) Selling a business - This is the real payoff. A lemonade stand may make 5k/mo profit after a year with two 20k concurrent contracts. However, after a year it's also probably work 250k to sell. Other businesses are worth a lot more.

Some advice:

---I highly suggest in the early game keeping 2-3 lemonade stands going (working the bookkeeping/janitorial jobs yourself and hiring cashiers), and selling them when they hit like 200-250k value. This takes several months, and you need to have all the adverts going except the ones where you have to advertise on the street. This first infusion of cash should be used to expand into more businesses.
---My experience is that you don't want to open an advanced business until you have like 500k+. The medical office is a great starter "advanced" business, but be aware is does take like 100k a month in expenses and takes a few months to break even, and you DO need to be able to pay wages at month-end.
---Your employees level up and become more efficient over time. With the medical office you may find that you need 500k startup and a bunch of employees, hiring new ones as time goes on. However, at some point you can fire some employees due to them having all leveled up and become more efficient (the game tells you how many hours each employee can work still in a given month). This medical office, after like a year, sells for like $3m or so.
---I haven't gotten to the point of creating a public company, so I don't know how well that obviates the need to manage individual businesses, but you are prompted at month end for anything requiring intervention (lease renewals, employees quitting or demanding pay raise).

review:
I highly recommend this game.  Great fun, lots of strategy to consider, and built-in flexibility for how you try to overcome each challenge.

Every run can be very different with the options of character selection and firepit modifications as well as different tower combinations, block card combinations, and path to get to the boss.  Talents give you a type of progression, too.  

There are no micro-transactions - and at this point there is three types of "currency".  Coins are earned and used within a single level to build/upgrade towers or to get more block cards.  Gems are earned in each level along the way to target a boss and are used between levels to make modifications to your cards, towers, or heal / strengthen your firepit before getting to the boss.   Finally, experience is used to unlock additional talents, which carry through between boss runs.

Once you've completed each area, you unlock additional types of levels.  

Infernal shards allow you to attempt additional boss runs with harder settings and are completely customizable as you can pick up to 8 shards to apply to your run.  Each shard has it's own impact on your run so you can tailor the difficulty as much as you want.

Outside of boss runs, there are endless modes.  The main endless mode I haven't tried yet, but the daily and weekly challenges are a welcome addition to the game.  They let you try to beat the leaderboard by staying in the level as long as possible. 

In the end, there is so much variability that there is always something to learn and new strategies to try given the hand that you're dealt each time through.  Excellent game, worth the money.

Remove damage cap on the chomper for endless mode or make it scale based on what wave you're on.

The "roguelike" endless mode where you choose buffs AND downsides as you progress is good. It falls off around wave 20+ though and starts to get to the point around 25-28 where enemy scaling is so agressive it's just not possible to put out more DPS because you've built a full maze and everything is upgraded.  Some way to keep upgrading your towers (or upgrading blocks to buff towers on them) would be great for this. 

The characters are interesting and varied but some of them are not really useful, or their buffs tend to work against them. The tiny builder for example, is described as a character who can build faster and gets a buff that gives you more maze tiles (3) times per round when you play one.  3 free tiles is cool, right?  Except you are locked to tiles 3 squares or smaller on that character. A full hand of 4-5 square tiles will cover more area and build you more maze than the builder will get. So the real buff the builder gets is that all his tiles have runes. This makes it good late game but the character can struggle in the middle waves to get a maze that's big enough, on the more open maps. 

The "Chronomancer" gets significantly less prep time but doesn't really get any buffs in exchange, other than an AOE "Slow" effect that be used twice per wave. 

The scrap character is amazing and I spent a crazy amount of time messing around with it.  It's a shame you can't use that char in Endless mode.

The quality of the game looks to be good enough and polished enough for the early access asking price and I bought 3 copies, one for husband, one for BIL's bday. I also played with my friend all day who got it.

Since looking at some of the Alpha gameplay trailers and streams of the game, they got VA's already replacing several of the characters that are great and do a good job and was one of the first thing's I noticed. I did immediately notice a typo with one of the words in the start up scenes that will need an easy fix.  Compared to what another reviewer said- there is an above radial menu that notifies you of where enemies are, the enemies also have sound bites that do let you know they are nearby, there are SFX and blood and body parts fly and when you slice the enemies with your 3rd weapon you're given a good amount of gore-- the enemies DO spawn away almost immediately but I imagine that's because the amount of game design that went into the world so it wouldn't be so heavily cluttered. I'm playing on max graphic settings, IDK if that makes a difference.

The game was released on time, which is a good sign compared to another game with similar specs that me and my husband were notified of this early access from a TikTok Game Review (hotsoss) that we saw a video recc.-ing this has been delayed into oblivion. 

I can't wait to spend more time and see where this goes!

Edited Addition:

So, far I have not seen any evidence of AI neither has my friend who scraped the forums looking for proof, IDK. Maybe we aren't good at identifying it. I think they did a good job with the graphics and everything.

Honestly, we were laughing a lot about a lot of the references. I think this is a game enjoyed heavily with friends. We got up to level 15 as far as today even looping back to help my husband and BIL catch up a bit.

I think this game to be honest would be best described as a combination of: Killing Floor [my friend and husband's says, I never played], Overcooked! (or other games like it), and Deep Rock Galactic as someone who played in early access DRG. 

I feel like there is not a HUGE ton of content released yet but that's subject to change if the dev's continue to develop like they should and DRG was similar that it quickly got grindy with only cosmetics and some stuff being out then. Only difference is DRG has generated maps that change, where as this has different mission spots that are going to be the same along with the Overcooked mini games that you kind of play per level spot.

As far as the music goes: I do think they need to expand heavily upon the soundtrack; the jukebox in the 4 person party HUB area only chooses 1 track and can get repetitive as it is a single track and they are all instrumental. The mission areas can feel the same to a degree. 

The combat does feel a lot like DRG in it's somewhat grindy plainness- which is fine to me personally and doesn't bother me.

I think there's a lot of potential if dev's keep at it, and if this sounds like a game that interests you and you have a good set of friends to play with it will be wayyyy more enjoyable just like DRG.

The online play with people was nice, but considering that unlike in DRG you don't share the special pick ups for ingredients to make beer - which in this game is pizza, can be a little annoying if a rando or friend is greedy in the party.

There is definitely need for QOL, HUD, a little bit of buginess, and other general improvement, but  I personally feel like it's on the right track.

Score: 6.9/10
Fun, unique mix of co-op shooter and restaurant sim. 
With more updates this could really pop off. Right now: Very enjoyable, alot of potential for further replayabillity if developers add more depth: game-modes think rogue-lite, boss only modes, endless waves, tower defense mode, difficulty-modifiers, mutators.

Here a list:

✅Great base-editing, social hub idea same as Deep Rock Galactic
✅Alot of Steam Achievements to complete
✅Many maps, diverse maps they all feel unique and missions arent all copy-paste. They have their own charm. 
✅ Combat is fun enough very arcady / nostalgic yet has room for improvement 
✅ Fluid co-op, you press ESC -> Multiplayer -> Get a list of matches -> Join, boom play with others.
❌Floaty combat, lack of weapon sway no recoil, weird bullet drop.
❌Very small maps that could easily be better by being a bit bigger with more objectives / things to find.
❌FPS issues, frames are playable but very inconsistent.
❌ Replay ability suffers — core loop is “do bounty → return to restaurant → pick a mission -> repeat” with little grind/progression compared to DRG. Its just too easy to unlock anything in this game which is a missed opportunity. review:
Potential for a cult classic is here, but it's going to take a lot longer in the oven. 

I added Pizza Bandit to my wishlist a couple of months ago after perusing my discovery queue to be met with a game that looked like it was doing something different. Going in my biggest concern was that this would be a UE5 asset flip with little more to offer than an idea. I was wrong. Performance is solid, haven't had any issues so far. Gameplay is fun, but the combat feels light, not much impact or weight to melee combat. Gunplay reminds me of a 3rd person Borderlands. While Pizza Bandit does feel new the inspirations are evident. Take a bit of Dave the Diver, Borderlands-esque gunplay, Monster Hunter type customization, and Killing Floor gameplay loop and you've got this fresh yet familiar co-op shooter in Pizza Bandit.

For as much as I like the game so far there are plenty of issues. For starters the asking price is a bit steep. Matchmaking is iffy and I'd highly recommend going into this with friends. Solo is fun, but the experience was definitely designed for multiplayer. Music is VERY generic, sounds like something that was crafted in AI test kitchen, I'd go as far as to say borderline soulless on that front. Enemy variety leaves a lot to be desired. There's the typical light, medium, heavy fodder rushing you as you're completing objectives, but the aesthetic of the enemies could use some work- they all look very similar. 

With more TLC Pizza Bandit can be a real underground hit, but the big IF is post launch support. I think it's commendable what the devs have put together for their initial offering and would love to see this get the chance to bake with some more toppings thrown on.

review:
I want to address the AI generated art claims here.  First off, the year is 2025, and AI is everywhere, get used to it.  Second, this is not a AAA title game, this is a small game being developed by 6 people in South Korea.  Small dev teams do not have the capital to invest in hiring voice actors.  If you want a game like that, go buy BL4 for $80.  Remember, this is an early access game.  Third, most importantly, they have addressed the issue in their discord, and plan on removing any content thought to be AI generated.  The dev team has been very active about addressing this.

Alright, now that that is out of the way, lets get down to business.  This is a 3rd person 4 player coop shooter where people work towards mission objectives on various difficulties in client-based servers.  You have a primary weapon, a secondary weapon, two specials, and 1 melee weapon.  All of the weapons/specials can be changed or upgraded to your play-style. 

This game plays like PD2 (weapons upgrades/customization, reviving team members, objective based missions).  The enemies spawn in and move like they are form KF2, except they can spawn around you at any given moment.  There is a call down for more ammo/life just like in DRG, but it is currently limited to once per mission.  

Missions are time based and can be failed before the mission time runs out.  I am averaging roughly 15 min on solo missions, difficulty 2.  

You get to decorate your pizza restaurant and that allows you to unlock perks.  You can cook pizza before a mission that will give you and 3 others some mission buffs.  You cook them with ingredients that you find while playing missions. 

Lastly, there is a lot of replay value with all the unlocks.  The game-play loop is there, and it is fun.  Remember, this game is still in development and the devs are very active on Discord so if you have questions, drop by.  Solo play can be hard, but there is a dodge/roll (spacebar key) that negates ALL damage, so it may also just be a skill issue :p.  I do recommend this game.

review:
Highly recommended.

A lot of people try to explain this game by comparing it to Overcooked or some well-known shooter, but that doesn’t really work. Calling it Overcooked ignores the combat, the layers of sarcastic humor, and the bizarre, sometimes gory gameplay. Calling it Payday misses the fact that you’re literally rolling through enemies in the middle of chaotic fights. Honestly, this game is just Pizza Bandit.

People seem to reach for familiar titles just because there are guns, and since it’s co-op they feel the need to compare it to other co-op shooters. But from my experience, those comparisons don’t mean much. This game is simply different. Saying “it’s a co-op shooter” explains about as much as saying “it’s side-scrolling or top-down.” It tells you nothing about what it actually is. All it really does is drag in the bias of whatever the most famous game with that system happens to be.

For players who come in because of the Steam tags, it’ll probably feel confusing at first. It did for me too. But the more you play, the more you realize: this isn’t an imitation, it’s its own thing. And that’s why so many reviews say it “feels full of potential but not quite refined yet.” To me, it feels like an egg. It clearly is something, but it hasn’t hatched into its final form. What I’m sure of is that whatever it becomes, it won’t be anything we’ve seen before.

Do games really need explanations? Since when? If it’s fun, you keep playing. If it’s not, you move on.

review:
exactly what i hoped/paid for:
Not quite sure what other folks were expectin but this is exactly what i thought it would be and i'm having a lot of fun playing it...If i would compare it to a recent game (both in gameplay mechanics as well as its "readiness" state upon early-release), i would compare it to FBC: Firebreak with a dash of base-building and more character customization (heck, in many ways, Pizza Bandit plays better than FBC upon release - and at only half the price!).  It's a co-op horde survival with a quirky "hold 'E' as your game-character completes complex task that will be reset upon being attacked" game function.  in the case of FBC, one was repairing the various supernatural machinery whilst battling the Hiss.  Conversely, in PizzaBandit, one is preparing various food items (from sushi to cocaine-laced chicken) all whilst battling hordes of the typical enemy types that all of these games feature (e.g. fast melee, slow long range, long range with explosions, kamikaze, and Goliath-type classes. you know the ones).

solo playing:
it CAN be played solo (as i prefer to play all these sorts of games, regardless of dev intentions) but as is always the case for games meant to be played co-op, the difficulty scales up rather quickly  (by the third stage, i had to start "playing smart" rather than just runnin n gunnin).

the words of others:
Thus far, i've greatly enjoyed what i've played and see the potential for a lot of growth.   Some have criticized the plot or lack-thereof (i wasn't expecting much of one...) but the trailers promised pizza, guns, and monsters and that's exactly what's been delivered.  Others have criticized the voice-acting, which is odd because its good. not bad or great but better than amateur and certainly better than one would expect from a niche-pizza-themed scifi co-op TPS.   Yet others have focused their entire criticism on the use of A.I. assets - its true, i have caught a few (e.g. the background music and the images representing said music when one interacts with the jukebox) but its minimal and i only noticed because so many reviews focused on this insignificant aspect of the overall game-to dismiss and negatively review an early-release game on 0.06% of is content (which may even be placeholder content) is not only weird, its seemingly political.  AI is part of our world now - boycotting and review-bombing indie games for their usage of such a tool, is not going to stop it. 

what i want for the full version:
I would love to see more varied enemy types or enemies themed to the locations that one is fighting in.  I would like to see a heavier focus on the ability to earn upgrades for the character and his weapons rather than toward decorating the pizza parlor. review:
I usually get really bad 3D motion sickness, but this game didn’t trigger it at all.

- Battle: The combat isn’t heavy; it’s light and focused on dodging. The invincibility frames on rolls are super generous. I wouldn’t exactly call it a shooter either — every fight turns into a chaotic brawl, so it feels more like an action game with guns. For melee weapons, like in most action games, you’ll want to roll right after swinging to cancel the animation. That’s why I’m calling it “battle” rather than “shooting.”

- Narrative: The basic setup is just as described on the store page. But it’s not really narrative-driven; story moments only pop up occasionally. Most of the time it plays like a co-op shooter (or action game?).

- Restaurant & Cooking: The restaurant and cooking elements aren’t super tightly woven into the combat. Honestly, the pace of the battles is way too fast for any kind of full-on cooking sim anyway. And you don’t actually perform cooking actions directly.

- Playtime: Probably around 15–20 hours to finish. Going for 100% will take longer, but for most players, 15–20 hours sounds about right.

- Visuals: Pretty much what you see is what you get. The graphics aren’t particularly distinctive despite the concept; they’re pretty average. Also, the framerate isn’t great.

- Sound: The BGM and voice acting are excellent, but the sound effects especially hit sounds are pretty underwhelming.

- Optimization: Honestly, it struggles on a 1060.

- Communication & Dev Support: Very responsive. It’s a small team, but they reply quickly and are super friendly feels like chatting with friends.

- Overall: lol this game is wild (in a good way). I hesitated because of some of the reviews, but I had a blast. That said, it might be a bit rough for players with pickier tastes. Still, where else are you gonna find a game like this? No one else would pull off something this crazy but this team.

review:
Gameplay is fun and engaging, enemies keep you on your toes while not providing too difficult a challenge too early on. It's easy to learn from mistakes and grasp the game's mechanics, even if those mechanics are explained somewhat loosely.
Visuals and textures are trippy and unorthodox, befitting the game's "dreamlike" aesthetic, but certain levels might be a little hard on the eyes. Due to its simple graphics, the game runs well on lower end computers.
Sound design is very good, the music especially so.
Unique mechanics include the magic casting system and rings which both require you too make important decisions as you progress through The Dungeons of Blood and Dream, while the notebook allows you to document important discoveries and interactions.
The lore is deep and you often get the sense that the world of blood, within which you dream, is immense and rich with culture and mystery, but one can still play without needing to understand it.

In summery, I highly recommend this work of art to those who enjoy the visuals of games such as Cruelty Squad, and gameplay mechanics similar to FlyKnight or Kings Field, mixed with traditional roguelike elements from The Binding of Isaac.

review:
After some tweaking and playing later levels, it got better.

I was able to use Loseless Scaling to enhance the Sharpness and remove most of the blurry factor.  That was a HUGE benefit.  Also, the first aarea was very detailed.  So, hopefully the game continues more like the second area which isn't cluttered as much.

I will update my review to a passing score.  It still needs graphics and audio adjustments in the settings, and those background extras that appear in the search list but are really just part of the background image need to be dealt with.

----- Original Review -----

This game is a hard pass.

I find the lack of settings Disturbing.  Language choices, Window/Fullscreen, Cursor Custom/Normal, Sound On/Off and Music On/Off.  That's it.  No resolution options, no Music or Sound volume sliders, just those. 

Several of the cardinal sins of hidden objects games are present.  It asked me to find a bellflower, and a hint showed me a bell.  It asked me to find a mushroom when the game had at least five mushrooms in the scene and only one was correct.  Some objects are blurred and appear to be part of the background ... some of these are in the list.  These are all throughout the game.

The objects in the game are blurry and often intentionally hard blended in the scene.  You need to find those.  Using a magnifying glass that makes blurry objects slightly larger and blurrier.  Some parts of the scene are dark enough to not see some things.  No video options to change this.

One of the mini games is for a color by number type coloring sequence.  You select part of the image, and it identifies all areas of the same color in the image with little dots.  Some areas are small enough that you can't see the dots there and would miss coloring them.  

Do not buy this at full price.  If you really, really like this theme for the game and like these kinds of games, then wait for a really, really big discount.  I am going to try and play the game in a window and use Lossless Scaling (adds scaling and other options to games that don't have these.  It's mostly for older games, but it can be used with any game).  These things should be in there, but I really do like the theme.  The music, while too loud for my liking, isn't bad.

review:
This is the first game of the Laruaville series to incorporate the puzzle-M3 fusion concept in order to collect all the coins, instead of playing like a "traditional" M3.  Many of the features of the later games were originally introduced in Laruaville 3, including the help book explaining the assorted gadgets which is a feature in all the other games this developer makes except the very first 2 Laruaville games.

The puzzles are a little rough around the edges, which makes this game surprisingly challenging because things like having a few more torches placed in the playfields weren't introduced yet, and the bombs from the first 2 games are still present, albeit with a different look.  There are also a lot more ladybugs.  Even though you aren't tasked to remove them like most of the newer games, having that many insects gets annoying at times.

There are 90 levels to play, and a ton of minigames, mostly mahjong, which in this game has the "parking spot" and undo buttons along with better looking playing tiles.  IMO there were too many mahjong games, but it does get your town built a little faster.  The only other minigame type in Laruaville 3 are spot the difference games, which do have a nifty feature of 2 hidden bonus coins in every scene.

The town scene to build this time is the size of the one in Laruaville 2, so you have to scroll the screen quite a bit to see it all and it'll get crowded with all the things to build.  The bonus sparkles are back from Laruaville 2.  The story of the ghosts finding a new place to live and having to restore the seasons is charming and much less hokey than the previous game.  I also liked that once the town is finished, the seasons will change periodically if you keep playing.

No Steam Achievements, but I'm pretty sure this is the last Laruaville to feature in-game achievements, one of which is bugged in the Steam version. :(  But if you enjoyed the newer games of this series, still recommended for discovering the ancestry of the "modern" Laruaville games.

review:
I've played video games for the past 40 years. This game is a throwback game with above average difficulty featuring a variety of themes on each level along with the entertaining original music. The variety offered by this game is refreshing change to most games these days. 

The game appears to be basic from the marketing but it's anything but another attempt by game developers to bait you into another "basic" and "mindless" trap to make the happy buck. This is a genuine classic development of a game that is entertaining and difficult for any level of player. 

There are a limited number of shots you can take on each level forcing the player to be frugal. Pay attention to your health as it is also a scarce resource. I liked both features of the game as so many games these days allow for unlimited ammunition and health. 

This is a game I purchased with the intent of passive interest as I'm a turn based strategy gamer. I find myself playing more often than I thought I would. It's enjoyable, relaxing, and challenging. I recommend the game.

Changing my tether to my mouse helped me get farther, but I think that is because of my FPS-goober brain.

The music was good enough for the duration I played, but I hope more tracks come with future updates! The audio options are more robust than I thought they would be by having multiple sliders for master, music, hostiles, game.

Graphics are good and the aesthetics are cool. I dig the different environments and having the objectives fit/change with the setting is a nice touch. The menu feels like a 'ye olde' flash game and I hope to see it evolve. That being said, I don't exactly know if that is the style, but the text is affected by this, so it could be difficult for some to read certain prompts or story beats.

Overall, the game will improve in time and more will be added, but it gave me a good first impression. I'll have to get this installed on my Steam Deck and see how well it works on the go!

review:
DERE Vengeance is without a doubt one of the biggest contenders for the most disappointing game I've ever played. When I saw the art, and the horror tags? I was hooked. I mean, this is my absolute FAVOURITE style of game. So, to say I'm disappointed, is an understatement, to be honest. I think this game failed at basically every aspect, so I'll break down the major flaws.

1. Platforming
The platforming in this game, is dreadful. The ENTIRE game is platforming, there is nothing else, which admittedly, is a bit disappointing, is what some people want, so fine. I can overlook it. But, the platforming itself is bad. The physics are terrible, controlling moving objects is borderline impossible, trying to control your character on moving slopes is the most inconsistent aspect of all time, hitboxes are slightly bigger than they appear to be, and it's not always clear on where to go. I'm sure there are other issues I may have missed, but this sums up the overall problems with the platforming.

2. The horror/Psychological horror
Now, when I got this game, I was expecting PSYCHOLOGICAL horror. What I got, was none of that. None of the "horror" in this game was psychological. In fact, to call it horror in the first place, is an absolute insult to the genre itself. There is nothing scary in this game, there's a few very cheap jumpscares, but that's it. Horror is not an aspect in this game that is well utilised, it does not properly utilise any of the player's senses to make them feel on edge or uneasy, instead, the gameplay is very frustrating, which just makes you feel annoyed or irritated, rather than, say, uneasy. This makes the game fail at not only the platforming aspects of the game, but also the horror aspects. 

3. Miscellaneous problems
Some issues that I couldn't quite fit in the first two categories include:
- Bad storyline (Inconsistencies, predictable, lack of effective foreshadowing)
- Bland characters (Very self explanatory. None of the characters have any depth to them, besides, ironically, the Ai)
- Bad savepoint placement (Often will be lacking savepoints after very difficult jumps, but will have many in easy jumps)
- Very repetitive gameplay. You essentially have to replay the same game twice with some minor changes, and then replay it partially for a third time, before finally getting into some fresh content. 

Overall:
This game, is definitely a huge let down. To say I don't recommend it, is frankly an understatement. I honestly hated my experience with this game as a whole. I liked it starting out, but after awhile, it became very low quality, and I was just about done, and only finished the game, because I was so close to the end at that point. 

Final Score: 2/10

review:
A fun, if short, metroidvania with unique controls and interesting items.

Full Disclosure: I was one of the play testers for this game, so while I do have some bias towards this game. I will attempt my best to remain objective in this review. I was not paid for this review and these are my own thoughts.

So, quick summary: Honey's Sweet Revenge is a short Metroidvania game staring the main character Honey on a journey to rescue her girlfriend from her evil creator in a world based on candy, vegetables, and mushrooms. The controls of the game play a bit similar to some popular plat-former fighters with charge attacks and aerials. As well as dodge rolls and aerial dodging.

However, what I think sets Honey's Sweet Revenge apart from other games is the items you collect in this game. These items provide attack methods and movement options for the cost of "sugar" that collect from hitting and killing enemies. These items can then be bound to a certain input in the "select" menu to provide freedom of choice to the player in what they want to play. Some items like the soda and the peanut buttercup were probably my favorites since they provided a lot of vertical and horizontal movement options to me. I usually put the soda on down+b and the peanut butter cup on up+b for my layout. There's also a few collectibles that can be found around the world, that when traded, can provide upgrades to your attack strength and health points. 

Collision in the game, can be a bit odd at times. And the movement can take some getting used to if you aren't familiar with platform fighters. But there's quite a few open areas to experiment with movement and a tutorial right at the beginning to help with the basics. The game never crashed on me, and I get a consistent 120 fps at 4k res.

This game is quite a short one and it took me around 2-3 hours to beat on the steam version. For full completion it took me around 5~ hours to collect every collectible.

Overall, I think Honey's Sweet Revenge is a fun, if short, metroidvania with a unique art style, interesting items, and unique controls.

the core gameplay loop is the same as unpacking, yes, but this game has way more optional and side content. there are lots, and i mean LOTS of easter eggs, item interactions, and little puzzles tucked away. you could speed through the quests in just a few hours, but slowing down and taking your time is so much more rewarding. i've seen a few reviews say they finished the game within 3 hours... but i'm almost positive those people missed some content.

review:
Have you ever wanted to move to a mysterious town to become a housekeeper, interior designer, and paranormal investigator all at once? Well boy do I have the game for you! Whisper of the House drops you into a cute and vibrant little town, where the townspeople will pay you to clean, organize, and design homes and businesses. But you start to encounter some... weird objects, not to mention the anonymous and vaguely threatening letters you start receiving in the mail. 

Oh, and you can pet cats!

The gameplay primarily consists of completing jobs for the townspeople (which progresses the story), fixing "anomalies," decorating your own homes (you start with one, and acquire 2 more throughout the game), and taking "model home" requests. There are also a few minigames -- making potions, mixing drinks, and growing unique plants (which you can then use to decorate with). Finally, you can wander around the town, which is just so cute and cozy!! It's rewarding to explore, because there are anomalies and secrets hidden around town, and sometimes you'll also run into characters you've helped previously. You can also raid crates and trash cans to find items, and you can find tokens scattered around.

The decorating mechanics are super simple and satisfying! Everything you pick up/set down makes a little sound that relates to what it is, which I love. The organization and decorating are VERY reminiscent of unpacking (another game I love, and probably a majority of Whisper players also love, LOL) but Whisper is more focused on the aesthetic/creativity aspect than the organization aspect (for example, there are a lot less drawers/cabinets to organize things in; there are a few, but mostly items are placed where they're visible). You can layer certain objects and even cause some objects to interact with each other (such as the ice cream cones and ice cream maker) to create new ones. 

Different jobs require different things from you as the housekeeper -- some are more focused on cleaning, some require you to place items in specific spots, and some simply ask you to decorate as you see fit. One of the cool things about this game is the variety of places you get to work on -- not only homes and apartments, but also different businesses, and even a cemetery. 

There is a huge variety of items, some of which make up themed sets. Furniture, appliances, decor, print items, plants, rugs, and food/drink can all be bought at different stores and vending machines around town, which are marked on the map. They're acquired through a blind box/gacha mechanic, but it's really easy to get tokens, so it's not stressful or difficult to unlock all the items. You'll be paid tokens after each job, when you're "promoted" by the company, and after completing model home requests. 

At the mall, you can buy duplicates of any furniture you have unlocked. For food and drink, you can buy duplicates at the convenience stores, and for plants, at the Flower Shop. I spent SO MUCH time just decorating and making spaces look cute and cozy, I'm sure I could have finished the game faster but I was having so much fun. There are no time penalties or deadlines, so I suggest taking it at whatever pace you want! 

Throughout the game, you get to know some really fun characters and help them with more than just organizing their homes. The little character stories are actually really heartwarming and adorable! Make sure to return to the homes and businesses you worked on, because some of the characters have secondary requests. I thought I was stuck for a while because no more requests were triggering, but I still had a missing character and anomalies... turns out I didn't know how to trigger one of the character's secondary requests. 

Overall, the game is pretty straightforward, and you can get most of the achievements and find most of the anomalies as long as you thoroughly explore and investigate everything. I got around 80/89 achievements by myself, and used a guide for the rest. There are a few things that are a little convoluted, the worst one (in my opinion) being the issue I mentioned before about triggering a characters request. Quick spoilers ahead in the following paragraph:

/BEGIN SPOILERS/

I got stuck after having completed all but one of the jobs in town, because I didn't know how to trigger Luna's secondary request. I had found the secret room and even interacted with the mousetrap, but when I returned to talk to her in response to her letter, I didn't get the hint about what I was supposed to do. She says something like "I hear sobbing at night, and noises in the bathroom." Ok, so I thought, I need to go check the secret room again as well as the bathroom. I click around, nothing happens. What you're meant to do is take the mousetrap from the secret room, put it in the bathroom, then wait a day and you'll receive a Daily Whisper about a homeless person being found in her apartment, as well as a letter from her asking you to come help her again (her secondary request). Honestly I don't get how you're expected to figure that out, the mousetrap is just one of many random cluttered items in the secret room and she makes no mention of rats or animals of any kind, just "noises" and "sobbing." I think if she had said something like "I wonder if there are animals?" after mentioning the noises, it might have clicked? I dunno if this is just me but that was frustrating because you're meant to finish that quest line early in the game, but I didn't get to it until near the end when I finally looked at a guide.

/END SPOILERS/ 

Besides my issue with Luna's requests, I only have small complaints about the game. Honestly, it instantly became one of my favorites -- it's just basically everything I love in one game. But here are my small criticisms, and some requests:

-All items should be able to be rotated all 4 ways. Certain items in the game can only be rotated 2 ways. Also, sometimes items that normally CAN be rotated 4 ways become locked into 2-way rotation when they're stacked (ex. a TV on top of a TV stand: both items by themselves can normally rotate 4 ways, but when stacked, they can't. If you un-stack them, rotate them to the position you want, then stack them again, it works). 
-Please add a search function for the storage! The filters are sometimes helpful, but sometimes not so much. Especially once you have all the items, finding a specific one can be very tedious. I think the best solution would be the option to search items by name. Being able to narrow down into smaller categories would also be good (ex. "bedframes," "computers")
-This one is probably a long shot, and it's not so much a criticism as just a request for future development. I would looveeee character customization! Doesn't have to be crazy or anything, but a few hair styles/colors and different outfits would be amazing. It made me sad looking at the cute clothes and wigs used as decor items in the game and wishing my character could wear them T_T
-Also perchance a long shot but... pets? Cats are a pretty big part of the game, and there's already the coding allowing us to pet the ones in town, plus lots of pet-related decor items. I would love it if we could take in a cat (or dog) that could either just sit or walk around one of our houses (and could be pet of course). 
-And finally... please more content!!! Pretty please a sequel or DLC or something. I want more jobs and more Whisper Town lore!!! No pressure, I know it takes time and effort but I hope there will be more eventually! <3

review:
I enjoyed this game a great deal, and it's a bummer to not be able to recommend this game on the merits of what it does well - but it truly does feel like a half-finished experience.

The parts that work are wonderful and memorable - two levels early in the story have incredible hidden secrets that truly make you feel smart for figuring them out. But the back half of the game becomes repetitive and relatively uninteresting.

The game promises a great deal about a hidden story to unravel, but its most interesting ideas go totally unexplored and unexplained. There are big missing chunks of story here that can't help but feel like the dev just ran out of time, and disappointingly, it takes what could have been, I think, a truly incredible game to a pretty unmemorable one. The decorating is fun, but the economy has zero challenge whatsoever. You get thousands of 'vouchers' for completing easy in-game tasks, and after that can just spam the merchants, which only award furniture at random, to get everything you need. You can buy individual pieces - but only if you've unlocked them already, completely removing any incentive for doing so.

The decorating challenges, which I suspect were added to pad playtime, are pointless. Unlike some decorating games that 'tag' furniture with associated characteristics, adding an actual mechanic to decorating, the challenges in this game simply give you four or five pieces of furniture to put in a giant room, and then arbitrarily let you put down an amount of furniture (it never tells you how much). You could literally plonk down random items for ten seconds and would be rewarded with completing the challenge with full marks, which completely took the fun out of it for me.

The world-building is charming and the little interactions are super cool. The first two hours of this game showcase what it could have been, and I'm disappointed that it couldn't keep up that level of quality. Buy it on sale and enjoy it for what it is, but I can't recommend it for the listed price.

I have been following the developer and this game for two years. Hearing and watching it come together has been one of the most inspirational experiences I've been lucky enough to be a part of.

I've played through the demo and was fortunate enough to make it to the game's beta release. The developer was incredibly welcoming and was open to hearing any feedback he could get. Panoptia is the truest form of an independent passion project, and the game itself is filled with small details and incredible visual pieces that can leave a player either completely enamored at a scene or horrified upon questioning it.

During the beta I reached one of the endings in about seven hours and it left a lot for me to think about in terms of my playthrough and what I saw. There is more to explore in the game then I had time to look around however, so I expect some more pieces for people to discover as they roam through each area tucked deeply away. The game sells you on a experience filled with twisted and beautiful imagery, somber and exciting music, and several charming characters that were wonderfully memorable.

To take it one step further, this game invites you to what can only be described as a human mind. But take it from the developer who said it himself:

"This game means a lot to me, it has a much more serious tone compared to everything else I've made, as I tried to explore my emotions in the story. It is reflective of some of the worst times of my life."

I urge you to take a look at this game, and if nothing else, try the demo yourself. This indie project has been a joy to experience and I am so excited to be able to take another jump in. Thank you.

As a twin stick enthusiast, I didn't understand how I could've missed a twin stick game from 2024. Listen when I say RUN away from this game.

Baffling design decisions abound, that when stacked on top of each other, make for a horrible gaming experience. Mages with predictive fireball aim. Killed enemies drop arrow blocking tombstones. The second enemy you encounter CAN STEAL YOUR ONLY WEAPON, rendering you useless. The only equipment you'll get is an arrow; you'll get the fire arrow in the first 20 minutes, and then a poison arrow and you'll never get another upgrade for hours. All enemies respawn on a short timer and since there's no map, you'll constantly be running around killing the same creatures. The boss drops nothing but a respec potion, but there isn't much to respec to because the three trees are very basic and provide single digit bonuses to attack, movement, and crit. You upgrades are very incremental and won't be noticed until about 12 levels in. And if all that's not enough, playing for more than 2 hours and you'll get fps under 20 (despite my 3080 Ti and 32 core chip with 32 GB ram).

So the gameplay loop boils down to kiting around a large group of skellies, dodging away from flies that will steal your bow, while zigzagging to avoid mage fireballs. Every now and then a fly will steal your bow making you chase after it while everything else chases after you. And after you've dealt with his cluster **** your reward is almost always a visibility potion (which uncovers an already cleared fog of war, i.e. useless) or an arrow you'll just throw away. 

It's rare I encounter a game that's such a huge FU to the player. Even at $2, this game is a waste of your time. There are literally dozens of better games at this price point.

review:
This game was pretty good. It had a good story to follow throughout the game and the ending I didn't see coming.
The visuals looked great except for the very beginning in the woods. The game is so dark there and to see well I had to turn the gamma way up which just made it super bright on top of dark colors. After I got inside the house it looked great though! The sounds where good as well as the overall atmosphere was great. I do recommend playing this game if your a fan of horror or indie games. It took me an hour to beat without ever seeing it before. If I played again or had watched someone play first it would be more like a 40 minute play through.
There are a few things that stood out to me that I didn't like but they where small to medium and didn't effect the overall game play too much. The first was the jump scares where good, at first. At a certain point it felt like there was a jump scare every 2 minutes like clock work every time I entered a room or went down a hallway. After awhile I wasn't even phased by it because I was fully expecting them. I think if they took 2/3's pf them out the ones left would have a great effect.
I like exploration games and games where I can find a lot of items and this game had a plethora of drawers, closets, cupboards and such to open with 99% empty or having objects you couldn't interact with. That felt disappointing and got to the point it was annoying. Again something there should have been 2/3's less of.
Lastly a bulk of the story's background info was in form of written notes left around the house. I love a good story in a game but I don't like to read as much as I like to listen to it. This is kind of to each there own and maybe the devs felt the opposite way about it which is ok.
Overall I give this game a 4/5 stars and the devs seem to have the potential to make some longer AA games in the future.
This game is worth $10 and if you see it on sale you will be missing out not to buy it on the spot.

review:
Alright. [i]A Game About Flicking A Switch[/i] is done and dusted. This is another in the fine tradition of troll games on Steam, where breaking the Fourth Wall and engaging directly with the player is the focal point; the very thing that makes this game both hilarious and awesome.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3535440156

Everything is triggered by....you guessed it...flicking switches. As you progress, the game will continue to mess with you and attempt to get you to quit playing the game, lol. However, the level design and the sequence of events is actually very well thought out and a joy to behold, and so the game is destined to fail in its attempt to provoke you into rage quitting. The variety of different levels and challenges was quite impressive. Most noteworthy was the dark level, which, if you don't uncover the secret to, will actually put you in a position where the only solution is to quit and come back to try again. Except, in order to restart the game from the beginning, you actually need to delete your save file (or select a specific switch at one point in the game). Otherwise, you always re-enter the game where you left off. And so, I would like to share a bit of vague advice regarding the dark level. Don't just go traipsing about. Be thorough when entering that level and try to find the one secret that makes the level doable.

There are a fair few achievements in the game. Most are triggered by static events, but some are also triggered randomly. Some will require multiple playthroughs in order to select divergent options available at a couple moments in the game. In keeping with the spirit of the game, the achievements also are messages designed to be read at that moment in the game and tie directly into the story such as it is.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3535440078

Although gameplay is centered around flicking switches, there are actually a few very interesting puzzles to be solved in order to progress. Where you find notes, take those notes literally, would be my advice. The puzzle design was pretty clever in my estimation. And there are a decent number of unique areas to explore as well. Which also tie into the story. I really enjoyed a sequence towards the end where you can actually take a look at these levels again, but from the perspective of a guest rather than the protagonist. That was a cool addition to the game.

The audio is also tied to certain achievements, and you will want to actually be listening while playing this game. There is a particular piano piece that is tied to two achievements and is simply an excellent listen. Or not. Depending on your musical preferences, lol. Visually, one of the areas in particular is quite the feat for the eyes, but everything in general looks really cool. Even the most generic closet with a switch is actually visually effective.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3535439989

I bought this for like 59 cents during a recent sale, but actually, you will get your $1.99 out of it if you decide not to wait for a sale. I had a good time with this game. There were a fair few laughs, some solid puzzles, and it was a very cohesive experience in general. Worth a look for sure.

review:
Alright. It's a nice game so far.

If you are looking for a metroidvania, that's not it. It's mostly turn-based combat with some exploration.

Monster have a little too much hp in "hard" difficulty (considering that everything I fought so far only use a 2 turn-skill-rotation, I quickly end up doing the exact same thing each turn since once you saw it you know what to do). The difficulty feel alright.

Outside of combat you will explore, but it's nothing fancy. Jump around a bit, push a lever, rotate a thing, find a key. In case of, you can teleport at every tree you unlock, so you are at worst two minutes away (with loading) from any spot you want to go back if you think you missed something.

there is a few hidden spot here and here but they seems quite obvious.

The art is good/ok, looks nice and nothing seems out of place. Could score more point from me if there was more contrast (everything is about the same color depending on the area - for example in the corruption monster, ground, background, platform - everything is red).

There is a bunch of items/skill/etc you find here and here, I end up swapping stuff around quite often early on (I'm not done yet, Iv done about 5h now). It's quite nice, there is some variety.

You level up but you can respec if you messed up. Some stats are better than other : unlike some other games, you can take your time killing boss and monster (well, you need to do enough dmg to go trough shield/regen/respawn), since buff and debuff stack are very limited (no infinite scalling).

Haven't encounter any crash, bug, exploit so far. It's quite rare for me to play an indie game that doesn't have any. Well, I only played 5h so ... I'll see.

Seems to use machine translation (even if the dev say otherwise), it's between terrible and passable. I have no effing clue what's going on sometime (especially with short item description or names) but I personally don't care too much, so whatever. If you ever read some manga/manwa/etc you will feel right at home.

Overall it's a good game. Especially for the price. Give the demo a try, but just so you know save aren't compatible.

[h2]Scream or Die Review[/h2]

[h1]Five Nights At Fredeez Nuts[/h1]
Let’s take a moment to talk about Scream or Die, a horror game that seems to have taken a misstep in its journey to scare and entertain. Designed to be a heart-pounding experience in a maze filled with animatronics, it turns out to be more of a frustration fest. Let's dive into the nitty-gritty of why this game might not be the scream you're looking for.

[h1]About This Game [/h1]

[h2]Storyline [/h2]

The concept is pretty straightforward – you're stuck in a maze, and you need to escape the creepy clutches of animatronics. Sounds like a thrill, right? But here's the twist: you have to scream (by pressing the 'F' key) to scare these mechanical nightmares away. The idea has potential, but the execution? Not so much. 

[h2]Gameplay Mechanics[/h2]

The gameplay hinges on balancing between screaming and running. Your screams have a cooldown, which means you need to strategize when to let out a yelp and when to leg it. This could have been an interesting mechanic, but it's overshadowed by the game's shortcomings.

[h2]Visuals and Audios[/h2]

It does deliver on eerie vibes. The maze is dark, and the animatronics are the stuff of nightmares. However, the game's audio is where it falls flat. You'll hear the same looping dialogue, "Please don't scare me," so many times it'll haunt your dreams. Not in a good way. It gets really annoying very fast.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Kinda intriguing concept with a somewhat strategic gameplay.
[*] Eerie atmosphere and visuals.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Repetitive and annoying audio.
[*] Buggy achievement system where you unlock everything upon launching the game. (Hopefully they patched it by the time I post this review)
[*] Lackluster execution that doesn't live up to its potential.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

While Scream or Die promises an adrenaline-fueled escape from animatronics in a maze, it unfortunately ends up being more of a repetitive and slightly irritating experience. The constant looping of "Please don't scare me" will test your patience more than your nerves. Plus, the achievement system glitch that gives you all the accolades right at the start strips away any sense of accomplishment. This game has potential, but it's a long way from delivering the scares and fun it aims for. As of now, I'd say approach this one with caution, unless you're in for a scream of frustration rather than fear.

Rating: 1/10

Really cool concept!
I wanna say first things first, the way the monster moves is super creepy and the way the game is explained sorta felt like a scary movie when it cuts off and leaves cliff hangers.

That can be a good and a bad thing though.

It really left me terrified but it also left me without direction, for example, I was told to "contain the enemy" but never told how, or they never brought attention to mechanics that would contain it.

The area was very large, which is cool for scale purposes, but when you only have 2 enemies and youre only looking for one item (the keycard to the next floor) 10's of rooms is kinda excessive. 

I've never made a game before but maybe reduce it (significantly) to a couple rooms per floor, explain important information fully and only let cliff hangers exist when either A. we are given enough explanation to complete the tasks and a clear path forward or B. you're just cutting off plot and not actual necessary mechanics.

As far as the computer goes, i like typing but im never gonna remember what to type or want to spend that much time in a horror scenario realistically typing things out, maybe just using the up and down arrow to select a prompt or making them as simple as possible like "A for audio check and V for video check" 

also it seemed a little obnoxious (but not too bad) to switch between all the different things at the desk (Again, it's not bad just could use some polishing, actually worked kinda well imo)

And clearly splitting between desk time and free roam time, maybe you maintain the monsters through some mechanic at the pc and after a little while there's some kind of objective change and the computers become unusable to help guide the player, sorta like different segments of the game, my main thinking is that if i cant do anything from the pc, and theres always monsters lurking, then im never gonna use them if that makes sense.

Another thought I just has is maybe you could even separate the floors, like you manage the monster contained on floor one so youre not overwhelmed, and get to learn his mechanics while you complete objectives in order to find the keycard and contain him to floor 1, then you move on to floor 2 with a new monster, again, clearly dividing the different sections in some way, maybe using the computer in the inbetween sections and then swapping back to free roam.

Overall really good concept, takeaways:
- FAR less map space to help guide player
- More descriptive descriptions on everything including mechanics (No cliff hangers there)
   - Maybe an objective telling us how to do these things "trap monster using cage on 2nd floor"
- Monster was good, I liked the design, movement, and tension from it
- Idk if I would buy this for money, atm it needs a lot more polish, Don't plan on refunding just to help support the creator because there's so much potential here but keep these notes in mind^
- Potentially more clearly splitting between different functional segments of the game, reducing the overwhelming and completely lost feeling, I understand being thrown into a job with no training but this just felt like I had no reason to complete the objective, or even a clear picture of what the objective was other than dont die. No "Survive until 6" "Find the key to escape" "Fight this main enemy" 
- I really do like the concept of the game, there's a ton of potential here

My yt is https://www.youtube.com/@SnowyBlizzard and I'll put a video up of me playing the game for the first time soon if you want that as a reference too :) Thank you for making a super cool game!

Despite its simplicity, each level presents a satisfying challenge that encourages thoughtful planning and strategic thinking. Combined with the soothing background music, playing "Ignis" feels like a peaceful escape from the hustle and bustle of everyday life.
While "Ignis" may not have the depth or complexity of other strategy games, its accessibility and relaxing nature make it a perfect choice for casual gamers looking to unwind. Whether you're a seasoned strategist or a newcomer to the genre like myself, "Ignis" offers a delightful journey that's sure to leave you feeling refreshed and satisfied.

review:
[b]Grub Truck[/b] isn't a great game, but it is arguably the best food truck-themed management sim available on Steam as of November 2024.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
You start by selecting one of several premade characters (each with their own goals, backstories, and unlockable perks), taking out a loan, kitting out your first food truck with secondhand appliances, and buying supplies.  From there, you [strike]take over the city[/strike] launch your food truck empire!

During the day, you serve customers by moving food from the fridge to your limited-slot tray, then placing the food in the correct appliance, waiting until it cooks, and moving to the window to fill orders. Successful orders increase your reputation, which then unlocks new menu items and neighborhoods.  After hours, you can expand your fleet of food trucks, set them up, hire managers, purchase supplies, etc.

[h3]Review[/h3]
[b]Grub Truck[/b]'s gameplay loop is repetitive but all chill vibes, and the decorating mechanics are surprisingly flexible.  I've spent more time than I care to admit lining up salt and pepper shakers [i]just so[/i], and have yet to turn down the music.

That said, the game is rough around the edges.  The UI looks like it was created in Microsoft Paint; the world, characters, and customers are all Synty Studios Polygons (which is fine, but I'm personally tired of seeing these same assets everywhere); and the mechanics are pretty bare-bones.  Cooking is more about inventory management than anything that feels like cooking in a food truck, and the camera moves strangely between appliances. Everything from hiring managers to ordering supplies is extremely simple, which likely appeals to more relaxed gamers but - as a stress junkie who has been playing management sims for 20-odd years - I feel that I've seen everything this game has to offer in ~2 hours total playtime.  

[h3]Recommendation[/h3]
I recommend this if you're looking for an easy business simulation game to kick back with for a few hours, or really want to run a food truck.  I don't recommend this if you were particularly interested in decorating or cooking, if you want a crunchy-ish business sim, or if you're looking for an artsty indie game.

review:
Anno 1602 might be the foundation of the Anno series, but actually playing it today is an exercise in frustration.

Terrible UI & Hidden Mechanics

Repairs are buried in tiny buttons and never explained.

Warships spin around uselessly, with clumsy firing arcs and awful pathfinding.

Worst of all: ships must be manually loaded with cannons before they can fight — something the game never tells you.
Bad Tutorial & Hints

The campaign “tutorial” teaches almost nothing. It doesn’t mention that ports can’t defend themselves, that towers are weak, or that warships need equipping. Instead, players get punished for mechanics hidden behind bad UI.

Pirates = Softlock

Pirates spawn early with ships stronger than yours, blockade trade routes, and even a single pirate can sink your defenses. This often leaves you unable to progress — not because of poor strategy, but because the game doesn’t give you tools to fight back.

Final Verdict

Anno 1602 is historically important but practically unplayable. The bad UI, lack of explanations, and softlocking pirates make it more of a prototype than a finished game. Later entries like Anno 1404 or Anno 1800 fix all of this and are far more enjoyable.

2/10 – important history, but not worth playing.

review:
Drill Core was a very pleasant surprise when I first tried it out about a year ago during a Steam Next Fest. Back then it didn't have the same amount of stuff as it does today, but even then I could see the potential for many hours of fun that this game had. I've been playing it on and off over the course of its time in Early Access, and now that it has hit 1.0, I feel it's the right time to write a review for it.

This game is a session-based management game where you manage a team of diggers while descending into the deep on a large mining platform, collecting resources to upgrade your platform with various upgrades that makes your personnel faster, stronger, more resilient, while also fitting out the platform with various guns, cannons, lasers, and mine deployers in order to protect you from the incoming hostile fauna that shows up during the night. The sheer amount of different buildings and gun platforms in this game is staggering to say the least, and all of them work in their own unique and interesting way. There's a lot of creativity on display, and due to the random nature of each session, you'll never end up with exactly the same setup on each run.

The game has many elements of Rogue-likes, but thanks to its lengthy sessions and ability to "check out" of a run fairly early, it doesn't *feel* like a Rogue-like, does that make sense? Like, in most other rogue-likes you get a random upgrade after a clearing a wave of enemies, and the amount of upgrades you get is usually only a handful, unless it's the type that can go on for a really long time. And in most other Rogue-likes you're almost always on the edge of failure if you make just a few mistakes. Drill Core is very different in this regard, as it is very generous with the amount of upgrades you can get throughout just one run, and there's so much meta-progression for you to unlock, that your mining platform starts out quite strong, even on the hardest difficulty. So if you crack the code on how to do well in the early game, the rest of the game can potentially become a cakewalk if you're smart with the upgrades you find.

An obvious parallel to draw to Drill Core is, of course, Dome Keeper, as both of these game have the same basic premise: You drill down and mine resources and upgrades by day, and defend against monsters coming from above by night. Rinse-repeat until you hit the goal and then you peace out. The difference between these two games is, however, that Dome Keeper has you control a single individual doing all the mining and defending yourself, while Drill Core lets control a whole team of dudes, or dwarves, or bugs, depending on which platform you decide to use, and Dome Keeper is also very minimalist with a muted color scheme, while Drill Core is far more colourful and vibrant, and has a far bigger array of enemy types, soil block types, upgrades, and more. Both games have a pixel graphics style that lend themselves well to both games, but I think I prefer the more interesting looks of Drill Core.

Comparison to other games aside, the gameplay in Drill Core is the "easy to learn, hard to master" kind, where early game can be a bit frustrating, but as you learn the ropes and unlock upgrades, the game becomes easier to grasp, and you get a very nice sense of progression. Every meta-upgrade feels significant and worth the investment, and it makes the later difficulties possible to beat, because they do get incredibly hard.

The three biomes you drill through are also varied and distinct. The normal rock type, the ice world type and jungle world type all have their own unique enemy types and block types which makes tackling each biome its own challenge. For instance, the ice world has ice blocks that freeze your personnel solid and if they fall too far down, they'll shatter and die, and the jungle world has "living" blocks that will randomly move around and crush any personnel in their path. The normal rock world has lava geysers that spews fire everywhere, lighting your dudes on fire and killing them if you're not careful, so you have to micro-manage them so they remove these blocks from the one angle where they don't spew fire. And these kinds of blocks can potentially make or break an entire run if you're particularly unlucky. I've had a few runs where a falling sand block completely wiped out all my drillers, and I had no resources to make new ones, so I had to bail and restart the run. Very annoying, but also kind of my own fault for not watching where they were drilling. 

This is the kind of hectic micro-managing gameplay you'll deal with during the day time. At night, it's an entirely different ballgame, as the locals will descend the mine shaft to destroy your core, and you have to make sure your defenses are good enough to withstand the onslaught. You also get the opportunity to use "active abilities" during both day time and night time, and these usually come in the shape of gun turrets, or turret boosters, or deployable drones, and they can save your butt if a new type of enemy just breezes through your defenses and makes mincemeat of your core. I've had several runs that barely made it through a night because a gun turret came in clutch and allowed me to wipe out a specific enemy type.

As you can see by the gameplay time, I've spent around 75 hours on this game, and I feel like I've gotten my money's worth and then some, because I'm not done unlocking everything yet, and I'm also not max level yet (I'm currently level 41 out of 50), but I've had a lot of fun during all those 75 hours (except the one time where I had a challenge to complete a run without losing a single worker, which was unbelievably frustrating because of the "instant death" nature of some of the blocks in the caves), and for that, I can whole-heartedly recommend this to anyone who wants a session-based management game with heavy rogue-like elements and a craving for digging deep and greedily.

However, when the miners go idle they may as well be asleep. The guards also frequently find terrible spots to stop and idle.

5. Too much of a grind. Im 20hrs in and have unlocked around a quarter of the upgrades.

review:
PegIdle takes the classic pachinko/pegboard style mechanic and blends it with idle progression, and honestly? It works way better than I expected. Watching the little balls bounce around, rack up points, and unlock upgrades scratches that same satisfying itch as watching numbers climb in other idle games — but with a fun, visual twist.

The appeal is in its simplicity. You drop balls, they bounce around, and you earn resources. Then you use those resources to unlock more pegs, boosts, and upgrades that make every drop feel more rewarding. It’s relaxing to watch, but there’s always a sense of “just one more upgrade” keeping you invested.

Progression feels fair — slow at first, sure, but once you get rolling, the upgrades layer on in a way that makes you want to keep optimizing your board. It’s got that “idle zen” energy while still giving you enough control to strategize how you want to build.

It won’t blow your mind like some of the more feature-heavy idle games, but it doesn’t have to. PegIdle knows exactly what it is — a satisfying mix of pachinko and incremental growth — and it delivers.

⭐ Final Score: 7.5/10.
Fun, relaxing, and addictive in short bursts. Perfect for when you just want to kick back and watch progress literally bounce around the screen.
