review:
Overture was a beautiful, but terribly short-lived experience that advances the base games combat with new upgrades to the P-Organ Tree and new weapons. And expands upon the tale of our protagonist and it's loveable cast of characters... BUT BOY DO I HAVE SOME FAT GRIEVANCES.

Before I get into spoilers I'll just say this. If you love the game and it's combat, yes, get this DLC; the weapons and challenges are truly interesting and I think your going to get a kick out of the new boss rush mode they added into the base game. However, I do mean it when I say it's very short, especially if you lower the difficulty. (Yes there's a Difficulty Setting now.)

Ok, so... I'll just bullet point it for ya'll.

*The DLC is short, painfully so and I felt like I didn't get enough time with any of the characters at all. This is even more true with a handful of characters that either have a very significant connection to Pinocchio, or have a major role in the lore, but are never seen or rarely spoken openly in the DLC.
* I couldn't form any meaningful connections with any of the bosses either, and unlike the base game where NG+ helps you get more context; I'm pretty sure Overture doesn't have anything similar.
* Baldur's Gate 3's Neil Newbon is a boss in the DLC and I am SEETHING at the fact that he's not available in the Boss Rematch mode! He's arguably THE best boss in the entire DLC!
* Yes there are new additions to the base game when you complete the DLC, but it's all just new conversations and a freaking portrait, that's it. Oh and you can give the hotel cat a collar, I guess.
* Only two-three bosses were genuinely good but the rest were pretty terrible. Especially the second and final boss where they start the second phase with a waterfowl style combo that will one shot you.  Also, while there are like 8 bosses, only TWO of them give you a boss soul to turn in for a boss weapon/trinket. And there is 4 special weapons in the whole DLC. -_- Only two weapons truly stood out to me. The Bow at the start of the DLC which has some really nice combos from Rapid Fire light and heavy to a supercharged heavy; and the Gunblade which you get from the anti-penultimate boss; which is just... amazing. I long for the days when Final Fantasy can make me feel this powerful with a Gunblade in an ARPG.

The final boss encounter was incredible in part because of their build-up throughout the game. I even cried at the end...!

I think this studio has got a great formula going. They've nailed a fun gameplay loop with an interesting combat system and challenging bosses. They've crafted a beautiful , atmospheric world with wonderfully poignant stories. Fantastic optimisation too - I've faced no issues on my steam deck. The only thing is that, while I enjoy the linearity, I'd like a bit more branching paths and exploration. 

So excited for the sequel!

Honestly the main game's a fun little time killer but this a) doesn't really add anything, and b) is a bug-ridden mess.

Concept is that you can take the containers to disposal yourself to make a bit of money instead of paying to dispose, but it isn't fully integrated as not all containers can be moved (shredder and glass banks, for example). The driving system is pointless, with a grand total of two blocks and one turn to the plant, the first block is the fuel station, only there because for some asinine reason there's a fuel system where you burn 1/4 tank on the run. Also you can teleport back after unloading, and there is literally zero reason not to as the bonus doesn't change versus driving home, you just burn twice the fuel doing it manually.

So even if it's kind of a weird development decision, it's rendered utterly useless due to bugs; namely after a single use the skip truck booms stop working, even with a restart. And the hooklift follows suit soon after with certain containers (drum roller being a major culprit). The other one is sometimes a container won't count as emptied, and you only find out after the driving 'experience' and have to abort.

Dev really needs to slow their roll with DLC and just actually fix gamebreaking bugs, or even better come up with a GDD and actually put some joined-up thinking into what they do.

review: I originally discovered Mark Leung from his Final Fantasy YouTube parody from over 10+ years ago. Sometimes I'll go and look up those parodies just because they were a fun part of my childhood and how I originally got into Final Fantasy. One day I was just curious and decided to do more research on Leung, because I was always familiar with his parody, but not with him as a creator. That led me down a rabbit hole of various things, including his passion for ice skating, his accident, and how much effort he's put into making this game possible. I have to give you so much credit, Leung, for being able to make a game like this and to make it as beautifully smooth, fun, and overall just as wonderful as it is. Despite the condition you are currently going through, you persevered and you've once again given us the gift of a world inside your head. Valentina's story is a lot of fun to go through. The game is very slice of life. You can tell that Leung put a lot of effort into the characters, the world, the dialogue, the OST, and more. Everything about this visual novel just has so much heart and love put into it. This game is also very educational as well, giving readers the opportunity to learn more about figure skating. review:
I am almost exclusively a Singleplayer / Co-op gamer. I cannot handle the stress of PvP. I get the shakes so bad that my teeth chatter for 45-75 minutes once I log in. I used to avidly play Natural Selection 2, Planetside 2, and Battlefield 3 but I just don't have enough time to recover from the exhaustion to make it worth it any more. 

That stress does not apply to Tribes, however. The gameplay of the Tribes series is the best gaming experience I have ever had. Singleplayer, Co-op, PvP, doesn't matter. My favorite time gaming ever, and I am a hardcore gamer. I am usually an unfortunately dour gamer, but Tribes makes me shout in joy and laugh for hours. Getting in endless, high-skill, back-and-forth honor duels with other players, punctuated by landing unlikely and extremely difficult shots, and supported by fast respawns is both low stress and extremely engaging. A winning formula.

I would still have been playing the previous entry to this franchise - Tribes: Ascend - to this very day, had the community not shrunk to such a degree that the only players you could find to fight against were cynically using only the overpowered weapons and equipment, including 80% of those 100 or so remaining players playing exclusively heavy classes. Getting killed by the same names using the same weapons and seeing them succeed day after day using the slowest classes in this supposedly fast paced and skillful formula was an absolute turn-off. Throw in the fact that many of these remaining people were complete jerks (typical PvP) sealed the deal for me.

Hearteningly, Tribes 3 has no noticeable balancing issues after my couple days of playing. There are lots of smart balancing decisions made, which I applaud! My wish to just be able to enjoy this game without being killed by another NJ-5B or Fractal Grenade has been granted. Gone are the days of playing a Light Class and being one-shot by a Heavy Class' Spinfusor, while I have to direct hit him 3 times in return to kill him! I'm 28 now, and I'm having even more fun with Tribes 3 than 16 year old me ever wanted.

However. Tribes: Ascend died for three reasons, not just balancing. The top two factors were ->insulting<- monetization, and unrealistic Free To Play grind. Balancing was third, and I would say it was a distant third. While in Tribes 3, all equipment is currently unlocked by default [A VERY PLAYER FRIENDLY DECISION], these skin packs for Tribes 3 are the spectre of the old, draconian, "squeeze blood from a stone" approach to Free To Play that Tribes: Ascend (And Planetside 2 at one point) drove off most of its player base with. These packs, being the only cosmetic options other than getting insane 50-victories-with-one-class ingame achievements, should not be so expensive.

My absolute priority with my current involvement with this game's community, is retention of players. I want enough people to play this game with for years to come. I have already gotten 2 friends into this game with me, I even bought one of them their copy. I might end up getting 2 of my coworkers into this game with me as well. This game needs to be more inviting to new players. I've put 350 hours into Helldivers in the last couple months, and that game has a universally acclaimed, new-player-friendly monetization system.

<==MY ULTIMATE FEEDBACK==> would be to split these DLC packs up as much as possible, without simply dropping the price on them any time soon. Dropping the price means you are alienating players who recently bought them at a higher price. Splitting these packs up so that you can access the Blood Eagle and Diamond Sword skins separately from the yearly skins (And then bundling them all for less than freakin $50), makes it more monetarily friendly for players who are new and curious about the game to invest $10 more, so they don't feel like they're wearing a punishing "Free To Play Gimp Suit" while playing their first few hours figuring the game out. Whoever made the decision to put all the players in Gray Gimp Suits until they've spent an extra $50 or gotten 1,000 kills, fundamentally sees monetization as a hostile relationship between the players and dev team, and that is clearly obvious. Microtransaction monetization should be the bundle/scaling system of a buffet, not the "In For A Penny, In For A Pound" scheme of a timeshare.

review:
Finding Sparky is what I believe to be a masterpiece in visual storytelling, with a dark tone that perfectly amplifies the themes of guilt, desperation, and what can happen when to someone when they lose everything they hold close to them.

The game is primarily a side-scrolling puzzle game, with a large emphasis on telling the story of a village boy named Tom whose beloved dog has been stolen from him, going to find him with help from the ghost of someone he once knew. Between each cutscene, whether it be dialogue between Tom and a villager, descriptions of Tom's memories, or even a couple of scenes mimicking a puppet show, there are puzzles involving ghosts, and later on, cats. To progress, Tom has to "mark," or petrify, Ghosts with a weapon he picks up during the prologue. He must petrify a specific number of ghosts and leave the rest in order to "slaughter" them all before progressing; when cats start appearing in the levels, he has to have a specific number of them nearby to do so. If a Ghost is being problematic, Tom can push them away with a wooden stick that he starts the game with. There are some extra mechanics at times, but this is how it is for the bulk of the game, and said extra gimmicks tie into the themes of the story.

Tom himself harbors a fear of the ghosts that surround him, or more specifically, being touched by them. The top of the screen shows a bar called the "Vision Gauge," which will drain quickly if Tom touches a ghost without either trying to mark it or without swinging the stick at them. Marked Ghosts are completely harmless, but unmarked ones will cause Tom's field of view to shrink along with the Vision Gauge, and if a Ghost is colliding with Tom while the bar is too low, he'll begin to rapidly hallucinate before you get a Game Over. Ghosts aren't the only thing that make the Vision Gauge lower, however, as Rolling, an ability you can use to quickly move past Ghosts, as well as using the stick use up a small piece of the gauge. Don't worry about using it too much, as it recovers over time and you can make it heal even faster by pressing a key to breathe deeply. The Vision Gauge being both a health bar and an active resource for the player makes it feel very impactful, reflecting Tom's mental state and one of the themes I pointed out (Which one? I'm not spoiling that!).

Certain ghosts are far more relevant to Tom's life than the ones you see in most levels, becoming giant animals that Tom needs to butcher. While the ghosts seen in every normal level can be petrified with one marking, Bosses require three marks and have set conditions that make them vulnerable to it. Each boss has unique mechanics, and they're all at least somewhat easy to beat once you figure out the right strategy. The only one I have an issue with is (and actually, the only real issue I have with the game in general) is the second boss, which has an attack that can cover the entire area. It has a short-ranged form that's avoidable, but the main issue is the long-ranged version. Even if you start the attack with a full Vision Gauge, you'll nearly be knocked out by the time it ends; if the boss then uses a certain "spawning" attack afterwards, there is a good chance that you'll miss your cue to use the stick and just die immediately. The second boss feels like it should be the fourth one, since I was able to clear the fourth boss in one go, and that one even has a way to instantly kill you. Story-wise, their placement makes sense, I just wish their difficulty reflected that.

I won't get too in-depth on how I feel about the storytelling, since it is the central focus of the game, but what I will say is that the characterization is sheer perfection. The way Tom talks reflects the tone of the game down to the wire, and the personalities of other characters such as his parents give way to how his personality during the game takes shape initially before evolving over time. I write stories myself, and Finding Sparky is an example of the quality that I strive to achieve. After you beat the game for the first time, you unlock Story Mode, which lets you go through the game without having to care about the puzzles between each cutscene, which is nice. It's not anything major, but I wish it wasn't labeled as "Tom's Diary" on the menu screen; that made me hope I could read more into Tom's personality and make more sense of the ending, but alas, it's just a mode that lets you refresh your memory on the chain of events.

While that is all I have to say on the game itself, I do have something I want to say about the game's obscurity. The fact that Finding Sparky is barely on the internet is depressing, and the possibility of it staying that way hurts even more. It's such a brilliant work of art, yet when I looked the game up, I didn't find any form of discussion outside of a few YouTube videos, with only two posts from two different people. Sure, I did find a couple of posts involving the game on Bluesky, but that was limited to a link to the Steam Store page and nothing more. Outside of those two sites, I only found unrelated stuff such as a Borderlands Steam Discussion post (wild leap in tone, huh?), pictures of actual dogs, subreddits about learning Korean, and... allegations towards a Megaman fan? It's weird that you can search up the game's title, and almost every search result is a complete 180 from what you want to see.

All that aside, Finding Sparky is a genuine masterpiece, with a tone and set of themes that are clear as day, yet unnerving to approach. The way the story was told as I played was beautiful, combined with a constant array of narrative twists that left me guessing what the game would show next. The gameplay itself was interesting, if frustrating on occasion, but it didn't bring down my experience and thoughts on what the game truly wanted to bring my attention to. However, most importantly, the story made me feel emotional. It made me curious, it made me feel depressed, and most importantly, it was the first game to make me actually cry out of genuine despair. Games have irritated me before, they have made me feel somber before. No other game has actually jerked the tears out of my eyes prior to Finding Sparky, and that is an amazing accomplishment to me.

Finding Sparky is simply brilliant, and I hope more attention gets brought to it soon.

In fact, you know what? I'll say it right now: Finding Sparky is now my favorite game of all time.

review:
This is a strange one.

On one hand, I can't say I didn't enjoy it at all, but on the other - I can't bring myself to recommend it, because the game doesn't deliver what it seems to be promising at all.

To start with the good stuff:
- It's beautifully drawn and very pleasant to loot at.
- It has lovely music - and for the length of the game surprisingly wide variety of it.

Next, here are the things I'm mostly meh about:
- The writing wasn't bad, but it didn't really work for me. The narrative starts off as wistful and melancholic, and then you meet all those whimsical characters who somehow turn out to be very plain as soon as you start talking to them. Like, you were whisked into a dream realm, wandered through the mystical grove to the moonlit meadow, and there you met him: your neighbor Fred, walking his dog (but in a slightly cryptic manner). Additionally I didn't feel like characters have any real distinction in their writing and dialogue - though it turns out that was a part of a much bigger issue I'll touch upon later.
- The story itself felt not very well paced. You start off spending the first third of the game going about your day making a lot of fairly inconsequential choices: read or play the game, follow the path or go into the woods. As it turns out those determine which character's route you land on, but, yeah, more on that later. Then you get a very brief exposition and option to pursue romance, and then suddenly you are supposed to make some bigger-than-life choices. The end. It's like as if the entirety of the first book of Lord of the Rings were about Frodo doing his hobbit things in Shire, the second one was about the meeting in Rivendell, and then the third was about literally everything else that happened after that. I think a story describing something this grand could be successfully told in an hour-long game, but not like that.
- The romance is, uh, weird. The main four characters start to touch you immediately (in the situation you seemingly cannot escape), then quite literally about an hour after you met they try to kiss you, and your options are either to push them away (no romance) or let them (yes romance). I mean, call me a buzzkill but I believe that in the year of our lord 2024 one shouldn't have to physically push away a mysterious fantasy man to stop unwanted advances.

And finally, the reason for this negative review:
- The four main LIs are - literally - the same character. Seriously. Apart from the names being different in each of their respective routes, there are maybe a couple of unique lines for each. I'm not trying to say that they are too similar, or generic, or follow the same archetype, or whatever. I'm pretty sure all four routes literally use the same lines with variable for the character's name from start to finish. So you basically have to only choose which one's sprite you like better, there is no reason to finish routes for other three. I often see people complain about lack of unique content in character routes, but, hey, this is a new low.
There is a 'secret' fifth route that has a different final climactic part, but even there you get a bunch of reused narration and dialogue lines.
- And as an extra little nitpick: despite text being exactly the same, you cannot skip it in a different route.

open space allows for room to run

overall i think this game has the potential to become something really neat, it just needs some extra pushes to really push it to its full abilities.

review:
I played this game on Android and really liked the non P2W aspect of the game which you can unlock everything by using the hacker coin. The game feels like one of those F2P games riddled with microtransactions except you can unlock everything for free. The game has lots of replayability with 6 characters to choose from, many weapons and items to unlock and can be a bit grindy which I really like.

I highly recommend everyone to try the Android version because the PC version still needs work.

While this is an early review and the developers can fix and update the game, here's what I noticed that I don't really like about the game compared to the Android version.

1. Character movement is too slow compared the Android version.
2. Manual aiming joystick dead zone is too big and the character doesn't aim where I want most of the time.
3. Character Animation becomes laggy with certain weapons and when you move the character.
4. Areas or Visions around the character is too dark compared to the Android version.
5. No keybinds for pausing the game.
6. No Controller Support
7. Missing skills compared to the Android version.
8. No keybinds to turn auto fire on or off using keyboard.
9. Can't skip some of the screen which can get annoying.

I'm glad I'm able to experience this game on a bigger screen but I find the Android version more enjoyable. I hope the developer addresses these issues.

review:
Last Box Standing May Go On is a delightfully challenging puzzle game.
The game is designed in such a way that the player learns its mechanics in an organic and intuitive way, which is highly appreciated.
While the game has a simple concept, a lot of the puzzles demand both cognitive and creative thinking.

For its price, Last Box is a bargain and offers more than enough entertainment and fun for many hours. However, a level editor would have vastly enriched an already great experience.

The graphics, backgrounds, and music add plenty of nuance to the game. All these aspects are reduced to the essentials so that the player can truly be immersed in the fresh challenges each new level provides. Thus, the reward for each completed stage feels all the more earned, and one can only wonder what difficulties still await later in the game. The short, solemn jingle one gets is the cherry on top.

Philosophically, the game presents a Darwinian approach: Bigger boxes eat smaller ones to either grow or to remove competition. Only the last box remaining is allowed to move on into the great unknown. Why these boxes live an arguably cruel life such as this is left for the players imagination to fill in the blanks.
However, in contrast to this, if two of the biggest purple boxes try to eat each other, they will turn into smaller boxes again. Thus, in certain stages it is not the biggest boxes but rather the smaller ones which are the last ones remaining standing - Stage 41 is a perfect example of this. Whether or not this might illuminate a criticism of an unrestricted Darwinian world view is left for the player to decide for themselves.

Overall ask yourself: Do you want to play this game and be the last box standing, or skip it and thus be eaten in the process. I highly recommend Last Box Standing May Go On and you should give it a try.

Pretty straightforward to understand, get into and play. I guess without this rogue-lite aspect, the experience would have been over much faster and have gotten more criticism for not being deep or varied enough.  I think the game would play better if the resource type camps were all unlocked at the start, and instead more defense towers were created and added as the unlocks.  Maybe that would run into its own problems though, people just beating the game on their third or fourth run and being done with it.

I do think the core concept and base of this game is fun, but the cheap price is very justified because you'd need a lot more variety and content for a longer, richer experience.  

The rarity of the rarest towers is pretty bad.  I found a couple of rare towers in some of my first runs, then never again.

A lot of the fogged events aren't equal.  I almost beat the game at 3.5 hours played, just happened to get a good RNG on which shrouded buildings appeared (+resources is inferior to +skillpoints for instance).   

Anyway, Stronghold Defenders is alright.  I had fun beating it but I wish it had waaaay more content because the core of this is fun and the potential is not fully realised.

review:
Was having a real TCG itch so I bought this on sale for $39.99. Decided to wait until I got all the achievements until I wrote a review. I'll write a quick review for each game in the collection along with it's biggest pro and con.

Duel Monsters:
Very reminiscent of the original few anime episodes where they make rules up as they go. 98% of the cards are normal monsters.
Pro: Pixel art is good
Con: basically just the card game 'War' where big number wins and you slam fatter monsters into each other. No tributes, just play Black Skull Dragon with its 3200 atk or Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth with 3500 atk and swing.

Duel Monsters II:
Like Madden in the sense where it's a slightly upgraded version of last year's game. Remember in Duel Kingdom where they added elemental weaknesses? This game now has those.
Pro: They took more effort to balance the game, which can't be said about the first game.
Con: Kuriboh will one shot your Blue Eyes White Dragon due to type chart

Monster Capsule:
The first YGO game in the collection that isn't just 'vanilla YuGiOh'. It's a really awful tactics game. And trust me tactics games are my favorite genre of games but this is one of the worst I've played in many years.
Pro: An attempt was made to call back to the manga where they play more than just card games.
Con: Extremely grindly, long, slow, permadeath to set you back hours, most guides don't go more than halfway through the game. Honestly this is probably the worst game in the collection.

Dark Duel Stories:
Earliest English released YGO game in the collection. Very similar to Duel Monsters II but with better graphics, some censorship, and a weird card combo mechanic that can be used to easily make powerful cards.
Pro: the card combo mechanic is specific to this where you have a suffix and prefix combined to make a unique card.
Con: elemental weaknesses and deck capacity mean you'll be fighting with 300-700 normal monsters for awhile until later in the game.

Duel Monsters 4: Battle of Great Duelists
This game has 3 versions (Yugi, Kaiba, Joey). The Kaiba achievement takes awhile to get but the others can be obtained quickly. Same game, probably really cool back in the day where each had exclusive cards and you could trade with your friends but nowadays they're a bit redundant.
Pro: I bet this game was amazing to play in 2001 with friends and link cables
Con: for achievement hunters, you gotta do 51 duels in each game to get the achievement or you can use cheats to get 2/3 of those achievments.

Dungeon Dice Monsters:
More of a tactics/board game but significantly better than Monster Capsule which came out only a year earlier. Probably the second best game in the collection.
Pro: actually a really fun game in it's own right. Not your standard YGO by any means but a very unique creature collection/tactics game.
Con: since it isn't a vanilla YGO, it lacks a tutorial so you gotta figure things out. Which isn't hard because the collection comes with instruction manuals but thought I'd throw trhat out there.

The Eternal Duelist Soul:
Aside from Falsebound Kingdom, this is my most played YGO game. The oldest vanilla YGO that doesn't use made up anime rules, strictly following the card game rules.
Pro: just duels, nothing else. Play games, win cards.
Con: the harder AI cheats by not attacking your face down cards if they know they can't destroy it.

Duel Monsters 6: Expert
This is the only game in the collection that is strictly in Japanese so I didn't play it much.
Pro: the achievement is easy to obtain with cheats
Con: It's Japanese so I can't read anything and have to rely on card art

The Sacred Cards:
The first YGO "RPG" but they brought back elemental type matchups, deck capacity, and duelist level to add more grinding. The easier of the two.
Pro: this is the most whack game in the collection to speedrun. If you like speedruns, I recommend looking up a vid for this one on YouTube.
Con: kinda obtuse sometimes on where you're supposed to go

Reshef of Destruction:
Oh my double gosh! By far the hardest game in the entire collection. By far the grindiest game in the collection. However, it isn't without merits. An effort was made to write a compelling story and it isn't revolutionary but it's got some neat characterization for otherwise one note characters. A fun game to play with cheats to skip all the grind. It's a direct sequel to Sacred Cards.
Pro: very fun if you use the built-in cheats to supercede the grind and never once did I need to look up what I was supposed to be doing as Ishizu tells you at anytime.
Con: the cursor rapidly goes through all 10 spots on both fields and both graveyards everytime anything happens to check for effects that might need to be triggered. This wasn't in Sacred Cards and wastes a lot of time.

Worldwide Edition: Stairway to the Destined Duel:
I don't know why Duel Monsters 6 is in the collection because this is just the English translation of that game. For the record, you can change the language of any game in the collection except that one so weird that they separated it into two games.
Pro: it's in English
Con: The first part of the game has you fight against random opponents and if you run into Kaiba you will get smoked

World Championship Tournament 2004:
Kinda like Eternal Duelist Soul but not as great. For starters a lot of characters cheat. It has the returned "don't attack face down monsters if I will lose life points" mechanic but also has 'luck' stats which actually allowed characters to use multiple limited cards. Someone like Yugi who has very high luck can run 3 Monster Reborns and 3 Raigeki for example while you're stuck with 1.
Pro: this was the vanilla YGO game in the collection to allow multiplayer, so that's nice.
Con: this is probably the worst singleplayer vanilla YGO game in the collection because of the AI and them running so many limited cards

Destiny Board Traveler:
It's a board game because every franchise needs a board game. And not a good one like Dungeon Dice Monsters
Pro: the achievement is fast
Con: not really my cup of tea but I can appreciate the effort

7 Trials to Glory: World Championship Tournament 2005
This is the cream of the crop in the collection if you were looking to play some vanilla YuGioH this here is your game. You don't get one random card after every duel and thus farm Mako for a specific card, you get money based off how well you did in the duel and use that money to go buy packs that you want to build the deck you want. Then it has the RPG mechanics of walking around the city, talking to people, and finding the many secrets hidden within. The ultimate goal of the game is to win the... 7 tournaments as the title suggest but it was a fun romp regardless.
Pro: best vanilla YuGiOh game in collection hands down
Con: I didn't want to use cheats for this one and the online guides have outright wrong information a lot of the time. For example I wanted to use an Exodia deck and the fandom said "win a tournament" when it really means wins the championship tournament late in the game.

Overall, had a fun time playing the collection and hope we get an "early console collection" including Monster Capsule: Breed and Battle (JP/PS1), Forbidden memories (PS1), Duelist of the Roses (PS2), Falsebound Kingdom (GCN), Power of Chaos Yugi the Destiny (PC), the Dawn of Destiny (Xbox), Power of Chaos: Kaiba the Revenge (PC), Power of Chaos: Joey the Passion (PC), Capsule Monster Coliseum (PS2). Also throw in 5D's Wheelie Breakers for the Wii because that game actually looks good please Konami xoxoxo

review:
Amber Alert — Cool idea, rough execution

I’m a long-time fan of horror games, tactical FPS titles, and I shoot IRL. Amber Alert has a neat premise, but a lot of the experience feels rough around the edges.

Controls / Sensitivity
The mouse settings are janky. Every time I hit Esc, my sensitivity resets. That’s brutal for anyone who keeps a consistent feel (I tune for a 360° in ~5–6 inches of movement). Please lock settings in and stop them from reverting.

Pacing & Spawns
I didn’t expect Ready or Not—and honestly, a real officer would wait for backup after the first body—but the enemy spawning is frustrating. Enemies pop into rooms I’ve already cleared, and sometimes visibly blink around corners if you move fast or pick up a key. The lore says the bad guys arrive in two G-Wagons (what, 5–6 seats each?), yet after the first three houses I’d already fought a small platoon. I get that it’s a horror mechanic to keep players on edge, but it breaks the fiction and feels more “clown car” than creeping dread.

Gunplay
The free-aim/floating aim makes the weapon drift before the camera, which ends up feeling like a plastic airsoft gun instead of something weighty. Also nitpicky, but a 1911 with 15 rounds is immersion-breaking unless it’s clearly a double-stack variant.

Value
For $5, it’s not a bad curiosity, but the sloppiness adds up.

Wish list for the devs

Don’t reset mouse sensitivity on Esc; add raw-input and a proper sensitivity slider.

Offer a toggle for free-aim (or reduce the dead-zone) and beef up weapon feedback.

Rework spawn logic: no spawning in cleared rooms; tie reinforcements to believable triggers.

Keep the tension, but keep the headcount consistent with the story.

There’s a solid horror-tactical hybrid hiding in here. Tighten the fundamentals and Amber Alert could punch way above its price.

The Holy Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit1 was a soldier in the city of Amáseia in Pontus (Asia Minor) on the coast of the Euxine (Black) Sea, under the command of the Praepositus (regimental commander) Brincus. Saint Theodore was ordered to offer sacrifice to idols, but he proclaimed his faith in Christ the Savior in a loud voice. Brincus gave him a few days to think it over, during which time the Saint prayed.

Theodore was accused of setting a pagan temple on fire and destroying the idol of Rhea, and so he was thrown into prison to be starved to death. The Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him there, comforting and encouraging him. When he was brought before the Governor Publius, Theodore boldly confessed his faith, for which he was subjected to new torments and condemned to be burnt alive. The Great Martyr Theodore mounted an enormous pyre, and after he made the Sign of the Cross, the wood was lit, but the Holy Spirit cooled the flames. Saint Theodore stood in the flames, praising and glorifying God. Then he gave his holy soul into God's hands, and the onlookers saw his soul ascending to Heaven, according to the author of his Life, who was also an eyewitness.

This occurred in about the year 306 under the Roman Emperor Galerius (305-311). Unharmed by the fire, Saint Theodore's body was buried under a widow's house in the city of Eukháϊta, not far from Amáseia. Later, his relics were transferred to Constantinople, to the church which bears his name. His head is in the city of Gaeto, Italy.

Fifty years after the Saint Theodore's martyrdom, Emperor Julian the Apostate (reigned 361-363), planned to commit an outrage upon the Christians during the first week of Great Lent. He ordered the city magistrate of Constantinople to sprinkle all the food in the marketplaces with blood which had been offered to idols. Saint Theodore appeared to Archbishop Eudoxios in a dream, and told him to inform all the Christians that no one should buy anything in the marketplaces, but to eat boiled wheat with honey (kolyva) instead.

In remembrance of this occurrence, the Orthodox Church commemorates the holy Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit each year on the first Saturday of Great Lent. On Friday evening, at the Divine Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, after the prayer at the Ambo, the Canon to the Holy Great Martyr Theodore, composed by Saint John of Damascus, is sung. After this, kolyva is blessed and distributed to the faithful. The celebration of the Great Martyr Theodore on the first Saturday of Great Lent was established by Patriarch Nektarios of Constantinople (381-397).

The Troparion to Saint Theodore is very similar to the Troparion for the Prophet Daniel and the Three Holy Youths (on the Sunday Before the Nativity of the Lord). The Kontakion to Saint Theodore, who suffered martyrdom by fire, reminds us that he also had faith as his breastplate (see I Thessalonians 5:8).

In iconography, Saint Theodore the Recruit is depicted in four different ways: either alone in military garb, battling a large snake, or together with Saint Theodore the Commander, standing upright or riding horses. He always wears his military uniform.

We pray to Saint Theodore the Recruit for the recovery of stolen articles.

1 His title comes from the Latin word tiro, because he was a newly-enlisted recruit, not because he came from the city of Tyre, as some misinformed persons imagine.

OH. MY. GOODNESS!

I'm usually not a fan of Visual Novels, but this one takes every cake in the bakery. The characters are adorable, the writing is so special, and the plot gripped me by the throat and would not let me go until I finished it. 

It's a tense story about lucid dreams with real-life consequences, with a protagonist Sonny that is used to being rejected by other people and suffering through his problems alone. But the context of the story is a charming town full of caring and unique people who want the best for Sonny and vice versa, even if they don't really know him. Sonny approaches people like they are explosives who haven't gone off yet, and picks apart every smile and compliment, not from bitterness but genuine surprise. I was so moved and engaged by this story seeing them come together into an organic community where Sonny actually belongs, where exchanging care is a given and his presence is truly wanted. It took me back to a time in middle school re-learning how to be around humans, taking the hard step of trusting people again after so long being alone.  

The game play is the classic VN setup you've seen around, excellently executed. The text is funny and engaging, with crisp characterizations, and genuinely hard puzzles about the characters that tests your attention to detail and understanding about how different people behave. With the right solutions you get an incredibly sweet epilogue but it took me a few tries to make it. And the plot-centric choices were SO HARD TO MAKE! I knew exactly what they meant and had to agonize over how to proceed. 

Truly a must play. 
Great as a gift for someone with a big heart.

To the devs: thanks * 1,000,000

I would at least expect a public statement on why everything is progressing so slow or why the roadmap was not just extended in timeframe but also moved around within. Assetto Corsa Evo – A Racing Masterpiece in the Making

From the moment I dropped into Assetto Corsa Evo, I was already vibing with the ambition and attention to detail. This is the next-level evolution in sim racing—I could feel the love the developers poured into it, and it’s already delivering something truly special.

Visuals & Atmosphere:
The graphical fidelity is off the charts. Tracks are rendered with jaw-dropping realism—crisp tarmac textures, weather effects that feel almost tactile, and car liveries that drape over body panels like real cloth. Whether you're rip-roaring down rain-slicked straights or blasting through sunlit corners, every frame feels cinematic.

Controls & Physics:
Let me say this loud and clear: the driving physics in Evo are next-gen. Every throttle blip, counter-steer, and brake lock-up feels grounded in reality. It’s no arcade fluff—it’s precise, demanding, and oh-so satisfying. Whether I was chasing the perfect late-braking apex or gently drifting through a sharp curve, the car responded exactly how I wanted it to.

Feature Set:
The developers have really earned my trust so far—every announced feature isn’t just talk, it’s delivered. From nuanced tire wear to dynamic weather, you can sense the methodical care behind it all. Anticipation for Freeroam:
Here’s the real deal breaker: once freeroam drops, Assetto Corsa Evo is set to shift into beast mode. Just imagining the open environments, the pure joy-rides, and the endlessly creative track layouts is putting me on cloud nine. I already trust the devs—I know they’re gonna make it pop exactly how we want it to.

Overall Thoughts:
Assetto Corsa Evo isn’t just a sim—it’s a commitment to realism, progression, and community promise kept. The devs are walking their talk, and I’m here for it. If you’re into precision driving, crave evolving content, and wanna be part of something innovative, jump in now and watch the evolution unfold.

The price seems a bit much for what it seems to be, but I can still recommend it to someone who wants a difficult and active tower defense game.

top down, more crpg than top-down-shooter

just be warned that the early minutes might take some getting used to.

review:
Very solid game, and enjoyable from start to finish. It has quite a few jumpscares but it definitely tries to rely on atmosphere. The way the game builds up lore and progresses is fantastic to me, and the objectives flow really nicely. The graphics have a gritty feel which really elevates the setting of the game, making it seem creepy, barren, abandoned, and worn down. The game is incredibly dark, making you feel vulnerable at all times. The story was also surprisingly good and ambiguous.

I have quite a few gripes but they are all pretty minor. Also minor spoiler warning:
- The sound design for the first half to two-thirds I think could be improved quite a lot. While I think the visuals were great, I think more creepy sound effects and music would really amplify the fear factor, as I honestly wasn't really scared.
- The walking and running speed is very slow when I played, but looking back on it, it does complement the tension and vulnerability.
- The darkness I think is a bit too dark, especially before you enter the house as I struggled greatly to find a wall that was like a meter away from me, even with the flashlight.
- Some jumpscares were a bit predictable and a bit lackluster. Even the unpredictable ones I don't think made me visibly jump or anything.
- I only found one segment really scary but I think it could be a bit more fair by adding a few hiding spots or making the location a bit bigger to avoid the monster more easily. This segment I think also had an overlook where there's one little open section that the monster cant get to, it will just chase you then forget you exist once you enter that area. But again, this part was terrifying and the highlight of the game for me.
- The monster AI could have more randomisation and unpredictability.

Overall, this is a super good horror game for the first time developers. I hope in their next games they can improve on these  aspects greatly to a make a super terrifying and haunting game.

It was great atmospheric horror until it wasn't. 
Ghostcase does a great job building up fear until finally throwing the player in to absolute horror.  There's many scenes where the player has nothing they can do but sit, watch, and anticipate.  The story elements are more compelling than most short horror games have to offer as well.

However, it falls flat in the last ~1/4 of the game.  The "stealth" is awful.  It's reminiscent of Sorcerer's Garden from Runescape in 2007.  Wait for entity to path past, then go.  "Hiding" in this game is absolutely ridiculous as well.  The entity can chase you right up to furniture, but if you crouch and go under it, it immediately forgets you exist.  Fear is very quickly replaced by annoyance.
Additionally there're many chase sequences where the character runs at a snails pace, and the entity is no faster.

It is a shame that such a great start to the game was ended with such a bad taste.

review:
DREAD FLATS is a unique blend of narrative-driven adventure and survival mechanics set against the backdrop of a harsh, unforgiving wasteland. Developed by Paranoid Productions, the game invites players to step into the boots of a lone protagonist struggling to survive in a world that is both mysterious and hostile. Its atmospheric storytelling, coupled with a minimalist yet striking art style, creates a tense and immersive experience that gradually unfolds as players explore the desolate environment, gather resources, and unravel the secrets lurking beneath the surface.

The game’s strongest asset lies in its narrative approach, which unfolds in a slow, deliberate manner that encourages exploration and reflection. Players traverse an expansive but barren landscape, encountering cryptic clues, environmental storytelling, and scattered remnants of a civilization long past. Dialogue and journal entries reveal bits and pieces of the lore, often delivered through hauntingly sparse conversations and unsettling audio logs. This fragmented storytelling fosters a pervasive sense of isolation and desperation, amplifying the game’s emotional weight and creating an atmosphere thick with suspense and melancholy.

Gameplay in DREAD FLATS combines survival elements with exploration and light puzzle-solving. Managing hunger, thirst, and stamina becomes a critical aspect, demanding careful planning and resource management. The wasteland offers limited supplies, so scavenging becomes a tense and often risky endeavor. Players must weigh the benefits of venturing further into unknown territory against the dangers posed by environmental hazards and lurking enemies. The survival mechanics are designed to be challenging but fair, creating a constant sense of urgency without feeling punishing, which keeps players engaged and invested in their character’s fate.

Visually, the game employs a distinct low-poly art style that complements the bleak and desolate setting. The muted color palette and stark lighting effects convey a world stripped of vitality, emphasizing the loneliness and decay that define the environment. This minimalist approach not only serves the narrative tone but also helps maintain clarity during exploration and encounters. Animations are subtle but effective, and the sound design enhances the immersive quality, with ambient noises that echo the emptiness of the wasteland and sudden bursts of tension when threats emerge.

Combat, while not the primary focus, plays a significant role in heightening the game’s tension. Encounters with hostile creatures or desperate survivors require quick thinking and strategic use of the limited weapons and tools at the player’s disposal. Combat mechanics are straightforward but demand precision and resourcefulness, reinforcing the game’s themes of survival against overwhelming odds. The scarcity of ammunition and health items adds to the sense of vulnerability, making every fight a potentially life-or-death situation.

One of the more innovative aspects of DREAD FLATS is its emphasis on atmosphere and mood over traditional gameplay structures. The pacing is deliberately measured, allowing players to absorb the world’s bleak beauty and unsettling mysteries. This approach may not appeal to everyone, particularly those seeking fast-paced action or extensive narrative exposition, but it rewards patience with a deeply immersive and emotionally resonant experience. The game’s minimal UI and controls further strip away distractions, placing the player firmly in the moment and heightening the impact of each discovery or challenge.

While the game succeeds in many areas, it is not without its flaws. Some players might find the sparse storytelling and slow pacing frustrating, especially early in the experience when much remains ambiguous. The survival mechanics, while engaging, occasionally feel repetitive due to limited variety in resources and environmental interaction. Additionally, the game’s low-poly aesthetic, though stylistically fitting, may not appeal to those who prefer more detailed or realistic graphics. Technical issues are relatively minor but can include occasional frame rate drops and minor bugs that momentarily disrupt immersion.

Audio design plays a pivotal role in establishing the game’s tone. The soundtrack is haunting and minimalist, weaving eerie melodies with environmental sounds that evoke a constant sense of unease. Voice acting, where present, is subdued but effective, adding emotional depth without overshadowing the game’s atmospheric focus. The careful layering of sound effects, from the crunch of footsteps on dry earth to the distant howls of unseen creatures, immerses players fully into the barren world.

In summary, DREAD FLATS offers a compelling and atmospheric survival adventure that stands out through its strong narrative undertones and evocative world-building. Its challenging survival mechanics and minimalist art style create a distinct experience that prioritizes mood and exploration over conventional gameplay thrills. While its deliberate pacing and sparse storytelling may not be for everyone, those who appreciate thoughtful, immersive experiences in bleak and mysterious settings will find much to admire here. It’s a game that invites players to linger, observe, and survive against all odds, crafting a memorable journey through a haunting wasteland.

Rating: 8/10

Dread Flats is a tense, atmospheric indie horror experience set in a desolate apartment complex where something isn’t right. It blends exploration, light puzzle-solving, and creeping dread into a short but memorable package. While not as chaotic as a co-op title, it thrives on isolation and slow-building fear.

Pros:

Strong atmosphere with unsettling audio design

Environmental storytelling that rewards exploration

Tension builds naturally without relying on constant jump scares

A few genuinely chilling set pieces

Runs well on modest hardware

Cons:

Short runtime — may leave you wanting more

Puzzles are simple and could use more variety

Minimal replay value once you’ve learned the scares

Story is intentionally vague but may feel underdeveloped to some

Dread Flats isn’t here to hold your hand or drown you in exposition. It’s a slow-burn horror game best enjoyed in one sitting with the lights off and headphones on. You won’t be screaming nonstop — but the unease will stick with you after the credits roll.

review:
"The Backrooms: Expedition" feels like one of the developer's first projects. They just wanted to take a shot at the Backrooms and have a bit of fun. The game isn't outright bad, I've played way worse, but I don't think it deserves to be paid; that's why this is a negative review.

The Good:
- Good graphics, admittedly.
- Responsive controls
- While the game feels like an asset flip, the assets actually feel like they belong to a common art style and they mesh relatively well together, which most games of this caliber can't pull off.

The Bad:
- Very short. Finished the game in exactly 20 minutes.
- Level design feels uninspired. The point of a Backrooms game is to be able to make a barren environment interesting; this game doesn't quite cut it. It mostly feels like an empty map with random models added as an afterthought, more than being designed with its decoration in mind.
- Low quality horror. The painted arrows and text such as "He's watching" on the walls were more corny than anything else, and the occasional random noise barely made me flinch.
- Very boring entity chase. The entity (whose appearance is straight up stolen from Kane Pixels) doesn't look nor sound scary, and the atmosphere really didn't build up for it either. It's just, you're walking down a long corridor, and suddenly the most generic chase music you can think of starts playing out of nowhere. The music is what triggers you to run, not the entity. And not because it's scary, only because you don't want to get caught and restart.
- Uninteresting gameplay. In short: walk to a place, door is locked, walk to a different place, door is unlocked, get to the next room, rinse and repeat. The "maze" part in the Poolrooms level was more annoying than anything else.
- Backrooms clichés. Oh no, Level Run. Red lights = scary.
- No settings: The only settings are four graphical options. Also, only changeable in the pause menu; can't do it from the main menu.

Extra: Influence From Other Games
- The Complex: Expedition
I think any of you that are like me and have played that game will agree that this feels like the main inspiration for this one. The name is nearly identical; the first level has an instance of unusually large chairs, something that was done in The Complex; even the camera bobbing feels similar (albeit stronger in this game).

- Pools:
This one is admittedly a bit more far fetched, but the use of monobloc chairs in the Poolrooms level definitely feels like it might be taken from Pools.

Extra Stuff:
- My flashlight didn't work until the Poolrooms level for some reason. I had to traverse several dark sections by hugging the walls.
- Camera zoom is a nice touch, however it's not adjustable. It's just click only to zoom in, click again to zoom out.

In its current state the game is basically just a standard roguelite with a shared lobby.

review:
Tldr; As of now, 20$ seems a bit too much for the game. I refunded because I don't think as of the early access, it seems to be not ready/ worth my money. I have high hopes for the game.

Pros:
Art styles, music and GAME IDEA is good. 
The ART style and character designs are really cute. 
The MUSIC is catchy. 
The IDEA for the game play is good. It's a bullet-hell style rogue-like where you and up to 3 other members can beat the boss together. The play styles of unit seems to be well thought out; each character have 2+ playstyles that the player can match, melee bruiser character can go Physical Damage whack em up or a CC unit with magic damage. Marksman Girl can go AoE or Single Target DPS and so on for other characters.

Cons:
The ideas of the games are executed very poorly. On paper it is really well thought out! On gameplay not so much. 
For dialogue wise, I don't think you need to do 4 screen-wipe transition for the same story within 6 lines of dialogue. 
Gameplay wise it's a bit clunky, dodging shouldn't lock you out of doing anything, either reduce the dodge time for fast-pace action dodging or allow players to cast some kind of attack during dodging. 
Attacking also felt a bit "delay", damage should be instant to give the dopamine feeling, but there's about 0.2-0.5s delay until the damage is finally calculated in. (Minor stuff)
Visual Clarity also need improvement, the indicator for an upcoming attack and ally AoE zones are the exact same, sure the first few area with only 1 to 3 enemy is fine, But this is a bullet hell game, so on later areas, it get really really messy.
This game has ideas for MMO, but currently this is just a social hub with fishing and crafting, it felt like a big matchmaking lobby rather than an MMO. Also almost no clear instructions on the stuff you can do in this hub.

So yeah, need more time to improve the game better. I have really high hopes for the game when I saw the designs, builds potential.
Regarding the company history, while it might be shady, but I have faith on these people to do good. Tbh the hate just seems to be on the CEO and not the company? Cuz I think art and music team is really good.
Did I refund this game? Yes. Will I buy the game in the future if they polished and fix it? YES!

review:
It makes me very sad to say this, especially because I have been so excited for this game's EA launch, but I cannot recommend this game in its current state.
The core issue for me, is there is nothing keeping you playing this game. It has no driving points, anything for you to push to gain. It does not have a plot, or any kind of quest line, or like...really even any NPCs you can interact with. With how small the rooms are for servers, it just looks like a dead game right off the bat. It's really sad.

The game does a really good job with its art direct and gameplay loop. It's really addicting to play, but those aren't the only things that make up a game. I think the only benefits to going through the gameplay loop right now are gaining materials for fishing poles and cosmetics, but I'm not really someone who can keep with a game through such superficial things. This game has really interesting lore, and it was a big selling point for me. The fact that it hasn't developed anymore than it was when they released the few open beta demos is honestly shocking.

I think instead of beefing it with that one guy in the Discussions tab and spending their money getting Youtubers to play their game at cons and do music/voice overs for them, they should just lock in and hire some writers, or at least put more attention towards the one they have hired, and start making a plot so people don't get bored of their game within the month.

I hope this isn't too harsh, like I genuinely enjoy this game and what it's leading to, but I do not see it being able to get out of EA and be fully developed with what their current focus is. Looking at their roadmap, they're putting higher priority over Steamdeck compatibility over creating a story for their game. It's a huge red flag for me, and the reason I posted this. They call themselves an MMO but it just doesn't hold to any kind of MMO standard. The MMO community is quite niche and usually prefer the games that have been running for years. I've played smaller MMO's from indie devs that did not last long at all that have complete and interesting stories, good mechanics, and nice enough art. Right now the game is too superficial for anyone to play. I think at least seeing on the roadmap they're investing more into the games story/questline would make me feel better about its future.

I have many other complaints about this game but I think they are very small in comparison to what I have already written about, and probably will be fixed with the ongoing development through EA.

[b]TL;DR I do not recommend this game, there's nothing that will make you want to keep playing after the initial thrill of beating your first run in the dungeon. It is not worth $20 in its current state. Needs to work on developing a quest line if they want to last any longer than the year or two of EA they're predicting to be in.[/b]

It's good and definitely more polished than what it was in the closed beta and demo. It's smooth, but the only complaints I have is:
- Certain UI aspects + map change: Instead of being able to choose either or, you get matchmade into an instance for the Sky map or the new Castle map varying on the difficulties you set on up. There's no unlock conditions specified for the extra difficulty and map either. No information is given in regards to that at all.
- Dodging: It did get severely nerfed from the last beta. Kira suffers from this the most as she is not able to dodge at all to make use of her dodge attack. Other characters get on by just fine. Kira does have an ability that helps mitigate this however.
- No fast travel in the hub: Pretty self explanatory. The game told me to go southwest for the new crafting area of trinkets and there's definitely no compass to help lead the way in regards to that, let alone quest markers beyond the quest pop-up one time that only tells you a cardinal direction. 
- Fishing rods: The fact the standard one breaks is a bit wack, especially for people who are purely fishers. The higher rarity ones could be the ones to break rather than the standard one, allowing for people to fish whenever they want, but not to the proficiency of other rods.
- Lack of a streamer mode: Some people are wack and have wack names and should be able to be hidden in all streaming purposes. This ties into at least wanting to have only the names of your friends more distinguished over others. So, hide the names of others but keep friends visible is one thing. Same with the chat to be able to be toggled off.

Other than that, the game is solid for what it is and has proper repetition for the gameplay loop. People in the chat are clueless about some things unfortunately like where to use fish, which may either just be a problem of literacy and a lack of a tutorial that guides users in the actual hub world outside of the combat tutorial.

While the game's art direction is very well executed, I do feel the actual co op/ community aspect of the game is very weak for being descried as an MMO. If you just want a game where you can turn your brain off and fight with your friends, I'd recommend it.

The game follows a more "Play the game with your friends," rather then a "Work together with your friends." This is an issue for the game because having little coordination in the game play is going to lead to less and less conversation in game, hurting the MMO idea of the game. I don't feel like I am contributing to the team differently when I play Kira or Effy, I'm just another guy on the team that does damage. Mu personal issue is I feel like the single player experience is not a priority. Us solo Q player should be able to hop into a dive by our selves easier.

The fix that the game needs is to have better synergy and team play between the character to encourage a more cooperative feeling. Along with making it easier to communicate in game.

Also for those worried about the whole AI/ crypto thing, most of it seams like it is a big misunderstanding. the CEO addressed it so I'd read his comment and make your own judgment.

Which is all the more disrespectful to the entire team of artists and engineers to imply they would spend their energy and risk their reputations just to allow that. I appreciate the desire to be transparent and not appear like silencing dissent, but it's genuinely a wonder that the post hasn't been locked and the user banned at this point for frankly some of the most unhinged borderline stalker behavior toward multiple devs I've seen on a Steam board so far.

There needs to be a option in the in game menu to change characters because having to log out to the main screen just to do that is a little convoluted and does not feel good at all.


Those are some of my main concerns for now. Looking forward to see how it progresses given the devs clear desire to fix things and improve the game. If you're comfortable trying out Early Access titles, I highly recommend giving it a try and see if you enjoy it.

review:
I wont bore you with a long well written paragraph, here's my review in bullet points:

PROS
- visually appealing
- music and sound design are very good

CONS
- NIM area feels bland and way too spread out. I feel like im doing the pacer test every time I try to go and unlock stuff 
- Combat feels off, sometimes it's fluid and other times I rubber band across the screen and get hit by 40 people. 
- Mob pathing can be super jank. Sometimes they just dont stop running away at full speed before you can even attack them
- Not really a competitive players cup of tea
- Doesn't feel like im working towards any "end goal," there are really only 2 biombs and the game doesn't give me enough to care about in terms of story when playing
- The maps are quite rigid, there arent a whole lot of them so most runs end up feeling the same apart from upgrades 
- No So Mi time leaderboard
- No rewards for having the fastest clear

Thats all I can really think of rn, idk I just felt like I was wasting my time when I played after a few hours. Like it was fun for a bit but there's not much depth to care enough to keep playing

Oh one more thing that kinda left a bad taste in my mouth. This doesn't have to do with gameplay but when I was at Anime NYC and tested this game there was an event going on where the fastest clear time would get to play with Ironmouse and CdawgVA. I had asked if I could keep trying if I failed and was told yes. I sat around the booth for 2-4 hours and around 2pm which was when the booth was a bit more busy, I was pulled aside almost like I was at a casino being told to walk away from the blackjack table by a pit boss. They pretty much said "ohh real close this time, did you beat it (the golem) no alright well im gonna have you talk to my friend over here" and then they passed me off to some dude who was like "so uh thanks for playing, ugh here's a Keychain, and uhh have a good rest of your day."

I was the one that was like so I cant play anymore? And they were like "no the lines too long, but we hope you have fun on wednesday" (implying I was going to buy the game which just felt kinda demeaning) (also mind you the line wasnt an issue to me, I would have stayed and kept playing). Was just really off putting. But yeah, don't recommend the game overall even based off pure gameplay alone. Just not a finished product.

review:
Beyond the art style which seemingly everyone agrees is a universal positive this game is too shallow and buggy to even recommend at this point. Even the bug reporter comes with bugs! 

The music is fitting but I'd personally like to be able to toggle the vocal tracks off for just instrumentals since I'm just not a fan of them. 

I don't know what it is about the animations but there is a constant jittering on the model with texture tearing which was present in the last demo. Menus got new assets but changing tabs has pop in and the gear tab has clipping assets. Minor issues sure but honestly hard not for me to see. 

Combat and movement still feels floaty. Yes dodging feels a bit better but as a whole something tighter, faster, and snappier. If this game wants to push for more bullet hell great but outside of dodging its just molasses. Hit feedback was another thing that was touch on before but still seems lacking. Perhaps its the sfx on hit. For example: If Effie swings her giant metal hammer and it sounds like I'm wacking them with a paper fan there is no satisfying impact. But lets say in this same example you get a knockback and it was more of a metal baseball bat hitting a homerun? Now THAT sounds good while watching the enemy fly backwords. As of this review remapping keybinds do not exist.

Microtransactions will be a part of the game at some point. While I do understand that its a necessary evil to help with server costs and the like judgement is reserved on when the pricing becomes apparent. This is a turn off for some people for a Buy 2 Play so it bears mentioning even if its not required for them to interact with. As for the limited drops like were present during testing will be pushed to generate FOMO or if its something if you miss it for free it will be purchasable later on. Purely speculation. 

There is no driving force to do much. You do a dive to get materials, craft items back at NIM, then go back to diving. Once that's all done then what? Yes there is only 2 stages right now but what is the plan for endgame? Fashion is true endgame as always but that isn't a substantial enough of a carrot to keep playing for some.

Devs seem to be responsive on feedback. Words only go so far so we'll see in the long haul. NGL some design choices seem just like oversight regardless if this is the studio's first game. Might be harsh but oh well. Maybe a sum of the marketing money and hiring youtuber talent should have been spent elsewhere.

As of now I feel like I've spent $20 to have the privilege to QA this game more than most EA games and it should have been in a more polished presentable state before now for how much they wants to get eyes on it. Can I ignore it? Sure. Will I? Yes that's what the refund is for. Hopefully I'll see enough changes to warrant a revisit down the line.

review:
This game is extremely ambitious and given that this is the studio's first ever release, the negative reviews are way too critical of them and are expecting perfection. While I agree, it could use some polishing that will come with time, I think it's a refreshing take on isometric rogue-lites. It has a very peppy vibe to it that capitalizes on the art style. The fact that there are cosmetic accessories and outfit unlocks for the characters, is such a nice inclusion in a genre that you otherwise don't find. 

Admittedly, there are some faults with the game, but I wouldn't say that they're game breaking, given that it just launched and there seemed to be a lot of anticipation surrounding the game, so servers seemed a little slow. I think that one thing that they could afford to improve upon, is change how players change characters, as you currently have to go back to the title screen and swap characters there once you get past the tutorial level, if you want to play as someone other than the default character—having the option to swap in the hub world would be nice, though I assume that option isn't initially available due to the potential issues it would cause with lag, but I'm not very knowledgeable on that sort of thing, so perhaps I'm way off the mark.  

The characters all feel unique between one another with each seemingly playing a key role in the party dynamic and offer a diverse enough gameplay, though perhaps some balancing might help—or perhaps it feels that way due to the power upgrades I was offered on each run with characters. Due to the nature of the unlockable collectibles, this game has a lot of replayability for me, so I can see myself getting my money's worth. 

If you're a fan of collectathons, rogue-lites and co-op gameplay, maybe this game is perfect for you. Or maybe you'll complain about linux support or a lack of competitive play in a game that I don't think ever advertised itself as having the latter. 

10/10, recommending to all my friends.

- Distinguish Artstyle, although its colors were too bright sometimes.
- Music is good with a vocal toggle option.
- Color-coded text for skills and charms, easy to read and understand.

[b]Not good things/things to improve[/b]
- Always online is dumb, having to queue into the lobby and into the game, and also, you have latency when playing solo.
- The town feels empty; it doesn't have much to do.
- The progression system is shallow.
- The time limit system kinda devolves the game into a DPS check, and you have to play perfectly / hitless to have more time.
- Coop feels like "Do your own things" rather than "synergize with others"
- SFX and Hit impact feel really weak.
- Friendly and Enemy VFX are hard to distinguish sometimes.
- Animation feels very jittery, and it's worse when you have latency.
- UI needs a lot of QoL updates.
- No key rebind.
- Bug report also got a bug (pretty funny ngl)

I will come back to try it later when it gets updated and polished enough for its price tag. 
You got a good fanbase and community already
Just don't fumble the game and this game will probably pop off.

review:
TL;DR: Good Graphics and sound, plays well, great fun with friends. Minor Bugs due to early access. Would recommend.

Honestly the game is a blast but there are some minor issues. Lets go over all the good first:

- The art is great. The characters look great, the enemies look cool (especially in the new area), the world looks nice and the cutscenes look amazing.

- Music is good to great throughout the entire thing.

- Gameplay is really fun. Each of the 4 character plays completely differently and then each one can be built in a multitude of ways depending on what your run gives you. The controls work well on mouse and keyboard.

- Everything feels weighty, attacks sound and look good, animations have weight, nothing feels "weak", everything that needs to pack a punch does.

- Upgrades and cosmetics can all be grinded for.

- Interesting twist on the roguelite genre with characters more focused on coop play and the stamina/soda mechanic.

- Endless revives as long as your teammates commit a decent amount of damage to beating you out of your death crystal, so you are never fully out of the game until its game over for everyone.

- Devs are communicating on discord, working on the known bugs and will open a feedback channel once the day 1 bugs are fixed.

- Game seems to scale to group size so even solo and duo runs are still fun.

- The fishing minigame is chill. It doesnt take long to get a bite and they made it a bit easier since the beta, so youll rarely battle a fish for more then a minute. Your rod does still break which is a bit annoying but not too horrible since you can just buy them in bulk. Shiny's make regular fishing more fun and rewarding since you can shiny hunt to complete your collection.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now for the few negatives:

- Bugs, its early access. I expect them to be fixed and dont see them as an issue at all. Its nothing gamebreaking ive experienced so far but they are there so i wanted to mention them.

- One or two enemies are a bit overtuned and annoying. Not impossible to deal with but there is a room or two you dont look forward to in each run. At the same time these do force you to adapt your strategy.

- Some of the movement with jumping over gaps needs some work. Its rare that its an issue but it can be a bit annoying.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------

In total the game is well worth the 20 / 25 bucks youll pay for it. Its great fun with friends or even just for a few solo runs on your own. Its early access so dont expect perfection but, if you are looking for a fun, coop, roguelite, youll have a good time with this.

Это не чилл геймплей, это просто будто вернулся лет на 20 назад и играешь в Resident Evil с "танковым" управлением. I'm into roguelikes, especially co-op ones, but I couldn't get into this one for a number of reasons:

Controller support is clunky compared to keyboard. I bound my ultimate ability to the same button as "interact"? Well, get ready to accidentally waste your ultimate when you miss an interactive point like a portal or a shop. The menu doesn't even have a visual layout for the controls; there's an option to change the keybind preset, but no diagram showing what actually changes.

The combat feels extremely tedious, both in terms of enemy design and overall pace. This isn't chill gameplay; it feels like going back 20 years to playing Resident Evil with its "tank" controls. I haven't even figured out the builds yet (though getting a +10 physical attack buff only gives you +1 damage to your basic attack scaling), but it feels like you're surrounded by damage sponges, likely due to the co-op scaling. The tutorial was brisk, but the first co-op run was a complete slog.

Visual clarity is a mess. Did your ally cast an AOE? Good luck seeing any enemy telegraphed attacks through their animations. It's a visual disco where you can't tell who's who.

A day-one bug literally prevents you from completing the tutorial if your Windows display language isn't set to English. It's an easy fix (you change it and change it back later), but hitting a hard stop in the tutorial because an enemy becomes invincible is unacceptable.

Yeah, I've seen the thread about the "echo chamber" and all the conspiracy theories surrounding the game's reception, but what I saw firsthand was enough for me to request a refund. Maybe I'll pick it up later at a deeper discount if they improve the core gameplay, visual presentation, and add proper Russian localization.

In summary: I liked the art style and the core idea, but the execution fell flat. Cannot recommend in its current state.

This is a game with a whole lot of heart and a whole lot of potential as it continues to grow and work out some launch kinks (disconnections/ping issues/etc - I will say I've now played almost 20 hours and I've yet to be disconnected) --- but I think it's 100% worth supporting and playing now.

I've never been a huge fan of roguelikes/roguelites and but Starlight has absolutely captured me. I love the social hub-world with other players to team up with, the cute little corners to explore and the fishing mechanic. 

They balance out the challenging work of doing a "Dive" (dungeon run) with the option to fish in the hub world between dives (you need fish to craft lots of different trinkets for your builds as well as cosmetics!) or just hang out and chat with other players while you run around to grab other resources that spawn.

Absolutely worth picking up if you are interested in a unique spin on a roguelight. The social aspect, art, music, characters and world are all brilliantly designed and incredibly charming.

From what I've seen (since picking up the game on day 1 EA) the devs have been transparent about their plans for EA with roadmaps and frequent announcements. They actively listen and respond to suggestions and/or concerns on discord and seem to prioritize the most pressing issues when they arise.
